\section{How to use this document}

\subsection{What is in each part}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Part I, The Python language.} Syntax, built-in types, the standard library and the
        behavior that interview code depends on. Use it as a reference when you forget a method or a rule.
  \item \textbf{Part II, Solving unseen problems.} A step-by-step method and how to read the constraints.
        The optimization moves that turn a brute force into a fast solution. A table from signals to techniques
        and a table that chooses a data structure from the operations. What to do when you are stuck.
        The pitfalls that cost points, how to debug and verify a solution, and a final checklist.
  \item \textbf{Part III, Techniques.} One section for each technique family. Each section gives the idea,
        the signals, a tested template, the variations, a checklist to adapt it, and the pitfalls.
        Each problem uses the most intuitive solution that fits the constraints. Its memory hook is a short sentence that
        brings back the whole solution. To find an algorithm by its name, use the table in Section~\ref{how:finder}.
  \item \textbf{Part IV, Retention.} A recall sheet with one row for each section of Part III.
        Transfer drills on problems that are not in NeetCode 150 or Blind 75. The answers are in the appendix.
  \item \textbf{Appendix.} The drill answers and a map of all NeetCode 150 and Blind 75 problems with their memory hooks.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{How to study with this document}
Knowledge of patterns fades fast without practice. Short, regular recall keeps it. Use this plan.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Every day, 15 minutes.} Run the review script in \cd{cheatsheet/retention} (command:
        \cd{python3 review.py}). For each card, say the technique, the memory hook and the first steps before you
        show the answer. Grade yourself honestly. The script schedules the next review.
  \item \textbf{For each card that you grade 1 or 2,} write the solution from its rebuild steps on the same day.
  \item \textbf{Every week,} do one set of transfer drills from Part IV without help. Then read the answers.
  \item \textbf{When you see a new problem,} follow the method in Part II. Look up the signals in the
        signal-to-technique table (Section~\ref{m1:signals}).
  \item \textbf{Before an assessment,} read these parts in this order:
        \begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*.]
          \item the recall sheet (Section~\ref{sec:recall}, p.~\pageref{sec:recall});
          \item the table of bug classes (Section~\ref{pit:check}, p.~\pageref{pit:check});
          \item the signal-to-technique table (Section~\ref{m1:signals}, p.~\pageref{m1:signals});
          \item the final checklist (Section~\ref{pit:final}, p.~\pageref{pit:final}).
        \end{enumerate}
        Then read the full pitfall subsections only for the bug classes that you often make.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{note}
Recall is the exercise. Reading a solution again feels productive, but it builds less memory than an attempt to
remember it first.
\end{note}

\subsection{Conventions}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Each topic has a short description and one or more examples.
  \item The comment \res{value} shows the value of the expression on that line.
  \item The comment \res{raises Error} shows that the line raises that exception.
  \item The comment {\frenchspacing\texttt{\# prints: text}} shows the text that the line writes to the screen.
  \item A CAUTION box tells you about a mistake that gives a wrong result or an error.
  \item A NOTE box gives more information.
  \item The tag \since{3.10} shows the first Python version that has the feature.
\end{itemize}

\begin{pyex}
x = 7
x * 2         # -> 14
x / 0         # -> raises ZeroDivisionError
print("hi")   # prints: hi
\end{pyex}

The script \cd{check_examples.py} runs every example in this document. It compares each

\subsection{Check the Python version of the judge}
Many online judges use an old Python version. Some features in this document need a newer version.
Run this line on the judge if you are not sure.
\begin{pyex}
import sys
sys.version_info >= (3, 8)   # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Find help inside Python}
Most assessments let you run code. If you forget a method name, ask Python.
\cd{dir(x)} lists the attributes of \cd{x}. \cd{help(x)} shows the documentation.
\begin{pyex}
[m for m in dir(list) if not m.startswith("_")]
# -> ['append', 'clear', 'copy', 'count', 'extend', 'index', 'insert', 'pop', 'remove', 'reverse', 'sort']
[m for m in dir(dict) if not m.startswith("_")]
# -> ['clear', 'copy', 'fromkeys', 'get', 'items', 'keys', 'pop', 'popitem', 'setdefault', 'update', 'values']
[m for m in dir(set) if not m.startswith("_")][:6]
# -> ['add', 'clear', 'copy', 'difference', 'difference_update', 'discard']
"removeprefix" in dir(str)        # -> True
len([m for m in dir(str) if not m.startswith("_")])   # -> 47
str.split.__doc__.splitlines()[0] # -> 'Return a list of the substrings in the string, using sep as the separator string.'
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyshow}
help(str.split)      # full documentation for one method
help(heapq)          # documentation for a module (after import heapq)
\end{pyshow}

\part{The Python language}\label{part:python}

% =====================================================================
\section{Program structure}

\subsection{Indentation and blocks}
Python uses indentation to make blocks. Use 4 spaces for each level. Do not mix tabs and spaces.
A colon starts a block.
\begin{pyex}
total = 0
for i in range(3):
    if i > 0:
        total += i
total   # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Statements and lines}
Put one statement on each line. A semicolon puts two statements on one line. Use this only for short code.
\begin{pyex}
a = 1; b = 2
a + b   # -> 3
\end{pyex}

A line continues inside parentheses, brackets and braces. A backslash also continues a line, but
parentheses are safer.
\begin{pyex}
total = (1 + 2 +
         3 + 4)
total   # -> 10
items = [
    "a",
    "b",     # a comma after the last element is permitted
]
len(items)   # -> 2
\end{pyex}
A long function header can also continue inside its parentheses.
\begin{pyex}
def clamp(value: int,
          lo: int,
          hi: int) -> int:
    return max(lo, min(value, hi))
clamp(15, 0, 10)   # -> 10
clamp(-3, 0, 10)   # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Put a long condition in parentheses to split it over lines. A call also continues over lines, and a comma
after the last argument is permitted. Give a long part of a condition a name to make the test clear.
\begin{pyex}
grid, r, c = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], 1, 1
inside = 0 <= r < len(grid) and 0 <= c < len(grid[0])   # a named condition
hit = False
if (inside
        and grid[r][c] == 1
        and r == c):
    hit = True
hit                                      # -> True
best = min(4,
           2,
           7,
           )
best                                     # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Comments and docstrings}
A \hsh{} starts a comment. A string that is the first statement of a function body is a docstring.
\begin{pyex}
def area(w, h):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return w * h     # multiply the two sides
area.__doc__        # -> 'Return the area of a rectangle.'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{The pass statement}
Use \cd{pass} when a block must exist but must do nothing.
\begin{pyex}
def todo():
    pass
todo() is None   # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{The main guard}
Code under \cd{if __name__ == "__main__":} runs only when you start the file directly.
It does not run when another file imports the file.
\begin{pyshow}
def solve():
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
\end{pyshow}

\subsection{The LeetCode solution format}\label{sec:leetcode-format}
LeetCode gives a class \cd{Solution} with one method. Write the code in the body of that method.
The first parameter of a method is \cd{self}. The judge makes one object and calls the method.
LeetCode compares the return value with the expected answer.
\begin{pyex}
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def twoSum(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
        seen = {}                          # value: index
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if target - x in seen:
                return [seen[target - x], i]
            seen[x] = i
        return []                          # not reached when the input has one answer

Solution().twoSum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)       # -> [0, 1]
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item LeetCode imports \cd{List}, \cd{Optional} and most standard modules for you. A local file needs the imports.
        Write the imports anyway. An extra import does no harm, and other judges need it.
  \item To test locally, call \cd{Solution().method(arguments)}.
  \item Call a helper method of the class as \cd{self.helper(...)}. A method calls itself as \cd{self.method(...)}.
  \item A name that starts with \cd{_} shows that the method is an internal helper. Python does not enforce this.
  \item LeetCode shows the node classes (\cd{ListNode}, \cd{TreeNode}) only as a comment. Define them yourself
        to run locally (Section~\ref{sec:leetcode-classes}).
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:                            # LeetCode defines this class for you
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

class Solution:
    def maxDepth(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        if not root:
            return 0
        return 1 + max(self.maxDepth(root.left), self.maxDepth(root.right))

    def isPalindrome(self, s: str) -> bool:
        t = self._clean(s)
        return t == t[::-1]

    def _clean(self, s: str) -> str:       # internal helper method
        """Keep letters and digits, in lowercase."""
        return "".join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())

Solution().maxDepth(TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(3))))   # -> 3
Solution().isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")    # -> True
\end{pyex}
Some problems give a function that the judge defines, for example \cd{isBadVersion}. Write a small stub
of that function to test locally.
\begin{pyex}
BAD = 4
def isBadVersion(v: int) -> bool:          # stub; the judge gives the real function
    return v >= BAD

class Solution:
    def firstBadVersion(self, n: int) -> int:
        lo, hi = 1, n
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if isBadVersion(mid):
                hi = mid
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        return lo

Solution().firstBadVersion(10)             # -> 4
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
A method with the return hint \cd{-> None} must change its argument in place. The judge reads the argument
after the call. An assignment to the parameter name makes a new local object. The caller does not see it.
Use slice assignment (\cd{nums[:] = ...}) or index assignment.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class Solution:
    def rotate(self, nums, k) -> None:
        k %= len(nums)
        nums = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]       # wrong: rebinds the local name only
    def rotate_ok(self, nums, k) -> None:
        k %= len(nums)
        nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]    # correct: changes the caller's list
a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Solution().rotate(a, 2)
a                                          # -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Solution().rotate_ok(a, 2)
a                                          # -> [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Names and assignment}

\subsection{Names are references}
A name refers to an object. Assignment does not copy the object. Two names can refer to the same object.
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2]
b = a            # b and a refer to the same list
b.append(3)
a                # -> [1, 2, 3]
a is b           # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Multiple assignment and swap}
Assign several names in one statement. \cd{x, y = y, x} swaps two values.
\begin{pyex}
x, y = 1, 2
x, y = y, x      # swap without a temporary name
(x, y)           # -> (2, 1)
a = b = 0        # two names, same value
(a, b)           # -> (0, 0)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{a = b = []} gives two names for one list. A change through \cd{a} also shows through \cd{b}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Simultaneous assignment}
In \cd{a, b = x, y}, Python first evaluates the full right side. Then it assigns the targets from left to right.
Use this form when each new value must read the old values. You do not need a temporary name.
\begin{pyex}
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(10):
    a, b = b, a + b              # a + b uses the old a and the old b
a                                # -> 55
prev2 = prev1 = 0
for x in [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]:        # rolling update with two states
    prev2, prev1 = prev1, max(prev1, prev2 + x)
prev1                            # -> 12
nums = [5, 6, 7]
nums[0], nums[2] = nums[2], nums[0]   # swap two list elements
nums                             # -> [7, 6, 5]
res = [0, 0]
carry, res[1] = divmod(17, 10)   # a target can be a list element
(carry, res)                     # -> (1, [0, 7])
class T:
    def __init__(self, left, right):
        self.left, self.right = left, right
t = T("a", "b")
t.left, t.right = t.right, t.left     # swap two attributes
(t.left, t.right)                # -> ('b', 'a')
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Python assigns the targets one at a time. A later target can use a value that an earlier target already changed.
Compute such an index first and store it in a name.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
nums, i = [3, 1, 2], 0
nums[i], nums[nums[i] - 1] = nums[nums[i] - 1], nums[i]   # wrong
nums                             # -> [2, 3, 2]
nums, i = [3, 1, 2], 0
j = nums[i] - 1                  # compute the second index first
nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
nums                             # -> [2, 1, 3]
\end{pyex}
In the wrong line, the second target \cd{nums[nums[i] - 1]} reads \cd{nums[i]} after the first target changed it.

\subsection{Chained assignment}
\cd{a = b = value} binds all the names to one object. This is safe for an immutable value (a number, a string,
\cd{None}, a tuple). It is also correct when two names must share one object, for example a dummy head node.
\begin{pyex}
lo = hi = 0
hi += 5                          # rebinds hi only; ints are immutable
(lo, hi)                         # -> (0, 5)
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
dummy = tail = Node()            # one sentinel node with two names
for v in [4, 7]:
    tail.next = Node(v)
    tail = tail.next             # tail moves; dummy stays at the start
dummy.next.val, tail.val         # -> (4, 7)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Unpacking}
Unpack a sequence into names. The number of names must match the number of elements.
A starred name collects the remaining elements into a list.
\begin{pyex}
first, second = [10, 20]
first             # -> 10
head, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
rest              # -> [2, 3, 4]
*init, last = "abc"
(init, last)      # -> (['a', 'b'], 'c')
a, (b, c) = 1, (2, 3)    # nested unpacking
c                 # -> 3
x, y = [1, 2, 3]  # -> raises ValueError
\end{pyex}

Use \cd{_} for a value that you do not need.
\begin{pyex}
_, count = ("ignored", 5)
count              # -> 5
\end{pyex}

Unpacking also works in a \cd{for} header, and it can be nested. Use \cd{*} in a list literal to join
sequences. Use \cd{**} in a dict literal to merge dicts. For a duplicate key, the later value wins.
\begin{pyex}
pairs = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)]
[f"{k}{v}" for k, v in pairs]                     # -> ['a1', 'b2']
gas, cost = [1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1]
[(i, g - c) for i, (g, c) in enumerate(zip(gas, cost))]   # -> [(0, -2), (1, 0), (2, 2)]
counts = {(0, 1): 3}
[(x, y, c) for (x, y), c in counts.items()]       # -> [(0, 1, 3)]
x, y, z = [7, 8, 9]                               # a list unpacks like a tuple
x, y = {"a", "b", "c"} - {"a"}                    # a set with two elements; the order is not fixed
sorted([x, y])                                    # -> ['b', 'c']
a, b = [1, 2], [3]
[*a, *b, 9]                                       # -> [1, 2, 3, 9]
{**{"k": 1}, **{"k": 2, "z": 0}}                  # -> {'k': 2, 'z': 0}
first, *_ = "xyz"
first                                             # -> 'x'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Augmented assignment}
\cd{x += 1} adds 1 to \cd{x}. Python has no \cd{x++} operator.
\begin{pyex}
x = 10
x += 5; x -= 3; x *= 2; x //= 4; x %= 4; x **= 3
x                  # -> 8
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
For a list, \cd{a += b} changes the list in place. \cd{a = a + b} makes a new list.
The difference is important when another name refers to the same list.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
a = [1]; alias = a
a += [2]
alias             # -> [1, 2]
a = a + [3]
alias             # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}
Each binary operator has an augmented form: \cd{+= -= *= /= //= **=}, \pct\cd{=}, \cd{&= |= ^=}, \shl\cd{=} and \shr\cd{=}.
The target can be a name, a list element or a dict value. Python computes the full right side first.
\begin{pyex}
flags = 0
flags |= 1 << 3              # set bit 3
flags ^= 1                   # flip bit 0
flags >>= 1                  # shift right by one bit
flags                        # -> 4
n = 12
n &= n - 1                   # same as n = n & (n - 1)
n                            # -> 8
found = False
found |= 3 > 2               # also works on bool values
found                        # -> True
cnt = [0, 0]
cnt[1] += 1                  # on a list element
cnt                          # -> [0, 1]
d = {"a": 1}
d["a"] += 1                  # on a dict value
d["b"] += 1                  # -> raises KeyError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{d[k] += 1} on a plain dict needs the key \cd{k}. Use \cd{d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1}, a \cd{defaultdict(int)} or a
\cd{Counter}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{The walrus operator} \since{3.8}
\cd{:=} assigns a value inside an expression.
\begin{pyex}
data = [5, 8, 1]
if (n := len(data)) > 2:
    msg = f"{n} items"
msg               # -> '3 items'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Delete a name}
\cd{del} removes a name, a list element or a dictionary key.
\begin{pyex}
x = 5
del x
x                 # -> raises NameError
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Built-in types overview}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule
Type & Example & Mutable & Hashable & Ordered \\
\midrule
\cd{int} & \cd{42} & no & yes & -- \\
\cd{float} & \cd{3.14} & no & yes & -- \\
\cd{bool} & \cd{True} & no & yes & -- \\
\cd{NoneType} & \cd{None} & no & yes & -- \\
\cd{str} & \cd{"abc"} & no & yes & yes \\
\cd{tuple} & \cd{(1, 2)} & no & yes (if elements are) & yes \\
\cd{list} & \cd{[1, 2]} & yes & no & yes \\
\cd{dict} & \cd{{"a": 1}} & yes & no & insertion order \\
\cd{set} & \cd{{1, 2}} & yes & no & no \\
\cd{frozenset} & \cd{frozenset({1})} & no & yes & no \\
\cd{range} & \cd{range(5)} & no & yes & yes \\
\cd{bytes} & \cd{b"ab"} & no & yes & yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Only hashable objects can be dictionary keys or set elements.
\begin{pyex}
type(3)             # -> int
type(3.0)           # -> float
type("3")           # -> str
isinstance(True, int)    # -> True
isinstance(5, (int, float))   # -> True
{[1, 2]: "x"}       # -> raises TypeError
{(1, 2): "x"}       # -> {(1, 2): 'x'}
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Type conversion}
\begin{pyex}
int("42")           # -> 42
int(" 42 ")         # -> 42
int(3.99)           # -> 3
int(-3.99)          # -> -3
float("2.5")        # -> 2.5
str(42)             # -> '42'
list("abc")         # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
tuple([1, 2])       # -> (1, 2)
set([1, 1, 2])      # -> {1, 2}
bool(0), bool("0")  # -> (False, True)
int("4.5")          # -> raises ValueError
int("-11"), int("+5"), int("007")   # -> (-11, 5, 7)
int("12\n")         # -> 12
int("")             # -> raises ValueError
float(3)            # -> 3.0
tuple([1, 2]) in {(1, 2)}           # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{int()} accepts a sign, leading zeros and whitespace around the digits.
Convert a list to a tuple to use it as a dict key or a set element.
\begin{caution}
\cd{int()} on a float truncates toward zero. It does not round.
\end{caution}

% =====================================================================
\section{Numbers}

\subsection{Integers}
Integers have no size limit. Integer overflow does not occur.
\begin{pyex}
2 ** 100              # -> 1267650600228229401496703205376
10 ** 18 + 1          # -> 1000000000000000001
1_000_000             # -> 1000000
0b1010, 0o17, 0xff    # -> (10, 15, 255)
import sys
sys.maxsize           # -> 9223372036854775807
INF = float("inf")    # a sentinel that is larger than every number
min(INF, 10**30)      # -> 1000000000000000000000000000000
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Use \cd{float("inf")} or \cd{math.inf} as an initial value for a minimum. \cd{sys.maxsize} is not the
largest integer. Python integers can be larger.
\end{note}
Arithmetic has no limit, but conversion between \cd{int} and \cd{str} has one \since{3.11}.
\cd{str()} and \cd{int()} raise \cd{ValueError} for a number with more than 4300 digits.
Late patch releases of 3.7 to 3.10 have the same limit. \cd{sys.set_int_max_str_digits(0)} removes it.
\begin{pyex}
import sys
len(str(10**4299))                # -> 4300
str(10**4300)                     # -> raises ValueError
sys.set_int_max_str_digits(0)     # 0 means no limit
len(str(10**4300))                # -> 4301
\end{pyex}
Because integers do not overflow, \cd{(lo + hi) // 2} is always safe in Python. In C or Java, \cd{lo + hi} can
overflow, so code from those languages writes \cd{lo + (hi - lo) // 2}. Both forms give the same result.
\begin{pyex}
lo, hi = 2**62, 2**62 + 10
(lo + hi) // 2                    # -> 4611686018427387909
lo + (hi - lo) // 2               # -> 4611686018427387909
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Floats}
A float is a 64-bit IEEE 754 value. It has about 15 to 17 significant digits.
\begin{pyex}
0.1 + 0.2             # -> 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3      # -> False
1e9                   # -> 1000000000.0
float("inf") > 10**100    # -> True
float("-inf") < -10**100  # -> True
float("nan") == float("nan")   # -> False
2 ** 0.5              # -> 1.4142135623730951
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Do not compare floats with \cd{==}. Use \cd{math.isclose} or a tolerance.
Use integers when the problem lets you.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import math
math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)            # -> True
abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9           # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Infinity and sentinel values}
Use \cd{float("inf")} (or \cd{math.inf}) as the start value of a minimum, and as a mark for ``not reached''.
Infinity compares correctly with every int. Use \cd{float("-inf")} as the start value of a maximum,
or as a mark for an impossible state.
\begin{pyex}
INF = float("inf")
dist = [INF] * 3
dist[0] = 0
min(dist)                        # -> 0
5 < INF, -INF < -10**100         # -> (True, True)
max(float("-inf"), 3)            # -> 3
type(max(float("-inf"), 3))      # -> int
INF + 1 == INF                   # -> True
-INF + 7                         # -> -inf
INF - INF                        # -> nan
0 * INF                          # -> nan
int(INF)                         # -> raises OverflowError
d = INF
-1 if d == INF else d            # -> -1
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
A result that can stay infinite is a float. Convert it before you return it, for example
\cd{return -1 if d == INF else d}. \cd{int(float("inf"))} raises \cd{OverflowError}.
\end{caution}
An integer sentinel keeps every value an int. Use a value that no real answer can reach, for example
\cd{amount + 1} for a count of coins or \cd{2**31 - 1} for a 32-bit limit. Use \cd{-1} or \cd{None}
for ``not found''.
\begin{pyex}
amount = 11
dp = [0] + [amount + 1] * amount     # amount + 1 means not reachable
dp[3]                                # -> 12
BIG = 2**31 - 1
min(BIG, 7)                          # -> 7
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Mix int and float}
An int and a float with the same value are equal, and they are the same dict key.
An operation on an int and a float gives a float.
\begin{pyex}
3 == 3.0                         # -> True
{3: "x"}[3.0]                    # -> 'x'
type(6 / 2), 6 / 2               # -> (float, 3.0)
(2 + 3) / 2                      # -> 2.5
7.0 // 2                         # -> 3.0
(2.0).is_integer()               # -> True
1e18 == 10**18                   # -> True
float(2**53 + 1) == 2**53        # -> True
10**20 // 3                      # -> 33333333333333333333
int(10**20 / 3)                  # -> 33333333333333331968
float(10**400)                   # -> raises OverflowError
idx = 4 / 2                      # 2.0, a float
[1, 2, 3][idx]                   # -> raises TypeError
[1, 2, 3][4 // 2]                # -> 3
range(6 / 2)                     # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{/} always gives a float, also when the division is exact. A float cannot be a list index or a \cd{range}
argument. A float has only 53 bits of precision, so it loses digits of a big integer. Use \cd{//} for integer results.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Arithmetic operators}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Operator & Meaning & Example \\
\midrule
\cd{+  -  *} & add, subtract, multiply & \cd{7 * 2} is \cd{14} \\
\cd{/} & true division, result is always a float & \cd{7 / 2} is \cd{3.5} \\
\cd{//} & floor division & \cd{7 // 2} is \cd{3} \\
\pct & remainder (modulo) & \texttt{7 \% 2} is \cd{1} \\
\cd{**} & power & \cd{2 ** 3} is \cd{8} \\
\cd{-x} & negation & \cd{-(3)} is \cd{-3} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
7 / 2        # -> 3.5
6 / 2        # -> 3.0
7 // 2       # -> 3
7 % 2        # -> 1
2 ** 10      # -> 1024
2 ** -1      # -> 0.5
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Division and modulo with negative numbers}
\cd{//} rounds toward negative infinity. The result of \pct{} has the same sign as the divisor.
This is different from C, C++ and Java.
\begin{pyex}
-7 // 2      # -> -4
-7 % 2       # -> 1
7 // -2      # -> -4
7 % -2       # -> -1
int(-7 / 2)  # -> -3
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Use \cd{int(a / b)} to truncate toward zero like C. For very large integers, the float division
loses precision. Use \cd{a // b} if \cd{a} and \cd{b} have the same sign. Use \cd{-(-a // b)} if they
have different signs.
\end{note}

Use \pct{} to wrap an index around. The result is never negative for a positive divisor.
\begin{pyex}
(0 - 1) % 4      # -> 3
(3 + 1) % 4      # -> 0
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Ceiling division without floats}
\begin{pyex}
a, b = 7, 2
-(-a // b)       # -> 4
(a + b - 1) // b # -> 4
-(-7 // -2), (7 + -2 - 1) // -2   # -> (-3, -2)
\end{pyex}
\cd{-(-a // b)} is correct for all signs. \cd{(a + b - 1) // b} is correct only when \cd{b > 0}.

\subsection{Number functions}
\begin{pyex}
abs(-5)            # -> 5
divmod(17, 5)      # -> (3, 2)
divmod(-17, 5)     # -> (-4, 3)
pow(2, 10)         # -> 1024
pow(2, 10, 1000)   # -> 24
pow(3, -1, 7)      # -> 5
max(3, 9, 4)       # -> 9
min([3, 9, 4])     # -> 3
sum([1, 2, 3])     # -> 6
\end{pyex}
\cd{pow(a, b, m)} computes $a^b \bmod m$ fast. \cd{pow(a, -1, m)} gives the modular inverse \since{3.8}.

Fast exponentiation uses the bits of the exponent. Each step squares the base. When the lowest bit is 1,
the step multiplies the result by the base. The loop needs $O(\log n)$ multiplications.
\begin{pyex}
def power(x, n):
    if n < 0:
        x, n = 1 / x, -n
    res = 1.0
    while n:                      # int truthiness: stops when n is 0
        if n & 1:                 # the lowest bit of n is 1
            res *= x
        x *= x
        n >>= 1                   # drop the lowest bit
    return res
power(2.0, 10), power(2.0, -2)    # -> (1024.0, 0.25)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Modular arithmetic}
Many problems ask for the answer modulo $10^9 + 7$. Take the remainder after each addition and multiplication.
This keeps the numbers small and fast. In Python, \cd{(a - b)} \pct{} \cd{MOD} is never negative.
\begin{pyex}
MOD = 10**9 + 7
a, b = 10**9, 10**9 + 5
(a * b) % MOD                     # -> 14
(3 - 5) % MOD                     # -> 1000000005
ways = 1
for _ in range(100):
    ways = ways * 2 % MOD         # * and % have the same precedence; they run left to right
ways == pow(2, 100, MOD)          # -> True
pow(2, MOD - 2, MOD) * 2 % MOD    # -> 1
type(1e9 + 7)                     # -> float
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{1e9 + 7} is a float. A float modulus gives float results and loses precision. Write \cd{10**9 + 7}.
\end{caution}
\cd{pow(a, MOD - 2, MOD)} is the inverse of \cd{a} when \cd{MOD} is prime. Use it to divide modulo \cd{MOD}.

\subsection{Rounding}
\cd{round()} uses banker's rounding. A value exactly half-way goes to the nearest even number.
\begin{pyex}
round(2.5)         # -> 2
round(3.5)         # -> 4
round(-2.5)        # -> -2
round(2.675, 2)    # -> 2.67
round(1234, -2)    # -> 1200
import math
math.floor(2.7), math.ceil(2.1), math.trunc(-2.7)   # -> (2, 3, -2)
math.floor(-2.5)   # -> -3
math.floor(2.5 + 0.5)   # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{round(2.675, 2)} gives \cd{2.67} because \cd{2.675} has no exact float value.
To round half up for a positive number, use \cd{math.floor(x + 0.5)}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Base conversion}
\begin{pyex}
bin(10), oct(10), hex(255)   # -> ('0b1010', '0o12', '0xff')
bin(10)[2:]                  # -> '1010'
int("1010", 2)               # -> 10
int("ff", 16)                # -> 255
int("z", 36)                 # -> 35
format(10, "b")              # -> '1010'
format(5, "08b")             # -> '00000101'
format(255, "x")             # -> 'ff'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Digits of an integer}
\cd{divmod(x, 10)} splits off the last digit. \cd{while x:} stops when \cd{x} becomes 0.
For a negative number, keep the sign apart and work with \cd{abs(x)}.
\begin{pyex}
x, digits = 4207, []
while x:
    x, d = divmod(x, 10)
    digits.append(d)
digits                          # -> [7, 0, 2, 4]
[int(c) for c in str(4207)]     # -> [4, 2, 0, 7]
sum(map(int, str(4207)))        # -> 13
len(str(4207))                  # -> 4
def reverse_int(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    x, r = abs(x), 0
    while x:
        x, d = divmod(x, 10)
        r = r * 10 + d
    return sign * r
reverse_int(-120)               # -> -21
int(str(1200)[::-1])            # -> 21
r = reverse_int(1534236469)
r if -2**31 <= r <= 2**31 - 1 else 0   # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{divmod(-17, 10)} is \cd{(-2, 3)}, not \cd{(-1, -7)}. Digit loops on negative numbers give wrong digits.
Take \cd{abs(x)} first.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Exact arithmetic}
Use \cd{fractions.Fraction} for exact rational values. Use \cd{decimal.Decimal} for exact decimal values.
\begin{pyex}
from fractions import Fraction
Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 6)     # -> Fraction(1, 2)
from decimal import Decimal
Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2")     # -> Decimal('0.3')
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Operator precedence}
From highest to lowest. Use parentheses when you are not sure.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Operators & Notes \\
\midrule
\cd{()} \cd{[]} \cd{.} calls & grouping, index, attribute \\
\cd{**} & right to left: \cd{2 ** 3 ** 2} is \cd{2 ** 9} \\
\cd{-x  +x  ~x} & unary \\
\cd{*  /  //} \pct & \\
\cd{+  -} & \\
\shl{} \shr & shifts \\
\cd{&} & bitwise AND \\
\cd{^} & bitwise XOR \\
\cd{|} & bitwise OR \\
\cd{==  !=  <  >  <=  >=  in  not in  is  is not} & comparisons \\
\cd{not} & \\
\cd{and} & \\
\cd{or} & \\
\cd{x if c else y} & conditional expression \\
\cd{lambda} & \\
\cd{:=} & assignment expression \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
-2 ** 2          # -> -4
(-2) ** 2        # -> 4
2 ** 3 ** 2      # -> 512
1 + 2 * 3        # -> 7
5 & 3 == 1       # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
In Python, bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons. \cd{x & 1 == 1} means
\cd{(x & 1) == 1}. This is the opposite of C.
\end{note}
Arithmetic binds tighter than shifts, and shifts bind tighter than \cd{&}, \cd{^} and \cd{|}.
Put parentheses around each bit expression inside a sum.
\begin{pyex}
1 << 2 + 1           # -> 8
i = 6
(i >> 1) + (i & 1)   # -> 3
i >> 1 + i & 1       # -> 0
mask, j = 0b101, 2
mask >> j & 1        # -> 1
mask | 1 << 1        # -> 7
not 1 == 2           # -> True
x = 5
x > 0 and x % 2 == 1 # -> True
\end{pyex}
\texttt{i >{}> 1 + i \& 1} means \texttt{(i >{}> (1 + i)) \& 1}. \texttt{mask >{}> j \& 1} means \texttt{(mask >{}> j) \& 1}.
\cd{not a == b} means \cd{not (a == b)}. Comparisons bind tighter than \cd{and} and \cd{or}.

% =====================================================================
\section{Bit operations}

\subsection{Operators}
\begin{pyex}
a, b = 0b1100, 0b1010
bin(a & b)       # -> '0b1000'
bin(a | b)       # -> '0b1110'
bin(a ^ b)       # -> '0b110'
~5               # -> -6
1 << 4           # -> 16
40 >> 2          # -> 10
-8 >> 1          # -> -4
\end{pyex}
\cd{~x} equals \cd{-x - 1}. Negative integers act as if they have infinite leading 1 bits.

\subsection{Common bit tricks}
\begin{pyex}
x = 0b10110
x & 1              # -> 0
(x >> 2) & 1       # -> 1
bin(x | (1 << 0))  # -> '0b10111'
bin(x & ~(1 << 1)) # -> '0b10100'
bin(x ^ (1 << 4))  # -> '0b110'
bin(x & (x - 1))   # -> '0b10100'
x & -x             # -> 2
x.bit_length()     # -> 5
x.bit_count()      # -> 3
bin(x).count("1")  # -> 3
n = 64
n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0   # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{x & 1}: lowest bit. The value is 1 when \cd{x} is odd.
  \item \cd{x & (x - 1)}: removes the lowest set bit.
  \item \cd{x & -x}: keeps only the lowest set bit.
  \item \cd{x.bit_count()} \since{3.10}: number of set bits. On old versions, use \cd{bin(x).count("1")}.
  \item \cd{x.bit_length()}: number of bits that you need to write \cd{x}.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
n = 4
(1 << n) - 1                  # -> 15
m, bits = 0b10110, []
while m:                      # visit each set bit, lowest first
    low = m & -m
    bits.append(low.bit_length() - 1)
    m ^= low
bits                          # -> [1, 2, 4]
x, count = 0b10110, 0
while x:
    x &= x - 1                # remove the lowest set bit
    count += 1
count                         # -> 3
ans = [0] * 6                 # set-bit counts for 0 to 5
for i in range(1, 6):
    ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
ans                           # -> [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2]
seen = 0
for c in "abca":              # a bitmask as a small set of letters
    seen |= 1 << (ord(c) - ord("a"))
bin(seen), seen >> 2 & 1      # -> ('0b111', 1)
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{(1 <{}< n) - 1}: a mask with the \cd{n} lowest bits set.
  \item \cd{x &= x - 1} in a loop counts the set bits. The loop runs one time for each set bit.
  \item \texttt{ans[i >{}> 1] + (i \& 1)}: the bit count of \cd{i} from the bit count of \cd{i // 2}.
  \item \texttt{1 <{}< (ord(c) - ord("a"))}: one bit for each letter. A mask of 26 bits replaces a set of letters.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Reverse the bits}
\begin{pyex}
def reverse_bits(n):              # reverse the 32 low bits of n
    res = 0
    for _ in range(32):
        res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)    # move the lowest bit of n into res
        n >>= 1
    return res
reverse_bits(0b1011)              # -> 3489660928
format(reverse_bits(0b1011), "032b")[:4]   # -> '1101'
int(format(0b1011, "032b")[::-1], 2)       # -> 3489660928
\end{pyex}
The last line uses strings: \cd{format(n, "032b")} gives 32 binary digits, and \cd{int(s, 2)} reads them back.

\subsection{Emulate 32-bit integers}
Python integers never overflow. A negative integer acts as if it has infinite leading 1 bits.
When a problem expects 32-bit behavior, keep the low 32 bits with \cd{& 0xFFFFFFFF}.
Then convert the result back to a signed value.
\begin{pyex}
INT_MAX, INT_MIN = 2**31 - 1, -2**31
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF
def to_signed(x):                 # read the low 32 bits as a signed int
    x &= MASK
    return x if x <= INT_MAX else x - (1 << 32)
to_signed(INT_MAX + 1)            # -> -2147483648
to_signed(-1)                     # -> -1
hex(-1 & MASK)                    # -> '0xffffffff'
def add(a, b):                    # addition with bit operations only
    a, b = a & MASK, b & MASK
    while b:
        a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
    return to_signed(a)
add(-7, 3), add(5, 9)             # -> (-4, 14)
-1 ^ 5                            # -> -6
INT_MIN <= 2**31 <= INT_MAX       # -> False
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Without the mask, the carry loop above does not stop for some negative inputs. The carry moves to the left forever,
because a negative Python integer has no highest bit.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Subsets as bitmasks}
Bit \cd{i} of a mask shows if element \cd{i} is in the subset.
\begin{pyex}
items = ["a", "b", "c"]
subsets = []
for mask in range(1 << len(items)):
    subsets.append([items[i] for i in range(len(items)) if mask >> i & 1])
len(subsets)          # -> 8
subsets[5]            # -> ['a', 'c']
mask = 0b101
subs = []
s = mask
while s:              # every non-empty submask of mask
    subs.append(s)
    s = (s - 1) & mask
subs                  # -> [5, 4, 1]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{XOR properties}
\cd{x ^ x} is 0. \cd{x ^ 0} is \cd{x}. XOR is commutative and associative.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor
reduce(xor, [4, 1, 2, 1, 2])   # -> 4
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Booleans, None and comparisons}

\subsection{True, False and None}
\cd{bool} is a subclass of \cd{int}. \cd{True} equals 1 and \cd{False} equals 0.
\cd{None} shows that a value is not there.
\begin{pyex}
True + True          # -> 2
sum([True, False, True])   # -> 2
def f():
    pass
f() is None          # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Truthiness}
These values are false: \cd{False}, \cd{None}, \cd{0}, \cd{0.0}, \cd{""}, \cd{[]}, \cd{()}, \cd{{}},
\cd{set()}, \cd{range(0)}. All other values are true.
\begin{pyex}
bool([]), bool([0]), bool(""), bool(" ")   # -> (False, True, False, True)
items = []
"empty" if not items else "full"           # -> 'empty'
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Do not use \cd{if x:} when 0 or an empty string is a valid value. Use \cd{if x is not None:}.
\end{caution}
An integer is true when it is not 0. Use this for parity tests and for loops that count down.
An object of your own class is always true, unless the class defines \cd{__bool__} or \cd{__len__}.
A tree node with the value 0 is true. \cd{None} is false.
\begin{pyex}
total = 7
"odd" if total % 2 else "even"    # -> 'odd'
n, steps = 3, 0
while n:                          # stops when n is 0
    n -= 1
    steps += 1
steps                             # -> 3
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
node = Node(0)
bool(node), bool(node.val)        # -> (True, False)
head, length = Node(5, Node(0)), 0
while head:                       # stops at None, the end of the list
    length += 1
    head = head.next
length                            # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{if node:} tests that the node exists. \cd{if node.val:} tests the value, and it is false for the value 0.
Do not mix the two tests.
\end{caution}

\subsection{and, or, not}
\cd{and} and \cd{or} stop as soon as they know the result. They return one of the operands,
not always a \cd{bool}.
\begin{pyex}
0 or 5          # -> 5
3 or 5          # -> 3
0 and 5         # -> 0
3 and 5         # -> 5
not 3           # -> False
name = ""
name or "anonymous"     # -> 'anonymous'
\end{pyex}
Use short-circuit evaluation to protect an index.
\begin{pyex}
a = []
len(a) > 0 and a[0] == 1   # -> False
stack = []
not stack or stack[-1] < 5 # -> True
\end{pyex}
The left test runs first. If \cd{stack} is empty, Python does not evaluate \cd{stack[-1]}.
The same guard protects a chain of attributes. In \cd{fast and fast.next}, Python reads \cd{fast.next} only
when \cd{fast} is not \cd{None}.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:  # fast moves two steps, slow moves one step
    slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
slow.val                   # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\cd{x or y} returns the first true operand. Use it to pick the part that is not empty, for example the rest of
a linked list after a merge (\cd{tail.next = l1 or l2}). A loop condition can combine several kinds of values.
\begin{pyex}
l1, l2 = None, [3, 4]
l1 or l2                   # -> [3, 4]
None or None               # -> None
carry, steps = 1, 0
while l1 or l2 or carry:   # None, a list and an int in one test
    l2, carry = None, 0
    steps += 1
steps                      # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Comparison operators}
Comparisons can be chained. \cd{a < b < c} means \cd{a < b and b < c}.
\begin{pyex}
r, R = 2, 5
0 <= r < R            # -> True
1 < 3 > 2             # -> True
"apple" < "banana"    # -> True
"Z" < "a"             # -> True
"10" < "9"            # -> True
[1, 2] < [1, 3]       # -> True
(1, 2) < (1, 2, 0)    # -> True
1 < "a"               # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}
Strings, lists and tuples compare element by element (lexicographic order). Strings compare by
Unicode code point, so all uppercase letters come before lowercase letters.
\begin{caution}
A tuple never equals a list, also when the elements are the same. Convert one side before you compare.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
(1, 2) == [1, 2]              # -> False
list((1, 2)) == [1, 2]        # -> True
best, target = [2, 5], (2, 5)
best == list(target)          # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Identity and equality}
\cd{==} compares values. \cd{is} compares identity (the same object).
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]
a == b        # -> True
a is b        # -> False
x = None
x is None     # -> True
p, q = None, None
p is q        # -> True
\end{pyex}
For two tree nodes, \cd{p is q} is true only when both names refer to one node, or when both are \cd{None}.
\begin{caution}
Use \cd{is} only to compare with \cd{None} (and \cd{True}/\cd{False} singletons if necessary).
Do not use \cd{is} to compare numbers or strings. The result depends on the implementation.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Membership}
\begin{pyex}
3 in [1, 2, 3]        # -> True
"b" in "abc"          # -> True
"bc" in "abcd"        # -> True
"a" in {"a": 1}       # -> True
1 in {"a": 1}         # -> False
4 not in {1, 2}       # -> True
5 in range(0, 10, 5)  # -> True
rows, r = 10, 9
r in (0, rows - 1)    # -> True
"*" in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}   # -> True
None in {(0, 0), (1, 2)}      # -> False
\end{pyex}
\cd{in} on a dict checks the keys. \cd{in} is $O(n)$ for a list and $O(1)$ on average for a set or dict.
A small tuple literal is a short way to test for one of a few values.

\subsection{Return a boolean}
A comparison already gives a \cd{bool}. Return it directly. \cd{sum} of booleans counts the true values,
because \cd{True} equals 1.
\begin{pyex}
def is_balanced(depth):
    return depth == 0         # not: if depth == 0: return True, else: return False
is_balanced(0)                # -> True
sum(x > 2 for x in [1, 3, 5]) # -> 2
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Control flow}

\subsection{if, elif, else}
\begin{pyex}
def sign(x):
    if x > 0:
        return 1
    elif x < 0:
        return -1
    else:
        return 0
[sign(-4), sign(0), sign(9)]   # -> [-1, 0, 1]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Conditional expression}
\cd{a if condition else b} gives \cd{a} when the condition is true. Otherwise it gives \cd{b}.
\begin{pyex}
x = 7
"odd" if x % 2 else "even"     # -> 'odd'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{for loops}
\cd{for} iterates over any iterable: list, string, tuple, dict, set, range, file, generator.
\begin{pyex}
out = []
for ch in "hey":
    out.append(ch.upper())
out                   # -> ['H', 'E', 'Y']
\end{pyex}
Loop over a tuple literal of offsets to visit the neighbors of a grid cell. Unpack each pair in the header.
\begin{pyex}
r, c, R, C = 0, 1, 2, 3
[(r + dr, c + dc) for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))
 if 0 <= r + dr < R and 0 <= c + dc < C]     # -> [(1, 1), (0, 2), (0, 0)]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{range}
\cd{range(stop)}, \cd{range(start, stop)}, \cd{range(start, stop, step)}. The stop value is not included.
\begin{pyex}
list(range(5))            # -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
list(range(2, 5))         # -> [2, 3, 4]
list(range(0, 10, 3))     # -> [0, 3, 6, 9]
list(range(5, 0, -1))     # -> [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
list(range(4, -1, -1))    # -> [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
list(range(3, 3))         # -> []
\end{pyex}
To include the end value \cd{n}, write \cd{range(1, n + 1)}. A range with a start at or after its stop is empty,
so the loop body does not run. Use \cd{max(0, i - k)} as the start to clip a window at index 0.
\begin{pyex}
n = 3
list(range(1, n + 1))             # -> [1, 2, 3]
list(range(5, 2))                 # -> []
i, k = 2, 4
list(range(max(0, i - k), i))     # -> [0, 1]
\end{pyex}
\cd{range()} reads its arguments one time, before the loop starts. Elements that the loop adds to a list do not
make the loop longer. A level-by-level BFS uses \cd{for _ in range(len(q))} for this reason: it processes
only the nodes of the current level.
\begin{pyex}
q = [1]
for _ in range(len(q)):   # len(q) is 1 here, and it stays 1 for this loop
    q.append(q[-1] + 1)
q                         # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{while loops}
\begin{pyex}
n, steps = 27, 0
while n != 1:
    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
    steps += 1
steps                     # -> 111
\end{pyex}

\subsection{while True (do-while) and a manual index}
Python has no do-while loop. Use \cd{while True:} with \cd{break} or \cd{return} as the exit.
The body then runs at least one time. Use a \cd{while} loop with a manual index when the step size changes.
\begin{pyex}
n, steps = 19, 0
while True:                  # the body runs at least one time
    n = sum(int(d) ** 2 for d in str(n))
    steps += 1
    if n == 1 or steps > 50:
        break
(n, steps)                   # -> (1, 4)
s, i, runs = "aaabcc", 0, []
while i < len(s):            # run-length encoding: each step skips one run
    j = i
    while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:
        j += 1
    runs.append(f"{s[i]}{j - i}")
    i = j
"".join(runs)                # -> 'a3b1c2'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{break, continue and loop else}
\cd{break} stops the loop. \cd{continue} goes to the next iteration.
The \cd{else} block of a loop runs only when the loop ends without \cd{break}.
\begin{pyex}
def first_even(nums):
    for x in nums:
        if x % 2 == 0:
            result = x
            break
    else:
        result = None        # no break: no even number
    return result
first_even([3, 5, 8, 9])     # -> 8
first_even([3, 5])           # -> None
\end{pyex}

To stop two nested loops, put them in a function and use \cd{return}.
\begin{pyex}
def find(grid, target):
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, v in enumerate(row):
            if v == target:
                return (r, c)
    return None
find([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 3)    # -> (1, 0)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{enumerate, zip, reversed}
\cd{enumerate} gives pairs of (index, value). \cd{zip} walks several sequences in parallel.
\cd{reversed} reads a sequence from the end. All three return iterators and make no copy.
\begin{pyex}
list(enumerate("ab"))              # -> [(0, 'a'), (1, 'b')]
list(enumerate("ab", start=1))     # -> [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
list(enumerate("ab", 1))           # -> [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
list(zip([1, 2, 3], "ab"))         # -> [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
list(reversed([1, 2, 3]))          # -> [3, 2, 1]
a = [5, 7, 9]
[y - x for x, y in zip(a, a[1:])]  # -> [2, 2]
\end{pyex}
\cd{zip} stops at the shortest input. \cd{zip(..., strict=True)} \since{3.10} raises
\cd{ValueError} if the lengths are different.
\begin{pyex}
list(zip([1, 2], [3], strict=True))   # -> raises ValueError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Loop over a sequence backwards}
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2, 3]
[a[i] for i in range(len(a) - 1, -1, -1)]   # -> [3, 2, 1]
[x for x in reversed(a)]                    # -> [3, 2, 1]
a[::-1]                                     # -> [3, 2, 1]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Change a collection while you loop over it}
\begin{caution}
Do not add or remove elements of a list, set or dict while you iterate over it.
Iterate over a copy, or build a new collection.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
for k in d:
    d[k + k] = 0          # -> raises RuntimeError
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
nums                      # -> [2, 4]
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
for k in list(d):         # iterate over a copy of the keys
    if d[k] == 1:
        del d[k]
d                         # -> {'b': 2}
\end{pyex}

\subsection{match statement} \since{3.10}
\cd{match} compares a value with patterns. The first pattern that matches runs.
\begin{pyex}
def describe(cmd):
    match cmd:
        case "F" | "B":
            return "move"
        case "L" | "R":
            return "turn"
        case (x, y):
            return f"point {x},{y}"
        case {"op": op}:
            return f"op {op}"
        case [first, *rest] if len(rest) > 1:
            return f"list from {first}"
        case _:
            return "unknown"
[describe("F"), describe("R"), describe((1, 2))]   # -> ['move', 'turn', 'point 1,2']
[describe({"op": "add"}), describe([7, 8, 9]), describe(3)]   # -> ['op add', 'list from 7', 'unknown']
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
A bare name in a \cd{case} captures the value. It does not compare with a variable.
Use a dotted name (for example \cd{Color.RED}) or a literal to compare.
\end{note}

% =====================================================================
\section{Functions}

\subsection{Define and call}
A function without a \cd{return} statement returns \cd{None}.
\begin{pyex}
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
add(2, 3)             # -> 5
def nothing():
    x = 1
nothing() is None     # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Return more than one value}
Return a tuple. Unpack it at the call.
\begin{pyex}
def min_max(nums):
    return min(nums), max(nums)
lo, hi = min_max([4, 1, 9])
(lo, hi)              # -> (1, 9)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Default arguments}
\begin{pyex}
def greet(name, greeting="hello"):
    return f"{greeting} {name}"
greet("ana")              # -> 'hello ana'
greet("ana", "hi")        # -> 'hi ana'
greet(greeting="yo", name="bo")   # -> 'yo bo'
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Python evaluates a default value one time, when it defines the function. All calls share a mutable default
(list, dict, set). Use \cd{None} and make a new object in the body.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def bad(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
bad(1); bad(2)        # -> [1, 2]
def good(x, acc=None):
    if acc is None:
        acc = []
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
good(1); good(2)      # -> [2]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Positional, keyword, *args and **kwargs}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{*args} collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
  \item \cd{**kwargs} collects extra keyword arguments into a dict.
  \item Parameters after \cd{*} are keyword-only.
  \item Parameters before \cd{/} are positional-only \since{3.8}.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def f(a, b=2, *args, c, d=4, **kwargs):
    return a, b, args, c, d, kwargs
f(1, c=3)                 # -> (1, 2, (), 3, 4, {})
f(1, 5, 6, 7, c=3, z=9)   # -> (1, 5, (6, 7), 3, 4, {'z': 9})
def g(x, /, y):
    return x + y
g(1, y=2)                 # -> 3
g(x=1, y=2)               # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Unpack arguments at the call}
\cd{*seq} in a call passes the elements of a sequence as positional arguments.
\cd{**d} passes the items of a dict as keyword arguments.
\begin{pyex}
def add3(a, b, c):
    return a + b + c
nums = [1, 2, 3]
add3(*nums)               # -> 6
opts = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}
add3(**opts)              # -> 6
print(*[1, 2, 3])         # prints: 1 2 3
print(*[1, 2, 3], sep=",")   # prints: 1,2,3
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Lambda functions}
A lambda is a small function with one expression. Use it for \cd{key=} arguments.
\begin{pyex}
square = lambda x: x * x
square(4)                       # -> 16
pairs = [(1, "b"), (2, "a")]
sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1])   # -> [(2, 'a'), (1, 'b')]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Functions are objects}
You can store a function in a variable, a list or a dict. You can pass it to another function.
\begin{pyex}
ops = {"+": lambda a, b: a + b, "*": lambda a, b: a * b}
ops["*"](3, 4)                  # -> 12
def apply_twice(f, x):
    return f(f(x))
apply_twice(lambda v: v + 3, 1) # -> 7
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Scope: LEGB}
Python looks for a name in this order: Local, Enclosing function, Global, Built-in.
\begin{pyex}
x = "global"
def outer():
    x = "enclosing"
    def inner():
        return x          # finds the enclosing x
    return inner()
outer()                   # -> 'enclosing'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{global and nonlocal}
An assignment to a name inside a function makes the name local. To assign to a name of an
enclosing function, declare it \cd{nonlocal}. To assign to a module name, declare it \cd{global}.
\begin{pyex}
def counter():
    count = 0
    def bump():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
    bump(); bump()
    return count
counter()                 # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
def broken():
    count = 0
    def bump():
        count += 1        # count is local here, but it has no value yet
    bump()
broken()                  # -> raises UnboundLocalError
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
calls = 0
def tick():
    global calls          # assign to the module-level name
    calls += 1
tick(); tick()
calls                     # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
You do not need \cd{nonlocal} to change a list or dict in place (\cd{res.append(x)}, \cd{d[k] = v}).
You need it only to assign a new object to the name.
\end{note}
\begin{pyex}
def collect():
    res = []
    def visit(x):
        res.append(x)     # no nonlocal needed: res is not reassigned
    visit(1); visit(2)
    return res
collect()                 # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Closures and late binding}
A closure remembers the variables of the enclosing function. It reads the variable when it runs,
not when you create it.
\begin{pyex}
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]         # -> [2, 2, 2]
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]   # bind the value now
[f() for f in fs]         # -> [0, 1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Nested helper functions}\label{sec:nested-helpers}
Define a recursive helper inside the method. The helper reads the variables of the method directly
(a closure). It can change a list, a set or a dict of the method without \cd{nonlocal}.
It needs \cd{nonlocal} only when it assigns a new value to the name.
\begin{pyex}
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res, path = [], []
        def dfs(i: int) -> None:          # type hints on the helper are optional
            if i == len(nums):
                res.append(path[:])       # append a copy of the path
                return
            path.append(nums[i])          # take nums[i]
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()                    # undo the choice
            dfs(i + 1)                    # skip nums[i]
        dfs(0)
        return res

    def longest_run(self, s: str) -> int:
        best = 0
        def update(length: int) -> None:
            nonlocal best                 # best gets a new value, so nonlocal is necessary
            best = max(best, length)
        run = 0
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            run = run + 1 if i and s[i - 1] == ch else 1
            update(run)
        return best

Solution().subsets([1, 2])                # -> [[1, 2], [1], [2], []]
Solution().longest_run("abbbcc")          # -> 3
\end{pyex}
Put \cd{@cache} on a nested helper. Each call of the method then makes a new helper with an empty cache.
The cache does not keep results from an earlier input.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

class Solution:
    def climbStairs(self, n: int) -> int:
        @cache
        def ways(i: int) -> int:          # number of ways to reach step i
            if i <= 1:
                return 1
            return ways(i - 1) + ways(i - 2)
        return ways(n)

Solution().climbStairs(10)                # -> 89
Solution().climbStairs(3)                 # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Recursion}
\begin{pyex}
def fact(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1)
fact(10)                  # -> 3628800
import sys
sys.getrecursionlimit()   # -> 1000
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
The default recursion limit is 1000 frames. A deeper recursion raises \cd{RecursionError}.
Raise the limit with \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)}, or use a loop and an explicit stack.
Section~\ref{sec:recursion} gives more information.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Decorators}
A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new function.
\cd{@name} above \cd{def} applies it.
\begin{pyex}
import functools
def logged(f):
    @functools.wraps(f)           # keeps the name and docstring of f
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        wrapper.calls += 1
        return f(*args, **kwargs)
    wrapper.calls = 0
    return wrapper
@logged
def double(x):
    return 2 * x
double(3); double(4)              # -> 8
double.calls                      # -> 2
double.__name__                   # -> 'double'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Memoization with functools.cache}
\cd{@cache} stores the result for each argument tuple. The arguments must be hashable.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
@cache
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
fib(90)                   # -> 2880067194370816120
fib.cache_info().currsize # -> 91
fib.cache_clear()
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{@cache} \since{3.9} is the same as \cd{@lru_cache(maxsize=None)}. On Python 3.8, use
\cd{@lru_cache(maxsize=None)}. Convert a list argument to a tuple before the call.
A recursive \cd{@cache} function can fail at a depth of a few thousand (Section~\ref{sec:recursion}).
\end{note}

\subsection{Type hints}
Python does not check type hints when the program runs. They are documentation.
\begin{pyex}
from typing import Optional
def find(nums: list[int], target: int) -> Optional[int]:
    return nums.index(target) if target in nums else None
find([4, 5], 5)           # -> 1
find([4, 5], "x")         # -> None
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{list[int]} works on Python 3.9 and later. On old versions, use \cd{from typing import List}
and \cd{List[int]}. LeetCode writes \cd{Optional[TreeNode]} for a value that can be \cd{None}.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Type hints in LeetCode signatures}
LeetCode signatures use the \cd{typing} forms. Section~\ref{sec:leetcode-format} shows the full format of a solution.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.8cm}L{5.2cm}L{5.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
\cd{typing} form (all versions) & Built-in form & Meaning \\
\midrule
\cd{List[int]} & \cd{list[int]} \since{3.9} & list of int \\
\cd{List[List[str]]} & \cd{list[list[str]]} & 2D grid of strings \\
\cd{Dict[str, int]} & \cd{dict[str, int]} & dict from str to int \\
\cd{Set[int]} & \cd{set[int]} & set of int \\
\cd{Tuple[int, int]} & \cd{tuple[int, int]} & pair of int \\
\cd{Optional[TreeNode]} & \cd{TreeNode | None} \since{3.10} & a node or \cd{None} \\
\cd{-> None} & \cd{-> None} & the method changes its argument in place \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
from typing import List, Optional, Dict
def count_rows(grid: List[List[str]], k: int = 0) -> Dict[str, int]:
    return {"rows": len(grid)}
count_rows([["a"], ["b"]])              # -> {'rows': 2}
def stats(xs: list[int] | None = None) -> tuple[int, int]:   # X | None needs 3.10
    xs = xs or []
    return len(xs), sum(xs)
stats([1, 2])                           # -> (2, 3)
count_rows.__annotations__["k"]         # -> int
def same(node: "TreeNode") -> Optional["TreeNode"]:   # TreeNode is not defined yet
    return node
same(None) is None                      # -> True
def copy(head: "Optional[Node]") -> "Optional[Node]":  # no import of Optional is necessary
    return head
copy(None) is None                      # -> True
\end{pyex}
A hint in quotes is a forward reference. Python stores the string and does not evaluate it.
Use it when the class is defined later in the file, or inside its own class body.
LeetCode uses this form, for example \cd{'Node'}, in some problems.

% =====================================================================
\section{Iterators and generators}

\subsection{The iterator protocol}
\cd{iter(x)} gets an iterator. \cd{next(it)} gets the next element. At the end,
\cd{next} raises \cd{StopIteration}, or returns the default value if you give one.
\begin{pyex}
it = iter([10, 20])
next(it)              # -> 10
next(it)              # -> 20
next(it, "done")      # -> 'done'
next(it)              # -> raises StopIteration
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Share one iterator between recursive calls}
An iterator remembers its position. Create it one time and read it from all recursive calls (through a
closure or an argument). Each \cd{next()} call takes the next token. You do not need an index variable.
\begin{pyex}
def build(tokens):                        # preorder tokens; "N" marks an empty child
    it = iter(tokens)
    def rec():
        v = next(it)
        if v == "N":
            return None
        return (int(v), rec(), rec())     # (value, left, right)
    return rec()
build("1 2 N N 3 N N".split())            # -> (1, (2, None, None), (3, None, None))
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Generator functions}
A function with \cd{yield} returns a generator. The generator makes values one at a time, when you ask.
\begin{pyex}
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
list(countdown(3))    # -> [3, 2, 1]
def chain_all(*seqs):
    for s in seqs:
        yield from s
list(chain_all([1, 2], "ab"))   # -> [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
\end{pyex}
A generator can call itself with \cd{yield from}. Use this for a lazy tree traversal. The caller can stop early,
and the generator then does no more work. The recursion depth equals the height of the tree.
\begin{pyex}
def inorder(t):                   # t is (value, left, right) or None
    if t:
        yield from inorder(t[1])
        yield t[0]
        yield from inorder(t[2])
tree = (2, (1, None, None), (3, None, None))
list(inorder(tree))               # -> [1, 2, 3]
it = inorder(tree)
next(it), next(it)                # -> (1, 2)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Generator expressions}
A generator expression is like a list comprehension in parentheses. It does not build a list.
\begin{pyex}
sum(x * x for x in range(4))        # -> 14
any(x > 2 for x in [1, 5])          # -> True
max(len(w) for w in ["a", "abc"])   # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Iterators run one time}
\begin{caution}
A generator, \cd{map}, \cd{filter}, \cd{zip} and file object give their values one time only.
A second loop gets nothing. Convert to a list if you need the values again.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
squares = (x * x for x in range(3))
list(squares)     # -> [0, 1, 4]
list(squares)     # -> []
z = zip([1, 2], [3, 4])
list(z); list(z)  # -> []
\end{pyex}

\subsection{First element that matches}
\begin{pyex}
nums = [3, 8, 5, 10]
next(x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)         # -> 8
next((x for x in nums if x > 100), None)    # -> None
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Strings}

\subsection{String literals}
\begin{pyex}
'single' == "single"          # -> True
"it's"                        # -> "it's"
'say "hi"'                    # -> 'say "hi"'
"line1\nline2".count("\n")    # -> 1
len("tab\there")              # -> 8
r"C:\new"                     # -> 'C:\\new'
len(r"\n")                    # -> 2
"""two
lines"""                      # -> 'two\nlines'
"ab" "cd"                     # -> 'abcd'
\end{pyex}
A raw string (\cd{r"..."}) does not process backslash escapes. Use it for regular expressions.

\subsection{Strings are immutable}
You cannot change a character in place. Build a new string.
\begin{pyex}
s = "cat"
s[0] = "b"                    # -> raises TypeError
"b" + s[1:]                   # -> 'bat'
chars = list(s)
chars[0] = "h"
"".join(chars)                # -> 'hat'
code, i = "0000", 2
code[:i] + "9" + code[i + 1:] # -> '0090'
\end{pyex}
\cd{s[:i] + ch + s[i + 1:]} makes a copy with one changed character. It takes $O(n)$ time.
For many changes, convert the string to a list, change the list, and join it at the end.

\subsection{Indexing and slicing}
\begin{pyex}
s = "python"
s[0], s[-1]           # -> ('p', 'n')
s[1:4]                # -> 'yth'
s[:2], s[2:]          # -> ('py', 'thon')
s[::-1]               # -> 'nohtyp'
s[::2]                # -> 'pto'
s[10:]                # -> ''
s[10]                 # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}
A slice never raises \cd{IndexError}. It clips the bounds to the string.

\subsection{Concatenation and repetition}
\begin{pyex}
"ab" + "cd"           # -> 'abcd'
"ab" * 3              # -> 'ababab'
"-" * 5               # -> '-----'
"n=" + str(5)         # -> 'n=5'
"n=" + 5              # -> raises TypeError
"." * 2 + "Q" + "." * 1   # -> '..Q.'
"ab" * 0              # -> ''
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{s += c} in a loop can take $O(n^2)$ time. Collect the parts in a list. Then use
\cd{"".join(parts)} one time.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
parts = []
for i in range(5):
    parts.append(str(i))
"".join(parts)        # -> '01234'
",".join(["a", "b"])  # -> 'a,b'
" ".join(map(str, [1, 2, 3]))   # -> '1 2 3'
",".join([1, 2])      # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}
\cd{join} accepts only strings. Convert numbers with \cd{map(str, ...)} first.

\subsection{Find and count}
\begin{pyex}
s = "banana"
"nan" in s            # -> True
s.find("an")          # -> 1
s.rfind("an")         # -> 3
s.find("x")           # -> -1
s.index("an")         # -> 1
s.index("x")          # -> raises ValueError
s.count("a")          # -> 3
s.count("ana")        # -> 1
s.startswith("ba"), s.endswith("na")   # -> (True, True)
s.startswith(("x", "b"))               # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{count} counts occurrences that do not overlap. To count overlapping occurrences, test each start position.
\begin{pyex}
"aaaa".count("aa")                                  # -> 2
sum("aaaa".startswith("aa", i) for i in range(4))   # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\cd{find}, \cd{index}, \cd{count} and \cd{startswith} accept a start and an end position.
The search starts at the start position, and the result is still an index in the full string.
\begin{pyex}
"banana".find("a", 2)                # -> 3
"banana".find("a", 2, 3)             # -> -1
def decode(s):                       # each word is stored as length, "#", word
    res, i = [], 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = s.index("#", i)          # the next "#" at or after position i
        n = int(s[i:j])
        res.append(s[j + 1:j + 1 + n])
        i = j + 1 + n
    return res
encoded = "".join(f"{len(w)}#{w}" for w in ["a#b", "", "xyz"])
encoded                              # -> '3#a#b0#3#xyz'
decode(encoded)                      # -> ['a#b', '', 'xyz']
grid = ["..S", "T.."]
[(r, row.find("S")) for r, row in enumerate(grid) if "S" in row]   # -> [(0, 2)]
\end{pyex}
The length prefix makes the encoding safe for every character, also for the separator inside a word.

\subsection{Change case}
\begin{pyex}
"Hello World".lower()        # -> 'hello world'
"Hello World".upper()        # -> 'HELLO WORLD'
"hello world".title()        # -> 'Hello World'
"hello world".capitalize()   # -> 'Hello world'
"Hello".swapcase()           # -> 'hELLO'
"HeLLo".casefold() == "hello"  # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Split and join}
\begin{pyex}
"a b  c".split()             # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
"a b  c".split(" ")          # -> ['a', 'b', '', 'c']
"a,b,,c".split(",")          # -> ['a', 'b', '', 'c']
"a,b,c".split(",", 1)        # -> ['a', 'b,c']
"a,b,c".rsplit(",", 1)       # -> ['a,b', 'c']
"l1\nl2\r\nl3".splitlines()  # -> ['l1', 'l2', 'l3']
"key=val=x".partition("=")   # -> ('key', '=', 'val=x')
"key=val=x".rpartition("=")  # -> ('key=val', '=', 'x')
"-".join("abc")              # -> 'a-b-c'
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{split()} without an argument splits on any run of whitespace and ignores leading and trailing
whitespace. \cd{split(" ")} splits on each single space and keeps empty strings.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Strip, remove, replace}
\begin{pyex}
"  hi  ".strip()             # -> 'hi'
"  hi  ".lstrip()            # -> 'hi  '
"xxhixx".strip("x")          # -> 'hi'
"0042".lstrip("0")           # -> '42'
"test_case.py".removesuffix(".py")   # -> 'test_case'
"test_case".removeprefix("test_")    # -> 'case'
"a-b-c".replace("-", "+")    # -> 'a+b+c'
"a-b-c".replace("-", "", 1)  # -> 'ab-c'
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{strip("abc")} removes any of the characters a, b, c from both ends. It does not remove the
substring \cd{"abc"}. Use \cd{removeprefix} / \cd{removesuffix} \since{3.9} for a substring.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
"cabbage".strip("abc")       # -> 'ge'
"000".lstrip("0")            # -> ''
"000".lstrip("0") or "0"     # -> '0'
"0120".lstrip("0") or "0"    # -> '120'
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{lstrip("0")} removes all the zeros of \cd{"0"} and \cd{"000"}. Add \cd{or "0"} when the result must be a number.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Character tests}
\begin{pyex}
"123".isdigit(), "12a".isdigit()       # -> (True, False)
"abc".isalpha(), "ab1".isalnum()       # -> (True, True)
"  ".isspace(), "".isspace()           # -> (True, False)
"abc".islower(), "ABC".isupper()       # -> (True, True)
"-5".isdigit()                         # -> False
"--5".lstrip("-").isdigit()            # -> True
"--5".removeprefix("-").isdigit()      # -> False
"\u00b2".isdigit()                     # -> True
int("\u00b2")                          # -> raises ValueError
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{isdigit()} is false for \cd{"-5"} and \cd{"1.5"}. It is true for some non-ASCII digits, for example the
superscript two, that \cd{int()} rejects. To test for an integer, use \cd{try: int(s)} and catch \cd{ValueError}.
For ASCII input, \cd{s.removeprefix("-").isdigit()} \since{3.9} also works. Do not use \cd{lstrip("-")}: it accepts \cd{"--5"}.
\end{note}

\subsection{Characters and codes}
\begin{pyex}
ord("a"), ord("A"), ord("0")   # -> (97, 65, 48)
chr(98)                        # -> 'b'
ord("c") - ord("a")            # -> 2
chr(ord("a") + 25)             # -> 'z'
[chr(ord("a") + i) for i in range(3)]   # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
int("7") == ord("7") - ord("0")         # -> True
\end{pyex}
Use \cd{ord(c) - ord("a")} to map a lowercase letter to 0 to 25. Use it as an index in a list of 26 counts.
\begin{pyex}
counts = [0] * 26
for c in "hello":
    counts[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
counts[ord("l") - ord("a")]    # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Characters compare by code point. Use a chained comparison to test a range. Use \pct{} 26 to wrap around the alphabet.
\begin{pyex}
c = "q"
"a" <= c <= "z"                # -> True
"0" <= "7" <= "9"              # -> True
def shift(c, k):               # move a lowercase letter k places, wrap after z
    return chr(ord("a") + (ord(c) - ord("a") + k) % 26)
shift("y", 3), shift("b", -3)  # -> ('b', 'y')
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Padding and alignment}
\cd{zfill} adds zeros on the left and keeps a sign in front. \cd{ljust}, \cd{rjust} and \cd{center}
pad to a width with a fill character. The default fill character is a space.
\begin{pyex}
"7".zfill(3)          # -> '007'
"-7".zfill(3)         # -> '-07'
"ab".rjust(5)         # -> '   ab'
"ab".ljust(5, ".")    # -> 'ab...'
"ab".center(6, "*")   # -> '**ab**'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{translate}
\cd{str.maketrans(old, new)} makes a table that maps each character of \cd{old} to the character at the same
position in \cd{new}. A third argument lists the characters to delete. \cd{s.translate(table)} applies the table.
\begin{pyex}
table = str.maketrans("abc", "xyz")
"aabbcc".translate(table)                    # -> 'xxyyzz'
"hello, world!".translate(str.maketrans("", "", ",!"))   # -> 'hello world'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{The string module}
\begin{pyex}
import string
string.ascii_lowercase     # -> 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
string.ascii_uppercase[:3] # -> 'ABC'
string.digits              # -> '0123456789'
string.ascii_letters[-1]   # -> 'Z'
"!" in string.punctuation  # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{f-strings}
Put an expression in braces inside an \cd{f"..."} string. After a colon, add a format specification.
\begin{pyex}
name, n, x = "ana", 42, 3.14159
f"{name} has {n} points"   # -> 'ana has 42 points'
f"{x:.2f}"                 # -> '3.14'
f"{n:5d}|"                 # -> '   42|'
f"{n:<5}|"                 # -> '42   |'
f"{n:^6}|"                 # -> '  42  |'
f"{n:*>6}"                 # -> '****42'
f"{n:05d}"                 # -> '00042'
f"{n:+d}"                  # -> '+42'
f"{1234567:,}"             # -> '1,234,567'
f"{1234567:_}"             # -> '1_234_567'
f"{0.256:.1%}"             # -> '25.6%'
f"{1e-5:.2e}"              # -> '1.00e-05'
f"{255:b} {255:x} {255:X} {255:o}"   # -> '11111111 ff FF 377'
f"{5:08b}"                 # -> '00000101'
f"{name!r}"                # -> "'ana'"
f"{n=}"                    # -> 'n=42'
f"{{literal braces}}"      # -> '{literal braces}'
width = 6
f"{n:>{width}}"            # -> '    42'
\end{pyex}
Format specification order: \cd{[fill][align][sign][0][width][,][.precision][type]}.
Align: \cd{<} left, \cd{>} right, \cd{^} center. \cd{f"{x=}"} \since{3.8} shows the name and the value.

\subsection{Other formatting methods}
\begin{pyex}
"{} + {} = {}".format(1, 2, 3)   # -> '1 + 2 = 3'
"{0}{1}{0}".format("a", "b")     # -> 'aba'
"%d items, %.1f%%" % (3, 99.5)   # -> '3 items, 99.5%'
format(3.14159, ".3f")           # -> '3.142'
str(3.0), repr("a")              # -> ('3.0', "'a'")
\end{pyex}

\subsection{String comparison and sorting}
\begin{pyex}
sorted(["banana", "apple", "Cherry"])                 # -> ['Cherry', 'apple', 'banana']
sorted(["banana", "apple", "Cherry"], key=str.lower)  # -> ['apple', 'banana', 'Cherry']
sorted(["bb", "a", "ccc"], key=len)                   # -> ['a', 'bb', 'ccc']
"".join(sorted("dcba"))                               # -> 'abcd'
max(["apple", "fig", "banana"], key=len)              # -> 'banana'
\end{pyex}
Without a key, all uppercase letters sort before all lowercase letters. Use \cd{key=str.lower} to ignore case.

\subsection{Common string idioms}
\begin{pyex}
s = "racecar"
s == s[::-1]                         # -> True
sorted("listen") == sorted("silent") # -> True
from collections import Counter
Counter("hello").most_common(1)      # -> [('l', 2)]
" ".join(reversed("the sky is blue".split()))   # -> 'blue is sky the'
"".join(c for c in "a1b2" if c.isdigit())        # -> '12'
[s[i:i + 3] for i in range(len(s) - 2)][:3]      # -> ['rac', 'ace', 'cec']
\end{pyex}

\subsection{String method summary}
All string methods return a new string (or another value). They never change the original string.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.2cm}L{12.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Task & Methods \\
\midrule
Search & \cd{in}, \cd{find}, \cd{rfind}, \cd{index}, \cd{rindex}, \cd{count}, \cd{startswith}, \cd{endswith} \\
Change case & \cd{lower}, \cd{upper}, \cd{title}, \cd{capitalize}, \cd{swapcase}, \cd{casefold} \\
Test characters & \cd{isdigit}, \cd{isdecimal}, \cd{isnumeric}, \cd{isalpha}, \cd{isalnum}, \cd{isspace}, \cd{islower}, \cd{isupper}, \cd{isascii} \\
Split and join & \cd{split}, \cd{rsplit}, \cd{splitlines}, \cd{partition}, \cd{rpartition}, \cd{join} \\
Trim and pad & \cd{strip}, \cd{lstrip}, \cd{rstrip}, \cd{removeprefix}, \cd{removesuffix}, \cd{zfill}, \cd{ljust}, \cd{rjust}, \cd{center} \\
Replace & \cd{replace}, \cd{translate}, \cd{str.maketrans}, \cd{expandtabs} \\
Format & \cd{format}, \cd{format_map}, f-strings \\
Bytes & \cd{encode} (and \cd{bytes.decode}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
"banana".rindex("a")                    # -> 5
"12".isdecimal(), "x".isascii()         # -> (True, True)
"ab\n".rstrip("\n")                     # -> 'ab'
"a\tb".expandtabs(4)                    # -> 'a   b'
"{a}-{b}".format_map({"a": 1, "b": 2})  # -> '1-2'
"hi".encode(), b"hi".decode()           # -> (b'hi', 'hi')
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Regular expressions}
Use the \cd{re} module for patterns. Use a raw string for the pattern.
\begin{pyex}
import re
re.findall(r"\d+", "a12b345")              # -> ['12', '345']
re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "a   b \t c")          # -> 'a b c'
re.split(r"[,;]", "a,b;c")                 # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
m = re.match(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.com", "ana@mail.com")
m.group(1), m.group(2)                     # -> ('ana', 'mail')
bool(re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", "abc"))       # -> True
re.search(r"\d", "abc") is None            # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{match} checks at the start of the string. \cd{search} checks anywhere. \cd{fullmatch} checks the full string.

% =====================================================================
\section{Lists}

\subsection{Create a list}
\begin{pyex}
[]                         # -> []
[1, "a", None]             # -> [1, 'a', None]
list("abc")                # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
list(range(3))             # -> [0, 1, 2]
[0] * 4                    # -> [0, 0, 0, 0]
[x * x for x in range(4)]  # -> [0, 1, 4, 9]
[-1] * 3                   # -> [-1, -1, -1]
[False] * 2                # -> [False, False]
[float("inf")] * 2         # -> [inf, inf]
list(range(1, 4))          # -> [1, 2, 3]
[1] + [0] * 3              # -> [1, 0, 0, 0]
\end{pyex}
When you fill a list by index, make it at its final size first. Common start values:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{[0] * n} for counts, and \cd{[-1] * n} for ``no answer yet''.
  \item \cd{[False] * n} for flags, and \cd{list(range(n))} for a parent array.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Create a 2D list}
\begin{caution}
Do not use \cd{[[0] * cols] * rows}. It repeats one inner list. All rows are the same object.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
bad = [[0] * 3] * 2
bad[0][0] = 1
bad                        # -> [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]]
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
good[0][0] = 1
good                       # -> [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{[0] * 3} is safe because integers are immutable. \cd{[[]] * 3} and \cd{[set()] * 3} are not safe.
\end{note}
Use the same comprehension form for a list of empty lists (an adjacency list) or a list of sets.
\begin{pyex}
adj = [[] for _ in range(3)]       # a new list for each node
adj[0].append(1)
adj                                # -> [[1], [], []]
cols = [set() for _ in range(3)]   # a new set for each column
cols[2].add("5")
cols                               # -> [set(), set(), {'5'}]
shared = [[]] * 3                  # wrong: one list three times
shared[0].append(1)
shared                             # -> [[1], [1], [1]]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Index and slice}
Negative indexes count from the end. A slice \cd{a[start:stop:step]} makes a new list.
The \cd{stop} index is not included.
\begin{pyex}
a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
a[0], a[-1], a[-2]         # -> (10, 50, 40)
a[1:3]                     # -> [20, 30]
a[:2], a[3:]               # -> ([10, 20], [40, 50])
a[::2]                     # -> [10, 30, 50]
a[::-1]                    # -> [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
a[-2:]                     # -> [40, 50]
a[3:1:-1]                  # -> [40, 30]
a[100:]                    # -> []
a[5]                       # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
A negative index does not raise an error. \cd{a[i - 1]} with \cd{i = 0} silently reads the last element.
