Guard the index, for example \cd{i > 0 and a[i - 1] == x}. Also, \cd{a[-k:]} with \cd{k = 0} gives the
full list, not an empty list.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
a = [10, 20, 30]
i = 0
a[i - 1]                   # -> 30
i > 0 and a[i - 1] == 30   # -> False
k = 0
a[-k:]                     # -> [10, 20, 30]
a[len(a) - k:]             # -> []
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Assign to a slice and delete a slice}
\begin{pyex}
a = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
a[1:3] = ["x", "y", "z"]   # the new part can have a different length
a                          # -> [0, 'x', 'y', 'z', 3, 4]
del a[1:4]
a                          # -> [0, 3, 4]
a[::2] = [9, 9]            # an extended slice needs the same length
a                          # -> [9, 3, 9]
a[:] = []                  # clear in place
a                          # -> []
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Add elements}
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2]
a.append(3)                # add one element at the end
a.extend([4, 5])           # add all elements of an iterable
a.insert(0, 0)             # insert before index 0
a                          # -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
a.append([6, 7])           # append adds the list as ONE element
a[-1]                      # -> [6, 7]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Remove elements}
\begin{pyex}
a = [5, 3, 7, 3]
a.pop()                    # -> 3
a.pop(0)                   # -> 5
a                          # -> [3, 7]
a.remove(7)                # remove the first element equal to 7
a                          # -> [3]
a.remove(99)               # -> raises ValueError
a.clear()
a                          # -> []
[].pop()                   # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Search and count}
\begin{pyex}
a = [4, 2, 4, 1]
a.index(4)                 # -> 0
a.index(4, 1)              # -> 2
a.count(4)                 # -> 2
4 in a                     # -> True
a.index(9)                 # -> raises ValueError
a.index(4, 1, 3)           # -> 2
0 in [3, 0, 5]             # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{a.index(x, start, stop)} searches only \cd{a[start:stop]}, but it returns an index in the full list.

\subsection{Sort and reverse in place}
\cd{sort()} and \cd{reverse()} change the list and return \cd{None}.
\cd{sorted()} returns a new list. \cd{reversed()} returns an iterator that reads the list from the end.
\begin{pyex}
a = [3, 1, 2]
a.sort()
a                          # -> [1, 2, 3]
a.sort(reverse=True)
a                          # -> [3, 2, 1]
a.reverse()
a                          # -> [1, 2, 3]
b = [3, 1, 2]
sorted(b), b               # -> ([1, 2, 3], [3, 1, 2])
print(b.sort())            # prints: None
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Do not write \cd{a = a.sort()}. The result is \cd{None}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Operators and built-in functions}
\begin{pyex}
[1, 2] + [3]               # -> [1, 2, 3]
[1, 2] * 2                 # -> [1, 2, 1, 2]
len([1, 2, 3])             # -> 3
min([4, 2, 8]), max([4, 2, 8]), sum([4, 2, 8])   # -> (2, 8, 14)
max([], default=0)         # -> 0
max([])                    # -> raises ValueError
any([0, 0, 3]), all([1, 0])   # -> (True, False)
[1, 2] == [1, 2], [1, 2] < [1, 2, 0]   # -> (True, True)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{min and max with a key}
\begin{pyex}
words = ["kiwi", "apple", "fig"]
max(words, key=len)                 # -> 'apple'
min(words, key=lambda w: w[-1])     # -> 'apple'
points = [(1, 5), (3, 2), (0, 9)]
min(points, key=lambda p: p[1])     # -> (3, 2)
a = [7, 3, 9]
max(range(len(a)), key=lambda i: a[i])   # -> 2
max(["bb", "aa", "c"], key=len)     # -> 'bb'
b = [4, 9, 9]
max(range(len(b)), key=lambda i: b[i])   # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\cd{max} and \cd{min} return the first element if two elements have the same key.
The \cd{max(range(len(a)), key=...)} idiom gives the index of the largest element.

\subsection{Use a list as a stack}
\cd{append} (amortized) and \cd{pop()} at the end are $O(1)$.
\begin{pyex}
stack = []
stack.append(1); stack.append(2)
stack[-1]                 # -> 2
stack.pop()               # -> 2
bool(stack)               # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{pop(0)} and \cd{insert(0, x)} are $O(n)$. For a queue, use \cd{collections.deque}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Copy a list}
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, [2, 3]]
b = a[:]                  # shallow copy (same as list(a) or a.copy())
b[0] = 99
a                         # -> [1, [2, 3]]
b[1].append(4)            # the inner list is shared
a                         # -> [1, [2, 3, 4]]
import copy
c = copy.deepcopy(a)
c[1].append(5)
a                         # -> [1, [2, 3, 4]]
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
g2 = [row[:] for row in grid]   # copy a 2D grid, fast
g2[0][0] = 0
grid[0][0]                # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\subsection{The loop variable is a name, not a slot}
\cd{for x in a} binds the name \cd{x} to each element. An assignment to \cd{x} does not change the list.
Use an index to change the elements. In a list of lists, \cd{row} is the inner list itself.
A change through \cd{row} changes the grid.
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2, 3]
for x in a:
    x *= 10                # rebinds the name x only
a                          # -> [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(a)):
    a[i] *= 10             # changes the list
a                          # -> [10, 20, 30]
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
for row in grid:
    row.reverse()          # changes each inner list in place
grid                       # -> [[2, 1], [4, 3]]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{List methods and their cost}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.9cm}L{8.9cm}L{2.8cm}@{}}
\toprule
Method & Action & Time \\
\midrule
\cd{append(x)} & add \cd{x} at the end & $O(1)$ amortized \\
\cd{extend(it)} & add all elements of \cd{it} at the end & $O(k)$ \\
\cd{insert(i, x)} & insert \cd{x} before index \cd{i} & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{pop()} & remove and return the last element & $O(1)$ \\
\cd{pop(i)} & remove and return the element at index \cd{i} & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{remove(x)} & remove the first element equal to \cd{x}; \cd{ValueError} if there is none & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{index(x, start, stop)} & index of the first \cd{x}; \cd{ValueError} if there is none & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{count(x)} & number of elements equal to \cd{x} & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{sort(key=, reverse=)} & sort in place (stable); returns \cd{None} & $O(n \log n)$ \\
\cd{reverse()} & reverse in place; returns \cd{None} & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{copy()} & shallow copy, the same as \cd{a[:]} & $O(n)$ \\
\cd{clear()} & remove all elements & $O(n)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Grid and matrix idioms}
\begin{pyex}
m = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6]]
len(m), len(m[0])                       # -> (2, 3)
[list(col) for col in zip(*m)]          # -> [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
[list(r) for r in zip(*m[::-1])]        # -> [[4, 1], [5, 2], [6, 3]]
[list(r) for r in zip(*m)][::-1]        # -> [[3, 6], [2, 5], [1, 4]]
[row[::-1] for row in m]                # -> [[3, 2, 1], [6, 5, 4]]
m[::-1]                                 # -> [[4, 5, 6], [1, 2, 3]]
[v for row in m for v in row]           # -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
sum(map(sum, m))                        # -> 21
[m[r][r] for r in range(2)]             # -> [1, 5]
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{zip(*m)} transposes. \cd{zip(*m[::-1])} rotates 90 degrees clockwise.
        \cd{list(zip(*m))[::-1]} rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise.
  \item On a diagonal from top-left to bottom-right, \cd{r - c} is constant. On the other diagonal, \cd{r + c} is constant.
  \item To store a cell as one integer, use \cd{k = r * cols + c}. Get it back with \cd{r, c = divmod(k, cols)}.
  \item In a $9 \times 9$ board, the $3 \times 3$ box of cell \cd{(r, c)} has the number \cd{(r // 3) * 3 + c // 3}.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
cols = 4
k = 2 * cols + 3
divmod(k, cols)                         # -> (2, 3)
r, c = 4, 7
(r // 3) * 3 + c // 3                   # -> 5
(r // 3, c // 3)                        # -> (1, 2)
m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
n = len(m)
for i in range(n):                      # transpose in place: swap across the diagonal
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        m[i][j], m[j][i] = m[j][i], m[i][j]
for row in m:
    row.reverse()
m                                       # -> [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]
\end{pyex}
The last example rotates a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place: transpose, then reverse each row.

To read a rectangle, slice the rows, then slice each row. A nested generator expression adds the values
without a temporary list.
\begin{pyex}
m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
sum(sum(row[1:3]) for row in m[0:2])    # -> 16
[row[1:3] for row in m[0:2]]            # -> [[2, 3], [5, 6]]
\end{pyex}
The example reads rows 0 to 1 and columns 1 to 2. For many rectangle queries, use a 2D prefix sum.

\subsection{Grid of strings}
A grid often comes as a list of strings. \cd{grid[r][c]} reads one character.
A string is immutable, so an assignment to \cd{grid[r][c]} raises \cd{TypeError}.
Convert each row to a list when you must mark cells.
\begin{pyex}
rows = ["#.", ".."]
rows[0][1]                              # -> '.'
rows[0][1] = "#"                        # -> raises TypeError
grid = [list(row) for row in rows]      # a list of lists of characters
grid[0][1] = "#"
["".join(row) for row in grid]          # -> ['##', '..']
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Directions and turns in a grid}
Store the four directions in clockwise order. An index \cd{d} gives the current facing.
\cd{(d + 1)} \pct{} \cd{4} turns right, and \cd{(d - 1)} \pct{} \cd{4} turns left.
In Python, \cd{(0 - 1)} \pct{} \cd{4} is 3, so a left turn from north correctly gives west.
\begin{pyex}
DIRS = ((-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1))   # north, east, south, west
r, c, d = 0, 0, 0                            # at (0, 0), facing north
for cmd in "RFFLF":
    if cmd == "R":
        d = (d + 1) % 4                      # turn right
    elif cmd == "L":
        d = (d - 1) % 4                      # turn left
    else:
        dr, dc = DIRS[d]                     # move one step forward
        r, c = r + dr, c + dc
(r, c, d)                                    # -> (-1, 2, 0)
(0 - 1) % 4                                  # -> 3
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Tuples}

\subsection{Create a tuple}
A tuple is an immutable sequence. A comma makes a tuple, not the parentheses.
\begin{pyex}
t = (1, 2, 3)
t2 = 1, 2
type(t2)                  # -> tuple
single = (5,)             # one element needs a comma
type((5))                 # -> int
type(single)              # -> tuple
tuple("ab")               # -> ('a', 'b')
() == tuple()             # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Use tuples}
\begin{pyex}
t = (3, 1, 3)
t[0], t[-1], t[1:]        # -> (3, 3, (1, 3))
t.count(3), t.index(1)    # -> (2, 1)
t + (4,)                  # -> (3, 1, 3, 4)
t[0] = 9                  # -> raises TypeError
seen = {(0, 0), (1, 2)}   # tuples can be set elements and dict keys
(1, 2) in seen            # -> True
\end{pyex}
Convert a list to a tuple to use it as a key. For example, a tuple of 26 letter counts is a key that is the same
for all anagrams.
\begin{pyex}
def signature(word):
    counts = [0] * 26
    for c in word:
        counts[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
    return tuple(counts)      # a list is not hashable; a tuple is
groups = {}
for w in ["eat", "tea", "tan"]:
    groups.setdefault(signature(w), []).append(w)
list(groups.values())         # -> [['eat', 'tea'], ['tan']]
point = [3, 4]
{tuple(point): 1}             # -> {(3, 4): 1}
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
A tuple that contains a list is not hashable, and you can change the list.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
t = (1, [2])
t[1].append(3)
t                         # -> (1, [2, 3])
hash(t)                   # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Tuples compare element by element}
Use tuples to sort by more than one key and to store heap entries.
\begin{pyex}
(1, "b") < (1, "c") < (2, "a")      # -> True
sorted([(2, "x"), (1, "z"), (1, "y")])   # -> [(1, 'y'), (1, 'z'), (2, 'x')]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{namedtuple}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p = Point(1, 2)
p.x, p[1]                 # -> (1, 2)
p                         # -> Point(x=1, y=2)
p._replace(x=5)           # -> Point(x=5, y=2)
p._asdict()               # -> {'x': 1, 'y': 2}
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Ranges}
A \cd{range} does not store its elements. Length, index and membership of an \cd{int} are $O(1)$.
Membership of another type (for example a float) checks each element.
\begin{pyex}
r = range(0, 20, 5)
len(r), r[2], r[-1]       # -> (4, 10, 15)
15 in r, 16 in r          # -> (True, False)
15.0 in r                 # -> True
list(reversed(r))         # -> [15, 10, 5, 0]
range(5)[1:3]             # -> range(1, 3)
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Dictionaries}

\subsection{Create a dictionary}
\begin{pyex}
{"a": 1, "b": 2}                  # -> {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
dict(a=1, b=2)                    # -> {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
dict([("a", 1), ("b", 2)])        # -> {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
dict(zip("ab", [1, 2]))           # -> {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
{c: ord(c) for c in "ab"}         # -> {'a': 97, 'b': 98}
dict.fromkeys("ab", 0)            # -> {'a': 0, 'b': 0}
{}                                # -> {}
type({})                          # -> dict
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{dict.fromkeys(keys, [])} gives every key the same list. Use a comprehension:
\cd{{k: [] for k in keys}}.
\end{caution}
In a comprehension or a loop, a later value for the same key replaces the earlier value.
So \cd{{v: i for i, v in enumerate(a)}} keeps the last index of each value.
\begin{pyex}
{v: i for i, v in enumerate("abca")}       # -> {'a': 3, 'b': 1, 'c': 2}
{a: b for a, b in [("x", 1), ("y", 2)]}    # -> {'x': 1, 'y': 2}
{c: set() for w in ["ab", "bc"] for c in w}   # -> {'a': set(), 'b': set(), 'c': set()}
MOVES = {"U": (-1, 0), "D": (1, 0), "L": (0, -1), "R": (0, 1)}
dr, dc = MOVES["L"]
(dr, dc)                                   # -> (0, -1)
OPEN = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}      # closing bracket: its opening bracket
OPEN["]"]                                  # -> '['
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Get values}
\begin{pyex}
d = {"a": 1}
d["a"]                    # -> 1
d["z"]                    # -> raises KeyError
d.get("z")                # -> None
d.get("z", 0)             # -> 0
"a" in d                  # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Set, update and delete}
\begin{pyex}
d = {"a": 1}
d["b"] = 2                         # add or replace
d.update({"b": 3, "c": 4})
d                                  # -> {'a': 1, 'b': 3, 'c': 4}
d.setdefault("d", 0)               # -> 0
d.setdefault("a", 99)              # -> 1
d.pop("a")                         # -> 1
d.pop("zz", None)                  # -> None
del d["b"]
d                                  # -> {'c': 4, 'd': 0}
d.popitem()                        # -> ('d', 0)
d | {"x": 1}                       # -> {'c': 4, 'x': 1}
d |= {"c": 5}
d                                  # -> {'c': 5}
\end{pyex}
\cd{setdefault(k, v)} returns the value of \cd{k}. If \cd{k} is not there, it first sets it to \cd{v}.
\cd{popitem()} removes the last inserted item. \cd{|} and \cd{|=} \since{3.9} merge dictionaries.
\begin{caution}
Python evaluates the arguments before the call. \cd{d.setdefault(k, Node())} makes a new \cd{Node} on every call,
also when \cd{k} is already there. For an expensive default, test with \cd{in} first, or use a \cd{defaultdict}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
made = []
def new_node():
    made.append(1)
    return {}
children = {}
node = children.setdefault("a", new_node())
node = children.setdefault("a", new_node())   # "a" is there, but new_node() runs again
len(made)                                     # -> 2
if "b" not in children:
    children["b"] = new_node()
len(made)                                     # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Iterate over a dictionary}
Dictionaries keep insertion order \since{3.7}.
\begin{pyex}
d = {"b": 2, "a": 1}
list(d)                   # -> ['b', 'a']
list(d.keys())            # -> ['b', 'a']
list(d.values())          # -> [2, 1]
list(d.items())           # -> [('b', 2), ('a', 1)]
[k for k, v in d.items() if v > 1]   # -> ['b']
\end{pyex}
\cd{next(iter(d))} gives the oldest key in $O(1)$. \cd{keys()}, \cd{values()} and \cd{items()} return views.
A view shows later changes to the dict. Key views and item views support set operations.
\begin{pyex}
d = {"x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3}
next(iter(d))                 # -> 'x'
d.pop(next(iter(d)))          # -> 1
list(d)                       # -> ['y', 'z']
keys = d.keys()
d["w"] = 0
list(keys)                    # -> ['y', 'z', 'w']
d.keys() & {"y", "q"}         # -> {'y'}
{"a": 1, "b": 2}.items() - {("a", 1)}   # -> {('b', 2)}
max(d.values()), len(d)       # -> (3, 3)
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Many deletions at the front of a dict make \cd{next(iter(d))} slower in CPython. For an LRU cache, use
\cd{OrderedDict} (Section~\ref{sec:collections}) or a dict with a doubly linked list.
\end{note}

\subsection{Sort and search by value}
\begin{pyex}
scores = {"ana": 7, "bo": 9, "cy": 7}
max(scores, key=scores.get)                    # -> 'bo'
sorted(scores, key=scores.get)                 # -> ['ana', 'cy', 'bo']
sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))   # -> [('bo', 9), ('ana', 7), ('cy', 7)]
dict(sorted(scores.items()))                   # -> {'ana': 7, 'bo': 9, 'cy': 7}
{v: k for k, v in {"a": 1, "b": 2}.items()}    # -> {1: 'a', 2: 'b'}
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Counting and grouping idioms}
\begin{pyex}
counts = {}
for w in ["a", "b", "a"]:
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
counts                         # -> {'a': 2, 'b': 1}
groups = {}
for w in ["eat", "tea", "tan"]:
    groups.setdefault("".join(sorted(w)), []).append(w)
groups                         # -> {'aet': ['eat', 'tea'], 'ant': ['tan']}
\end{pyex}
\cd{collections.Counter} and \cd{collections.defaultdict} make these idioms shorter (Section~\ref{sec:collections}).

\subsection{Dictionary rules}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Keys must be hashable: numbers, strings, tuples of hashable values, frozensets.
  \item \cd{1}, \cd{1.0} and \cd{True} are the same key because they are equal. The first key object stays,
        and the last value replaces the earlier values.
  \item Two dictionaries are equal if they have the same items. The order does not matter.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
{1: "a", 1.0: "b"}             # -> {1: 'b'}
{"a": 1, "b": 2} == {"b": 2, "a": 1}   # -> True
{[1]: 0}                       # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}
An object of your own class is hashable by identity when the class does not define \cd{__eq__}.
Use such objects as keys to map each original node to its copy. The key \cd{None} maps a missing pointer to
\cd{None}, so the copy code needs no test for \cd{None}.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
a = Node(1, Node(2))
copies = {None: None}                 # original node: its copy
n = a
while n:
    copies[n] = Node(n.val)
    n = n.next
n = a
while n:
    copies[n].next = copies[n.next]   # copies[None] is None
    n = n.next
b = copies[a]
(b.val, b.next.val, b.next.next)      # -> (1, 2, None)
b is not a, Node(1) in copies         # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Sets}

\subsection{Create a set}
\begin{pyex}
{1, 2, 2, 3}              # -> {1, 2, 3}
set("aab") == {"a", "b"}  # -> True
set()                     # -> set()
type({})                  # -> dict
{x % 3 for x in range(10)}   # -> {0, 1, 2}
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{{}} is an empty dict. Use \cd{set()} for an empty set.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Add and remove}
\begin{pyex}
s = {1, 2}
s.add(3)
s.update([4, 5])
s.discard(10)             # no error if the element is not there
s.remove(1)
s                         # -> {2, 3, 4, 5}
s.remove(10)              # -> raises KeyError
len(s), 3 in s            # -> (4, True)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Set operations}
\begin{pyex}
a, b = {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}
a | b                     # -> {1, 2, 3, 4}
a & b                     # -> {2, 3}
a - b                     # -> {1}
a ^ b                     # -> {1, 4}
{1, 2} <= a               # -> True
{1, 2} < a                # -> True
a >= {1}                  # -> True
a.isdisjoint({7, 8})      # -> True
a.union([9]), a.intersection(b, {3})   # -> ({1, 2, 3, 9}, {3})
a |= {10}
a                         # -> {1, 2, 3, 10}
\end{pyex}
The methods (\cd{union}, \cd{intersection}, \cd{difference}) accept any iterable. The operators need sets.

\subsection{More set methods}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{6.2cm}L{9.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Method & Same as / action \\
\midrule
\cd{s.issubset(t)}, \cd{s.issuperset(t)} & \cd{s <= t}, \cd{s >= t} \\
\cd{s.union(t)}, \cd{s.update(t)} & \cd{s | t}, \cd{s |= t} \\
\cd{s.intersection(t)}, \cd{s.intersection_update(t)} & \cd{s & t}, \cd{s &= t} \\
\cd{s.difference(t)}, \cd{s.difference_update(t)} & \cd{s - t}, \cd{s -= t} \\
\cd{s.symmetric_difference(t)} & \cd{s ^ t} \\
\cd{s.pop()} & remove and return an arbitrary element; \cd{KeyError} if \cd{s} is empty \\
\cd{s.copy()}, \cd{s.clear()} & shallow copy; remove all elements \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
s = {3, 1, 2}
t = s.copy()
x = t.pop()                       # removes an arbitrary element
len(t), x in s                    # -> (2, True)
{1, 2}.issubset([1, 2, 3]), {1, 2, 3}.issuperset({3})   # -> (True, True)
a = {1, 2, 3}
a.difference_update({1})
a.intersection_update({2, 9})
a                                 # -> {2}
{1, 2}.symmetric_difference([2, 3])   # -> {1, 3}
set().pop()                       # -> raises KeyError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{frozenset}
A \cd{frozenset} is an immutable set. You can put it in a set or use it as a dict key.
\begin{pyex}
regions = {frozenset({(0, 0), (0, 1)}), frozenset({(5, 5)})}
frozenset({(5, 5)}) in regions       # -> True
{{1, 2}}                             # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Set idioms}
\begin{pyex}
nums = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]
len(set(nums))                       # -> 3
list(dict.fromkeys(nums))            # -> [3, 1, 2]
sorted(set(nums))                    # -> [1, 2, 3]
seen, dupes = set(), set()
for x in nums:
    (dupes if x in seen else seen).add(x)
sorted(dupes)                        # -> [1, 3]
\end{pyex}
\cd{list(dict.fromkeys(nums))} removes duplicates and keeps the first order. \cd{set} does not keep order.
\begin{pyex}
nums = [1, 2, 2]
len(set(nums)) < len(nums)        # -> True
seen = set()
for r, c, v in [(0, 0, "5"), (1, 1, "5")]:   # one set of tuples replaces many sets
    keys = [("row", r, v), ("col", c, v), ("box", r // 3, c // 3, v)]
    dup = any(k in seen for k in keys)
    seen.update(keys)
dup                               # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{len(set(a)) < len(a)} tests for a duplicate in one line. A tuple that includes a tag
(\cd{"row"}, \cd{"col"}, \cd{"box"}) puts several kinds of keys in one set.
\begin{note}
A set has no order. Its print order is not the sorted order (\cd{{1, 2, 3, 10}} can print as \cd{{10, 1, 2, 3}}).
For strings, the order changes from run to run. Do not depend on it. Use \cd{sorted()}.
\end{note}

% =====================================================================
\section{Comprehensions}

\subsection{List, dict and set comprehensions}
\begin{pyex}
[x * 2 for x in range(4)]                  # -> [0, 2, 4, 6]
[x for x in range(10) if x % 3 == 0]       # -> [0, 3, 6, 9]
["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(3)]   # -> ['even', 'odd', 'even']
{x: x * x for x in range(3)}               # -> {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 4}
{len(w) for w in ["a", "bb", "cc"]}        # -> {1, 2}
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
A filter \cd{if} goes at the end. A conditional value \cd{a if c else b} goes at the start.
\end{note}

\subsection{Nested comprehensions}
The \cd{for} clauses run in the same order as nested loops.
\begin{pyex}
[(r, c) for r in range(2) for c in range(2)]    # -> [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]
[[r * 3 + c for c in range(3)] for r in range(2)]   # -> [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]
[x for row in [[1, 2], [3]] for x in row]       # -> [1, 2, 3]
[(a, b) for a in range(3) for b in range(a)]    # -> [(1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 1)]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Generator expressions as arguments}
A function call with one argument can take a generator expression without extra parentheses.
Python makes the values one at a time, so it builds no temporary list.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter, deque
board = [["a", "b"], ["b", "c"]]
Counter(ch for row in board for ch in row)["b"]   # -> 2
indeg = [0, 2, 0]
deque(i for i in range(3) if indeg[i] == 0)       # -> deque([0, 2])
offsets = [(dr, dc) for dr in (-1, 0, 1) for dc in (-1, 0, 1) if (dr, dc) != (0, 0)]
len(offsets)                                      # -> 8
words = ["apple", "fig"]
max(map(len, words))                              # -> 5
sum(len(w) for w in words if "p" in w)            # -> 5
[(w, n) for w in words if (n := len(w)) > 3]      # -> [('apple', 5)]
\end{pyex}
The walrus operator computes \cd{len(w)} one time and uses it in the filter and in the value.

\subsection{Comprehension scope}
The loop variable of a comprehension does not leak out of the comprehension.
A name that \cd{:=} assigns inside a comprehension is different: it belongs to the enclosing scope.
\begin{pyex}
x = "outer"
[x for x in range(3)]
x                                          # -> 'outer'
[y for v in [1, 2, 3] if (y := v * 10) > 15]   # -> [20, 30]
y                                          # -> 30
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Mutability and copies}

\subsection{Mutable and immutable objects}
You can change a mutable object (list, dict, set) in place. You cannot change an immutable object
(int, float, str, tuple, frozenset). An operation on an immutable object makes a new object.
\begin{pyex}
s = "ab"
t = s
s += "c"                  # makes a new string; t does not change
(s, t)                    # -> ('abc', 'ab')
a = [1]
b = a
a += [2]                  # changes the list in place; b sees it
b                         # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Arguments are passed by object reference}
A function gets a reference to the same object. A change in place is visible to the caller.
Assignment to the parameter name is not visible.
\begin{pyex}
def mutate(lst):
    lst.append(99)
def rebind(lst):
    lst = [0]
a = [1]
mutate(a); rebind(a)
a                         # -> [1, 99]
\end{pyex}
To replace all the contents of an argument, assign to the full slice. A method that sorts its argument also
changes the caller's list. Use \cd{sorted(xs)} when the caller needs the old order.
\begin{pyex}
def reset(lst):
    lst[:] = [0] * len(lst)   # changes the caller's list
a = [1, 2]
reset(a)
a                         # -> [0, 0]
def middle(xs):
    xs.sort()             # sorts the caller's list too
    return xs[len(xs) // 2]
data = [3, 1, 2]
middle(data), data        # -> (2, [1, 2, 3])
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Shallow copy and deep copy}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.2cm}L{4.4cm}L{6.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Operation & Copies & Notes \\
\midrule
\cd{b = a} & nothing & same object \\
\cd{a[:]}, \cd{list(a)}, \cd{a.copy()} & outer list only & inner objects are shared \\
\cd{[row[:] for row in a]} & two levels & correct for a 2D grid of numbers \\
\cd{copy.deepcopy(a)} & everything & slow; avoid in loops \\
\cd{d.copy()}, \cd{dict(d)} & outer dict only & lists inside are shared \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
import copy
d = {"k": [1]}
shallow = d.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(d)
d["k"].append(2)
shallow["k"], deep["k"]   # -> ([1, 2], [1])
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Keep the old values in a rolling update}
Sometimes each new value must read only old values. Then write the new values to a separate list.
Rebind the name to the new list at the end of the step. If one list is read and written in the same step,
the update reads some new values by mistake.
\begin{pyex}
prev = [1, 1, 1]
for _ in range(2):            # grid paths, one row at a time
    cur = [1] * 3             # a new list for each row
    for j in range(1, 3):
        cur[j] = cur[j - 1] + prev[j]
    prev = cur                # rebind; no copy is necessary
prev                          # -> [1, 3, 6]
dist = [0, 5, 9]
new = dist.copy()             # read from dist, write to new
for u, v, w in [(0, 1, 1), (1, 2, 1)]:
    if dist[u] + w < new[v]:
        new[v] = dist[u] + w
new                           # -> [0, 1, 6]
\end{pyex}
In the second example, one round uses only the distances of the previous round. An in-place update
gives \cd{2} for the last node, because it uses the new value of node 1 in the same round.

\subsection{Copy the current path in backtracking}
\begin{caution}
\cd{res.append(path)} stores a reference to the same list. Later changes to \cd{path} change the stored
result. Append a copy: \cd{res.append(path[:])}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
res, path = [], []
for x in [1, 2]:
    path.append(x)
    res.append(path)      # wrong: the same list two times
res                       # -> [[1, 2], [1, 2]]
res, path = [], []
for x in [1, 2]:
    path.append(x)
    res.append(path[:])   # correct
res                       # -> [[1], [1, 2]]
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{The collections module}\label{sec:collections}

\subsection{deque}
A deque is a double-ended queue. Add and remove at both ends in $O(1)$ time.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4)               # right end
q.appendleft(0)           # left end
q                         # -> deque([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
q.pop(), q.popleft()      # -> (4, 0)
q[0], q[-1]               # -> (1, 3)
q.extend([7, 8]); q.extendleft([-1, -2])   # extendleft adds -1, then -2: the order reverses
q                         # -> deque([-2, -1, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8])
q.rotate(2)               # move 2 elements from right to left
q                         # -> deque([7, 8, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3])
q.rotate(-2)
len(q), 3 in q            # -> (7, True)
deque().popleft()         # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}
Use \cd{maxlen} to keep only the last \cd{n} elements.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
last3 = deque(maxlen=3)
for x in range(6):
    last3.append(x)
last3                     # -> deque([3, 4, 5], maxlen=3)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Indexing in the middle of a deque is $O(n)$. Do not use a deque for random access.
\end{caution}
\cd{deque(iterable)} accepts any iterable, also a generator expression. An empty deque is false, so
\cd{while q:} runs until the queue is empty. A deque also has \cd{remove}, \cd{reverse}, \cd{index},
\cd{count}, \cd{insert} and \cd{clear}.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
q = deque(x * x for x in range(4))
q                         # -> deque([0, 1, 4, 9])
bool(deque())             # -> False
q.remove(4); q.reverse()
q                         # -> deque([9, 1, 0])
q.index(1), q.count(9)    # -> (1, 1)
q.insert(1, 7)
q                         # -> deque([9, 7, 1, 0])
q.clear()
len(q)                    # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Process a breadth-first search one level at a time. Read the size of the level before the inner loop.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
children = {1: [2, 3], 2: [4], 3: [], 4: []}
q, levels = deque([1]), []
while q:
    level = []
    for _ in range(len(q)):           # only the nodes of this level
        u = q.popleft()
        level.append(u)
        q.extend(children[u])
    levels.append(level)
levels                    # -> [[1], [2, 3], [4]]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{defaultdict}
A \cd{defaultdict} calls a factory function to make a value for a missing key.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict
graph = defaultdict(list)
for u, v in [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)]:
    graph[u].append(v)
    graph[v].append(u)
graph[1]                  # -> [2, 3]
counts = defaultdict(int)
for ch in "abca":
    counts[ch] += 1
counts["a"], counts["z"]  # -> (2, 0)
dict(counts)              # -> {'a': 2, 'b': 1, 'c': 1, 'z': 0}
nested = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
nested["x"]["y"] += 5
nested["x"]["y"]          # -> 5
groups = defaultdict(set)
groups["k"].add(1)
groups["k"]               # -> {1}
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
When you read a missing key, the \cd{defaultdict} inserts it (see \cd{"z"} above).
To test for a key, use \cd{key in d}. Do not use \cd{d[key]}.
\end{caution}
\cd{d.get(key, default)} reads a \cd{defaultdict} without an insert. A loop over \cd{d[key]} inserts the key.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict
g = defaultdict(list)
g.get("x", [])            # -> []
"x" in g                  # -> False
for v in g["y"]:          # reading g["y"] inserts an empty list
    pass
"y" in g                  # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Counter}
A \cd{Counter} counts hashable objects. A missing key has the count 0. It does not insert the key.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
c = Counter("abracadabra")
c["a"], c["z"]            # -> (5, 0)
c.most_common(2)          # -> [('a', 5), ('b', 2)]
Counter([1, 1, 2])        # -> Counter({1: 2, 2: 1})
Counter({"x": 2, "y": 1}).total()   # -> 3
sorted(Counter("aab").elements())   # -> ['a', 'a', 'b']
c.update("aa")            # add counts
c["a"]                    # -> 7
c.subtract({"a": 6})      # subtract counts (can go negative)
c["a"]                    # -> 1
del c["a"]
"a" in c                  # -> False
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
a, b = Counter("aab"), Counter("abc")
a + b                     # -> Counter({'a': 3, 'b': 2, 'c': 1})
a - b                     # -> Counter({'a': 1})
a & b                     # -> Counter({'a': 1, 'b': 1})
a | b                     # -> Counter({'a': 2, 'b': 1, 'c': 1})
Counter("listen") == Counter("silent")    # -> True
Counter("ab") <= Counter("aabb")          # -> True
not (Counter("ab") - Counter("aabb"))     # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{a - b} keeps only positive counts. Use it to find what is missing.
  \item \cd{most_common()} without an argument gives all items from the highest count to the lowest.
  \item \cd{total()} \since{3.10} gives the sum of the counts. On old versions, use \cd{sum(c.values())}.
  \item Comparisons \cd{<=} and \cd{>=} between counters \since{3.10} check multiset inclusion.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
c = Counter("aab")
c["z"] -= 1                       # a missing key starts at 0
c["z"]                            # -> -1
+c                                # -> Counter({'a': 2, 'b': 1})
Counter(a=1, b=0) == Counter(a=1) # -> True
len(Counter("aab"))               # -> 2
sorted(Counter([3, 1, 3]))        # -> [1, 3]
Counter([(0, 0), (0, 0), (1, 2)])[(0, 0)]   # -> 2
max(Counter("aabbb").values())    # -> 3
Counter("aab").most_common()[-1]  # -> ('b', 1)
[k for k, v in Counter("abca").items() if v == 1]   # -> ['b', 'c']
c.get("q") is None, c.get("q", 0) # -> (True, 0)
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{c[k]} gives 0 for a missing key. \cd{c.get(k)} gives \cd{None}, like a plain dict. Write \cd{c.get(k, 0)}.
  \item \cd{+c} removes the keys with a count of 0 or less.
  \item Equality treats a count of 0 as a missing key \since{3.10}. On older versions, the two counters
        in the equality example above are not equal.
  \item \cd{len(c)} is the number of keys. A key stays in the counter when its count falls to 0.
\end{itemize}
\begin{caution}
In a sliding window, \cd{len(window)} counts the distinct values only if you delete each key whose count
reaches 0.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
window = Counter("ab")
window["a"] -= 1
len(window)                       # -> 2
if window["a"] == 0:
    del window["a"]
len(window)                       # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\subsection{OrderedDict}
A normal dict keeps insertion order. An \cd{OrderedDict} also has \cd{move_to_end} and
\cd{popitem(last=False)}. Use it for an LRU cache.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import OrderedDict
cache = OrderedDict()
for k in "abc":
    cache[k] = k.upper()
cache.move_to_end("a")            # "a" is now the most recent
cache.popitem(last=False)         # -> ('b', 'B')
list(cache)                       # -> ['c', 'a']
cache.move_to_end("a", last=False)
list(cache)                       # -> ['a', 'c']
\end{pyex}

\subsection{ChainMap}
A \cd{ChainMap} searches several dictionaries in order.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import ChainMap
defaults, user = {"color": "red", "size": 1}, {"size": 3}
cfg = ChainMap(user, defaults)
cfg["size"], cfg["color"]         # -> (3, 'red')
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{heapq: priority queues}

\subsection{Basic operations}
\cd{heapq} makes a min-heap on a normal list. \cd{h[0]} is always the smallest element.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
h[0]                      # -> 1
heapq.heappop(h)          # -> 1
heapq.heappop(h)          # -> 3
len(h)                    # -> 2
a = [9, 4, 7, 1]
heapq.heapify(a)          # O(n), in place
a[0]                      # -> 1
heapq.heappushpop(a, 0)   # -> 0
heapq.heapreplace(a, 10)  # -> 1
sorted(a)                 # -> [4, 7, 9, 10]
heapq.heappop([])         # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{heappush}, \cd{heappop}: $O(\log n)$. \cd{heapify}: $O(n)$. \cd{h[0]}: $O(1)$.
  \item \cd{heappushpop(h, x)}: push \cd{x}, then pop the smallest. Faster than two calls.
  \item \cd{heapreplace(h, x)}: pop the smallest, then push \cd{x}.
  \item The list is not sorted. Only \cd{h[0]} has a known position.
  \item \cd{heapify} changes the list in place. Copy the input first if the caller needs it.
  \item A list with zero or one element is already a valid heap. It needs no \cd{heapify}.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
nums = [5, 2, 8]
h = list(nums)            # copy, then heapify the copy
heapq.heapify(h)
nums, h[0]                # -> ([5, 2, 8], 2)
h = [(0, "src")]          # one element: already a heap
heapq.heappush(h, (3, "b"))
h[0][0]                   # -> 0
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Max-heap}
\cd{heapq} has only a min-heap. Push negative values to get a max-heap.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 8]:
    heapq.heappush(h, -x)
-h[0]                     # -> 8
-heapq.heappop(h)         # -> 8
counts = {"a": 3, "b": 1}
mh = [(-n, ch) for ch, n in counts.items()]   # max-heap by count
heapq.heapify(mh)
n, ch = heapq.heappop(mh)
(-n, ch)                  # -> (3, 'a')
n += 1                    # use one copy: -3 becomes -2
if n:
    heapq.heappush(mh, (n, ch))
mh[0]                     # -> (-2, 'a')
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Python 3.14 adds \cd{heapq.heappush_max}, \cd{heapq.heappop_max} and \cd{heapq.heapify_max}.
Most judges run an older version. Use negated keys.
\end{note}

\subsection{Priorities with tuples}
Push tuples \cd{(priority, value)}. Tuples compare by the first element, then the next one.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "read"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "test"))
[heapq.heappop(tasks) for _ in range(3)]   # -> [(1, 'read'), (2, 'test'), (2, 'write')]
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
If two priorities are equal, Python compares the next element. If that element cannot be compared
(for example a dict or a node object), you get \cd{TypeError}. Put a unique counter in the middle.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq, itertools
counter = itertools.count()
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, next(counter), {"id": "a"}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, next(counter), {"id": "b"}))
heapq.heappop(h)[2]       # -> {'id': 'a'}
bad = []
heapq.heappush(bad, (1, {"id": "a"}))
heapq.heappush(bad, (1, {"id": "b"}))   # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{k largest, k smallest and merge}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
nums = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]
heapq.nlargest(2, nums)                  # -> [9, 7]
heapq.nsmallest(2, nums)                 # -> [1, 3]
heapq.nlargest(1, ["aa", "b"], key=len)  # -> ['aa']
list(heapq.merge([1, 4], [2, 3], [0]))   # -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
list(heapq.merge([4, 1], [2]))           # -> [2, 4, 1]
k, h = 3, []
for x in nums:                           # keep the k largest in a min-heap
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
    if len(h) > k:
        heapq.heappop(h)
sorted(h)                                # -> [5, 7, 9]
h[0]                                     # -> 5
\end{pyex}
\cd{h[0]} of a size-$k$ min-heap is the $k$-th largest element.
\cd{heapq.merge} needs sorted inputs. It does not check them, so unsorted inputs give an unsorted result.

\subsection{Lazy deletion}
\cd{heapq} cannot change or remove an element inside the heap. Push a new entry instead.
When you pop an entry that is out of date, skip it. Dijkstra's algorithm uses this method.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
best = {"a": 5, "b": 4}
h = [(4, "b"), (5, "a")]
best["a"] = 2                         # a better value for "a": push a new entry
heapq.heappush(h, (2, "a"))
out = []
while h:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(h)
    if d != best[u]:
        continue                      # an old entry: skip it
    out.append((u, d))
out                                   # -> [('a', 2), ('b', 4)]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Heap of custom objects}
Define \cd{__lt__} so that the heap can compare the objects.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.val < other.val
h = [Node(3), Node(1)]
heapq.heapify(h)
h[0].val                  # -> 1
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{bisect: binary search on sorted lists}
\begin{pyex}
import bisect
a = [1, 3, 3, 3, 7]
bisect.bisect_left(a, 3)      # -> 1
bisect.bisect_right(a, 3)     # -> 4
bisect.bisect(a, 3)           # -> 4
bisect.bisect_left(a, 4)      # -> 4
bisect.bisect_left(a, 0)      # -> 0
bisect.bisect_left(a, 100)    # -> 5
bisect.bisect_right(a, 3) - bisect.bisect_left(a, 3)   # -> 3
bisect.insort(a, 5)
a                             # -> [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 7]
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{bisect_left(a, x)}: the first index \cd{i} with \cd{a[i] >= x}.
  \item \cd{bisect_right(a, x)}: the first index \cd{i} with \cd{a[i] > x}.
  \item The count of elements in \cd{[lo, hi]} is \cd{bisect_right(a, hi) - bisect_left(a, lo)}.
  \item \cd{insort} is $O(n)$ because the list must shift elements.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Floor and ceiling in a sorted list}
\begin{pyex}
import bisect
a = [10, 20, 30]
def floor(x):                 # largest element <= x
    i = bisect.bisect_right(a, x)
    return a[i - 1] if i else None
def ceiling(x):               # smallest element >= x
    i = bisect.bisect_left(a, x)
    return a[i] if i < len(a) else None
floor(25), ceiling(25), floor(5), ceiling(35)   # -> (20, 30, None, None)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{bisect with a key} \since{3.10}
\begin{pyex}
import bisect
events = [(1, "a"), (4, "b"), (9, "c")]
bisect.bisect_left(events, 4, key=lambda e: e[0])   # -> 1
i = bisect.bisect_right(events, 5, key=lambda e: e[0]) - 1   # last time <= 5
events[i][1] if i >= 0 else ""                      # -> 'b'
\end{pyex}
\cd{bisect_right(a, t) - 1} is the index of the last element with a time at or before \cd{t}.
The result \cd{-1} means that no such element exists.

\subsection{Search part of a list}
\cd{lo} and \cd{hi} limit the search to \cd{a[lo:hi]} without a slice copy. The result is an index in the full list.
For a list in descending order, search a negated copy, or use \cd{key=lambda x: -x} \since{3.10}.
\begin{pyex}
import bisect
a = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
i = 1
bisect.bisect_left(a, 7, lo=i + 1)        # -> 3
bisect.bisect_left(a, 7, 0, 2)            # -> 2
desc = [9, 7, 5]
bisect.bisect_left([-x for x in desc], -7)       # -> 1
bisect.bisect_left(desc, -7, key=lambda x: -x)   # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Binary search on the answer}
\cd{first_true} and \cd{last_true} search a half-open range \cd{[lo, hi)}. The search never calls \cd{ok(hi)}.
\begin{pyex}
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):   # first x in [lo, hi) with ok(x) True, or hi if no x passes
    while lo < hi:            # ok is False...False True...True on [lo, hi)
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def last_true(lo, hi, ok):    # last x in [lo, hi) with ok(x) True, or lo - 1
    return first_true(lo, hi, lambda x: not ok(x)) - 1   # ok is True...True False...False

first_true(0, 100, lambda x: x * x >= 50)   # -> 8
first_true(0, 100, lambda x: x > 500)       # -> 100
last_true(0, 100, lambda x: x * x <= 50)    # -> 7
last_true(0, 100, lambda x: x < 0)          # -> -1
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
The direct form of the last true search uses a closed range \cd{[lo, hi]} and needs \cd{ok(lo)} True.
It uses \cd{mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2} and \cd{lo = mid}.
If you round down there, the loop does not stop when \cd{hi = lo + 1}.
Do not mix this form with \cd{last_true} above: for the same arguments, the results are different by one.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def last_true_closed(lo, hi, ok):   # last x in [lo, hi] with ok(x) True; ok(lo) must be True
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2    # round up
        if ok(mid):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo
last_true_closed(0, 100, lambda x: x * x <= 50)   # -> 7
last_true_closed(0, 100, lambda x: True)          # -> 100
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Sorting}

\subsection{sort and sorted}
\cd{list.sort()} sorts in place. \cd{sorted()} accepts any iterable and returns a new list.
Both are stable and take $O(n \log n)$ time.
\begin{pyex}
sorted([3, 1, 2])                 # -> [1, 2, 3]
sorted("bca")                     # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
sorted({"b": 1, "a": 2})          # -> ['a', 'b']
sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True)   # -> [3, 2, 1]
intervals = [[5, 6], [1, 3], [2, 4]]
intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])   # in place, by start
intervals                         # -> [[1, 3], [2, 4], [5, 6]]
sorted([[2, 1], [1, 9], [1, 2]])  # -> [[1, 2], [1, 9], [2, 1]]
\end{pyex}
Lists and tuples sort element by element. Without a key, a list of intervals sorts by start, then by end.

Sort in reverse order, then use \cd{pop()} from the end. Each \cd{pop()} gives the next smallest element in $O(1)$.
\begin{pyex}
stack = sorted(["b", "c", "a"], reverse=True)
stack.pop(), stack.pop()          # -> ('a', 'b')
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Sort with a key}
The key function gets each element and returns the value to compare.
\begin{pyex}
words = ["banana", "Kiwi", "apple", "fig"]
sorted(words, key=len)                       # -> ['fig', 'Kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']
sorted(words, key=str.lower)                 # -> ['apple', 'banana', 'fig', 'Kiwi']
sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w))     # -> ['fig', 'Kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']
sorted(words, key=lambda w: (-len(w), w))    # -> ['banana', 'apple', 'Kiwi', 'fig']
\end{pyex}
Return a tuple to sort by more than one key. Negate a number to sort that key in descending order.

\subsection{Descending order for a string key}
You cannot negate a string. Use two stable sorts: first the secondary key, then the primary key.
\begin{pyex}
people = [("bo", 30), ("ana", 25), ("cy", 30)]
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[0], reverse=True)   # secondary: name descending
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])                 # primary: age ascending
people                    # -> [('ana', 25), ('cy', 30), ('bo', 30)]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{itemgetter and attrgetter}
\begin{pyex}
from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter
rows = [("b", 2), ("a", 2), ("c", 1)]
sorted(rows, key=itemgetter(1))        # -> [('c', 1), ('b', 2), ('a', 2)]
sorted(rows, key=itemgetter(1, 0))     # -> [('c', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 2)]
from collections import namedtuple
P = namedtuple("P", "name age")
min([P("x", 9), P("y", 3)], key=attrgetter("age"))   # -> P(name='y', age=3)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Argsort and ranks}
\begin{pyex}
x = [30, 10, 20]
order = sorted(range(len(x)), key=lambda i: x[i])
order                     # -> [1, 2, 0]
[x[i] for i in order]     # -> [10, 20, 30]
rank = [0] * len(x)
for r, i in enumerate(order):
    rank[i] = r
rank                      # -> [2, 0, 1]
\end{pyex}
\cd{order[k]} is the original index of the $k$-th smallest value. \cd{rank[i]} is the sorted position of \cd{x[i]}.
A bound method can be the key. \cd{x.__getitem__} is the same as \cd{lambda i: x[i]}, and it is faster.
\begin{pyex}
x = [30, 10, 20]
sorted(range(len(x)), key=x.__getitem__)   # -> [1, 2, 0]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Sort by a custom alphabet}
Map each character to its rank. The key of a word is the list of ranks of its characters.
\begin{pyex}
order = "hlabcdefgijkmnopqrstuvwxyz"
rank = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(order)}
words = ["hello", "leetcode"]
words == sorted(words, key=lambda w: [rank[c] for c in w])   # -> True
sorted(["ab", "ha", "l"], key=lambda w: [rank[c] for c in w])   # -> ['ha', 'l', 'ab']
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Custom comparison}
Use \cd{functools.cmp_to_key} when you cannot write a key. The function returns a negative number,
zero, or a positive number.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cmp_to_key
def cmp(a, b):            # order numbers to make the largest concatenation
    return -1 if a + b > b + a else (1 if a + b < b + a else 0)
"".join(sorted(["3", "30", "34", "5", "9"], key=cmp_to_key(cmp)))   # -> '9534330'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Sort pitfalls}
\begin{pyex}
sorted([3, None, 1])      # -> raises TypeError
sorted([3, None, 1], key=lambda v: (v is None, v or 0))   # -> [1, 3, None]
sorted(["10", "9", "100"])                # -> ['10', '100', '9']
sorted(["10", "9", "100"], key=int)       # -> ['9', '10', '100']
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Built-in iteration functions}
\begin{pyex}
list(map(int, ["1", "2"]))                 # -> [1, 2]
list(map(lambda a, b: a * b, [1, 2], [3, 4]))   # -> [3, 8]
list(filter(None, [0, 1, "", "a"]))        # -> [1, 'a']
list(filter(lambda x: x > 1, [1, 2, 3]))   # -> [2, 3]
sum([[1], [2, 3]], [])                     # -> [1, 2, 3]
sum([1, 2, 3], 10)                         # -> 16
all([]), any([])                           # -> (True, False)
list(zip(*[(1, "a"), (2, "b")]))           # -> [(1, 2), ('a', 'b')]
dict(enumerate("ab"))                      # -> {0: 'a', 1: 'b'}
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{zip(*pairs)} unzips a list of pairs. \cd{all([])} is \cd{True}. \cd{any([])} is \cd{False}.
The second argument of \cd{sum} is the start value. \cd{sum(lists, [])} copies the result for each list,
so it takes $O(n^2)$ time for many lists. Use \cd{list(chain.from_iterable(lists))} for many lists.
\end{note}

% =====================================================================
\section{The itertools module}

\subsection{Infinite iterators}
\cd{count}, \cd{cycle} and \cd{repeat} without a count never stop. Stop them with \cd{islice} or with \cd{break}.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import count, cycle, repeat, islice
list(islice(count(10, 5), 3))     # -> [10, 15, 20]
list(islice(cycle("ab"), 5))      # -> ['a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a']
list(repeat(0, 3))                # -> [0, 0, 0]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{accumulate}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import accumulate
import operator
list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4]))                # -> [1, 3, 6, 10]
list(accumulate([1, 2, 3], initial=0))        # -> [0, 1, 3, 6]
list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1], max))           # -> [3, 3, 4, 4]
list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4], operator.mul))  # -> [1, 2, 6, 24]
\end{pyex}
\cd{accumulate(a, initial=0)} \since{3.8} gives prefix sums where \cd{P[i]} is the sum of \cd{a[:i]}.

\subsection{Combinatorics}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import product, permutations, combinations, combinations_with_replacement
list(product("ab", [0, 1]))                # -> [('a', 0), ('a', 1), ('b', 0), ('b', 1)]
len(list(product(range(3), repeat=4)))     # -> 81
list(permutations([1, 2, 3], 2))           # -> [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 3), (3, 1), (3, 2)]
len(list(permutations(range(4))))          # -> 24
list(combinations("abc", 2))               # -> [('a', 'b'), ('a', 'c'), ('b', 'c')]
list(combinations_with_replacement("ab", 2))   # -> [('a', 'a'), ('a', 'b'), ('b', 'b')]
["".join(p) for p in product("01", repeat=2)]  # -> ['00', '01', '10', '11']
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
These functions return tuples. They treat elements by position, not by value. Duplicates in the input give
duplicate results.
\end{note}

\subsection{Group, chain, slice, pair}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import groupby, chain, islice, pairwise, zip_longest, batched
[(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby("aaabcc")]   # -> [('a', 3), ('b', 1), ('c', 2)]
[k for k, _ in groupby([1, 1, 2, 1])]               # -> [1, 2, 1]
list(chain([1, 2], "ab"))                 # -> [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
list(chain.from_iterable([[1], [2, 3]]))  # -> [1, 2, 3]
list(islice(range(10), 2, 8, 2))          # -> [2, 4, 6]
list(pairwise([1, 2, 4]))                 # -> [(1, 2), (2, 4)]
list(zip_longest("ab", "x", fillvalue="-"))   # -> [('a', 'x'), ('b', '-')]
list(batched(range(5), 2))                # -> [(0, 1), (2, 3), (4,)]
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{groupby} groups only consecutive equal elements. Sort the input first if you need one group for each key.
\cd{pairwise} needs \since{3.10}. \cd{batched} needs \since{3.12}.
\end{caution}
Use \cd{pairwise} with \cd{all} or \cd{any} to test adjacent elements. On old versions, use \cd{zip(a, a[1:])}.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import pairwise
a = [1, 2, 2, 5]
all(x <= y for x, y in pairwise(a))      # -> True
any(x == y for x, y in zip(a, a[1:]))    # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Filtering iterators}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import takewhile, dropwhile, filterfalse, compress, starmap
list(takewhile(lambda x: x < 3, [1, 2, 5, 1]))    # -> [1, 2]
list(dropwhile(lambda x: x < 3, [1, 2, 5, 1]))    # -> [5, 1]
list(filterfalse(lambda x: x % 2, range(5)))      # -> [0, 2, 4]
list(compress("abcd", [1, 0, 1, 0]))              # -> ['a', 'c']
list(starmap(pow, [(2, 3), (3, 2)]))              # -> [8, 9]
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{The functools and operator modules}

\subsection{functools}
\cd{reduce(f, items, start)} combines the items into one value, from left to right.
\cd{partial(f, ...)} makes a new function with some arguments fixed.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import reduce, partial, lru_cache, cache
reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, [1, 2, 3, 4], 1)   # -> 24
int2 = partial(int, base=2)
int2("101")                                    # -> 5
@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def slow_square(n):
    return n * n
slow_square(4); slow_square(4)                 # -> 16
slow_square.cache_info().hits                  # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import total_ordering
@total_ordering
class Version:
    def __init__(self, major, minor):
        self.key = (major, minor)
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.key == other.key
    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.key < other.key
Version(1, 2) >= Version(1, 0)                 # -> True
\end{pyex}
\cd{total_ordering} makes \cd{<=}, \cd{>} and \cd{>=} from \cd{__eq__} and \cd{__lt__}.

\subsection{operator}
\begin{pyex}
import operator
from functools import reduce
operator.add(2, 3), operator.mul(2, 3), operator.neg(4)   # -> (5, 6, -4)
reduce(operator.xor, [1, 2, 3])                # -> 0
reduce(operator.or_, [{1}, {2}, {1, 3}])       # -> {1, 2, 3}
operator.itemgetter(0, 2)("abc")               # -> ('a', 'c')
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{The math module}
\begin{pyex}
import math
math.sqrt(16), math.isqrt(17)          # -> (4.0, 4)
math.gcd(12, 18), math.lcm(4, 6)       # -> (6, 12)
math.gcd(12, 18, 30)                   # -> 6
math.factorial(5)                      # -> 120
math.comb(5, 2), math.perm(5, 2)       # -> (10, 20)
math.prod([2, 3, 4])                   # -> 24
math.floor(-1.5), math.ceil(-1.5)      # -> (-2, -1)
math.log2(1024), math.log10(1000)      # -> (10.0, 3.0)
math.log(math.e), math.log(8, 2)       # -> (1.0, 3.0)
math.hypot(3, 4)                       # -> 5.0
math.dist((0, 0), (3, 4))              # -> 5.0
math.inf > 10**300, -math.inf < 0      # -> (True, True)
math.isinf(math.inf), math.isnan(math.nan)   # -> (True, True)
round(math.pi, 4), round(math.e, 4)    # -> (3.1416, 2.7183)
math.isclose(1.0, 1.0 + 1e-12)         # -> True
math.fsum([0.1] * 10)                  # -> 1.0
total = 0.0
for x in [0.1] * 10:
    total += x
total                                  # -> 0.9999999999999999
round(math.degrees(math.atan2(1, 1)))  # -> 45
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{math.isqrt(n)} gives the exact integer square root. Use it, not \cd{int(math.sqrt(n))}, for big integers.
  \item \cd{math.lcm} needs \since{3.9}. A \cd{math.gcd} call with more than two arguments also needs \since{3.9}.
        \cd{math.comb}, \cd{math.perm}, \cd{math.prod}, \cd{math.isqrt} and \cd{math.dist} need \since{3.8}.
  \item \cd{math.fsum} adds floats with less rounding error. A plain loop with \cd{+=} collects the error.
        \cd{sum()} of floats also corrects the error \since{3.12}, but not on older versions.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
import math
n = 10**30 + 1
math.isqrt(n) ** 2 <= n                # -> True
int(math.sqrt(10**30 - 1))             # -> 1000000000000000
math.isqrt(10**30 - 1)                 # -> 999999999999999
math.log(1000, 10), math.log(243, 3)   # -> (2.9999999999999996, 4.999999999999999)
int(math.log(243, 3))                  # -> 4
def is_power(n, b):                    # exact test with integers only
    while n > 1 and n % b == 0:
        n //= b
    return n == 1
is_power(243, 3), is_power(244, 3)     # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{math.log(n, b)} is a float. It can be a little below the exact integer, so \cd{int()} of it can be 1 too small.
Do not use it to test for a power or to count digits. Use integer division, or compare with \cd{b ** k}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{statistics}
\begin{pyex}
import statistics
statistics.mean([1, 2, 3, 4])          # -> 2.5
statistics.median([3, 1, 2])           # -> 2
statistics.median([1, 2, 3, 4])        # -> 2.5
statistics.mode([1, 2, 2, 3])          # -> 2
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{The random module}
Use \cd{random} to make test data. Set a seed to get the same values each run.
\begin{pyex}
import random
random.seed(0)
a = random.randint(1, 6)       # 1 <= a <= 6 (both ends included)
1 <= a <= 6                    # -> True
b = random.randrange(10)       # 0 <= b < 10
c = random.choice("abc")
c in "abc"                     # -> True
deck = list(range(5))
random.shuffle(deck)           # in place
sorted(deck)                   # -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
len(random.sample(range(100), 3))   # -> 3
0 <= random.random() < 1       # -> True
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Classes and objects}

\subsection{Define a class}
\cd{__init__} sets up a new object. The first parameter of a method is the object itself (\cd{self}).
\begin{pyex}
class Account:
    bank = "PyBank"                 # class attribute: shared by all objects
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner          # instance attributes
        self.balance = balance
    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance
acc = Account("ana")
acc.deposit(50)                     # -> 50
acc.owner, acc.bank                 # -> ('ana', 'PyBank')
isinstance(acc, Account)            # -> True
hasattr(acc, "balance"), getattr(acc, "missing", None)   # -> (True, None)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
All objects share a mutable class attribute. Set lists and dicts in \cd{__init__}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class Bad:
    items = []
a, b = Bad(), Bad()
a.items.append(1)
b.items                             # -> [1]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{String representation}
\cd{__repr__} gives the text for debugging. \cd{__str__} gives the text for \cd{print} and \cd{str}.
\begin{pyex}
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"
    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"
p = Point(1, 2)
repr(p), str(p)                     # -> ('Point(1, 2)', '(1, 2)')
[p]                                 # -> [Point(1, 2)]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Equality, hashing and ordering}
By default, \cd{==} compares identity. Define \cd{__eq__} and \cd{__hash__} together to use objects
as dict keys by value. Define \cd{__lt__} to sort objects or to put them in a heap.
\begin{pyex}
class Cell:
    def __init__(self, r, c):
        self.r, self.c = r, c
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return (self.r, self.c) == (other.r, other.c)
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.r, self.c))
    def __lt__(self, other):
        return (self.r, self.c) < (other.r, other.c)
Cell(1, 2) == Cell(1, 2)            # -> True
len({Cell(1, 2), Cell(1, 2)})       # -> 1
[(c.r, c.c) for c in sorted([Cell(2, 0), Cell(1, 5)])]   # -> [(1, 5), (2, 0)]
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
If you define \cd{__eq__} but not \cd{__hash__}, the objects become unhashable.
\end{note}

\subsection{Dataclasses}
\cd{@dataclass} writes \cd{__init__}, \cd{__repr__} and \cd{__eq__} for you.
\begin{pyex}
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
@dataclass
class Item:
    name: str
    qty: int = 0
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)   # a new list for each object
it = Item("pen", 3)
it                                  # -> Item(name='pen', qty=3, tags=[])
it == Item("pen", 3)                # -> True
@dataclass(order=True, frozen=True)
class Task:
    priority: int
    name: str = field(compare=False)
sorted([Task(2, "b"), Task(1, "a")])[0].name   # -> 'a'
hash(Task(1, "a")) == hash(Task(1, "zzz"))      # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{order=True} adds \cd{<}, \cd{<=}, \cd{>}, \cd{>=}. It compares the fields in order.
  \item \cd{frozen=True} makes the objects immutable and hashable.
  \item \cd{field(compare=False)} removes a field from comparisons.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Inheritance and super}
\cd{class Dog(Animal)} makes a subclass. The subclass gets all methods of \cd{Animal}, and it can replace them.
\cd{super().__init__(...)} runs the \cd{__init__} of the base class.
\begin{pyex}
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def speak(self):
        return "..."
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.breed = breed
    def speak(self):
        return "woof"
d = Dog("rex", "lab")
d.name, d.speak(), isinstance(d, Animal)   # -> ('rex', 'woof', True)
issubclass(Dog, Animal)                    # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Properties, static methods and class methods}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{@property}: a method that you read like an attribute, without parentheses.
  \item \cd{@staticmethod}: a function in the class body. It gets no \cd{self}.
  \item \cd{@classmethod}: it gets the class as \cd{cls}. Use it for a second constructor.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r):
        self.r = r
    @property
    def diameter(self):             # read it like an attribute, without ()
        return 2 * self.r
    @staticmethod
    def unit():                     # no self, no cls
        return Circle(1)
    @classmethod
    def from_diameter(cls, d):      # cls is the class
        return cls(d / 2)
Circle(2).diameter                  # -> 4
Circle.unit().r                     # -> 1
Circle.from_diameter(10).r          # -> 5.0
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Special methods}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Method & Called by \\
\midrule
\cd{__len__} & \cd{len(x)} \\
\cd{__getitem__}, \cd{__setitem__} & \cd{x[k]}, \cd{x[k] = v} \\
\cd{__contains__} & \cd{v in x} \\
\cd{__iter__} & \cd{for v in x} \\
\cd{__call__} & \cd{x(...)} \\
\cd{__add__}, \cd{__mul__} & \cd{x + y}, \cd{x * y} \\
\cd{__eq__}, \cd{__lt__} & \cd{x == y}, \cd{x < y} \\
\cd{__hash__} & \cd{hash(x)}, set, dict key \\
\cd{__bool__} & \cd{if x:} \\
\cd{__repr__}, \cd{__str__} & \cd{repr(x)}, \cd{str(x)}, \cd{print(x)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
class Vec:
    def __init__(self, *xs):
        self.xs = list(xs)
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.xs)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.xs[i]
    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vec(*[a + b for a, b in zip(self.xs, other.xs)])
    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.xs)
v = Vec(1, 2) + Vec(3, 4)
len(v), v[1], list(v), 4 in v       # -> (2, 6, [4, 6], True)
\end{pyex}
Python uses \cd{__bool__} to decide if an object is true. If the class has no \cd{__bool__}, Python uses
\cd{__len__}. An object with neither method is always true.
\begin{pyex}
class Bag:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)
b = Bag()
bool(b)                             # -> False
b.items.append(1)
bool(b)                             # -> True
class Plain:
    pass
bool(Plain())                       # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{\texttt{\_\_slots\_\_}}
\cd{__slots__} saves memory and makes attribute access faster. The object cannot get new attributes.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    __slots__ = ("val", "next")
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
n = Node(1)
n.other = 5                         # -> raises AttributeError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{LeetCode node classes}\label{sec:leetcode-classes}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
def build_list(values):             # helper to test locally
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next             # save the rest of the list
        head.next = prev            # point this node backwards
        prev, head = head, nxt      # move both pointers one step
    return prev
to_list(reverse(build_list([1, 2, 3])))   # -> [3, 2, 1]
def reverse_short(head):            # the same loop in one line
    prev = None
    while head:
        head.next, prev, head = prev, head, head.next
    return prev
to_list(reverse_short(build_list([4, 5])))   # -> [5, 4]
root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2), TreeNode(3, TreeNode(4)))
def height(t):
    return 0 if t is None else 1 + max(height(t.left), height(t.right))
height(root)                        # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
In a multiple assignment, Python evaluates the full right side first, then assigns from left to right.
In the one-line form \cd{head.next, prev, head = prev, head, head.next}, the order of the targets is important.
If \cd{head} changes before \cd{head.next}, the code writes to the wrong node. The form with \cd{nxt} is easier to get right.
\end{caution}
A graph problem gives a node with a list of neighbors. The class uses \cd{None} as the default, not \cd{[]},
because a mutable default is shared by all calls. To copy a graph, map each original node to its copy in a
dict. Objects without \cd{__eq__} are dict keys by identity.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:                            # LeetCode graph node
    def __init__(self, val=0, neighbors=None):
        self.val = val
        self.neighbors = neighbors if neighbors is not None else []
def clone(node):
    copies = {}                        # original node: its copy
    def dfs(n):
        if n in copies:
            return copies[n]
        copies[n] = Node(n.val)        # store the copy before the recursion
        copies[n].neighbors = [dfs(m) for m in n.neighbors]
        return copies[n]
    return dfs(node) if node else None
a, b = Node(1), Node(2)
a.neighbors, b.neighbors = [b], [a]
c = clone(a)
c.val, c.neighbors[0].val, c is not a  # -> (1, 2, True)
c.neighbors[0].neighbors[0] is c       # -> True
clone(None) is None                    # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Design-problem classes}
A design problem gives a class with \cd{__init__} and several methods. Keep the state in instance attributes.
The judge makes one object and calls its methods in order. The judge input is two lists: the method names
and the argument lists. A short helper replays this input locally. \cd{getattr(obj, name)} gets a method by its name.
\begin{pyex}
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []                 # pairs (value, minimum so far)
    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        low = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val
        self.stack.append((val, low))
    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stack.pop()
    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][0]
    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][1]

def replay(cls, ops, args):             # run the judge input format
    obj, out = None, []
    for op, a in zip(ops, args):
        if op == cls.__name__:
            obj = cls(*a)
            out.append(None)
        else:
            out.append(getattr(obj, op)(*a))
    return out

replay(MinStack, ["MinStack", "push", "push", "getMin", "pop", "top", "getMin"],
       [[], [3], [1], [], [], [], []])  # -> [None, None, None, 1, None, 3, 3]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{A doubly linked list with sentinels}
Two sentinel nodes (\cd{head} and \cd{tail}) remove the special cases at the ends. Every real node always has
a \cd{prev} and a \cd{next}. A dict from key to node gives $O(1)$ access to any node. An LRU cache uses this design.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "prev", "next")
    def __init__(self, key=None):
        self.key, self.prev, self.next = key, None, None

class Recent:                          # the most recent key is at the front
    def __init__(self):
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head
        self.nodes = {}
    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev
    def _add_front(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node
    def touch(self, key):
        if key in self.nodes:
            self._remove(self.nodes[key])
        else:
            self.nodes[key] = Node(key)
        self._add_front(self.nodes[key])
    def keys(self):
        out, cur = [], self.head.next
        while cur is not self.tail:
            out.append(cur.key)
            cur = cur.next
        return out

r = Recent()
for k in "abca":
    r.touch(k)
r.keys()                               # -> ['a', 'c', 'b']
r.tail.prev.key                        # -> 'b'
\end{pyex}
The least recent key is \cd{tail.prev}. To evict it, call \cd{_remove(tail.prev)} and delete its key from the dict.

\subsection{Enum}
An \cd{Enum} gives names to a fixed set of constant values. Each member has a \cd{name} and a \cd{value}.
\begin{pyex}
from enum import Enum
class Dir(Enum):
    UP = (-1, 0)
    DOWN = (1, 0)
Dir.UP.value, Dir.UP.name           # -> ((-1, 0), 'UP')
Dir((1, 0))                         # -> <Dir.DOWN: (1, 0)>
Dir((1, 0)) is Dir.DOWN, Dir["UP"] is Dir.UP   # -> (True, True)
[d.name for d in Dir]               # -> ['UP', 'DOWN']
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Exceptions}

\subsection{try, except, else, finally}
Python runs the first \cd{except} clause that matches the exception type. A tuple of types catches any of them.
The \cd{else} block runs only when the \cd{try} block raises nothing. The \cd{finally} block always runs.
\begin{pyex}
def parse(s):
    try:
        value = int(s)
    except ValueError:
        return "bad"
    except (TypeError, OverflowError) as e:
        return type(e).__name__
    else:
        return value * 2            # runs only if no exception
    finally:
        pass                        # always runs (close files, release locks)
parse("21"), parse("x"), parse(None)   # -> (42, 'bad', 'TypeError')
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Raise an exception}
\begin{pyex}
def sqrt_int(n):
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"negative input: {n}")
    return int(n ** 0.5)
sqrt_int(-1)                        # -> raises ValueError
try:
    sqrt_int(-4)
except ValueError as e:
    msg = str(e)
msg                                 # -> 'negative input: -4'
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Common exceptions}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lL{11cm}@{}}
\toprule
Exception & Typical cause \\
\midrule
\cd{IndexError} & list or string index out of range; \cd{pop()} from an empty list \\
\cd{KeyError} & missing dict key; \cd{set.remove} of a missing element \\
\cd{ValueError} & right type, wrong value: \cd{int("x")}, \cd{list.index} of a missing value, unpack count \\
\cd{TypeError} & wrong type: \cd{"a" + 1}, unhashable key, compare \cd{None < 1}, wrong argument count \\
\cd{AttributeError} & missing attribute, often a method call on \cd{None} \\
\cd{NameError} & name not defined (spelling, scope) \\
\cd{UnboundLocalError} & local name used before assignment (missing \cd{nonlocal}) \\
\cd{ZeroDivisionError} & \cd{x / 0}, \cd{x // 0}, \texttt{x \% 0} \\
\cd{RecursionError} & recursion deeper than the limit \\
\cd{StopIteration} & \cd{next()} on an empty iterator \\
\cd{RuntimeError} & dict or set changed size during iteration \\
\cd{OverflowError} & float result too large, for example \cd{math.exp(1000)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
[][0]                 # -> raises IndexError
{}["k"]               # -> raises KeyError
int("3.5")            # -> raises ValueError
None + 1              # -> raises TypeError
None.append(1)        # -> raises AttributeError
undefined_name        # -> raises NameError
1 % 0                 # -> raises ZeroDivisionError
import math
math.exp(1000)        # -> raises OverflowError
\end{pyex}

\subsection{EAFP and LBYL}
Python code often tries an operation and handles the exception (EAFP: easier to ask forgiveness than permission).
The other style checks first (LBYL: look before you leap). Both are correct.
\begin{pyex}
d = {"a": 1}
try:
    v = d["b"]
except KeyError:
    v = 0
v                     # -> 0
v = d["b"] if "b" in d else 0
v                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Context managers}
A \cd{with} block sets up a resource and always cleans it up, also after an exception.
\begin{pyex}
from contextlib import suppress, contextmanager
with suppress(KeyError):          # ignore one exception type
    {}["missing"]
log = []
@contextmanager
def section(name):
    log.append(f"start {name}")
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        log.append(f"end {name}")
with section("bfs") as s:
    log.append(f"inside {s}")
log                               # -> ['start bfs', 'inside bfs', 'end bfs']
\end{pyex}

\subsection{assert}
Use \cd{assert} to check your own assumptions while you test. \cd{python -O} removes all \cd{assert} statements,
so do not use \cd{assert} to check input in real code.
\begin{pyex}
def mean(xs):
    assert xs, "empty input"
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)
mean([1, 2])          # -> 1.5
mean([])              # -> raises AssertionError
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Recursion}\label{sec:recursion}

\subsection{The recursion limit}
The default limit is 1000 frames. A depth-first search on a large grid or a long linked list
goes deeper than this.
\begin{pyex}
def depth(n):
    return 0 if n == 0 else 1 + depth(n - 1)
depth(500)            # -> 500
depth(5000)           # -> raises RecursionError
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)
depth(5000)           # -> 5000
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
A higher limit is not always enough, because deep recursion can also use the C stack.
\begin{itemize}
  \item On Python 3.10 and older, a depth of a few times $10^4$ can crash the interpreter with no error message.
  \item A function with \cd{@cache} or \cd{@lru_cache} runs C code at each level. On 3.11, it can crash at a
        similar depth. On 3.12 and 3.13, it raises \cd{RecursionError} at a depth of about 3000, also after
        \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit}.
\end{itemize}
Find the largest possible depth. With \cd{@cache}, the safe depth is about 3000. Without it, the safe depth is
about $10^4$. Above that, use a loop with an explicit stack or a bottom-up table.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Convert recursion to a loop}
\begin{pyex}
def dfs_recursive(graph, u, seen):
    seen.add(u)
    for v in graph[u]:
        if v not in seen:
            dfs_recursive(graph, v, seen)
def dfs_iterative(graph, start):
    seen = {start}
    stack = [start]
    while stack:
        u = stack.pop()
        for v in graph[u]:
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)       # mark when you push
                stack.append(v)
    return seen
g = {0: [1, 2], 1: [3], 2: [], 3: []}
s = set(); dfs_recursive(g, 0, s)
s == dfs_iterative(g, 0)          # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Memoized recursion}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
@cache
def paths(r, c):                  # number of grid paths to (r, c)
    if r == 0 or c == 0:
        return 1
    return paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1)
paths(16, 16)                     # -> 601080390
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Define a memoized helper inside the main function when the main function gets new input each call.
Then the cache starts empty for each input. A global \cd{@cache} keeps old results.
\end{note}
\begin{caution}
Do not put \cd{@cache} on a method of \cd{Solution}. The cache key then includes \cd{self}, and the cache keeps every
\cd{Solution} object alive. Put \cd{@cache} on a nested helper (Section~\ref{sec:nested-helpers}).
\end{caution}

\subsection{Return several values from a recursive call}
Return a tuple when the parent needs more than one value from a child. This avoids global state and
\cd{nonlocal} names.
\begin{pyex}
def check(t):                         # t is (left, right) or None
    if t is None:
        return True, 0                # (balanced, height)
    lb, lh = check(t[0])
    rb, rh = check(t[1])
    return lb and rb and abs(lh - rh) <= 1, 1 + max(lh, rh)
check(((None, None), None))           # -> (True, 2)
check((((None, None), None), None))   # -> (False, 3)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Run deep recursion in a thread}
On some judges, a deep recursion crashes also after \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit}, because the C stack is too small.
Run the solution in a new thread with a larger stack. Use this only when you cannot write a loop.
On Python 3.12 and 3.13, a larger stack does not raise the depth limit of a \cd{@cache} function.
\begin{pyshow}
import sys, threading
def main():
    ...                              # the recursive solution
sys.setrecursionlimit(1 << 25)
threading.stack_size(1 << 27)        # 128 MB for threads made after this call
t = threading.Thread(target=main)
t.start()
t.join()
\end{pyshow}

% =====================================================================
\section{Input and output}

\subsection{print}
\begin{pyex}
print(1, 2, 3)                   # prints: 1 2 3
