print(1, 2, sep="-")             # prints: 1-2
print("a", end="")               # prints: a
print(*["x", "y"])               # prints: x y
print("\n".join(["l1", "l2"]))   # prints: l1 | l2
print(f"{2/3:.3f}")              # prints: 0.667
print([1, 2], (3,), {"k": 1})    # prints: [1, 2] (3,) {'k': 1}
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Read standard input}
Some assessments give the input on standard input. These patterns read it.
The examples use \cd{io.StringIO} to act as the input.
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("3\n1 2 3\nhello\n")
n = int(input())                          # one integer
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))    # integers on one line
word = input().strip()
(n, nums, word)                           # -> (3, [1, 2, 3], 'hello')
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("2 3\n1 2 3\n4 5 6\n")
data = sys.stdin.read().split()           # all tokens at one time (fast)
r, c = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
grid = [list(map(int, data[2 + i * c: 2 + (i + 1) * c])) for i in range(r)]
grid                                      # -> [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("a b\nc\n")
lines = [line.rstrip("\n") for line in sys.stdin]   # read until end of input
lines                                     # -> ['a b', 'c']
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{input()} is slow for $10^5$ or more lines. Use \cd{sys.stdin.readline} or read all input at one time
with \cd{sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()}. \cd{input()} removes the newline. \cd{readline()} keeps it.
\end{note}
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("2\n5 1\n7 3\n")
input = sys.stdin.readline                # a common speed trick
n = int(input())                          # int() ignores the newline
pairs = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]
pairs                                     # -> [(5, 1), (7, 3)]
sys.stdin.readline()                      # -> ''
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__
\end{pyex}
At the end of the input, \cd{readline()} returns \cd{""} and \cd{input()} raises \cd{EOFError}.
Use this to read when the input does not give the number of lines.
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("4\n9\n")
total = 0
while True:
    try:
        total += int(input())
    except EOFError:                      # no more lines
        break
total                                     # -> 13
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Fast output}
\begin{pyex}
import sys, io
buf = io.StringIO()
results = [3, 1, 4]
buf.write("\n".join(map(str, results)) + "\n")   # one write instead of many prints
buf.getvalue()                            # -> '3\n1\n4\n'
\end{pyex}
For many lines, build one string and call \cd{sys.stdout.write} one time.
\begin{pyex}
import sys
sys.stdout.write("1 2\n")                 # prints: 1 2
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(map(str, [3, 1, 4])) + "\n")   # prints: 3 | 1 | 4
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Debug output}
Write debug text to standard error. The judge reads only standard output, so the debug text does not change the answer.
Remove debug output before you submit, because it costs time.
\begin{pyex}
import io, sys
sys.stderr = io.StringIO()                # stands in for the real standard error here
print("debug: n =", 5, file=sys.stderr)   # not part of the answer
print(42)                                 # prints: 42
sys.stderr.getvalue()                     # -> 'debug: n = 5\n'
sys.stderr = sys.__stderr__
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Files}
\begin{pyex}
import os, tempfile
path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "demo.txt")
with open(path, "w") as f:                # the file closes at the end of the block
    f.write("line1\nline2\n")
with open(path) as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()
lines                                     # -> ['line1', 'line2']
os.remove(path)
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Performance}

\subsection{Time budget}\label{sec:time-budget}
CPython does about $10^7$ simple operations per second. Most judges give 1 to 4 seconds per test.
Use the input size to choose the algorithm before you write code.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Largest $n$ & Algorithm that fits in Python \\
\midrule
$\le 10$ & $O(n!)$ \\
$\le 20$ & $O(2^n)$, $O(n \cdot 2^n)$ \\
$\le 200$ & $O(n^3)$; up to about 500 if the loops cover only $i < k < j$ \\
$\le 5000$ & $O(n^2)$ \\
$\le 10^5$ & $O(n \log n)$ \\
$\le 10^6$ & $O(n)$; $O(n \log n)$ only with the built-in sort \\
$\le 10^9$ & $O(\sqrt n)$, $O(\log n)$ or a formula \\
$\le 10^{18}$ & $O(\log n)$ or a formula \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Cost of common operations}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lL{6.2cm}L{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Type & Fast: $O(1)$ (average) & Slow: $O(n)$ or more \\
\midrule
\cd{list} & \cd{a[i]}, \cd{a[i] = x}, \cd{append}, \cd{pop()}, \cd{len} & \cd{x in a}, \cd{insert(0, x)}, \cd{pop(0)}, \cd{remove}, \cd{index}, slice, \cd{a + b}, \cd{min}, \cd{max}, \cd{sum} \\
\cd{dict} & get, set, delete, \cd{k in d}, \cd{len} & iterate, copy \\
\cd{set} & \cd{add}, \cd{discard}, \cd{x in s} & iterate, copy; \cd{a & b} is $O(\min(|a|,|b|))$ \\
\cd{deque} & \cd{append}, \cd{appendleft}, \cd{pop}, \cd{popleft} & \cd{q[i]} in the middle \\
\cd{heapq} & \cd{h[0]} & \cd{heappush}, \cd{heappop}: $O(\log n)$; \cd{heapify}: $O(n)$ \\
\cd{str} & \cd{s[i]}, \cd{len} & slice, \cd{+}, \cd{in}, \cd{find}, \cd{replace}, \cd{join} \\
\cd{sorted} & -- & $O(n \log n)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Speed rules}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Convert a list to a \cd{set} before many membership tests.
  \item Use a list with integer indexes, not a dict, when the keys are \cd{0..n-1}.
  \item Use built-in functions (\cd{sum}, \cd{max}, \cd{sorted}, \cd{str.join}, \cd{Counter}, slicing). They run in C.
  \item Move work out of inner loops. Store \cd{grid[r]} in a local name before the inner loop.
  \item Keep a running total. Do not call \cd{sum(path)} in each recursive call.
  \item Do not call \cd{copy.deepcopy} in a loop. Copy only what changes.
  \item Do not \cd{print} inside a hot loop.
  \item Use a big integer as a bitset: \cd{bits |= bits} \shl{} \cd{x} finds subset sums fast.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
nums = [3, 5, 7]
bits = 1                          # bit s is set when sum s is possible
for x in nums:
    bits |= bits << x
[s for s in range(16) if bits >> s & 1]   # -> [0, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15]
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Make a hot loop faster}
These changes do not change the complexity. They make a tight inner loop faster by a constant factor.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Store a row in a local name: \cd{row = grid[r]}, then read \cd{row[c]}.
  \item Compute values that do not change in the inner loop before the loop.
  \item Use \cd{if v > best: best = v} in place of \cd{best = max(best, v)}. A function call costs more than a comparison.
  \item Store a bound method in a local name, for example \cd{push = res.append}.
  \item Use a bound method as a sort key (\cd{key=x.__getitem__}) in place of a lambda.
  \item Pass index bounds (\cd{lo}, \cd{hi}) to a recursive call. Do not pass slices: each slice copies its elements.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
best = float("-inf")
for row in grid:                  # one lookup for each row
    for v in row:
        if v > best:              # compare and assign
            best = v
best                              # -> 6
vals, total = [2, 3, 4], 0
for l in range(3):
    left = vals[l]                # computed one time for each l
    for r in range(l + 1, 3):
        total += left * vals[r]
total                             # -> 26
res = []
push = res.append                 # a bound method in a local name
for i in range(3):
    push(i)
res                               # -> [0, 1, 2]
def total_slices(a):              # O(n^2): each call copies a[1:]
    return 0 if not a else a[0] + total_slices(a[1:])
def total_bounds(a, lo=0):        # O(n): the call passes an index
    return 0 if lo == len(a) else a[lo] + total_bounds(a, lo + 1)
total_slices([1, 2, 3]), total_bounds([1, 2, 3])   # -> (6, 6)
\end{pyex}

\subsection{Measure time}
\begin{pyex}
import time, timeit
start = time.perf_counter()
total = sum(range(10**5))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
elapsed < 5                       # -> True
t = timeit.timeit("x in s", setup="s = set(range(1000)); x = 999", number=1000)
t < 5                             # -> True
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{Common mistakes}
Each item gives the mistake and the correct form. The sections above have more information.

\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{5.2cm}L{5.4cm}L{5.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Mistake & Wrong & Correct \\
\midrule
\endhead
2D list shares rows & \cd{[[0] * c] * r} & \cd{[[0] * c for _ in range(r)]} \\
Mutable default argument & \cd{def f(a=[])} & \cd{def f(a=None)} \\
Store a reference, not a copy & \cd{res.append(path)} & \cd{res.append(path[:])} \\
Sort result is None & \cd{a = a.sort()} & \cd{a.sort()} or \cd{a = sorted(a)} \\
Empty set & \cd{s = {}} & \cd{s = set()} \\
One-element tuple & \cd{(5)} & \cd{(5,)} \\
Integer division & \cd{7 / 2} gives \cd{3.5} & \cd{7 // 2} \\
Truncate toward zero & \cd{-7 // 2} gives \cd{-4} & \cd{int(-7 / 2)} \\
Round half up & \cd{round(2.5)} gives \cd{2} & \cd{math.floor(x + 0.5)} \\
Float equality & \cd{a == b} & \cd{math.isclose(a, b)} \\
Test for missing value & \cd{if not x:} & \cd{if x is None:} \\
Compare with None & \cd{x == None} & \cd{x is None} \\
Membership in a list in a loop & \cd{x in lst} & \cd{x in set_of_lst} \\
Queue with a list & \cd{q.pop(0)} & \cd{deque.popleft()} \\
String building & \cd{s += c} in a loop & \cd{"".join(parts)} \\
Read a defaultdict key & \cd{if d[k]:} & \cd{if k in d:} \\
Change dict while iterating & \cd{for k in d: del d[k]} & \cd{for k in list(d):} \\
Rebind enclosing name & \cd{count += 1} & \cd{nonlocal count} first \\
Lambda in a loop & \cd{lambda: i} & \cd{lambda i=i: i} \\
Strip a substring & \cd{s.strip("abc")} & \cd{s.removesuffix("abc")} \\
Split on spaces & \cd{s.split(" ")} & \cd{s.split()} \\
Iterator used two times & \cd{list(z); list(z)} & \cd{z = list(zip(...))} \\
Deep recursion & recursive DFS on a big grid & explicit stack \\
Heap ties with objects & \cd{(p, node)} & \cd{(p, counter, node)} \\
Max of an empty list & \cd{max([])} & \cd{max(a, default=0)} \\
Shadow a built-in & \cd{sum = 0}, \cd{list = []} & \cd{total = 0}, \cd{items = []} \\
Bitwise vs comparison & \cd{x & 1 == 0} works, but & \cd{(x & 1) == 0} is clearer \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

\begin{pyex}
sum = 0                    # shadows the built-in sum
sum([1, 2])                # -> raises TypeError
del sum
sum([1, 2])                # -> 3
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================

\part{Solving unseen problems}\label{part:method}

% =====================================================================
% Part II: how to find a solution to a problem you have never seen
% =====================================================================
\section{A method for unseen problems}\label{m1:method}
A new problem is usually an old technique behind new words. The method in this section finds that
technique by reasoning, not by memory. It starts from a slow solution that is surely correct.
Then it finds the waste in that solution and removes it.
Each step has one question. Write a short answer to the question before you go to the next step.

\begin{center}
\setlength{\extrarowheight}{1.5pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4.0cm}L{5.8cm}L{6.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Step & Question to ask & A good answer \\
\midrule
\endhead
1. Restate the task and the exact output & What goes in, what comes out, and what exactly does the output count or choose? &
  One sentence in your own words, the type of the output, and a decision for each word with two meanings. \\
2. Work small examples by hand & What is the answer on three to six elements, and what did my hand do? &
  Three or more input and output pairs, with edge cases. A note on the work that the hand repeats. \\
3. Read the constraints and set a time budget & Which complexity fits the largest input? What do the constraints give for free? &
  A target such as $O(n \log n)$ with the arithmetic behind it, and a list of useful facts (sorted, small values, negative values). \\
4. Write the brute force & What is the most direct correct solution? &
  Short code that follows the definition: try every candidate and test it. \\
5. Find the repeated or wasted work & What does the inner loop compute again and again? What does it search for? &
  One sentence: ``for each X, the inner loop searches Y for Z''. Then the kind of Z: an exact key, an extreme, a boundary, a repeated subproblem. \\
6. Choose the move that removes it & Which optimization move removes exactly that waste? &
  The name of a move from Section~\ref{m1:moves}, and one reason why each other likely move fails. \\
7. State the invariant or the state definition & What does each variable hold at the top of each iteration? What does \cd{dp[i]} mean? &
  One sentence for each variable, with a start value that makes the sentence true before the first iteration. \\
8. Code from the invariant & Which lines keep each sentence of step 7 true? &
  Code where each line maps to one part of the invariant. The order of the lines follows from it. \\
9. Test against the brute force & Do the fast and the slow solutions agree on many small inputs? &
  A seeded random test with small sizes and small values, and zero mismatches. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

\textbf{Short form to remember:} restate, examples, budget, brute force, waste, move, invariant, code, test.

\begin{note}
Steps 1 to 3 take a few minutes, and they prevent most wrong turns. Steps 4 to 7 are where the idea appears.
Do not skip step 4. The brute force is the reference for step 9. It is also a correct answer when no
faster idea comes. A correct slow solution is worth more than a fast wrong one.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The running example}\label{m1:example}
The steps below use one problem: Subarray Sums Divisible by K (LeetCode 974).

\textbf{Statement.} You get an integer list \cd{nums} and an integer \cd{k}. Return the number of
non-empty subarrays whose sum is divisible by \cd{k}.
Constraints: $1 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$, $-10^4 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^4$, $2 \le k \le 10^4$.
Example: \cd{nums = [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1]} and \cd{k = 5} give 7.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 1: Restate the task and the exact output}
\textbf{Ask.} What is the input? What is the output? Which objects does the output count or choose?

\textbf{A good answer.} Write one sentence in your own words. Write the type of the output: a count,
an index, a list, a boolean or a string. Write what to return when no answer exists.
Then decide each word that has two meanings:
\begin{itemize}
  \item contiguous (subarray, substring) or not (subsequence, subset);
  \item order matters (sequence, permutation) or not (combination, set);
  \item strict (``greater'') or not strict (``at least'');
  \item distinct values or distinct positions;
  \item empty answer permitted or not;
  \item ends that touch: do \cd{[1, 2]} and \cd{[2, 3]} overlap or not;
  \item indexes that start at 0 or at 1, in the input and in the output.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example.} ``Count the pairs $(i, j)$ with $i \le j$ such that $\mathit{nums}[i] + \dots + \mathit{nums}[j]$ is a
multiple of $k$. Return an int.'' Decisions: a subarray is contiguous and non-empty.
The count is over positions, so two equal subarrays at different places count two times.
A zero sum and a negative sum such as $-5$ are multiples of 5.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 2: Work small examples by hand}
\textbf{Ask.} What is the answer on three to six elements? Which operations did my hand do?

\textbf{A good answer.} Three or more input and output pairs that you computed yourself.
Include the edge cases: one element, all equal values, negative values, no answer.
These pairs become your first tests. Also write down the work that your hand repeats.
That work is often the key to the fast solution.

\textbf{Example.} For \cd{[4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1]} and $k = 5$, the good subarrays are
\cd{[5]}, \cd{[5, 0]}, \cd{[0]}, \cd{[5, 0, -2, -3]}, \cd{[0, -2, -3]}, \cd{[-2, -3]} and the whole list: 7.
To get each sum, the hand reuses a running total. The sum of $\mathit{nums}[i..j]$ is the running total after $j$
minus the running total before $i$. Edge cases: \cd{[5]} with $k = 9$ gives 0.
\cd{[-5]} with $k = 5$ gives 1. \cd{[0, 0]} with $k = 3$ gives 3.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 3: Read the constraints and set a time budget}
\textbf{Ask.} Which complexity fits the largest input? What else do the constraints allow or forbid?

\textbf{A good answer.} A target complexity, with the arithmetic that supports it.
A list of facts that the constraints give for free: sorted input, small values, a small $k$, negative values.
Section~\ref{m1:constraints} has the full tables.

\textbf{Example.} $n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$, so there are about $n^2/2 = 4.5 \cdot 10^8$ subarrays.
CPython does about $10^7$ simple steps per second, so $O(n^2)$ needs about 45 seconds.
The target is $O(n)$ or $O(n \log n)$. The values can be negative.
Thus a running sum can go down, and a sliding window on sums does not work.
Also $k \le 10^4$, so a list of size $k$ is cheap.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 4: Write the brute force}
\textbf{Ask.} What is the most direct correct solution, with no attention to speed?

\textbf{A good answer.} Code that follows the definition: try every candidate and test it.
Keep it simple, because it is the reference for step 9. Remove only the obvious waste,
such as a sum that you compute again from zero for each subarray.

\textbf{Example.} Try every left end. Extend the right end and keep a running sum.
This is $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space: correct, and too slow for the limits.
\begin{pyex}
def count_div_brute(nums, k):
    n, count = len(nums), 0
    for i in range(n):                   # left end
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, n):            # right end: extend the running sum
            total += nums[j]
            if total % k == 0:
                count += 1
    return count

count_div_brute([4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5)   # -> 7
count_div_brute([5], 9)                    # -> 0
count_div_brute([-5], 5)                   # -> 1
count_div_brute([0, 0], 3)                 # -> 3
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 5: Find the repeated or wasted work}
\textbf{Ask.} What does the inner loop compute again and again? What does it search for?

\textbf{A good answer.} One sentence of the form ``for each X, the inner loop searches Y for Z''.
Then classify Z, because the kind of Z selects the move:
\begin{itemize}
  \item an exact key or value: remember what you saw (hashing);
  \item an extreme of a range (a minimum or maximum): keep a running best or precompute it;
  \item a boundary in ordered data: binary search, two pointers or a monotonic stack;
  \item a subproblem that the recursion solves many times: memoization or DP.
\end{itemize}
The table at the start of Section~\ref{m1:moves} lists all twelve kinds of waste and the move for each one.

\textbf{Example.} Let $P[i]$ be the sum of the first $i$ elements, with $P[0] = 0$.
Then the sum of $\mathit{nums}[i..j]$ is $P[j+1] - P[i]$. This difference is a multiple of $k$ exactly when
$P[i]$ and $P[j+1]$ have the same remainder modulo $k$.
So for each right end, the inner loop searches the earlier prefixes for one exact key:
the remainder of the current prefix.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
from itertools import accumulate
from math import comb

nums, k = [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5
P = [0] + list(accumulate(nums))         # P[i] = sum of the first i elements
P                                        # -> [0, 4, 9, 9, 7, 4, 5]
rem = [p % k for p in P]
rem                                      # -> [0, 4, 4, 4, 2, 4, 0]
P[5] - P[1], rem[5] == rem[1]            # -> (0, True)
sum(comb(c, 2) for c in Counter(rem).values())   # -> 7
\end{pyex}
Each pair of equal remainders is one good subarray. The remainder 0 occurs 2 times (1 pair),
and the remainder 4 occurs 4 times (6 pairs). The total is 7, as in the hand count of step 2.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 6: Choose the move that removes it}
\textbf{Ask.} Which optimization move removes exactly that waste? Why do the other moves fail?

\textbf{A good answer.} The name of a move from Section~\ref{m1:moves}, and one reason for each rejected
alternative. A rejected alternative with a reason is useful: it shows which property of the problem matters.

\textbf{Example.} Two moves work together.
\emph{Precompute}: the running total gives each prefix sum in $O(1)$.
\emph{Remember what you saw}: a count of the remainders of earlier prefixes replaces the inner loop.
Rejected moves: a sliding window needs a condition that stays true when the window shrinks.
Divisibility does not: \cd{[2, 3]} has the sum 5, but \cd{[3]} has the sum 3. Negative values also let the sum go down.
A sort loses the order $i < j$. A binary search needs sorted data, and the prefix sums are not sorted.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 7: State the invariant or the state definition}
\textbf{Ask.} What does each variable hold at the top of each loop iteration?
For a DP: what does one entry of the table mean, in words?

\textbf{A good answer.} One sentence for each variable, with its start value.
The start value must make the sentence true before the first iteration.
If you cannot write the sentence, you cannot yet write the code.

\textbf{Example.} At the top of the iteration for element $j$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{total} is $P[j]$, the sum of the first $j$ elements;
  \item \cd{seen[r]} is the number of prefixes $P[0], \dots, P[j]$ with remainder $r$;
  \item \cd{count} is the number of good subarrays that end before index $j$.
\end{itemize}
Start values: \cd{total = 0}, \cd{count = 0}, and \cd{seen = {0: 1}}, because the empty prefix
$P[0] = 0$ exists before the first element.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 8: Code from the invariant}
\textbf{Ask.} Which lines keep each sentence of step 7 true?

\textbf{A good answer.} Code where each line maps to one part of the invariant.
The invariant also gives the order of the lines: read the state, then update it.

\textbf{Example.} Add the element to \cd{total}, so that \cd{total} is $P[j+1]$.
Each earlier prefix with the same remainder gives one good subarray that ends at $j$, so add \cd{seen[r]} to \cd{count}.
Then add the new prefix to \cd{seen}. Now the invariant is true for $j + 1$.
The result is $O(n)$ time and $O(\min(n, k))$ extra space.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def count_div(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1                          # the empty prefix P[0] = 0
    total = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x                       # total is now the next prefix sum
        r = total % k                    # in Python, 0 <= r < k also for a negative total
        count += seen[r]                 # one good subarray for each earlier equal remainder
        seen[r] += 1                     # then add this prefix
    return count

count_div([4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5)       # -> 7
count_div([-5], 5)                       # -> 1
count_div([0, 0], 3)                     # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Read the state before you update it. If \cd{seen[r] += 1} comes before \cd{count += seen[r]},
each prefix pairs with itself, and the code counts empty subarrays.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
In Python, \cd{x}~\pct~\cd{k} is in \cd{0..k-1} when $k > 0$, also for a negative \cd{x}.
In C++ and Java the remainder of a negative value can be negative. There, use $((x \bmod k) + k) \bmod k$.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Step 9: Test against the brute force}
\textbf{Ask.} Do the fast and the slow solutions agree on many small random inputs and on the edge cases?

\textbf{A good answer.} A short loop with a fixed seed. Use small sizes and a small value range,
so that equal values, zeros and edge cases occur often. The loop finds zero mismatches.
On a mismatch, keep the smallest failing input and trace it by hand.
\begin{pyex}
import random
from collections import defaultdict

def count_div_brute(nums, k):            # step 4
    count = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, len(nums)):
            total += nums[j]
            count += total % k == 0
    return count

def count_div(nums, k):                  # step 8
    seen, total, count = defaultdict(int), 0, 0
    seen[0] = 1
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen[total % k]
        seen[total % k] += 1
    return count

random.seed(7)
bad = []
for _ in range(500):
    nums = [random.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    k = random.randint(2, 6)
    if count_div(nums, k) != count_div_brute(nums, k):
        bad.append((nums, k))
bad                                      # -> []
\end{pyex}

\begin{note}
Step 5 can find no waste that you can remove. Then do two checks. First, compare the brute force with
the budget of step 3: sometimes the brute force already fits. Second, go to Section~\ref{m1:stuck}
and try the reframings in order.
\end{note}

% =====================================================================
\section{Read the constraints}\label{m1:constraints}
The constraints are part of the hint. The problem author picks the limits so that the intended solution
passes and a slower solution fails. Read them before you choose an approach. They tell you the target complexity,
and they often tell you which properties of the input you can use.

\subsection{Input size and feasible complexity in CPython}
CPython does about $10^7$ simple steps per second. A simple step is one loop iteration with a few
arithmetic operations, or one dict access. Built-in functions that run in C (\cd{sorted}, \cd{sum},
\cd{Counter}, string methods, slicing) are 10 to 50 times faster for each element.
Most judges give 1 to 4 seconds for each test. Plan for about $10^7$ Python steps.
Between $2 \cdot 10^7$ and $4 \cdot 10^7$ steps, the code passes only with simple loop bodies and built-ins.
At $10^8$ steps, the code takes about 10 seconds.
The table extends the time-budget table in Section~\ref{sec:time-budget}.

\begin{center}
\setlength{\extrarowheight}{1.5pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{1.9cm}L{3.3cm}L{2.9cm}L{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Largest $n$ & Feasible in CPython & Steps at the largest $n$ & Typical techniques \\
\midrule
\endhead
$\le 10$ & $O(n!)$; $O(n! \cdot n)$ is borderline & $10! \approx 3.6 \cdot 10^6$ & All permutations; try every order (Section~\ref{bt:top}). \\
$\le 20$ & $O(2^n)$; $O(2^n \cdot n)$ is borderline & $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ & All subsets, bitmask DP over the set of used items. \\
$\le 40$ & $O(2^{n/2} \cdot n)$ & $2^{20} \cdot \log_2 2^{20} \approx 2 \cdot 10^7$ & Meet in the middle: enumerate each half, then combine with sort or hashing. \\
$\le 200$ & $O(n^3)$; $O(n^4)$ only up to about 50 & $8 \cdot 10^6$ & Three nested loops, Floyd--Warshall, DP with a split point. \\
$\le 500$ & $O(n^3)$ only with loops over $i < k < j$; $O(n^2 \log n)$ & $500^3/6 \approx 2 \cdot 10^7$ & Interval DP (Burst Balloons has $n \le 300$). \\
$\le 5000$ & $O(n^2)$ & $2.5 \cdot 10^7$ & Two-sequence DP tables, all pairs, DP over (index, previous index). \\
$\le 10^5$ & $O(n \log n)$; $O(n \sqrt{n})$ is borderline & $1.7 \cdot 10^6$ & Sort, heap, binary search, two pointers, sliding window, monotonic stack. \\
$\le 10^6$ & $O(n)$; $O(n \log n)$ only with the built-in sort & $10^6$ & One pass with $O(1)$ work for each element. Prefer built-ins. \\
$\le 10^9$ & $O(\sqrt{n})$, $O(\log n)$ & $3 \cdot 10^4$ & Math, divisor loops, binary search on the answer. \\
$\le 10^{18}$ & $O(\log n)$ & $60$ & Fast power, binary search with integer math, digit-by-digit methods. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

Use the arithmetic, not a feeling. Multiply the sizes of nested loops. Count each query separately.
\begin{pyex}
import math
STEPS_PER_SECOND = 10**7                 # simple CPython steps, a rough figure

def seconds(steps):
    return steps / STEPS_PER_SECOND

n = 10**5
seconds(n * n)                           # -> 1000.0
round(seconds(n * math.log2(n)), 2)      # -> 0.17
q = 10**5                                # q queries, each one O(n): too slow
seconds(q * n) > 60                      # -> True
seconds(n + q * math.log2(n)) < 1        # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item With two inputs of sizes $m$ and $n$, the budget uses both: $O(m \cdot n)$ with $m, n \le 10^3$ is $10^6$ and fits.
  \item With $q$ queries, the cost is the build cost plus $q$ times the cost of one query.
  \item A table of $10^4 \times 10^4$ cells is $10^8$ entries, about 800 MB of list slots in CPython. It does not fit a typical memory limit. Keep only the rows that the recurrence reads.
  \item A chain of $10^4$ nodes (a list, a skewed tree, a path graph) is deeper than the default recursion limit of 1000. Use an explicit stack.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Other signals in the constraints and the statement}
Some constraints say more than a size. They permit a structure, or they forbid one.
\begin{center}
\setlength{\extrarowheight}{1.5pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4.8cm}L{5.6cm}L{5.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Signal & What to try & Why it helps \\
\midrule
\endhead
The input is sorted, or ``non-decreasing'' & Binary search; two pointers; a merge instead of a new sort & One comparison discards a half or one end. \\
Small values, for example $0 \le v \le 10^4$ & A list indexed by value: counting sort, buckets, DP over values & No hashing and no comparison sort: $O(n + \text{range})$. \\
Values up to $10^9$ and $n \le 10^5$ & A dict or a set; sort plus coordinate compression & A list over the value range does not fit in memory. \\
A small alphabet (26 lowercase letters) & A list of 26 counts; a 26-bit mask; $O(26 n)$ loops & A fixed-size state compares in constant time. \\
$k$ much smaller than $n$ (top $k$, window of $k$) & A heap of size $k$: $O(n \log k)$; a window of size $k$ & Keep only $k$ candidates, not all $n$. \\
$n \le 20$, or $n \le 16$ & Subsets, bitmask DP, backtracking & $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ states fit. \\
$n \le 40$ & Meet in the middle & Each half has only $2^{20}$ subsets. \\
A grid with $R \cdot C$ up to $10^5$ or $10^6$ cells & $O(1)$ work for each cell: BFS, flood fill, grid DP; an explicit stack & One region can hold every cell, and recursion then fails. \\
$R, C \le 300$ and the answer is a size & Binary search on the size plus 2-D prefix sums & $O(R C \min(R, C)) \approx 2.7 \cdot 10^7$ is slow in Python. \\
Up to $10^5$ queries on static data & Precompute once: prefix sums, sort plus \cd{bisect}, tables & Each query then costs $O(1)$ or $O(\log n)$. \\
You get all queries in advance & Answer offline: sort the queries and sweep & A pointer over sorted queries moves in one direction only. \\
Updates between the queries & A heap, a sorted list, union-find or a Fenwick tree (Section~\ref{m1:fenwick}) & A precomputed table becomes wrong after an update. \\
``Return any valid answer'', ``in any order'' & Build one answer directly: a greedy, any topological order & You do not search for a special answer. \\
``Return the answer modulo $10^9 + 7$'' & Count with DP or combinatorics; take the modulo after each addition & The count is too large to enumerate. \\
``The answer fits in a 32-bit integer'' (for a count) & Count with DP & The number of objects can be near $2 \cdot 10^9$. \\
Values can be negative & An exact sum: prefix sums plus a hash map. A shortest segment with a sum at least $k$: a deque of prefix indexes (Section~\ref{m1:negsum}). A best sum: Kadane; DP & A sliding window on sums and Dijkstra need non-negative values. A hash map finds only exact keys. \\
All values are positive & A sliding window on sums; binary search on prefix sums; an early break in backtracking & A sum grows when the range grows. \\
The values are distinct & Simple comparisons with no tie rules & Equal values break some binary searches and stack rules. \\
A step count or a budget up to $10^9$ or $10^{18}$ & A formula, a division, cycle detection plus modulo, fast power & A step-by-step simulation does not finish. \\
``At most $k$'' changes, deletions or stops & A budget inside a window; an extra DP dimension; $k + 1$ rounds of relaxation & The budget is part of the state. \\
``Exactly $k$'' & Count ``at most $k$'' minus ``at most $k - 1$'' & ``At most'' stays true when a window shrinks. ``Exactly'' does not. \\
Follow-up: $O(1)$ extra space & Two pointers; marks in the input; the output list as storage; Floyd; XOR or sum & The bookkeeping goes into the input or into a few variables. \\
Follow-up: $O(n)$ when a sort gives $O(n \log n)$ & Hashing, bucket sort, a monotonic stack, union-find & These remove the comparison sort. \\
Required $O(\log n)$ & Binary search on the index or on the answer & A search that halves the range at each step takes logarithmic time. \\
A tiny $n$ with many detailed rules & Simulate the rules literally; test each rule & Speed is not the risk. Correctness is. \\
$V$ and $E$ up to $10^5$ & Adjacency lists; $O(V + E)$ traversal; $O(E \log V)$ Dijkstra & An adjacency matrix needs $V^2$ cells. \\
A complete graph from a formula, $V \le 10^3$ & $O(V^2)$ Prim with weights computed on demand & A list of about $5 \cdot 10^5$ edges is slow to build and sort. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

\subsection{A range-sum inequality with negative values}\label{m1:negsum}
With negative values, a running sum can go down. Thus a sliding window on sums fails.
A hash map also fails, because it finds only an exact key, not ``at least $k$''.
For the shortest segment with a sum at least $k$, keep a deque of prefix indexes whose prefix values increase.
Two rules keep the deque small:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Front: while the current prefix minus the front prefix is at least $k$, record the length and remove the front.
    A later end gives only a longer segment for that start.
  \item Back: remove each index whose prefix is not lower than the current prefix.
    The current index starts later with a lower or equal prefix, so it is always a better or equal start.
\end{itemize}
Each index enters and leaves the deque one time, so the scan is $O(n)$
(Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K, LeetCode 862).
\begin{pyex}
import random
from collections import deque
from itertools import accumulate

def shortest_at_least(a, k):             # values can be negative
    P = [0] + list(accumulate(a))
    best = len(a) + 1
    starts = deque()                     # prefix indexes; their P values increase
    for j, p in enumerate(P):
        while starts and p - P[starts[0]] >= k:
            best = min(best, j - starts.popleft())   # no later end beats this start
        while starts and P[starts[-1]] >= p:
            starts.pop()                 # a later, lower prefix is a better start
        starts.append(j)
    return best if best <= len(a) else -1

def shortest_brute(a, k):
    n = len(a)
    lens = [j - i + 1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i, n) if sum(a[i:j + 1]) >= k]
    return min(lens, default=-1)

shortest_at_least([1, -5, 4, 3], 7)      # -> 2
shortest_at_least([84, -37, 32, 40, 95], 167)   # -> 3
random.seed(3)
cases = [([random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))], random.randint(1, 15))
         for _ in range(500)]
all(shortest_at_least(a, k) == shortest_brute(a, k) for a, k in cases)   # -> True
\end{pyex}

% =====================================================================
\section{From brute force to fast: the optimization moves}\label{m1:moves}
A fast solution is a brute force minus some waste. The waste has few forms.
This section gives twelve moves, and each move removes one form of waste.
The table names the Part III sections by a short form of their titles and by their numbers.
First find the waste (step 5 of the method). Then pick the move that removes it.
Often two moves work together, as in the running example: precompute, then remember what you saw.

\begin{center}
\setlength{\extrarowheight}{1.5pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4.6cm}L{6.4cm}L{5.0cm}@{}}
\toprule
Move & Waste that it removes & Main sections in Part III (number) \\
\midrule
\endhead
Remember what you saw & An inner loop that searches earlier items for an exact value & Hashing (\ref{tech:T01}) \\
Precompute & A range aggregate that you compute again for each query or index & Prefix sums (\ref{tech:T02}) \\
Sort first & Comparisons between all pairs when only neighbors in order matter & Intervals (\ref{tech:T20}); Two pointers (\ref{tech:T03}); Greedy (\ref{tech:T19}) \\
Exploit monotonic order & A scan over candidates that one comparison already ruled out & Two pointers (\ref{tech:T03}); Binary search (\ref{tech:T06}); Sliding window (\ref{tech:T04}); Stacks and monotonic stacks (\ref{tech:T05}) \\
Keep only the best candidates & Storage or a sort of all items when only the top or the current best matters & Heaps and priority queues (\ref{tech:T10}); Greedy (\ref{tech:T19}) \\
Reuse subproblems & A recursion that solves the same subproblem many times & The four DP sections (\ref{tech:T15} to \ref{tech:T18}) \\
Change the representation & A representation that hides the structure & Hashing (\ref{tech:T01}); Graph traversal (\ref{tech:T12}); Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}) \\
Work backward or from the complement & A search from every source, or a direct test of a hard property & Graph traversal (\ref{tech:T12}); Intervals (\ref{tech:T20}); DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
Fix one part and solve the rest & Nested loops over all parts of a tuple & Two pointers (\ref{tech:T03}); Trees (\ref{tech:T08}); Stacks and monotonic stacks (\ref{tech:T05}) \\
Count by contribution & A list of all structures (subarrays, pairs, paths, moves) only to add up one value for each & Stacks and monotonic stacks (\ref{tech:T05}); Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}); Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
Track offsets or extremes & A simulation that moves every item at every step & Prefix sums (\ref{tech:T02}); Stacks and monotonic stacks (\ref{tech:T05}); Greedy (\ref{tech:T19}) \\
Prune the search & Branches that cannot give a valid or better answer & Backtracking (\ref{tech:T11}); Tries (\ref{tech:T09}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Remember what you saw (hashing)}\label{m1:move-hash}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} For each item, an inner loop searches the earlier items for one exact value:
a partner, a duplicate, or an earlier prefix with the same key.

\textbf{Signal.} The partner of an item is fully known from the item: $t - x$, $x - 1$, the same remainder,
the same sorted word. The relation is an equality, not ``near'' or ``less than''.

\textbf{The move.} Keep a set or a dict of what you saw. Ask it for the partner, then add the current item.
Store the value that the question needs: a flag (set), an index (dict), or a count (\cd{Counter}).
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def count_pairs_brute(a, t):             # pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] == t
    n = len(a)
    return sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if a[i] + a[j] == t)

def count_pairs(a, t):
    seen, count = Counter(), 0
    for x in a:
        count += seen[t - x]             # partners among the earlier items
        seen[x] += 1                     # then remember this item
    return count

a = [1, 5, 3, 3, 7, 1]
count_pairs_brute(a, 6), count_pairs(a, 6)   # -> (3, 3)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} The brute force compares each item with all earlier items: about $n^2/2$ tests.
The partner is one exact key, so one dict lookup finds it in $O(1)$ on average.
The dict holds all earlier items at the same time, so one scan is enough: $O(n)$.
In the example, the brute force tests 15 pairs, and the scan does 6 lookups.

\textbf{Problems.} Two Sum; Contains Duplicate; Longest Consecutive Sequence; Subarray Sum Equals K;
Continuous Subarray Sum (LeetCode 523).
\begin{caution}
Hashing finds only exact matches. When the inner loop looks for a value in a range (``the nearest'',
``at most $d$ away''), sort the data or use buckets.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Precompute (prefix and suffix data)}\label{m1:move-prefix}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} A sum, product, minimum or maximum over a range that you compute again
for each query or for each index.

\textbf{Signal.} Many range sums on data that does not change. An answer for each index that uses
``everything on the left'' and ``everything on the right''. The words ``except self''.

\textbf{The move.} Build the prefix aggregate one time in $O(n)$. Then each range sum is a difference of
two prefix values. For an operation with no inverse (max, min, a product with zeros), build a prefix
list and a suffix list, and combine the two sides.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import accumulate

a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2]
P = [0] + list(accumulate(a))            # P[i] = sum(a[:i])

def range_sum(l, r):                     # sum of a[l..r], both ends included
    return P[r + 1] - P[l]

range_sum(2, 4), sum(a[2:5])             # -> (10, 10)
left = list(accumulate(a, max))                  # max of a[0..i]
right = list(accumulate(reversed(a), max))[::-1] # max of a[i..n-1]
left                                     # -> [3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 9, 9]
right                                    # -> [9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 2]
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} A range sum in the brute force adds up to $n$ items. Ranges that overlap
add the same items again and again. The prefix list adds each item one time, and all ranges share it.
Thus $q$ range sums cost $O(n + q)$, not $O(n q)$.
In the example, \cd{range_sum(2, 4)} is one subtraction: $P[5] - P[2] = 14 - 4 = 10$.

\textbf{Problems.} Product of Array Except Self; Trapping Rain Water; Range Sum Query - Immutable (LeetCode 303);
Maximum Side Length of a Square with Sum Less than or Equal to Threshold (2-D prefix sums).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Sort first}\label{m1:move-sort}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} A comparison of all pairs, when after a sort only neighbors can matter.

\textbf{Signal.} The answer does not depend on the input order. The question is about overlaps,
closest values, groups of equal values, or a greedy choice of ``the smallest first''.
The budget permits $O(n \log n)$.

\textbf{The move.} Sort, then scan one time and compare each item with its neighbor or with the last group.
Sort pairs \cd{(value, index)} when the output needs the original indexes.
\begin{pyex}
def min_gap_brute(a):
    return min(abs(x - y) for i, x in enumerate(a) for y in a[i + 1:])

def min_gap(a):
    b = sorted(a)                        # the closest pair is now adjacent
    return min(y - x for x, y in zip(b, b[1:]))

a = [40, 3, 18, 25, 7, 31]
min_gap_brute(a), min_gap(a)             # -> (4, 4)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} After a sort, the closest partner of an item is one of its two neighbors.
An item that is farther away in the sorted list is also farther away in value.
Thus $n - 1$ neighbor pairs replace $n(n - 1)/2$ pairs. The sort costs $O(n \log n)$, and the scan costs $O(n)$.
In the example, the sorted list is \cd{[3, 7, 18, 25, 31, 40]}. Its 5 neighbor gaps replace 15 pairs.

\textbf{Problems.} Merge Intervals; Meeting Rooms; 3Sum; Car Fleet;
Minimum Absolute Difference (LeetCode 1200).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Exploit monotonic order}\label{m1:move-mono}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} A scan over candidates that one comparison already ruled out.

\textbf{Signal.} Something only grows or only shrinks. Examples are sorted data and a sum of positive values.
Other examples are a feasibility that stays true for all larger parameters, and a validity that stays true
when a window shrinks. Or a new item makes some old items useless for all later questions.

\textbf{The move.} Pick the tool from the shape of the order:
\begin{itemize}
  \item two ends of sorted data, and each comparison discards one end: converging two pointers;
  \item a true-or-false property that changes one time along an index or a value: binary search;
  \item a window whose best left end never moves back: a sliding window;
  \item ``the nearest greater or smaller item'': a monotonic stack; the best item of a moving window: a monotonic deque.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def has_pair(b, t):                      # b is sorted
    lo, hi = 0, len(b) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = b[lo] + b[hi]
        if s == t:
            return True
        if s < t:
            lo += 1                      # b[lo] is too small for every partner
        else:
            hi -= 1                      # b[hi] is too big for every partner
    return False

has_pair([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 10), has_pair([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 11)   # -> (True, False)

def next_greater(a):
    res = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []                           # indexes that wait for a greater value
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
            res[stack.pop()] = x         # x answers every smaller waiting item
        stack.append(i)
    return res

next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3])            # -> [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} Each comparison removes one candidate for all later questions, and that candidate
never comes back. Thus each pointer moves at most $n$ times in total, and each index enters and leaves a stack
one time: $O(n)$. A binary search removes half of the candidates with each check: $O(\log n)$ checks.
In \cd{has_pair} with $t = 11$, the sum $1 + 9 = 10$ is too small. Thus 1 is too small for every partner, and it leaves.
The search ends after 4 pointer moves. The brute force tests 10 pairs.

\textbf{Problems.} Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted; Koko Eating Bananas; Longest Substring Without
Repeating Characters; Daily Temperatures; Sliding Window Maximum.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Keep only the best candidates (heap, greedy)}\label{m1:move-best}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} You store or sort all items, but the answer uses only the top $k$ items,
or only the current best item.

\textbf{Signal.} ``$k$ largest'', ``$k$ closest'', ``$k$ most frequent''. A process that repeatedly takes
the smallest or the largest item. A choice where one candidate dominates the others,
for example the farthest reach or the earliest end.

\textbf{The move.} Keep a heap of size $k$ whose root is the weakest kept item.
For a greedy, keep one number that summarizes all candidates.
Then prove with a small exchange argument that the dominated candidates never win.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq

def k_largest(a, k):
    h = []                               # min-heap of the k largest items so far
    for x in a:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k:
            heapq.heappop(h)             # drop the weakest kept item
    return sorted(h, reverse=True)

k_largest([5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 6], 3)         # -> [9, 7, 6]
heapq.nlargest(3, [5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 6])    # -> [9, 7, 6]

def can_reach_end(jumps):                # jumps[i] = longest jump from i
    far = 0                              # the farthest reachable index dominates all others
    for i, j in enumerate(jumps):
        if i > far:
            return False
        far = max(far, i + j)
    return True

can_reach_end([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]), can_reach_end([3, 2, 1, 0, 4])   # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} A full sort orders all $n$ items, but the answer uses only $k$ of them.
In a heap of size $k$, each push and pop costs $O(\log k)$. The total is $O(n \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ memory.
A greedy removes even more work: one number summarizes all candidates, so each item costs $O(1)$.
In \cd{can_reach_end}, every index up to \cd{far} is reachable. Thus \cd{far} replaces the set of reachable indexes.

\textbf{Problems.} Kth Largest Element in an Array; K Closest Points to Origin; Merge k Sorted Lists;
Meeting Rooms II; Jump Game.
\begin{caution}
A greedy needs a reason. Before you code a greedy, try two or three small inputs where a different
choice looks better. If you find a counterexample, use DP.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Reuse subproblems (memoization, DP)}\label{m1:move-dp}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} A recursion that solves the same subproblem many times through different paths.

\textbf{Signal.} ``How many ways'', ``minimum cost'', ``is it possible''. A choice at each step.
The future depends only on a few numbers (an index, a remaining amount), not on the full history.

\textbf{The move.} Write the brute-force recursion. Find the arguments that alone decide the future.
Cache the function on those arguments. Later, if necessary, turn the cache into a table filled in order.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

calls = 0
def ways(n):                             # steps of size 1, 2 or 3
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n < 0:
        return 0
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) + ways(n - 3)

ways(20)                                 # -> 121415
calls                                    # -> 433993

@cache
def ways_memo(n):
    if n < 0:
        return 0
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return ways_memo(n - 1) + ways_memo(n - 2) + ways_memo(n - 3)

ways_memo(20)                            # -> 121415
ways_memo.cache_info().misses            # -> 23
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} The plain recursion reaches the same argument through many paths,
so the number of calls grows exponentially with $n$. The cache computes each distinct argument one time.
The cost becomes the number of states times the work for each state.
In the example, the plain recursion makes 433993 calls. The cached version solves each of the 23 subproblems
one time, and each one reads at most 3 cached values.

\textbf{Problems.} Climbing Stairs; Coin Change; Word Break; Longest Common Subsequence; Edit Distance.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Change the representation}\label{m1:move-repr}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} Work that a better encoding makes cheap or removes.
A comparison of two sets letter by letter, a search over pairs of states, a check of a diagonal cell by cell.

\textbf{Signal.} The items are equal ``up to'' some detail. The input is a configuration, not a graph,
but the question is about moves between configurations. The objects are small sets.
A grid has diagonals or blocks.

\textbf{The move.} Pick an encoding that makes the question one operation:
\begin{itemize}
  \item a canonical key (sorted word, count tuple, \cd{frozenset}) groups equal items in a dict;
  \item a graph whose nodes are states and whose edges are single moves turns ``fewest moves'' into BFS;
  \item a bitmask turns a small set into one integer: a test for common letters is one AND;
  \item coordinate keys: \cd{r * C + c} for a cell id, $r - c$ and $r + c$ for the two diagonals, \cd{(r // 3, c // 3)} for a block.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]:
    groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w) # canonical key: the sorted letters
sorted(groups.values())                  # -> [['bat'], ['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat']]

def max_product(words):                  # two words with no common letter
    masks = []
    for w in words:
        m = 0
        for ch in w:
            m |= 1 << (ord(ch) - ord("a"))
        masks.append(m)
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(words)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(words)):
            if masks[i] & masks[j] == 0: # no shared letter: one AND
                best = max(best, len(words[i]) * len(words[j]))
    return best

max_product(["abcw", "baz", "foo", "bar", "xtfn", "abcdef"])   # -> 16
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} You build each encoding one time, and then every comparison uses it.
The sorted-letter key replaces a comparison of each word with each group: one dict lookup for each word.
The 26-bit mask replaces a letter-by-letter test of two words: one AND, in place of up to $|w_1| \cdot |w_2|$
letter comparisons. A state graph replaces a search over all move sequences: BFS visits each state one time.

\textbf{Problems.} Group Anagrams; Word Ladder; N-Queens; Search a 2D Matrix;
Maximum Product of Word Lengths (LeetCode 318).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Work backward or from the complement}\label{m1:move-back}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} One search from each source toward a fixed target. A direct test of a property
that is hard to test, when its opposite is easy.

\textbf{Signal.} Many sources and a few fixed targets (a border, an ocean, a gate). Words such as
``cannot escape'', ``at least one'', ``minimum number to remove''. A choice of the first action
that leaves two coupled sides.

\textbf{The move.} Search once from the targets on reversed edges. Count the opposite and subtract it
from the total. Turn ``fewest removed'' into ``most kept''. In interval DP, choose the last action, not the first.
\begin{pyex}
def count_with_even_brute(a):            # subarrays with at least one even value
    n = len(a)
    return sum(any(x % 2 == 0 for x in a[i:j + 1])
               for i in range(n) for j in range(i, n))

def count_with_even(a):
    n = len(a)
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2             # all subarrays
    all_odd = run = 0
    for x in a:
        run = run + 1 if x % 2 else 0    # length of the odd run that ends here
        all_odd += run                   # subarrays with only odd values that end here
    return total - all_odd

a = [1, 3, 2, 5, 7, 9, 4]
count_with_even_brute(a), count_with_even(a)   # -> (19, 19)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} One search from the targets answers the question for every source at the same time.
Thus the cost is one traversal, not one traversal for each source.
The complement is often a simpler shape that one pass counts.
In the example, a subarray with no even value lies inside a run of odd values.
A run of length $m$ holds $m(m + 1)/2$ such subarrays, and a running length counts them in $O(n)$.
The runs \cd{[1, 3]} and \cd{[5, 7, 9]} give $3 + 6 = 9$, and the answer is $28 - 9 = 19$.

\textbf{Problems.} Surrounded Regions; Pacific Atlantic Water Flow; Non-overlapping Intervals;
Burst Balloons.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Fix one part and solve the rest}\label{m1:move-fix}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} Nested loops over all parts of a tuple: a pair, a triple or a path.
Often one fixed part makes the rest a known, easier problem.

\textbf{Signal.} The answer is a tuple or a path of a fixed shape. One part has a special role:
the middle element, the middle edge, the minimum of a range, the highest node of a tree path.
Once you fix that part, the other parts become independent.

\textbf{The move.} Loop over the special part. Solve the rest with a count, a lookup, two pointers or a
precomputed table. For independent sides, multiply the counts.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import combinations

def teams_brute(r):                      # triples i < j < k, strictly up or strictly down
    return sum(1 for x, y, z in combinations(r, 3) if x < y < z or x > y > z)

def teams(r):
    total = 0
    for j, mid in enumerate(r):          # fix the middle soldier
        left_less = sum(x < mid for x in r[:j])
        left_more = j - left_less        # the ratings are distinct
        right_less = sum(x < mid for x in r[j + 1:])
        right_more = len(r) - 1 - j - right_less
        total += left_less * right_more + left_more * right_less
    return total

teams_brute([2, 5, 3, 4, 1]), teams([2, 5, 3, 4, 1])   # -> (3, 3)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} With the middle fixed, the left choice and the right choice do not depend on each other.
Thus the number of triples through this middle is a product of two counts, and you do not list the pairs.
One loop level disappears: $O(n^3)$ becomes $O(n^2)$.
In the example, fix the middle value 3. On the left, 2 is smaller and 5 is larger.
On the right, 1 is smaller and 4 is larger. The middle gives $1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 = 2$ teams.

\textbf{Problems.} 3Sum (fix the first value); Largest Rectangle in Histogram (fix the shortest bar);
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (fix the highest node); Detect Squares (fix the diagonal corner);
Count Number of Teams (LeetCode 1395).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Count by contribution}\label{m1:move-contrib}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} You list every subarray, pair, path or move only to add up one value for each.

\textbf{Signal.} A sum over all subarrays, all substrings, all pairs or all paths.
The total number of unit moves of items along the edges of a tree.
There are $O(n^2)$ or more structures, but $n$ is up to $10^5$.

\textbf{The move.} Swap the order of the sum. For each element, bit or edge, count the structures where it counts.
Multiply that count by the value of the element, and add the products.
When the value of a structure is its minimum or maximum, a monotonic stack gives the reach of each element
on each side.
\begin{pyex}
def sum_all_subarrays_brute(a):
    n = len(a)
    return sum(sum(a[i:j + 1]) for i in range(n) for j in range(i, n))

def sum_all_subarrays(a):
    n = len(a)
    return sum(x * (i + 1) * (n - i) for i, x in enumerate(a))   # starts times ends

a = [3, 1, 4, 2]
sum_all_subarrays_brute(a), sum_all_subarrays(a)   # -> (50, 50)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} The brute force lists $n(n + 1)/2$ subarrays and adds up to $n$ items for each one.
The element $a[i]$ is in each subarray that starts at or before $i$ and ends at or after $i$.
The start and the end are independent, so there are $(i + 1)(n - i)$ such subarrays.
Thus one pass with $O(1)$ work for each element gives the total: $O(n)$.
In the example, the value 4 at index 2 is in $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ subarrays, so it adds 24.

\textbf{Problems.} Vowels of All Substrings (LeetCode 2063); Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays (LeetCode 1588);
Count Unique Characters of All Substrings of a Given String (LeetCode 828: an occurrence counts in each substring
that holds no other occurrence of its letter); Distribute Coins in Binary Tree (LeetCode 979: the coins that cross
an edge equal the absolute value of the coins minus the nodes below that edge).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Track offsets or extremes instead of simulating every step}\label{m1:move-offset}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} A simulation that moves every item at every step.
Or a step-by-step replay of a process when only a summary decides the answer.

\textbf{Signal.} The same move applies to all items at the same time. An item survives only if it stays
inside bounds at every step. A step count or a budget is too large to simulate.
Objects cannot pass each other, so only a finish value per object matters.

\textbf{The move.} Keep one shared offset instead of the positions. Keep its running minimum and maximum.
The surviving starts form one interval. In other problems, replace the motion of each object by one
number, such as a finish time, and scan with a running maximum.
\begin{pyex}
def count_starts_brute(diffs, lower, upper):
    good = 0
    for start in range(lower, upper + 1):
        x, ok = start, True
        for d in diffs:
            x += d
            ok = ok and lower <= x <= upper
        good += ok
    return good

def count_starts(diffs, lower, upper):
    off = lo = hi = 0                    # offset from the start, and its extremes
    for d in diffs:
        off += d
        lo, hi = min(lo, off), max(hi, off)
    return max(0, (upper - hi) - (lower - lo) + 1)

count_starts_brute([1, -3, 4], 1, 6), count_starts([1, -3, 4], 1, 6)   # -> (2, 2)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} The brute force replays all steps for each start: starts times steps.
All starts move by the same amount, so their distances never change, and one offset describes all of them.
A start $s$ is valid when $s + \mathit{lo} \ge \mathit{lower}$ and $s + \mathit{hi} \le \mathit{upper}$.
The cost is $O(n)$ for any range of starts.
In the example, the offsets are $1$, $-2$ and $2$, so $\mathit{lo} = -2$ and $\mathit{hi} = 2$.
With $\mathit{lower} = 1$ and $\mathit{upper} = 6$, the valid starts are $3 \le s \le 4$.

\textbf{Problems.} Count the Hidden Sequences (LeetCode 2145); Car Fleet; Gas Station;
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock; Jump Game.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Prune the search}\label{m1:move-prune}
\textbf{Waste it removes.} Branches of a search that cannot give a valid or a better answer.

\textbf{Signal.} The task asks for all solutions, or the input is tiny, so a search is the plan.
A partial answer can already break a rule: a sum above the target, a conflict, a prefix that no word has.

\textbf{The move.} Test the rule on the partial answer, and stop the branch at once.
Sort the choices so that one failure ends the loop (\cd{break}, not \cd{continue}).
Keep the conflict data in sets or a trie, so that each test is $O(1)$ or one step.
\begin{pyex}
def subsets_with_sum(vals, target, prune):
    vals = sorted(vals)
    nodes = 0
    def dfs(start, remain):
        nonlocal nodes
        nodes += 1
        found = 1 if remain == 0 else 0
        for i in range(start, len(vals)):
            if prune and vals[i] > remain:
                break                    # sorted: every later value is too big too
            found += dfs(i + 1, remain - vals[i])
        return found
    return dfs(0, target), nodes         # (number of subsets, nodes visited)

subsets_with_sum(range(1, 13), 10, prune=False)   # -> (10, 4096)
subsets_with_sum(range(1, 13), 10, prune=True)    # -> (10, 43)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Why it is faster.} A stopped branch removes its whole subtree, not one node.
A cut near the root removes the most work. In the example, the plain search visits all $2^{12} = 4096$
subsets. The pruned search visits 43 nodes and finds the same 10 subsets.

\textbf{Problems.} Combination Sum; N-Queens; Word Search; Word Search II (the trie prunes);
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets.

Non-negative weights; cheapest cost or earliest arrival & Dijkstra with a heap & Weighted and advanced graphs (\ref{tech:T14}) \\
Path cost = the highest cell on the path; the earliest time two cells connect & Dijkstra with max; or binary search plus BFS; or union-find by value & Weighted and advanced graphs (\ref{tech:T14}) \\
Cheapest path with at most $k$ stops, that is $k + 1$ edges & Bellman-Ford: $k + 1$ rounds, each on a frozen copy & Weighted and advanced graphs (\ref{tech:T14}) \\
Connect all points at a minimum total cost & Minimum spanning tree: Prim for dense, Kruskal for sparse & Weighted and advanced graphs (\ref{tech:T14}) \\
Use every edge (ticket) exactly one time & Hierholzer: post-order, then reverse & Weighted and advanced graphs (\ref{tech:T14}) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{@{}l}{\textbf{Optimize or count over choices}} \\*
``How many ways'', or the minimum cost, to reach step $n$ with a few step sizes & \cd{dp[i]} from the few entries before it: a sum or a minimum over the last step & DP: foundations and 1-D (\ref{tech:T15}) \\
Take or skip each item; neighbors conflict & \cd{dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + v)} & DP: foundations and 1-D (\ref{tech:T15}) \\
The circular version of a line problem & Two runs: without the first item, without the last item & DP: foundations and 1-D (\ref{tech:T15}) \\
Split a string into valid pieces: is it possible, or how many ways (words, letter codes)? & DP over the end of the prefix: \cd{dp[i]} from \cd{dp[j]} and a valid \cd{s[j:i]} & DP: foundations and 1-D (\ref{tech:T15}) \\
Fewest coins, or number of ways, with unlimited items & Unbounded knapsack; the loop order selects combinations or orderings & DP: knapsack family (\ref{tech:T16}) \\
Each item at most one time; reach a target sum; equal halves & 0/1 knapsack, capacity loop downward; or a set of reachable sums & DP: knapsack family (\ref{tech:T16}) \\
Count or optimize subsets with a total of at least $T$ (profit, score), often with a second limit & Cap the total: write to \cd{dp[min(T, t + w)]}; one dimension for each limit & DP: knapsack family (\ref{tech:T16}) \\
A plus or minus sign on each number to hit a target & Memoized DFS on (index, running sum); or a subset sum with $P = (\mathit{total} + \mathit{target}) / 2$ & DP: knapsack family (\ref{tech:T16}) \\
$n \le 16$ to 20; assign items to $k$ groups (equal sums) or find an order & Bitmask DP over the set of used items; or backtracking with items in decreasing order that skips equal empty groups & DP: knapsack family (\ref{tech:T16}); Backtracking (\ref{tech:T11}) \\
Two strings: align, edit, common subsequence, count matches & A table over prefix pairs $(i, j)$ with three neighbors & DP on strings and sequences (\ref{tech:T17}) \\
A pattern with a repeat operator; interleave two strings & DP over $(i, j)$; a repeat means skip it, or use one and stay & DP on strings and sequences (\ref{tech:T17}) \\
Palindromic substrings (contiguous), $n$ up to a few thousand & Expand around $2n - 1$ centers & DP on strings and sequences (\ref{tech:T17}) \\
Fewest inserts or deletes that make a string a palindrome & An interval table on \cd{s[i..j]}: equal ends go inside at no cost; else 1 plus the better of the two ranges with one end dropped & DP on strings and sequences (\ref{tech:T17}) \\
Grid moves only right and down; count or best paths & Each cell from the cell above and the cell on the left & DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
Longest path where each move strictly increases a value & Visit the cells from the largest value down: 1 plus the best larger neighbor; or a memoized DFS on the implicit DAG & DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
Remove items one by one; the score uses the current neighbors & Interval DP; choose the last item to remove & DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
Two players take from the ends; both play optimally & Score difference: $f(i, j) = \max(\text{gain} - f(\text{rest}))$ & DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
Buy and sell with cooldown, fee or $k$ transactions & A state machine: one best value per status & DP on grids, intervals, games and states (\ref{tech:T18}) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{@{}l}{\textbf{Trees and linked lists}} \\*
A value at a node from its children: height, balance, size & Post-order DFS that returns a summary & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
Two trees: the same, mirror images, or one inside the other & Recurse on both roots together; for a subtree, run that check at each node & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
Best path between any two nodes & Return the best one-sided chain; record the two-sided path in a global & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
A condition that depends on all ancestors (path maximum, bounds) & Pass the state down as arguments & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
One answer per level: level order, side view, level average & BFS with a snapshot of the level size & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
A BST and an order question: $k$-th smallest, validate, ancestor & In-order is sorted; pass bounds; find the split point & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
Rebuild a tree from traversals; serialize a tree & Root from preorder, split by an index map; null markers & Trees (\ref{tech:T08}) \\
Reverse (all, or in groups of $k$), reorder or rotate a singly linked list in place & \cd{prev}, \cd{curr} and a saved \cd{next}; a dummy head & Linked lists (\ref{tech:T07}) \\
The $k$-th node from the end in one pass; the middle node & Two pointers with a gap; fast and slow pointers & Linked lists (\ref{tech:T07}) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{@{}l}{\textbf{Numbers, bits and matrices}} \\*
Every value two times except one; $O(1)$ space & XOR of all values; if the input is sorted and $O(\log n)$ is required, binary search for the first pair index $p$ with \cd{nums[2*p] != nums[2*p+1]} & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}); Binary search (\ref{tech:T06}) \\
One missing value in $0..n$ & Expected sum minus actual sum, or XOR & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}); Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
Number of 1 bits of one value & \cd{n &= n - 1} removes the lowest 1 bit; or \cd{bin(n).count("1")} & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}) \\
Number of 1 bits for every value $0..n$ & Answer of $i$ = answer of $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$ plus the last bit & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}) \\
Reverse the bits of a 32-bit value & 32 rounds: shift the result left, add \cd{n & 1}, shift \cd{n} right & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}) \\
Add without $+$; fixed 32-bit width & XOR for the sum, AND shifted left for the carry, a 32-bit mask & Bit manipulation (\ref{tech:T23}) \\
The digits of an integer: digit sums, reverse, palindrome number & \cd{n, d = divmod(n, 10)} in a loop; remove the sign first & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
Numbers as digit lists or strings, longer than 64 bits & Column arithmetic with a carry from the least significant end & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}); Linked lists (\ref{tech:T07}) \\
An exponent up to $2^{31}$ & Fast power by repeated squaring & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
Apply $x \to f(x)$ again and again: does it end or loop? & Cycle detection with a set or with fast and slow values & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
A fixed 32-bit range and no wider type & Test for overflow before the operation & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
The gradient of a function that sorts or selects items (sort, median, max) & Keep the argsort; send each upstream gradient back to its original index; add one term for each other path, such as a divisor & Math and number manipulation (\ref{tech:T22}) \\
Rotate or flip a square matrix in place & Transpose, then reverse each row & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
Spiral or ring order & Four bounds that move inward & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
A walker moves and turns on a grid & A list of four direction vectors and an index into it; a right turn adds 1 to the index, modulo 4 & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
Mark the row and the column of each zero with $O(1)$ extra space & Store the marks in the first row and the first column, plus one flag for the first column; apply those two last & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
All cells update at the same time, in place & Store old and new state in one cell (two bits) & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
Each output cell is a function of its neighbors & An offset list, a bounds check and a new grid & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
Change exactly one step of a process so that it succeeds & Forward state after each prefix; built backward, the set of states from which each suffix still reaches the goal; one lookup for each edit & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
Detailed rules, a tiny $n$, rounds that repeat until nothing changes & A literal simulation; stop after a round with no change & Matrices and simulation (\ref{tech:T21}) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{@{}l}{\textbf{Design problems}} \\*
A class with a list of operations and a required cost for each & List the operations; pick a structure for each; link the structures (Section~\ref{m1:ds}) & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}) \\
$O(1)$ get and put with eviction of the least recently used item & A dict plus a doubly linked list, or \cd{OrderedDict} & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}); Linked lists (\ref{tech:T07}) \\
A stack with $O(1)$ minimum & Push the pair (value, minimum so far) & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}); Stacks and monotonic stacks (\ref{tech:T05}) \\
Minimum or maximum over entries that change in place (update, increment, decrement) & A dict as the truth plus heaps with lazy deletion; for changes of $\pm 1$, a linked list of count buckets & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}); Heaps and priority queues (\ref{tech:T10}) \\
A feed of the 10 most recent items from many sources & A global timestamp plus a heap merge of the sources & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}); Heaps and priority queues (\ref{tech:T10}) \\
Pack a list of any strings into one string & A length prefix before each item & Design problems (\ref{tech:T24}); Hashing (\ref{tech:T01}) \\
\end{longtable}
}

% =====================================================================
\section{Choose a data structure from the operations}\label{m1:ds}
List the operations that the algorithm needs, and how often each one runs.
Then pick the cheapest structure that supports all of them.
If no single structure does, combine two structures that point into each other.
For example, a dict finds a node, and a linked list keeps the order.

\begin{center}
\setlength{\extrarowheight}{1.5pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{5.6cm}L{4.2cm}L{6.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Operations you need & Structure & Cost in Python \\
\midrule
\endhead
Read and write by position; add and remove at the end & \cd{list} (array) & \cd{a[i]}, \cd{append}, \cd{pop()}: $O(1)$. Insert or delete in the middle, \cd{x in a}: $O(n)$. \\
Membership; remove duplicates; a visited mark & \cd{set} & \cd{add}, \cd{in}, \cd{discard}: $O(1)$ average. \\
Key to value: an index, a last position, a parent, a memo & \cd{dict}, \cd{defaultdict} & Get, set, \cd{in}, delete: $O(1)$ average. A \cd{dict} keeps insertion order. \\
Count occurrences; compare two multisets & \cd{Counter} & One update: $O(1)$. A missing key reads as 0 and adds nothing. \cd{most_common(k)}: $O(n \log k)$. \\
Keys are $0..m - 1$ with a small $m$ & \cd{list} of size $m$ & $O(1)$, with a smaller constant than a \cd{dict}. \\
A key made of several parts: a cell, a state, a pair, a set of letters & \cd{tuple} or \cd{frozenset} & Hashable, so it can be a \cd{dict} key or a \cd{set} item. A \cd{list} or a \cd{set} cannot. Hashing costs $O(\text{length})$. \\
Visited marks on a grid & A \cd{set} of \cd{(r, c)}, or a list of lists of \cd{bool} & Both $O(1)$. The list of lists is faster and smaller when most cells get a mark. \\
Add and remove at both ends; a FIFO queue; BFS & \cd{collections.deque} & \cd{append}, \cd{appendleft}, \cd{pop}, \cd{popleft}: $O(1)$. An index in the middle: $O(n)$. \\
Take the smallest item many times; insert at any time & \cd{heapq} on a list & Push and pop: $O(\log n)$. Read \cd{h[0]}: $O(1)$. \cd{heapify}: $O(n)$. For a max-heap, push $-x$. \\
The $k$ best items of a stream & A heap of size $k$ & $O(n \log k)$ time, $O(k)$ space. \\
A moving middle rank (median) & Two heaps & Insert: $O(\log n)$. Read: $O(1)$. \\
Delete an arbitrary item from a heap & A heap plus a set or \cd{Counter} of deleted items & Delete lazily when the item reaches the top: $O(\log n)$ amortized. \\
Sorted order with floor, ceiling and rank queries & A sorted \cd{list} plus \cd{bisect} & Search: $O(\log n)$. \cd{insort}: $O(n)$ memory move, fast up to about $10^5$ items. \\
Last in, first out; matching; undo; next greater item & \cd{list} as a stack & \cd{append}, \cd{pop()}, \cd{a[-1]}: $O(1)$. \\
Lookup by key, move an item to the end, evict the oldest & \cd{OrderedDict}, or a \cd{dict} plus a doubly linked list & \cd{move_to_end}, \cd{popitem(last=False)}, get, set: $O(1)$. \\
A random item, plus insert and delete by value & A \cd{list} plus a \cd{dict} from value to index & Delete: swap with the last item, then \cd{pop()}: $O(1)$. \\
Prefix queries over many strings & A trie (\cd{dict} of \cd{dict}) & Insert, search, prefix test: $O(L)$ for a string of length $L$. \\
Merge groups; ``same group?'' & Union-find (a parent list) & \cd{find}, \cd{union}: almost $O(1)$ amortized with path compression and union by size; $O(\log n)$ amortized with path compression only. \\
Range sums on static data & A prefix-sum list & Build: $O(n)$. Query: $O(1)$. In 2-D, a query is $O(1)$ by inclusion and exclusion. \\
Range sums with point updates & A Fenwick tree & Update and query: $O(\log n)$. \\
Maximum or minimum of a sliding window & A monotonic \cd{deque} & $O(1)$ amortized per step. \\
Neighbors of each node & A \cd{dict} of lists, or a list of lists & Build: $O(V + E)$. Neighbors of one node: $O(\text{degree})$. \\
Values for each key, ordered by time & A \cd{dict} of lists plus \cd{bisect} & Append: $O(1)$ when the times increase. Floor query: $O(\log k)$. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

The structures below occur often. Each block shows the operations and their results.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import OrderedDict

cache = OrderedDict()                    # the order of keys is the order of use
for key in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    cache[key] = key.upper()
cache.move_to_end("a")                   # "a" is now the most recently used key
cache.popitem(last=False)                # -> ('b', 'B')
list(cache)                              # -> ['c', 'a']
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
parent = list(range(6))                  # union-find: each item starts as its own group

def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]    # path halving keeps the trees flat
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra == rb:
        return False                     # one group already: this edge closes a cycle
    parent[ra] = rb
    return True

[union(0, 1), union(1, 2), union(3, 4), union(2, 0)]   # -> [True, True, True, False]
len({find(x) for x in range(6)})         # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\begin{pyex}
import bisect

times = [1, 4, 4, 9, 12]                 # sorted

def floor_index(t):                      # last index with times[i] <= t, or -1
    return bisect.bisect_right(times, t) - 1

floor_index(4), floor_index(0), floor_index(10)   # -> (2, -1, 3)
bisect.insort(times, 7)
times                                    # -> [1, 4, 4, 7, 9, 12]
\end{pyex}

\textbf{Fenwick tree.}\label{m1:fenwick} A Fenwick tree keeps prefix sums that stay correct after a point update.
Both \cd{add} and \cd{prefix} cost $O(\log n)$. The sum of \cd{a[l..r]} is \cd{prefix(r + 1) - prefix(l)}.
To count the smaller items after each index, rank the values, scan from the right,
and keep a count for each rank (Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, LeetCode 315).
The same scan counts the inversions of a list.
\begin{pyex}
import random

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
