        self.tree = [0] * (n + 1)        # 1-based inside
    def add(self, i, v):                 # a[i] += v, 0-based i
        i += 1
        while i < len(self.tree):
            self.tree[i] += v
            i += i & -i                  # the next node that covers i
    def prefix(self, i):                 # sum of a[0..i-1]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.tree[i]
            i -= i & -i                  # drop the lowest set bit
        return s

def count_smaller_after(nums):
    ranks = {v: r for r, v in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}
    fw, out = Fenwick(len(ranks)), []
    for x in reversed(nums):
        out.append(fw.prefix(ranks[x]))  # smaller values already seen
        fw.add(ranks[x], 1)
    return out[::-1]

count_smaller_after([5, 2, 6, 1])        # -> [2, 1, 1, 0]
random.seed(5)
lists = [[random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))] for _ in range(300)]
all(count_smaller_after(a) == [sum(y < x for y in a[i + 1:]) for i, x in enumerate(a)]
    for a in lists)                      # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
Look for a hidden $O(n)$ operation inside a loop. It turns an $O(n)$ plan into $O(n^2)$.
The usual ones are \cd{x in some_list}, \cd{list.pop(0)}, \cd{list.insert(0, x)}, \cd{list.remove(x)},
\cd{list.index(x)}, a slice such as \cd{a[1:]}, and \cd{min}, \cd{max}, \cd{sum} or \cd{sorted} over a whole list.
Use a set, a \cd{deque}, an index, or a running value instead.
\end{caution}

% =====================================================================
\section{When you are stuck}\label{m1:stuck}
Sometimes step 5 finds the waste, but no move removes it. Sometimes the brute force itself is not clear.
Then change the question, not the code. Try the reframings below in this order.
Give each one a short, honest try before you go to the next one.
\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Solve a smaller or special case.} Use $n = 1, 2, 3$, $k = 1$, all values equal, or only positive values.
    The answers for small cases often show the recurrence.
    Example: count the binary strings of length $n$ with no two adjacent 1s.
    A brute force gives 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. This is the Fibonacci pattern.
    A last character 0 follows any valid string of length $n - 1$.
    A last character 1 follows a 0 and a valid string of length $n - 2$.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import product

def brute(n):
    return sum("11" not in "".join(bits) for bits in product("01", repeat=n))

[brute(n) for n in range(1, 8)]          # -> [2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34]
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Draw it.} Draw the array as bars, the intervals on a line, the grid, or the graph.
    Example: draw the bars of Trapping Rain Water. The water over a bar rises to the lower of two walls:
    the highest bar on its left and the highest bar on its right.
  \item \textbf{Model it as a graph.} Make each item or state a node, and each allowed move or relation an edge.
    Then ``fewest moves'' is a BFS, ``an order'' is a topological sort, and ``groups'' are components.
    Example: in Open the Lock (LeetCode 752), each 4-digit code is a node, and one turn of one wheel is an edge.
    The fewest turns is the BFS distance from \cd{"0000"}.
  \item \textbf{Sort it.} If the answer does not depend on the input order, sort, and look again.
    Example: in Meeting Rooms, after a sort by start, if any two meetings overlap, then two neighbors overlap.
    So one scan over the neighbors finds a conflict.
  \item \textbf{Think about the last step.} Ask which choice comes last. The rest is a smaller version of the same problem.
    Example: in Coin Change, the last coin is one of the coins, so the best count for $a$ is
    $1 + \min_c \text{best}(a - c)$. In Burst Balloons, the last balloon of a range splits it into two independent ranges.
  \item \textbf{Fix one variable.} Loop over one part of the answer and solve the rest.
    Example: in Largest Rectangle in Histogram, fix the shortest bar of the rectangle.
    Then the width is the gap between the nearest shorter bars on each side.
  \item \textbf{Reverse the process.} Run time backward, or search from the goal.
    Example: in Pacific Atlantic Water Flow, let the water climb from each ocean.
    When a process deletes edges, add them in reverse order with union-find.
  \item \textbf{Look at the complement.} Count or test the opposite, then subtract.
    Example: in Non-overlapping Intervals, the fewest removals equal $n$ minus the most intervals that you can keep.
  \item \textbf{Add a dummy element.} A sentinel removes a special case at an edge.
    Examples: a dummy head node for list edits; $P[0] = 0$ before the prefix sums;
    a bar of height 0 at the end of a histogram to empty the stack; a 1 at each end in Burst Balloons.
  \item \textbf{Bound the answer and binary search.} If you can check one candidate answer fast, and the check is
    monotone, search for the boundary.
    Example: Split Array Largest Sum (LeetCode 410). A greedy pass counts the parts for a cap.
    A larger cap never needs more parts. The problem asks for exactly $k$ parts. A further cut never raises
    the largest sum, so ``at most $k$ parts'' gives the same answer when $k \le n$.
\begin{pyex}
def min_largest_sum(a, k):               # split a into at most k contiguous parts
    def parts_needed(cap):               # greedy: fill each part up to cap
        parts, cur = 1, 0
        for x in a:
            if cur + x > cap:
                parts, cur = parts + 1, 0
            cur += x
        return parts
    lo, hi = max(a), sum(a)              # the answer is in [lo, hi]
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if parts_needed(mid) <= k:
            hi = mid                     # mid is feasible: try a smaller cap
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

min_largest_sum([7, 2, 5, 10, 8], 2)     # -> 18
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Ask what to remember from the prefix.} Scan from left to right. At each item, ask which
    summary of the items before it is enough to answer for this item.
    Example: in Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, it is the minimum price so far.
    In Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, it is the last index of each character.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{note}
If no reframing works, go back to step 4. Improve the brute force one small step at a time,
and test each version against the previous one. A memoized brute-force recursion is often the intended
solution. A correct $O(n^2)$ solution also passes many tests when the intended one is $O(n \log n)$.
\end{note}

% =====================================================================
\section{Pitfalls that cost points}
Most lost points come from a small set of mistakes that repeat across problems.
Often the algorithm is correct, but one detail is wrong: a bound, a tie, a copy, or one word of the statement.
Each item in this section gives the wrong form and the right form.
Most items also have a tested example that shows the bug and the fix.

The Common mistakes table in Part I lists the traps of the Python language.
This section covers the traps one level higher: the specification, the boundaries of an algorithm,
and the state that the code keeps.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Bug classes at a glance}\label{pit:check}
Use this list when time is short. Each line names one class of bug and the subsection with the details.
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{3.3cm}L{11.3cm}L{1.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Class & Check & Details \\
\midrule
\endhead
Specification & Strict or non-strict words; contiguous or not; order matters or not; ``ends at'' or ``visits''. & \ref{pit:spec} \\
Rules on the method & Extra space, forbidden operations, change in place. The judge does not check them. & \ref{pit:spec} \\
Off-by-one & Inclusive or exclusive ends; arrays of size $n + 1$; nodes or edges. & \ref{pit:index} \\
Negative indexes & Both bounds tested before each index: \cd{0 <= i < n}. & \ref{pit:index} \\
Work after the loop & The last group, the rest of a stack, a final carry, the rest of a list. & \ref{pit:index} \\
Termination & Each path of a loop makes progress; the binary search midpoint; a repeated state stops the loop. & \ref{pit:loop} \\
Shared objects & Rows made with \cd{*}; a stored path; an alias of the input; a new value read too early. & \ref{pit:mut} \\
Linked lists & \cd{next} saved before a rewire; the tail moved after each link; \cd{dummy.next} returned. & \ref{pit:mut} \\
State & One fact in one place; three states for a cycle check; new state for each call. & \ref{pit:state} \\
Recursion & Depth above 1000; a memo key with all the state; a return on every path. & \ref{pit:rec} \\
Greedy and DP & A small counterexample tried for each greedy; the base case; the meaning of \cd{dp[i]}; the loop order. & \ref{pit:dp} \\
Hashing & Lookup before insert; keys that keep all the information; no insert on a read. & \ref{pit:hash} \\
Comparisons & Ties; the start value of a best; a comparison with the running value. & \ref{pit:cmp} \\
Numbers & Integer math for large values; \cd{//} and the modulo of negative values; operator precedence. & \ref{pit:num} \\
Speed & No hidden $O(n)$ step in a loop; mark on push; no debug output. & \ref{pit:perf} \\
Input shapes & Empty input, a \cd{None} root, an empty stack; strings in a grid; rows and columns. & \ref{pit:shape} \\
Output & The requested value; the impossible case; integer or float; return or print. & \ref{pit:out} \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
Then run the checks of Section~\ref{pit:debug}: a hand trace, the edge cases, and a brute-force cross-check.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Read the specification}\label{pit:spec}
A wrong reading of the statement is the most frequent cause of a wrong answer.
The code then solves a different problem, and it solves it correctly.
Read the statement two times: one time for the idea, and one time for each rule and each word.

\begin{longtable}{@{}L{5.2cm}L{11.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Word in the statement & Meaning in the code \\
\midrule
\endhead
at most $k$, no more than $k$ & \cd{<= k}. A value equal to $k$ is valid. \\
less than $k$, fewer than $k$ & \cd{< k}. A value equal to $k$ is not valid. \\
strictly larger, warmer, increasing & Equal values do not count. \\
non-decreasing, at least as large & Equal values count. \\
subarray, substring & Contiguous. You cannot skip elements. \\
subsequence & Keeps the order. You can skip elements. \\
subset, combination & The order does not matter: $[1, 2]$ and $[2, 1]$ are one answer.
Check the examples: a title can say ``combination'' and still count orders. \\
permutation, sequence of choices & The order matters: $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$ are two answers. \\
non-empty & The answer has at least one element. Do not start the best value at 0. \\
distinct & Distinct values, or distinct positions? Find the answer in the examples. \\
in place & Change the given object. The judge reads that object, not a return value. \\
1-indexed & Labels or answers start at 1. Size arrays $n + 1$, or subtract 1 from each label. \\
in any order & The judge accepts any order. Your own tests must sort before they compare. \\
ends at, final & Test only the last state. \\
reaches, visits, at some time & Test every state on the way. \\
every, all & \cd{all(...)}: one failure gives \cd{False}. \\
some, any, exists & \cd{any(...)}: one success gives \cd{True}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The exact success condition.}
Wrong: return success as soon as a walk touches the target.
Right: finish the walk, then test the final state.
``Ends at the target'' and ``passes through the target'' are two different problems.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
MOVES = {"U": (-1, 0), "D": (1, 0), "L": (0, -1), "R": (0, 1)}
def cells_on_walk(start, program):
    r, c = start
    cells = [(r, c)]
    for ch in program:
        dr, dc = MOVES[ch]
        r, c = r + dr, c + dc
        cells.append((r, c))
    return cells
def reaches(start, goal, program):          # "the walk visits the goal"
    return goal in cells_on_walk(start, program)
def ends_at(start, goal, program):          # "the walk stops on the goal"
    return cells_on_walk(start, program)[-1] == goal
reaches((0, 0), (0, 1), "RR")               # -> True
ends_at((0, 0), (0, 1), "RR")               # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Every rule implemented, every rule tested.}
Wrong: copy the code of one rule to make a similar rule, and miss one change.
An example is a ``move backward'' command that moves forward.
Right: list the rules of the statement. Write one small test for each rule.
Raise an error on an input value that no rule covers, so that a missing rule fails loudly.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
DIRS = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]   # up, right, down, left: clockwise
def run(program):
    r, c, d = 0, 0, 0                        # start at (0, 0) and face up
    for ch in program:
        if ch == "L":
            d = (d - 1) % 4                  # turn counterclockwise
        elif ch == "R":
            d = (d + 1) % 4                  # turn clockwise
        elif ch == "F":
            r, c = r + DIRS[d][0], c + DIRS[d][1]
        elif ch == "B":                      # move backward and keep the facing
            r, c = r - DIRS[d][0], c - DIRS[d][1]
        else:
            raise ValueError(ch)
    return (r, c, d)
TESTS = {"L": (0, 0, 3), "R": (0, 0, 1), "F": (-1, 0, 0),
         "B": (1, 0, 0), "RF": (0, 1, 1), "RB": (0, -1, 1)}   # one test per rule
def failing(solution):
    return [p for p, want in TESTS.items() if solution(p) != want]
def run_wrong(program):                      # acts like a copied rule: B moves like F
    return run(program.replace("B", "F"))
failing(run_wrong)                           # -> ['B', 'RB']
failing(run)                                 # -> []
run("X")                                     # -> raises ValueError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rules on the method, not only on the answer.}
Wrong: ignore a rule that the judge cannot see. Examples are $O(1)$ extra space, ``no division'',
``do not convert the input to an integer'', and ``relink the nodes, do not change their values''.
Right: list these rules together with the other rules of the statement.
A judge often accepts a solution that breaks them, but an interviewer does not.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Assumptions that the statement does not give.}
Wrong: assume that the input is sorted, that the values are distinct or positive,
or that a graph is connected, because the examples look like that.
Right: check each assumption against the constraints. If the constraints do not promise it, handle the other case.
\end{caution}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Two pointers on unsorted input give wrong answers. Sort first, or use a hash map.
  \item A sliding window on sums needs sums that only grow when the window grows. Negative values break this.
        Use prefix sums with a hash map instead (Subarray Sum Equals K).
  \item A traversal from node 0 misses the other components. Start a traversal from every unvisited node.
  \item Isolated nodes do not appear in the edge list. Take the node count from $n$, not from the edges.
  \item Edge direction: a pair \cd{[a, b]} can mean ``$b$ comes before $a$''. Check the direction on the first example.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Indexing and off-by-one}\label{pit:index}
Most off-by-one bugs come from a mixed convention.
For each range, decide whether the end is included. Then use the same decision everywhere.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Inclusive and exclusive ends.}
Wrong: \cd{s[i:j]} for the piece from $i$ to $j$ with both ends included.
Right: \cd{s[i:j + 1]}. A slice and \cd{range} exclude the end.
The number of elements from $i$ to $j$ is $j - i + 1$. The distance between them is $j - i$.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
s = "abcdef"
i, j = 1, 3                       # the piece from index 1 to index 3, both included
s[i:j]                            # -> 'bc'
s[i:j + 1]                        # -> 'bcd'
len(range(i, j + 1)), j - i + 1   # -> (3, 3)
list(range(3, 0, -1))             # -> [3, 2, 1]
list(range(3, -1, -1))            # -> [3, 2, 1, 0]
\end{pyex}
A downward \cd{range} also excludes its end. To include 0, stop at \cd{-1}.
Formulas that often go wrong by one:
\begin{itemize}
  \item A window from \cd{l} to \cd{r}, both included, has length \cd{r - l + 1}.
        The width between two walls at \cd{l} and \cd{r} is \cd{r - l} (Container With Most Water).
  \item A prefix table has $n + 1$ entries. \cd{P[i]} is the sum of the first $i$ elements,
        so the sum of \cd{a[i..j]} is \cd{P[j + 1] - P[i]}.
  \item In a DP over prefix lengths, entry \cd{dp[i]} covers \cd{s[:i]}, so its last character is \cd{s[i - 1]}.
  \item A path with $k$ stops has $k + 1$ edges. A path of $k$ nodes has $k - 1$ edges.
        Tree depth counts nodes, but a diameter counts edges.
  \item A cooldown of $n$ steps between two runs puts the next run at time $t + n + 1$, not $t + n$.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative indexes do not fail.}
Wrong: test only the upper bound, \cd{nr < R}. The index \cd{-1} then reads the last row, and no error appears.
Right: test both bounds with a chained comparison, \cd{0 <= nr < R}, before you index.
The same trap appears in \cd{dp[a - c]} when \cd{c > a}, in an index sentinel of \cd{-1},
and in \cd{s[i - 1:i + 1]} when \cd{i} is 0.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
grid = ["ab",
        "cd"]
R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
STEPS = ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))
def neighbors_wrong(r, c):
    return sorted(grid[r + dr][c + dc] for dr, dc in STEPS
                  if r + dr < R and c + dc < C)          # no lower bound
def neighbors(r, c):
    return sorted(grid[r + dr][c + dc] for dr, dc in STEPS
                  if 0 <= r + dr < R and 0 <= c + dc < C)
neighbors_wrong(0, 0)       # -> ['b', 'b', 'c', 'c']
neighbors(0, 0)             # -> ['b', 'c']
dp = [10, 20, 30, 40]
a, coin = 1, 3
dp[a - coin]                # -> 30
\end{pyex}
The last line reads \cd{dp[-2]} silently. Test \cd{coin <= a} before you read \cd{dp[a - coin]}.
A guard that skips the move is correct only when the move must land exactly, as with a coin.
When the move covers a span that can start before index 0, as with a 7-day pass, do not skip the move.
Clamp the index with \cd{max(0, i - k)} (Minimum Cost For Tickets).
\begin{pyex}
def min_cost(days, costs, clamp=True):     # passes of 1, 7 and 30 days
    travel, last = set(days), days[-1]
    dp = [0] * (last + 1)                   # dp[i]: cheapest cover of the travel days up to day i
    for i in range(1, last + 1):
        if i not in travel:
            dp[i] = dp[i - 1]
        elif clamp:
            dp[i] = min(dp[max(0, i - k)] + c for k, c in zip((1, 7, 30), costs))
        else:                               # wrong: skips a pass that starts before day 1
            dp[i] = min(dp[i - k] + c for k, c in zip((1, 7, 30), costs) if i - k >= 0)
    return dp[last]
min_cost([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 15], clamp=False)   # -> 6
min_cost([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 15])                # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Empty and single-element input.}
Wrong: start a result at 1, or read \cd{a[0]} before a length check.
Right: decide the answer for an empty input and for one element first.
Then check that the general code gives these answers, or add a guard.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_run_wrong(a):         # longest run of equal neighbors
    best = cur = 1
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        cur = cur + 1 if a[i] == a[i - 1] else 1
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
def longest_run(a):
    if not a:
        return 0
    best = cur = 1
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        cur = cur + 1 if a[i] == a[i - 1] else 1
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
longest_run_wrong([])             # -> 1
longest_run([]), longest_run([7]), longest_run([4, 4, 1])   # -> (0, 1, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Work left after the loop.}
Wrong: finish an item only when the next item starts. The last item then never gets into the output.
Examples are the last group of a merge, the bars left on a stack, a final carry, and the rest of the longer list.
Right: after the loop, handle what is left.
For groups, keep the current group as the last element of the output, \cd{out[-1]}. Then there is no step to forget.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def merge_wrong(intervals):
    intervals = sorted(intervals)
    out = []
    st, ed = intervals[0]
    for s, e in intervals[1:]:
        if s <= ed:
            ed = max(ed, e)
        else:
            out.append([st, ed])
            st, ed = s, e
    return out                         # the last group is never added
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])         # a new list, not the input list
    return out
merge_wrong([[1, 3], [2, 4], [6, 7]])  # -> [[1, 4]]
merge([[1, 3], [2, 4], [6, 7]])        # -> [[1, 4], [6, 7]]
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Loops and termination}\label{pit:loop}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Every loop makes progress.}
Wrong: a \cd{while} loop with a path that does not change the loop variables.
An example is a two-pointer swap that never moves the pointers. The program then hangs.
Right: for every path through the body, find the variable that moves toward the exit condition.
While you debug, add a step counter that raises an error after too many steps.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def reverse_wrong(a, limit=100):
    l, r, steps = 0, len(a) - 1, 0
    while l < r:
        steps += 1
        if steps > limit:                    # a debug guard against an endless loop
            raise RuntimeError("no progress")
        a[l], a[r] = a[r], a[l]              # l and r never move
    return a
def reverse(a):
    l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
    while l < r:
        a[l], a[r] = a[r], a[l]
        l += 1                               # both pointers move on every pass
        r -= 1
    return a
reverse_wrong([1, 2, 3])                     # -> raises RuntimeError
reverse([1, 2, 3])                           # -> [3, 2, 1]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The binary search midpoint.}
Wrong: \cd{lo = mid} together with \cd{mid = (lo + hi) // 2}.
When \cd{hi = lo + 1}, \cd{mid} equals \cd{lo}. If the test is true, \cd{lo} does not change, and the loop never ends.
Right: choose one template from the table below and keep all of its rules.
\end{caution}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.2cm}L{1.9cm}L{3.6cm}L{2.8cm}L{3.0cm}@{}}
\toprule
Goal & Loop & Midpoint & Moves & Result \\
\midrule
Find an exact value & \cd{lo <= hi} & \cd{(lo + hi) // 2} & \cd{lo = mid + 1}\newline\cd{hi = mid - 1} & \cd{mid} on a match \\
First \cd{True} & \cd{lo < hi} & \cd{(lo + hi) // 2} & \cd{hi = mid}\newline\cd{lo = mid + 1} & \cd{lo} \\
Last \cd{True} (closed range, \cd{ok(lo)} true) & \cd{lo < hi} & \cd{(lo + hi + 1) // 2} & \cd{lo = mid}\newline\cd{hi = mid - 1} & \cd{lo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In the first row, the first move is for \cd{a[mid] < x}, and a match returns at once.
In the other rows, the first move is for a true test, and the second move is for a false test.
Section~\ref{t06:sec} uses \cd{first_true} on the half-open range \cd{[lo, hi)}.
It gets the last true value as the first false value minus 1, so it needs no second template.
\begin{pyex}
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):     # on [lo, hi): returns hi if no x passes
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2    # round down, because the update is hi = mid
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo
def last_true_closed(lo, hi, ok):   # closed [lo, hi]; ok(lo) must be True
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2   # round up, because the update is lo = mid
        if ok(mid):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo
def last_true_closed_wrong(lo, hi, ok, limit=100):
    steps = 0
    while lo < hi:
        steps += 1
        if steps > limit:
            raise RuntimeError("no progress")
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2    # rounds down: lo = mid can leave lo unchanged
        if ok(mid):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo
first_true(0, 100, lambda x: x * x >= 50)          # -> 8
last_true_closed(0, 10, lambda x: x <= 3)          # -> 3
last_true_closed_wrong(0, 10, lambda x: x <= 3)    # -> raises RuntimeError
\end{pyex}
Other binary search traps:
\begin{itemize}
  \item The start range must contain the answer. Start at the smallest valid value: a speed of 0 divides by zero.
        Start at 0 when 0 is a possible answer.
  \item The test must be monotonic: all \cd{False}, then all \cd{True}. Negative values can break this for sums.
  \item \cd{bisect_left} can return \cd{len(a)}. Test \cd{i < len(a)} before you read \cd{a[i]}.
  \item After the loop of the exact-value template, \cd{lo} is the insertion point, not a match.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Inner loops need the outer bound.}
Wrong: an inner \cd{while} loop that skips elements and tests only the element.
On an input with nothing to keep, the index runs off the end.
Right: repeat the outer bound in the inner condition: \cd{while i < j and ...}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def is_pal_wrong(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while not s[i].isalnum():           # no i < j test
            i += 1
        while not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i, j = i + 1, j - 1
    return True
def is_pal(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i, j = i + 1, j - 1
    return True
is_pal_wrong("!!")                          # -> raises IndexError
is_pal("!!"), is_pal("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")   # -> (True, True)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Loops that wait for a value.}
Wrong: \cd{while n != 1: n = step(n)}. If the sequence enters a cycle without 1, the loop never ends.
Right: stop on a repeated state too. Keep a set of seen states, or use fast and slow pointers.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def step(n):
    return sum(int(d) ** 2 for d in str(n))
def is_happy(n):
    seen = set()
    while n != 1 and n not in seen:      # stop on success or on a repeat
        seen.add(n)
        n = step(n)
    return n == 1
is_happy(19), is_happy(2)                # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Fast and slow pointers start on the same node. Test for equality after the first move.
        A test before the move ends the loop at once.
  \item A simulation in rounds stops only after a full round with no change.
        A round with fewer changes is not the end.
  \item When time can be large (up to $10^9$), do not step one time unit per pass. Jump to the next event.
  \item A level-by-level BFS reads the queue size one time, before the inner loop: \cd{for _ in range(len(q))}.
        A \cd{while} loop that reads \cd{len(q)} again mixes the levels.
  \item A level BFS that runs until the queue is empty also counts the last level, which changes nothing.
        For ``minutes until all cells change'', stop when no target is left, or subtract that last level.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A condition that can never be true.}
Wrong: a test inside a loop for a state that exists only after the loop, such as \cd{i == len(s)} inside
\cd{for i in range(len(s))}. The test never passes, so its branch never runs, and no error appears.
Right: put the final test after the loop. For each \cd{if}, find one input that makes it true.
If no such input exists, the condition is dead, and the logic around it is wrong.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def back_to_start_wrong(program):
    pos = 0
    for i in range(len(program)):
        pos += 1 if program[i] == "R" else -1
        if i == len(program):          # never true: i stops at len(program) - 1
            return pos == 0
    return False
def back_to_start(program):
    pos = 0
    for ch in program:
        pos += 1 if ch == "R" else -1
    return pos == 0                    # test the final state after the loop
back_to_start_wrong("RL"), back_to_start("RL")   # -> (False, True)
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Mutation, copying and aliasing}\label{pit:mut}
A name refers to an object. An assignment, an append, or a call does not copy the object.
Most state bugs have one of two causes: two names for one object, or a write that a later read sees too early.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Shared rows.}
Wrong: \cd{[[0] * C] * R} or \cd{[[]] * n} to make a table.
Also wrong: \cd{grid.copy()}, \cd{grid[:]} or \cd{list(grid)} to get an independent grid.
With \cd{[[0] * C] * R}, all rows are one list, so a write to one row changes every row.
With \cd{grid.copy()}, \cd{grid[:]} or \cd{list(grid)}, the copy shares each row with the original,
so a write to the copy also changes the original.
Right: \cd{[[0] * C for _ in range(R)]}, \cd{[[] for _ in range(n)]}, and \cd{[row[:] for row in grid]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
table = [[0] * 2] * 2             # one row object, two times
table[0][0] = 1
table                             # -> [[1, 0], [1, 0]]
table = [[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)]
table[0][0] = 1
table                             # -> [[1, 0], [0, 0]]
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = grid.copy()             # grid[:] and list(grid) do the same
shallow[0][0] = 9
grid[0][0]                        # -> 9
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
deep = [row[:] for row in grid]   # a new list for every row
deep[0][0] = 9
grid[0][0]                        # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Synchronous updates.}
Wrong: write new values into the grid while later cells still read their neighbors from that grid
(Game of Life, an image blur). Later cells then read new values.
Right: read only old values. Write into a new grid,
or store the new state in extra bits and decode it in a second pass.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def step_wrong(a):                # new a[i] = old a[i - 1] + old a[i + 1]
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        left = a[i - 1] if i > 0 else 0
        right = a[i + 1] if i + 1 < n else 0
        a[i] = left + right       # the next cell reads this new value
    return a
def step(a):
    n = len(a)
    return [(a[i - 1] if i > 0 else 0) + (a[i + 1] if i + 1 < n else 0)
            for i in range(n)]    # reads only the old list
step_wrong([1, 2, 3])             # -> [2, 5, 5]
step([1, 2, 3])                   # -> [2, 4, 2]
\end{pyex}
A one-dimensional DP table that is reused for each item has the same problem.
For a choice that each item can make only one time, loop over the sums downward.
Then each read sees the value from before this item.
\begin{pyex}
def can_sum(nums, target, downward):
    dp = [True] + [False] * target          # dp[s]: some subset has the sum s
    for x in nums:
        sums = range(target, x - 1, -1) if downward else range(x, target + 1)
        for s in sums:
            dp[s] = dp[s] or dp[s - x]
    return dp[target]
can_sum([3], 6, downward=False)             # -> True
can_sum([3], 6, downward=True)              # -> False
\end{pyex}
The upward loop uses the 3 two times. That is correct only when each item can repeat (Coin Change).

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rolling variables.}
Wrong: update two rolling variables in two statements, when the second statement needs the old value of the first.
Right: use one tuple assignment. Python evaluates the full right side before it assigns.
The same rule applies to a pair such as the current maximum and minimum (Maximum Product Subarray).
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def rob_wrong(nums):
    prev2 = prev1 = 0                 # best total up to i - 2, and up to i - 1
    for x in nums:
        prev2 = prev1                 # the next line reads this new prev2
        prev1 = max(prev1, prev2 + x)
    return prev1
def rob(nums):
    prev2 = prev1 = 0
    for x in nums:
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, max(prev1, prev2 + x)
    return prev1
rob_wrong([2, 1, 1, 2])               # -> 6
rob([2, 1, 1, 2])                     # -> 4
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rolling rows.}
Wrong: \cd{prev = cur} at the end of a row, followed by writes into \cd{cur} in the next row.
The two names are now one list, so \cd{prev[j - 1]} already holds a value of the new row.
Right: \cd{prev = cur[:]}, or build a new \cd{cur} list for each row.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def lcs(a, b, copy_row):              # longest common subsequence with two rows
    prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    cur = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                cur[j] = prev[j - 1] + 1
            else:
                cur[j] = max(prev[j], cur[j - 1])
        prev = cur[:] if copy_row else cur
    return prev[-1]
lcs("ab", "bb", copy_row=False)       # -> 2
lcs("ab", "bb", copy_row=True)        # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Tuple assignment evaluates the right side first, but it assigns the targets from left to right.
A target such as \cd{curr.next} uses the value of \cd{curr} at the time of that assignment.
Put \cd{curr.next} before \cd{curr} in the target list, or use a temporary name.
\end{note}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def values(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next   # curr.next is assigned first
    return prev
def reverse_wrong(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        prev, curr, curr.next = curr, curr.next, prev   # curr changes first
    return prev
values(reverse(Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))))      # -> [3, 2, 1]
reverse_wrong(Node(1, Node(2, Node(3))))        # -> raises AttributeError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Pointer changes in a linked list.}
Wrong: change \cd{node.next} before you save the old value, or link a node and then not move the tail.
Right: obey these rules on every change of a pointer.
\end{caution}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Save \cd{nxt = curr.next} before you change \cd{curr.next}. Otherwise the rest of the list is lost.
  \item Start an output list with a dummy node. Move the tail after each link. Return \cd{dummy.next}, not \cd{dummy}.
  \item After a split or a reorder, set the last \cd{next} to \cd{None}. An old link can make a cycle.
  \item Compare nodes with \cd{is}, and use the node object as a map key. Two nodes can have the same value.
  \item Test \cd{fast and fast.next} before a step of two nodes.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def values(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out
def merge(a, b, move_tail):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        if move_tail:
            tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b                 # attach the rest of the longer list
    return dummy.next
values(merge(Node(1, Node(3)), Node(2, Node(4)), move_tail=False))   # -> [4]
values(merge(Node(1, Node(3)), Node(2, Node(4)), move_tail=True))    # -> [1, 2, 3, 4]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A stored reference to the input.}
Wrong: append an input list to the output, and later change that output element. The caller's data changes too.
Right: append a new object, such as \cd{[s, e]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def merge_alias(intervals):
    out = []
    for iv in sorted(intervals):
        if out and iv[0] <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], iv[1])   # changes a list of the caller
        else:
            out.append(iv)                        # stores the input list itself
    return out
data = [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
merge_alias(data)        # -> [[1, 4]]
data                     # -> [[1, 4], [2, 4]]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A change to the caller's input.}
Wrong: sort, heapify, negate, or mark the input when the caller still needs it.
Right: work on a copy (\cd{sorted(nums)}, \cd{[row[:] for row in grid]}), or keep a separate visited set.
Some problems require a change in place. Then the opposite rule applies.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def kth_smallest_wrong(nums, k):
    nums.sort()                     # sorts the list of the caller
    return nums[k - 1]
def kth_smallest(nums, k):
    return sorted(nums)[k - 1]      # sorts a new list
data = [3, 1, 2]
kth_smallest_wrong(data, 1), data   # -> (1, [1, 2, 3])
data = [3, 1, 2]
kth_smallest(data, 1), data         # -> (1, [3, 1, 2])
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A new object assigned to a parameter.}
Wrong: assign a new object to the parameter name when the function must change its input in place.
The assignment changes only the local name. The caller still sees the old object.
Right: change the object itself: \cd{m[:] = new_rows}, or write into its cells.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def rotate_wrong(m):
    m = [list(row) for row in zip(*m[::-1])]      # binds the local name only
def rotate(m):
    m[:] = [list(row) for row in zip(*m[::-1])]   # changes the object of the caller
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
rotate_wrong(a); a          # -> [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
rotate(a); a                # -> [[3, 1], [4, 2]]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A change to a collection during a loop over it.}
Wrong: add or remove elements of a list, a set or a dict in a \cd{for} loop over that collection.
A dict or a set raises \cd{RuntimeError}. A list raises no error, but the loop skips elements.
Right: loop over a copy (\cd{list(d)}, \cd{a[:]}), or build a new collection.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
a = [1, 2, 2, 3]
for x in a:
    if x == 2:
        a.remove(x)                    # the next element moves into this slot and is skipped
a                                      # -> [1, 2, 3]
a = [1, 2, 2, 3]
[x for x in a if x != 2]               # -> [1, 3]
s = {1, 2}
for x in s:
    s.add(x + 10)
# -> raises RuntimeError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A stored path that keeps changing.}
Wrong: \cd{res.append(path)} in a backtracking search. Every entry of \cd{res} is then the same list,
and the later pops make it empty.
Right: \cd{res.append(path[:])}, or append a new object, such as \cd{"".join(path)} or \cd{tuple(path)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def subsets(nums, copy):
    res, path = [], []
    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:] if copy else path)
            return
        path.append(nums[i])           # take nums[i]
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.pop()                     # undo, then skip nums[i]
        dfs(i + 1)
    dfs(0)
    return res
subsets([1, 2], copy=False)            # -> [[], [], [], []]
subsets([1, 2], copy=True)             # -> [[1, 2], [1], [2], []]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Backtracking state.}
Wrong: return from inside the loop before you undo a mark.
The board then stays changed for the caller and for each later search on the same board, such as the next word.
Right: compute the result, undo every change, and then return.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def exists_wrong(board, word):
    R, C = len(board), len(board[0])
    def dfs(r, c, i):
        if i == len(word):
            return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or board[r][c] != word[i]:
            return False
        board[r][c] = "#"                          # mark the cell as used
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if dfs(nr, nc, i + 1):
                return True                        # returns before the undo
        board[r][c] = word[i]
        return False
    return any(dfs(r, c, 0) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))
def exists(board, word):
    R, C = len(board), len(board[0])
    def dfs(r, c, i):
        if i == len(word):
            return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or board[r][c] != word[i]:
            return False
        board[r][c] = "#"
        found = any(dfs(nr, nc, i + 1)
                    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)))
        board[r][c] = word[i]                      # undo on every path
        return found
    return any(dfs(r, c, 0) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))
board = [list("ab"), list("cd")]
exists_wrong(board, "ab"), board      # -> (True, [['#', '#'], ['c', 'd']])
board = [list("ab"), list("cd")]
exists(board, "ab"), board            # -> (True, [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd']])
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Each change before a recursive call needs its undo after the call: \cd{append} and \cd{pop},
        mark and unmark, add and remove.
  \item With equal values in the input, sort first. Then skip a value equal to the previous value only at the same level:
        \cd{j > start}, not \cd{j > 0}. The test \cd{j > 0} also blocks answers with two equal values, such as $[2, 2]$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def subsets_no_dup(nums, right):
    nums, res, path = sorted(nums), [], []
    def dfs(start):
        res.append(path[:])
        for j in range(start, len(nums)):
            first = start if right else 0      # right: j > start; wrong: j > 0
            if j > first and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
                continue                       # an equal value at the same level
            path.append(nums[j])
            dfs(j + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return res
subsets_no_dup([2, 2], right=False)    # -> [[], [2]]
subsets_no_dup([2, 2], right=True)     # -> [[], [2], [2, 2]]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{State that lives longer than one call.}
Wrong: keep results in a class attribute, a default argument, or a global name.
A judge can call the method many times, and old results then leak into new answers.
Right: create all state inside the method. Define a cached helper inside the method too,
so that its cache starts empty for each input.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class SolutionWrong:
    found = []                     # a class attribute: one list for all calls
    def evens(self, nums):
        for x in nums:
            if x % 2 == 0:
                self.found.append(x)
        return self.found
class Solution:
    def evens(self, nums):
        found = []                 # new state for each call
        for x in nums:
            if x % 2 == 0:
                found.append(x)
        return found
SolutionWrong().evens([2, 3])      # -> [2]
SolutionWrong().evens([4])         # -> [2, 4]
Solution().evens([2, 3]), Solution().evens([4])   # -> ([2], [4])
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{State design}\label{pit:state}
Keep each fact in one place, and give each state an explicit value.
Clever shortcuts in the state save a line, but they are hard to check.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{One fact, one place.}
Wrong: two parallel structures for one fact, such as a list of values and a list of flags,
or a DP array together with a separate ``reachable'' array.
A change to one structure without the other moves the facts out of line.
Right: keep one list of records, or let one value encode every case, for example \cd{float("inf")} for ``not reachable''.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
names, alive = ["a", "b", "c"], [True, False, True]
del names[0]                         # the flag list still has its old first entry
list(zip(names, alive))              # -> [('b', True), ('c', False)]
items = [["a", True], ["b", False], ["c", True]]
del items[0]                         # one list: the facts move together
items                                # -> [['b', False], ['c', True]]
\end{pyex}
The same rule applies to a design with two structures, such as a dict and a linked list in a cache.
Change both structures in the same method, every time.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Explicit states, not destructive tricks.}
Wrong: one visited set for a cycle check in a directed graph, or a ``done'' mark that destroys the input,
such as an emptied adjacency list. One set cannot tell ``on the current path'' from ``finished'',
so two paths to one node look like a cycle.
Right: three states: 0 for new, 1 for on the current path, 2 for finished.
Kahn's algorithm (Section~\ref{sec:graph-structure}, Template 1) avoids the problem too.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def has_cycle_wrong(graph):
    seen = set()
    def dfs(u):
        if u in seen:
            return True                  # "seen before" is not "on the current path"
        seen.add(u)
        return any(dfs(v) for v in graph[u])
    return any(dfs(u) for u in graph if u not in seen)
def has_cycle(graph):
    state = {u: 0 for u in graph}        # 0 new, 1 on the current path, 2 finished
    def dfs(u):
        state[u] = 1
        for v in graph[u]:
            if state[v] == 1 or (state[v] == 0 and dfs(v)):
                return True
        state[u] = 2
        return False
    return any(state[u] == 0 and dfs(u) for u in graph)
diamond = {0: [1, 2], 1: [3], 2: [3], 3: []}
has_cycle_wrong(diamond), has_cycle(diamond)     # -> (True, False)
has_cycle({0: [1], 1: [0]})                      # -> True
\end{pyex}
Other rules for visited state:
\begin{itemize}
  \item In an undirected graph, the edge back to the parent is not a cycle. Pass the parent to the search, and skip it.
  \item Union-find: compare \cd{find(a)} with \cd{find(b)}, never \cd{parent[a]} with \cd{parent[b]}. Link a root to a root.
  \item Two searches that answer two questions need two visited sets (Pacific Atlantic Water Flow).
  \item BFS marks a node when it pushes the node (Section~\ref{pit:perf}).
        Dijkstra makes a node final only when it pops the node, because a later push can carry a smaller distance.
        Skip a popped entry that is larger than the best known distance.
  \item A search with a limit, such as at most $k$ stops, can need a second visit to one node with fewer stops.
        Put the limit in the state, or do not mark the nodes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Progress as an index.}
Wrong: build a new string or list in each step to record how far a search is,
when an index already holds that information.
Right: pass the index, and build the output one time at the end.
The code is shorter, and each step costs $O(1)$ instead of $O(n)$.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recursion}\label{pit:rec}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The depth limit.}
Wrong: a recursive search on a structure with a long path. The default limit is 1000 frames.
Examples are a $300 \times 300$ grid (depth up to 90{,}000), a linked list with 5000 nodes,
a skewed tree, and a memoized \cd{f(i - 1)} for $i$ up to $10^4$.
Right: use a loop with an explicit stack or queue.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def corridor_wrong(n):             # flood fill a row of n open cells
    seen = set()
    def dfs(c):
        if c < 0 or c >= n or c in seen:
            return
        seen.add(c)
        dfs(c + 1)
        dfs(c - 1)
    dfs(0)
    return len(seen)
def corridor(n):
    seen, stack = {0}, [0]
    while stack:
        c = stack.pop()
        for nc in (c + 1, c - 1):
            if 0 <= nc < n and nc not in seen:
                seen.add(nc)
                stack.append(nc)
    return len(seen)
corridor_wrong(300)                # -> 300
corridor_wrong(5000)               # -> raises RecursionError
corridor(5000)                     # -> 5000
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A function that calls itself is a DFS with a depth limit, whatever its name.
        A BFS uses a queue and a loop, and it has no depth limit.
  \item The depth is the longest chain of nested calls, not the number of calls.
        Estimate it from the worst input shape: one long path, a grid that is all land, a tree that is a chain.
  \item Some judges raise the limit. Code can then pass on one platform and fail on another platform or on a local run.
  \item \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit} raises the Python limit only. Very deep recursion can still overflow the
        C stack and stop the process with no Python traceback. The risk is highest on Python 3.10 and older,
        and when the calls go through C code, such as a \cd{@cache} wrapper.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion that should be a loop.}
Wrong: one recursive call for each step of a simulation that never branches.
Python does not remove tail calls, so 3000 steps need 3000 frames.
Right: a \cd{for} loop.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def final_pos_wrong(program, i=0, pos=0):
    if i == len(program):
        return pos
    step = 1 if program[i] == "R" else -1
    return final_pos_wrong(program, i + 1, pos + step)   # one frame per command
def final_pos(program):
    pos = 0
    for ch in program:
        pos += 1 if ch == "R" else -1
    return pos
final_pos_wrong("R" * 3000)        # -> raises RecursionError
final_pos("R" * 3000)              # -> 3000
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A missing memo.}
Wrong: a correct recurrence with overlapping states and no cache. The number of calls grows like $2^n$.
Right: add \cd{@cache}, or fill a table.
The cost with a cache is the number of distinct states times the work for one state.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
def best_margin(nums, use_cache):   # first player's best score minus the second player's
    calls = [0]
    def f(i, j):
        calls[0] += 1
        if i > j:
            return 0
        return max(nums[i] - f(i + 1, j), nums[j] - f(i, j - 1))
    if use_cache:
        f = cache(f)                # the recursive calls also go through the cache
    return f(0, len(nums) - 1), calls[0]
nums = [3, 9, 1, 2] * 4             # 16 numbers
best_margin(nums, False)            # -> (28, 131071)
best_margin(nums, True)             # -> (28, 153)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The memo key and the ``not computed'' mark.}
Wrong: a key that leaves out state that the answer depends on.
Also wrong: a test such as \cd{if memo.get(i):}, which treats a stored 0 as ``not computed''.
Right: put every changing input in the key. Test with \cd{i in memo}, or use \cd{None} as the empty mark.
\end{caution}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A path search that marks used cells cannot use \cd{(r, c, i)} as a key.
        The answer also depends on the used cells (Word Search).
  \item A search that fills $k$ groups must put the set of used elements in the key, for example as a bitmask.
  \item Check that a move is allowed before you use the cached answer of the next state.
        The cache does not know the move (Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix).
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def calls_needed(test_with_in):
    memo, calls = {}, 0
    def ways(i):                         # every answer is 0 in this example
        nonlocal calls
        calls += 1
        if i < 2:
            return 0
        if test_with_in:
            if i in memo:                # right: a stored 0 is found
                return memo[i]
        elif memo.get(i):                # wrong: a stored 0 looks like "not computed"
            return memo[i]
        memo[i] = ways(i - 1) + ways(i - 2)
        return memo[i]
    ways(20)
    return calls
calls_needed(False), calls_needed(True)  # -> (21891, 39)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A value on every path.}
Wrong: a recursive call whose result is not returned. The function then falls off the end and returns \cd{None}.
Right: return a value on every path. Combine the results of the branches with \cd{or}, \cd{and}, \cd{max} or \cd{+}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def contains_wrong(t, x):               # t is None or (value, left, right)
    if t is None:
        return False
    if t[0] == x:
        return True
    contains_wrong(t[1], x) or contains_wrong(t[2], x)    # the result is lost
def contains(t, x):
    if t is None:
        return False
    return t[0] == x or contains(t[1], x) or contains(t[2], x)
tree = (1, (2, None, None), None)
contains_wrong(tree, 2)                 # -> None
contains(tree, 2)                       # -> True
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Greedy choices and DP tables}\label{pit:dp}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A greedy with no proof.}
Wrong: take the choice that looks best now, such as the largest coin, the larger end, or the longest word that matches.
Right: try to break the rule on a small input first. If a choice now removes a better choice later, use DP.
A brute-force cross-check on all small inputs finds a counterexample quickly (Section~\ref{pit:brute}).
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def coins_greedy(coins, amount):           # the largest coin first
    count = 0
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        count += amount // c
        amount %= c
    return count if amount == 0 else -1
def coins_dp(coins, amount):
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount              # dp[a]: the fewest coins for the amount a
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] < INF else -1
coins_greedy([1, 3, 4], 6), coins_dp([1, 3, 4], 6)   # -> (3, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The base case.}
Wrong: \cd{dp[0] = 0} in a count of ways. Every later entry is then 0.
Right: the empty case has one way, which is to do nothing. Use \cd{dp[0] = 1} for a count,
and \cd{dp[0] = True} for a yes-or-no question.
Fill the first row and the first column of a 2-D table from the meaning of an empty prefix.
An example is \cd{dp[i][0] = i} in an edit distance.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def ways(coins, amount, base):             # the number of coin combinations
    dp = [base] + [0] * amount
    for c in coins:
        for a in range(c, amount + 1):
            dp[a] += dp[a - c]
    return dp[amount]
ways([1, 2], 3, base=0), ways([1, 2], 3, base=1)   # -> (0, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The meaning of dp[i], and the place of the answer.}
Wrong: define \cd{dp[i]} as ``the best result that ends at index $i$'', and then return \cd{dp[-1]}.
Right: write the meaning of \cd{dp[i]} in one sentence before you write code.
If \cd{dp[i]} ends at $i$, the answer is \cd{max(dp)}. If \cd{dp[i]} covers the first $i$ elements, the answer is \cd{dp[n]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def lis_ending_at(a):          # dp[i]: the longest increasing subsequence that ends at index i
    dp = [1] * len(a)
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(i):
            if a[j] < a[i]:
                dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)
    return dp
dp = lis_ending_at([1, 2, 3, 0])
dp[-1], max(dp)                # -> (1, 3)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The loop order decides what the DP counts.}
Wrong: swap the two loops of a count of ways.
Right: put the items in the outer loop to count combinations, where the order does not matter.
Put the amounts in the outer loop to count ordered sequences.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def combinations(coins, amount):           # items outside: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are one answer
    dp = [1] + [0] * amount
    for c in coins:
        for a in range(c, amount + 1):
            dp[a] += dp[a - c]
    return dp[amount]
def sequences(coins, amount):              # amounts outside: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are two answers
    dp = [1] + [0] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] += dp[a - c]
    return dp[amount]
combinations([1, 2], 3), sequences([1, 2], 3)      # -> (2, 3)
\end{pyex}
Other DP rules:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Fill each entry after the entries that it reads. If \cd{dp[i][j]} reads \cd{dp[i + 1][j - 1]}, loop \cd{i} downward,
        or fill by the length of the range (palindromes, interval DP, two-player games).
  \item A 1-D table that is reused for each item changes its meaning with the direction of the loop.
        See the synchronous updates in Section~\ref{pit:mut}.
  \item Keep one convention for each state. For example, \cd{dp[i]} includes \cd{cost[i]}, or it does not.
        A mix of the two adds or drops one cost.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Hashing and membership}\label{pit:hash}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The order of lookup and insert.}
Wrong: add the current element to the map before you look up its partner. The element can then pair with itself.
Right: look up first, then insert. For prefix-sum counts, start the map with \cd{{0: 1}} for the empty prefix.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def two_sum_wrong(nums, target):
    pos = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        pos[x] = i                       # insert before the lookup
        if target - x in pos:
            return [pos[target - x], i]
def two_sum(nums, target):
    pos = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in pos:            # look up first: x cannot pair with itself
            return [pos[target - x], i]
        pos[x] = i
two_sum_wrong([3, 2, 4], 6)              # -> [0, 0]
two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6), two_sum([3, 3], 6)   # -> ([1, 2], [0, 1])
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Unhashable keys and keys that lose information.}
Wrong: a list as a set element or a dict key. This raises \cd{TypeError}.
Also wrong: a key that loses information, such as a set of letters, a sum of character codes,
or numbers joined with no separator. Different inputs then get the same key.
Right: a tuple, a sorted string, a tuple of counts, or a \cd{frozenset} when the order does not matter and no element repeats.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
seen = set()
seen.add([1, 2])                                # -> raises TypeError
seen.add((1, 2))
(1, 2) in seen                                  # -> True
set("aab") == set("abb")                        # -> True
sum(map(ord, "bc")) == sum(map(ord, "ad"))      # -> True
"".join(map(str, [1, 11])) == "".join(map(str, [11, 1]))   # -> True
def count_key(word):                            # a full count vector as a tuple
    counts = [0] * 26
    for ch in word:
        counts[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
    return tuple(counts)
count_key("aab") == count_key("abb"), count_key("bc") == count_key("ad")   # -> (False, False)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A read that inserts.}
Wrong: \cd{d[k]} on a \cd{defaultdict} to test or read a key. The read inserts the key with a default value.
Later membership tests then pass, and a loop over the dict can raise \cd{RuntimeError}.
Right: \cd{k in d}, \cd{d.get(k, default)}, or a \cd{Counter}. A \cd{Counter} returns 0 for a missing key and does not insert it.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict, Counter
d = defaultdict(list)
len(d["x"])                    # -> 0
"x" in d                       # -> True
d = defaultdict(int, {"a": 1})
for k in d:
    d[k + "!"] += 0
# -> raises RuntimeError
c = Counter()
c["x"]                         # -> 0
"x" in c                       # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The truth value of a stored value.}
Wrong: \cd{if cache.get(k):} when 0, \cd{""} or \cd{[]} are valid stored values.
Right: \cd{if k in cache:}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
cache = {"a": 0}
"hit" if cache.get("a") else "miss"      # -> 'miss'
"hit" if "a" in cache else "miss"        # -> 'hit'
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Counter subtraction drops negative counts.}
Wrong: test that two strings have equal letter counts with \cd{Counter(a) - Counter(b) == Counter()}.
The subtraction keeps only positive counts, so the test proves only that \cd{b} covers \cd{a}.
Right: \cd{Counter(a) == Counter(b)}, or check that the lengths are equal too.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
Counter("ab") - Counter("abc") == Counter()     # -> True
Counter("ab") == Counter("abc")                 # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Equal-looking values of different types.}
Wrong: compare a tuple with a list, or a digit character with an integer. The result is always \cd{False}, and no error appears.
Right: convert one side, so that both sides have the same type.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
(2, 7) == [2, 7]                 # -> False
tuple([2, 7]) == (2, 7)          # -> True
"1" == 1                         # -> False
len({1, "1"})                    # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Membership in a list costs $O(n)$. Convert the list to a set one time, before the loop.
        Look for hidden list scans: \cd{x in nums[:i]}, \cd{nums.index(x)}, and a test against an input list
        of forbidden states.
  \item A set lookup is $O(1)$ on average, not in the worst case. Say ``expected time'' in an interview.
  \item An array indexed by value works only for a small value range. For values up to $10^9$, use a dict.
  \item The iteration order of a set of strings can change between runs. Sort before you print or compare.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Comparison, ties and sorting}\label{pit:cmp}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Strict or non-strict.}
Wrong: \cd{<} where the statement needs \cd{<=}, or the opposite.
Right: take the strictness from the statement, and then test an input with equal values.
Equal values are the only inputs where the two forms differ.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def days_to_warmer(t, pop_on_equal):
    res, stack = [0] * len(t), []          # the stack keeps indexes
    for i, x in enumerate(t):
        while stack and (t[stack[-1]] <= x if pop_on_equal else t[stack[-1]] < x):
            j = stack.pop()
            res[j] = i - j
        stack.append(i)
    return res
days_to_warmer([70, 70, 71], pop_on_equal=True)    # -> [1, 1, 0]
days_to_warmer([70, 70, 71], pop_on_equal=False)   # -> [2, 1, 0]
\end{pyex}
``Warmer'' is strict, so the second result is correct. Other places where strictness decides the answer:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Intervals that touch: Merge Intervals joins \cd{[1, 2]} and \cd{[2, 3]}, so its overlap test is \cd{s <= end}.
        A meeting that ends at $t$ does not conflict with one that starts at $t$,
        so the conflict test is \cd{s < end} (Meeting Rooms).
  \item Validate Binary Search Tree needs a strict order: an equal value in a subtree makes the tree invalid.
  \item ``No ancestor is greater'' means \cd{>=}: a node equal to the path maximum counts (Count Good Nodes).
  \item Equal arrival times form one group (Car Fleet).
  \item A sliding window ``at most $k$'' shrinks while the window is above $k$, not while it equals $k$.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Ties in a best choice.}
Wrong: update the best index on \cd{>=} when the statement asks for the first maximum.
Right: \cd{>} keeps the first maximum, and \cd{>=} keeps the last. \cd{max} and \cd{min} return the first one.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
sizes = [3, 5, 5]
best = 0
for i in range(1, len(sizes)):
    if sizes[i] >= sizes[best]:
        best = i
best                                             # -> 2
max(range(len(sizes)), key=lambda i: sizes[i])   # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The start value of a running best.}
Wrong: start a maximum at 0, or a minimum at 0. For all-negative input, a maximum of 0 is not a real answer.
For all-positive input, a minimum of 0 never changes.
Right: start from the first element, or from \cd{float("-inf")} or \cd{float("inf")}.
Do not use a sentinel that can be a real value, such as \cd{-2**31} when the input can hold \cd{-2**31}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def max_sub_wrong(a):                  # largest sum of a non-empty subarray
    best = cur = 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
def max_sub(a):
    best, cur = float("-inf"), 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
max_sub_wrong([-3, -1])                # -> 0
max_sub([-3, -1])                      # -> -1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Compare with the running value, not with the neighbor.}
Wrong: compare an element only with the previous element, or a tree node only with its parent.
Right: compare with a summary of everything before it (Car Fleet, Count Good Nodes, Validate Binary Search Tree).
Examples are the end of the current merged group, the running maximum, and the bounds from all ancestors.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def groups_wrong(iv):                  # iv is sorted by start; count the merged groups
    count = 1
    for k in range(1, len(iv)):
        if iv[k][0] > iv[k - 1][1]:    # compares with the previous interval only
            count += 1
    return count
def groups(iv):
    count, end = 1, iv[0][1]
    for s, e in iv[1:]:
        if s > end:
            count += 1
        end = max(end, e)              # the running end of the current group
    return count
iv = [[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]]
groups_wrong(iv), groups(iv)           # -> (2, 1)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Sort keys and pairs.}
Wrong: sort two parallel lists separately, or sort the queries and lose their original positions.
Right: sort pairs made with \cd{zip}, or sort a list of indexes and write each answer at its original index.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
position, speed = [10, 0, 5], [1, 3, 2]
sorted(zip(position, speed))           # -> [(0, 3), (5, 2), (10, 1)]
queries = [50, 10, 30]
order = sorted(range(len(queries)), key=lambda i: queries[i])
smaller = [0] * len(queries)           # how many queries are smaller
for rank, i in enumerate(order):
    smaller[i] = rank                  # the answer goes to the original index
smaller                                # -> [2, 0, 1]
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Python sorts are stable. Sort by a tuple key, or sort by the secondary key first and by the primary key second.
  \item A heap is not stable. Equal priorities compare the next field of the tuple.
        Put a counter before a payload that cannot be compared.
  \item \cd{heapq} is a min-heap. For a max-heap, negate the key when you push and again when you pop.
        To keep the $k$ largest values, keep a min-heap and pop its smallest value when the size goes above $k$.
  \item A greedy depends on its sort key. Sort intervals by start to merge them.
        Sort them by end to keep the most intervals that do not overlap. A wrong key gives a plausible wrong count.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Numbers}\label{pit:num}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Floats in integer problems.}
Wrong: \cd{a / b}, \cd{math.ceil(a / b)} or \cd{int(a / b)} with large integers.
A float keeps 53 bits of precision, so integers above $2^{53} \approx 9 \times 10^{15}$ can lose digits.
Right: stay in integers. Use \cd{a // b}, \cd{-(-a // b)} for the ceiling,
and cross-multiplication to compare fractions.
When the answer is a float, compare it in your tests with \cd{math.isclose}, not with \cd{==}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import math
a = 10**17 + 1
int(a / 1) == a                          # -> False
a // 1 == a                              # -> True
math.ceil(a / 10) == -(-a // 10)         # -> False
-(-a // 10)                              # -> 10000000000000001
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3                         # -> False
math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)             # -> True
p, q, r, s = 1, 3, 2, 6                  # compare p/q with r/s (q and s positive)
p * s == r * q                           # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative numbers with // and the modulo operator.}
Wrong: expect \cd{-7 // 2} to give \cd{-3}, or \cd{-123} \pct{} \cd{10} to give \cd{3}.
Python rounds toward negative infinity, and \pct{} takes the sign of the divisor.
Right: for a quotient toward zero, divide the absolute values and restore the sign.
For digits, work on \cd{abs(n)} and keep the sign apart.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
-7 // 2, -123 % 10, -123 // 10       # -> (-4, 7, -13)
def div_toward_zero(a, b):           # exact, also for very large integers
    q = abs(a) // abs(b)
    return q if (a < 0) == (b < 0) else -q
div_toward_zero(-7, 2)               # -> -3
def digits(n):
    sign, n = (-1 if n < 0 else 1), abs(n)
    out = []
    while n:
        n, d = divmod(n, 10)
        out.append(d)
    return sign, out[::-1]
digits(-123)                         # -> (-1, [1, 2, 3])
(0 - 1) % 10                         # -> 9
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
The modulo of a negative number is useful for wrap-around: a wheel digit 0 turned down gives
\cd{(0 - 1)} \pct{} \cd{10}, which is 9. C, C++ and Java round toward zero, and there \cd{-1} \pct{} \cd{10} is \cd{-1}.
In those languages, write \cd{(d + 9)} \pct{} \cd{10}.
\end{note}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Overflow in other languages.}
Python integers never overflow. But an interviewer can ask about a fixed-width language,
and some problems define 32-bit limits.
Wrong: assume that a value fits because each input value fits.
Right: compare the largest intermediate value with $2^{31} - 1 \approx 2.1 \times 10^9$
and with $2^{63} - 1 \approx 9.2 \times 10^{18}$.
\end{caution}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A product of two values up to $10^5$ is up to $10^{10}$.
  \item A sum of $10^5$ values up to $10^9$ is up to $10^{14}$.
  \item A count of pairs or segments, $n(n + 1)/2$ for $n = 10^5$, is about $5 \times 10^9$.
  \item \cd{lo + hi} in a binary search can overflow. Write \cd{lo + (hi - lo) / 2} in those languages.
  \item Intermediate DP counts can be much larger than the final answer.
  \item For a problem that defines a 32-bit result, test the range in Python too: \cd{-2**31 <= x <= 2**31 - 1}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative numbers in bit tricks.}
Wrong: \cd{while n: n &= n - 1} on a negative Python integer.
Python integers have no fixed width, so a negative number has infinitely many leading 1 bits, and the loop never ends.
Right: mask to 32 bits first with \cd{n & 0xFFFFFFFF}.
To get the sign back, subtract \cd{2**32} when the masked value is above \cd{0x7FFFFFFF}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
n = -5
bin(n)                                   # -> '-0b101'
m = n & 0xFFFFFFFF                       # the 32-bit pattern of -5
bin(m).count("1")                        # -> 31
m if m <= 0x7FFFFFFF else m - 2**32      # -> -5
2 ^ 3, 2 ** 3                            # -> (1, 8)
3 + 1 & 1, 3 + (1 & 1)                   # -> (0, 4)
1 << 2 + 1, (1 << 2) + 1                 # -> (8, 5)
\end{pyex}
The last three lines show two more traps. First, \cd{^} is XOR, not a power.
Second, \cd{+} and \cd{-} bind more tightly than \shl{} and \shr{}, and these bind more tightly than \cd{&}, \cd{^} and \cd{|}.
Put parentheses around each bit operation in a mixed expression, for example \cd{ans[i // 2] + (i & 1)}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Performance traps}\label{pit:perf}
A time limit result often comes from one line that does hidden $O(n)$ work inside a loop.
The code looks like $O(n)$, but it runs in $O(n^2)$.
Part I lists the cost of each operation. The table below lists the patterns that hide this cost, and the fix for each one.
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{5.4cm}L{4.0cm}L{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Code inside a loop & Hidden cost & Fix \\
\midrule
\endhead
\cd{x in lst}, \cd{lst.index(x)} & a scan of the list & a set, or a dict from value to index \\
\cd{q.pop(0)}, \cd{q.insert(0, x)} & a shift of all elements & \cd{collections.deque} \\
\cd{s[i + 1:]} in a recursive call & a copy of the rest & pass the index \cd{i + 1} \\
\cd{sum(path)} & a pass over the path & carry a running total as an argument \\
\cd{len(set(window))} & a pass over the window & keep a count map of the window \\
\cd{max(a[i:i + k])} & a copy and a pass & a monotonic deque \\
\cd{s += ch}, \cd{path + [x]} & a copy of the whole list, and often of the whole string & append to a list; \cd{"".join} once at the end \\
a slice of the best answer at each update & a copy per update & keep the start and the length; slice once \\
\cd{sorted(...)} for each query & $O(n \log n)$ per query & sort once, or keep a heap \\
a new copy of the grid in each step, when few cells change & $O(R \cdot C)$ per step & change only the cells that change \\
\cd{print(...)} & slow output & remove it, or collect the output and print once \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The same value computed again at every node.}
Wrong: call a helper such as \cd{height(node)} at every node of a tree. On a chain-shaped tree this is $O(n^2)$.
Right: one post-order pass that returns every value that the parent needs, for example \cd{(height, best)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
calls = 0
def height(t):                         # t is None or (left, right)
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return 0 if t is None else 1 + max(height(t[0]), height(t[1]))
def diameter_slow(t):                  # calls height() at every node
    if t is None:
        return 0
    through = height(t[0]) + height(t[1])
    return max(through, diameter_slow(t[0]), diameter_slow(t[1]))
def diameter_fast(t):                  # one pass returns (height, best)
    if t is None:
        return 0, 0
    lh, lb = diameter_fast(t[0])
    rh, rb = diameter_fast(t[1])
    return 1 + max(lh, rh), max(lb, rb, lh + rh)
t = None
for _ in range(200):
    t = (t, None)                      # a chain of 200 nodes
diameter_slow(t), calls                # -> (199, 40200)
diameter_fast(t)[1]                    # -> 199
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Mark a node when you push it.}
Wrong: mark a cell as visited when you pop it. The same cell can then enter the queue several times.
The answer stays correct, but the work grows.
Right: mark the cell when you push it.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
def pushes(R, C, mark_on_push):        # BFS over an open R x C grid
    seen = {(0, 0)} if mark_on_push else set()
    q, count = deque([(0, 0)]), 1
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        if not mark_on_push:
            if (r, c) in seen:
                continue
            seen.add((r, c))
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r - 1, c), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and (nr, nc) not in seen:
                if mark_on_push:
                    seen.add((nr, nc))
                q.append((nr, nc))
                count += 1
    return count
pushes(30, 30, True), pushes(30, 30, False)    # -> (900, 1741)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Debug output in a hot loop.}
Wrong: \cd{print} calls inside a loop that runs $10^5$ times. The output is slow, and the run looks like a time limit.
Right: remove debug output before you submit, or send it through one function that you can switch off
(see the \cd{log} helper in the next section).
\end{caution}

Input shapes that make a correct solution slow:
\begin{itemize}
  \item A quickselect with a fixed pivot is $O(n^2)$ on sorted input. Use a random pivot.
        Many equal values can make the parts uneven, even with a random pivot.
        Use a three-way partition: less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot.
  \item A loop over a list with many duplicates repeats work. A loop over a set does the work once for each value.
  \item A backtracking search that passes small tests can time out on a crafted input, such as many equal values
        or a board of one repeated letter. Prune early, and skip equal choices at the same level.
  \item A full table of $10^4 \times 10^4$ cells is $10^8$ entries: too slow and too large in Python.
        Keep only the rows that the recurrence reads.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Input shapes}\label{pit:shape}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A grid of strings.}
Wrong: compare a cell with the integer 1, or assign to a cell of a string row. Strings are immutable.
Right: compare with \cd{"1"}. Convert with \cd{[list(row) for row in grid]} when you must write,
or keep a separate visited set.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
grid = ["10",
        "01"]
grid[0][0] == 1              # -> False
grid[0][0] == "1"            # -> True
grid[0][0] = "#"             # -> raises TypeError
cells = [list(row) for row in grid]
cells[0][0] = "#"
cells[0]                     # -> ['#', '0']
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rows and columns.}
Wrong: use the row count where the column count belongs. A square test input hides this bug.
Right: name \cd{R = len(grid)} and \cd{C = len(grid[0])} one time.
For a flat index \cd{i}, the cell is \cd{(i // C, i} \pct{} \cd{C)}.
Test a $2 \times 3$ grid, a $3 \times 2$ grid, a $1 \times n$ grid and an $n \times 1$ grid.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
m = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6]]                       # 2 rows, 3 columns
R, C = len(m), len(m[0])
[m[i // C][i % C] for i in range(R * C)]    # -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
m[4 // R][4 % R]                      # -> raises IndexError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Empty input, None, and an empty stack.}
Wrong: read \cd{grid[0]}, \cd{nums[0]}, \cd{root.val}, \cd{stack[-1]} or \cd{heap[0]} before a check.
Right: guard first, for example \cd{C = len(grid[0]) if grid else 0}, \cd{if root is None: return 0},
or \cd{while stack and ...}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
grid = []
len(grid[0])                          # -> raises IndexError
C = len(grid[0]) if grid else 0
C                                     # -> 0
stack = []
stack[-1]                             # -> raises IndexError
bool(stack and stack[-1] == ")")      # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A value of 0 is not a missing node.}
Wrong: \cd{if not node.val} or \cd{if not x} to find a missing node or a missing value.
A node with the value 0 is still a node.
Right: \cd{if node is None}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
def size_wrong(node):
    if not node or not node.val:      # a node with value 0 looks missing
        return 0
    return 1 + size_wrong(node.left) + size_wrong(node.right)
def size(node):
    if node is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + size(node.left) + size(node.right)
root = TreeNode(0, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(2))
size_wrong(root), size(root)          # -> (0, 3)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Tokens.}
Wrong: find an operator by its first character or by a substring test. The number \cd{"-11"} starts with \cd{"-"}.
Right: compare the whole token with a set of operators. Read a number as one whole token, not digit by digit.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
tokens = ["-11", "3", "-"]
[t for t in tokens if t[0] in "+-*/"]         # -> ['-11', '-']
OPS = {"+", "-", "*", "/"}
[t for t in tokens if t in OPS]               # -> ['-']
text = "12,-3,7"
[int(t) for t in text.split(",")]             # -> [12, -3, 7]
[ch for ch in text if ch.isdigit()]           # -> ['1', '2', '3', '7']
\end{pyex}
The last line shows why a digit-by-digit read fails: it splits 12 and loses the sign of $-3$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Labels from 1 to $n$: size the arrays $n + 1$, or subtract 1 from each label.
  \item An undirected edge goes into both adjacency lists.
