  \item Node ids are not always $0$ to $n - 1$. Size an array by the largest id, or use a dict.
  \item The input is not sorted unless the statement says so, even when all the examples are sorted.
  \item A linked list or a tree can be empty. The head or the root is then \cd{None}.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Output format}\label{pit:out}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The requested value.}
Wrong: return values when the statement asks for indexes, a count when it asks for the items,
or a margin when it asks for a score.
Right: read the return type in the signature and in the examples before you write code.
Frequent pairs: index or value, size or string, node or \cd{node.val}, 0-based or 1-based index.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The impossible case.}
Wrong: return \cd{None}, infinity, or an internal sentinel such as \cd{amount + 1}.
Right: convert to the value that the statement gives, such as \cd{-1}, \cd{[]}, \cd{""} or \cd{0}, in one place at the end.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Integer or float.}
Wrong: \cd{(a + b) // 2} for a median or an average that can end in .5.
Right: \cd{(a + b) / 2}. Do not round a float result unless the statement asks for it.
Decimal places in the examples are often only for display.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
a, b = 2, 3
(a + b) // 2, (a + b) / 2             # -> (2, 2.5)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Return or print.}
Wrong: print the answer in a function problem, or return it in a program that reads standard input.
Right: a function problem needs \cd{return}. A standard-input problem needs output in the exact format:
the separators, one answer on each line, and the spelling of booleans.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
res = [3, 1, 4]
print(*res)                           # prints: 3 1 4
print(res)                            # prints: [3, 1, 4]
print("\n".join(map(str, res)))       # prints: 3 | 1 | 4
print(f"{2 / 3:.6f}")                 # prints: 0.666667
print(str(True).lower())              # prints: true
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Keep the original order of the answers when the queries were sorted.
  \item When the judge accepts any order, sort the outputs in your own tests before you compare them.
  \item Use the exact method name and signature of the template, including names such as \cd{startsWith}.
  \item Return lists when the checker compares lists. A strict local checker sees \cd{(1, 2) != [1, 2]}.
\end{itemize}

% =====================================================================
\section{Debug and verify a solution}\label{pit:debug}
Test a solution before you submit it. Three checks find most bugs:
a hand trace of a small example, a list of edge cases, and a comparison with a brute force on many small inputs.
A fourth check, a timed run on a maximum-size input, finds time limit problems.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Hand-trace a small example}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Choose the smallest input that uses every branch of the code. Three to six elements are usually enough.
  \item Make one column for each variable that changes, and one row for each loop pass.
  \item Fill the rows from the code, not from what the code should do.
  \item Compare each row with the value that you expect. The first row that is different shows the bug.
\end{enumerate}
In an interview, trace the example of the statement aloud. The trace also finds rules that you read wrongly.
A debug print gives the same table quickly:
\begin{pyex}
def lower_bound(a, x, debug=False):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if debug:
            print(f"lo={lo} hi={hi} mid={mid} a[mid]={a[mid]}")
        if a[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo
lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 7], 5, debug=True)
# prints: lo=0 hi=4 mid=2 a[mid]=5 | lo=0 hi=2 mid=1 a[mid]=3
lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 7], 5)          # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Send debug output through one function. Then one flag switches all of it off, and standard error
keeps it apart from the answer.
\begin{pyex}
import sys
DEBUG = False
def log(*args):
    if DEBUG:
        print(*args, file=sys.stderr)
log("state:", [1, 2])                 # prints nothing while DEBUG is False
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Test the edge cases}
Run each case that fits the input type. Decide the expected answer from the statement before you run the code.
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{2.6cm}L{13.8cm}@{}}
\toprule
Input type & Cases to test \\
\midrule
\endhead
Array & empty; one element; two elements; all equal; all distinct; sorted; reverse sorted;
negative values; zeros; duplicates of the answer value; the target at the first and the last index; no valid answer \\
String & empty; one character; all one letter; no letter repeats; upper and lower case; digits and punctuation;
the pattern longer than the text \\
Grid & $1 \times 1$; $1 \times n$; $n \times 1$; not square ($2 \times 3$ and $3 \times 2$); all one value;
no target cell; a region that touches the border; a long snake-shaped path \\
Graph & one node; no edges; isolated nodes; two components; a self loop; a cycle; a duplicate edge;
a long chain (depth); a star (high degree); labels from 1 to $n$ \\
Tree or list & empty (\cd{None}); one node; a chain to the left; a chain to the right; a value of 0;
negative values; duplicate values \\
Intervals & touching end points; one inside another; equal intervals; unsorted input; one interval \\
Numbers & 0; 1; negative; the minimum and the maximum of the constraints; values near $2^{31}$ \\
Parameters & $k = 0$; $k = 1$; $k = n$; $k$ larger than $n$; a target of 0; an answer of 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
A small generator keeps the edge cases in one place. Run the solution on each case,
and compare each result with the answer that you expect.
\begin{pyex}
def edge_arrays(n=6, lo=-3, hi=3):
    yield []                              # empty
    yield [lo]                            # one element
    yield [hi] * n                        # all equal
    yield [0] * n                         # all zero
    yield list(range(n))                  # sorted
    yield list(range(n, 0, -1))           # reverse sorted
    yield [lo, hi] * (n // 2)             # alternating
    yield [lo] * (n - 1) + [hi]           # the special value at the last index
def longest_run(a):                       # the solution under test
    if not a:
        return 0
    best = cur = 1
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        cur = cur + 1 if a[i] == a[i - 1] else 1
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
[longest_run(a) for a in edge_arrays()]   # -> [0, 1, 6, 6, 1, 1, 1, 5]
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-check with a brute force}\label{pit:brute}
Write the simplest correct solution: try all subarrays, all subsets, or all orders.
It is slow, but it is easy to get right.
Then compare it with the fast solution on every small input and on many random inputs.
The template below returns the first input where the two solutions give different results.
\begin{pyex}
import random
from itertools import product
def brute(a):                          # simple and slow: try every subarray
    return max(sum(a[i:j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a) + 1))
def fast_wrong(a):                     # the solution under test
    best = cur = 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
def fast(a):
    best, cur = float("-inf"), 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
def all_small_inputs():                # every list of length 1 to 4, values -2 to 2
    for n in range(1, 5):
        for t in product(range(-2, 3), repeat=n):
            yield list(t)
def random_inputs(count, seed=1):
    rng = random.Random(seed)          # a fixed seed: a failure repeats
    for _ in range(count):
        n = rng.randint(1, 8)
        yield [rng.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(n)]
def first_failure(solution, inputs):
    for a in inputs:
        got, want = solution(a), brute(a)
        if got != want:
            return a, got, want
    return None
first_failure(fast_wrong, all_small_inputs())       # -> ([-2], 0, -2)
first_failure(fast, all_small_inputs()) is None     # -> True
first_failure(fast, random_inputs(500)) is None     # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Generate the inputs in order of size. The first failure is then the smallest one, and it is easy to trace.
  \item Keep the value range small, for example $-2$ to $2$. Small ranges make duplicates, zeros and ties,
        which are the risky cases.
  \item Use \cd{random.Random(seed)}, so that a failure repeats on the next run.
  \item When many answers are valid, compare a normal form (for example, the sorted output),
        or write a checker that tests the properties of the answer.
  \item For a greedy, the brute force is a practical proof check. If all small inputs agree, the greedy is probably correct.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Assert invariants}
An invariant is a fact that must be true at a fixed point of each loop pass.
Write it as an \cd{assert} while you test. A failed assert stops at the first wrong step,
not at a wrong final answer many steps later.
\begin{pyex}
def longest_unique_wrong(s):           # longest substring with no repeated character
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last:
            left = last[ch] + 1        # wrong: left can move back
        last[ch] = right
        window = s[left:right + 1]
        assert len(set(window)) == len(window), (s, left, right)   # O(n): test only
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
def longest_unique(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last:
            left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)   # left never moves back
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
longest_unique_wrong("abba")           # -> raises AssertionError
longest_unique("abba")                 # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Invariants that are worth an assert:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Sliding window: after the shrink step, the window satisfies the condition.
  \item Binary search: the answer stays in \cd{[lo, hi]}, and the range gets smaller on every pass.
  \item Two heaps for a median: every value in the lower heap is at most every value in the upper heap,
        and the sizes differ by at most one.
  \item Monotonic stack: the values on the stack stay in order.
  \item Union-find: the number of components is $n$ minus the number of successful unions.
\end{itemize}
Remove expensive asserts before you submit. An $O(n)$ assert inside a loop makes the solution $O(n^2)$.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Read the error message}
Read the last line first. It gives the exception type and the message.
Then find the lowest frame in the traceback that is in your own code. That line raised the error.
\begin{pyshow}
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "solution.py", line 9, in <module>
    print(longest([]))
  File "solution.py", line 2, in longest
    best = nums[0]
IndexError: list index out of range
\end{pyshow}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{5.6cm}L{10.8cm}@{}}
\toprule
Error & Frequent cause \\
\midrule
\endhead
\cd{IndexError} & an off-by-one bound; an empty input; \cd{a[i + 1]} at the last index; \cd{stack[-1]} on an empty stack \\
\cd{KeyError} & a read of a missing key; use \cd{in}, \cd{get} or a \cd{defaultdict} \\
\cd{TypeError} that names \cd{NoneType} & a function with no \cd{return} on some path; \cd{a = a.sort()}; a missing node \\
\cd{TypeError}: unhashable type & a list or a dict used as a key or as a set element \\
\cd{TypeError}: \cd{<} not supported & a heap tie that compares payloads; a sort of mixed types or of \cd{None} \\
\cd{AttributeError} that names \cd{NoneType} & a step past the end of a linked list or a tree; a missing \cd{None} check \\
\cd{RecursionError} & depth above 1000; a base case that the code never reaches \\
\cd{UnboundLocalError} & an assignment to a name of an outer function without \cd{nonlocal}, or to a module name without \cd{global} \\
\cd{RuntimeError}: changed size & an insert or a delete during a loop over a dict or a set; a \cd{defaultdict} read in that loop \\
\cd{ValueError} from \cd{max} or \cd{min} & an empty input; use \cd{default=} or a guard \\
\cd{ZeroDivisionError} & a count of 0, for example no neighbors or a speed of 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Time a maximum-size input}
Build an input at the largest size that the constraints allow. Choose the shape that is worst for the code.
Then time the solution on that input.
\begin{pyex}
import random, time
def solve(a):                          # the solution under test
    best, cur = float("-inf"), 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
rng = random.Random(7)
n = 10**5                              # the largest n in the constraints
big = [rng.randint(-10**4, 10**4) for _ in range(n)]
start = time.perf_counter()
answer = solve(big)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
elapsed < 1.0                          # -> True
\end{pyex}
Shapes that often give the worst case:
\begin{itemize}
  \item sorted, reverse sorted, and all-equal arrays;
  \item a graph that is one long chain (depth), and a star graph (one node with every edge);
  \item a grid that is all one value, and a snake-shaped path through a grid;
  \item a string of one repeated letter, and a pattern that almost matches everywhere;
  \item the largest values, to check overflow in a fixed-width language.
\end{itemize}
To find the slow part, run the profiler: \cd{python3 -m cProfile -s cumtime solution.py}.
It lists the functions, with the largest cumulative time first.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{When a hidden test fails}
A judge result names the kind of failure. Each kind has a short list of usual causes.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.4cm}L{13cm}@{}}
\toprule
Result & Check first \\
\midrule
Wrong answer & the success condition and each rule of the statement; strict or non-strict comparisons;
the output format; empty and single-element input; negative indexes that wrap; shared rows or aliases;
work left after the loop; a greedy with no proof; the DP base case. Then run the brute-force cross-check. \\
Runtime error & empty input; index bounds; \cd{None} nodes; recursion depth; missing keys; division by zero. \\
Time limit & the complexity against the constraints; hidden $O(n)$ work in a loop; a loop with no progress
on a special input; a recursion with no memo; debug output. \\
Memory limit & a full table where two rows are enough; stored copies of every path; one copy of the input per step;
very deep recursion. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
After a fix, search the rest of the code for the same pattern.
A bug class, such as a missing lower bound check, usually appears in more than one place.

\section{Final checklist}\label{pit:final}
Do these checks in order after the code passes the given examples.
Section~\ref{pit:check} gives the detailed checklist by class of bug.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Read the output definition again. Check the type (int, bool, list, string) and the exact format.
  \item Check 0-based and 1-based indexes.
  \item Test the smallest input: empty list, one element, $1 \times 1$ grid, \cd{n = 1}.
  \item Test equal values, negative values and duplicates.
  \item Find hidden $O(n)$ work inside loops: \cd{in list}, \cd{pop(0)}, slices, \cd{sum}, string \cd{+=}.
  \item Check the recursion depth. Use a loop or raise the limit.
  \item Check that BFS marks nodes when it adds them to the queue.
  \item Check that backtracking appends copies.
  \item Check that a simultaneous update reads only old values.
  \item Check integer division, negative modulo and rounding rules.
  \item Remove debug \cd{print} calls.
\end{enumerate}

\part{Techniques}\label{part:techniques}

% =====================================================================
\section{Hashing: counting, membership and canonical keys}\label{tech:T01}

\subsection{The idea}
A hash set or a hash map is a memory of the items that a scan has already seen.
The hash function turns a key into a slot number. So a lookup goes straight to one slot and does not scan the items.
This gives $O(1)$ average time for each question about one exact key:
``did this key occur?'', ``where did it occur?'', ``how many times did it occur?'' and ``which items have it?''.
Many brute-force solutions have an inner loop that searches the earlier items for one exact value.
Replace that inner loop with one lookup. Then $O(n^2)$ work becomes $O(n)$ work.

The second use is the canonical key. Often two items are ``the same'' under a rule that ignores one detail,
for example the order of the letters. Compute a key that erases that detail.
Then equal keys mean the same class. One dictionary insert per item replaces all pairwise comparisons.

\textbf{Worked example: complement lookup.} Find two indexes in \cd{[3, 2, 4]} whose values add up to 6.
At index 0, the value is 3 and its partner must be $6 - 3 = 3$. The map is empty, so store \cd{3: 0}.
At index 1, the value is 2 and its partner must be 4. The map has no 4, so store \cd{2: 1}.
At index 2, the value is 4 and its partner must be 2. The map holds \cd{2: 1}, so the answer is \cd{[1, 2]}.
The brute force tests every pair. The map visits each element one time.

\textbf{Worked example: canonical key.} Group the words \cd{eat}, \cd{tea} and \cd{tan} by anagram class.
Sort the letters of each word. The keys are \cd{aet}, \cd{aet} and \cd{ant}.
The first two words have the same key, so they go into the same bucket.

The output of the problem tells you what to store for each key.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.2cm}L{6.4cm}L{5.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Store & Example \\
\midrule
Did this key occur? & a \cd{set} & Contains Duplicate \\
Where did it occur? & a \cd{dict} from key to index (first index for the longest range, last index for the nearest) & Two Sum \\
How many times? & a \cd{Counter} from key to count & Valid Anagram, Subarray Sum Equals K \\
Which items have it? & a \cd{defaultdict(list)} from key to items & Group Anagrams \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The statement asks if any value repeats, if all values are distinct, or for the first repeated value.
  \item The statement asks for a pair with an exact relation: a sum, a difference or a remainder equal to a target.
        One element then fixes the exact key of its partner.
  \item The output is a pair of original indexes, not values. A sort loses the indexes, so a map from value to index fits.
  \item The words anagram, permutation of, rearrange or same characters appear. Compare counts, not order.
  \item The statement asks to group items, or to count distinct items, that are equal up to one detail:
        order, shift, rotation or position.
  \item The statement compares whole collections between two inputs, such as the regions of two grids.
        Store each collection as a \cd{frozenset} and match them by hash.
  \item The statement asks for the $k$ most frequent items. Count first, then select.
  \item The statement asks for runs of consecutive values in an unsorted array and demands $O(n)$ time.
        Sorting solves it in $O(n \log n)$, so set lookups must replace the sort.
  \item An item belongs to several groups at the same time (a row, a column, a box, a diagonal),
        and each group forbids repeats.
  \item The statement counts contiguous subarrays with an exact sum, and values can be negative.
        A range sum is a difference of two prefix sums, so this is a pair problem on prefix sums.
  \item A design problem stores points and counts shapes through a query point.
        The query and one more point force the rest of the shape.
  \item The statement packs many strings into one string and must recover them exactly.
        The strings can hold any character, so no delimiter is safe. Use a length header.
  \item The constraints give $n$ up to $10^4$ or $10^5$. This rules out $O(n^2)$ pair checks in Python.
  \item Values go up to $10^9$. An array indexed by value does not fit, but a hash map does.
        A small fixed alphabet (26 lowercase letters) allows a list of 26 counts.
\end{itemize}
\begin{note}
A hash finds only exact keys. If the relation is ``at most'', ``nearest'' or ``inside a range'',
a lookup of the value itself does not help. Sort and use two pointers or binary search.
Or hash each value to its bucket of a fixed width, and look up only the neighbor buckets.
\end{note}

\subsection{Core template}
\textbf{Template A: the seen-before scan.} Walk the items one time.
For each item, compute the key that a valid partner must have, and ask the structure for that key.
Then record the item under its own key. Only the type of the stored value changes from problem to problem.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def has_duplicate(nums):                 # yes or no: a set
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:                    # 1. ask
            return True
        seen.add(x)                      # 2. record
    return False

def two_sum(nums, target):               # where: value -> index
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x                # the key of the partner
        if need in seen:                 # 1. ask
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i                      # 2. record
    return []

def count_pairs(nums, target):           # how many: value -> count
    seen = Counter()
    pairs = 0
    for x in nums:
        pairs += seen[target - x]        # 1. ask
        seen[x] += 1                     # 2. record
    return pairs

has_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1])              # -> True
has_duplicate([1, 2, 3])                 # -> False
two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6)                    # -> [1, 2]
two_sum([3, 3], 6)                       # -> [0, 1]
count_pairs([1, 5, 3, 3, 3], 6)          # -> 4
\end{pyex}
Invariant: before step $j$, the structure holds facts about the items $0 \ldots j-1$ only.
Ask first, then record. So the scan tests every pair $i < j$ exactly one time, at step $j$,
and an item never pairs with itself.

\textbf{Template B: group by a key.} Compute the key of each item and append the item to the bucket of that key.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def group_by(items, key):
    groups = defaultdict(list)           # key -> items with that key
    for item in items:
        groups[key(item)].append(item)
    return list(groups.values())

group_by(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"], lambda w: "".join(sorted(w)))
# -> [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']]
group_by([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], lambda x: x % 2)   # -> [[1, 3, 5], [2, 4]]
\end{pyex}
Invariant: two items share a bucket exactly when their keys are equal.
So the key must be equal for two items of one class, and different for two items of different classes.
A dict keeps the insertion order, so the groups come out in the order of their first item.

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Membership: seen before}
The question for each element is ``did an equal value occur earlier?''. A set answers it.
Return at the first hit (Contains Duplicate).
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Ask the set if you saw it, then add it.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item For a one-line answer, compare sizes: \cd{len(set(nums)) < len(nums)}. This has no early exit.
  \item To avoid the set, sort and compare neighbors in $O(n \log n)$. Equal values become neighbors.
        A sorted copy costs $O(n)$ memory. An in-place sort saves the copy but changes the input.
  \item If the two equal values must be at most $k$ indexes apart, store the last index of each value.
  \item If the values are $1 \ldots n$, a list of $n + 1$ flags replaces the set.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def first_repeat(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return x
        seen.add(x)
    return None

def near_duplicate(nums, k):             # equal values at most k indexes apart
    last = {}                            # value -> last index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if x in last and i - last[x] <= k:
            return True
        last[x] = i
    return False

len(set([1, 2, 3, 1])) < 4               # -> True
first_repeat([2, 5, 1, 5, 2])            # -> 5
near_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1], 3)          # -> True
near_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], 2)    # -> False
s = sorted([3, 1, 3])
any(s[i] == s[i + 1] for i in range(len(s) - 1))   # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Complement lookup: the partner fixes its own key}
A pair must satisfy an exact relation, so one element gives the exact key of its partner.
Do not search for the partner. Look it up among the earlier elements (Two Sum).
Store the index when the output is a position. Store a count when the output is a number of pairs.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Ask the map for the partner, then add yourself.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Sum equal to $t$: the partner key is $t - x$.
  \item Difference equal to $k > 0$: the partner keys are $x - k$ and $x + k$.
  \item Sum divisible by $m$: store $x \bmod m$. The partner key is $(-x) \bmod m$.
  \item Equal values such as \cd{[3, 3]} need no special case. The lookup comes before the insert.
  \item To put every item into exactly one pair, consume the partner. When the lookup finds a waiting partner,
        subtract 1 from its count. Otherwise, add the item. At the end, no item may wait
        (Check If Array Pairs Are Divisible by k).
  \item The same test with counts only: remainder $r$ needs as many items as remainder $m - r$.
        The remainders 0 and $m/2$ need even counts.
  \item A count of pairs does not answer ``can all items pair up?''.
        \cd{[3, 3, 3, 1]} with $m = 6$ has 3 pairs, but no full pairing.
  \item The consume scan works in any order because the relation is symmetric: $r$ needs $m - r$, and $m - r$ needs $r$.
        If the relation goes one way only, such as $x$ with $2x$, the order matters.
        Process the values from the smallest absolute value up (Array of Doubled Pairs).
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def pairs_sum_divisible(nums, m):        # count i < j with m dividing a[i] + a[j]
    seen = Counter()                     # remainder -> count
    pairs = 0
    for x in nums:
        pairs += seen[(-x) % m]          # remainder of the partner
        seen[x % m] += 1
    return pairs

def pairs_with_diff(nums, k):            # count i < j with |a[i] - a[j]| == k, k > 0
    seen = Counter()
    pairs = 0
    for x in nums:
        pairs += seen[x - k] + seen[x + k]
        seen[x] += 1
    return pairs

def can_pair_all(nums, m):               # every item in exactly one pair, m divides each sum
    waiting = Counter()                  # remainder -> items that wait for a partner
    for x in nums:
        need = (-x) % m
        if waiting[need]:
            waiting[need] -= 1           # consume one waiting partner
        else:
            waiting[x % m] += 1          # wait for a partner
    return not any(waiting.values())     # no item waits

pairs_sum_divisible([30, 20, 150, 100, 40], 60)   # -> 3
pairs_with_diff([1, 2, 2, 1], 1)                  # -> 4
can_pair_all([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 6, 7, 8, 9], 5)  # -> True
can_pair_all([-1, 1, -2, 2], 3)                   # -> True
can_pair_all([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 10)              # -> False
pairs_sum_divisible([3, 3, 3, 1], 6)              # -> 3
can_pair_all([3, 3, 3, 1], 6)                     # -> False
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
If the input is sorted and the extra memory must be $O(1)$, use two converging pointers instead.
If the relation is an inequality, sort and use two pointers. A hash map does not help there.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Complement lookup on running values}
A sum over a contiguous range is a difference of two prefix sums: $\mathrm{sum}(a[i..j-1]) = P[j] - P[i]$.
So a range with sum $k$ is a pair of prefixes with $P[j] - P[i] = k$.
This is Two Sum on prefix sums (Subarray Sum Equals K).
Seed the map with the empty prefix, \cd{{0: 1}}, so that a range can start at index 0.
This works with negative values, where a sliding window fails.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Two Sum on prefix sums: look up prefix minus k, then store prefix.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item To count ranges, store the count of each prefix value.
  \item To find the longest range, store the first index of each prefix value. Seed it with \cd{{0: -1}}.
  \item For a sum divisible by $m$, store the prefix $\bmod\ m$ instead of the prefix.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def count_subarrays(nums, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})               # the empty prefix
    prefix = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen[prefix - k]        # 1. ask
        seen[prefix] += 1                # 2. record
    return count

def longest_subarray(nums, k):
    first = {0: -1}                      # prefix value -> first index
    prefix = best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix += x
        if prefix - k in first:
            best = max(best, i - first[prefix - k])
        first.setdefault(prefix, i)      # keep the first index only
    return best

count_subarrays([1, 1, 1], 2)            # -> 2
count_subarrays([1, 2, 3], 3)            # -> 2
count_subarrays([1, -1, 0], 0)           # -> 3
count_subarrays([0, 0], 0)               # -> 3
longest_subarray([1, -1, 5, -2, 3], 3)   # -> 4
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Frequency counts: compare multisets}
Two sequences are equal up to order exactly when their counts are equal (Valid Anagram).
A \cd{Counter} works for any alphabet. A list of 26 counts works for lowercase letters only.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Count both, compare counts.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The optimal form keeps one table. Check the lengths first. Count the letters of $s$,
        then subtract 1 for each letter of $t$, and return \cd{False} at the first negative count.
        It has the same $O(n)$ time. In CPython the two-\cd{Counter} form is faster, because \cd{Counter} counts in C.
  \item \cd{is_anagram26} below adds and subtracts in one pass over both strings.
        A count can go negative before the end there, so it checks for all zeros only at the end.
  \item For a one-sided check (``build the note from the letters''), subtract the counters.
        An empty result means that the letters cover the note. \cd{a <= b} on counters also works \since{3.10}.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def is_anagram(s, t):
    return Counter(s) == Counter(t)

def is_anagram26(s, t):                  # lowercase letters only, one table
    if len(s) != len(t):
        return False
    count = [0] * 26
    for a, b in zip(s, t):
        count[ord(a) - ord("a")] += 1
        count[ord(b) - ord("a")] -= 1
    return all(c == 0 for c in count)

def can_build(note, letters):            # one-sided: letters cover note
    return not (Counter(note) - Counter(letters))

is_anagram("anagram", "nagaram")         # -> True
is_anagram("rat", "car")                 # -> False
is_anagram26("aab", "abb")               # -> False
is_anagram26("listen", "silent")         # -> True
can_build("aab", "baac")                 # -> True
can_build("aa", "ab")                    # -> False
Counter("aab") <= Counter("aabc")        # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Canonical keys: group items that are equal up to a detail}
Map each item to a key that erases the ignored detail, then group by the key (Group Anagrams).
The sorted word is the simplest key for anagrams.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Sort each word, group by the sorted word.}
The optimal key is a tuple of 26 letter counts. It costs $O(k + 26)$ per word instead of $O(k \log k)$.
In CPython the sorted key is as fast or faster, because \cd{sorted} runs in C.
Use the count tuple only when you must show $O(k)$ work per word.
Before you trust a new key, test two items that must collide and two items that must not.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{6.2cm}L{10.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Items are equal up to & Key \\
\midrule
the order of the letters & \cd{"".join(sorted(w))}, or a tuple of 26 counts \\
the order, any alphabet & the sorted string, or \cd{frozenset(Counter(w).items())} \\
the same shift of every letter & the tuple of differences of neighbor letters, modulo 26 \\
order and repeats (a set of elements) & \cd{frozenset(items)} \\
a rotation of a sequence & the smallest rotation \\
the position of a shape on a grid & a \cd{frozenset} of offsets from the smallest cell \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(groups.values())

def count_key(w):                        # O(k) key for lowercase words
    count = [0] * 26
    for ch in w:
        count[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
    return tuple(count)                  # a list is not hashable

def smallest_rotation(seq):              # O(k^2), fine for short items
    return min((seq[i:] + seq[:i] for i in range(len(seq))), default=seq)

group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"])
# -> [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']]
group_anagrams(["", "b", ""])            # -> [['', ''], ['b']]
count_key("aab") == count_key("aba")     # -> True
count_key("aab") == count_key("abb")     # -> False
smallest_rotation("cab"), smallest_rotation("bca")   # -> ('abc', 'abc')
smallest_rotation("")                    # -> ''
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Whole regions as keys: frozensets of cells}
To compare whole collections, such as the regions of two grids, store each collection as a \cd{frozenset}.
Then one hash lookup finds an equal collection, with no pairwise comparisons.
A set intersection counts the common collections in time linear in the total number of cells
(for example, count the islands that are identical in two binary grids of the same size).
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Collect each grid's islands as frozensets, then intersect.}
Use an explicit stack for the flood fill. One region can hold the whole grid, and recursion fails at that depth.
The optimal solution floods only the first grid and builds no sets.
A region matches when the second grid has \cd{1} on every region cell and \cd{0} on every border cell.
A connected region can grow only through a neighbor, so the border ring decides ``no extra cell''.
\begin{pyex}
def regions(grid):                       # set of frozensets of (r, c)
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    seen = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    found = set()
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] != "1" or seen[r][c]:
                continue
            seen[r][c] = True            # mark on push
            stack, cells = [(r, c)], []
            while stack:
                i, j = stack.pop()
                cells.append((i, j))
                for x, y in ((i - 1, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j - 1), (i, j + 1)):
                    inside = 0 <= x < rows and 0 <= y < cols
                    if inside and grid[x][y] == "1" and not seen[x][y]:
                        seen[x][y] = True
                        stack.append((x, y))
            found.add(frozenset(cells))
    return found

def shape(cells):                        # a key that ignores the position
    r0, c0 = min(cells)
    return frozenset((r - r0, c - c0) for r, c in cells)

len(regions(["001", "011", "100"]) & regions(["001", "011", "101"]))   # -> 1
len(regions(["101", "010", "101"]))      # -> 5
len({shape(cells) for cells in regions(["101", "010", "101"])})   # -> 1
len(regions(["000"]))                    # -> 0
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Count, then select by count: bucket sort}
Count each value with a hash map. Then select the $k$ values with the largest counts (Top K Frequent Elements).
A count is an integer from 1 to $n$. So a list of $n + 1$ buckets, indexed by count, sorts the values by count
in $O(n)$ time without comparisons.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Bucket values by count, read buckets top down, take the first k.}
The general rule: when a sort key has a small known range, use the key as an index instead of comparing keys.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{Counter(nums).most_common(k)} is the quick version. It uses a heap, $O(m \log k)$ for $m$ distinct values.
  \item A size-$k$ min-heap gives $O(n + m \log k)$ when the key is not a small integer.
  \item If ties at the boundary are possible, define a tie rule and sort inside the boundary bucket.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    count = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]   # buckets[f]: values that occur f times
    for value, freq in count.items():
        buckets[freq].append(value)
    by_freq = []
    for freq in range(len(nums), 0, -1):           # highest count first
        by_freq.extend(buckets[freq])
    return by_freq[:k]

top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2)    # -> [1, 2]
top_k_frequent([4], 1)                   # -> [4]
[v for v, _ in Counter([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]).most_common(2)]   # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Neighbors in value space: walk only from run starts}
If a solution sorts only to find the neighbor of a value ($x + 1$, $x + d$, $2x$), a set finds that neighbor in $O(1)$.
Put the values in a set. A value starts a run exactly when $x - 1$ is not in the set.
Walk forward only from a run start (Longest Consecutive Sequence).
Each value is then visited by one walk only, so the total work is $O(n)$.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Only start counting where x-1 is missing.}
The general rule: to do the work of each group one time, find a cheap local test that is true
for exactly one member of the group. Start the work only from that member.
\begin{pyex}
def longest_run(nums):
    values = set(nums)
    longest = 0
    for start in values:                 # loop over the set: each start walks once
        if start - 1 in values:
            continue                     # not a run start
        length = 1
        while start + length in values:
            length += 1
        longest = max(longest, length)
    return longest

def count_runs(nums):
    values = set(nums)
    return sum(1 for x in values if x - 1 not in values)

longest_run([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2])      # -> 4
longest_run([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1])   # -> 9
longest_run([])                          # -> 0
count_runs([1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 20])        # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Several groups per item: group ids from coordinates}
Each item belongs to several groups, and each group forbids repeats (Valid Sudoku).
Give every group its own seen-set. Compute the group ids of a cell from its coordinates:
the row is $r$, the column is $c$, and the $k \times k$ box is \cd{(r // k, c // k)}.
On a diagonal from top left to bottom right, $r - c$ is constant. On the other diagonal, $r + c$ is constant.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Each digit checks in at its row, its column and its box (r // 3, c // 3).
A second check-in at any of the three fails.}
The flat box id \cd{(r // 3) * 3 + c // 3} lets you keep the boxes in a list of 9 sets.
The sum \cd{r // 3 + c // 3} is wrong: boxes \cd{(0, 1)} and \cd{(1, 0)} get the same id.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def valid_board(board, k):               # N x N board, k x k boxes, "." is empty
    seen = defaultdict(set)              # group id -> values in that group
    for r, row in enumerate(board):
        for c, v in enumerate(row):
            if v == ".":
                continue
            groups = (("row", r), ("col", c), ("box", r // k, c // k))
            if any(v in seen[g] for g in groups):
                return False
            for g in groups:
                seen[g].add(v)
    return True

valid_board(["12..", "..1.", "....", "...."], 2)   # -> True
valid_board(["1...", ".1..", "....", "...."], 2)   # -> False
valid_board(["1...", "....", "1...", "...."], 2)   # -> False
r, c = 4, 7
(r // 3, c // 3), (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3  # -> ((1, 2), 5)
\end{pyex}
The 9 by 9 board is the call with \cd{k = 3}. The tag in each group id (\cd{"row"}, \cd{"col"}, \cd{"box"})
keeps a row id and a column id apart in one dict.

\subsubsection{Shapes through a query point: enumerate the free part, look up the forced part}
Count the shapes that contain a query point (Detect Squares).
Fix the query corner $(q_x, q_y)$. Then one more point fixes an axis-aligned square: the diagonal corner $(x, y)$,
with $|x - q_x| = |y - q_y| \neq 0$. The other two corners are forced: $(x, q_y)$ and $(q_x, y)$.
Look them up in a \cd{Counter} of points. Duplicate points are different choices, so multiply the counts.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Pick the diagonal, the other two corners are forced, multiply the counts.}
The general rule: find the smallest set of elements that fixes the whole shape.
Enumerate only those elements, and look up the rest.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

class DetectSquares:
    def __init__(self):
        self.points = Counter()          # (x, y) -> number of copies

    def add(self, point):
        self.points[tuple(point)] += 1

    def count(self, point):
        qx, qy = point
        total = 0
        for (x, y), copies in self.points.items():
            if x == qx or abs(x - qx) != abs(y - qy):
                continue                 # not the diagonal corner of a real square
            total += copies * self.points.get((x, qy), 0) * self.points.get((qx, y), 0)
        return total

ds = DetectSquares()
for p in ([3, 10], [11, 2], [3, 2]):
    ds.add(p)
ds.count([11, 10])                       # -> 1
ds.count([14, 8])                        # -> 0
ds.add([11, 2])
ds.count([11, 10])                       # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Length-prefixed encoding}
Pack a list of strings into one string and get the list back (Encode and Decode Strings).
A delimiter fails when the data can contain it: \cd{["a,b"]} and \cd{["a", "b"]} join to the same text.
Write each item as its length in digits, then a marker, then the item.
The header holds only digits, so the first marker after the header start ends the header.
Then take exactly that many characters and jump over them. Never search inside the payload.
\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Write length, hash, string; read length, then jump.}
The general rule: put the data that a reader needs before the item that it describes.
Write that header in an alphabet that cannot contain the marker.
\begin{pyex}
def encode(strs):
    return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)

def decode(s):
    res, i = [], 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = s.index("#", i)              # the marker that ends the header
        length = int(s[i:j])
        start = j + 1
        res.append(s[start:start + length])
        i = start + length               # jump over the payload
    return res

encode(["a#b", "", "12"])                # -> '3#a#b0#2#12'
decode(encode(["a#b", "", "12"]))        # -> ['a#b', '', '12']
decode(encode([""])), decode(encode([]))   # -> ([''], [])
",".join(["a,b"]) == ",".join(["a", "b"])  # -> True
\end{pyex}
Move an index. Do not cut the used prefix off the string in each step. Each cut copies the rest, and decode becomes $O(n^2)$.

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What does the inner loop of the brute force search for? If it searches for one exact key,
        replace the loop with a lookup. If it searches for a range or the nearest value, use sorting instead.
  \item What is the key? It can be the value itself, the partner key (\cd{target - x}),
        a running value (\cd{prefix - k}, the prefix modulo $m$), a canonical form (sorted, counts, offsets),
        or a group id (\cd{(r // k, c // k)}).
  \item Does the relation mix two elements, or an index and a value? Move all terms of one element to one side.
        For example, \cd{a[j] - a[i] == j - i} becomes \cd{a[i] - i == a[j] - j}.
        Then each side is a key of one element, and equal keys form the pairs.
  \item What is the stored value? Read it from the output: a set for yes or no, an index for a position,
        the first index for a longest range, a count for a number of pairs, a list for groups.
  \item When do you record? For pairs $i < j$, ask first and record second.
        Put the start state (the empty prefix) into the map before the loop.
  \item Is the key hashable and exact? Use a tuple, a \cd{frozenset} or a string. Keep the counts.
        Put a separator between numbers in a string key. Test two items that must collide and two that must not.
  \item Which container? Use a list when the keys are small dense integers (26 letters, values $1 \ldots n$,
        counts $0 \ldots n$). Use a dict or a set for all other keys.
  \item Do duplicates count as different choices? If yes, store counts and multiply them.
        If no, use a set, and loop over the set.
  \item Must every item go into exactly one pair? Then a pair count is not the answer.
        On a hit, consume the waiting partner. At the end, check that no item waits.
  \item Does every member of a group repeat the same work? Find a cheap test that selects one member per group,
        such as ``$x - 1$ is absent''. Start the work only there.
  \item Is the last step a selection by count? Bucket by count (a count is at most $n$),
        keep a size-$k$ heap, or call \cd{most_common(k)}.
  \item Does each query force most of a shape? Enumerate the free part only, and look up the forced part in a counter.
  \item Must many strings go into one string and come back? Write a length header before each item.
        Read the header, then jump by the length.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Record before you ask.} The current item then finds itself.
In Two Sum it pairs with itself. In prefix counting with $k = 0$ it counts empty ranges.
Always ask first, then record.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def two_sum_wrong(nums, target):         # records before it asks
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        seen[x] = i
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]

two_sum_wrong([3, 2, 4], 6)              # -> [0, 0]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A missing start state.} In a prefix scan, the empty prefix is an earlier prefix too.
Without the seed \cd{{0: 1}}, every range that starts at index 0 is lost.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def count_subarrays(nums, k, seed):
    seen = Counter(seed)
    prefix = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen[prefix - k]
        seen[prefix] += 1
    return count

count_subarrays([1, 2, 3], 3, {0: 1})    # -> 2
count_subarrays([1, 2, 3], 3, {})        # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A key that loses information.} A set of letters loses the counts. A sum or an XOR of character codes collides.
Numbers joined with no separator collide. Each wrong key merges two different classes.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
set("aab") == set("abb")                 # -> True
sum(map(ord, "bc")) == sum(map(ord, "ad"))   # -> True
"".join(map(str, [1, 11])) == "".join(map(str, [11, 1]))   # -> True
",".join(map(str, [1, 11])) == ",".join(map(str, [11, 1]))   # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A mutable key.} A list or a set cannot be a dict key or a set element. Convert it to a tuple or a \cd{frozenset}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
d = {}
d[[1, 2]] = "x"                          # -> raises TypeError
d[(1, 2)] = "x"
frozenset({1, 2}) in {frozenset({2, 1})}   # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A read that inserts.} A read of a missing key in a \cd{defaultdict} inserts that key.
Inside a loop over the same dict, this raises \cd{RuntimeError}. A \cd{Counter} read and \cd{dict.get} do not insert.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int, {1: 1})
d[5]                                     # -> 0
len(d)                                   # -> 2
def look_ahead(table):
    for key in table:
        table[key + 100]                 # inserts a key during the loop
look_ahead(d)                            # -> raises RuntimeError
c = Counter({1: 1})
c[5], len(c)                             # -> (0, 1)
look_ahead(c)
len(c)                                   # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A hidden linear scan.} \cd{x in some_list}, \cd{nums.index(x)} and \cd{x in nums[:i]} each cost $O(n)$.
Inside a loop, the total becomes $O(n^2)$ again. Keep the seen items in a set or a dict.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Shared buckets.} \cd{[[]] * n} repeats one list $n$ times. Build buckets with a comprehension.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
buckets = [[]] * 3
buckets[1].append(7)
buckets                                  # -> [[7], [7], [7]]
buckets = [[] for _ in range(3)]
buckets[1].append(7)
buckets                                  # -> [[], [7], []]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Counter comparison details.} Subtraction drops counts that are zero or negative.
So an empty \cd{a - b} proves only that \cd{b} covers \cd{a}, not that they are equal. Check the lengths too.
Since Python 3.10, \cd{Counter} equality treats a missing key as count 0. A plain dict does not.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
Counter("ab") - Counter("abc")           # -> Counter()
Counter("ab") == Counter("abc")          # -> False
Counter(a=1, b=0) == Counter(a=1)        # -> True
{"a": 1, "b": 0} == {"a": 1}             # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Run starts over the list, not over the set.} If one run start occurs many times in the input,
a loop over the list walks the same run many times. The time becomes $O(n^2)$. Loop over the set.
Do not add to or remove from a set while a loop runs over it. Python raises \cd{RuntimeError}.
\end{caution}

\begin{note}
Hash operations are $O(1)$ on average only. The order of a set of strings changes from run to run.
Sort a result before you compare it in a test, and do not print a set as an answer.
\end{note}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Contains Duplicate & A set of seen values. Return at the first hit. & Ask the set if you saw it, then add it. \\
Two Sum & A map from value to index. Look up \cd{target - x}. & Ask the map for the partner, then add yourself. \\
Subarray Sum Equals K & Two Sum on prefix sums. A count map seeded with the empty prefix. & Two Sum on prefix sums: look up prefix minus k, then store prefix. \\
Valid Anagram & Two count tables, compared. & Count both, compare counts. \\
Group Anagrams & Canonical key: the sorted word. A dict of lists. & Sort each word, group by the sorted word. \\
Top K Frequent Elements & Count, then bucket by count. A count is at most $n$. & Bucket values by count, read buckets top down, take the first k. \\
Longest Consecutive Sequence & A set of values. Walk only from a run start. & Only start counting where x-1 is missing. \\
Valid Sudoku & One seen-set per row, column and box. Box id \cd{(r // 3, c // 3)}. & Each digit checks in at its row, its column and its box (r // 3, c // 3). A second check-in at any of the three fails. \\
Detect Squares & A counter of points. Enumerate the diagonal corner, look up the forced corners, multiply the counts. & Pick the diagonal, the other two corners are forced, multiply the counts. \\
Encode and Decode Strings & A length header and a marker. Jump by the length, never search the payload. & Write length, hash, string; read length, then jump. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T01} (page~\pageref{drill:T01}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T01} (page~\pageref{ans:T01}).
