\section{Prefix sums, running aggregates and offsets}\label{tech:T02}

\subsection{The idea}
A brute force often computes the same aggregate many times.
For each index, it adds, multiplies or compares all the earlier elements again.
A prefix sum, a running minimum or a running offset does that work one time.
One pass carries a summary of everything seen so far.
Each later step reads the summary in $O(1)$ instead of a new inner loop.
This usually changes $O(n^2)$ into $O(n)$.
In this section, a \emph{range} is a contiguous part of an array, also called a subarray.
\cd{nums[l..r]} includes both ends.

\textbf{Worked example.} Take \cd{nums = [3, -1, 4, 2]}.
The prefix sums are \cd{P = [0, 3, 2, 6, 8]}.
\cd{P[i]} is the sum of the first \cd{i} elements, and \cd{P[0] = 0} is the empty prefix.
The sum of \cd{nums[1..2]} is \cd{P[3] - P[1]}, that is $6 - 3 = 3$. Check: $-1 + 4 = 3$.
So a range sum is the difference of two prefix values.
A question about a range becomes a question about a pair of prefixes.

\textbf{A second example.} Take the prices \cd{[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]} and sell on day 4 at price 6.
The best earlier day to buy is the cheapest day so far, at price 1. The profit is 5.
The cheapest price so far is one variable. It replaces the loop over all earlier days.

Three questions pick the main tool:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Does the operation have an inverse?} Addition and XOR have one.
        Remove one prefix from another (subtract a sum, XOR an XOR) to get any range.
        Maximum, minimum, gcd and a product with zeros have no usable inverse.
        For them, a prefix pass and a suffix pass answer ``all except \cd{i}'' and ``left and right of \cd{i}''.
        They do not give an arbitrary range.
  \item \textbf{What do you need from the past?} A count or the first index of each prefix value needs a hash map.
        The best earlier partner needs one running minimum or maximum.
  \item \textbf{Does everything move together?} Then one shared offset describes all the items.
        Move the frame, not the items. Track the offset and its extremes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.0cm}L{5.2cm}L{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Summary of the past & Build step & Answers \\
\midrule
Prefix sum \cd{P} & \cd{P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i]} & Any range sum in $O(1)$. With a hash map: count or find ranges with an exact sum. \\
Prefix and suffix aggregate & A left pass and a right pass & ``All except \cd{i}'', ``left of \cd{i} and right of \cd{i}''. \\
Running minimum or maximum & \cd{low = min(low, x)} & The best pair \cd{i < j} when the best left partner is an extreme. \\
2D prefix table & Cell + top + left $-$ overlap & Any rectangle sum in $O(1)$. \\
Difference array & \cd{+v} at \cd{l}, \cd{-v} at \cd{r + 1} & Many range updates, then one read. \\
Shared offset and its extremes & \cd{off += step}, then min and max & Rigid moves of all items, with loss at a boundary. \\
Running left bound & \cd{left = max(left, ...)} & Count the ranges whose property survives shrinking. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The statement asks for the sum of a contiguous range, or for many range sums of static data.
  \item The task counts ranges with an exact sum, a sum divisible by $m$, or a balance of two kinds of items.
        The values can be negative or zero, so a sliding window fails.
  \item The answer at index \cd{i} uses ``all elements except \cd{i}'', or ``the elements left of \cd{i} and right of \cd{i}''.
        The statement forbids the inverse operation, for example division.
  \item A per-index formula uses \cd{min(best on the left, best on the right)}, as with walls and water.
  \item The task maximizes a score of a pair with the order \cd{i < j}: ``buy before sell'', ``an earlier day''.
  \item A static grid needs many rectangle or square sums.
  \item The task asks for the largest size of a region under a sum limit, and all values are non-negative.
  \item Many updates add a value to a range: bookings, trips, shifts over an index range.
        The task reads the final values, or the peak value, one time.
  \item The same move applies to every item at the same time, and items that cross a boundary are lost.
        The number of steps times the number of items is far above $10^7$.
  \item The input gives moves or differences, not positions. Each position is a running sum of the moves,
        and every position must stay inside bounds.
  \item The task counts contiguous ranges that must not contain something. Every range inside a valid range is valid.
  \item $n$ is $10^4$ or more, so $O(n^2)$ is too slow in Python. The target is one or a few linear passes.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
\textbf{The prefix array.} Pad it with one zero at the front. Then no range needs a special case.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import accumulate

nums = [3, -1, 4, 2]
P = [0]
for x in nums:
    P.append(P[-1] + x)
P                                   # -> [0, 3, 2, 6, 8]
list(accumulate(nums, initial=0))   # -> [0, 3, 2, 6, 8]

def range_sum(l, r):                # sum of nums[l..r], both ends included
    return P[r + 1] - P[l]

range_sum(1, 2)                     # -> 3
range_sum(0, 3)                     # -> 8
range_sum(2, 2)                     # -> 4
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant:} \cd{P[i]} is the sum of \cd{nums[0..i-1]}, and \cd{P[0] = 0} is the empty prefix.
The sum of \cd{nums[l..r]} is \cd{P[r + 1] - P[l]}.
The \cd{initial} argument of \cd{accumulate} needs \since{3.8}.

\textbf{The one-pass sweep.} Most problems in this family do not store \cd{P}.
They sweep one time and keep a summary of the earlier prefixes.
Each step has four parts: seed, extend, ask, add.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def count_ranges_with_sum(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1                     # 1. seed: the empty prefix is an earlier prefix
    prefix = 0
    count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x                 # 2. extend: the prefix that ends here
        count += seen[prefix - k]   # 3. ask: earlier prefixes p with prefix - p == k
        seen[prefix] += 1           # 4. add: only now is this prefix in the past
    return count

count_ranges_with_sum([1, 1, 1], 2)       # -> 2
count_ranges_with_sum([1, 2, 3], 3)       # -> 2
count_ranges_with_sum([3, -1, 4, 2], 3)   # -> 2
count_ranges_with_sum([0, 0], 0)          # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant:} before the step for index \cd{j}, the summary holds exactly the prefixes that end before \cd{j}, plus the empty prefix.
Ask before you add. Then a range never pairs a prefix with itself, and every range is non-empty.

The variations fill the same four slots in different ways:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.8cm}L{4.2cm}L{2.2cm}L{5.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem shape & Summary of the past & Seed & Ask at each step \\
\midrule
Count ranges with sum \cd{k} & Count of each prefix value & \cd{{0: 1}} & \cd{seen[prefix - k]} \\
Longest range with sum \cd{k} & First index of each prefix value & \cd{{0: -1}} & \cd{j - first[prefix - k]} \\
Best pair with \cd{i < j} & Running minimum or maximum & \cd{a[0]}, or $\pm\infty$ & \cd{a[j] - low} \\
Rigid moves, loss at a bound & Minimum and maximum of the offset & \cd{0} and \cd{0} & After the loop: the interval of surviving starts \\
Ranges that survive shrinking & Smallest valid left end & The first index & \cd{r - left + 1} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Ranges with an exact sum: prefix sums and a hash map}
The core template above is \textbf{Subarray Sum Equals K}.
\textbf{Memory hook:} Two Sum on prefix sums: look up prefix minus k, then store prefix.
A range \cd{nums[i..j]} has sum \cd{k} exactly when an earlier prefix equals \cd{prefix - k}.
A sliding window does not work here, because negative values make the window sum go up and down.

Change the key or the stored value for related shapes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Divisible by $m$:} use \cd{prefix} \pct{} \cd{m} as the key. Two equal remainders bound a divisible range.
        Python gives a non-negative remainder for $m > 0$. (Subarray Sums Divisible by K;
        Continuous Subarray Sum needs a length of at least 2, so it stores first indexes.)
  \item \textbf{Longest range:} store the first index of each prefix value, and seed \cd{{0: -1}}.
        Do not overwrite an index that is already in the map. (Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k)
  \item \textbf{Balance of two kinds of items:} map one kind to $+1$ and the other kind to $-1$.
        A balanced range has sum 0, so it starts and ends at equal prefix values.
  \item \textbf{Paths in a tree:} run the same map along the root-to-node path. Undo the insert when you backtrack. (Path Sum III)
  \item \textbf{Submatrices:} fix a pair of rows, collapse the columns into one array, and run the 1D sweep.
        (Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target)
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def count_divisible(nums, m):
    seen = {0: 1}
    prefix = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix = (prefix + x) % m             # never negative for m > 0
        count += seen.get(prefix, 0)
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count

def longest_with_sum(nums, k):
    first = {0: -1}                           # the empty prefix ends at index -1
    prefix = best = 0
    for j, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix += x
        if prefix - k in first:
            best = max(best, j - first[prefix - k])
        if prefix not in first:               # keep the FIRST index only
            first[prefix] = j
    return best

count_divisible([4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5)      # -> 7
longest_with_sum([1, -1, 5, -2, 3], 3)        # -> 4
longest_with_sum([-2, -1, 2, 1], 1)           # -> 2
longest_with_sum([1, 2], 7)                   # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
When all values are positive and the condition is ``sum at least $k$'' or ``sum at most $k$'',
a sliding window is simpler and uses $O(1)$ space. The hash map handles exact targets and negative values.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Everything except one index: a prefix pass and a suffix pass}
The answer at \cd{i} is the aggregate of the left side combined with the aggregate of the right side.
In \textbf{Product of Array Except Self}, division is forbidden, and zeros break it anyway.
\textbf{Memory hook:} Answer = left product times right product. In each pass, use the running product, then multiply in nums[i].

Write the left products into the output. Then sweep from the right with one scalar and multiply it in.
This uses $O(1)$ extra space, because the output array does not count.
The same two passes work for any associative operation. Start each pass at the identity, which is the value of an empty side.
The identity is 1 for a product, 0 for a sum, \cd{-inf} for a maximum, \cd{inf} for a minimum, and 0 for gcd and OR.
The two passes matter most when the operation has no inverse.
\begin{pyex}
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):                  # answer[i] = product of nums[0..i-1]
        answer[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):      # multiply in the product of nums[i+1..n-1]
        answer[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return answer

product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])       # -> [24, 12, 8, 6]
product_except_self([-1, 1, 0, -3, 3])  # -> [0, 0, 9, 0, 0]
product_except_self([0, 0, 5])          # -> [0, 0, 0]
\end{pyex}
\textbf{General rule:} when a result needs two directional aggregates, store one direction and stream the other.

\subsubsection{Two walls: prefix maximum and suffix maximum}
In \textbf{Trapping Rain Water}, the water at index \cd{i} rises to the lower of two walls.
One wall is the tallest bar in \cd{height[0..i]}. The other wall is the tallest bar in \cd{height[i..n-1]}.
\textbf{Memory hook:} Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height.
Both maxima include \cd{height[i]}, so no term is negative and the end bars add 0.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import accumulate

def trap(height):
    n = len(height)
    left_max = [0] * n
    left_max[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], height[i])
    right_max = [0] * n
    right_max[n - 1] = height[n - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], height[i])
    return sum(min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i] for i in range(n))

trap([0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1])       # -> 6
trap([4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5])                         # -> 9
trap([5])                                        # -> 0
a = [0, 2, 1, 3, 1]
list(accumulate(a, max))                         # -> [0, 2, 2, 3, 3]
list(accumulate(reversed(a), max))[::-1]         # -> [3, 3, 3, 3, 1]
\end{pyex}
\cd{accumulate(a, max)} builds a running maximum in one line.
Apply it to \cd{reversed(a)} and reverse the result to get the suffix maximum.

\begin{note}
The optimal solution uses two converging pointers and $O(1)$ extra space.
Only the lower wall matters. If \cd{left_max < right_max}, the true right wall of the next left index is at least \cd{right_max}.
So \cd{left_max} alone sets its level. Settle the side with the smaller running maximum and move that pointer inward.
Use this form only when the problem asks for constant extra space.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{The best earlier partner: a running minimum or maximum}
\textbf{Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock} asks for the largest \cd{prices[j] - prices[i]} with \cd{i < j}, or 0.
Fix the sell day \cd{j}. The best buy day is the cheapest day at or before \cd{j}.
\textbf{Memory hook:} Remember the cheapest day, sell today.

In general, maximize a score of a pair \cd{i < j}. If the score splits into \cd{f(i) + g(j)},
keep the running best of \cd{f(i)} and combine it with \cd{g(j)} at each step.
For the stock, \cd{f(i) = -prices[i]} and \cd{g(j) = prices[j]}.
If the best left partner is not an extreme but an exact value, keep a hash map instead (Two Sum).
\begin{pyex}
def max_profit(prices):
    min_price = prices[0]           # cheapest buy price so far
    best = 0                        # 0 means "do not trade"
    for price in prices:
        min_price = min(min_price, price)
        best = max(best, price - min_price)
    return best

max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4])      # -> 5
max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1])         # -> 0
max_profit([2, 4, 1])               # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Here the update of the minimum comes before the ask. That is safe, because a pair of one day with itself gives profit 0.
That value never beats the start value 0.

The same scan on prefix sums gives the largest range sum (Maximum Subarray).
A range sum is \cd{P[j] - P[i]}, so keep the smallest earlier prefix.
Here the order matters: ask before you add, so the range is not empty.
This is Kadane's algorithm seen through prefix sums.
\begin{pyex}
def max_subarray(nums):             # the subarray must not be empty
    prefix, low, best = 0, 0, float("-inf")
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        best = max(best, prefix - low)   # ask first
        low = min(low, prefix)           # then add this prefix to the past
    return best

max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])   # -> 6
max_subarray([-3, -1])                          # -> -1
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{2D prefix sums and the largest square under a limit}
A direct sum of a $k \times k$ square reads $k^2$ cells.
A padded table \cd{P} with \cd{(rows + 1) x (cols + 1)} cells gives any rectangle sum with four lookups.
\cd{P[r][c]} is the sum of the block above row \cd{r} and left of column \cd{c}.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Build:} the cell, plus the block above, plus the block to the left, minus their overlap.
  \item \textbf{Query:} the whole block, minus the top strip, minus the left strip, plus the corner that you subtracted two times.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{Memory hook:} whole, minus top, minus left, plus the corner.
When all values are non-negative, a larger square has a larger or equal sum than a square inside it.
So the condition ``a square of side \cd{k} fits'' is monotone in \cd{k}. Binary search the largest side.
Each check scans all corners in $O(R \cdot C)$. The total is $O(R \cdot C \log \min(R, C))$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Maximum Side Length of a Square with Sum Less than or Equal to Threshold} needs \emph{some} square of side \cd{k} to fit: \cd{any}.
        \textbf{Memory hook:} Prefix table for O(1) squares, then binary search the biggest side that fits.
  \item \textbf{A largest side where all squares must fit} needs \emph{every} square of side \cd{k} to fit: \cd{all}.
        \textbf{Memory hook:} Cells are non-negative, so if size k fails, every bigger size fails.
        Binary search k, and check all k x k squares with 2D prefix sums.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def build(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    P = [[0] * (cols + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)]
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            P[r + 1][c + 1] = grid[r][c] + P[r][c + 1] + P[r + 1][c] - P[r][c]
    return P

def rect_sum(P, r1, c1, r2, c2):        # corners (r1, c1) and (r2, c2), both included
    return P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1]

def largest_side(grid, limit, every):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    P = build(grid)
    def fits(k):
        ok = (rect_sum(P, r, c, r + k - 1, c + k - 1) <= limit
              for r in range(rows - k + 1) for c in range(cols - k + 1))
        return all(ok) if every else any(ok)
    lo, hi, best = 1, min(rows, cols), 0    # side 0 always fits
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if fits(mid):
            best, lo = mid, mid + 1         # mid fits: try bigger
        else:
            hi = mid - 1                    # mid fails: try smaller
    return best

P = build([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
P                                       # -> [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 3], [0, 4, 10]]
rect_sum(P, 1, 0, 1, 1), rect_sum(P, 0, 1, 1, 1)   # -> (7, 6)
mat = [[1, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2] for _ in range(3)]
largest_side(mat, 4, every=False)       # -> 2
largest_side([[2] * 5 for _ in range(5)], 1, every=False)   # -> 0
largest_side([[1] * 3 for _ in range(3)], 4, every=True)    # -> 2
largest_side([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 4, every=True)               # -> 1
largest_side([[5, 0], [0, 0]], 4, every=True)               # -> 0
largest_side([[5, 0], [0, 0]], 4, every=False)              # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Both problems have an $O(R \cdot C)$ refinement.
For ``some square'', scan the bottom-right corners in row-major order and test only side \cd{best + 1} at each corner.
A valid square of side $K$ contains valid squares of sides 1 to $K$ along its diagonal, and the scan meets them in order.
For ``every square'', a two-pointer walk along each diagonal removes the log factor.
The binary search is fast enough for grids up to $300 \times 300$.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Difference arrays: many range updates, one read}
A direct update touches every index of its range, so $q$ updates cost $O(q \cdot n)$.
A difference array is the inverse of a prefix sum. It stores only where the value changes.
To add \cd{v} to \cd{a[l..r]}, do \cd{diff[l] += v} and \cd{diff[r + 1] -= v}. Each update costs $O(1)$.
One prefix sum pass at the end gives the final array.
\textbf{Memory hook:} plus at the start, minus just past the end, then run the sum.
Use it for the final values after many range additions and for the peak number of overlapping intervals.
Also use it to check that the load never goes above a capacity. (Corporate Flight Bookings, Range Addition)
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import accumulate

def apply_updates(n, updates):
    diff = [0] * (n + 1)                # one extra slot for r + 1 == n
    for l, r, v in updates:             # add v to a[l..r], both ends included
        diff[l] += v
        diff[r + 1] -= v
    return list(accumulate(diff[:n]))

apply_updates(5, [(1, 3, 2), (0, 1, 5), (3, 4, -1)])   # -> [5, 7, 2, 1, -1]
intervals = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (4, 6)]                   # closed integer intervals
max(apply_updates(7, [(s, e, 1) for s, e in intervals]))   # -> 2
\end{pyex}
For a half-open interval \cd{[s, e)}, put the \cd{-v} at \cd{e}, not at \cd{e + 1}.
In 2D, to add \cd{v} to the rectangle from \cd{(r1, c1)} to \cd{(r2, c2)}, add \cd{v} at \cd{(r1, c1)} and at \cd{(r2 + 1, c2 + 1)}.
Subtract \cd{v} at \cd{(r1, c2 + 1)} and at \cd{(r2 + 1, c1)}. Then run the 2D prefix sum build.

\subsubsection{A shared offset and its extremes instead of a simulation}
A simulation moves every item at every step, so it costs the number of steps times the number of items.
But when the same move applies to every item, all items keep their relative positions.
One shared offset per axis describes every item. Move the frame, not the items.
Take a grid of leaves where each gust of wind moves every leaf one cell.
A leaf that leaves the garden never comes back.
\textbf{Memory hook:} Move the frame, not the leaves: track the offset's min and max, then sum the surviving box.

A leaf that starts at row \cd{r} survives if \cd{0 <= r + d <= rows - 1} for the offset \cd{d} after every prefix of gusts.
This depends only on the minimum and the maximum of the offset.
So the surviving start rows are exactly \cd{-min_dr} to \cd{rows - 1 - max_dr}. Columns follow the same rule.
In general, with bounds \cd{lower} and \cd{upper}, the valid start values form the interval
\cd{[lower - min_off, upper - max_off]}. It is empty when the extremes are too far apart.
\begin{pyex}
def remaining_leaves(garden, gusts):
    rows, cols = len(garden), len(garden[0])
    step = {"U": (-1, 0), "D": (1, 0), "L": (0, -1), "R": (0, 1)}
    dr = dc = 0
    min_dr = max_dr = min_dc = max_dc = 0     # the empty prefix counts
    for g in gusts:
        sr, sc = step[g]
        dr += sr
        dc += sc
        min_dr, max_dr = min(min_dr, dr), max(max_dr, dr)
        min_dc, max_dc = min(min_dc, dc), max(max_dc, dc)
    top, bottom = -min_dr, rows - 1 - max_dr
    left, right = -min_dc, cols - 1 - max_dc
    if top > bottom or left > right:          # guard: negative slice ends count from the end
        return 0
    return sum(sum(row[left:right + 1]) for row in garden[top:bottom + 1])

g = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
remaining_leaves(g, "R")                      # -> 12
remaining_leaves(g, "RL")                     # -> 12
remaining_leaves(g, "")                       # -> 21
remaining_leaves(g, "UD")                     # -> 15
remaining_leaves(g, "UU")                     # -> 0
remaining_leaves(g, "DLL")                    # -> 3
\end{pyex}
The net offset of \cd{"RL"} is 0, but the \cd{R} gust already removed the right column.
So track the extremes over all prefixes, not only the final offset.
Each axis is independent, so the survivors form one rectangle.
For many gust strings on the same garden, build a 2D prefix table one time. Then each rectangle sum costs $O(1)$.

\subsubsection{A monotone left bound while sweeping}
A brute force checks all $n^2 / 2$ ranges one by one.
Some properties survive shrinking: if a range is valid, every range inside it is valid.
Then, for each right end \cd{r}, the valid starts form one block \cd{[left, r]}, and \cd{left} never moves back.
Count \cd{r - left + 1} ranges for each right end. The total work is $O(n)$.
\textbf{Memory hook:} valid stays valid when it shrinks, so keep the smallest left and add \cd{r - left + 1}.

Take the task to count the ranges of \cd{1..n} that contain no forbidden pair.
A range is invalid when it contains both numbers of a forbidden pair.
A pair \cd{{a, b}} is the interval \cd{[lo, hi]}. A range contains the pair when it covers that interval.
\textbf{Memory hook:} A pair closes at its max and pushes left past its min.

Many constraints have the form ``a range that ends at or after \cd{p} must start after \cd{q}''.
Bucket them by \cd{p} and keep the largest \cd{q} in each bucket. A running maximum during the sweep applies them.
This replaces a search over the constraints with $O(1)$ work per step.
\begin{pyex}
def count_valid_sequences(n, pairs):
    block = [0] * (n + 1)                 # block[hi] = largest lo of a pair that closes at hi
    for a, b in pairs:
        lo, hi = min(a, b), max(a, b)
        block[hi] = max(block[hi], lo)
    total = 0
    left = 1                              # smallest valid start for the current right end
    for right in range(1, n + 1):
        left = max(left, block[right] + 1)    # left never moves back
        total += right - left + 1
    return total

count_valid_sequences(4, [[1, 3]])            # -> 8
count_valid_sequences(3, [])                  # -> 6
count_valid_sequences(5, [[1, 2], [4, 5]])    # -> 8
count_valid_sequences(4, [[3, 1], [1, 3]])    # -> 8
\end{pyex}
The running maximum is essential. A pair that closed earlier still blocks every later right end.
The same sweep counts ranges of positive values with a product below $k$,
or ranges with at most $k$ distinct values (see Sliding window).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What is the brute force? Write the quantity for one range or one index as a formula.
  \item Is it a contiguous range? Write it as \cd{f(j) - f(i)} with a running value \cd{f}. Then the task is about pairs of prefixes.
  \item Is the condition an exact value, a remainder or a balance? Keep a hash map of earlier prefix values:
        a count to count ranges, the first index to find the longest range.
  \item Is the condition an inequality? With non-negative values, use a sliding window or a binary search on \cd{P}.
        With negative values, use a sorted list of earlier prefixes or a monotonic deque.
  \item Does the answer at \cd{i} need both sides of \cd{i}? Use a prefix pass and a suffix pass.
        If the operation has an inverse, the total minus one part is simpler.
  \item Is it the best pair with \cd{i < j}? Split the score into \cd{f(i) + g(j)} and keep the running best of \cd{f(i)}.
  \item Are there many range updates before one read? Use a difference array.
  \item Does every item get the same move? Track one shared offset. If items drop out at a bound, track its minimum and maximum too.
  \item Does validity survive shrinking? Keep the smallest valid left end and add \cd{r - left + 1}.
  \item Is it a grid? Build a padded 2D table. If the question asks for a size, check that the condition is monotone, then binary search.
  \item What is the empty prefix? Seed it: 0 for a sum, 1 for a product, \cd{{0: 1}} for counts, \cd{{0: -1}} for first indexes, 0 for an offset.
  \item Ask before you add. Decide if the problem allows a pair of one position with itself.
  \item Test the small cases by hand: one element, a zero value, \cd{k = 0}, and a range that starts at index 0.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Off-by-one in the prefix array.} \cd{P} has \cd{n + 1} entries.
The sum of \cd{nums[l..r]} is \cd{P[r + 1] - P[l]}, not \cd{P[r] - P[l]}.
A padded table (one zero row and one zero column in 2D) removes all bounds checks.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The empty prefix.} Without \cd{seen[0] = 1}, the sweep misses every range that starts at index 0.
Without \cd{first[0] = -1}, the longest range from index 0 is lost.
Offsets and their extremes start at 0, not at the first move.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Add before ask.} An insert before the lookup pairs a prefix with itself.
With \cd{k = 0}, this counts empty ranges.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def wrong(nums, k):
    seen, prefix, count = {0: 1}, 0, 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1    # add first: wrong
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)
    return count

wrong([0, 0], 0)                                  # -> 5
wrong([1, 1, 1], 2)                               # -> 2
\end{pyex}
The correct answer for \cd{[0, 0]} and \cd{k = 0} is 3. The bug is invisible when \cd{k} is not 0.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Sliding window on negative values.} A window needs a sum that never drops when the window grows.
Negative values break that. For an exact count, zeros also break a simple window, because several starts give the same sum.
Use prefix sums with a hash map.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong identity.} A running product starts at 1, a running minimum at \cd{inf} or the first element,
a running maximum at \cd{-inf}. A minimum price that starts at 0 never changes.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Global extremes ignore the order.} The global minimum can come after the global maximum.
For prices \cd{[2, 4, 1]} the answer is 2, not 3. Keep the minimum of the prefix only.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The final offset is not enough.} With permanent loss, an item can leave and the offset can come back.
Track the minimum and the maximum over all prefixes.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{2D tables.} \cd{[[0] * n] * m} makes all rows one list. Use a comprehension for any table that you write to.
Check the signs: subtract the top strip and the left strip, then add back the corner.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Binary search on a size.} The search for a maximum with \cd{lo = mid} needs the upper mid \cd{(lo + hi + 1) // 2}.
The upper bound is \cd{min(rows, cols)}, not \cd{max(rows, cols)}.
The answer can be 0, so side 0 must be a possible result. The search is valid only for non-negative values.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Empty slices.} When a computed range is empty, its end can be negative.
A negative slice end counts from the end of the list, so the slice returns real elements. Guard the empty case first.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Difference array size.} An update that ends at index \cd{n - 1} writes to \cd{diff[n]}. Allocate \cd{n + 1} slots.
\end{caution}

\begin{note}
A \cd{defaultdict} lookup inserts the missing key. The count stays correct, but the map grows.
Use \cd{dict.get} or \cd{Counter} to read a missing key without an insert.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Product of Array Except Self & Exclude one index. No division. A left pass writes prefix products. A right pass multiplies in a scalar suffix. & Answer = left product times right product. In each pass, use the running product, then multiply in nums[i]. \\
Subarray Sum Equals K & Exact range sum with negative values. Count earlier prefixes \cd{prefix - k} in a map seeded with \cd{{0: 1}}. & Two Sum on prefix sums: look up prefix minus k, then store prefix. \\
Maximum Side Length of a Square with Sum Less than or Equal to Threshold & 2D prefix table. \emph{Some} square of side \cd{k} fits. Monotone in \cd{k}, so binary search the side. & Prefix table for O(1) squares, then binary search the biggest side that fits. \\
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock & Best pair with \cd{i < j}. The best partner is the running minimum. The answer starts at 0. & Remember the cheapest day, sell today. \\
Trapping Rain Water & Per index: \cd{min} of prefix maximum and suffix maximum, minus the bar. Two pointers give $O(1)$ space. & Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T02} (page~\pageref{drill:T02}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T02} (page~\pageref{ans:T02}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Two pointers}\label{tech:T03}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
A pointer is an index into an array or a reference to a list node.
Two pointers walk the data at the same time, and each pointer moves in one direction only.
Each pointer makes $O(n)$ moves, so the total work is $O(n)$.
A brute force over pairs checks about $n^2/2$ pairs.
The two pointers do less work because each step proves a fact about one element.
The element cannot be part of any answer, or of a better answer than the best so far.
That element is then discarded for good.

\textbf{Worked example.} Find two values with the sum 9 in the sorted list $[1, 3, 4, 6, 9]$.
Put \cd{lo} on 1 and \cd{hi} on 9. The sum 10 is too large.
The value 9 is too large even with the smallest partner, 1. So no pair uses 9: move \cd{hi} to 6.
The sum $1 + 6 = 7$ is too small.
The value 1 is too small even with the largest partner that is left, 6. So no pair uses 1: move \cd{lo} to 3.
The sum $3 + 6 = 9$ is the answer. Three steps replace the ten pairs of the brute force.

The pointers can move in four shapes. Each shape keeps a different fact true.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.5cm}L{3.6cm}L{4.3cm}L{5.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Shape & Moves & Use it for & Fact that stays true \\
\midrule
Converging & \cd{lo} from the left, \cd{hi} from the right, toward each other &
  pair sums on sorted data, symmetric checks, the best pair with a bottleneck &
  Every answer lies inside \cd{[lo, hi]}, or the best answer outside it is already recorded. \\
Fast and slow & same direction, two speeds or a fixed gap &
  cycles, the middle, the $k$th node from the end on forward-only data &
  After $t$ steps, slow is at position $t$ and fast is at $2t$. Or fast is $k$ nodes ahead of slow. \\
Read and write & same direction, write never ahead of read &
  filter, remove, deduplicate or partition in place &
  \cd{a[:w]} is the finished output. \\
One per sequence & each pointer walks its own sorted input &
  merge, intersection, subsequence check &
  The output so far is final and sorted. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Only the converging shape removes pairs. The other three shapes remove memory or a second pass.
Fast and slow pointers replace a visited set, a node array or a length count.
Read and write pointers replace a second output array.
One pointer per sorted input replaces a new sort of all the values.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
\item The input is sorted. Or you can sort it, because neither the output nor the score uses the original positions.
\item The task asks for a pair or a triple with a sum condition, and $n$ is too large to try every pair ($n \geq 10^4$)
  or every triple ($n$ in the thousands).
\item The score of a pair depends only on the two endpoints. One endpoint caps the score (a minimum of the two),
  and the distance between them grows toward the ends.
\item The task compares element $k$ with element $n-1-k$: a palindrome, a mirror, a front-back order.
\item The task asks for $O(1)$ extra space, and the easy answer uses a hash set or a cleaned copy.
\item The data is a singly linked list, and the question is about a cycle, the middle or the $k$th node from the end.
\item Each value is a valid index into the same array, or one deterministic step repeats on a finite set of states.
  The data is then a functional graph, and a walk must enter a cycle.
\item The task says ``in place'' and asks to remove, filter or deduplicate elements of an array.
\item The task groups the elements in place and in one pass.
  The keys are few: 0, 1 and 2, or below, equal to and above a pivot.
\item Two or more sorted inputs give one sorted output, or one check walks two sequences together.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
The converging skeleton fits all pair searches on sorted data and all ``best pair'' searches.
Only the use of the pair and the discard rule change from problem to problem.
\begin{pyshow}
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo < hi:
    use the pair (lo, hi): return it, count it, or update the best
    if the element at lo cannot be in a better answer:
        lo += 1
    else:
        hi -= 1
\end{pyshow}
The sorted pair sum is the basic instance.
\begin{pyex}
def pair_with_sum(a, target):        # a is sorted; return (i, j) with i < j, or None
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target:
            return lo, hi
        if s < target:
            lo += 1                  # a[lo] is too small even with the largest partner
        else:
            hi -= 1                  # a[hi] is too large even with the smallest partner
    return None

pair_with_sum([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 9)    # -> (1, 3)
pair_with_sum([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 2)    # -> None
pair_with_sum([3, 3], 6)             # -> (0, 1)
pair_with_sum([1, 2, 5], 10)         # -> None
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} Every answer pair $(i, j)$ stays inside the range \cd{[lo, hi]}: \cd{lo <= i} and \cd{j <= hi}.
Each step discards one end and keeps the invariant. So \cd{hi - lo} decreases by one, and the loop ends in at most $n - 1$ steps.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Pair search on sorted data: find, count, closest}
\textbf{Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted} is the core template with 1-based output indices.
The template returns 0-based indices. For this problem, return \cd{[lo + 1, hi + 1]}.
Memory hook: \emph{Sorted pair sum: start at both ends. Too small, move left up. Too big, move right down.}
The same loop answers three more questions. Only the action on the pair changes.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Count the pairs below a target.} If \cd{a[lo] + a[hi] < target}, then \cd{a[lo]} pairs with every index in
  \cd{lo+1..hi}. Add \cd{hi - lo} at once, then move \cd{lo}.
\item \textbf{The closest sum.} Keep the sum with the smallest \cd{abs(s - target)}. Move the pointers as in the template.
\item \textbf{Unsorted input.} Sort first in $O(n \log n)$ when the output needs values only.
  When it needs the original indices, sort \cd{(value, index)} pairs, or use a hash map.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import combinations

def count_pairs_below(a, target):    # pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] < target
    a = sorted(a)
    lo, hi, count = 0, len(a) - 1, 0
    while lo < hi:
        if a[lo] + a[hi] < target:
            count += hi - lo         # a[lo] works with every index in lo+1..hi
            lo += 1
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return count

count_pairs_below([-1, 1, 2, 3, 1], 2)                          # -> 3
a = [5, -2, 7, 0, 3, 3, -4]
count_pairs_below(a, 4) == sum(x + y < 4 for x, y in combinations(a, 2))
# -> True
\end{pyex}
(Count Pairs Whose Sum is Less than Target, 3Sum Closest, Two Sum IV on a BST.)

\subsubsection{Same-direction pointers for a pair difference}
A difference needs another shape. From the two ends, a difference that is too large does not tell you which end to move:
both moves make it smaller. Start both pointers at the left instead.
If the gap \cd{a[j] - a[i]} is too small, move \cd{j}. If it is too large, move \cd{i}.
Each move changes the gap in one known direction, so each comparison again discards one index for good.
Memory hook: \emph{Difference: both start left. Gap too small, move the leading pointer. Gap too big, move the trailing pointer.}
\begin{pyex}
def pair_with_difference(a, k):      # a is sorted, k >= 0; i != j and a[j] - a[i] == k
    i, j = 0, 1
    while j < len(a):
        d = a[j] - a[i]
        if i == j or d < k:
            j += 1                   # the gap is too small: widen it
        elif d > k:
            i += 1                   # the gap is too large: shrink it
        else:
            return i, j
    return None

pair_with_difference([1, 3, 5, 8], 3)    # -> (2, 3)
pair_with_difference([1, 4, 6], 5)       # -> (0, 2)
pair_with_difference([1, 1, 4], 0)       # -> (0, 1)
pair_with_difference([1, 2], 0)          # -> None
\end{pyex}
(K-diff Pairs in an Array; the pair count inside Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance.)

\subsubsection{k-sum: fix one element, then squeeze}
\textbf{3Sum} asks for all value triples with sum 0 and no repeated triples.
Sort, fix an anchor \cd{a[i]}, and run the sorted pair search on the suffix with target \cd{-a[i]}.
The cost is $n$ anchors times $O(n)$, so $O(n^2)$.
Memory hook: \emph{Sort, fix one, squeeze two pointers, skip repeats.}

Sorting also removes duplicate triples without a set. At each choice level, use a value only the first time it appears.
Compare with the previous element (\cd{a[i] == a[i - 1]}), not the next one.
Then the first copy still pairs with its own repeats, as in $[-1, -1, 2]$.
After a match, move \cd{lo} past all copies of the value just used.
When the anchor is positive, every later value is positive too, so stop.
\begin{pyex}
def three_sum(nums):
    a = sorted(nums)                 # sorted() keeps the caller's list unchanged
    n, res = len(a), []
    for i in range(n - 2):
        if a[i] > 0:
            break                    # every later value is positive too
        if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]:
            continue                 # this anchor value was already used
        lo, hi = i + 1, n - 1
        while lo < hi:
            s = a[i] + a[lo] + a[hi]
            if s < 0:
                lo += 1
            elif s > 0:
                hi -= 1
            else:
                res.append([a[i], a[lo], a[hi]])
                lo += 1
                hi -= 1
                while lo < hi and a[lo] == a[lo - 1]:
                    lo += 1          # skip copies of the left value just used
    return res

three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4])     # -> [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0])              # -> [[0, 0, 0]]
three_sum([0, 1, 1])                 # -> []
\end{pyex}
The same idea works for any $k$: fix one element and solve $(k-1)$-sum on the rest.
The base case is the pair search. The cost is $O(n^{k-1})$.
\begin{pyex}
def k_sum(a, k, target, start=0):    # a is sorted; value lists of size k, no repeats
    res = []
    if k == 2:
        lo, hi = start, len(a) - 1
        while lo < hi:
            s = a[lo] + a[hi]
            if s < target:
                lo += 1
            elif s > target:
                hi -= 1
            else:
                res.append([a[lo], a[hi]])
                lo += 1
                hi -= 1
                while lo < hi and a[lo] == a[lo - 1]:
                    lo += 1
        return res
    for i in range(start, len(a) - k + 1):
        if i > start and a[i] == a[i - 1]:
            continue                 # same value at the same level: skip it
        for rest in k_sum(a, k - 1, target - a[i], i + 1):
            res.append([a[i]] + rest)
    return res

k_sum(sorted([1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2]), 4, 0)
# -> [[-2, -1, 1, 2], [-2, 0, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 0, 1]]
k_sum(sorted([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]), 3, 0)    # -> [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
\end{pyex}
(4Sum, 3Sum Closest.)
To count index triples instead of value triples, add \cd{hi - lo} at once, as in the pair count (3Sum Smaller).
For an exact sum with many repeated values, count each value and use combinatorics (3Sum With Multiplicity).

\subsubsection{Symmetric checks from both ends}
A palindrome check compares the $k$th item from the left with the $k$th item from the right.
\textbf{Valid Palindrome} keeps only letters and digits and ignores case.
The intuitive solution builds the cleaned list and compares it with its reverse.
Memory hook: \emph{Clean it, flip it, compare.}
The converging form is the aside. It needs $O(1)$ extra space and stops at the first mismatch.
Use it when the task asks for $O(1)$ extra space, or when the check must react to the first mismatch.
Each loop step does one thing: it skips one invalid character, or it consumes one matched pair.
So the loop needs no inner skip loops and no extra bound checks.
\begin{pyex}
def is_pal_clean(s):
    cleaned = [ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum()]
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

def is_pal_pointers(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        if not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1                   # skip an invalid character on the left
        elif not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1                   # skip an invalid character on the right
        elif s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        else:
            i += 1                   # one matched pair is done
            j -= 1
    return True

s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
is_pal_clean(s), is_pal_pointers(s)            # -> (True, True)
is_pal_clean("0P"), is_pal_pointers("0P")      # -> (False, False)
is_pal_pointers(".,"), is_pal_pointers("aA")   # -> (True, True)
\end{pyex}
Swap instead of compare, and the same loop reverses an array in place.
Add the same skips, and it reverses only selected characters.
(Reverse String, Reverse Only Letters, Palindrome Number.)

\subsubsection{Discard the weaker endpoint}
Some problems ask for the best pair, and the score is a bottleneck times a distance.
In \textbf{Container With Most Water}, the area of lines $i < j$ is \cd{min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i)}.
Start with the widest pair. Suppose \cd{h[lo] < h[hi]}.
Every inner partner of \cd{lo} is narrower, and the height stays at most \cd{h[lo]}.
So \cd{lo} has already met its best partner. Record the area and discard \cd{lo}.
On a tie, discard either line.
Memory hook: \emph{Start widest, keep the best area, and move the shorter wall in.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_area(h):
    lo, hi, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
    while lo < hi:
        best = max(best, min(h[lo], h[hi]) * (hi - lo))
        if h[lo] < h[hi]:
            lo += 1                  # the shorter wall is done
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return best

max_area([1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7])    # -> 49
max_area([1, 1])                         # -> 1
max_area([2, 9, 9, 2])                   # -> 9
\end{pyex}
The general rule: move the pointer whose element cannot appear in a better answer.
Write a one-sentence proof that every skipped pair is no better than a pair already checked.
If the score uses a maximum instead of a minimum, this proof fails. Think again about which end is dominated.

\subsubsection{Settle the side with the smaller bound}
In \textbf{Trapping Rain Water}, the water above bar $i$ is the lower of two walls minus the bar:
\cd{min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - h[i]}.
The intuitive solution computes both walls with a prefix maximum pass and a suffix maximum pass.
Memory hook: \emph{Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height.}

The converging form removes both arrays.
Keep \cd{left_max} for \cd{h[0..lo]} and \cd{right_max} for \cd{h[hi..n-1]}.
If \cd{left_max < right_max}, the true right wall of index \cd{lo + 1} is at least \cd{right_max}.
So \cd{left_max} alone decides the level there. Settle that index now, then do the mirror step on the other side.
The general rule: if the answer is \cd{min(A, B)} and you know $A \leq$ a lower bound of $B$, the answer is $A$.
\begin{pyex}
def trap_arrays(h):                  # intuitive: two passes, O(n) space
    n = len(h)
    left_max, right_max = h[:], h[:]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], h[i])
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], h[i])
    return sum(min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - h[i] for i in range(n))

def trap_pointers(h):                # converging: O(1) space
    lo, hi = 0, len(h) - 1
    left_max, right_max = h[lo], h[hi]
    water = 0
    while lo < hi:
        if left_max < right_max:
            lo += 1
            left_max = max(left_max, h[lo])    # update first, then add
            water += left_max - h[lo]
        else:
            hi -= 1
            right_max = max(right_max, h[hi])
            water += right_max - h[hi]
    return water

h = [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]
trap_arrays(h), trap_pointers(h)         # -> (6, 6)
trap_pointers([4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5])        # -> 9
trap_pointers([5])                       # -> 0
trap_arrays([3, 0, 1]), trap_pointers([3, 0, 1])    # -> (1, 1)
\end{pyex}
Use the arrays first. Switch to the pointers only when the task asks for $O(1)$ extra space.

\subsubsection{Read and write pointers: compact in place}
The read pointer \cd{r} visits every element. The write pointer \cd{w} marks the end of the kept part.
Copy \cd{a[r]} to \cd{a[w]} only when the element stays.
\textbf{Invariant:} \cd{a[:w]} holds the kept elements in their original order, and $w \leq r$.
So a write never destroys an element that is not read yet.
To keep a condition on the output itself, compare with the written part, for example \cd{a[w - 1]}.
Memory hook: \emph{Read every element, write only the keepers. The prefix before w is done.}
\begin{pyex}
def remove_value(a, val):            # keep every element that is not val
    w = 0
    for r in range(len(a)):
        if a[r] != val:
            a[w] = a[r]
            w += 1
    return w

def dedupe_sorted(a):                # keep the first copy of each value
    w = 0
    for r in range(len(a)):
        if w == 0 or a[r] != a[w - 1]:
            a[w] = a[r]
            w += 1
    return w

a = [3, 2, 2, 3, 4]
k = remove_value(a, 3)
a[:k]                                # -> [2, 2, 4]
b = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
k = dedupe_sorted(b)
b[:k]                                # -> [0, 1, 2, 3]
\end{pyex}
To keep the removed elements at the end, swap \cd{a[w]} and \cd{a[r]} instead of a copy.
(Remove Element, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, Move Zeroes, String Compression.)

\subsubsection{Three-way partition: three pointers}
Some tasks put each element into one of three groups, in place: below, equal to and above a pivot.
\textbf{Sort Colors} (values 0, 1 and 2) is the usual example.
The easy answer counts each value and writes the counts back. That takes two passes.
For one pass, use three pointers. \cd{lo} and \cd{hi} are write pointers at the two ends. \cd{mid} is the read pointer.
\textbf{Invariant:} \cd{a[:lo]} holds the small keys, \cd{a[lo:mid]} the middle keys and \cd{a[hi + 1:]} the large keys.
\cd{a[mid:hi + 1]} is not read yet, so the loop runs while \cd{mid <= hi}.
A small key at \cd{mid} goes to \cd{lo}, and both pointers move: the value that comes back was read already.
A large key goes to \cd{hi}, and only \cd{hi} moves.
After a swap with \cd{hi}, do not move \cd{mid}: the new \cd{a[mid]} is not read yet.
Memory hook: \emph{Small to the front, large to the back, middle stays. After a swap with the back, look again.}
\begin{pyex}
def partition3(a, pivot):                # in place, one pass
    lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, len(a) - 1
    while mid <= hi:
        if a[mid] < pivot:
            a[lo], a[mid] = a[mid], a[lo]
            lo += 1
            mid += 1                     # the old a[lo] was read already
        elif a[mid] > pivot:
            a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]
            hi -= 1                      # mid stays: the new a[mid] is not read yet
        else:
            mid += 1
    return lo, hi + 1                    # a[lo:hi + 1] holds the keys equal to pivot

a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]
partition3(a, 1)                         # -> (2, 4)
a                                        # -> [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
b = [5, 1, 5, 9, 5, 3, 7]
i, j = partition3(b, 5)
sorted(b[:i]), b[i:j], sorted(b[j:])     # -> ([1, 3], [5, 5, 5], [7, 9])
partition3([], 1)                        # -> (0, 0)
\end{pyex}
For Sort Colors, use the pivot 1. The swaps do not keep the original order inside a group.
(Sort Colors, the partition step of quickselect when many values are equal.)

\subsubsection{Fast and slow pointers: cycle and middle}
\textbf{Linked List Cycle} asks if a list loops, with $O(1)$ extra memory.
Move \cd{slow} one node and \cd{fast} two nodes per step.
Without a cycle, \cd{fast} reaches the end. With a cycle, both pointers enter it.
Inside the cycle, \cd{fast} gains exactly one node per step, so the gap counts down to 0 and cannot skip it.
Memory hook: \emph{Hare runs two, tortoise runs one. If they meet, it loops. If the hare falls off the end, it does not.}
The same loop finds the middle: when \cd{fast} reaches the end, \cd{slow} is halfway.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:            # fast can take two steps
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:                 # the same node object
            return True
    return False                         # fast fell off the end

def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow                          # the right middle for an even length

head = build([1, 2, 3, 4])
middle(head).val                         # -> 3
middle(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])).val       # -> 3
has_cycle(head), has_cycle(None)         # -> (False, False)
head.next.next.next.next = head.next     # the tail now links back to node 2
has_cycle(head)                          # -> True
\end{pyex}
Start \cd{fast} at \cd{head.next} to get the left middle, the last node of the front half.
Use the left middle when you cut a list into two halves.
(Middle of the Linked List, Happy Number, Palindrome Linked List.)

\subsubsection{Cycle entry: an array as a linked list}
\textbf{Find the Duplicate Number} has $n + 1$ values in $[1, n]$, a read-only array and $O(1)$ extra space.
Read the array as a linked list: index \cd{i} points to index \cd{nums[i]}.
No value is 0, so nothing points to index 0. A walk from index 0 must enter a cycle.
The cycle entry has two incoming edges, so two indexes hold its value: the entry is the duplicate.

Floyd's algorithm finds the entry in two phases.
Phase 1 runs fast and slow pointers until they meet.
Phase 2 puts one pointer back at the head and moves both pointers one step at a time. They meet at the entry.
The reason: at the meeting, \cd{slow} walked $m$ steps and \cd{fast} walked $2m$ steps.
Both stand on the same node, so the extra $m$ steps are a whole number of laps.
Let $\mu$ be the tail length, the number of steps from the head to the entry.
After $\mu$ more steps, the pointer from the meeting point is $\mu + m$ steps from the head: the entry plus whole laps.
The pointer from the head is on the entry after the same $\mu$ steps.
Memory hook: \emph{Index points to value: tortoise and hare from 0, then reset one to 0, walk together, and meet at the duplicate.}
\begin{pyex}
def find_duplicate(nums):
    slow, fast = nums[0], nums[nums[0]]  # both pointers after their first move
    while slow != fast:                  # phase 1: meet inside the cycle
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
    start = 0
    while start != slow:                 # phase 2: meet at the cycle entry
        start = nums[start]
        slow = nums[slow]
    return slow

find_duplicate([1, 3, 4, 2, 2])          # -> 2
find_duplicate([3, 1, 3, 4, 2])          # -> 3
find_duplicate([3, 3, 3, 3, 3])          # -> 3
\end{pyex}
The same two phases find the entry of a cycle in a real linked list (Linked List Cycle II).
A second $O(1)$-space approach: binary search on the value.
If more than \cd{mid} values are at most \cd{mid}, the duplicate is in \cd{[1, mid]}.

\subsubsection{Fixed gap: the kth node from the end}
\textbf{Remove Nth Node From End of List} gives a position from the end, but a singly linked list only walks forward.
The intuitive solution lines up the nodes in a Python list behind a dummy node.
Then \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} is the predecessor of the target.
Memory hook: \emph{Line up the nodes behind a dummy, then \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} skips its next.}

The pointer form needs $O(1)$ extra memory. Give \cd{fast} a lead of $n$ nodes and then move both pointers.
The gap stays $n$. Stop when \cd{fast} is on the last node: \cd{slow} is then the predecessor of the target.
Start both pointers at a dummy node, so that the removal of the head needs no special code.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def remove_nth_array(head, n):           # intuitive: O(n) extra memory
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    nodes, node = [], dummy
    while node:
        nodes.append(node)
        node = node.next
    prev = nodes[-n - 1]
    prev.next = prev.next.next
    return dummy.next

def remove_nth_gap(head, n):             # gap pointers: O(1) extra memory
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    slow = fast = dummy
    for _ in range(n):
        fast = fast.next                 # fast leads by n nodes
    while fast.next:                     # stop with fast on the last node
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next           # slow is the predecessor of the target
    return dummy.next

to_list(remove_nth_gap(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2))     # -> [1, 2, 3, 5]
to_list(remove_nth_gap(build([1]), 1))                 # -> []
to_list(remove_nth_gap(build([1, 2]), 2))              # -> [2]
to_list(remove_nth_array(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 5))   # -> [2, 3, 4, 5]
\end{pyex}
Run until \cd{fast} is past the last node, and \cd{slow} lands on the target itself.
(Kth node from the end, Rotate List, Swapping Nodes in a Linked List.)

\subsubsection{Mirror pairs on a forward-only list}
\textbf{Reorder List} changes $L_0, L_1, \ldots, L_{n-1}$ into $L_0, L_{n-1}, L_1, L_{n-2}, \ldots$.
Node $i$ pairs with node $n - 1 - i$, but a singly linked list has no backward step.
The intuitive solution copies the node references into an array.
Two converging indexes then give the order front, back, front, back. Chain the nodes and end the list with \cd{None}.
Memory hook: \emph{Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reorder(head):
    nodes = []
    while head:
        nodes.append(head)
        head = head.next
    order = []
    lo, hi = 0, len(nodes) - 1
    while lo <= hi:                      # lo <= hi: the middle node needs a step
        order.append(nodes[lo])
        if lo < hi:
            order.append(nodes[hi])
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1
    for a, b in zip(order, order[1:]):
        a.next = b
    order[-1].next = None                # end the list, or it has a cycle

head = build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
reorder(head)
to_list(head)                            # -> [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]
head = build([1, 2, 3, 4])
reorder(head)
to_list(head)                            # -> [1, 4, 2, 3]
\end{pyex}
The $O(1)$-space form composes three linked-list routines.
Find the left middle with fast and slow pointers and cut the list there.
Reverse the back half in place, so that a forward walk reads it from the last node. Then weave the two halves, front first.
The same three steps check a palindrome list and find the maximum twin sum. Only the last step changes.

\subsubsection{Merge two sorted sequences}
Each input is sorted, so the smallest value that is left is always one of the current fronts.
Keep one pointer per input. Compare the fronts, take the smaller one, and move that pointer.
When one input runs out, append the rest of the other input.
\begin{pyex}
def merge(a, b):
    i = j = 0
    out = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:                 # <= takes from a first on a tie: stable
            out.append(a[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(a[i:])                    # at most one of these is not empty
    out.extend(b[j:])
    return out

merge([1, 4, 6], [2, 3, 7, 8])           # -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8]
merge([], [5])                           # -> [5]
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Merge Two Sorted Lists} does the same on linked lists. A dummy node removes the special case for the first node.
A \cd{tail} pointer marks the end of the output.
Memory hook: \emph{Dummy and tail. Take the smaller head, move the tail. Glue the rest.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def merge_lists(l1, l2):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.val <= l2.val:
            tail.next, l1 = l1, l1.next
        else:
            tail.next, l2 = l2, l2.next
        tail = tail.next                 # move the tail after each link
    tail.next = l1 or l2                 # glue the rest
    return dummy.next

to_list(merge_lists(build([1, 2, 4]), build([1, 3, 4])))   # -> [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]
to_list(merge_lists(None, build([0])))                     # -> [0]
to_list(merge_lists(None, None))                           # -> []
\end{pyex}
For an intersection, move the pointer at the smaller front.
When the two fronts are equal, emit the value and move both pointers. For $k$ inputs, keep the $k$ fronts in a min-heap.
A subsequence check is also a merge. The pointer of the long sequence moves on every step.
The pointer of the short sequence moves only on a match.
Sometimes the two sorted runs sit at the two ends of one array. Then merge from the ends inward and take the larger value first.
For example, the squares of a sorted array with negative values are largest at the two ends.
(Squares of a Sorted Array, Intersection of Two Arrays II, Is Subsequence, Sort List.)

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item What does the brute force check? If it checks all pairs, can one comparison rule out a full row of pairs?
\item Is the order useful? Is the input sorted, or can you sort it?
  Sorting is safe when neither the output nor the score uses the original positions.
  It is not safe when the output needs original indices, or when the score uses a distance between indices, as in Container With Most Water.
\item Which shape fits?
  A sum, a bottleneck or a mirror: converging.
  A position from the end, the middle or a cycle on forward-only data: fast and slow.
  An in-place filter: read and write. Three groups in place: three pointers.
  Several sorted inputs: one pointer per input.
\item Write the discard rule as one sentence: ``the element at \cd{lo} cannot be in a better answer, because \ldots''.
  If you cannot prove it for either end, the two ends are the wrong start. Try the same direction, or another technique.
\item Decide the action on a match: return it, count \cd{hi - lo} pairs at once, or record it and skip the repeats.
\item Choose the loop condition. Use \cd{lo < hi} when the two pointers must be different elements.
  Use \cd{lo <= hi} when the middle element needs its own step.
\item More than two elements in a group? Fix $k - 2$ elements with loops and run the pair search inside.
\item A linked list? Add a dummy node when the head can change. Aim the trailing pointer at the predecessor of the node to change.
\item Test the edges: an empty input or one element, all values equal, no answer, and an answer at the two ends.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Move exactly one pointer per comparison, and move the right one.}
Moving both pointers on a step without a match can skip the answer.
Moving the taller wall can skip the optimum.
Settling the side with the larger running maximum adds too much water: on $[3, 0, 1]$ it gives 5, not 1.
Move the pointer that your proof discards.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{\cd{lo <= hi} pairs an element with itself.}
The pair search then uses one element two times when no real pair exists.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def pair_bad(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:                      # wrong: lo == hi is one element
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target:
            return lo, hi
        if s < target:
            lo += 1
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return None

pair_bad([1, 2, 5], 10)                  # -> (2, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Bound every inner skip loop.}
Write \cd{while lo < hi and a[lo] == a[lo - 1]}. Without \cd{lo < hi}, the input $[0, 0, 0, 0]$ walks off the end.
In a palindrome check with inner skip loops, each loop needs \cd{i < j}, or \cd{"!!"} raises \cd{IndexError}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Skip repeats by a comparison with the previous element.}
\cd{a[i] == a[i + 1]} skips the first copy of a value, and $[-1, -1, 2]$ is lost.
\cd{a[i] == a[i - 1]} uses the first copy and skips only the later ones.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Fast pointers: check before you jump, compare after you move.}
Test \cd{fast and fast.next} before \cd{fast.next.next}, or a \cd{None} raises \cd{AttributeError}.
Both pointers start on the head, so compare them only after the first move.
Compare nodes with \cd{is}. Two nodes with equal values are not the same node.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The first meeting point of Floyd's algorithm is, in general, not the cycle entry.}
Run phase 2. Put one pointer back on the same head where phase 1 started, not on another node.
In the duplicate problem, the head is index 0, which is never inside the cycle.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]
slow, fast = nums[0], nums[nums[0]]
while slow != fast:
    slow = nums[slow]
    fast = nums[nums[fast]]
slow                                     # -> 4
start = 0
while start != slow:
    start = nums[start]
    slow = nums[slow]
slow                                     # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Linked lists: end the list and return the real head.}
After you rewire nodes, set the next link of the new last node to \cd{None}. Otherwise the list has a cycle.
Return \cd{dummy.next}, not the old head: the old head can move or be removed.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Sorting has side effects.}
\cd{nums.sort()} changes the caller's list, and it loses the original indices.
Use \cd{sorted(nums)}, or sort \cd{(value, index)} pairs when the output needs indices.
\end{caution}

\begin{note}
Converging pointers need a rule that names the end to discard.
For a sum search, a move of \cd{lo} must push the sum up and a move of \cd{hi} must push it down.
For a best pair, one end must be dominated, like the shorter wall.
A difference, a product of signed values or a score with \cd{max} in place of \cd{min} often breaks this rule.
Then use same-direction pointers, a hash map, or another technique.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Valid Palindrome & Keep the letters and digits in lowercase and compare the list with its reverse. Aside: converging pointers for $O(1)$ space. &
  Clean it, flip it, compare. \\
Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted & The core pair search on sorted data. Discard the end that cannot pair. 1-based indices. &
  Sorted pair sum: start at both ends. Too small, move left up. Too big, move right down. \\
3Sum & Sort, fix an anchor, run the pair search on the suffix. Skip a repeated value at each level. &
  Sort, fix one, squeeze two pointers, skip repeats. \\
Container With Most Water & Best pair with a min-times-width score. The shorter wall has met its best partner. &
  Start widest, keep the best area, and move the shorter wall in. \\
Trapping Rain Water & Water at each index is min(prefix max, suffix max) minus the bar. Aside: settle the side with the smaller running maximum for $O(1)$ space. &
  Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height. \\
Linked List Cycle & Fast pointer two steps, slow pointer one step. A meeting proves a cycle. &
  Hare runs two, tortoise runs one. If they meet, it loops. If the hare falls off the end, it does not. \\
Find the Duplicate Number & The array is a functional graph \cd{i -> nums[i]}. Floyd phase 2 finds the cycle entry. &
  Index points to value: tortoise and hare from 0, then reset one to 0, walk together, and meet at the duplicate. \\
Remove Nth Node From End of List & Line up the nodes behind a dummy; \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} is the predecessor. Aside: a gap of $n$ nodes for $O(1)$ memory. &
  Line up the nodes behind a dummy, then \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} skips its next. \\
Reorder List & Mirror pairs $i$ and $n-1-i$ on a forward-only list. Converging indexes on an array of nodes. &
  Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None. \\
Merge Two Sorted Lists & One pointer per sorted input. Take the smaller front; a dummy and a tail build the output. &
  Dummy and tail. Take the smaller head, move the tail. Glue the rest. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
