% =====================================================================
\section{Sliding window}\label{tech:T04}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
A window is a contiguous part \cd{a[left..right]} of an array or a string.
Both ends of the window move only to the right.
In each step, the right end moves one position and one element enters the window.
When the window breaks the rule of the problem, the left end moves and elements leave the window.
Each element enters the window one time and leaves it at most one time.
So the scan does $O(n)$ updates in total.

A brute force checks all $n(n+1)/2$ contiguous segments, and it often scans each segment again.
That is $O(n^2)$ or $O(n^3)$ work.
The window saves this work for two reasons:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{The left end never moves back.} A brute force restarts the left end at 0 for each right end.
        The window keeps the left end where it is. Take a ``longest'' or a ``count'' goal, and suppose
        \cd{a[l..r]} is invalid. Then every longer window \cd{a[l..r2]} contains it and is invalid too.
        So a start that fails one time fails for all later right ends. The scan never tries it again.
        For a ``shortest'' goal, suppose \cd{a[l..r]} is valid. Then every longer window from \cd{l} is worse.
        So the scan records \cd{a[l..r]} and drops \cd{l}.
  \item \textbf{The window keeps a state.} The state is a set, a count map, a sum or a deque.
        It changes in $O(1)$ when one element enters or leaves. The validity test reads the state.
        It does not scan the window again.
\end{itemize}

The first reason needs a \emph{monotone} rule.
For a ``longest'' goal, a valid window must stay valid when it shrinks.
For a ``shortest'' goal, a valid window must stay valid when it grows.
A ``count'' goal can use either direction. The table in the core template shows the two loop shapes.
If the rule is not monotone, the correct left end can be behind the current left end. Then the method gives wrong answers.

\textbf{Worked example.} Find the longest substring of \cd{"pwwkew"} with no repeated character.
The state is the set of characters in the window.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{right = 0} adds \cd{p}. The window is \cd{"p"}, length 1.
  \item \cd{right = 1} adds \cd{w}. The window is \cd{"pw"}, length 2.
  \item \cd{right = 2} reads \cd{w}, which is already in the set. Remove \cd{p} and then \cd{w} from the left.
        Now \cd{left = 2}. Add the new \cd{w}. The window is \cd{"w"}.
  \item \cd{right = 3} and \cd{right = 4} add \cd{k} and \cd{e}. The window is \cd{"wke"}, length 3.
  \item \cd{right = 5} reads \cd{w} again. Remove one \cd{w} from the left. The window is \cd{"kew"}, length 3.
\end{itemize}
The answer is 3. Six characters entered the window and three characters left it. The work is linear.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The answer is a \textbf{contiguous} segment: a subarray, a substring, a run of days, a block of
        consecutive values. A subsequence or a subset is not a window problem.
  \item The goal is the longest, the shortest, the number of, or the existence of a segment with a property.
        Or the goal is one value (a maximum, a sum, a match) for every segment of a fixed size $k$.
  \item The property is monotone. Words such as ``at most $k$'', ``no repeated'', ``does not contain''
        and ``less than'' (with non-negative values) usually give a rule that survives shrinking.
        Words such as ``contains all of'', ``at least'' and ``covers'' usually give a rule that survives growing.
  \item A budget limits the bad elements in the segment: at most $k$ changes, flips, zeros, deletions or
        distinct values.
  \item The statement says ``anagram'' or ``permutation'' of a pattern, together with ``substring''.
        The length is then fixed, and only the counts matter.
  \item The statement asks for the number of segments with \emph{exactly} $k$ of something
        (odd numbers, distinct values, ones). Count two windows: at most $k$, and at most $k - 1$.
  \item The statement asks for the maximum or the minimum of every window of size $k$. Or the rule uses the
        maximum or the minimum of the window, such as \cd{max - min <= limit}.
  \item The length is up to about $10^5$. An $O(n^2)$ scan of all segments is too slow, and the target is $O(n)$.
  \item The statement asks for the best pair \cd{i < j}, such as ``buy before you sell''.
        The left end of the window then jumps to the best earlier element.
\end{itemize}
\begin{note}
Sums with negative values are not monotone: a shrink can make the sum larger or smaller.
For such problems, use prefix sums with a hash map, or a monotonic deque of prefix sums.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Answer three questions before you write code.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{State.} What data tells you if the window is valid? It must update in $O(1)$
        when one element enters and when one element leaves.
  \item \textbf{Rule.} Write the validity test as an expression of the state.
  \item \textbf{Record.} Where in the loop is the window an answer candidate? See the table below.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{pyshow}
left = 0
for right, x in enumerate(a):
    add x to the state                       # grow on the right
    while the window a[left..right] is invalid:
        remove a[left] from the state        # shrink on the left
        left += 1
    record the answer for a[left..right]     # longest: right - left + 1
\end{pyshow}
The tested template below finds the longest valid window. The state is a \cd{Counter} of the window.
Only the rule changes from problem to problem, so the rule is a parameter.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def longest_window(a, invalid):
    count = Counter()                  # value -> count in a[left..right]
    left = best = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        count[x] += 1                  # grow: x enters on the right
        while invalid(count, right - left + 1):
            out = a[left]              # shrink: a[left] leaves on the left
            count[out] -= 1
            if count[out] == 0:
                del count[out]         # keep len(count) = number of distinct values
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)   # a[left..right] is valid here
    return best

def has_repeat(count, size):
    return len(count) < size           # fewer distinct values than elements

def more_than_two_kinds(count, size):
    return len(count) > 2

def needs_more_than_one_change(count, size):
    return size - max(count.values()) > 1

longest_window("pwwkew", has_repeat)                    # -> 3
longest_window([1, 2, 1, 2, 3], more_than_two_kinds)    # -> 4
longest_window("AABABBA", needs_more_than_one_change)   # -> 4
longest_window("", has_repeat)                          # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} After the shrink loop, \cd{a[left..right]} is valid, and \cd{left} is the smallest
valid start for this right end. The left end never moves back, so the total time is $O(n)$ times the cost
of one rule test.

The goal decides the loop shape and the place of the record step.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.7cm}L{4.0cm}L{4.9cm}L{4.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Goal & Left end moves & Record & Needs \\
\midrule
Longest valid & \cd{while} the window is invalid & after the loop: \cd{best = max(best, right - left + 1)} &
  a rule that stays true when the window shrinks \\
Count valid, rule survives shrinking & \cd{while} the window is invalid & after the loop: \cd{total += right - left + 1} &
  a rule that stays true when the window shrinks \\
Count valid, rule survives growing & \cd{while} the window is valid & after the loop: \cd{total += left} &
  a rule that stays true when the window grows \\
Shortest valid & \cd{while} the window is valid & inside the loop, before the removal:
  \cd{best = min(best, right - left + 1)} & a rule that stays true when the window grows \\
Fixed size $k$ & remove \cd{a[right - k]} when \cd{right >= k} & when \cd{right >= k - 1} &
  a state with add and remove \\
Max or min of each window & pop the front index when it leaves & when the window is full: \cd{a[dq[0]]} &
  a monotonic deque of indices \\
Best pair \cd{i < j} & jump to a better start & after the update of the start &
  one summary of the past, such as a minimum \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{The left end jumps: a running minimum}
In Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, the left end is the buy day and the right end is the sell day.
When a price is lower than the price at the left end, no later sell day prefers the old buy day.
So the left end jumps to the new low. Only the price at the left end matters, so keep the running minimum.
Memory hook: \emph{Remember the cheapest day, sell today.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_profit(prices):
    min_price = prices[0]                    # cheapest buy price so far
    best = 0                                 # 0 means "do not trade"
    for price in prices:
        min_price = min(min_price, price)    # buy at the lowest price so far
        best = max(best, price - min_price)  # sell today
    return best

max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4])   # -> 5
max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1])      # -> 0
max_profit([2, 4, 1])            # -> 2
\end{pyex}
The general idea is the best pair with an order \cd{i < j}. Fix the right element \cd{j}.
Keep one summary of the prefix that gives the best partner: a minimum, a maximum, or a hash map.
For example, Two Sum keeps a hash map of the earlier values.

\subsubsection{Longest window with a set}
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters is the base case of the template.
The state is the set of characters in the window. The window is invalid when the new character is already
in the set. Shrink until it is not, then add it.
Memory hook: \emph{Drop from the left until the new character is unique, then add it on the right.}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_unique(s):
    window = set()                 # characters in s[left..right]
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in window:        # shrink until ch is unique
            window.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        window.add(ch)             # grow
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

longest_unique("abcabcbb")   # -> 3
longest_unique("bbbbb")      # -> 1
longest_unique("pwwkew")     # -> 3
longest_unique("")           # -> 0
\end{pyex}
A second form stores the last index of each character. The left end then jumps past the old copy in one step.
This form needs \cd{left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)}. See the pitfalls.

\subsubsection{Longest window under a budget}
Many problems allow at most $k$ changes, flips or deletions. Write the cost of a window as an
expression of the state. The cost must not decrease when the window grows. Then shrink while the cost is
more than $k$.

In Longest Repeating Character Replacement, the cheapest way to make a window uniform keeps its most
common letter and changes all other letters. So the cost is the window length minus the top count.
Memory hook: \emph{Window length minus top count must be at most k.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def character_replacement(s, k):
    count = Counter()
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1
        # changes needed = window length - count of the most common letter
        while (right - left + 1) - max(count.values()) > k:
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

character_replacement("ABAB", 2)      # -> 4
character_replacement("AABABBA", 1)   # -> 4
character_replacement("ABCD", 0)      # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The scan \cd{max(count.values())} costs $O(26)$ per step. That is fast for a small alphabet.
For other budgets, the cost is often simpler. In Max Consecutive Ones III, the cost is the number of zeros
in the window. For at most $k$ distinct characters, the cost is the number of keys in the \cd{Counter}.
\begin{note}
The optimal solution keeps \cd{max_freq} as a running maximum that never decreases. It removes the
factor of 26. A stale \cd{max_freq} can keep a window that is not valid now.
That window is never longer than the best valid window so far.
The answer grows only when a count goes above the old \cd{max_freq}.
This trick works only when the goal is the maximum length.
\end{note}
In the optimal form, the window slides and never shrinks. When the window is too long, exactly one element
leaves, so an \cd{if} replaces the \cd{while}.
\begin{pyex}
def character_replacement_fast(s, k):
    count = {}
    left = max_freq = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] = count.get(ch, 0) + 1
        max_freq = max(max_freq, count[ch])      # never decreases
        if (right - left + 1) - max_freq > k:    # slide: the length never shrinks
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

character_replacement_fast("AABABBA", 1)   # -> 4
character_replacement_fast("ABAB", 2)      # -> 4
character_replacement_fast("ABCD", 0)      # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The general rule: when the goal is the maximum length, a bound that can only be too high is safe.
The condition is that the answer can grow only when that bound grows.

\subsubsection{Fixed-size window}
When the length of the answer is known, the window has a fixed size $k$.
In each step, one element enters at \cd{right}, and the element \cd{a[right - k]} leaves when \cd{right >= k}.
The window is full when \cd{right >= k - 1}.

In Permutation in String, a permutation of \cd{s1} is any string with the same letter counts.
So slide a window of length \cd{len(s1)} over \cd{s2} and compare two count arrays.
Memory hook: \emph{Slide a window of len(s1) over s2 and compare its letter counts to s1's counts.}
\begin{pyex}
def check_inclusion(s1, s2):
    k = len(s1)
    need = [0] * 26                 # letter counts of s1
    window = [0] * 26               # letter counts of the last k letters of s2
    for ch in s1:
        need[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
    for right, ch in enumerate(s2):
        window[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1                 # enters on the right
        if right >= k:
            window[ord(s2[right - k]) - ord("a")] -= 1  # leaves on the left
        if window == need:                              # same counts: a permutation
            return True
    return False

check_inclusion("ab", "eidbaooo")   # -> True
check_inclusion("ab", "eidboaoo")   # -> False
check_inclusion("abc", "ab")        # -> False
\end{pyex}
The compare \cd{window == need} costs $O(26)$. That is fast for lowercase letters.
\textbf{Optimal aside.} For a large or unknown alphabet, keep one map \cd{diff}.
It holds the window count minus the pattern count for each key.
Also keep an integer \cd{bad}: the number of keys with a nonzero \cd{diff}.
Only the entering key and the leaving key can change \cd{bad}. The window matches when \cd{bad == 0}.
\begin{pyex}
def check_inclusion_fast(s1, s2):
    k = len(s1)
    diff = {}                       # count in window - count in s1
    for ch in s1:
        diff[ch] = diff.get(ch, 0) - 1
    bad = len(diff)                 # keys with a nonzero diff
    def update(ch, delta):
        nonlocal bad
        old = diff.get(ch, 0)
        diff[ch] = old + delta
        bad += (old == 0) - (old + delta == 0)   # +1 if it left 0, -1 if it came back
    for right, ch in enumerate(s2):
        update(ch, 1)
        if right >= k:
            update(s2[right - k], -1)
        if bad == 0:
            return True
    return False

check_inclusion_fast("ab", "eidbaooo")   # -> True
check_inclusion_fast("aab", "abba")      # -> False
check_inclusion_fast("aab", "cbaa")      # -> True
\end{pyex}
A fixed window also gives the sum, the average or the number of vowels of each block of $k$ elements.
Add the entering value and subtract the leaving value.

\subsubsection{Shortest window: shrink while valid}
For a ``shortest'' goal, flip the loop. Grow the window until it is valid. Then shrink it while it stays
valid, and record the window \emph{inside} the shrink loop, before each removal.
The simplest case uses a sum of non-negative values and a positive target.
\begin{pyex}
def shortest_sum_at_least(a, target):     # values >= 0, target > 0
    total = left = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        total += x
        while total >= target:            # valid: record, then shrink
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= a[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

shortest_sum_at_least([2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3], 7)   # -> 2
shortest_sum_at_least([1, 1, 1], 5)            # -> 0
\end{pyex}
When the rule is ``the window contains every required item with its count'', use a \textbf{need/have}
pair of counters. \cd{need} holds the required counts. \cd{have} counts the keys that meet their requirement.
The window is valid when \cd{have == required}. Change \cd{have} only when one count crosses its threshold:
up when \cd{window[c]} becomes equal to \cd{need[c]}, down when it falls below \cd{need[c]}.
This is Minimum Window Substring.
Memory hook: \emph{Grow right until have equals required, then shrink left while it holds.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    window = Counter()
    have, required = 0, len(need)     # keys that meet their count; keys in t
    best_len, best_start = float("inf"), 0
    left = 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        window[c] += 1
        if c in need and window[c] == need[c]:          # c just reached its count
            have += 1
        while have == required:                         # valid: record, then shrink
            if right - left + 1 < best_len:
                best_len, best_start = right - left + 1, left
            out = s[left]
            window[out] -= 1
            if out in need and window[out] < need[out]:  # out just fell short
                have -= 1
            left += 1
    if best_len == float("inf"):
        return ""
    return s[best_start:best_start + best_len]

min_window("ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC")   # -> 'BANC'
min_window("a", "aa")                # -> ''
min_window("aa", "aa")               # -> 'aa'
\end{pyex}
Store the start and the length of the best window, and slice one time at the end.
A slice at each improvement copies the window each time.

\subsubsection{Counting windows: add right - left + 1}
Count the valid segments when the rule survives shrinking. Fix the right end. After the shrink loop,
every start from \cd{left} to \cd{right} gives a valid segment. So \cd{right - left + 1} valid segments
end at \cd{right}. Add this number for each right end. This counts up to $n(n+1)/2$ segments in $O(n)$.
Memory hook: \emph{Every start from left to right is valid, so add right - left + 1.}

In a problem with forbidden pairs, the segments are runs \cd{l, l + 1, ..., r} of the numbers \cd{1..n}.
A run is invalid when it contains both numbers of a forbidden pair. So the pair $\{a, b\}$ acts as the
interval \cd{[lo, hi]}, and a run is invalid when it covers that interval. A pair has no effect until the
right end reaches \cd{hi}. From then on, every valid start is after \cd{lo}.
Keep \cd{block[hi]}, the largest \cd{lo} for each \cd{hi}, and move \cd{left} with a running maximum.
Memory hook: \emph{A pair closes at its max and pushes left past its min.}
\begin{pyex}
def count_valid_sequences(n, pairs):
    block = [0] * (n + 1)          # block[r] = largest lo of a pair with hi = r
    for a, b in pairs:
        lo, hi = min(a, b), max(a, b)
        block[hi] = max(block[hi], lo)
    total = 0
    left = 1                       # smallest valid start for this right end
    for right in range(1, n + 1):
        left = max(left, block[right] + 1)   # left never moves back
        total += right - left + 1            # starts left, left + 1, ..., right
    return total

count_valid_sequences(4, [[1, 3]])           # -> 8
count_valid_sequences(3, [])                 # -> 6
count_valid_sequences(5, [[1, 2], [4, 5]])   # -> 8
\end{pyex}
The trick is reusable. Many constraints can say ``a window that ends at or after \cd{p} must start after
\cd{q}''. Bucket them by \cd{p}, keep the largest \cd{q} per bucket, and take a running maximum in the sweep.

A rule with ``exactly $k$'' does not survive shrinking. Count two windows that do:
\emph{exactly $k$ = at most $k$ minus at most $k - 1$}.
The example counts the subarrays with exactly $k$ distinct values ($k \ge 1$).
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def count_at_most(a, k):           # subarrays with at most k distinct values
    count = Counter()
    left = total = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        count[x] += 1
        while len(count) > k:
            count[a[left]] -= 1
            if count[a[left]] == 0:
                del count[a[left]]
            left += 1
        total += right - left + 1
    return total

def count_exactly(a, k):
    return count_at_most(a, k) - count_at_most(a, k - 1)

count_at_most([1, 2, 1, 2, 3], 2)    # -> 12
count_exactly([1, 2, 1, 2, 3], 2)    # -> 7
count_exactly([1, 2, 1, 3, 4], 3)    # -> 3
\end{pyex}

Some count rules survive growing: ``contains all of'', ``at least $k$''. Then flip the loop.
Shrink while the window is valid. After the loop, \cd{a[left..right]} is invalid, but every start before
\cd{left} gives a valid window. So add \cd{left} for each right end.
Memory hook: \emph{Shrink while valid, then every start before left is valid, so add left.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def count_with_all(s, letters):    # substrings that contain every letter
    count = Counter()
    left = total = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1
        while all(count[c] > 0 for c in letters):   # valid: shrink
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        total += left              # starts 0, 1, ..., left - 1 are valid
    return total

count_with_all("abcabc", "abc")    # -> 10
count_with_all("aaacb", "abc")     # -> 3
count_with_all("ab", "abc")        # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Another way: count the invalid windows with \cd{right - left + 1} and subtract them from $n(n+1)/2$.
(Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters, Count Subarrays Where Max Element Appears at Least
K Times.)

\subsubsection{Window maximum: a monotonic deque}
A running maximum cannot handle a removal. When the maximum leaves the window, the next maximum is unknown.
Use dominance: if an older element is not larger than a newer element, the older one leaves first and never
wins again. Delete it when the newer element arrives. The remaining candidates have decreasing values from
front to back, so the front is the maximum.
This is Sliding Window Maximum.
Memory hook: \emph{Kick out the old from the front, kick out the weak from the back, and the front is the max.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def max_sliding_window(nums, k):
    candidates = deque()     # indices; their values go down from front to back
    result = []
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if candidates and candidates[0] <= i - k:        # old: left the window
            candidates.popleft()
        while candidates and nums[candidates[-1]] <= x:  # weak: never a max again
            candidates.pop()
        candidates.append(i)
        if i >= k - 1:                                   # the window is full
            result.append(nums[candidates[0]])
    return result

max_sliding_window([1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], 3)   # -> [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
max_sliding_window([1], 1)                          # -> [1]
max_sliding_window([4, 2, 2, 1], 2)                 # -> [4, 2, 2]
\end{pyex}
Store indices, not values. The index tells you when the front leaves the window.
Each index enters and leaves the deque at most one time, so the time is $O(n)$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item For the window minimum, pop the back while its value is \cd{>= x}.
  \item In a variable window, the left end can pass several indices. Pop the front with a \cd{while} loop
        while its index is less than \cd{left}.
  \item A rule such as \cd{max - min <= limit} needs two deques: one for the maximum and one for the minimum.
  \item The same deque speeds up a DP of the form \cd{dp[i] = f(i) + max(dp[j])} over the last $k$ indices.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Is the answer one contiguous segment? If the answer can skip elements, use another technique.
  \item If the segment is not visible, reframe the input. If the order does not matter, sort first: the best
        group is then often a window of the sorted array. If you remove items from both ends, the items that
        stay form one window of fixed size.
  \item Is the length fixed? Then use a fixed window: one element in and one element out in each step.
  \item Write the rule for a valid window in one sentence. Is it monotone? Try a small example. For a longest
        goal, a valid window must stay valid when it shrinks. For a shortest goal, it must stay
        valid when it grows. For a count goal whose rule survives growing (contains all of, at least $k$),
        shrink while the window is valid, then add \cd{left}: every start before \cd{left} gives a valid window.
        Or count the invalid windows with \cd{right - left + 1} and subtract them from $n(n+1)/2$.
        Use prefix sums only when no direction is monotone, for example sums with negative values.
  \item Choose the state. It must update in $O(1)$ for one entering and one leaving element: a set, a
        \cd{Counter}, a sum, a count of bad elements, a need/have pair, or a deque.
  \item Write the rule as an expression of the state. Examples: ``at most $k$ changes'' gives
        \cd{length - top_count <= k}. ``Contains all of \cd{t}'' gives \cd{have == required}.
  \item Choose the loop shape from the table in the core template. Put the record step in the correct place.
  \item If the rule says ``exactly $k$'', count ``at most $k$'' minus ``at most $k - 1$''.
  \item If the rule needs the maximum or the minimum of the window, keep a monotonic deque.
  \item If constraints connect two positions, turn each one into an interval. Keep the largest blocking
        start per right end.
  \item Check the edges: an empty input, $k$ larger than $n$, no valid window. Use \cd{float("inf")} as the
        start value of a shortest length, and return the ``none'' value at the end.
  \item Compare with a brute force over all $O(n^2)$ segments on small random inputs.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A stale index moves the left end back.} In the last-index form of the longest unique substring,
the last copy of a character can be before \cd{left}. Then \cd{left = last[ch] + 1} moves the window
back and includes a repeat. Use \cd{left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def jump_bad(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last:
            left = last[ch] + 1              # wrong: can move left back
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

def jump_good(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last:
            left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)   # left never moves back
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

jump_bad("abba"), jump_good("abba")          # -> (3, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A \cd{Counter} keeps keys with a count of 0.} Then \cd{len(count)} is not the number of distinct
values in the window. Delete a key when its count reaches 0, or keep a separate counter of distinct values.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter
count = Counter("aab")
count["b"] -= 1              # "b" left the window
len(count)                   # -> 2
del count["b"]
len(count)                   # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative values break a sum window.} With negative values, a shrink can increase the sum.
The window below misses the full array, which has a sum of 0. Use prefix sums for such problems.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_sum_at_most(a, k):        # correct only when all values are >= 0
    total = left = best = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        total += x
        while left <= right and total > k:
            total -= a[left]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

longest_sum_at_most([1, 2, 3, 1], 4)  # -> 2
longest_sum_at_most([5, -10, 5], 0)   # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The record step in the wrong place.} For a shortest window, record inside the shrink loop,
before the removal. After the loop, the window is not valid. For a longest window, record after the loop.
Inside the loop, the window is not valid yet.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{\cd{if} instead of \cd{while}.} One removal does not always make the window valid. A repeated
character can be far inside the window. Use \cd{while} for the shrink step. The fixed window is an
exception, because exactly one element leaves in each step. The slide form with a stale \cd{max_freq}
is also an exception, because its window never shrinks.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Off-by-one errors.} The window length is \cd{right - left + 1}. In a fixed window, the leaving
element is \cd{a[right - k]}, and it leaves only when \cd{right >= k}. The first full window ends at
\cd{right = k - 1}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{An empty window.} If one element alone can break the rule, the shrink loop can empty the window.
Then \cd{left} is \cd{right + 1}, and a test such as \cd{max(count.values())} can raise \cd{ValueError}.
Add \cd{left <= right} to the loop condition, or make sure the rule is true for one element.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The have counter counts crossings, not elements.} Increase \cd{have} only when a count becomes
equal to its requirement. Decrease it only when a count falls below its requirement. A surplus copy
must not change \cd{have}. A key that is not in \cd{need} must not change \cd{have}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Hidden $O(k)$ work.} Do not call \cd{sum(a[left:right + 1])}, \cd{max(window)} or
\cd{Counter(s[left:right + 1])} inside the loop. Each call rescans the window and gives $O(nk)$.
Update the state with the one entering and the one leaving element.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The empty answer.} Start a longest length at 0 and a shortest length at \cd{float("inf")}.
In a profit problem, start at 0 when ``no trade'' is allowed. Return the value the statement gives
for ``no valid window'', such as \cd{""}, \cd{0} or \cd{-1}.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock & The left end jumps to a new low. The state is the running minimum. &
  Remember the cheapest day, sell today. \\
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters & Longest window. The state is a set. Shrink while the new
  character is in the set. & Drop from the left until the new character is unique, then add it on the right. \\
Longest Repeating Character Replacement & Longest window under a budget. The cost is the length minus the
  top count. & Window length minus top count must be at most k. \\
Permutation in String & Fixed window of length \cd{len(s1)}. Compare two count arrays. &
  Slide a window of len(s1) over s2 and compare its letter counts to s1's counts. \\
Minimum Window Substring & Shortest window. Need/have counters. Record inside the shrink loop. &
  Grow right until have equals required, then shrink left while it holds. \\
Sliding Window Maximum & Fixed window. The state is a monotonic deque of indices. &
  Kick out the old from the front, kick out the weak from the back, and the front is the max. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Stacks and monotonic stacks}\label{tech:T05}

\subsection{The idea}
A stack keeps the items that are still \emph{pending}: openers that wait for a closer, values that wait
for an operator, or indexes that wait for an answer. Each new item looks only at the newest pending item.
It finishes the newest pending items that it can finish (pop). Then, if it must wait too, it joins the
pile (push). This is last in, first out order. A brute force rescans the earlier items for each new item and costs $O(n^2)$. The stack removes
each finished item for good, so each item is pushed once and popped at most once. The total cost is
$O(n)$, even with a \cd{while} loop inside the \cd{for} loop.

There are two kinds of stack problems.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Matching stack.} Pairs nest but do not cross. The next closer can match only the most
        recent unmatched opener. Brackets, tags, postfix expressions and undo work this way.
  \item \textbf{Monotonic stack.} Each element waits for the first later element that beats it
        (greater or smaller). A new element resolves every waiting element that it beats. No element on
        the stack beats an element below it, so the values on the stack stay sorted.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Worked example (matching).} Check \cd{"([)]"}. Push \cd{(}, then push \cd{[}. Next comes
\cd{)}. The top is \cd{[}, which is the wrong opener, so the string is not valid. Two counters
(one per bracket type) accept this string, because counters forget the order of the openers.

\textbf{Worked example (monotonic).} For each day of \cd{[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76]}, find the
number of days until a warmer day. Day 0 (73) waits. Day 1 (74) is warmer, so day 0 gets 1 and leaves;
day 1 waits. Day 2 (75) resolves day 1. Days 3 (71) and 4 (69) are colder, so they wait on top of day 2.
Day 5 (72) pops day 4 (gap 1) and day 3 (gap 2). It stops at day 2, because 75 is not colder.
Day 6 (76) pops day 5 (gap 1) and day 2 (gap 4). The result is \cd{[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0]}.
The waiting temperatures never increase from bottom to top. So when the pops reach an element that is
not colder, no element below it is colder, and the pops can stop.

The same pass answers ``previous'' questions. Take the previous smaller element. A new element hides
every earlier element that is greater than or equal to it, because the new element is closer and not
larger. Those earlier elements can never be an answer again, so the pass pops them. What stays below the
new element is its answer.

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Items open and close. Each closer pairs with an earlier opener. Pairs nest and do not cross
        (brackets, HTML tags, start and end entries of function logs).
  \item An operator or a closing token acts on the most recent pending items (postfix expressions,
        nested decoding such as \cd{3[a2[c]]}, path simplification, backspace or undo).
  \item A design asks for an aggregate (min, max, sum) in $O(1)$ next to push and pop. Removals are LIFO,
        so every earlier state comes back after a pop.
  \item ``For each element, find the nearest element to the left or right that is greater or smaller'',
        or the distance to it, or the value of it.
  \item The output has one entry per element (an index, a distance or a value). A default such as
        \cd{-1} or \cd{0} marks an element with no answer.
  \item The score of a range is the minimum (or maximum) of the range times its length or sum. As the
        minimum, each element limits a range that stops just before the nearest smaller element on each
        side. For a maximum, use the nearest greater element.
  \item The amount at each index depends on the tallest element on its left and the tallest element on
        its right (water between bars).
  \item Remove items and keep the order of the others, so that the result is the smallest (or
        largest) possible. The limit is a count $k$, or a rule such as ``keep each letter exactly once''.
  \item Objects on a line cannot pass each other, and the question counts the groups that form.
  \item The task asks for all valid bracket strings (or other nested structures) of size $n$, and $n$ is
        small (about 8 or less). This is backtracking, and the state is two counts: openers used and
        closers used.
  \item $n$ is up to about $10^5$, and the brute force scans right from every index. That is $O(n^2)$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
\textbf{Matching stack.} Push each opener. A closer must find its own opener on top, and then it pops it.
At the end, the stack must be empty.
\begin{pyex}
def is_valid(s):
    opener_of = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []                       # openers that wait for a closer
    for c in s:
        if c in opener_of:           # c is a closer
            if not stack or stack[-1] != opener_of[c]:
                return False
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append(c)
    return not stack                 # leftover openers make it invalid

is_valid("([]{})")   # -> True
is_valid("([)]")     # -> False
is_valid("((")       # -> False
is_valid(")")        # -> False
\end{pyex}
Invariant: before each character, the stack holds the unmatched openers of the prefix, in their original
order. A closer is legal only if it matches the top.

\textbf{Monotonic stack.} Keep the indexes that still wait for an answer. Pop every waiting index that the
new element beats. There are two ways to read an answer. At pop time, the popped index gets the current
index as its \emph{next} element. After the pops, the index on top is the \emph{previous} element of the
current one.
\begin{pyex}
def next_greater(a):
    # ans[i] = index of the first j > i with a[j] > a[i], else -1
    ans = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []                       # indexes that wait for an answer
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
            ans[stack.pop()] = i     # x resolves each smaller waiting index
        stack.append(i)
    return ans

def prev_smaller(a):
    # ans[i] = index of the last j < i with a[j] < a[i], else -1
    ans = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] >= x:
            stack.pop()              # never a "previous smaller" again
        if stack:
            ans[i] = stack[-1]
        stack.append(i)
    return ans

a = [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]
next_greater(a)       # -> [3, 2, 3, -1, -1]
prev_smaller(a)       # -> [-1, -1, 1, 2, 2]

# check: compare with a brute force on all small arrays
from itertools import product

def brute_next_greater(a):
    return [next((j for j in range(i + 1, len(a)) if a[j] > a[i]), -1) for i in range(len(a))]

all(next_greater(list(t)) == brute_next_greater(list(t))
    for n in range(6) for t in product(range(3), repeat=n))   # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: the stack holds the indexes that are not popped yet, in increasing index order, and their
values are sorted. These indexes still wait for a \emph{next} answer, and only they can still be a
\emph{previous} answer. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the pass is $O(n)$.
Choose the pop condition from the question:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.2cm}L{4.4cm}L{4.2cm}L{3.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
For each \cd{i}, find & Pop while & Read the answer & Stack values \\
\midrule
next greater & \cd{a[top] < x} & popped index gets \cd{i} & non-increasing \\
next greater or equal & \cd{a[top] <= x} & popped index gets \cd{i} & strictly decreasing \\
next smaller & \cd{a[top] > x} & popped index gets \cd{i} & non-decreasing \\
previous greater & \cd{a[top] <= x} & top after the pops & strictly decreasing \\
previous smaller & \cd{a[top] >= x} & top after the pops & strictly increasing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Rule: pop what can never be an answer again. One pass gives two answers. The popped indexes get their
\emph{next} answer, and the top after the pops is the \emph{previous} answer with the opposite strictness.
For example, the pass with \cd{a[top] < x} gives the next greater and the previous greater-or-equal element.

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Match and validate nested pairs}
Push openers and pop on a matching closer (Valid Parentheses). Memory hook: \emph{push openers; each
closer must pop its own opener off the top; end with an empty stack.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item One bracket type and only a yes or no answer: a balance counter replaces the stack. Add 1 for an
        opener, subtract 1 for a closer, fail below 0, and require 0 at the end.
  \item Positions or lengths matter: push indexes instead of characters. The indexes that stay unmatched
        mark the parts to remove or the borders of valid runs.
  \item Tags or log entries: push the name or id on start, and check it on end.
  \item A token cancels the newest kept token (\cd{..} in a file path, a backspace, an undo): push the
        normal tokens, and pop on the cancel token. The stack holds the result.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Evaluate an expression: a stack of pending values}
In postfix order, each operator acts on the two newest pending values (Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation).
Push numbers. On an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left operand, and push the result.
Memory hook: \emph{push numbers; an operator pops b, then a, and pushes a op b; divide with
\cd{int(a / b)}.}
\begin{pyex}
OPS = {
    "+": lambda a, b: a + b,
    "-": lambda a, b: a - b,
    "*": lambda a, b: a * b,
    "/": lambda a, b: int(a / b),    # truncate toward zero
}

def eval_rpn(tokens):
    stack = []                       # values that wait for an operator
    for tok in tokens:
        if tok in OPS:               # compare the whole token: "-11" is a number
            b = stack.pop()          # the right operand is on top
            a = stack.pop()
            stack.append(OPS[tok](a, b))
        else:
            stack.append(int(tok))
    return stack[0]

eval_rpn(["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"])      # -> 9
eval_rpn(["4", "13", "5", "/", "+"])     # -> 6
eval_rpn(["7", "-2", "/"])               # -> -3
eval_rpn(["-11"])                        # -> -11
-7 // 2, int(-7 / 2)                     # -> (-4, -3)
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Prefix (Polish) notation: scan from the right with the same stack. Pop the left operand first.
  \item Infix with precedence and no parentheses: keep the previous operator. Push \cd{+num} or
        \cd{-num}. For \cd{*} and \cd{/}, pop the top, combine it with \cd{num}, and push the result.
        The answer is the sum of the stack.
  \item Infix with parentheses and only \cd{+} and \cd{-}: on \cd{(}, push the current result and sign,
        and start a new result. On \cd{)}, pop and combine. With all four operators and parentheses, use
        recursive descent: evaluate each part in parentheses with the method of the previous item.
\end{itemize}
\begin{note}
\cd{int(a / b)} is exact for 32-bit operands. For very large integers, use \cd{abs(a) // abs(b)} and
negate the result when the signs differ.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{A stack that carries extra state}
Store a snapshot of the aggregate with each push (Min Stack). Each entry is the pair (value, minimum of this
value and all values below it). A pop removes the value and its snapshot together, so the old minimum
comes back with no work. Memory hook: \emph{push the pair (value, min so far); pop removes both.}
\begin{pyex}
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []   # (value, min of this value and all values below it)

    def push(self, val):
        low = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val
        self.stack.append((val, low))

    def pop(self):
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self):
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def getMin(self):
        return self.stack[-1][1]

s = MinStack()
for v in [5, 3, 7, 3]:
    s.push(v)
s.getMin()             # -> 3
s.pop()
s.pop()
s.getMin(), s.top()    # -> (3, 3)
s.pop()
s.getMin(), s.top()    # -> (5, 5)
\end{pyex}
The same idea works for any aggregate that extends by one element: max, sum, count, gcd. Min and max
have no inverse: the current minimum and the popped value do not give back the old minimum. So save the
old value with each level instead.
Nested decoding uses the same idea. On an opener, push the current state (for example the text so far and
a repeat count), and start fresh. On the closer, pop the state and combine.
A common alternative splits the pairs into two parallel lists, with the same cost. Then each pop must remove from both lists.

\subsubsection{Generate balanced structures}
Generate every valid string of \cd{n} bracket pairs (Generate Parentheses). For one bracket type, the
stack is only a count of open brackets. So backtrack with two counts and allow only moves that keep the
prefix completable. Memory hook: \emph{open while opens remain; close only what is open; save at length 2n.}
\begin{pyex}
def generate_parentheses(n):
    result = []

    def build(text, opens, closes):
        if len(text) == 2 * n:
            result.append(text)
            return
        if opens < n:                # an opener is still free
            build(text + "(", opens + 1, closes)
        if closes < opens:           # close only what is open
            build(text + ")", opens, closes + 1)

    build("", 0, 0)
    return result

generate_parentheses(3)
# -> ['((()))', '(()())', '(())()', '()(())', '()()()']
len(generate_parentheses(4))   # -> 14
\end{pyex}
Every branch ends in a valid string, so the work is proportional to the output size. The output has
$C(n)$ strings (the Catalan number) of length $2n$, so the total is $O(n \cdot C(n)) = O(4^n / \sqrt{n})$.
With several bracket types, the state must hold the stack of open types.
The optimal version uses one shared list as the path (append, recurse, pop) and joins it at a leaf. It
saves a string copy per node. That is only a constant factor here.

\subsubsection{Next greater element: the answer at pop time}
Each new element is the answer for every smaller element that still waits (Daily Temperatures). Memory
hook: \emph{today pops every colder waiting day and writes the gap.}
\begin{pyex}
def daily_temperatures(temps):
    answer = [0] * len(temps)
    waiting = []                     # days that still wait for a warmer day
    for today, t in enumerate(temps):
        while waiting and temps[waiting[-1]] < t:
            day = waiting.pop()
            answer[day] = today - day
        waiting.append(today)
    return answer

daily_temperatures([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73])
# -> [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]
daily_temperatures([30, 30, 31])   # -> [2, 1, 0]
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Store indexes, not values. An index gives both the distance and the value.
  \item The question asks for the next value instead of the distance: write \cd{a[i]} into the popped slot.
  \item Circular array: loop \cd{i} over \cd{range(2 * n)}, read \cd{a[i} \pct{} \cd{n]}, and push only when
        \cd{i < n}.
  \item A stream of queries for the previous greater element: keep (value, span) pairs. A new value
        absorbs the spans of the values that it pops.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def next_greater_circular(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [-1] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(2 * n):
        x = nums[i % n]
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            ans[stack.pop()] = x     # the value, not the distance
        if i < n:                    # the second lap only resolves
            stack.append(i)
    return ans

next_greater_circular([1, 2, 1])       # -> [2, -1, 2]
next_greater_circular([5, 4, 3, 4])    # -> [-1, 5, 4, 5]
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Smallest subsequence: a greedy increasing stack}
Some problems remove items, keep the order of the others, and ask for the smallest result (Remove K
Digits, Remove Duplicate Letters). An earlier position weighs more than all later positions together. So
a smaller item that arrives replaces a larger item before it, if that larger item may still go. The stack
holds the result so far. Memory hook: \emph{pop a bigger top that you can still afford to lose.}
The problem sets the permission to pop.
\begin{itemize}
  \item A budget of $k$ removals (Remove K Digits): pop while removals remain, and count each pop. After
        the scan, cut the unused removals from the end, because the end holds the largest digits. Then
        strip the leading zeros.
  \item Each letter exactly once (Remove Duplicate Letters): pop the top only when it occurs again later.
        Keep the last index of each letter for this test. Also skip a letter that is already on the
        stack. The result needs it only once, and the copy on the stack already has its best position.
  \item The largest result: reverse the comparison, and pop a smaller top.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
def remove_k_digits(num, k):
    stack = []                       # the result so far
    for d in num:
        while k and stack and stack[-1] > d:
            stack.pop()              # a smaller digit replaces a larger one before it
            k -= 1
        stack.append(d)
    if k:
        stack = stack[:-k]           # unused removals come off the end
    return "".join(stack).lstrip("0") or "0"

def smallest_subsequence(s):         # each letter exactly once
    last = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(s)}    # last index of each letter
    stack, on_stack = [], set()
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in on_stack:
            continue                 # the result needs it only once
        while stack and stack[-1] > ch and last[stack[-1]] > i:
            on_stack.discard(stack.pop())   # the top comes again later
        stack.append(ch)
        on_stack.add(ch)
    return "".join(stack)

remove_k_digits("1432219", 3)        # -> '1219'
remove_k_digits("10200", 1)          # -> '200'
remove_k_digits("10", 2)             # -> '0'
smallest_subsequence("bcabc")        # -> 'abc'
smallest_subsequence("cbacdcbc")     # -> 'acdb'

# check: compare with a brute force on all small inputs
from itertools import combinations, product

def brute_remove(num, k):
    kept = ("".join(t) for t in combinations(num, len(num) - k))
    return min((t.lstrip("0") or "0" for t in kept), key=int)

def brute_smallest(s):
    m = len(set(s))
    return min("".join(t) for t in combinations(s, m) if len(set(t)) == m)

all(remove_k_digits(s, k) == brute_remove(s, k)
    for n in range(1, 6) for s in map("".join, product("0123", repeat=n))
    for k in range(n + 1))                                       # -> True
all(smallest_subsequence(s) == brute_smallest(s)
    for n in range(1, 7) for s in map("".join, product("abc", repeat=n)))   # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Sort first, then a stack of groups}
Objects on a line cannot pass each other, and the question counts groups (Car Fleet). Reduce each object
to one number: its finish time on an empty road. The general rule: when only the end state matters,
compute the outcome of each item alone first. Then apply the interaction rule in one ordered pass.

Here a car cannot pass the fleet ahead, so its real time is the maximum of its own time and the time of
the fleet ahead. Sort by position and scan from the front, because blocking flows from the front to the
back. A car joins the fleet ahead if it would arrive at the same time or earlier. Memory hook:
\emph{front car first: a car that arrives later than the fleet ahead starts a new fleet.}
\begin{pyex}
def car_fleet(target, position, speed):
    cars = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)   # front car first
    fleets = 0
    fleet_time = 0.0                 # arrival time of the fleet just ahead
    for pos, spd in cars:
        arrive = (target - pos) / spd    # time on an empty road
        if arrive > fleet_time:          # cannot catch the fleet ahead
            fleets += 1
            fleet_time = arrive
    return fleets

car_fleet(12, [10, 8, 0, 5, 3], [2, 4, 1, 1, 3])   # -> 3
car_fleet(10, [3], [3])                             # -> 1
car_fleet(100, [0, 2, 4], [4, 2, 1])                # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The usual stack version pushes each new fleet time onto a stack and returns the stack size. The stack only
uses its top, so it is a running maximum. Keep the stack when the question asks about each fleet, for
example its size. Then push (time, count), and add to the top count when a car joins.
The same scan without the sort finds the buildings with an ocean view. Scan from the ocean side, and
keep each strict new maximum.

\subsubsection{Nearest smaller on both sides: largest rectangle}
Enumerate the limiting element instead of the range (Largest Rectangle in Histogram). Suppose bar \cd{i}
is the shortest bar of the rectangle. Then the rectangle spans the gap between the nearest strictly
shorter bar on the left and the nearest strictly shorter bar on the right. The best rectangle has a
shortest bar, so this search finds it. It replaces $O(n^2)$ ranges with $n$ candidates.
Find both borders with one helper, called once in each direction. Memory hook:
\emph{each bar is the shortest: stretch it to the nearest shorter bar on both sides.}
\begin{pyex}
def largest_rectangle(heights):
    n = len(heights)

    def nearest_smaller(order, default):
        # result[i] = closest strictly shorter bar before i in this order
        result = [default] * n
        stack = []
        for i in order:
            while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
                stack.pop()
            if stack:
                result[i] = stack[-1]
            stack.append(i)
        return result

    left = nearest_smaller(range(n), -1)
    right = nearest_smaller(range(n - 1, -1, -1), n)
    return max(heights[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1) for i in range(n))

largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3])   # -> 10
largest_rectangle([2, 4])               # -> 4
largest_rectangle([4, 0, 4])            # -> 4
\end{pyex}
The optimal version does the work in one pass. A popped bar gets its area when the shorter bar arrives. The new
bar inherits the start index of the last bar that it popped, because it extends left over all of them.
A 0-height sentinel at the end flushes the stack. Use this ``absorb the span'' trick when the popped
element's range must pass to the new element.
\begin{pyex}
def largest_rectangle_one_pass(heights):
    best = 0
    stack = []                       # (start, height); heights never decrease
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):    # the 0 bar pops every bar
        start = i
        while stack and stack[-1][1] > h:
            start, top = stack.pop()
            best = max(best, top * (i - start))
        stack.append((start, h))     # h reaches left to the last popped start
    return best

largest_rectangle_one_pass([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3])   # -> 10

# check: compare with a brute force on all small arrays
from itertools import product

def brute(hs):
    return max(min(hs[l:r + 1]) * (r - l + 1)
               for l in range(len(hs)) for r in range(l, len(hs)))

all(largest_rectangle_one_pass(list(t)) == brute(list(t))
    for n in range(1, 6) for t in product(range(4), repeat=n))   # -> True
\end{pyex}
Some problems count over all subarrays, for example the sum of the subarray minimums. There, use a strict
comparison on one side and a non-strict comparison on the other side. Then each subarray with equal
minimums is counted once. When the score is the minimum times the sum (Maximum Subarray Min-Product), keep
the same borders and read the range sum from prefix sums. For a binary matrix, build one histogram per
row and run this on each row (Maximal Rectangle).

\subsubsection{Fill between walls: trapping water}
The water above index \cd{i} rises to the lower of two walls (Trapping Rain Water). The left wall is the
tallest bar on its left, and the right wall is the tallest bar on its right. A brute force scans both
sides for every index, which is $O(n^2)$. The intuitive solution needs no stack: precompute prefix maxima
and suffix maxima, then sum the levels. Memory hook: \emph{water at i is the lower wall minus the bar:
min(left max, right max) - height.}
The stack version fills water in horizontal layers. Keep a stack of indexes with non-increasing heights.
A taller bar pops the floor bar. The new top is the left wall, and the current bar is the right wall.
The layer has height \cd{min(left wall, right wall) - floor} and width \cd{i - left - 1}.
\begin{pyex}
def trap_walls(height):
    n = len(height)
    left_max, right_max = height[:], height[:]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], height[i])
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], height[i])
    return sum(min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i] for i in range(n))

def trap_stack(height):
    water = 0
    stack = []                       # indexes; heights never increase
    for i, h in enumerate(height):
        while stack and height[stack[-1]] < h:
            floor = height[stack.pop()]
            if not stack:
                break                # no left wall: water runs off
            left = stack[-1]
            level = min(height[left], h)
            water += (level - floor) * (i - left - 1)
        stack.append(i)
    return water

hs = [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]
trap_walls(hs), trap_stack(hs)       # -> (6, 6)
trap_stack([4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5])       # -> 9

# check: compare the two methods on all small arrays
from itertools import product
all(trap_stack(list(t)) == trap_walls(list(t))
    for n in range(1, 7) for t in product(range(4), repeat=n))   # -> True
\end{pyex}
The optimal solution uses two converging pointers with running maxima and $O(1)$ extra space. Move the side
with the smaller running maximum, because that maximum already sets the level there. Use it only when the
problem asks for constant extra space.

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Does each new item interact only with the newest pending item? If yes, use a stack.
        Name what ``pending'' means: an opener, a value that waits for an operator, or an index without
        an answer.
  \item Does the score of a range depend on its minimum or maximum? Then fix the limiting element. Find
        its nearest smaller (or greater) element on each side, and score the range between them.
  \item What do you push? Push an index when you need a distance or a width. Push a tuple when each level
        needs extra state. Examples are a snapshot of the minimum, a count, a start index and the text so far.
  \item When do you pop? Write the pop condition from the question: pop the items that can never be an
        answer again. Next greater pops smaller items. Previous smaller pops greater-or-equal items.
        A smallest subsequence pops a larger top that can still go.
  \item When do you read the answer? At pop time for the popped item (``next''), or after the pops for
        the current item (``previous'').
  \item How do ties work? Read the tie rule in the statement and choose \cd{<} or \cd{<=}. For counts over
        all subarrays, use strict on one side and non-strict on the other side.
  \item What stays on the stack at the end? Those items have no answer (keep the default), or they reach
        the end of the array (flush them, or add a sentinel).
  \item Does the input give objects on a line in no order? Sort by position first. Scan from the side that blocks.
  \item Does the stack only use its top? Then replace it with a variable (running maximum) or a counter
        (one bracket type). To generate balanced strings of one type, two counts replace the stack.
  \item Is the array circular? Loop twice with \cd{i} \pct{} \cd{n} and push only in the first lap.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
Check that the stack is not empty before \cd{stack[-1]} or \cd{stack.pop()}. A closer can arrive when the
stack is empty, as in \cd{")"}. Write \cd{while stack and ...}, with the emptiness test first.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
Return \cd{not stack} at the end of a matching check. Leftover openers, as in \cd{"(("}, make the input
invalid. Separate counters per bracket type accept crossed pairs such as \cd{"([)]"}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
In an expression, the top of the stack is the \emph{right} operand. Pop \cd{b} first, then \cd{a}.
Python \cd{//} rounds toward negative infinity: \cd{-7 // 2} is \cd{-4}. Use \cd{int(a / b)} to truncate
toward zero. Detect operators by the whole token, because \cd{"-11"} starts with \cd{-}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
Read the tie rule. An equal temperature is not warmer, so pop only on a strictly lower value. Two cars
with equal arrival times meet at the target and form one fleet, so start a new fleet only on a strictly
later time.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
Do not forget the items that stay on the stack after the loop. In the largest rectangle, they reach the
end of the array and often hold the answer (for example, an increasing array). Iterate over
\cd{heights + [0]} for a sentinel. Do not append to the caller's list.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
One cached minimum variable fails after a pop removes the current minimum. Store the minimum per level.
In Car Fleet, compare with the fleet time (the running maximum), not with the car directly ahead. Zip
position with speed before you sort.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
In Remove Duplicate Letters, skip a letter that is already on the stack. Without the skip,
\cd{"cbacdcbc"} gives \cd{"acdbc"} instead of \cd{"acdb"}. In Remove K Digits, cut the unused removals
from the end, and return \cd{"0"} for an empty result.
\end{caution}
\begin{note}
A \cd{while} loop inside a \cd{for} loop looks like $O(n^2)$. It is $O(n)$ in total, because each index
is pushed once and popped at most once.
\end{note}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Valid Parentheses (20) & Matching stack of openers; three bracket types need the stack, not counters. &
  Push openers. Each closer must pop its own opener off the top. End with an empty stack. \\
Min Stack (155) & Each level stores a snapshot of the minimum, so a pop restores the old minimum. &
  Push the pair (value, min so far). Pop removes both. \\
Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (150) & Stack of pending values; an operator pops two and pushes one. &
  Push numbers. An operator pops b, then a, and pushes a op b. Divide with int(a / b). \\
Generate Parentheses (22) & Generate instead of check; one bracket type, so two counts replace the stack. &
  Open while opens remain. Close only what is open. Save at length 2n. \\
Daily Temperatures (739) & Next greater element; the answer is the distance, written at pop time. &
  Today pops every colder waiting day and writes the gap. \\
Car Fleet (853) & Sort by position, scan from the front; the stack of fleet times is a running maximum. &
  Front car first: a car that arrives later than the fleet ahead starts a new fleet. \\
Largest Rectangle in Histogram (84) & Nearest strictly smaller bar on both sides; area = height times gap. &
  Each bar is the shortest: stretch it to the nearest shorter bar on both sides. \\
Trapping Rain Water (42) & Lower of two walls per index; a decreasing stack fills water in layers. &
  Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\medskip
