% =====================================================================
\section{Binary search}\label{tech:T06}\label{t06:sec}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
Binary search finds the place where a yes/no question changes its answer.
Put the candidates on a line in order. The candidates can be indexes, values, sizes, times or split points.
Ask one question \cd{ok(x)} about each candidate.
If the answers are \emph{monotone}, they form one block of ``no'' and then one block of ``yes'': F F F T T T T.
Then one question at the middle removes half of the candidates.
A brute force asks about every candidate. Binary search asks about $\log_2$ of their count:
20 questions for $10^6$ candidates, 30 questions for $10^9$ candidates.

\textbf{Worked example 1: a sorted array.}
Find the first value that is at least 7 in \cd{[2, 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15]}.
The question ``is \cd{a[i] >= 7}?'' gives F F T T T T T on indexes 0 to 6.
Ask at index 3. The value 7 passes, so the answer is index 3 or an index to its left. Keep indexes 0 to 3.
Ask at index 1. The value 4 fails, so the answer is to its right. Keep indexes 2 to 3.
Ask at index 2. The value 7 passes. Only index 2 is left, so the answer is index 2.
Three questions replace up to seven.

\textbf{Worked example 2: no array at all.}
Find the smallest eating speed that finishes the piles \cd{[3, 6, 7, 11]} in 8 hours.
One pile of $p$ bananas takes $\lceil p / k \rceil$ hours at speed $k$.
Ask ``does speed $k$ finish in time?''.
Speed 6 needs $1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6$ hours: yes. Speed 3 needs $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ hours: no.
Speed 4 needs $1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8$ hours: yes.
Speed 3 fails and speed 4 passes, so the answer is 4.
A faster speed never needs more hours. Thus the answers are monotone, and binary search applies.
A brute force tries speeds 1, 2, 3, and so on. Binary search tests only about $\log_2$ of the largest pile.

So binary search does not need a sorted array. It needs three things:
\begin{itemize}
  \item a range of candidates that surely holds the answer;
  \item a question \cd{ok(x)} that you can answer fast for one candidate;
  \item a reason why \cd{ok} changes from false to true at most one time along the range.
\end{itemize}
The work saved is large. A check that costs $O(n)$ and a range of $10^9$ values give about $30n$ steps, not $10^9 n$.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input is sorted, and the statement asks for $O(\log n)$ time. A scan is then not accepted.
  \item The output is a position in sorted data: an insertion point, the first or the last copy of a value,
        or the count of values below a limit.
  \item The input is sorted, but it is rotated, shifted or cut into rows. It is still a few sorted runs.
  \item The question asks for the minimum or the maximum value of a parameter that still meets a limit:
        a speed, a capacity, a size, a distance, a day.
        Typical phrases: ``the minimum $x$ such that it is possible'', ``minimize the largest'', ``maximize the smallest''.
  \item You can test one candidate fast, but no formula gives the answer directly.
  \item The statement asks for $O(\log n)$ time, but the values are not sorted.
        Look for a test at \cd{mid} and its neighbor that flips one time.
  \item The answer range is very large (up to $10^9$ or more). A scan over all values is too slow,
        but $\log_2$ of the range is only about 30.
  \item The test flips only one time. Typical reasons: sorted data, non-negative values,
        a bigger region that contains a smaller region, more capacity that always helps.
  \item A query asks for ``the latest value at or before time $t$'', a version, a snapshot, or a value ``as of'' a date.
        This is a floor query on a sorted history.
  \item The question asks for the median or the $k$-th smallest value of sorted inputs, and a full merge is too slow or not allowed.
  \item The question asks for the longest strictly increasing chain (a subsequence, or pairs that nest),
        and $n$ is up to $10^5$. The $O(n^2)$ DP is then too slow.
        A sorted helper array of chain tails gives $O(n \log n)$.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Two loops cover almost every problem. Use the first loop to find one exact value.
Use the second loop to find a boundary: the first candidate that passes a test.

\subsubsection{Exact match on a closed range}
Use this loop to find one value when any index that holds it is a correct answer.
Unique values give this case (Binary Search).
\begin{pyex}
def search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1          # closed range [lo, hi] can hold target
    while lo <= hi:                    # the range is not empty
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:         # mid and everything left of it are too small
            lo = mid + 1
        else:                          # mid and everything right of it are too big
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1                          # the range is empty: target is absent

nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12]
search(nums, 9)                        # -> 4
search(nums, 2)                        # -> -1
search([5], 5), search([5], 7)         # -> (0, -1)
\end{pyex}
Invariant: if \cd{target} is present, its index is in the closed range \cd{[lo, hi]}.
Both updates drop \cd{mid}, so the range shrinks at each step and the loop stops.
Memory hook: \emph{closed range, check the middle, drop the half that cannot hold the target.}

\subsubsection{First true on a half-open range}
Use this loop by default for a boundary question. It is the general template.
\begin{pyex}
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):
    # First x in [lo, hi) with ok(x) True, or hi if no x passes.
    # ok must be False ... False True ... True on [lo, hi).
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid             # mid passes: the answer is mid or left of it
        else:
            lo = mid + 1         # mid fails: the answer is right of it
    return lo

a = [2, 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15]
first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: a[i] >= 7)     # -> 2
first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: a[i] > 7)      # -> 4
first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: a[i] >= 99)    # -> 7
first_true(1, 10**9, lambda x: x * x >= 50)    # -> 8
\end{pyex}
Invariant: every candidate below \cd{lo} fails, and \cd{hi} passes or is the end of the range.
The lower midpoint gives \cd{mid < hi}, so \cd{hi = mid} always shrinks the range.
The loop stops when \cd{lo == hi}. That candidate is the first one that passes.
Memory hook: \emph{if mid passes, keep it; if mid fails, skip it.}

The \cd{bisect} module is this template on a sorted list.
\cd{bisect_left(a, x)} is the first index with \cd{a[i] >= x}.
\cd{bisect_right(a, x)} is the first index with \cd{a[i] > x}.
Both return \cd{len(a)} when no index passes.
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
a = [2, 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15]
bisect_left(a, 7), bisect_right(a, 7)       # -> (2, 4)
bisect_right(a, 7) - bisect_left(a, 7)      # -> 2
bisect_left(a, 99)                          # -> 7
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Last true}
Some questions are true first and false after: T T T F F. A ``largest value that works'' gives this shape.
The last true candidate is one position before the first false candidate.
So reuse \cd{first_true} with the negated question.
\begin{pyex}
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def last_true(lo, hi, ok):
    # Last x in [lo, hi) with ok(x) True, or lo - 1 if no x passes.
    # ok must be True ... True False ... False on [lo, hi).
    return first_true(lo, hi, lambda x: not ok(x)) - 1

last_true(0, 100, lambda x: x * x <= 50)    # -> 7
last_true(0, 100, lambda x: x < 0)          # -> -1
last_true(0, 100, lambda x: True)           # -> 99
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Two other forms find the last true. The direct form uses \cd{while lo < hi}, the upper midpoint
\cd{(lo + hi + 1) // 2}, \cd{lo = mid} and \cd{hi = mid - 1}.
The ``best'' form uses \cd{while lo <= hi}. On a pass it saves \cd{best = mid} and sets \cd{lo = mid + 1}.
On a fail it sets \cd{hi = mid - 1}.
When at least one candidate passes, all forms give the same result.
They differ only in the value that they return when no candidate passes.
Use \cd{first_true} by default. The ``best'' form is a safe alternative for a last-true question,
and some examples below use it. Do not mix the update rules of two forms in one loop.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Boundaries in a sorted list: lower bound, upper bound, floor, ceiling}
What changes: values can repeat, or the target can be absent, and the question asks for a position.
Do not stop on a match. Search for a boundary.
The \cd{bisect} functions give each boundary in one line.
(Search Insert Position, Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array.)
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.6cm}L{8.3cm}L{3.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Code & If none exists \\
\midrule
first index with \cd{a[i] >= x} (insertion point) & \cd{bisect_left(a, x)} & \cd{len(a)} \\
first index with \cd{a[i] > x} & \cd{bisect_right(a, x)} & \cd{len(a)} \\
count of values \cd{< x} & \cd{bisect_left(a, x)} & 0 \\
count of values \cd{<= x} & \cd{bisect_right(a, x)} & 0 \\
last index with \cd{a[i] <= x} (floor) & \cd{bisect_right(a, x) - 1} & $-1$ \\
last index with \cd{a[i] < x} & \cd{bisect_left(a, x) - 1} & $-1$ \\
count of values in \cd{[lo, hi]} & \cd{bisect_right(a, hi) - bisect_left(a, lo)} & 0 \\
first and last index of \cd{x} & \cd{bisect_left(a, x)}, \cd{bisect_right(a, x) - 1} & test \cd{first < len(a)}, then \cd{a[first] == x} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
def first_last(a, x):
    first = bisect_left(a, x)
    if first == len(a) or a[first] != x:       # x is absent
        return [-1, -1]
    return [first, bisect_right(a, x) - 1]

a = [1, 3, 3, 3, 8]
first_last(a, 3)                        # -> [1, 3]
first_last(a, 5), first_last(a, 9)      # -> ([-1, -1], [-1, -1])
def floor_index(a, x):                  # last index with a[i] <= x, or -1
    return bisect_right(a, x) - 1
floor_index(a, 5), floor_index(a, 0)    # -> (3, -1)
\end{pyex}
Memory hook: \emph{left gives the first \cd{>= x}, right gives the first \cd{> x}; minus one gives the last one before it.}

\subsubsection{A virtual sorted array: a flat index into a grid}
What changes (Search a 2D Matrix): each row is sorted, and each row starts above the end of the previous row.
Read row by row, the grid is one sorted list of length \cd{rows * cols}.
Do not copy the grid into a list. That costs $O(mn)$.
Binary search the flat index \cd{k}, and convert it to a cell with \cd{divmod(k, cols)}.
Memory hook: \emph{the grid is one sorted list cut into rows, so binary search the flat index and divmod by cols.}
\begin{pyex}
def search_matrix(matrix, target):
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    lo, hi = 0, rows * cols - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        r, c = divmod(mid, cols)       # divide by the number of columns
        val = matrix[r][c]
        if val == target:
            return True
        if val < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return False

m = [[1, 3, 5, 7], [10, 11, 16, 20], [23, 30, 34, 60]]
search_matrix(m, 3), search_matrix(m, 13)       # -> (True, False)
search_matrix([[1], [3]], 3)                    # -> True
\end{pyex}
The general rule: binary search works on any structure that gives its $k$-th element in sorted order in $O(1)$.
You do not have to build the sorted list.
\begin{note}
Sometimes rows and columns are sorted, but a row does not start above the end of the previous row (Search a 2D Matrix II).
Then the flat order is not sorted. Walk a staircase from the top-right corner in $O(m + n)$:
move left when the value is too big, and move down when it is too small.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Rotated sorted arrays: find the drop}
What changes: a rotated sorted array such as \cd{[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]} is two sorted runs, a high run and then a low run.
One comparison with \cd{nums[mid]} no longer tells which side holds a target.

To find the minimum (Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array), use a fixed reference value on a known side of the drop.
The last element is always in the low run.
Every value of the high run is greater than the last element. Every value of the low run is not.
So the test \cd{nums[i] <= nums[-1]} is F \ldots F T \ldots T, and the minimum is at its first true index.
An array that is not rotated passes the test everywhere, so the answer is index 0 with no special case.
Memory hook: \emph{low run means at most the last value; find the first one.}
\begin{caution}
Do not compare with \cd{nums[lo]}. When the window is already sorted, the minimum is at \cd{lo},
but the test sends the search to the right. On \cd{[1, 2, 3]}, the loop below returns 3.
The general rule: compare with a reference value that is surely on one known side of the boundary.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def find_min_wrong(nums):            # compares with the left end: wrong
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= nums[lo]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

find_min_wrong([4, 5, 1, 2, 3])      # -> 1
find_min_wrong([1, 2, 3])            # -> 3
\end{pyex}

To search for a target (Search in Rotated Sorted Array), split the problem into two searches that you know.
First find the drop, which is the index of the minimum.
A target \cd{<= nums[-1]} can only be in the low run \cd{nums[pivot:]}. A bigger target can only be in \cd{nums[:pivot]}.
Then run a lower-bound search on that one sorted run.
Memory hook: \emph{find the drop, then binary search the side that can hold the target.}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def find_min(nums):
    last = nums[-1]
    return nums[first_true(0, len(nums), lambda i: nums[i] <= last)]

def search_rotated(nums, target):
    n, last = len(nums), nums[-1]
    pivot = first_true(0, n, lambda i: nums[i] <= last)    # index of the minimum
    lo, hi = (pivot, n) if target <= last else (0, pivot)
    i = bisect_left(nums, target, lo, hi)                  # searches only nums[lo:hi]
    return i if i < hi and nums[i] == target else -1

nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]
find_min(nums), find_min([1, 2, 3]), find_min([2, 1])     # -> (0, 1, 1)
search_rotated(nums, 0), search_rotated(nums, 5)          # -> (4, 1)
search_rotated(nums, 3), search_rotated([1], 0)           # -> (-1, -1)
arrays = [[1, 3, 5, 7][k:] + [1, 3, 5, 7][:k] for k in range(4)]
all(search_rotated(a, t) == (a.index(t) if t in a else -1)
    for a in arrays for t in range(9))                    # -> True
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
The common one-pass form finds the target in a single loop.
At each step, one half of \cd{[lo, hi]} is sorted: the left half when \cd{nums[lo] <= nums[mid]}.
Keep that half only when the target is inside its value range:
\cd{nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]} for the left half, or \cd{nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]} for the right half.
It has the same $O(\log n)$ time and about half the steps.
With duplicate values, the test against \cd{nums[-1]} is not always monotone: \cd{[1, 1, 2, 1]} gives T T F T.
For Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II, compare \cd{nums[mid]} with \cd{nums[hi]}. On a tie, drop \cd{hi} with \cd{hi -= 1}.
For Search in Rotated Sorted Array II, use the one-pass form.
When \cd{nums[lo] == nums[mid]}, you cannot tell which half is sorted, so set \cd{lo += 1}.
This is safe, because \cd{nums[lo]} equals \cd{nums[mid]}, which is not the target. Do this test before the sorted-half test.
The two-pass form fails here, because its pivot test is not monotone.
In both problems, the worst case becomes $O(n)$.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{No sorted values: a test from local structure}
What changes: the values are not sorted, but the statement still asks for $O(\log n)$ time.
Binary search does not need sorted values. It needs a test that flips one time.
Build the test from \cd{mid} and its neighbor.
\begin{itemize}
  \item A slope (Peak Index in a Mountain Array, LeetCode 852): the values go up and then down.
        A downhill step \cd{a[i] > a[i + 1]} is F \ldots F T \ldots T. The peak is the first true index.
  \item A broken pairing (Single Element in a Sorted Array, LeetCode 540): each value occurs two times, except one value.
        Before the single value, each pair of indexes \cd{(2p, 2p + 1)} holds two equal values.
        At and after the single value, each pair is broken.
        So the test \cd{nums[2p] != nums[2p + 1]} is F \ldots F T \ldots T over the pairs \cd{p}.
\end{itemize}
Memory hook: \emph{no sorted values? Find a test at mid that flips one time: a downhill step, a broken pair.}
\begin{pyex}
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def peak_index(a):                   # a goes up, then down
    return first_true(0, len(a) - 1, lambda i: a[i] > a[i + 1])

def single_in_pairs(nums):           # sorted; each value two times except one
    p = first_true(0, len(nums) // 2, lambda p: nums[2 * p] != nums[2 * p + 1])
    return nums[2 * p]                # the first broken pair starts with the single value

peak_index([0, 2, 5, 9, 4, 1]), peak_index([0, 10, 5, 2])    # -> (3, 1)
single_in_pairs([3, 3, 7, 7, 10, 11, 11])                    # -> 10
single_in_pairs([1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 8, 8])                 # -> 2
single_in_pairs([5]), single_in_pairs([1, 1, 2])             # -> (5, 2)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
The XOR of all values also finds the single value, but it costs $O(n)$.
It does not meet a required $O(\log n)$ time. XOR is the correct tool when the values are not sorted (Single Number).
\end{caution}

\subsubsection{Binary search on the answer: the smallest value that works}
What changes: no array exists. The candidates are the possible answers.
Use four steps.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Write \cd{ok(x)}: can you do the task with the value \cd{x}? It is often a sum or a greedy pass.
  \item Prove that \cd{ok} is monotone: if \cd{x} works, \cd{x + 1} also works.
  \item Set the bounds: \cd{lo} is the smallest possible answer, and \cd{hi} surely works.
  \item Find the first true value. The total cost is the cost of one check times $\log_2(\text{hi} - \text{lo})$.
\end{enumerate}
In Koko Eating Bananas, \cd{ok(k)} is ``the hours at speed \cd{k} are at most \cd{h}''.
Each pile needs $\lceil p / k \rceil$ hours, and that value never grows when \cd{k} grows.
Speed 1 is the slowest. Speed \cd{max(piles)} always works, because each pile then takes one hour and \cd{h >= n}.
Memory hook: \emph{guess a speed, count the hours, and binary search for the first speed that fits.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    def hours_needed(k):
        return sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)    # ceil(p / k) in integers
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)        # hi always fits: one pile per hour
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if hours_needed(mid) <= h:
            hi = mid              # mid fits: it can be the answer
        else:
            lo = mid + 1          # mid is too slow
    return lo

min_eating_speed([3, 6, 7, 11], 8)          # -> 4
min_eating_speed([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 5)    # -> 30
min_eating_speed([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 6)    # -> 23
min_eating_speed([10**9], 10**9)            # -> 1
\end{pyex}
Only the check and the bounds change in the problems of this group: the capacity to ship packages in $D$ days,
the smallest largest sum of $k$ pieces, the smallest divisor under a threshold, the first day with enough bouquets.
For a ``maximize the smallest'' question, the check flips in the other direction. Then search for the last true value.
\begin{note}
For a real-valued answer, run a fixed number of steps and set \cd{lo = mid} or \cd{hi = mid} with no \cd{+ 1}.
Each step halves the range, but the range cannot become smaller than the gap between two neighbor floats.
From a range of $10^9$, about 80 steps make \cd{lo} and \cd{hi} neighbor floats for an answer near 1.
More steps do not make the answer more exact.
Thus 100 steps give an answer that is as exact as a float allows, which is enough for normal limits.
A very large range needs more steps: with 100 steps, the cube root below is wrong by 58\% for $v = 10^{45}$.
\end{note}
\begin{pyex}
def cube_root(v):                   # v >= 0
    lo, hi = 0.0, max(1.0, v)       # the answer is in [lo, hi]
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if mid ** 3 >= v:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid
    return hi

round(cube_root(2.0), 6), round(cube_root(27.0), 6)    # -> (1.259921, 3.0)
# 100 steps are too few for a huge range: the true ratio is 1.0
round(cube_root(1e45) / 1e15, 2)                       # -> 1.58
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Binary search on the answer: the largest value that works}
What changes: the test is T T T F F, so search for the last true value.
Two grid problems show this shape. Both have non-negative cells, and both ask for the largest side $k$ of a square under a sum limit.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Maximum Side Length of a Square with Sum Less than or Equal to Threshold: \emph{some} $k \times k$ square must fit.
        It is monotone because a fitting square contains a fitting smaller square.
  \item A variant that asks for the largest side where \emph{every} $k \times k$ square must fit.
        It is monotone because a square that fails makes each bigger square around it fail.
\end{itemize}
A 2D prefix table gives each square sum in $O(1)$, so one check costs $O(R C)$.
The total cost is $O(R C \log \min(R, C))$.
The loop below uses the ``best'' form: if \cd{mid} fits, save it and try bigger.
The only difference between the two problems is \cd{any} or \cd{all}.
Memory hooks: \emph{prefix table for $O(1)$ squares, then binary search the biggest side that fits} (some square);
\emph{cells are non-negative, so if size $k$ fails, every bigger size fails; binary search $k$, and check all
$k \times k$ squares with 2D prefix sums} (every square).
\begin{pyex}
def largest_side(grid, limit, need_all):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    pre = [[0] * (cols + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)]     # pre[r][c] = sum of the top-left r x c block
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            pre[r + 1][c + 1] = grid[r][c] + pre[r][c + 1] + pre[r + 1][c] - pre[r][c]

    def square_sum(r, c, k):            # k x k square with top-left cell (r, c)
        return pre[r + k][c + k] - pre[r][c + k] - pre[r + k][c] + pre[r][c]

    def fits(k):
        tests = (square_sum(r, c, k) <= limit
                 for r in range(rows - k + 1) for c in range(cols - k + 1))
        return all(tests) if need_all else any(tests)

    lo, hi, best = 1, min(rows, cols), 0    # best stays 0 if no side fits
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if fits(mid):
            best = mid                  # mid fits: save it and try bigger
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1                # mid fails: try smaller
    return best

mat = [[1, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2]] * 3       # read only, so shared rows are safe here
largest_side(mat, 4, need_all=False)    # -> 2
largest_side(mat, 4, need_all=True)     # -> 1
largest_side([[2] * 5] * 5, 1, need_all=False)   # -> 0
largest_side([[5, 5, 5]], 4, need_all=True)      # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Both problems also have an $O(R C)$ solution.
For ``some square'', scan the bottom-right corners in row order and test only the side \cd{best + 1} at each corner.
For ``every square'', walk each diagonal with two pointers.
The limits ($300 \times 300$) do not need them.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Sorted history: the latest value at or before a time}
What changes (Time Based Key-Value Store): the data groups by an exact key, and each key has a timeline.
A query asks for the value in effect at time $t$.
Split the query into two parts. A hash map finds the exact key.
A sorted list per key handles the time.
The set timestamps strictly increase, so \cd{append} keeps each list sorted for free.
A get is a floor query: \cd{bisect_right(times, t)} counts the times \cd{<= t}, and the answer is one position to the left.
Memory hook: \emph{two lists per key, times and values; \cd{bisect_right} counts the times at or before $t$, so take the value one to the left.}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict

class TimeMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.times = defaultdict(list)     # key -> timestamps, increasing
        self.values = defaultdict(list)    # key -> values, same order as times

    def set(self, key, value, timestamp):
        self.times[key].append(timestamp)  # timestamps increase: the list stays sorted
        self.values[key].append(value)

    def get(self, key, timestamp):
        times = self.times.get(key, [])    # .get does not add a missing key
        i = bisect_right(times, timestamp) # i = count of times <= timestamp
        return self.values[key][i - 1] if i > 0 else ""

tm = TimeMap()
tm.set("foo", "bar", 1)
tm.get("foo", 1), tm.get("foo", 3)      # -> ('bar', 'bar')
tm.set("foo", "bar2", 4)
tm.get("foo", 4), tm.get("foo", 5)      # -> ('bar2', 'bar2')
tm.get("foo", 0), tm.get("baz", 9)      # -> ('', '')
"baz" in tm.times                       # -> False
\end{pyex}
The same pattern answers snapshot arrays, election leaders by time, and prices ``as of'' a date.
For the earliest value at or after $t$, use \cd{i = bisect_left(times, t)} and read index \cd{i} when \cd{i < len(times)}.
Without \cd{bisect}, write the floor search by hand with the ``best'' form.
If the time at \cd{mid} is \cd{<= t}, save its value and set \cd{lo = mid + 1}. Else set \cd{hi = mid - 1}.
\begin{note}
Always check whether the input order already gives sorted data. Here it removes the need for a balanced tree.
If inserts can arrive out of order, insert at \cd{i = bisect_right(times, t)} in both lists
(\cd{bisect.insort} does this for one list). Each insert costs $O(k)$, because the list shifts.
For many such inserts, use an ordered container.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{A sorted helper array: longest increasing subsequence}
What changes (Longest Increasing Subsequence): the input is not sorted. The algorithm builds a sorted array as it goes.
For each chain length, keep only the smallest tail value seen so far.
A smaller tail is always at least as easy to extend, so the other chains of that length do not matter.
These tails stay strictly increasing. For a new value \cd{x}, \cd{bisect_left} finds the first tail \cd{>= x}.
Replace that tail with \cd{x}, or append \cd{x} when no tail is \cd{>= x}.
The length of \cd{tails} is the answer.
For \cd{[10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]}, the tails change as follows:
\cd{[10]}, \cd{[9]}, \cd{[2]}, \cd{[2, 5]}, \cd{[2, 3]}, \cd{[2, 3, 7]}, \cd{[2, 3, 7, 101]}, \cd{[2, 3, 7, 18]}. The length is 4.
Memory hook: \emph{smallest tail per length: \cd{bisect_left}, then replace or append.}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
def length_of_lis(nums, strict=True):
    find = bisect_left if strict else bisect_right   # right lets equal values chain
    tails = []        # tails[k] = smallest last value of a chain of length k + 1
    for x in nums:
        pos = find(tails, x)
        if pos == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)       # x extends the longest chain
        else:
            tails[pos] = x        # x is a smaller tail for length pos + 1
    return len(tails)

length_of_lis([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18])     # -> 4
length_of_lis([0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3])               # -> 4
length_of_lis([7, 7, 7, 7])                     # -> 1
length_of_lis([7, 7, 7, 7], strict=False)       # -> 4
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\cd{tails} is not a real subsequence. Only its length is correct.
To rebuild the sequence, store the index of each tail and a parent index for each element.
\end{caution}
The $O(n^2)$ DP (``the longest chain that ends at index $i$'') is the simple fallback when $n$ is a few thousand.

\subsubsection{Partition search across two sorted arrays}
What changes (Median of Two Sorted Arrays): the answer is a cut, not a value.
Put the smallest half of all values on the left side of the cut.
The left side has a fixed size \cd{half = (m + n + 1) // 2}.
If it takes \cd{i} values from array \cd{A}, it must take \cd{j = half - i} values from array \cd{B}.
So only \cd{i} is free. Binary search \cd{i} over the shorter array, so that \cd{j} always stays in range.
Check a cut with the four border values. Use $-\infty$ and $+\infty$ for a border outside an array.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \cd{A[i - 1] > B[j]}: the cut takes too many values from \cd{A}. Move \cd{i} left.
  \item \cd{B[j - 1] > A[i]}: the cut takes too few values from \cd{A}. Move \cd{i} right.
  \item Else the cut is correct. The median comes from the largest left border and the smallest right border.
\end{itemize}
Memory hook: \emph{cut the shorter array so the left half is full: too many from A, go left; too few, go right;
just right, read the borders.}
\begin{pyex}
def find_median(nums1, nums2):
    A, B = nums1, nums2
    if len(A) > len(B):
        A, B = B, A                    # search the shorter array
    m, n = len(A), len(B)
    half = (m + n + 1) // 2            # size of the left side

    def at(arr, k):                    # arr[k], with -inf and +inf outside the array
        if k < 0:
            return float("-inf")
        if k >= len(arr):
            return float("inf")
        return arr[k]

    lo, hi = 0, m                      # i = values that the left side takes from A
    while lo <= hi:
        i = (lo + hi) // 2
        j = half - i                   # the rest of the left side comes from B
        if at(A, i - 1) > at(B, j):
            hi = i - 1                 # too many from A
        elif at(B, j - 1) > at(A, i):
            lo = i + 1                 # too few from A
        else:                          # just right
            left_max = max(at(A, i - 1), at(B, j - 1))
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1:
                return float(left_max)
            return (left_max + min(at(A, i), at(B, j))) / 2

find_median([1, 3], [2])               # -> 2.0
find_median([1, 2], [3, 4])            # -> 2.5
find_median([], [5]), find_median([1, 1, 1], [1, 1])    # -> (5.0, 1.0)
import statistics
pairs = [([1, 4, 9], [2, 3]), ([5, 6], [1, 2, 3, 4]), ([], [1, 2]), ([0, 0], [0, 7])]
all(find_median(a, b) == statistics.median(a + b) for a, b in pairs)    # -> True
\end{pyex}
The same cut finds the $k$-th smallest value of two sorted arrays: make the left side size $k$, and keep
\cd{i} between \cd{max(0, k - n)} and \cd{min(k, m)}. The answer is the largest left border.
With more than one free count (many sorted arrays, a sorted matrix), binary search the answer value instead.
The answer is the first value \cd{v} where the count of values \cd{<= v} is at least $k$.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{What are the candidates?} Indexes, answer values, sizes, times, a split count, or a flat index.
  \item \textbf{What is the question for one candidate?} Write \cd{ok(x)} in words first.
  \item \textbf{Why does \cd{ok} flip only one time?} Name the reason: sorted data, non-negative values,
        a bigger region that contains a smaller one, more capacity that always helps,
        or a local pattern at \cd{mid} (a downhill step, a broken pair).
        If you cannot name a reason, compare with a brute force on small inputs.
  \item \textbf{Which boundary do you need?} The smallest value that works is a first true.
        The largest value that works is a last true. One exact value uses the closed-range loop.
  \item \textbf{What are the bounds?} \cd{lo} is the smallest possible answer. \cd{hi} surely works, or it is one past the end.
        Decide the return value when no candidate works.
  \item \textbf{What does one check cost?} The total is the cost of one check times $\log_2$ of the range.
        Make the check cheap with prefix sums, a greedy pass, or \cd{bisect} counts.
  \item \textbf{Is one comparison at \cd{mid} ambiguous?} Find a second fact that makes it safe
        (which half is sorted, which array gives too many values). Or split the problem into two searches that you know.
  \item \textbf{Test the edges:} one element, two elements, the answer at each end of the range, and no answer.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Mixed loop conventions.} Each loop form has one condition and one pair of updates.
A mix skips the last candidate or loops forever.
With \cd{lo = mid} and the lower midpoint, a range of two values never shrinks, because \cd{mid == lo}.
\end{caution}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.8cm}L{4.3cm}L{3.5cm}L{5.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Goal & Start & Loop & Updates \\
\midrule
Exact match & \cd{lo, hi = 0, n - 1} & \cd{while lo <= hi} & \cd{lo = mid + 1}, \cd{hi = mid - 1} \\
First true & \cd{lo, hi = 0, n} (hi is a sentinel) & \cd{while lo < hi}, lower mid & \cd{hi = mid}, \cd{lo = mid + 1} \\
Last true, direct & \cd{ok(lo)} is true & \cd{while lo < hi}, upper mid & \cd{lo = mid}, \cd{hi = mid - 1} \\
Last true, best & \cd{best} = the ``none'' value & \cd{while lo <= hi} & pass: \cd{best = mid}, \cd{lo = mid + 1}; fail: \cd{hi = mid - 1} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
lo, hi = 4, 5
(lo + hi) // 2             # -> 4
(lo + hi + 1) // 2         # -> 5
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A boundary index can be outside the list.} \cd{bisect_left} can return \cd{len(a)}.
Test \cd{i < len(a)} before you read \cd{a[i]}.
A floor index can be $-1$, and \cd{a[-1]} silently reads the last element. Test \cd{i >= 0} first.
In the count form \cd{i = bisect_right(a, x)}, test \cd{i > 0} before you read \cd{a[i - 1]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
a = [10, 20, 30]
bisect_left(a, 99)                  # -> 3
a[bisect_left(a, 99)]               # -> raises IndexError
i = bisect_right(a, 5) - 1          # no value <= 5
i, a[i]                             # -> (-1, 30)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A search on a question that is not monotone gives a wrong answer and no error.}
A search on the size of a region (a square, a window) needs non-negative values.
With negative values, a size can fail while a bigger size passes.
Prove monotonicity first, or test it against a brute force.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Wrong bounds.} Make the smallest possible answer reachable, including 0 when nothing can fit.
Start \cd{lo} at 0 in the direct form, or start \cd{best} at 0 in the ``best'' form.
A speed or a divisor starts at 1, because 0 divides by zero.
Do not set \cd{hi} above the largest real candidate.
For a side above \cd{min(rows, cols)}, no square exists, so an ``every square'' check passes with no work.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
all(s <= 4 for s in [])     # -> True
any(s <= 4 for s in [])     # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Ceiling division.} A partial pile or a partial load still costs a full unit. Floor division undercounts.
Use \cd{(p + k - 1) // k} or \cd{-(-p // k)}. Do not use \cd{math.ceil(p / k)} for large values,
because float division loses precision above $2^{53}$.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
p, k = 7, 2
p // k, (p + k - 1) // k, -(-p // k)    # -> (3, 4, 4)
int((2**53 + 1) / 1) == 2**53 + 1       # -> False
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{\cd{bisect} on tuples.} A probe \cd{(t,)} sorts before \cd{(t, "x")}, so \cd{bisect_right} misses an exact match.
Search a separate list of times, or pass \cd{key=} \since{3.10}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_right
pairs = [(1, "a"), (4, "b")]
pairs[bisect_right(pairs, (4,)) - 1]                       # -> (1, 'a')
pairs[bisect_right(pairs, 4, key=lambda p: p[0]) - 1]     # -> (4, 'b')
\end{pyex}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Strict or non-strict.} \cd{bisect_left} keeps equal values apart (strictly increasing).
        \cd{bisect_right} lets them chain (non-decreasing).
  \item \textbf{``Some'' or ``every''.} ``Some square fits'' and ``every square fits'' are two different checks.
        Read the statement again before you write \cd{any} or \cd{all}.
  \item \textbf{The wrong divisor in a flat index.} Divide by the number of columns, not by the number of rows.
  \item \textbf{A table with shared rows.} \cd{[[0] * (cols + 1)] * (rows + 1)} makes every row the same list.
        Build a prefix table with \cd{[[0] * (cols + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)]}.
  \item \textbf{A read that adds a key.} \cd{d[key]} on a \cd{defaultdict} adds an empty entry. Use \cd{d.get(key, [])} in a query.
  \item \textbf{Integer division of a median.} Use \cd{/ 2} for the average of two middle values, not \cd{// 2}.
  \item \textbf{A scan that meets the limits but breaks the rule.} A merge or a linear scan can pass the tests,
        but it does not meet a required $O(\log n)$ time.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Binary Search & Exact match on a closed range; return $-1$ when the range is empty. &
  Closed range, check the middle, drop the half that cannot hold the target. \\
Search a 2D Matrix & The grid is one sorted list; convert the flat index with \cd{divmod(k, cols)}. &
  The grid is one sorted list cut into rows, so binary search the flat index and divmod by cols. \\
Koko Eating Bananas & Search the answer (the speed); the check sums $\lceil p / k \rceil$ hours. &
  Guess a speed, count the hours, and binary search for the first speed that fits. \\
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array & First index with \cd{nums[i] <= nums[-1]}. &
  Low run means at most the last value; find the first one. \\
Search in Rotated Sorted Array & Find the drop, then a lower bound in the one run that can hold the target. &
  Find the drop, then binary search the side that can hold the target. \\
Time Based Key-Value Store & Floor query per key: \cd{bisect_right} on the times, then one to the left. &
  Two lists per key, times and values; \cd{bisect_right} counts the times at or before $t$, so take the value one to the left. \\
Median of Two Sorted Arrays & Search the cut in the shorter array; check four border values. &
  Cut the shorter array so the left half is full: too many from A, go left; too few, go right; just right, read the borders. \\
Maximum Side Length of a Square with Sum Less than or Equal to Threshold &
  Last true over the side; \emph{some} square must fit; 2D prefix sums for the check. &
  Prefix table for $O(1)$ squares, then binary search the biggest side that fits. \\
Longest Increasing Subsequence & The sorted array is the \cd{tails} list that the loop builds. &
  Smallest tail per length: \cd{bisect_left}, then replace or append. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}
