\section{Linked lists}\label{tech:T07}

\subsection{The idea}
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and one link, \cd{next}, to the node after it.
The list has no index, no stored length and no link back.
In this section, a \emph{link} is a field of a node that refers to another node: \cd{next}, and in some problems \cd{prev} or \cd{random}.
A \emph{pointer} is a variable that refers to a node.
A list algorithm is a plan of link changes: which links change, and in which order. The values do not move.

One rule controls all list code: a node that no pointer and no link refers to is lost.
Before you change a link, put a pointer on the node at its other end.
This rule explains the saved \cd{nxt} in a reversal and the saved \cd{after} in a block reversal.
It also explains the dummy node. The link \cd{dummy.next} always refers to the current first node, even when the first node changes.

\textbf{Worked example.} Reverse \cd{1 -> 2 -> 3}. Start with \cd{prev = None} and \cd{curr} on node 1.
Save \cd{nxt} on node 2. Point the link of node 1 at \cd{prev}. Step: \cd{prev} is now node 1 and \cd{curr} is node 2.
Do the same for node 2, then for node 3.
Now \cd{curr} is \cd{None} and \cd{prev} is node 3, the head of \cd{3 -> 2 -> 1}.
Each node changes one time, so the time is $O(n)$ and the extra memory is $O(1)$.

\textbf{What the techniques save.} The brute force copies the nodes into a Python list.
That gives index access, negative indexes and access from both ends, for $O(n)$ extra memory.
This copy is often the fastest correct solution to write, and the constraints often allow it.
The list techniques remove that memory. They also remove a node from the middle in $O(1)$.
A singly linked list needs a pointer on the predecessor. A doubly linked list needs only a pointer on the node itself.
An array cannot do that: a removal from the middle shifts all later items, $O(n)$.

\textbf{Five moves.} Almost every list problem is a composition of two or three of these moves:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Walk}: \cd{while node:} \ldots\ \cd{node = node.next}.
  \item \textbf{Build}: a dummy node in front, and a tail pointer on the last node of the output.
  \item \textbf{Reverse}: \cd{prev}, \cd{curr} and a saved \cd{nxt}.
  \item \textbf{Find a position}: fast and slow pointers (the middle, a cycle), or two pointers with a fixed gap (the $k$-th node from the end).
  \item \textbf{Map}: a dict keyed by node object (a deep copy), or a dict from key to node (an LRU cache).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input or the output is a chain of nodes. The statement says ``in place'', ``do not change the values'' or
        ``$O(1)$ extra memory''. Plan the link changes.
  \item The first node of the output can change: removal of the head, insertion at the front, a reversal, a merge.
        Put a dummy node in front of the head.
  \item The task needs a position from the end, the middle, or both ends at the same time.
        Use fast and slow pointers, a fixed gap, or reverse one half. If memory is free, copy the nodes into a Python list.
  \item The task changes a block or a range of the list: reverse in groups, swap pairs, rotate.
        Name four nodes: \cd{before}, \cd{first}, \cd{last} and \cd{after}.
  \item Two or more inputs are sorted, and the output must be sorted. Merge the fronts (the first unused node of each input):
        compare two fronts, or keep $k$ fronts in a min-heap.
  \item A number is stored as a chain of digits. Add column by column with a carry.
  \item The task asks for a deep copy of nodes with extra links (random, child) that can point to any node.
        Map each old node to its new node.
  \item One deterministic step repeats on a finite set of states: ``does it loop'', ``where does the loop start''.
        Use fast and slow pointers. An array whose values are valid indexes into the same array is such a walk:
        index \cd{i} links to index \cd{nums[i]}.
  \item Every operation must be $O(1)$, and you need lookup by key plus an order that changes (most recent, oldest).
        The statement asks you to design a class with methods such as \cd{get} and \cd{put}.
        Use a hash map from key to node and a doubly linked list.
  \item The constraint sizes. A list has at most about $10^5$ nodes. An $O(n)$ copy into a Python list fits,
        unless the statement or a follow-up asks for $O(1)$ extra memory.
        Python stops recursion near depth 1000. When the list can be longer, use loops, not one recursive call per node.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
Most examples in this section start with the same three helpers: a node class, \cd{build} (Python list to
linked list) and \cd{to_list} (linked list to Python list). Each block repeats them, because each block runs alone.

\textbf{Reverse.} This is the base move for all link rewiring.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head          # prev: reversed part, curr: the rest
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next              # 1. save the rest
        curr.next = prev             # 2. flip the link
        prev = curr                  # 3. step prev
        curr = nxt                   # 4. step curr
    return prev                      # curr is None; prev is the old tail

to_list(reverse(build([1, 2, 3])))   # -> [3, 2, 1]
to_list(reverse(build([7])))         # -> [7]
reverse(None) is None                # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: \cd{prev} is the head of a reversed list of all visited nodes, and \cd{curr} is the head of the
untouched rest. The two lists are disjoint. Each step moves one node from the front of the rest to the front of the reversed part.

\textbf{Build with a dummy and a tail.} This is the base move for every output list.
The example keeps the nodes that pass a test and splices them into a new chain.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def keep(head, test):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()        # tail: the last node of the output
    while head:
        if test(head.val):
            tail.next = head         # link the node
            tail = head              # move the tail
        head = head.next
    tail.next = None                 # end the output; cut the old links
    return dummy.next                # the head can change

to_list(keep(build([5, 1, 6, 2, 7]), lambda v: v < 3))   # -> [1, 2]
keep(build([5, 6]), lambda v: v < 3) is None             # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: the chain from \cd{dummy.next} to \cd{tail} is the finished output. The link of \cd{tail} is not part of the
output until the end, so set it to \cd{None} after the loop. The dummy removes all special code for the first node and for an empty output.

\textbf{Escape to an array.} When $O(n)$ extra memory is allowed, copy the node references into a Python list.
Write the new order with indexes, then relink the nodes in that order. This handles any reorder that you can write as a list of indexes.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def to_nodes(head):
    nodes = []
    while head:
        nodes.append(head)
        head = head.next
    return nodes
def relink(nodes):                   # chain the nodes in this order
    for a, b in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
        a.next = b
    if not nodes:
        return None
    nodes[-1].next = None            # end the list; no old link stays
    return nodes[0]

nodes = to_nodes(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
to_list(relink(nodes[1::2] + nodes[::2]))   # -> [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Reverse a whole list}
To reverse a whole list, use the core template with no change (Reverse Linked List).
Memory hook: \emph{Save next, flip the arrow, step both, return prev.}
Use the loop, not recursion. A recursive reversal goes one call deep per node, and Python stops near depth 1000.
The same loop is a subroutine in harder problems. Reverse one half to read it backward (Reorder List).
Reverse a block (Reverse Nodes in k-Group). Reverse digit lists to add from the low end (Add Two Numbers II).

\subsubsection{Merge two sorted lists}
Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list (Merge Two Sorted Lists).
The \emph{front} of an input is its first node that is not in the output yet.
Each input is sorted, so the smallest remaining value is at one of the two fronts.
Compare the two fronts, link the smaller one after the tail, and move the tail.
When one input is empty, link the rest of the other input in one step.
Memory hook: \emph{Dummy and tail. Take the smaller head, move the tail. Glue the rest.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:           # <= takes the node of a first on a tie
            tail.next = a
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b               # glue the rest (or None)
    return dummy.next

to_list(merge(build([1, 2, 4]), build([1, 3, 4])))   # -> [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]
to_list(merge(None, build([0])))                     # -> [0]
merge(None, None) is None                            # -> True
\end{pyex}
The same two-front comparison merges sorted arrays and gives the intersection or union of two sorted sequences.
It is also the merge step of merge sort on a linked list.

\subsubsection{Digit lists: add with a carry}
Two numbers are stored as lists of digits, and the output is their sum as a new list (Add Two Numbers).
Here the digits come least significant first, which is the order of column addition.
Walk both lists together. Use 0 for a list that has ended. Write the total mod 10 and carry the total div 10.
Keep the loop alive while a carry is left, so a final carry becomes a new node.
Memory hook: \emph{Add digits plus carry while anything is left; write mod 10, carry div 10.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def add(l1, l2):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:         # a final carry makes one more node
        total = carry
        if l1:
            total += l1.val
            l1 = l1.next
        if l2:
            total += l2.val
            l2 = l2.next
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

to_list(add(build([2, 4, 3]), build([5, 6, 4])))   # -> [7, 0, 8]
to_list(add(build([9, 9]), build([1])))            # -> [0, 0, 1]
\end{pyex}
The carry is 0 or 1, because the largest column total is $9 + 9 + 1 = 19$.
When the digits come most significant first, reverse both lists first, or push the digits on two stacks.

\subsubsection{Both ends at once: an array of nodes, or split, reverse and weave}
The new order is first, last, second, second to last, and so on (Reorder List). Node \cd{i} pairs with node \cd{n - 1 - i}.
A singly linked list reads only forward, so the task needs access from the back.
The intuitive solution copies the nodes into a Python list. Two indexes move inward and give the order.
Then chain the nodes and end the last one with \cd{None}.
Memory hook: \emph{Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reorder(head):
    nodes = []
    node = head
    while node:
        nodes.append(node)
        node = node.next
    order = []
    left, right = 0, len(nodes) - 1
    while left <= right:
        order.append(nodes[left])
        if left < right:             # the middle node of an odd list goes in once
            order.append(nodes[right])
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    for a, b in zip(order, order[1:]):
        a.next = b
    order[-1].next = None            # end the list, or it has a cycle

head = build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
reorder(head)
to_list(head)                        # -> [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]
head = build([1, 2, 3, 4])
reorder(head)
to_list(head)                        # -> [1, 4, 2, 3]
\end{pyex}
The $O(1)$ memory form composes three moves. Find the last node of the front half with fast and slow pointers.
Cut the list there and reverse the back half, so the back reads forward. Then weave the two halves.
The same split-and-reverse answers any mirror-pair question on a list: compare the pairs, add them, or weave them.
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev, head = head, nxt
    return prev

def middle(head):                    # the left middle for an even length
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow
def reorder(head):
    mid = middle(head)
    back = reverse(mid.next)         # the back half reads forward now
    mid.next = None                  # cut: the front half ends here
    front = head
    while back:                      # the back half is never longer
        f_next, b_next = front.next, back.next
        front.next = back
        back.next = f_next
        front, back = f_next, b_next

middle(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])).val   # -> 3
middle(build([1, 2, 3, 4])).val      # -> 2
head = build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
reorder(head)
to_list(head)                        # -> [1, 6, 2, 5, 3, 4]
\end{pyex}
With \cd{slow, fast = head, head.next}, \cd{slow} stops on node \cd{ceil(n/2) - 1}, the last node of the front half.
The front half is then never shorter than the back half. With \cd{slow = fast = head}, \cd{slow} stops on the right middle.

\subsubsection{A position from the end: line up the nodes, or keep a gap}
The task names a node by its position from the end, for example to delete it (Remove Nth Node From End of List).
To delete a node, you need its predecessor. The head has no predecessor, so put a dummy in front.
The intuitive solution lines up all nodes, dummy included, in a Python list.
Then \cd{nodes[-n]} is the target and \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} is its predecessor.
Memory hook: \emph{Line up the nodes behind a dummy, then \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} skips its next.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)        # the head gets a predecessor
    nodes = []
    node = dummy
    while node:
        nodes.append(node)
        node = node.next
    prev = nodes[-n - 1]             # nodes[-n] is the target
    prev.next = prev.next.next
    return dummy.next

def remove_with_gap(head, n):        # one pass, O(1) memory
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    slow = fast = dummy
    for _ in range(n):               # fast is n nodes ahead of slow
        fast = fast.next
    while fast.next:                 # stop when fast is on the last node
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next       # slow is the predecessor
    return dummy.next

to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2))   # -> [1, 2, 3, 5]
remove_nth_from_end(build([1]), 1) is None                # -> True
to_list(remove_with_gap(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2))       # -> [1, 2, 3, 5]
to_list(remove_with_gap(build([1, 2]), 2))                # -> [2]
\end{pyex}
The optimal form keeps a gap of $n$ nodes between two pointers. When the lead pointer is on the last node,
the trail pointer is on the predecessor. To land on the target itself, run until the lead pointer is \cd{None}.
The same gap finds the $k$-th node from the end and the cut point to rotate a list.

\subsubsection{Reverse a block in place: before, first, last, after}
The task reverses each block of $k$ nodes, and a short last block stays as it is (Reverse Nodes in k-Group).
Each full block is a plain reversal with two splice points.
Probe $k$ steps to find \cd{last}. If the probe reaches \cd{None}, the block is short: stop and change nothing.
Save \cd{first} and \cd{after}. Reverse the block with \cd{prev} starting at \cd{after}, so the reversed block is already
attached at its tail. Then link \cd{before} to \cd{last}, and move \cd{before} to \cd{first}, the new tail of the block.
Memory hook: \emph{Before, first, last, after: probe k, reverse with prev = after, link before to last, step to first.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy                   # the tail of the finished part
    while True:
        last = before
        for _ in range(k):           # 1. probe: is there a full block?
            last = last.next
            if last is None:
                return dummy.next    # a short block stays as it is
        first, after = before.next, last.next
        prev, curr = after, first    # 2. reverse; first ends up linked to after
        while curr is not after:
            nxt = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = nxt
        before.next = last           # 3. splice the block in
        before = first               # first is the tail of the block now

to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2))   # -> [2, 1, 4, 3, 5]
to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 3))   # -> [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]
to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2]), 1))            # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}
The four names fit most changes to a contiguous part of a list: reverse a range, swap pairs ($k = 2$), or move a block (rotate).
Save the outside neighbors first, change the inside, then splice.
Start an accumulator with the value that the boundary must have at the end. Here, \cd{prev = after} makes the tail link correct with no extra step.

\subsubsection{Merge many sorted lists: a heap of fronts}
Merge $k$ sorted lists into one sorted list (Merge k Sorted Lists).
The next output node is the smallest of the current fronts. Keep only the fronts in a min-heap.
Pop the smallest front, link it after the tail, and push its successor.
Each node costs one pop and at most one push, $O(\log k)$. With the $O(k)$ heap build, the total is $O(k + N \log k)$ for $N$ nodes.
Memory hook: \emph{Heap the fronts; pop the smallest, push its next.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def merge_k(lists):
    heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
    heapq.heapify(heap)              # i breaks ties, so nodes never compare
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

to_list(merge_k([build([1, 4, 5]), build([1, 3, 4]), build([2, 6])]))   # -> [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]
merge_k([]) is None, merge_k([None]) is None    # -> (True, True)
heapq.heappush([(1, ListNode())], (1, ListNode()))   # -> raises TypeError
\end{pyex}
The last line shows the reason for the index: two equal values make Python compare the nodes, and nodes have no order.
The list index is unique in the heap, because the heap holds at most one front per list.
An alternative merges the lists in pairs, round after round. There are $\log k$ rounds of $N$ nodes each.
Do not merge the lists one by one into a growing result. That re-reads the result and costs $O(N k)$.

\subsubsection{Copy a list with extra links: map old node to new node}
The task asks for a deep copy of a list (Copy List with Random Pointer). Each node has an extra link that can point to any node.
A \cd{random} link can point forward, so the copy of its target may not exist yet.
Use two passes. Pass 1 makes a copy of every node and stores old node to new node in a dict.
Pass 2 sets each \cd{next} and \cd{random} of the copies through the dict.
Key the dict by the node object, because values can repeat. The entry \cd{{None: None}} copies a missing link as \cd{None}, with no special case.
Memory hook: \emph{Make every copy first, then link copies through the old-to-new map.}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None, random=None):
        self.val, self.next, self.random = val, next, random

def copy_random_list(head):
    old_to_new = {None: None}        # a missing link maps to None
    cur = head
    while cur:                       # pass 1: make every copy
        old_to_new[cur] = Node(cur.val)
        cur = cur.next
    cur = head
    while cur:                       # pass 2: link the copies
        copy = old_to_new[cur]
        copy.next = old_to_new[cur.next]
        copy.random = old_to_new[cur.random]
        cur = cur.next
    return old_to_new[head]

a, b, c = Node(7), Node(7), Node(5)  # equal values: key by node, not by value
a.next, b.next = b, c
a.random, b.random, c.random = c, a, c
h = copy_random_list(a)
(h.val, h.next.val, h.next.next.val)              # -> (7, 7, 5)
h.random is h.next.next, h.next.random is h       # -> (True, True)
h is not a and h.random is not c                  # -> True
copy_random_list(None) is None                    # -> True
\end{pyex}
This is the pattern to clone any structure with arbitrary references: graphs, trees with parent links, objects with cycles.
In a DFS or BFS clone, put the new node in the map before you visit its neighbors, so a cycle ends.

The $O(1)$ memory form stores the map inside the list. Insert each copy right after its original, so
\cd{orig.next} is the copy. Set \cd{copy.random = orig.random.next} when \cd{orig.random} is not \cd{None}.
Then split the two lists and restore the original.

The general rule: when you need an extra map and the structure has a free slot or a change that you can undo,
store the map inside the structure. Undo the change at the end.
Index marking on arrays uses the same idea: to record value \cd{x}, negate \cd{nums[abs(x) - 1]}.
Morris traversal of a tree also uses it: a free right link points back to an ancestor for a short time.

\subsubsection{Detect a cycle: fast and slow pointers}
The task asks if a list loops back on itself (Linked List Cycle).
A visited set of nodes works with $O(n)$ memory. For $O(1)$ memory, move \cd{slow} one node and
\cd{fast} two nodes per step. Without a cycle, \cd{fast} reaches the end. With a cycle, both pointers enter it.
Inside the cycle, \cd{fast} gains exactly one node per step, so the gap counts down to 0 and cannot skip it.
Memory hook (\cd{fast} is the hare, \cd{slow} is the tortoise): \emph{Hare runs two, tortoise runs one. If they meet, it loops. If the hare falls off the end, it does not.}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:        # fast can take two steps
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:             # the same node object: a loop
            return True
    return False                     # fast fell off the end

head = build([3, 2, 0, -4])
has_cycle(head)                      # -> False
head.next.next.next.next = head.next # the tail links back to node 1
has_cycle(head)                      # -> True
has_cycle(None)                      # -> False
\end{pyex}
Compare after the move. Both pointers start on the head, so a test before the first move is always true.
The meeting comes within $n$ steps, so the time is $O(n)$.

The general rule: when two walkers move on one cycle, reason about their relative speed.
A relative speed of 1 shrinks the gap by 1 per step, so the walkers meet within one lap.
A relative speed of 2 or more can jump over the slow walker. From some start positions, the walkers never meet.
For example, on a cycle of 4 nodes with a gap of 1, a relative speed of 2 gives the gaps 1, 3, 1, 3, and so on.
Keep the speeds 1 and 2.

Fast and slow pointers work on any sequence that applies one deterministic step to a finite set of states.
An example is the sequence of digit-square sums in Happy Number.

\subsubsection{An array as a linked list: the cycle entrance}
An array has $n + 1$ values in the range $1..n$, so one value repeats (Find the Duplicate Number).
The array is read-only, and the extra memory must be $O(1)$. Sorting and a set are not allowed.
Read the array as a linked list: index \cd{i} links to index \cd{nums[i]}. Every value is a valid index.
No value is 0, so nothing links to index 0, and the walk from index 0 starts outside any cycle.
A walk on a finite set of indexes must enter a cycle. The cycle entrance has two incoming links: one from the path and one from inside the cycle.
Two indexes that hold the same value make those two links, so the entrance is the duplicate value.
Memory hook: \emph{Index points to value: tortoise and hare from 0, then reset one to 0, walk together, and meet at the duplicate.}
\begin{pyex}
def find_duplicate(nums):
    slow, fast = nums[0], nums[nums[0]]   # both after their first move
    while slow != fast:              # phase 1: meet inside the cycle
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
    start = 0
    while start != slow:             # phase 2: meet at the cycle entrance
        start = nums[start]
        slow = nums[slow]
    return slow

find_duplicate([1, 3, 4, 2, 2])      # -> 2
find_duplicate([3, 1, 3, 4, 2])      # -> 3
find_duplicate([3, 3, 3, 3, 3])      # -> 3
\end{pyex}
Why phase 2 works: let $\mu$ be the path length before the cycle and $L$ the cycle length.
At the meeting, \cd{slow} walked $m$ steps and \cd{fast} walked $2m$ steps. Both stand on the same node.
The extra $m$ steps of \cd{fast} are whole laps of the cycle, so $m$ is a multiple of $L$.
After $\mu$ more steps, \cd{slow} has walked $\mu + m$ steps: the path, then whole laps. So it stands on the entrance.
A pointer from the start also reaches the entrance after $\mu$ steps. The two pointers meet there.
The same two phases find the start of the cycle in a real linked list.
The first meeting point is not the answer. Phase 2 is necessary.
\begin{note}
Other $O(1)$ memory route: binary search on the value. If more than \cd{mid} elements are \cd{<= mid}, the duplicate is
in \cd{1..mid}. This is $O(n \log n)$. A sum or XOR formula fails, because the duplicate can appear more than two times.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Fast lookup plus fast reorder: hash map and doubly linked list}
A cache needs \cd{get} and \cd{put} in $O(1)$ and an order by last use (LRU Cache).
When the cache is full, it evicts the least recently used key.
A dict gives lookup but no order. A Python list gives order, but a move from the middle is $O(n)$.
In Python, \cd{collections.OrderedDict} is a dict plus a doubly linked list. It keeps the oldest key first.
On every use, move the key to the end. On overflow, pop the first key.
Memory hook: \emph{Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import OrderedDict
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = OrderedDict()   # the oldest key first, the newest key last
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)  # a get is a use
        return self.cache[key]
    def put(self, key, value):
        self.cache[key] = value
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)  # a put is a use
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)   # drop the oldest key

lru = LRUCache(2)
lru.put(1, 1)
lru.put(2, 2)
lru.get(1)                           # -> 1
lru.put(3, 3)                        # evicts key 2
lru.get(2)                           # -> -1
lru.put(4, 4)                        # evicts key 1
(lru.get(1), lru.get(3), lru.get(4))   # -> (-1, 3, 4)
\end{pyex}
Build the structure by hand when \cd{OrderedDict} is not allowed, or when the task asks for the list itself.
The dict maps key to node. The doubly linked list keeps the nodes from least recent (left) to most recent (right).
Two sentinel nodes at the ends remove all checks for an empty list. Each node stores its key, so an eviction can delete its dict entry.
Hook for this form: \emph{map finds the node, list keeps the order; remove then insert at the right; evict \cd{left.next}.}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key, self.val = key, val    # the key lets an eviction clean the dict
        self.prev = self.next = None
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}          # key: node
        self.left, self.right = Node(), Node()     # sentinels: LRU end, MRU end
        self.left.next, self.right.prev = self.right, self.left
    def _remove(self, node):
        prev, nxt = node.prev, node.next
        prev.next, nxt.prev = nxt, prev
    def _insert(self, node):                       # just before the right sentinel
        prev, nxt = self.right.prev, self.right
        prev.next = nxt.prev = node
        node.prev, node.next = prev, nxt
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._insert(node)
        return node.val
    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])            # no old node stays in the list
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._insert(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            lru = self.left.next
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]

lru = LRUCache(2)
lru.put(1, 1)
lru.put(2, 2)
lru.get(1)                           # -> 1
lru.put(3, 3)
lru.put(1, 10)                       # an existing key: update, no eviction
(lru.get(2), lru.get(3), lru.get(1))   # -> (-1, 3, 10)
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
A plain dict also keeps insertion order, and \cd{next(iter(d))} gives the oldest key. But many deletions at the front
make that call slow in CPython. Use \cd{OrderedDict} or the hand-built list.
\end{note}
The general rule: when one structure gives only half of the required operations, combine two structures that point into each other.
Each item must carry enough data to find itself in the other structure.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Draw the target for a list of 5 or 6 nodes. Mark each link that changes.
  \item Is $O(n)$ extra memory allowed? If yes, copy the nodes into a Python list, write the new order with indexes,
        and relink. End the last node with \cd{None}.
  \item Can the head change? If yes, start with a dummy node and return \cd{dummy.next}.
  \item Which nodes do you need after a link change? Name them (\cd{nxt}, \cd{before}, \cd{after}, the tail) and save them first.
  \item Do you need a position? Use a 2-to-1 speed for the middle and a fixed gap for the $k$-th node from the end.
        To delete or insert, stop on the predecessor.
  \item Do you need to read part of the list backward? Reverse that part in place. Reverse it again if the caller needs the original.
  \item Are there several sorted inputs and one sorted output? Merge the fronts. Compare two fronts, or keep $k$ fronts in a min-heap.
  \item Can a link point to any node (random, child, graph edge)? Map old node to new node. Make all nodes first, link them second.
  \item Does one deterministic step repeat on a finite set? Expect a cycle. Use fast and slow pointers for $O(1)$ memory,
        a visited set otherwise.
  \item Must every operation be $O(1)$ by key in an order that changes? Combine a dict with a doubly linked list.
  \item Test the empty list, one node, two nodes, odd and even lengths, and a change of the head.
        Check the last node of the result: its link must be \cd{None}.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A lost rest of the list.} Save \cd{curr.next} before you overwrite it. After the change, nothing refers to the rest.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Tuple assignment order.} Python evaluates the right side first, then assigns the targets from left to right.
If \cd{curr} changes before \cd{curr.next} is assigned, the write goes to the wrong node. A temporary variable is safer.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head
def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reverse_ok(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next
    return prev
def reverse_bad(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        prev, curr, curr.next = curr, curr.next, prev   # curr moves first
    return prev

to_list(reverse_ok(build([1, 2, 3])))   # -> [3, 2, 1]
reverse_bad(build([1, 2, 3]))           # -> raises AttributeError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong return value.} Return \cd{prev} after a reversal, not \cd{head}: the old head is now the tail.
Return \cd{dummy.next}, not \cd{dummy} (an extra 0 node) and not the old \cd{head} (it can be removed or moved).
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A tail that does not move.} After \cd{tail.next = node}, also move \cd{tail}. Otherwise each link overwrites the same field.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A cycle in the output.} The last node of a rebuilt list keeps its old link. Set it to \cd{None}.
After a split at the middle, cut the front half. Without the cut, the result has a cycle.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A read of \cd{next} on \cd{None}.} Test \cd{fast and fast.next} before you move \cd{fast} two nodes.
Treat an ended input as 0 or as empty before you read \cd{.val}. In a block reversal, probe for $k$ nodes before you change a link.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Values instead of nodes.} Compare nodes with \cd{is}. Key a map by the node object. Equal values do not mean the same node.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion on a long list.} A recursive reversal or merge goes one call deep per node. Python stops near depth 1000.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def reverse_rec(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_rec(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

reverse_rec(build([1, 2, 3])).val          # -> 3
reverse_rec(build(list(range(5000))))      # -> raises RecursionError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Heap entries without a tie-breaker.} Push \cd{(val, i, node)}, not \cd{(val, node)}. Equal values make Python compare nodes, which raises \cd{TypeError}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Floyd details.} Move first, then compare. The first meeting point is not the cycle entrance: run phase 2,
with both pointers at one step. For an array walk, start at an index that nothing links to (index 0 when no value is 0).
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{LRU details.} A successful \cd{get} is a use. A \cd{put} on an existing key is a use and must not evict.
Store the key in each node. Test membership with \cd{in}, not with the truth value of a stored value, because 0 is a legal value.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Reverse Linked List & The core template: flip every link. & Save next, flip the arrow, step both, return prev. \\
Merge Two Sorted Lists & Build with a dummy and a tail; compare two fronts. & Dummy and tail. Take the smaller head, move the tail. Glue the rest. \\
Reorder List & Both ends at once: array of nodes (or middle, reverse, weave). & Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None. \\
Remove Nth Node From End of List & A position from the end; stop on the predecessor; dummy for the head. & Line up the nodes behind a dummy, then \cd{nodes[-n - 1]} skips its next. \\
Copy List with Random Pointer & Pointers go anywhere: two passes and a map keyed by node. & Make every copy first, then link copies through the old-to-new map. \\
Add Two Numbers & Build new nodes; column addition with a carry. & Add digits plus carry while anything is left; write mod 10, carry div 10. \\
Linked List Cycle & Fast and slow pointers; meet means loop. & Hare runs two, tortoise runs one. If they meet, it loops. If the hare falls off the end, it does not. \\
Find the Duplicate Number & Array as a list (\cd{i} links to \cd{nums[i]}); Floyd phase 2 finds the entrance. & Index points to value: tortoise and hare from 0, then reset one to 0, walk together, and meet at the duplicate. \\
LRU Cache & Dict plus doubly linked list (\cd{OrderedDict}). & Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow. \\
Merge k Sorted Lists & Many fronts: a min-heap with a tie-breaker. & Heap the fronts; pop the smallest, push its next. \\
Reverse Nodes in k-Group & Block surgery with four names; probe before you change. & Before, first, last, after: probe k, reverse with prev = after, link before to last, step to first. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
