\section{Trees}\label{tech:T08}

\subsection{The idea}
A binary tree is a recursive structure. A tree is empty, or it is a node with a left subtree and a right subtree.
So a question about a tree splits into the same question about each subtree.
Write a function that answers the question for one node.
Let it use the answers of the two children, or the facts that come down from the ancestors.
Each node then does $O(1)$ work, and one traversal costs $O(n)$.

The brute force repeats work at each node.
It scans the whole subtree again to get a height, or it walks the path from the root again to see the ancestors.
On a skewed tree (each node has at most one child, so the height is $n$), both cost $O(n^2)$.
The traversal removes this repeated work: each node reuses the answers of its children and the facts from its parent.

Information moves in one of three directions.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Down (top-down).} A parent gives each child a fact about the path above it:
        the depth, the largest value so far, the allowed value range.
        Pass the fact as an argument, or keep it in the stack entry with the node.
  \item \textbf{Up (bottom-up).} A child gives its parent a summary of its subtree: the height, the size, the best path down.
        Return the summary from the call. The parent combines the two summaries after both calls return (postorder).
  \item \textbf{Across (level order).} A queue visits the nodes one level at a time (BFS).
        Use it when the question is about depth, levels or rows.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Worked example.} Take the tree \cd{[3, 1, 4, 3, None, 1, 5]} (LeetCode level order):
\begin{pyshow}
        3
       / \
      1   4
     /   / \
    3   1   5
\end{pyshow}
A node is ``good'' when no value on the path above it is larger.
This is a fact about the ancestors, so pass the path maximum down.
The root gets no maximum and is good. It gives 3 to its children.
Node 1 gets 3, so it is not good. The leaf 3 below it gets 3, so it is good.
Node 4 gets 3, so it is good, and it gives 4 to its children. Leaf 1 is not good. Leaf 5 is good. The count is 4.

Now find the height. This is a fact about the subtree, so return it up.
Each leaf returns 1. Node 1 returns $1 + \max(1, 0) = 2$. Node 4 returns $1 + \max(1, 1) = 2$.
The root returns $1 + \max(2, 2) = 3$.

Some questions need a returned value and a separate answer.
The longest path between two nodes has one highest node, where the path bends.
A chain is a path that starts at a node and goes only down.
At the highest node, the path uses one chain from each child.
But the node can give only one chain to its parent, because a path cannot branch.
So the function returns the one-sided chain and records the two-sided path in an outer variable.
In the example tree, the root records $2 + 2 = 4$ edges (leaf 3 to leaf 5) and returns 3 to its (missing) parent.

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input is a root node, or data where each item has one parent: a file system, an org chart, nested expressions.
  \item The answer for a node comes from the answers of its children: height, size, sum, ``balanced'', the best chain.
        Use bottom-up DFS.
  \item The rule for a node uses all its ancestors: ``no ancestor is larger'', ``the path sum so far'', a value range.
        Use top-down DFS.
  \item The words ``path between any two nodes'' or ``may not pass through the root''.
        Return one value to the parent and record the answer at each node.
  \item The words ``level'', ``depth'', ``row'', ``view from the side'', ``minimum depth''. Use BFS by levels.
        The output is a list of lists (one list for each depth), or one value for each depth.
  \item The input is a binary search tree (BST) and the question is about order: the $k$th value, a successor,
        a range, the closest value, a split point. Compare with \cd{node.val} to discard one side,
        or read the in-order stream, which is sorted.
  \item Two trees go into one question (equal, mirror, contains). Recurse on pairs of nodes.
  \item The input is two traversals or a string, and the task is to rebuild the tree.
        One traversal names the root; null markers keep the shape.
  \item The tree has up to $10^4$ or $10^5$ nodes. Plan one $O(n)$ traversal.
        A scan of the subtree at each node is $O(n^2)$ on a skewed tree, which is too slow.
  \item The tree can be skewed, with a height of $10^4$ or more. The recursion depth then passes the CPython limit of 1000.
        Plan an explicit stack or BFS.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
All examples use the LeetCode node class. LeetCode defines it for you.
Build a small test tree with nested calls: \cd{T(2, T(1), T(3))} is the root 2 with the children 1 and 3.
For the empty child in the middle of a call, write \cd{None}: \cd{T(1, None, T(2))}.

\subsubsection{The three DFS orders}
A DFS visits each node one time. The order tells when a node does its own work, relative to its two subtrees.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Preorder} (node, left, right). Top-down work goes here: the node passes its state before it visits the children.
  \item \textbf{In-order} (left, node, right). In a BST, this order gives the values in ascending order.
  \item \textbf{Postorder} (left, right, node). Bottom-up work goes here: the node needs both child results first.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def orders(node, pre, ino, post):
    if node is None:
        return
    pre.append(node.val)                # before both subtrees
    orders(node.left, pre, ino, post)
    ino.append(node.val)                # between the subtrees
    orders(node.right, pre, ino, post)
    post.append(node.val)               # after both subtrees

pre, ino, post = [], [], []
orders(T(1, T(2, T(4)), T(3, T(5), T(6))), pre, ino, post)
pre, ino, post      # -> ([1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6], [4, 2, 1, 5, 3, 6], [4, 2, 5, 6, 3, 1])
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Bottom-up: return a summary of the subtree}
Write the contract first, in one sentence: ``\cd{f(node)} returns X for the subtree at \cd{node}''.
Then write the value for the empty tree. Then combine the two child values.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def height(node):                   # nodes on the longest downward path
    if node is None:
        return 0                    # the empty tree
    left = height(node.left)        # trust the contract for each child
    right = height(node.right)
    return 1 + max(left, right)     # combine after both calls return

def total(node):                    # sum of all values in the subtree
    if node is None:
        return 0
    return node.val + total(node.left) + total(node.right)

root = T(3, T(1, T(3)), T(4, T(1), T(5)))
height(root)                        # -> 3
total(root)                         # -> 17
height(None), height(T(7))          # -> (0, 1)
\end{pyex}
Invariant: when \cd{f(node)} returns, its value is correct for the whole subtree,
because both child values were correct. The empty case starts the induction.

\subsubsection{Top-down: pass the path state down}
Keep the state in each stack entry, next to its node. Each branch then has its own copy.
Compute the state of a child from the state of its parent in $O(1)$.
The example lists the sums of all root-to-leaf paths.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def leaf_sums(root):
    out = []
    stack = [(root, 0)]                     # (node, sum of the path above it)
    while stack:
        node, above = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        s = above + node.val                # the state for this node
        if node.left is None and node.right is None:
            out.append(s)                   # a leaf ends a path
        stack.append((node.left, s))        # each child gets its own copy
        stack.append((node.right, s))
    return sorted(out)

def leaf_sums_rec(node, above=0):           # recursive form: the state is an argument
    if node is None:
        return []
    s = above + node.val
    if node.left is None and node.right is None:
        return [s]
    return leaf_sums_rec(node.left, s) + leaf_sums_rec(node.right, s)

root = T(3, T(1, T(3)), T(4, T(1), T(5)))
leaf_sums(root)                             # -> [7, 8, 12]
leaf_sums_rec(root)                         # -> [7, 8, 12]
leaf_sums(None)                             # -> []
\end{pyex}
Invariant: each stack entry carries the exact state of the path from the root to the parent of its node.

\subsubsection{Level by level: BFS}
Keep the nodes of one whole level in a list. Read what you need from the level.
Then replace the list with the children of its nodes, left child first.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def levels(root):
    out = []
    level = [root] if root else []
    while level:
        out.append([node.val for node in level])   # use the whole level here
        next_level = []
        for node in level:
            if node.left:
                next_level.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                next_level.append(node.right)
        level = next_level                          # swap in the children
    return out

root = T(3, T(1, T(3)), T(4, T(1), T(5)))
levels(root)                                # -> [[3], [1, 4], [3, 1, 5]]
levels(None)                                # -> []
len(levels(root))                           # -> 3
\end{pyex}
Invariant: at the start of each loop, \cd{level} holds exactly the nodes of one depth, from left to right.
The number of loops is the height.

\subsubsection{Deep trees: no recursion}
CPython stops a recursion at a depth of about 1000. A skewed tree with 5000 nodes makes a recursive DFS raise
\cd{RecursionError}. LeetCode raises the limit, but a local run or another judge may not.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Top-down and BFS: the loops above use no recursion.
  \item Bottom-up: list the nodes with a stack so that each parent comes before its children.
        Then walk the list backward. Both children of a node are then done before the node.
        Keep the child results in a dict that starts as \cd{h = {None: 0}}, so an empty child has a value.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def height_rec(node):
    return 0 if node is None else 1 + max(height_rec(node.left), height_rec(node.right))

def parents_first(root):
    order, stack = [], [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node:
            order.append(node)
            stack.append(node.left)
            stack.append(node.right)
    return order

def height_iter(root):
    h = {None: 0}                                # the empty child has height 0
    for node in reversed(parents_first(root)):   # children before parents
        h[node] = 1 + max(h[node.left], h[node.right])
    return h[root]

skewed = None
for v in range(5000):
    skewed = TreeNode(v, skewed)                 # skewed to the left, 5000 levels deep
height_rec(skewed)                               # -> raises RecursionError
height_iter(skewed)                              # -> 5000
height_iter(None)                                # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)} also helps (Section~\ref{sec:recursion}).
The explicit stack is safe on all judges. The recursive form is shorter. Use it when the height is small.
\end{note}

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{The same rule at every node}
Apply one local change at each node and let the traversal reach all nodes.
The order of the visits does not matter, so recursion, a stack or a queue all work.
Invert Binary Tree swaps the two children of every node.
Memory hook: \emph{swap the two children, then invert each child.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def invert(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left   # one statement: both sides at once
    invert(root.left)
    invert(root.right)
    return root

def preorder(n):
    return [] if n is None else [n.val] + preorder(n.left) + preorder(n.right)

preorder(invert(T(4, T(2, T(1), T(3)), T(7, T(6), T(9)))))   # -> [4, 7, 9, 6, 2, 3, 1]
invert(None) is None                                         # -> True
\end{pyex}
Another problem of this shape: mirror an N-ary tree (reverse the list of children).
Symmetric Tree and Merge Two Binary Trees look similar, but they walk two trees in lockstep (see below).

\subsubsection{Bottom-up with a check at every node}
The rule must hold at every node, and each node needs a number from its subtrees.
A helper that scans the subtree again at each node costs $O(n^2)$ on a skewed tree.
Merge the helper and the check into one bottom-up pass.
Balanced Binary Tree compares the two child heights at each node.
The main solution uses the parents-first list from the core template.
Memory hook: \emph{list parents first, walk backward, compare child heights.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def is_balanced(root):
    order, stack = [], [root] if root else []
    while stack:                            # each parent before its children
        node = stack.pop()
        order.append(node)
        if node.left:
            stack.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            stack.append(node.right)
    height = {None: 0}
    for node in reversed(order):            # children before parents
        left, right = height[node.left], height[node.right]
        if abs(left - right) > 1:
            return False
        height[node] = 1 + max(left, right)
    return True

def height_or_fail(node):                   # recursive form: -1 means "not balanced"
    if node is None:
        return 0
    left = height_or_fail(node.left)
    if left == -1:
        return -1                           # pass the failure up at once
    right = height_or_fail(node.right)
    if right == -1 or abs(left - right) > 1:
        return -1
    return 1 + max(left, right)

ok = T(3, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7)))
bad = T(1, T(2, T(3, T(4), T(4)), T(3)), T(2))
is_balanced(ok), is_balanced(bad), is_balanced(None)   # -> (True, False, True)
height_or_fail(ok), height_or_fail(bad)                # -> (3, -1)
two_chains = T(1, T(2, T(3, T(4))), T(2, None, T(3, None, T(4))))
# the root sees heights 3 and 3; node 2 below it sees 2 and 0
is_balanced(two_chains)                                # -> False
\end{pyex}
The recursive form returns a value outside the valid range (\cd{-1}) as the failure signal.
It stops at the first failure and needs no dict. A tuple \cd{(ok, height)} also works.
Use the same shape when a rule at every node needs the size, the sum, the minimum or the maximum of the subtrees.

\subsubsection{Answer through the node, value up to the parent}
This split is the most important tree idea.
Every path between two nodes has one highest node. At that node the path is a left chain, the node and a right chain.
So enumerate the highest node:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Record} the two-sided path at the node in an outer best.
  \item \textbf{Return} only the one-sided chain, because the parent can extend only one side.
\end{itemize}
The brute force tries each node as the bend and computes its two chains from scratch: $O(n^2)$ on a skewed tree.
The bottom-up pass gets every chain from the child values, so the whole search is one $O(n)$ walk.
Diameter of Binary Tree counts edges: the candidate is \cd{left + right}, and the node stores \cd{1 + max(left, right)}.
Memory hook: \emph{parents first, then walk backward: add the two heights for best, store one plus the bigger height.}
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum adds values, which can be negative. Cut a negative child chain to 0: it is better to not take it.
Memory hook: \emph{list parents first, then walk back. At each node, cut negative sides to 0,
record left plus me plus right, and store me plus the better side.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def parents_first(root):
    order, stack = [], [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node:
            order.append(node)
            stack.append(node.left)
            stack.append(node.right)
    return order

def diameter(root):
    height, best = {None: 0}, 0
    for node in reversed(parents_first(root)):
        left, right = height[node.left], height[node.right]
        best = max(best, left + right)              # record: edges of the bend here
        height[node] = 1 + max(left, right)         # return: one side only
    return best

def max_path_sum(root):
    gain, best = {None: 0}, root.val                # a single node is a valid path
    for node in reversed(parents_first(root)):
        left = max(gain[node.left], 0)              # drop a negative branch
        right = max(gain[node.right], 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + left + right)   # record: left + me + right
        gain[node] = node.val + max(left, right)    # return: me + the better side
    return best

off_root = T(1, T(2, T(3, T(5)), T(4, None, T(6))))     # longest path avoids the root
diameter(off_root), diameter(T(1))                      # -> (4, 0)
max_path_sum(T(-10, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7))))          # -> 42
max_path_sum(T(-3)), max_path_sum(T(-2, T(-1)))         # -> (-3, -1)
\end{pyex}
Aside: the usual textbook solution is the recursive form of the same idea. It is shorter and has the same $O(n)$ time.
Use it when the height is small. The outer best needs \cd{nonlocal}.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def max_path_sum(root):
    best = root.val
    def gain(node):                         # best downward chain that starts at node
        nonlocal best                       # without it: UnboundLocalError
        if node is None:
            return 0
        left = max(gain(node.left), 0)
        right = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + left + right)
        return node.val + max(left, right)
    gain(root)
    return best

max_path_sum(T(-10, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7))))   # -> 42
max_path_sum(T(1, T(2), T(3)))                   # -> 6
\end{pyex}
Other problems of this shape: the diameter of an N-ary tree (add the two largest child chains),
and the longest path in a general tree.
The array version is Maximum Subarray: a tree path is two Kadane chains that meet at the highest node.

Moves along edges use the same split, with a sum in place of a maximum.
In Distribute Coins in Binary Tree (LeetCode 979), each node must end with one coin.
One move sends one coin along one edge. The balance of a subtree is its coins minus its nodes.
A surplus must leave the subtree and a deficit must come in, so exactly the absolute balance crosses the edge above it.
Return the balance to the parent, and add the absolute balance of each child to the total.
Memory hook: \emph{return coins minus nodes; each edge costs the absolute balance below it.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def distribute_coins(root):
    order, stack = [], [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node:
            order.append(node)
            stack.append(node.left)
            stack.append(node.right)
    balance, moves = {None: 0}, 0                     # balance = coins minus nodes
    for node in reversed(order):                      # children before parents
        left, right = balance[node.left], balance[node.right]
        moves += abs(left) + abs(right)               # record: coins that cross each child edge
        balance[node] = node.val - 1 + left + right   # return: the balance for the parent edge
    return moves

distribute_coins(T(3, T(0), T(0))), distribute_coins(T(0, T(3), T(0)))   # -> (2, 3)
distribute_coins(T(1, T(0, None, T(3)), T(0)))                           # -> 4
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Two trees in lockstep}
Walk two trees together, one pair of nodes at a time. Treat \cd{None} as a real value that must match \cd{None}.
Same Tree checks the empty pairs first, then the values, then the two child pairs.
Memory hook: \emph{both null is true, one null or different values is false, else check left pair and right pair.}
Subtree of Another Tree runs the same check from every node of the large tree.
It is pattern search: one loop lists the start positions, and one exact check runs at each start.
Memory hook: \emph{try every node as a start, and ask Same Tree at each one.
Both loops pop, skip the empty case, check, and push the children.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def same(p, q):                              # Same Tree, recursive
    if p is None and q is None:
        return True
    if p is None or q is None or p.val != q.val:
        return False
    return same(p.left, q.left) and same(p.right, q.right)

def same_iter(a, b):                         # the same check with a stack of pairs
    pairs = [(a, b)]
    while pairs:
        x, y = pairs.pop()
        if x is None and y is None:
            continue
        if x is None or y is None or x.val != y.val:
            return False
        pairs.append((x.left, y.left))
        pairs.append((x.right, y.right))
    return True

def is_subtree(root, sub):
    stack = [root]                           # every node of root is a possible start
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        if same_iter(node, sub):
            return True
        stack.append(node.left)
        stack.append(node.right)
    return False

same(T(1, T(2)), T(1, None, T(2)))                         # -> False
sub = T(4, T(1), T(2))
is_subtree(T(3, T(4, T(1), T(2)), T(5)), sub)              # -> True
is_subtree(T(3, T(4, T(1), T(2, T(0))), T(5)), sub)        # -> False
\end{pyex}
The check is $O(n \cdot m)$. Aside: for large trees, serialize both trees in preorder.
Write a null marker for each empty child and a delimiter before each value.
Then search for the small string in the large string with a linear matcher.
Other problems of this shape: Symmetric Tree (pair the left child of one side with the right child of the other),
Flip Equivalent Binary Trees (accept the straight or the swapped pairing), Merge Two Binary Trees.

\subsubsection{A path state from the ancestors}
The rule for a node uses all its ancestors. Reduce the path to a small summary, such as a maximum,
a minimum, a sum, a bitmask or a value range. Each parent computes the summary of its children in $O(1)$.
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree carries the largest value above each node.
Memory hook: \emph{carry the path max down; count a node when it is at least the max.}
Validate Binary Search Tree carries an open window \cd{(low, high)}. A left turn sets a new ceiling,
and a right turn sets a new floor. A check of each parent against its children is not enough.
Memory hook: \emph{every node lives in a window: going left lowers the ceiling, going right raises the floor.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def good_nodes(root):
    count = 0
    stack = [(root, root.val)]          # (node, biggest value above it on the path)
    while stack:
        node, path_max = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        if node.val >= path_max:
            count += 1
        path_max = max(path_max, node.val)
        stack.append((node.left, path_max))
        stack.append((node.right, path_max))
    return count

def is_bst(root):
    stack = [(root, float("-inf"), float("inf"))]
    while stack:
        node, low, high = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        if not (low < node.val < high):
            return False
        stack.append((node.left, low, node.val))    # left side: new ceiling
        stack.append((node.right, node.val, high))  # right side: new floor
    return True

good_nodes(T(3, T(1, T(3)), T(4, T(1), T(5))))   # -> 4
good_nodes(T(3, T(3, T(4), T(2))))               # -> 3
is_bst(T(2, T(1), T(3)))                         # -> True
is_bst(T(5, T(4), T(6, T(3), T(7))))             # -> False
is_bst(T(2, T(2)))                               # -> False
\end{pyex}
In the second BST test, 3 is a correct left child of 6, but it is in the right subtree of 5.
Other problems of this shape: Path Sum (carry the remaining sum), Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
(carry the number so far), Pseudo-Palindromic Paths (carry a parity bitmask).

\subsubsection{One answer per level}
Use the BFS level loop of the core template and reduce each level to what the question asks for.
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal keeps the whole level. This is the core template.
Memory hook: \emph{take the whole level, save its values, swap in its children.}
Maximum Depth of Binary Tree counts the levels.
Memory hook: \emph{depth is 1 plus the deeper child; for a very deep tree, count the BFS levels instead.}
The short recursive form \cd{1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))} is the base shape of most bottom-up problems.
Binary Tree Right Side View keeps the last node of each level.
Following only the right pointers fails when the left subtree is deeper.
Memory hook: \emph{level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one you see.}
The example uses the second common form of BFS: one deque, and a loop over the level size, read one time.
Read the answer for a level before the inner loop removes its nodes.
At that moment \cd{queue[-1]} is the rightmost node and \cd{queue[0]} is the leftmost node, so you need no extra variable.
Use the same read for any first or last value of each level.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def max_depth(root):
    depth, level = 0, [root] if root else []
    while level:
        depth += 1
        level = [c for n in level for c in (n.left, n.right) if c]
    return depth

def right_side_view(root):
    if root is None:
        return []
    view, queue = [], deque([root])
    while queue:
        view.append(queue[-1].val)          # the queue holds one level, left to right
        for _ in range(len(queue)):         # the range reads the size one time
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
    return view

max_depth(T(3, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7)))), max_depth(None)   # -> (3, 0)
right_side_view(T(1, T(2, None, T(5)), T(3, None, T(4))))    # -> [1, 3, 4]
right_side_view(T(1, T(2)))                                  # -> [1, 2]
\end{pyex}
A DFS can also give one value per depth. Carry the depth, visit the right child first,
and append a value when \cd{depth == len(view)}. The first node at each new depth is the rightmost one.
Other problems of this shape: Zigzag Level Order (reverse every other level), Average of Levels,
Largest Value in Each Row, Minimum Depth (stop at the first leaf).

\subsubsection{BST: compare and go one way}
In a BST, one comparison with \cd{node.val} tells which subtree holds a value.
So a search follows one path and costs $O(h)$, not $O(n)$.
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree walks down while both targets are on the same side.
The first node where they split (or where one target sits) is the answer.
Memory hook: \emph{both smaller go left, both bigger go right, else this node is the split.}
The example takes the two target values. LeetCode passes two nodes, so compare \cd{p.val} and \cd{q.val}.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def lca_bst(root, p, q):                # p and q are values that exist in the tree
    node = root
    while node:
        if p < node.val and q < node.val:
            node = node.left            # both targets are in the left subtree
        elif p > node.val and q > node.val:
            node = node.right           # both targets are in the right subtree
        else:
            return node                 # they split here, or one target is here
    return None

bst = T(6, T(2, T(0), T(4, T(3), T(5))), T(8, T(7), T(9)))
lca_bst(bst, 2, 8).val, lca_bst(bst, 2, 4).val, lca_bst(bst, 5, 3).val   # -> (6, 2, 4)
\end{pyex}
Use strict \cd{<} and \cd{>} to move. A node is its own ancestor, so an equal value stops the walk.
The same descent finds a value, an insert position, a floor, a ceiling or the closest value.
In a tree without order, this descent does not work, because one comparison does not tell the side.

\subsubsection{BST: the in-order stream is sorted}
An in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a BST gives the values in ascending order.
Read the BST as a sorted list, one value at a time, and stop early.
A sort of all values costs $O(n \log n)$. The stack walk stops after $k$ values, so it costs $O(h + k)$.
Kth Smallest Element in a BST pops $k$ values from an iterative in-order walk.
The left spine of a node is the node, its left child, the left child of that child, and so on.
The smallest value of a subtree is at the bottom of its left spine.
Memory hook: \emph{push the left spine; pop, count, push the right child's left spine.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack = []
    def push_left(node):
        while node:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
    push_left(root)                     # the top of the stack is the smallest value
    while True:
        node = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return node.val
        push_left(node.right)           # the next smallest value is now on top

def inorder(root):                      # the same walk as a generator: a sorted stream
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        yield node.val
        node = node.right

bst = T(5, T(3, T(2, T(1)), T(4)), T(6))
kth_smallest(bst, 3), kth_smallest(bst, 1)       # -> (3, 1)
list(inorder(bst))                               # -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
vals = list(inorder(T(5, T(4), T(6, T(3), T(7)))))
all(a < b for a, b in zip(vals, vals[1:]))       # -> False
\end{pyex}
The last two lines are a second way to validate a BST: the in-order stream must be strictly increasing.
For the $k$th largest, walk in reverse in-order (right, node, left).
Other problems of this shape: Binary Search Tree Iterator,
Two Sum IV (a forward and a backward iterator as two pointers).

\subsubsection{Build a tree from two traversals}
One traversal names the root: preorder starts with the root, and postorder ends with it.
In-order splits the other values: the values before the root form the left subtree.
Every subtree is a contiguous block in preorder, in-order and postorder (not in level order), so recurse on the blocks.
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal slices both lists and keeps a stack of jobs.
Memory hook: \emph{preorder names the root. In-order splits at the root. Slice both lists and push each side as a job.}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def build(preorder, inorder):
    root = TreeNode(preorder[0])
    stack = [(root, preorder, inorder)]     # job: node, preorder and in-order of its subtree
    while stack:
        node, pre, ino = stack.pop()
        mid = ino.index(node.val)           # the size of the left subtree
        left_pre, left_ino = pre[1:mid + 1], ino[:mid]
        right_pre, right_ino = pre[mid + 1:], ino[mid + 1:]
        if left_pre:
            node.left = TreeNode(left_pre[0])
            stack.append((node.left, left_pre, left_ino))
        if right_pre:
            node.right = TreeNode(right_pre[0])
            stack.append((node.right, right_pre, right_ino))
    return root

def pre(n):
    return [] if n is None else [n.val] + pre(n.left) + pre(n.right)
def ino(n):
    return [] if n is None else ino(n.left) + [n.val] + ino(n.right)

root = build([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
root.val, root.left.val, root.right.val, root.right.left.val   # -> (3, 9, 20, 15)
pre(root), ino(root)            # -> ([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
\end{pyex}
The slices and \cd{index} make this $O(n^2)$ on a skewed tree. Aside: the optimal form is $O(n)$ with two changes.
Look up the root position in a dict from value to in-order index.
Pass in-order bounds \cd{(lo, hi)} instead of lists, and read the roots with one shared preorder pointer.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def build(preorder, inorder):
    pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    roots = iter(preorder)                  # one shared cursor into preorder
    def make(lo, hi):                       # the subtree that holds inorder[lo..hi]
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        node = TreeNode(next(roots))
        mid = pos[node.val]
        node.left = make(lo, mid - 1)       # left first: preorder lists it first
        node.right = make(mid + 1, hi)
        return node
    return make(0, len(inorder) - 1)

def pre(n):
    return [] if n is None else [n.val] + pre(n.left) + pre(n.right)
root = build([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
pre(root), root.right.right.val             # -> ([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], 7)
\end{pyex}
The shared cursor works only because the code builds the left subtree before the right subtree.
That is the order in which preorder lists the nodes.
The dict and the in-order split need unique values.
The general rule: when a stream lists a recursive structure in the same order as your recursion visits it,
read the stream with one shared cursor. You then compute no offsets.
The preorder decoder for serialization (next variation) uses the same rule.

\subsubsection{Serialize with null markers}
A list of values loses the shape. The root 1 with the left child 2 gives the values 1, 2.
The root 1 with the right child 2 gives the same values.
Write a marker \cd{N} for every empty child. Then one preorder, postorder or level-order traversal fully defines the tree.
The decoder reads the tokens in the same order as the encoder wrote them.
In-order with markers is not enough: \cd{T(1, T(2))} and \cd{T(2, None, T(1))} both give \cd{N,2,N,1,N}.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree uses level order, like the LeetCode list format.
Memory hook: \emph{write it level by level like the example list, with N for every null;
each real node in the queue takes the next two tokens as its children.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def serialize(root):
    out, queue = [], deque([root])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node is None:
            out.append("N")                 # the null marker keeps the shape
            continue
        out.append(str(node.val))
        queue.append(node.left)             # the queue holds None children too
        queue.append(node.right)
    return ",".join(out)

def deserialize(data):
    tokens = iter(data.split(","))
    def make(tok):
        return None if tok == "N" else TreeNode(int(tok))
    root = make(next(tokens))
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node is None:
            continue                        # a null has no children to read
        node.left = make(next(tokens, "N")) # the next two tokens are its children
        node.right = make(next(tokens, "N"))
        queue.append(node.left)
        queue.append(node.right)
    return root

s = serialize(T(1, T(2), T(3, T(4), T(5))))
s                                           # -> '1,2,3,N,N,4,5,N,N,N,N'
serialize(deserialize(s)) == s              # -> True
serialize(None), deserialize("N") is None   # -> ('N', True)
serialize(deserialize("-1,N,20"))           # -> '-1,N,20,N,N'

def inorder_marks(n):                       # in-order with markers: not reversible
    if n is None:
        return "N"
    return inorder_marks(n.left) + "," + str(n.val) + "," + inorder_marks(n.right)
inorder_marks(T(1, T(2))), inorder_marks(T(2, None, T(1)))   # -> ('N,2,N,1,N', 'N,2,N,1,N')
\end{pyex}
The default \cd{"N"} in \cd{next(tokens, "N")} also reads a LeetCode list, which drops the trailing nulls
(write \cd{N} for \cd{null}). So \cd{deserialize} is a good helper to build test trees.
Join the tokens with a delimiter and split on it, so negative and multi-digit values stay whole.
Aside: the usual textbook solution writes preorder with null markers. It decodes with the grammar
\emph{tree = N, or a value, a left tree and a right tree}, and reads the tokens with one shared iterator.
Part I (``Share one iterator between recursive calls'') shows that decoder.
The grammar form is the base for problems that check or reuse a preorder encoding.
Other problems of this shape: the N-ary version (write the child count after each value), Encode and Decode Strings (length prefixes),
Find Duplicate Subtrees (the serialized subtree is a dict key).

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Write the brute force in one sentence. Find the work that it repeats at each node.
  \item Does the answer for a node need its ancestors (down), its subtree (up), or its level (across)?
  \item Write the contract in one sentence: ``\cd{f(node)} returns \ldots{} for the subtree'',
        or ``each stack entry carries \ldots{} of the path above''.
  \item Write the empty case first. Decide what \cd{None} gives: 0, \cd{True}, \cd{float("-inf")} or a sentinel.
  \item Does the parent need two facts from each child? Return a tuple, for example \cd{(ok, height)},
        or use a sentinel such as \cd{-1} for ``failed''.
  \item Is the answer always at the root, or can it be at any node?
        If at any node, record a best at each node and return only the part that the parent can extend.
  \item Can a part of the answer make it worse (negative values)? Clamp that part at 0.
  \item Is the tree a BST? Compare with \cd{node.val} to go one way, or read the sorted in-order stream.
  \item Do two structures move together? Recurse on pairs, and handle the \cd{None} pairs first.
  \item Can the height reach $n$ with $n > 1000$? Use a stack with state, BFS, or the parents-first list.
  \item Test the empty tree, one node, a tree skewed to the left, a tree skewed to the right,
        negative values and equal values.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Return and record are two different values.}
Do not return the two-sided value (\cd{left + right} or \cd{node.val + left + right}) to the parent.
A path cannot branch, so return \cd{1 + max(left, right)} or \cd{node.val + max(left, right)}.
Also, the answer at the root only is wrong when the best path avoids the root.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The start value of a best.}
When the values can be negative and the answer is not empty, start the best at \cd{root.val} or \cd{float("-inf")}, not 0.
Clamp only the child chains at 0. The node itself is always on its own path.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A node, not a value.}
Test \cd{node is None}. A node with the value 0 is still a node.
Read \cd{node.val} only after the \cd{None} test.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{All ancestors, not only the parent.}
A BST rule compares a node with every ancestor. A check of each node against its two children accepts
\cd{[5, 4, 6, None, None, 3, 7]}. Pass the window \cd{(low, high)} down, use strict comparisons,
and start with infinite bounds, not with the smallest or largest integer of the input range.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right
T = TreeNode

def local_check(n):                     # wrong: compares only with the children
    if n is None:
        return True
    if n.left and not n.left.val < n.val:
        return False
    if n.right and not n.val < n.right.val:
        return False
    return local_check(n.left) and local_check(n.right)

def window_check(n, low=float("-inf"), high=float("inf")):
    if n is None:
        return True
    if not (low < n.val < high):
        return False
    return window_check(n.left, low, n.val) and window_check(n.right, n.val, high)

t = T(5, T(4), T(6, T(3), T(7)))
local_check(t), window_check(t)        # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{State that two branches share.}
In a top-down walk, one global ``path maximum'' is wrong after the walk returns from a branch.
Keep the state in the argument or in the stack entry.
In a recursive walk, a nested function that assigns to an outer counter needs \cd{nonlocal}.
Without it, Python raises \cd{UnboundLocalError}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def count_wrong(values):
    count = 0
    def visit(i):
        if i < len(values):
            count += 1                  # assignment makes count a local name
            visit(2 * i + 1)
    visit(0)
    return count

def count_right(values):
    count = 0
    def visit(i):
        nonlocal count
        if i < len(values):
            count += 1
            visit(2 * i + 1)
    visit(0)
    return count

count_wrong([1, 2, 3, 4])               # -> raises UnboundLocalError
count_right([1, 2, 3, 4])               # -> 3
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The level size and the queue.}
Read the level size one time before the inner loop: \cd{for _ in range(len(queue))}.
A \cd{while} loop that reads \cd{len(queue)} again also takes the children of this level.
Do not use \cd{list.pop(0)} as a queue: each pop is $O(n)$.
Push the left child before the right child, or the order inside a level breaks.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Nodes or edges.}
Height in nodes gives \cd{height(None) = 0}, and \cd{left + right} is then an edge count.
Height in edges needs \cd{height(None) = -1}. Then \cd{-1} cannot be a failure sentinel.
A single node has depth 1 and diameter 0.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Two assignments for a swap.}
\cd{root.left = root.right} followed by \cd{root.right = root.left} loses the old left child.
Swap in one statement: \cd{root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion depth.}
A skewed tree with $n$ nodes makes a recursion $n$ calls deep. CPython stops at about 1000.
For $n$ up to $10^4$ or $10^5$, use an explicit stack, BFS, or the parents-first list.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Encodings that lose information.}
Values alone lose the shape. Write a null marker for each empty child.
Put a delimiter between tokens, or \cd{"-1"} splits into two characters.
For a substring search, put the delimiter before every token, or \cd{"2,N,N"} matches inside \cd{"12,N,N"}.
The rebuild from preorder plus in-order needs unique values.
With repeats, \cd{T(1, T(1))} and \cd{T(1, None, T(1))} give the same two lists.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Invert Binary Tree & The same local rule (swap the children) at every node; any order of visits. &
  Swap the two children, then invert each child. \\
Maximum Depth of Binary Tree & The bottom-up height template itself; BFS counts the levels with no recursion. &
  Depth is 1 plus the deeper child; for a very deep tree, count the BFS levels instead. \\
Diameter of Binary Tree & Record \cd{left + right} at each node; return \cd{1 + max(left, right)}. &
  Parents first, then walk backward: add the two heights for best, store one plus the bigger height. \\
Balanced Binary Tree & Bottom-up heights from the parents-first list; compare the two child heights at every node. Aside: the recursive form returns \cd{-1} on failure. &
  List parents first, walk backward, compare child heights. \\
Same Tree & Two trees in lockstep; the \cd{None} pairs first. &
  Both null is true, one null or different values is false, else check left pair and right pair. \\
Subtree of Another Tree & Same Tree from every node of the large tree. &
  Try every node as a start, and ask Same Tree at each one. Both loops pop, skip the empty case, check, and push the children. \\
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree & One guided descent in a BST; stop where the targets split. &
  Both smaller go left, both bigger go right, else this node is the split. \\
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal & BFS; keep the whole level. &
  Take the whole level, save its values, swap in its children. \\
Binary Tree Right Side View & BFS; keep the last node of each level. &
  Level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one you see. \\
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree & Top-down; carry the path maximum. &
  Carry the path max down; count a node when it is at least the max. \\
Validate Binary Search Tree & Top-down; carry an open window \cd{(low, high)}. &
  Every node lives in a window: going left lowers the ceiling, going right raises the floor. \\
Kth Smallest Element in a BST & Iterative in-order is a sorted stream; stop after $k$ values. &
  Push the left spine; pop, count, push the right child's left spine. \\
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal & Preorder gives the root; in-order splits the rest. &
  Preorder names the root. In-order splits at the root. Slice both lists and push each side as a job. \\
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum & Record \cd{left + me + right}; return \cd{me + max(left, right)}; clamp at 0. &
  List parents first, then walk back. At each node, cut negative sides to 0, record left plus me plus right, and store me plus the better side. \\
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree & Level order with a marker for each null child. &
  Level by level with N for every null; each real node takes the next two tokens as its children. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Tries}\label{tech:T09}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
Many stored words share their first letters. A trie (prefix tree) stores each shared beginning one time only.
Each edge holds one letter. Each node stands for one prefix: the letters on the path from the root to that node.
The root stands for the empty string.
A flag on a node tells whether its prefix is also a whole stored word.

\textbf{Worked example.} Insert \cd{car}, \cd{cat}, \cd{cart} and \cd{dog}.
The root gets two children, \cd{c} and \cd{d}.
Three words start with \cd{ca}, but the path c-a exists one time.
Below \cd{ca}, the path splits into \cd{r} and \cd{t}.
The four nodes where a word ends carry the end flag.
\begin{pyshow}
(root)
 +-- c
 |   +-- a
 |       +-- r  *        * = end flag (car)
 |       |   +-- t  *    (cart)
 |       +-- t  *        (cat)
 +-- d
     +-- o
         +-- g  *        (dog)
\end{pyshow}
Now ask about \cd{ca}. The walk takes two steps and reaches a node, so some stored word starts with \cd{ca}.
That node has no end flag, so \cd{ca} itself is not a stored word.
Ask about \cd{cab}. The walk takes two steps, and then stops: the node for \cd{ca} has no child \cd{b}.
The number of stored words does not change the cost of the walk.

\textbf{What a trie saves.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Brute force compares the query with every stored word: $O(N \cdot L)$ for each query.
  \item A hash set of every prefix answers a prefix query in $O(L)$.
        But each insert builds $L$ prefix strings, so it copies $O(L^2)$ characters.
  \item A trie does each insert and each query in $O(L)$ steps.
        It has at most one node for each stored letter, and shared beginnings cost nothing extra.
\end{itemize}
The larger gain appears when a search branches.
A wildcard letter or the neighbors of a grid cell give several next letters at one position.
At each step, the search must ask: ``is this string still the start of some target word?''
The current trie node answers this in $O(1)$: the next letter is a child, or it is not.
A missing child stops the branch at once. This pruning is the main reason to use a trie.

\textbf{Trie or set.} A trie is not always the best tool. Use this table to choose.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{8.2cm}L{8.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
The task needs & Use \\
\midrule
Exact lookups only & A hash set. \\
Prefix queries, with inserts and queries mixed & A trie. \\
Prefix queries on a list that does not change & Sort the list and use \cd{bisect}, or a trie. \\
Wildcard queries with few wildcards (1 or 2) & A set of masked patterns (one letter replaced by a dot). Fill a second dot with each letter. \\
Many wildcards, or a search that grows a string (grid, stream) & A trie and a DFS that walks it. \\
All stored words below a prefix (autocomplete) & A trie, or a sorted list and \cd{bisect}. \\
The shortest or longest stored prefix of a query & A trie walk that watches the end flags. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
A sorted list answers a static prefix query with one binary search.
All words with prefix $p$ are next to each other, and the first one is at \cd{bisect_left(words, p)}.
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left
words = sorted(["mouse", "mobile", "moneypot", "monitor", "mousepad"])
def has_prefix(p):
    i = bisect_left(words, p)          # the first word that is >= p
    return i < len(words) and words[i].startswith(p)
has_prefix("mou"), has_prefix("mox")   # -> (True, False)
i = bisect_left(words, "mon")
words[i:i + 2]                         # -> ['moneypot', 'monitor']
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input has many strings (a dictionary, a word list), and the queries ask about prefixes:
        ``starts with'', autocomplete, ``shortest root'', ``common prefix''.
  \item Inserts and queries interleave, so one sort at the start does not work.
  \item A query contains a wildcard that matches any one letter. One query then stands for many strings.
        A small bound on the wildcards (``at most 2 dots'') also allows a set of masked patterns.
  \item A search builds a string one letter at a time: a path in a grid, a stream of letters, a split of a string.
        At each step, the search must test many target words.
  \item Many patterns must be found in one search space.
        You know the search for one pattern, but a repeat of it for each pattern is too slow.
  \item The output is a subset of a given word list: ``return all words that appear on the board''.
  \item The sizes: $10^4$ or more stored words, and $10^4$ or more calls. Each word is short, often 10 to 30 letters.
        Each call must then cost $O(L)$ for its string, not $O(N \cdot L)$ for all stored strings.
  \item The keys are sequences of small parts: lowercase letters, digits, the bits of an integer, the parts of a file path.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Give each node a dict of children and an end flag.
Write one helper that walks a string down from the root. Then \cd{search} and \cd{startsWith} differ only in the last check.
\begin{pyex}
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}      # letter to TrieNode
        self.is_end = False     # True if a whole word ends here

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.is_end = True      # flag the last node only

    def _walk(self, s):         # the node for prefix s, or None
        node = self.root
        for ch in s:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def search(self, word):     # is word a whole stored word?
        node = self._walk(word)
        return node is not None and node.is_end

    def startsWith(self, prefix):   # does a stored word start with prefix?
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None

t = Trie()
t.insert("apple")
t.search("apple"), t.search("app"), t.startsWith("app")   # -> (True, False, True)
t.insert("app")
t.search("app")                                           # -> True
t.startsWith("apple"), t.startsWith("b")                  # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} A node other than the root exists if and only if its string is a prefix of an inserted word.
\cd{is_end} is \cd{True} if and only if its string was inserted as a whole word.
Each operation costs $O(L)$ for a string of length $L$. The memory is $O(\text{total letters inserted})$.

\begin{note}
The judge uses the method names of the statement, often in camelCase: \cd{startsWith}, \cd{addWord}.
A snake\_case name fails the judge.
\end{note}

A shorter form uses nested dicts. Each node is a dict, and a special key marks the end of a word.
The end key must never be a letter of the alphabet.
Write this form fast when the trie is only a helper inside a larger solution.
\begin{pyex}
END = "$"                       # a key that is never a letter

def insert(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        node = node.setdefault(ch, {})   # create the child only on insert
    node[END] = True

def find(root, s):              # the node for prefix s, or None
    node = root
    for ch in s:
        if ch not in node:
            return None
        node = node[ch]
    return node

root = {}
for w in ["car", "cat", "cart", "dog"]:
    insert(root, w)
END in find(root, "car"), END in find(root, "ca")   # -> (True, False)
find(root, "cab") is None                           # -> True
sorted(find(root, "ca"))                            # -> ['r', 't']
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Whole word or prefix}
This is the core template (Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)).
A path can exist only because a longer word passes through it.
So \cd{search} returns the end flag of the last node, and \cd{startsWith} returns ``the walk reached a node''.
A word counts as a prefix of itself. A second insert of the same word walks the same nodes and changes nothing.
Memory hook: \emph{One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end.}

\subsubsection{Store data on the nodes}
Put more data on each node. The same walk then answers richer questions.
\begin{itemize}
  \item A pass count (the number of words that go through the node) answers ``how many words start with $p$''.
        An end count answers ``how many copies of $w$ are stored''. An erase decrements the counts along the path.
  \item The whole word at its end node gives the answer at once. You do not rebuild the path string.
  \item A best value below the node (a sum, a minimum, the 3 smallest words) answers a query in one walk.
        Update the value at each node on the path during the insert.
  \item The sum of the pass counts on the query walk (without the root) answers more than one prefix at a time.
        It adds up, for each prefix of the query, the number of stored words with that prefix
        (Sum of Prefix Scores of Strings, LeetCode 2416).
\end{itemize}
Memory hook: \emph{Update every node on the insert path; read the last node of the query walk, or add up all its nodes.}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.pass_count = 0     # words that go through this node
        self.end_count = 0      # words that end at this node

class CountTrie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = Node()

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        node.pass_count += 1
        for ch in word:
            node = node.children.setdefault(ch, Node())
            node.pass_count += 1
        node.end_count += 1

    def _walk(self, s):
        node = self.root
        for ch in s:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def count_prefix(self, p):
        node = self._walk(p)
        return node.pass_count if node else 0

    def count_equal(self, w):
        node = self._walk(w)
        return node.end_count if node else 0

    def prefix_score(self, w):  # add up count_prefix over every prefix of w
        node, total = self.root, 0
        for ch in w:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                break
            total += node.pass_count
        return total

    def erase(self, word):      # word must be stored
        node = self.root
        node.pass_count -= 1
        for ch in word:
            child = node.children[ch]
            child.pass_count -= 1
            if child.pass_count == 0:
                del node.children[ch]   # no word is left below: cut the branch
                return
            node = child
        node.end_count -= 1

t = CountTrie()
for w in ["apple", "apple", "app"]:
    t.insert(w)
t.count_equal("apple"), t.count_prefix("app")    # -> (2, 3)
t.erase("apple")
t.count_equal("apple"), t.count_prefix("app")    # -> (1, 2)
t.erase("apple")
t.count_prefix("appl"), t.count_equal("app")     # -> (0, 1)
t._walk("app").children                          # -> {}
s = CountTrie()
for w in ["abc", "ab", "bc", "b"]:
    s.insert(w)
[s.prefix_score(w) for w in ["abc", "ab", "bc", "b"]]   # -> [5, 4, 3, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Shortest stored prefix and autocomplete}
Two more walks come up often.
The first walk follows a query word and stops at the first end flag.
It gives the shortest stored prefix of the word (Replace Words). For the longest one, keep the last end flag.
The second walk goes down to the node of a prefix. Then a DFS visits the children in sorted order.
It lists all words with that prefix in lexicographic order (autocomplete).
Memory hook: \emph{Stop at the first flag; list below the prefix node in sorted order.}
\begin{pyex}
def build(words):
    root = {}
    for w in words:
        node = root
        for ch in w:
            node = node.setdefault(ch, {})
        node["$"] = w           # store the whole word at its end node
    return root

def shortest_root(root, word):  # the shortest stored prefix of word, else word
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in node:
            break
        node = node[ch]
        if "$" in node:
            return node["$"]
    return word

def words_below(node, out):     # all words at or below node, sorted
    if "$" in node:
        out.append(node["$"])   # a word comes before its extensions
    for ch in sorted(k for k in node if k != "$"):
        words_below(node[ch], out)
    return out

roots = build(["cat", "bat", "rat", "ca"])
[shortest_root(roots, w) for w in "the cattle was rattled".split()]
# -> ['the', 'ca', 'was', 'rat']
shop = build(["mouse", "mobile", "moneypot", "monitor", "mousepad"])
words_below(shop["m"]["o"]["u"], [])     # -> ['mouse', 'mousepad']
words_below(shop, [])[:3]                # -> ['mobile', 'moneypot', 'monitor']
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Wildcard search by branching}
A query can contain a wildcard: a dot that matches any one letter (Design Add and Search Words Data Structure).
The query and the stored word must then have the same length.
The statement often bounds the number of dots, for example at most 2 for each query.
Inserts and queries interleave, so the structure must grow one word at a time.

\textbf{Intuitive solution: a set of masked patterns.}
When the number of dots is small, move the work to the insert.
Store each word, and each copy of it with one letter replaced by a dot.
A query with at most one dot is then one set lookup.
A query with two dots fills its first dot with each of the 26 letters and searches again.
An insert costs $O(L^2)$. A query with $k \ge 1$ dots costs $26^{k-1}$ set lookups.
Memory hook: \emph{Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search.}
\begin{pyex}
class WordDictionary:
    def __init__(self):
        self.patterns = set()   # each word, and each copy with one letter masked

    def addWord(self, word):
        self.patterns.add(word)
        for i in range(len(word)):
            self.patterns.add(word[:i] + "." + word[i + 1:])

    def search(self, word):
        if word.count(".") <= 1:
            return word in self.patterns
        i = word.index(".")     # fill the first dot, then search again
        return any(self.search(word[:i] + letter + word[i + 1:])
                   for letter in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")

d = WordDictionary()
for w in ["bad", "dad", "mad"]:
    d.addWord(w)
d.search("pad"), d.search("bad"), d.search(".ad"), d.search("b..")   # -> (False, True, True, True)
d.search("..."), d.search("ba"), d.search("....")                   # -> (True, False, False)
\end{pyex}

\textbf{General solution: DFS over the trie.}
A letter in the query follows one edge. A dot follows every edge at that depth.
The search succeeds if one branch succeeds.
At the end of the query, the walk succeeds only if the node has the end flag.
The state is \cd{dfs(i, node)}: \cd{node} matches \cd{word[:i]}, and the call matches the rest.
For example, with \cd{bad} and \cd{dad} stored, the query \cd{.ad} tries the children \cd{b} and \cd{d} of the root.
The branch through \cd{b} reaches the end flag of \cd{bad}, so the search returns \cd{True}.
Memory hook: \emph{A letter follows one edge; a dot follows every edge.}
\begin{pyex}
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False

class WordDictionary:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def addWord(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.is_end = True

    def search(self, word):
        def dfs(i, node):               # node matches word[:i]
            if i == len(word):
                return node.is_end
            ch = word[i]
            if ch == ".":               # branch: try every child
                return any(dfs(i + 1, child) for child in node.children.values())
            child = node.children.get(ch)
            return child is not None and dfs(i + 1, child)
        return dfs(0, self.root)

d = WordDictionary()
for w in ["bad", "dad", "mad"]:
    d.addWord(w)
d.search("pad"), d.search("bad"), d.search(".ad"), d.search("b..")   # -> (False, True, True, True)
d.search("..."), d.search("ba"), d.search("....")                   # -> (True, False, False)
\end{pyex}
Use the trie form when the statement asks for a trie, when you also need prefix queries,
or when a query can have many dots. A trie search never visits more nodes than the trie has.
In CPython the trie does not save memory here, because each node is an object with its own dict.
\begin{note}
The bound ``at most 2 dots'' does not make the trie search fast in the worst case.
A crafted input with all 676 two-letter prefixes and two leading dots keeps 676 branches alive to the last letter.
\end{note}
The same walk handles other branching rules.
A query position can allow a set of letters: follow each child in the set.
A query can allow a budget of mismatches: carry the budget in the state, and spend it on a child with a different letter.

\subsubsection{Trie plus grid backtracking}
The task: find every word of a long list that a path on a letter grid spells (Word Search II).
A path moves up, down, left or right, and it uses each cell at most one time in one word.
One grid DFS for each word repeats the same work for shared prefixes, and $3 \cdot 10^4$ words make it too slow.
Start from the one-word solution: a DFS from each cell that marks the cell and unmarks it on return.
Then replace ``compare with \cd{word[i]}'' by ``step to the trie child''.
One DFS now tests all words at the same time, and a missing child ends the path.
For example, with the words \cd{oath} and \cd{oat}, the path o-a-t reaches the end node of \cd{oat}.
The DFS records \cd{oat} and continues, because the node still has the child \cd{h}.
Two tricks keep the search fast.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Store the whole word at its end node. When the DFS reaches it, record the word and set the field to \cd{None}.
        The DFS then reports each word one time, and it does not build path strings.
  \item On the way back, delete a node that has no children left.
        Later searches never enter a branch with nothing left to find.
\end{itemize}
Memory hook: \emph{Word Search I, but walk a trie instead of one word, and cut empty leaves on the way back.}
\begin{pyex}
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}      # letter to TrieNode
        self.word = None        # the whole word that ends here, if any

def find_words(board, words):
    root = TrieNode()
    for word in words:
        node = root
        for ch in word:
            node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())
        node.word = word
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
    found = []

    def dfs(r, c, parent):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r == rows or c == cols:
            return                          # off the board
        ch = board[r][c]
        if ch not in parent.children:
            return                          # no word goes on ('#' marks a used cell)
        node = parent.children[ch]
        if node.word:
            found.append(node.word)
            node.word = None                # report each word once
        board[r][c] = "#"                   # mark the cell as used on this path
        dfs(r + 1, c, node)
        dfs(r - 1, c, node)
        dfs(r, c + 1, node)
        dfs(r, c - 1, node)
        board[r][c] = ch                    # backtrack: restore the cell
        if not node.children:
            del parent.children[ch]         # prune: nothing left to find here

    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            dfs(r, c, root)
    return found

board = [list("oaan"), list("etae"), list("ihkr"), list("iflv")]
sorted(find_words(board, ["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"]))   # -> ['eat', 'oath']
board[0]                                                    # -> ['o', 'a', 'a', 'n']
find_words([list("ab"), list("cd")], ["abdc", "abcb"])      # -> ['abdc']
sorted(find_words([list("aa")], ["a", "aa", "aaa"]))        # -> ['a', 'aa']
\end{pyex}
The DFS state is (cell, trie node). The letters on the current path spell the string from the root to the node.
The marker \hsh{} is never a trie key, so the child test also blocks a second visit to a cell.
The recursion depth is at most one more than the length of the longest word.
The general rule: when a search consumes its targets, shrink the target structure as you find them.
The worst case is still exponential in the word length.
An all-\cd{a} board with the words \cd{aaaaaaab} to \cd{aaaaaaak} keeps long paths alive.
The DFS finds no word, so it prunes nothing.
A form that checks the bounds and the trie child before each call makes fewer calls.
In CPython it is not clearly faster, so write the form that you remember. Keep the leaf prune in both forms.
\begin{note}
Other searches use the same pair (search state, trie node). A Boggle grid with 8 directions changes only the neighbor list.
If cells can repeat, drop the used mark: the longest word still limits the depth.
To count paths instead of words, do not clear words and do not prune.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Walk the trie from each start index}
To find many dictionary words inside one string, walk the trie from each start index $i$.
Stop at the first missing child. Each end flag on the way marks a match \cd{s[i:j + 1]}.
The cost is $O(n \cdot L_{\max})$, where $L_{\max}$ is the length of the longest word.
A set of words must test every end index $j$. The trie walk stops at the first missing child.
Word Break uses this walk to fill a DP table over the indexes.
Memory hook: \emph{From each start, walk until the trie says no.}
\begin{pyex}
def word_break(s, words):
    root = {}
    for w in words:
        node = root
        for ch in w:
            node = node.setdefault(ch, {})
        node["$"] = True
    n = len(s)
    ok = [True] + [False] * n           # ok[i]: s[:i] splits into words
    for i in range(n):
        if not ok[i]:
            continue
        node = root
        for j in range(i, n):           # walk the trie along s[i:]
            node = node.get(s[j])
            if node is None:
                break
            if "$" in node:
                ok[j + 1] = True
    return ok[n]

word_break("leetcode", ["leet", "code"])                         # -> True
word_break("catsandog", ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"])   # -> False
\end{pyex}
When the questions are about suffixes, insert the reversed keys and walk the string from its end.
For a very long text and many patterns, the Aho-Corasick automaton adds failure links to the trie
and matches in linear time. Interview problems rarely need it.

\subsubsection{Binary trie for XOR}
The keys can be integers. Write each integer as a fixed number of bits, from the highest bit to the lowest.
The trie then has at most two children per node.
To get the largest \cd{x ^ y} over the stored \cd{y}, walk down from the root.
At each bit, take the child with the opposite bit if it exists, because a high bit outweighs all lower bits.
For example, $3 = 00011$ and $25 = 11001$ differ in the top bit, so their XOR is at least $2^4 = 16$.
Memory hook: \emph{Bits from the top; take the opposite bit when it exists.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_xor_pair(nums):
    B = max(nums).bit_length()          # the number of bits to use
    root, best = {}, 0
    for x in nums:
        node = root
        for b in range(B - 1, -1, -1):  # insert x, highest bit first
            node = node.setdefault((x >> b) & 1, {})
        node, cur = root, 0
        for b in range(B - 1, -1, -1):  # query: prefer the opposite bit
            bit = (x >> b) & 1
            if 1 - bit in node:
                cur |= 1 << b
                node = node[1 - bit]
            else:
                node = node[bit]
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

max_xor_pair([3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8])     # -> 28
max_xor_pair([7])                      # -> 0
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What are the keys, and what is the alphabet? Letters, digits, bits from the highest bit, the parts of a path.
        If the questions are about suffixes, reverse the keys.
  \item Which operations need prefixes? If every query is an exact lookup, use a hash set and stop.
  \item Do the stored strings change? A list that does not change can use a sorted list and \cd{bisect}.
  \item What must each node hold? An end flag, a pass count, the whole word, an index, a sum, a minimum.
        Update this data at each node on the path during the insert.
  \item Does a query branch? A wildcard, a grid neighbor and a budget of edits all branch.
        Write a DFS over the state (position in the query or cell, trie node). A missing child ends the branch.
  \item Is the number of branches small and bounded? Then a set of masked patterns can be simpler than a trie.
  \item Do found targets leave the search? Clear the stored word, and delete empty leaves on the way back.
  \item Check the cost. The trie has at most one node per inserted letter. Each walk is $O(L)$.
        The recursion depth grows with the length of the longest key, not with the number of keys.
  \item Write the code in layers. First the insert and the plain walk of the core template.
        Then the node data. Then the branching DFS. Last, the pruning.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A path is not a word.} After an insert of \cd{apple} only, \cd{search("app")} must return \cd{False}.
Return the end flag of the last node, not ``the walk finished''.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A query that creates nodes.} Use \cd{setdefault} or a \cd{defaultdict} only in the insert.
In a query, they add empty paths. A later \cd{startsWith} then returns \cd{True} for a word that was never inserted.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict
def make_node():
    return defaultdict(make_node)
root = make_node()
node = root
for ch in "cat":
    node = node[ch]                   # insert "cat"
node["$"] = True
def starts_with_bad(root, p):
    node = root
    for ch in p:
        node = node[ch]               # creates a node when ch is missing
    return True
def starts_with_good(root, p):
    node = root
    for ch in p:
        if ch not in node:
            return False
        node = node[ch]
    return True
starts_with_good(root, "dog")         # -> False
starts_with_bad(root, "dog")          # -> True
starts_with_good(root, "dog")         # -> True
\end{pyex}
The last line shows the damage: the bad query added the path d-o-g, so the correct query now returns \cd{True} too.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{One dict for all nodes.} A class attribute \cd{children = {}} or a mutable default argument
shares one dict between all nodes. Create a new dict in \cd{__init__} for each node.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class BadNode:
    children = {}                     # one dict for the class, not for each node
a, b = BadNode(), BadNode()
a.children["x"] = BadNode()
"x" in b.children                     # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Wildcard rules.} A dot matches exactly one letter, so the lengths must be equal.
At a dot, try every child, and return \cd{True} if any branch succeeds. Return that result at once:
the recursive calls already match the rest of the query.
Check for the dot before you compute a list index such as \cd{ord(ch) - ord("a")}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Grid search with a trie.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Restore the cell after the four recursive calls. Otherwise later searches see a damaged board.
  \item Do not return after the first word at a node. A longer word can continue the path (\cd{cat} and \cd{cats}).
  \item A word can be reachable along several paths. Clear the stored word, or use a set, so each word appears once.
  \item Delete a node only from its parent, and only after its own recursion returns.
  \item Use a used-cell marker that is never a trie key, such as \hsh{} for a trie of lowercase letters.
  \item Record a one-letter word at the start cell, before any step to a neighbor.
\end{itemize}
\end{caution}

\begin{note}
Python node objects are large. A list of 26 children per node wastes memory when few words share prefixes.
Prefer dict children, or add \cd{__slots__} to the node class.
A nested-dict trie is often smaller and faster than a trie of node objects.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) & The core template: insert, a whole-word search that reads the end flag, and a prefix search that does not. & One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end. \\
Design Add and Search Words Data Structure & A dot matches any one letter, at most 2 dots. Store masked patterns in a set, or run a trie DFS that tries every child at a dot. & Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search. (Trie: a letter follows one edge; a dot follows every edge.) \\
Word Search II & Many words on one grid. The grid DFS walks a trie, stores each word at its end node, clears it when found, and cuts empty leaves. & Word Search I, but walk a trie instead of one word, and cut empty leaves on the way back. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Heaps and priority queues}\label{tech:T10}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
A heap is a list with one rule: each parent is less than or equal to its children.
This rule puts the smallest item at index 0. The other items are only partly ordered.
A push or a pop moves one item along one path between the root and a leaf, so each costs $O(\log n)$.
A new sort costs $O(n \log n)$ and a new scan costs $O(n)$ each time the data changes.
The heap does only the work that is necessary to know the next smallest item.
Use a heap when a collection changes again and again, and each step needs only its best item.

Most heap solutions have one of three shapes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Keep the $k$ best.} A heap of size $k$ holds the best items so far. Its root is the weakest
        kept item. The root is the gate that a new item must beat.
  \item \textbf{Pop the best, push what follows.} The heap holds the candidates for the next step.
        Each pop can make new candidates: the next item of the same list, a combined stone, a task that is ready again.
  \item \textbf{Two heaps at a boundary.} A max-heap holds the lower part and a min-heap holds the upper part.
        The two roots face each other, so a middle rank is always at the top.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Worked example.} Find the 3rd largest value after each value of the stream 5, 1, 8, 3, 9.
Keep a min-heap of at most 3 values. After 5, 1 and 8, the heap holds $\{1, 5, 8\}$, and the root 1 is the answer.
Then 3 arrives. Push it, so the heap holds 4 values. Pop the root 1.
The value 1 can never be in the top 3 again, because values are only added.
The heap is $\{3, 5, 8\}$, and the answer is the root 3.
Then 9 arrives. Push it and pop 3. The heap is $\{5, 8, 9\}$, and the answer is 5.
Each step costs $O(\log k)$. A sort of the full history at each step costs $O(n \log n)$.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
