Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets & Interchangeable buckets: fill one at a time; the used mask is the full state, so memoize. &
  Mask of used numbers, fill is used sum mod target, try every unused number that fits. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Graph traversal: grids and implicit graphs}\label{tech:T12}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
Many problems contain a graph that the input does not show.
A grid is a graph: each cell is a node, and each pair of adjacent cells is an edge.
A word, a lock code or a board is also a node: each legal one-step change is an edge.
When you name the nodes and the edges, two traversals answer most questions.
\begin{itemize}
\item A \textbf{flood fill} (DFS or BFS, in any order) answers ``which nodes connect''.
  Use it to count regions, to measure them, or to test a property of each region.
\item A \textbf{BFS} answers ``how many steps''. BFS takes nodes from a queue in order of distance.
  When each step costs the same, the first time BFS reaches a node gives its shortest distance.
\end{itemize}
The visited mark saves the work. A brute force starts a new search from each cell, which costs $O((mn)^2)$ on a grid.
With a visited mark, each node is expanded (its edges are read) at most one time. The total work is then $O(V + E)$, or $O(mn)$ on a grid.

\textbf{Worked example: count components.}
Take the grid with the rows \cd{110}, \cd{010} and \cd{001}. Scan the cells row by row.
Cell (0, 0) is land and is not visited, so count one island.
A flood fill from (0, 0) marks (0, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1).
The scan skips (0, 1) and (1, 1), because they are marked.
Cell (2, 2) touches (1, 1) only at a corner, and corner contact does not connect.
So (2, 2) starts a second island, and the answer is 2.

\textbf{Worked example: BFS layers.}
In an open $3 \times 3$ grid, start a BFS at (0, 0). Layer 0 holds only (0, 0).
Layer 1 holds (1, 0) and (0, 1). Layer 2 holds (2, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 2).
The far corner (2, 2) is in layer 4, so the fewest steps to it are 4.
A DFS can reach (2, 2) first by a longer path, so a DFS does not give the shortest distance.
A brute force tries every path and keeps the shortest one, and the number of paths grows exponentially.
BFS removes that work. It reaches each node one time, and that first time is by a shortest path.

For each problem, decide three things: what a node is, what an edge is,
and what the traversal returns (a count, a size, a flag, a distance, or a copy).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
\item The input is a grid, and cells connect ``horizontally or vertically''. The words island, region, group,
  blob or province name connected components.
\item The question asks for the minimum number of moves, steps or minutes, and each move costs the same.
  This is a shortest path in an unweighted graph. Use BFS, not DFS.
\item A process spreads from many cells at the same time, one step per unit of time. Use one BFS with all sources
  in the queue at distance 0.
\item The question asks which cells can reach a border, an ocean or an exit, or which regions are surrounded.
  Many sources share a few fixed targets. Search backward from the targets.
\item The statement asks you to split the nodes into two groups, and each conflict or dislike must join the two groups.
  Color the nodes with two colors in a BFS.
\item The input is one configuration (a word, a code, a board), and a move changes it a little.
  Each configuration is a node of an implicit graph.
\item The input gives $n$ nodes and a list of pairs: edges, friendships, prerequisites or equal pairs.
  Build an adjacency list, then traverse it.
\item The input gives objects and a rule that relates two of them: a distance, a radius or a one-letter difference.
  Each object is a node, and each pair that obeys the rule is an edge.
  If the rule is not symmetric (``$i$ reaches $j$''), the edges are directed.
\item The statement says clone or deep copy, and the structure has shared nodes or cycles.
  Traverse it and keep a map from each old node to its copy.
\item The sizes allow one linear pass: about $10^5$ cells or $10^6$ states. One search from each cell is too slow.
\item The answer is $-1$, 0 or INF when a target is unreachable. A traversal with a reachability check gives this case.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}

\subsubsection{Flood fill: scan and sink}
Scan every cell. At each land cell that is not visited, add one to the count and flood fill its whole component.
The flood fill marks each cell that it reaches, so the scan never counts that component again.
This version pushes all four neighbors without a check, and it checks each cell when it pops the cell.
The check after the pop rejects cells off the grid, water cells, and cells that are already sunk.
Use this push-blindly form only for a flood fill with a stack, where no distance and no counter depend on the pushes.
In a BFS with a queue, mark each node when you push it (see the BFS template below).
\begin{pyex}
def num_islands(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

    def sink(r, c):
        stack = [(r, c)]                 # iterative DFS: no recursion limit
        while stack:
            i, j = stack.pop()
            if 0 <= i < rows and 0 <= j < cols and grid[i][j] == "1":
                grid[i][j] = "0"         # sink: the grid is the visited set
                stack += [(i + 1, j), (i - 1, j), (i, j + 1), (i, j - 1)]

    islands = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1":
                islands += 1
                sink(r, c)
    return islands

grid = [list("110"), list("010"), list("001")]
num_islands(grid)                       # -> 2
grid[0]                                 # -> ['0', '0', '0']
num_islands([list("11000"), list("11000"), list("00100"), list("00011")])   # -> 3
num_islands([["1"] * 200 for _ in range(200)])                              # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} Before the scan reaches a cell, every cell of each counted island is already \cd{"0"}.
So each \cd{"1"} that the scan finds starts a new island.
Memory hook (Number of Islands): \emph{count each new land cell, then sink its whole island; push blindly, check on pop.}

\textbf{Aside.} The optimal form checks each neighbor before it pushes it, and it sinks the neighbor at once
(see Max Area of Island below). Then each cell enters the stack at most one time. Both forms cost $O(mn)$.
The sink-on-push form also works with a deque, so it is the form to use in a BFS.

\begin{caution}
Use an explicit stack or a queue, not recursion. A recursive DFS on an all-land $300 \times 300$ grid
goes 90{,}000 calls deep. The default Python limit is 1000 calls, so the code raises \cd{RecursionError}.
\end{caution}

\subsubsection{BFS: fewest steps}
Put the start nodes in a deque. Pop from the left. Give each new neighbor the distance of its parent plus 1,
and mark it at that moment. The dict \cd{dist} does two jobs: it is the visited set, and it holds the answer.
The function takes a \cd{neighbors} function, so the same code runs on a grid, on an adjacency list, or on a state graph.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def bfs(starts, neighbors):
    dist = {s: 0 for s in starts}       # visited set and answer in one dict
    queue = deque(starts)
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        for nxt in neighbors(node):
            if nxt not in dist:         # mark on push
                dist[nxt] = dist[node] + 1
                queue.append(nxt)
    return dist

maze = ["..#",
        ".##",
        "..."]
rows, cols = len(maze), len(maze[0])

def open_cells(cell):
    r, c = cell
    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
        if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and maze[nr][nc] == ".":
            yield nr, nc

dist = bfs([(0, 0)], open_cells)
dist[(2, 2)]                            # -> 4
dist.get((0, 2), -1)                    # -> -1
len(dist)                               # -> 6
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} The queue holds nodes in nondecreasing order of distance, and two queued distances differ by at most 1.
So the first distance that a node gets is its shortest distance.
Mark a node when you push it. A node that you mark only when you pop it can enter the queue many times.

\begin{note}
There are three ways to keep the distance: a dict as above, (node, distance) pairs in the queue,
or a level loop \cd{for _ in range(len(queue))} with one counter.
Use the level loop when you must act on one whole level at a time, for example one minute of a spread.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Build an adjacency list from edges}
When the input is a list of edges, build an adjacency list first. For an undirected edge, store both directions.
Then the flood fill and the BFS above run without a change.
Loop over all node ids, not over the dict keys, so that a node with no edges still counts.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

n = 6
edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4)]
adj = defaultdict(list)
for a, b in edges:
    adj[a].append(b)
    adj[b].append(a)                    # undirected: store both directions
adj[1]                                  # -> [0, 2]

def count_components(n, adj):
    seen = set()
    count = 0
    for start in range(n):              # every node id, also node 5 with no edges
        if start in seen:
            continue
        count += 1
        seen.add(start)
        stack = [start]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            for nxt in adj[node]:
                if nxt not in seen:
                    seen.add(nxt)
                    stack.append(nxt)
    return count

count_components(n, adj)                # -> 3
\end{pyex}
Union-find, cycle checks and topological order are in the section on graph structure.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Measure each component}
\textbf{What changes:} the flood fill returns a value for its component, and the scan combines the values.
In \textbf{Max Area of Island}, the flood fill returns the cell count, and the scan keeps the largest count.
Sink each cell when you push it, and count each cell when you pop it.
Each cell enters the stack one time, so the number of pops is the area.
Memory hook: \emph{scan for land; sink on push, count on pop, keep the max.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_area(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

    def island_size(r, c):
        grid[r][c] = 0                  # sink on push
        stack = [(r, c)]
        size = 0
        while stack:
            i, j = stack.pop()
            size += 1                   # count on pop
            for x, y in ((i + 1, j), (i - 1, j), (i, j + 1), (i, j - 1)):
                if 0 <= x < rows and 0 <= y < cols and grid[x][y] == 1:
                    grid[x][y] = 0
                    stack.append((x, y))
        return size

    best = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 1:
                best = max(best, island_size(r, c))
    return best

max_area([[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 1]])   # -> 3
max_area([[0, 0]])                            # -> 0
\end{pyex}
The flood fill can return other values. Two examples are the number of sides that touch water (a perimeter)
and the offsets from the first cell (a shape key).
A third example is a flag that stays \cd{True} only if every cell passes a test.

\subsubsection{Compare regions by their cell sets}
\textbf{What changes:} there are two grids of the same shape.
A region of one grid matches a region of the other grid only if both have exactly the same coordinates.
To \textbf{count the regions that two binary grids share}, flood fill every region of each grid and store it as a
\cd{frozenset} of coordinates. The answer is the size of the intersection of the two sets of regions.
A \cd{frozenset} is hashable, so it can be a member of a set, and two frozensets with the same cells are equal.
Memory hook: \emph{collect each grid's islands as frozensets, then intersect.}
\begin{pyex}
def count_matching_regions(grid1, grid2):
    def regions(grid):
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        seen = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        found = set()
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(cols):
                if grid[r][c] != "1" or seen[r][c]:
                    continue
                seen[r][c] = True
                stack = [(r, c)]
                cells = []
                while stack:
                    i, j = stack.pop()
                    cells.append((i, j))
                    for x, y in ((i - 1, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j - 1), (i, j + 1)):
                        if (0 <= x < rows and 0 <= y < cols
                                and grid[x][y] == "1" and not seen[x][y]):
                            seen[x][y] = True
                            stack.append((x, y))
                found.add(frozenset(cells))
        return found

    return len(regions(grid1) & regions(grid2))

count_matching_regions(["110", "000", "011"], ["110", "000", "010"])   # -> 1
count_matching_regions(["10"], ["11"])                                 # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\textbf{The faster form: check the border ring.} A maximal region can grow only through a neighbor cell.
So a region $A$ of \cd{grid1} equals a region of \cd{grid2} exactly when two conditions are true.
First, \cd{grid2} has \cd{"1"} on every cell of $A$.
Second, \cd{grid2} has \cd{"0"} on every neighbor of $A$ outside $A$ (the border ring).
Check both conditions with one flag during one flood fill of \cd{grid1}. This needs no sets of coordinates.
The general idea: to compare a component with another structure, check the frontier where the component can leak.
\begin{pyex}
def count_matching_regions(grid1, grid2):
    rows, cols = len(grid1), len(grid1[0])
    seen = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    count = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid1[r][c] != "1" or seen[r][c]:
                continue
            seen[r][c] = True
            stack = [(r, c)]
            matches = True
            while stack:                            # finish the fill even after a mismatch
                i, j = stack.pop()
                if grid2[i][j] != "1":
                    matches = False                 # grid2 misses a region cell
                for x, y in ((i - 1, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j - 1), (i, j + 1)):
                    if not (0 <= x < rows and 0 <= y < cols):
                        continue
                    if grid1[x][y] == "1":
                        if not seen[x][y]:
                            seen[x][y] = True
                            stack.append((x, y))
                    elif grid2[x][y] == "1":
                        matches = False             # the grid2 region leaks out
            count += matches
    return count

count_matching_regions(["110", "000", "011"], ["110", "000", "010"])   # -> 1
count_matching_regions(["10"], ["11"])                                 # -> 0
count_matching_regions(["101"], ["101"])                               # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
Do not stop a flood fill at the first mismatch. The rest of the region then stays unmarked,
and the scan later starts a new search inside it. That search can count a false match. Finish the fill, then decide.
\end{caution}

\subsubsection{Search backward from the targets}
\textbf{What changes:} many sources ask if they can reach a small fixed set of targets.
Reverse each edge, and run one search that starts at all targets together.
The cells that this search reaches are exactly the cells that can reach a target.
One reverse search replaces one forward search per cell.

In \textbf{Pacific Atlantic Water Flow}, water flows to a neighbor that is lower or at the same height.
So the reverse search climbs to a neighbor that is higher or at the same height.
Run one search from the Pacific border: the top row and the left column.
Run one more search from the Atlantic border: the bottom row and the right column.
Return the cells that are in both results.
Memory hook: \emph{water flows down, so flood uphill from each ocean and keep the cells both floods reach.}
\begin{pyex}
def pacific_atlantic(heights):
    rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])

    def flood_uphill(starts):
        reached = set(starts)
        stack = list(starts)
        while stack:
            r, c = stack.pop()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and (nr, nc) not in reached
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]):   # reverse of "flows down"
                    reached.add((nr, nc))
                    stack.append((nr, nc))
        return reached

    top_left = [(0, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)]
    bottom_right = ([(rows - 1, c) for c in range(cols)]
                    + [(r, cols - 1) for r in range(rows)])
    both = flood_uphill(top_left) & flood_uphill(bottom_right)
    return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(both)]

heights = [[1, 2, 2, 3, 5],
           [3, 2, 3, 4, 4],
           [2, 4, 5, 3, 1],
           [6, 7, 1, 4, 5],
           [5, 1, 1, 2, 4]]
pacific_atlantic(heights)
# -> [[0, 4], [1, 3], [1, 4], [2, 2], [3, 0], [3, 1], [4, 0]]
pacific_atlantic([[7]])                 # -> [[0, 0]]
\end{pyex}
Each ocean has its own \cd{reached} set. A shared set stops the second search early on cells that the first search marked.

In \textbf{Surrounded Regions}, a region of \cd{"O"} cells survives if one of its cells is on the border.
Flood from all border cells, and change each \cd{"O"} that the flood reaches to a third symbol \cd{"T"}.
Then sweep the board one time: \cd{"O"} becomes \cd{"X"} (captured), and \cd{"T"} becomes \cd{"O"} (safe).
The third symbol replaces a visited set. Use this trick when you may change the input and need a temporary third state.
Memory hook: \emph{flood from the border, O becomes T; then O to X, T to O.}
\begin{pyex}
def solve(board):
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
    stack = [(r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols)
             if r in (0, rows - 1) or c in (0, cols - 1)]
    while stack:
        r, c = stack.pop()
        if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and board[r][c] == "O":
            board[r][c] = "T"           # safe: the border reaches it
            stack += [(r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)]
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if board[r][c] == "O":
                board[r][c] = "X"       # captured
            elif board[r][c] == "T":
                board[r][c] = "O"       # restored

board = [list("XXXX"), list("XOOX"), list("XXOX"), list("XOXX")]
solve(board)
["".join(row) for row in board]         # -> ['XXXX', 'XXXX', 'XXXX', 'XOXX']
\end{pyex}
The same border-first flood counts the land cells that cannot reach the edge, or the islands that do not touch it.

\subsubsection{Multi-source BFS}
\textbf{What changes:} the search starts from many cells at the same time.
Put all sources in the queue at distance 0 before the loop.
This is the same as a BFS from one virtual source that connects to every real source.
So the first distance that a cell gets is its distance to the nearest source.

In \textbf{Rotting Oranges}, put all rotten oranges in the queue, and count the fresh ones.
Process one BFS level per minute. Stop when no fresh orange is left or when the queue is empty.
Return $-1$ if a fresh orange remains.
Memory hook: \emph{all rotten in the queue, count the fresh, one level is one minute, stop when fresh is zero.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def oranges_rotting(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    queue = deque()
    fresh = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 2:
                queue.append((r, c))
            elif grid[r][c] == 1:
                fresh += 1
    minutes = 0
    while queue and fresh > 0:          # "fresh > 0" stops before an extra empty minute
        for _ in range(len(queue)):     # one level is one minute
            r, c = queue.popleft()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                    grid[nr][nc] = 2    # mark on push
                    fresh -= 1
                    queue.append((nr, nc))
        minutes += 1
    return minutes if fresh == 0 else -1

oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]])   # -> 4
oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]])   # -> -1
oranges_rotting([[0, 2]])                            # -> 0
\end{pyex}

In \textbf{Walls and Gates}, put all gates in the queue, then run a plain BFS.
Write the parent distance plus 1 into each room that still holds INF.
INF means ``not reached yet'', so the grid is the visited set.
Memory hook: \emph{push all gates first, then BFS and fill only INF rooms.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

INF = 2**31 - 1

def walls_and_gates(rooms):
    rows, cols = len(rooms), len(rooms[0])
    queue = deque((r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols) if rooms[r][c] == 0)
    while queue:
        r, c = queue.popleft()
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and rooms[nr][nc] == INF:
                rooms[nr][nc] = rooms[r][c] + 1   # first visit is the shortest
                queue.append((nr, nc))

rooms = [[INF, -1, 0, INF],
         [INF, INF, INF, -1],
         [INF, -1, INF, -1],
         [0, -1, INF, INF]]
walls_and_gates(rooms)
rooms
# -> [[3, -1, 0, 1], [2, 2, 1, -1], [1, -1, 2, -1], [0, -1, 3, 4]]
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Multi-source BFS gives a minimum over the sources. When the answer for a cell is a sum over all sources,
run one BFS per source and add the distances. When the steps have different costs, push all sources into a heap
at cost 0 and run Dijkstra (see the section on weighted graphs).
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Two sides: two-coloring}
\textbf{What changes:} the statement asks you to split the nodes into two groups,
and each edge (a conflict or a dislike) must join the two groups.
Such a graph is bipartite. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no cycle of odd length.
Run the BFS template with a dict \cd{color} in place of \cd{dist}.
Give each new neighbor the other color, \cd{1 - color[u]}.
If an edge joins two nodes of the same color, return \cd{False}: that edge closes an odd cycle.
The graph can have many components, so start a BFS from every node that has no color yet.
The first color of each component is free, because you can swap the two colors of a component.
Memory hook: \emph{give each new neighbor the other color; a same-color edge means an odd cycle.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def is_bipartite(graph):                 # graph[u] = list of neighbors
    color = {}
    for start in range(len(graph)):      # every component
        if start in color:
            continue
        color[start] = 0
        queue = deque([start])
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            for v in graph[u]:
                if v not in color:
                    color[v] = 1 - color[u]      # the other side, marked on push
                    queue.append(v)
                elif color[v] == color[u]:
                    return False                 # an edge inside one side: an odd cycle
    return True

def possible_bipartition(n, dislikes):  # people 1..n, pairs that must split
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]   # node 0 is not used and stays alone
    for a, b in dislikes:
        graph[a].append(b)
        graph[b].append(a)
    return is_bipartite(graph)

is_bipartite([[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 3], [0, 2]])         # -> True
is_bipartite([[1, 2, 3], [0, 2], [0, 1, 3], [0, 2]])   # -> False
is_bipartite([[1], [0]])                               # -> True
is_bipartite([[1], [0], [3, 4], [2, 4], [2, 3]])       # -> False
possible_bipartition(4, [[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 4]])      # -> True
possible_bipartition(3, [[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]])      # -> False
\end{pyex}
A DFS with a stack works the same way, because only the color matters, not the distance.
Example problems: Is Graph Bipartite (785) and Possible Bipartition (886).
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Do not union the two ends of each edge.} The two ends of an edge must go to different sides.
A union puts them in one group, so the check fails even on the single edge \cd{[[1], [0]]}, which is bipartite.
Union-find works only in this form: union all neighbors of one node with each other,
and return \cd{False} if the node is in the same group as one of its neighbors.
\end{caution}

\subsubsection{Implicit state graphs}
\textbf{What changes:} a node is a whole configuration, and a move generator lists its neighbors.
You do not build the graph in advance. Define three things: the state, the move generator,
and the forbidden or allowed states. Then count the states. Up to about $10^6$ states fit a plain BFS in Python.
Use a hashable state as the key of the visited set: a string, a tuple, or an integer.

In \textbf{Open the Lock}, a state is a 4-digit string. One move turns one wheel by $+1$ or $-1$ modulo 10,
so each state has 8 neighbors and there are $10^4$ states.
Put the dead ends in the \cd{seen} set before the search. Then one membership test blocks both the revisits and
the forbidden states.
Memory hook: \emph{BFS from 0000 with (code, turns) pairs; dead ends start in seen; 8 neighbors are each wheel
plus or minus 1 mod 10.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def open_lock(deadends, target):
    def neighbors(code):
        for i in range(4):
            digit = int(code[i])
            for step in (1, -1):
                yield code[:i] + str((digit + step) % 10) + code[i + 1:]

    seen = set(deadends)                # dead ends are walls: BFS never enters them
    if "0000" in seen:
        return -1
    seen.add("0000")
    queue = deque([("0000", 0)])        # (code, turns from "0000")
    while queue:
        code, turns = queue.popleft()
        if code == target:              # test on pop: also handles target == "0000"
            return turns
        for nxt in neighbors(code):
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                queue.append((nxt, turns + 1))
    return -1

open_lock(["0201", "0101", "0102", "1212", "2002"], "0202")    # -> 6
open_lock(["8888"], "0009")                                    # -> 1
ring = ["8887", "8889", "8878", "8898", "8788", "8988", "7888", "9888"]
open_lock(ring, "8888")                                        # -> -1
open_lock(["0000"], "8888")                                    # -> -1
open_lock([], "0000")                                          # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Aside.} The optimal code counts levels and tests the target when it generates a neighbor.
It stops about one level sooner, but it needs its own check for a target of \cd{"0000"}.
The test on pop is fast enough for $10^4$ states.

In \textbf{Word Ladder}, a state is a word, and a move changes one letter to give a word of the list.
Do not compare all pairs of words: that is $O(N^2 L)$. Generate the $26L$ candidates of each word and look each one up
in a set. Remove a word from the set when you enqueue it. The answer counts words, not moves, so the start has length 1.
Memory hook: \emph{BFS of (word, length) pairs: change one letter, keep the word only if it is still in the unvisited set.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque
from string import ascii_lowercase

def ladder_length(begin, end, word_list):
    unvisited = set(word_list)
    unvisited.discard(begin)            # the start counts as visited
    queue = deque([(begin, 1)])         # (word, words in the ladder so far)
    while queue:
        word, length = queue.popleft()
        if word == end:
            return length
        for i in range(len(word)):
            for c in ascii_lowercase:
                nxt = word[:i] + c + word[i + 1:]
                if nxt in unvisited:
                    unvisited.remove(nxt)       # mark visited when enqueued
                    queue.append((nxt, length + 1))
    return 0

ladder_length("hit", "cog", ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot", "log", "cog"])   # -> 5
ladder_length("hit", "cog", ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot", "log"])          # -> 0
\end{pyex}
The time is $O(26 \cdot N \cdot L^2)$: $N$ words, $26L$ candidates per word, and $O(L)$ to build and hash each one.
The optimal code is the same BFS. It processes one level per pass with one counter,
and it returns 0 at once when the end word is not in the list.
For a much larger graph, use bidirectional BFS: search from both ends, and always expand the smaller frontier.

\textbf{Trick: wildcard buckets.} When an edge means ``equal except at one position'', mask that position.
All words with the same masked key are neighbors. This turns an all-pairs search into hash lookups.
Building the buckets costs $O(N L^2)$ and has no loop over the alphabet.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

buckets = defaultdict(list)
for w in ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot"]:
    for i in range(len(w)):
        buckets[w[:i] + "*" + w[i + 1:]].append(w)
buckets["*ot"]                          # -> ['hot', 'dot', 'lot']
buckets["do*"]                          # -> ['dot', 'dog']
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Return the path, not only the distance}
Store the parent of each node when you push it. The parent dict is also the visited set.
At the goal, follow the parents back to the start, then reverse the list.
The example is an implicit graph on numbers: the moves are $+1$ and $\times 2$.
Memory hook: \emph{the parent dict is the visited set; walk back from the goal, then reverse.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def shortest_path(start, goal, neighbors):
    parent = {start: None}
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node == goal:
            path = []
            while node is not None:
                path.append(node)
                node = parent[node]
            return path[::-1]
        for nxt in neighbors(node):
            if nxt not in parent:
                parent[nxt] = node
                queue.append(nxt)
    return None

moves = lambda x: [y for y in (x + 1, x * 2) if y <= 20]
shortest_path(2, 9, moves)              # -> [2, 4, 8, 9]
shortest_path(5, 3, moves) is None      # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Clone a graph}
\textbf{What changes:} the traversal builds one new node for each old node.
A dict from each old node to its copy does two jobs. It is the visited set, and it translates old references
into new references. Create the copy and store it in the dict before you visit the neighbors.
Then a cycle that comes back to the node finds the copy and stops.
In \textbf{Clone Graph}, \cd{dfs(cur)} returns the copy of \cd{cur}.
Memory hook: \emph{copy a tree, but check the map first and register the copy before you recurse.}
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, neighbors=None):
        self.val = val
        self.neighbors = neighbors if neighbors is not None else []

def clone_graph(node):
    old_to_new = {}

    def dfs(cur):
        if cur in old_to_new:
            return old_to_new[cur]
        copy = Node(cur.val)
        old_to_new[cur] = copy          # register before recursing
        for nei in cur.neighbors:
            copy.neighbors.append(dfs(nei))
        return copy

    return dfs(node) if node else None

a, b, c, d = Node(1), Node(2), Node(3), Node(4)      # the cycle 1-2-3-4-1
a.neighbors, b.neighbors = [b, d], [a, c]
c.neighbors, d.neighbors = [b, d], [c, a]
a2 = clone_graph(a)
[n.val for n in a2.neighbors]           # -> [2, 4]
a2 is a, a2.neighbors[0] is b           # -> (False, False)
a2.neighbors[0].neighbors[0] is a2      # -> True
clone_graph(None) is None               # -> True
\end{pyex}
The same map copies a linked list with random pointers, and \cd{copy.deepcopy} keeps a memo dict for the same reason.
Recursion is safe here for 100 nodes. For a long graph, use BFS: create the copy and store it when you enqueue the node.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{What is a node?} A cell \cd{(r, c)}, an index, a word, or a tuple that holds the whole state.
  It must be hashable if a set or a dict holds it.
\item \textbf{What is an edge?} Write the move generator. List the offsets: 4 or 8 directions, a knight move, one wheel,
  one letter. Test the bounds first. Then apply the rule of the edge: a wall, a height rule, a wrap-around with modulo.
  Ask if the edge is directed. A rule such as ``$i$ reaches $j$'' is not always true in reverse.
  If the input is a list of pairs or objects, build the adjacency list now.
\item \textbf{What does the question ask?} Connectivity, a count, a size or a flag per region: flood fill in any order.
  Fewest steps with equal costs: BFS. Different costs: Dijkstra. Two groups with every edge between them: two-coloring.
  An order or a cycle: see the section on graph structure.
\item \textbf{How many sources and targets?} Many sources that act together: multi-source BFS.
  Many sources and a few fixed targets: search backward from the targets.
  One start and one goal in a large graph: plain BFS, then bidirectional BFS if necessary.
\item \textbf{How do you mark a visited node?} An unused value in the input (sink, \cd{"T"}, INF) if you may change it.
  A set if you may not. A dict if each node needs a value: a distance, a parent, or a copy. Mark on push.
\item \textbf{How large is the graph?} Nodes times moves must be about $10^7$ or less in Python.
  Use an explicit stack or a queue if the depth can pass 1000.
\item \textbf{What are the edge cases?} The start is the goal. The start is forbidden. There is no source.
  A target is unreachable. If the answer can be $-1$, count the targets before the search and check the count after it.
\item \textbf{Is one traversal enough?} Some problems chain two. For example, a flood fill collects the cells of one
  region, and a multi-source BFS from those cells measures the distance to something else.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative indexes.} Python reads \cd{grid[-1]} as the last row, with no error.
Test \cd{0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols} first in the \cd{and} chain, then read the cell.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
r, c = 0, 0
grid[r - 1][c]                          # -> 3
0 <= r - 1 < len(grid)                  # -> False
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Mark on push in a BFS.} If you mark a node only when you pop it, the node can enter the queue many times.
The work grows, and a counter that you change on each push (the fresh oranges) becomes wrong.
The push-blindly flood fill with a stack is the only exception. It has no distance and no counter,
and it tests each cell when it pops it. So a duplicate entry does no harm there.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion depth.} A recursive DFS can go as deep as the number of cells. Above 1000 calls, Python raises
\cd{RecursionError}. Use an explicit stack or a deque.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{DFS for a shortest path.} DFS finds a path, not the shortest path. Use BFS when each step costs the same.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Nodes or moves.} Word Ladder counts words, so the start has length 1. Open the Lock counts moves, so the start
has distance 0. You can test the goal when you generate a neighbor.
Then the answer is the parent value plus 1, and the case ``start equals goal'' needs its own check.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{An extra level.} A level loop that runs until the queue is empty also processes the last level, which
reaches nothing new. Stop when the targets are done, or subtract the last level.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong direction in a reverse search.} The reverse of ``flows to a lower or equal cell'' is ``climbs to a
higher or equal cell'': use \cd{>=}, not \cd{<=} and not \cd{>}. Give each search its own visited set.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Cell types.} A grid of strings holds \cd{"1"}, not \cd{1}. The test \cd{grid[r][c] == 1} is always
\cd{False} there. Diagonal cells connect only if the statement says so.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{The queue and the visited matrix.} \cd{list.pop(0)} is $O(n)$; use \cd{collections.deque}.
Build a visited matrix with a comprehension: \cd{[[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Changes to the input.} Sinking cells destroys the input. Copy the grid first if the caller needs it.
If you use a temporary marker such as \cd{"T"}, restore it in a final sweep.
A function that must change the input in place must not rebind the name to a new object.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Number of Islands & Count the flood fill starts. & Count each new land cell, then sink its whole island; push blindly, check on pop. \\
Max Area of Island & The flood fill returns its cell count; keep the maximum. & Scan for land; sink on push, count on pop, keep the max. \\
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow & Two reverse searches that climb from each ocean border; intersect the results. & Water flows down, so flood uphill from each ocean and keep the cells both floods reach. \\
Surrounded Regions & Flood from the border with a third symbol, then one sweep decodes the board. & Flood from the border, O becomes T; then O to X, T to O. \\
Rotting Oranges & Multi-source BFS by levels with a counter of fresh cells. & All rotten in the queue, count the fresh, one level is one minute, stop when fresh is zero. \\
Walls and Gates & Multi-source BFS from all gates; INF marks the cells not reached yet. & Push all gates first, then BFS and fill only INF rooms. \\
Open the Lock & BFS on $10^4$ codes with 8 moves each; dead ends start in the visited set. & BFS from 0000 with (code, turns) pairs; dead ends start in seen; 8 neighbors are each wheel plus or minus 1 mod 10. \\
Word Ladder & BFS on words; generate one-letter edits and look them up in a set; count words, not moves. & BFS of (word, length) pairs: change one letter, keep the word only if it is still in the unvisited set. \\

\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Graph structure: ordering, cycles and connectivity}\label{tech:T13}\label{sec:graph-structure}
The problems in this section ask about the shape of a graph, not about a distance.
Is there an order that respects all the rules? Which items belong together?
Does an extra link close a loop? Where does a forced walk stop?
Each question has a short template that visits every node and every edge a constant number of times.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
Many statements give a set of items and pairwise facts about them.
A fact ``$u$ comes before $v$'' is a directed edge $u \to v$.
A fact ``$a$ is linked to $b$'' is an undirected edge.
A brute force tries all $n!$ orders, or it starts a new search from every node.
The templates below do one pass over the graph, so they run in $O(V + E)$ or close to it (union-find adds a
small factor).
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Ordering (directed).} An order that respects every edge exists if and only if the graph has no
        directed cycle. In an acyclic graph, some node always waits for nothing, so it can go next.
        Kahn's algorithm takes such a node, removes its edges, and repeats.
        If it stops before it takes every node, the remaining nodes sit on a cycle or wait for one.
  \item \textbf{Grouping (undirected).} ``Linked to'' is symmetric. ``Connected by a path'' is also transitive,
        so the items fall into connected components. Flood fill from each unvisited node finds them.
        Union-find merges groups as the edges arrive, and it tells you when an edge joins a group to itself.
        That edge closes a cycle.
  \item \textbf{Forced walks (functional graph).} When each node has at most one next node, a walk has no choices.
        It is a chain that stops at a dead end, or a tail that runs into a cycle (a ``rho'' shape).
        The first repeated node proves a cycle, because from there the walk repeats the same steps forever.
        So one visited set stops the walk after at most $V$ steps.
  \item \textbf{Counting patterns.} A small pattern, such as a path of 3 edges, has exactly one center.
        Fix the center and multiply the independent choices on each side.
        A brute force lists every path, and the number of paths can be in the billions.
        The product counts them without listing them.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Worked example (ordering).} Take courses 0 to 3 with the rules 0 before 1, 0 before 2, 1 before 3 and
2 before 3. Count the unmet rules of each course: course 0 has 0, courses 1 and 2 have 1, course 3 has 2.
Take course 0. Now courses 1 and 2 have 0 unmet rules. Take course 1: course 3 drops to 1.
Take course 2: course 3 drops to 0. Take course 3. All four courses are taken, so the order 0, 1, 2, 3 is valid.
Now add the rule ``3 before 0''. Course 0 then has 1 unmet rule, and no course starts at 0.
The process takes no course, so a cycle exists.

\textbf{Worked example (grouping).} Take the undirected edges (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3) in this order.
Edge (1, 2) joins two groups. Edge (1, 3) joins group $\{1, 2\}$ and group $\{3\}$.
Edge (2, 3) finds both ends in the same group already. So this edge closes a cycle.

\textbf{Worked example (forced walk).} Take the next nodes $0 \to 1$, $1 \to 2$, $2 \to 3$ and $3 \to 1$.
The walk from 0 visits 0, 1, 2, 3. The next node of 3 is 1, and 1 is already visited.
So the walk has a tail of one node (0) and a cycle of three nodes (1, 2, 3).

\textbf{Worked example (counting).} Fix one middle edge $(a, b)$ of a path $p_0 - a - b - p_3$.
Node $a$ has 3 neighbors that can be $p_0$, and node $b$ has 4 neighbors that can be $p_3$.
The two choices are independent, so $3 \times 4 = 12$ paths use this middle edge. One multiplication replaces 12
listed paths.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{5.0cm}L{2.6cm}L{5.4cm}L{2.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Graph & Tool & Time \\
\midrule
Does an order exist? Give one. & directed & Kahn's algorithm (or DFS with three colors) & $O(V + E)$ \\
How many groups? Which group? & undirected & flood fill from each unvisited node & $O(V + E)$ \\
Does this new edge close a cycle? & undirected & union-find: same root means a cycle & $O(E \log V)$ or better \\
Is it a tree? & undirected & $n - 1$ edges and one flood reaches all nodes & $O(V + E)$ \\
Where does the walk stop? & out-degree $\le 1$ & successor map and a visited set & $O(V)$ \\
How many paths with 2 or 3 edges? & any & fix the middle, multiply side counts & $O(V + E)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input gives pairs such as ``take $b$ before $a$'', ``$a$ depends on $b$'', prerequisites, a build order,
        an install order or a deadlock. Each pair is a directed edge. Think topological sort.
  \item The task says ``return any valid order'' and ``return an empty result if it is impossible''.
        Impossible means a directed cycle. Kahn's algorithm finds both in one pass.
  \item A list is sorted by an unknown rule, and you must recover the rule. Neighbors in the list give the edges.
  \item The task asks how many groups, provinces, networks or clusters exist, or if two items are connected.
        The relation is symmetric and transitive. Think connected components.
  \item Edges arrive one at a time, and the task asks which edge creates a cycle or when two items become connected.
        Think union-find.
  \item The task asks if an undirected graph is a tree. Use the edge count $n - 1$ plus one connectivity check.
  \item Each node has at most one outgoing edge: a next pointer, an array \cd{i -> a[i]}, or a function applied
        again and again. Think functional graph: follow the only next node until a dead end or a repeat.
  \item The task counts paths of a small fixed length, $n$ and $m$ go up to $10^5$, and ``the answer can be large''.
        You cannot list the paths. Fix the middle and multiply.
  \item Groups come from a relation on values, such as $x$ and $x + 1$, and the task demands $O(n)$.
        Put the values in a hash set and start the work only at one member of each group.
  \item Chains can be thousands of nodes long. Avoid recursion, because CPython stops at a depth of about 1000.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Three templates cover most problems in this family. Learn them as three fixed shapes.

\subsubsection{Template 1: Kahn's topological sort}
Count the unmet requirements (the indegree) of each node. Put every node with indegree 0 in a queue.
Pop a node, append it to the order, and lower the indegree of each node that it points to.
Push a node when its indegree reaches 0. At the end, a short order means a cycle.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def topo_order(n, edges):              # edge (u, v): u must come before v
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n                 # unmet requirements of each node
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        indegree[v] += 1
    queue = deque(v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:             # u is done: v waits for one node less
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                queue.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []   # short order: a cycle blocks some nodes

topo_order(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])            # -> [0, 1, 2, 3]
topo_order(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 0)])    # -> []
topo_order(3, [])                                          # -> [0, 1, 2]
topo_order(2, [(1, 1)])                                    # -> []
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} \cd{indegree[v]} equals the number of requirements of \cd{v} that are not in the order yet.
The queue holds exactly the nodes with indegree 0 that are not in the order yet.
A node on a cycle always waits for another node of the cycle, so it never reaches 0.
So \cd{len(order) == n} holds if and only if the graph has no cycle.

\subsubsection{Template 2: flood fill to count components}
Loop over all nodes. Each unvisited node starts a new component. Mark everything that it reaches with a stack.
\begin{pyex}
def count_components(n, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in edges:
        graph[a].append(b)             # undirected: add both directions
        graph[b].append(a)
    seen = [False] * n
    count = 0
    for start in range(n):
        if seen[start]:
            continue                   # an earlier flood already reached it
        count += 1                     # a new start is a new component
        seen[start] = True
        stack = [start]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            for nxt in graph[node]:
                if not seen[nxt]:
                    seen[nxt] = True   # mark on push, not on pop
                    stack.append(nxt)
    return count

count_components(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4)])              # -> 2
count_components(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)])      # -> 1
count_components(3, [])                                    # -> 3
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} Every node in \cd{seen} is reachable from a start that the loop already counted.
Each node enters the stack at most once. When the stack is empty, the flood has marked the whole component of
\cd{start}. To get the group of each node, store the component number in a list instead of \cd{True}.

\subsubsection{Template 3: union-find}
Each group is a tree of parent links. The root names the group. \cd{find} walks up to the root.
\cd{union} links one root under the other root. A union of two nodes with the same root fails: the edge closes a cycle.
\begin{pyex}
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))   # every node starts as its own root
        self.groups = n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]   # path halving
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False               # same root already: this edge closes a cycle
        self.parent[ra] = rb           # link root to root
        self.groups -= 1
        return True

d = DSU(5)
[d.union(a, b) for a, b in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (3, 4)]]
# -> [True, True, False, True]
d.groups                                         # -> 2
d.find(0) == d.find(2), d.find(0) == d.find(3)   # -> (True, False)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} After the first $k$ edges, the sets are exactly the connected components of the graph with
those $k$ edges. \cd{groups} equals $n$ minus the number of successful unions.
Path halving is a one-pass form of path compression: each step points a node at its grandparent.
\begin{note}
For the tight bound, also keep a \cd{size} list and link the smaller root under the larger root (union by size).
Then each operation costs almost $O(1)$ ($O(\alpha(n))$ amortized). Path halving alone gives $O(\log n)$ amortized,
which is enough for $n$ up to about $10^5$. The recursive form \cd{parent[x] = find(parent[x])} also compresses
paths, but a long chain can pass the recursion limit before the first compression.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Can every task finish?}
Course Schedule gives pairs \cd{[a, b]}: take \cd{b} before \cd{a}. It asks only if all courses can finish.
Run Template 1 and compare the number of taken courses with the number of courses.
Memory hook: \emph{take what is ready, free its dependents, check that you took everything.}
Disconnected parts and self-loops need no special code: the queue starts with every free node, and a self-loop
never reaches indegree 0. A DFS with three colors (below) also works, but a chain of 2000 courses needs a
recursion depth of 2000.

\subsubsection{Return one valid order}
Course Schedule II returns the order itself, or an empty list. Now the edge direction matters.
The pair \cd{[a, b]} means the edge \cd{b -> a}, because \cd{b} comes first.
Reversed edges give a reversed order. Memory hook: \emph{count unmet prerequisites, take any course at zero;
a short order means a cycle.}
Two small changes to the queue answer two common follow-up questions.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Minimum number of rounds} (semesters, parallel steps): process the queue one level at a time.
        The number of levels is the answer. It equals the number of nodes on the longest path.
  \item \textbf{Lexicographically smallest order}: replace the deque with a min-heap of free nodes.
\end{itemize}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import deque

def build(n, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        indegree[v] += 1
    return graph, indegree

def rounds(n, edges):                  # minimum number of rounds; -1 on a cycle
    graph, indegree = build(n, edges)
    level = [v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0]
    count = done = 0
    while level:
        count += 1
        done += len(level)
        next_level = []
        for u in level:
            for v in graph[u]:
                indegree[v] -= 1
                if indegree[v] == 0:
                    next_level.append(v)
        level = next_level
    return count if done == n else -1

def smallest_order(n, edges):          # the smallest order in dictionary order
    graph, indegree = build(n, edges)
    heap = [v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    order = []
    while heap:
        u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(heap, v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

def fifo_order(n, edges):              # Template 1, for comparison
    graph, indegree = build(n, edges)
    queue = deque(v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                queue.append(v)
    return order

rounds(4, [(0, 3), (1, 3), (3, 2)])    # -> 3
rounds(2, [(0, 1), (1, 0)])            # -> -1
fifo_order(3, [(1, 0)])                # -> [1, 2, 0]
smallest_order(3, [(1, 0)])            # -> [1, 0, 2]
\end{pyex}
The order of Template 1 depends on when a node becomes free. Node 0 becomes free after node 2 is already in the
queue. The heap always takes the smallest free node.
The same idea of peeling free nodes works on an undirected tree: peel the leaves (degree 1) layer by layer to find
the center (Minimum Height Trees).
To compute a value for each node from its predecessors, such as an earliest finish time, update the value of
\cd{v} when you lower its indegree. Every input of a node is final before the node leaves the queue.

\subsubsection{DFS with three colors}
A DFS also finds a directed cycle and an order. Give each node one of three colors: white (not seen),
gray (on the current path) and black (finished). An edge to a gray node is a back edge, so it closes a cycle.
An edge to a black node is safe. A node finishes after every node that it points to, so the reversed finish
order is a topological order.
Memory hook: \emph{gray is the current path; an edge to gray is a cycle; reverse the finish order.}
\begin{pyex}
def dfs_topo(n, edges):                # edge (u, v): u before v; [] on a cycle
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
    WHITE, GRAY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2
    color = [WHITE] * n
    finished = []
    def visit(u):
        color[u] = GRAY
        for v in graph[u]:
            if color[v] == GRAY:
                return False           # back edge: a cycle
            if color[v] == WHITE and not visit(v):
                return False
        color[u] = BLACK
        finished.append(u)             # u finishes after all nodes that it points to
        return True
    for u in range(n):
        if color[u] == WHITE and not visit(u):
            return []
    return finished[::-1]

dfs_topo(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])              # -> [0, 2, 1, 3]
dfs_topo(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)])                      # -> []
dfs_topo(3000, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(2999)])          # -> raises RecursionError
\end{pyex}
Use the colors when you need the set of nodes that can reach a cycle (Find Eventual Safe States).
Then do not stop at the first cycle: run \cd{visit} from every node. A node is safe if its DFS finishes black,
and a node that stays gray can reach a cycle. Prefer Kahn's algorithm when a chain can be long.
If the edges point from a node to its prerequisites (\cd{a -> b}), the finish order is already correct; do not reverse it.

\subsubsection{Derive the edges from a sorted list}
In Alien Dictionary, the words are sorted by an unknown letter order, and the task is to recover that order.
Compare only neighboring words: the order is transitive, so other pairs add nothing new.
In each neighboring pair, only the first differing letters give a fact: the letter of the first word comes first.
The letters after that position give nothing. If the shared prefix is equal and the first word is longer,
no order can sort the list. Every letter is a node, also when no fact mentions it.
Memory hook: \emph{compare neighbors: a longer word before its prefix fails, else the first difference gives one
edge. Kahn gives the order. A short order means a cycle.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def alien_order(words):
    graph = {c: set() for w in words for c in w}   # every letter is a node
    indegree = {c: 0 for c in graph}
    for w1, w2 in zip(words, words[1:]):
        if len(w1) > len(w2) and w1.startswith(w2):
            return ""                              # a longer word before its own prefix
        for a, b in zip(w1, w2):
            if a != b:
                if b not in graph[a]:              # count each edge one time only
                    graph[a].add(b)
                    indegree[b] += 1
                break                              # only the first difference counts
    queue = deque(c for c in graph if indegree[c] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        c = queue.popleft()
        order.append(c)
        for nxt in graph[c]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return "".join(order) if len(order) == len(graph) else ""

alien_order(["wrt", "wrf", "er", "ett", "rftt"])   # -> 'wertf'
alien_order(["z", "x", "z"])                       # -> ''
alien_order(["abc", "ab"])                         # -> ''
alien_order(["ab", "ab"])                          # -> 'ab'
\end{pyex}
The general rule for a lexicographic comparison has three parts. The first difference gives a strict fact.
An equal prefix gives a length fact. Everything after the first difference gives nothing.
When many orders are valid, test an answer by checking every edge, not by comparing it with one fixed string.

\subsubsection{Cycle detection: directed or undirected}
The tool depends on the direction of the edges. Union-find ignores direction, so it reports false cycles in a
directed graph.
Memory hook: \emph{directed: Kahn or colors; undirected: union-find or skip the parent.}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.6cm}L{6.4cm}L{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Graph & Tool & Sign of a cycle \\
\midrule
directed & Kahn's algorithm & the order has fewer than $n$ nodes \\
directed & DFS with three colors & an edge to a gray node \\
undirected & union-find & an edge whose ends have the same root \\
undirected & DFS that skips the edge back to its parent & a neighbor that is seen and is not the parent \\
undirected & counting & a connected graph with $n$ nodes and at least $n$ edges \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
def undirected_cycle(n, edges):        # iterative DFS with a parent check
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in edges:
        graph[a].append(b)
        graph[b].append(a)
    seen = [False] * n
    for s in range(n):
        if seen[s]:
            continue
        seen[s] = True
        stack = [(s, -1)]
        while stack:
            node, parent = stack.pop()
            for nxt in graph[node]:
                if nxt == parent:
                    continue           # the edge back to the parent is not a cycle
                if seen[nxt]:
                    return True
                seen[nxt] = True
                stack.append((nxt, node))
    return False

def union_find_cycle(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    for a, b in edges:
        ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return True
        parent[ra] = rb
    return False

triangle = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)]
undirected_cycle(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2)])  # -> False
undirected_cycle(3, triangle)          # -> True
union_find_cycle(3, triangle)          # -> True
dag = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)]         # directed edges: no directed cycle
union_find_cycle(3, dag)               # -> True
\end{pyex}
The last line is wrong for a directed graph. Two paths from 0 to 2 are not a cycle when the edges have a direction.

\subsubsection{First edge that closes a cycle}
Redundant Connection gives a tree on nodes $1$ to $n$ plus one extra edge. It asks for the cycle edge that occurs
last in the input. Add the edges in input order. The first edge whose ends already share a root is the answer.
Memory hook: \emph{same root already? That edge closes the cycle.}
\begin{pyex}
def redundant_connection(edges):       # nodes 1..n and n == len(edges)
    parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1))   # index 0 is not used
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    for a, b in edges:
        ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return [a, b]              # already connected: this edge closes the cycle
        parent[ra] = rb
    return []

redundant_connection([[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]])                    # -> [2, 3]
redundant_connection([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 4], [1, 5]])    # -> [1, 4]
\end{pyex}
The tie-break ``the last one in the input'' needs no extra work. A cycle is complete only when its last edge arrives,
so the first conflict in a forward scan is the last cycle edge. This is a reusable idea: when a rule asks for the
last element that completes a structure, scan forward and stop at the moment of completion.
The optimal form adds union by size for the $O(n \alpha(n))$ bound. For $n \le 1000$, path halving alone is enough.
The same loop is the core of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree: sort the edges by weight and skip each edge that
closes a cycle.

\subsubsection{Count the groups}
Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph is Template 2 without changes.
Memory hook: \emph{count how many times you must start a new flood.}
Isolated nodes are components too, so loop over all $n$ nodes, not only over the nodes in the edges.
The optimal solution uses union-find: the count is $n$ minus the successful unions (Template 3).
It needs no adjacency list, and it reports the count after each new edge when edges arrive over time.
A grid is the same problem with an implicit graph (Number of Islands).
Other aggregates come from the same flood: the size of each group, or a list of its members.

\subsubsection{Is it a tree?}
Graph Valid Tree asks if $n$ nodes and an undirected edge list form one tree.
A graph on $n$ nodes is a tree when any two of these three facts hold: it has $n - 1$ edges, it is connected,
it has no cycle. Check the cheap fact first (the edge count). Then check connectivity with one flood.
With $n - 1$ edges, connected means acyclic, so you need no cycle logic.
Memory hook: \emph{a tree has $n - 1$ edges and reaches everyone.}
\begin{pyex}
def valid_tree(n, edges):
    if len(edges) != n - 1:
        return False                   # a tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in edges:
        adj[a].append(b)
        adj[b].append(a)
    seen = {0}
    stack = [0]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        for nei in adj[node]:
            if nei not in seen:
                seen.add(nei)
                stack.append(nei)
    return len(seen) == n              # n - 1 edges and connected: no cycle

valid_tree(5, [[0, 1], [0, 2], [0, 3], [1, 4]])             # -> True
valid_tree(5, [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 3], [1, 4]])     # -> False
valid_tree(4, [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0]])                     # -> False
valid_tree(1, [])                                           # -> True
\end{pyex}
The third call has $n - 1$ edges, but it is a triangle plus an isolated node. So the count alone is not enough.
A related counting fact: a forest (no cycle) with $n$ nodes and $E$ edges has exactly $n - E$ components.

\subsubsection{Groups on values: runs of consecutive numbers}
Longest Consecutive Sequence asks for the longest run of values $x, x + 1, x + 2, \ldots$ in an unsorted array,
in $O(n)$ time. Think of an edge between $x$ and $x + 1$. Each component is a run.
A walk up from every value repeats work, because each member of a long run walks the rest of the run again.
Instead, start the walk only at one member of each group: the value $x$ with $x - 1$ missing.
Memory hook: \emph{only start counting where $x - 1$ is missing.}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_consecutive(nums):
    values = set(nums)
    longest = 0
    for start in values:               # loop over the set, not over nums
        if start - 1 in values:
            continue                   # not the start of a run
        length = 1
        while start + length in values:
            length += 1
        longest = max(longest, length)
    return longest

longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2])           # -> 4
longest_consecutive([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1])   # -> 9
longest_consecutive([])                               # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Each value is visited by exactly one walk, so the total work is $O(n)$ on average.
The general rule: to process each group once, find a cheap local test that is true for exactly one member of each
group, and start the work only there. Union-find on values (union $x$ with $x + 1$) also works, and it handles
values that arrive one at a time. With a different neighbor rule, such as $x \to x^2$ on positive values, the same
idea applies: start only where the predecessor $\sqrt{x}$ is missing.

\subsubsection{Functional graphs: follow the only next node}
In a functional graph, each node has at most one outgoing edge. Linked lists, arrays read as \cd{i -> a[i]},
and a function applied again and again are all functional graphs.
A typical task walks from a start node through a network where each node has at most one next node.
It returns the dead end, or the last node before the walk repeats a node. Build a successor map, keep a visited set, and look at the next node before you move.
Then the current node is the answer in both stop cases.
Memory hook: \emph{map next, mark seen, peek before you step.}
\begin{pyex}
def find_endpoint(edges, start):
    nxt = {u: v for u, v in edges}     # each node has at most one next node
    seen = {start}
    cur = start
    while cur in nxt:                  # stop at a node with no next node
        step = nxt[cur]
        if step in seen:               # the next step would repeat a node
            return cur
        seen.add(step)
        cur = step
    return cur

find_endpoint([[1, 3], [7, 3], [3, 4], [4, 6], [2, 6], [6, 9], [9, 5]], 1)   # -> 5
find_endpoint([[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0]], 0)              # -> 2
find_endpoint([[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 1]], 0)      # -> 3
find_endpoint([[4, 4]], 4), find_endpoint([], 8)        # -> (4, 8)
\end{pyex}
To measure the rho shape, store the step index of each node instead of a plain visited set.
The first repeated node is the cycle entry. Its stored index is the tail length, and the difference of the two
indexes is the cycle length. Call these two numbers $t$ and $c$.
For $k \ge t$, the node after $k$ steps is the node after $t + ((k - t) \bmod c)$ steps.
So a huge $k$ needs no long walk.
\begin{pyex}
def rho(nxt, start):                   # nxt: dict from node to next node
    step_of = {}                       # node: its step index on the walk
    cur, step = start, 0
    while cur in nxt and cur not in step_of:
        step_of[cur] = step
        cur, step = nxt[cur], step + 1
    if cur not in step_of:
        return step, 0                 # dead end after step moves: no cycle
    return step_of[cur], step - step_of[cur]   # (tail length, cycle length)

rho({0: 1, 1: 2, 2: 3, 3: 1}, 0)       # -> (1, 3)
rho({4: 4}, 4)                         # -> (0, 1)
rho({0: 1, 1: 2}, 0)                   # -> (2, 0)
\end{pyex}
For $O(1)$ extra memory, use Floyd's tortoise and hare (Linked List Cycle, Find the Duplicate Number).
When many starts share one graph, mark each node as unvisited, in progress or done, so each node is resolved once.

\subsubsection{Count fixed-length paths: fix the middle}
Take a road network where each shop has one of the types 0, 1, 2 and 3.
The task counts the paths $p_0 - p_1 - p_2 - p_3$ in an undirected graph that use each type exactly once.
A path and its reverse count separately.
With $n$ and $m$ up to $10^5$, the number of paths can reach billions, so you cannot list them.
Every path with 3 edges has exactly one middle edge. Fix the middle edge $(a, b)$.
Then $p_0$ is any neighbor of $a$ with one missing type, and $p_3$ is any neighbor of $b$ with the other missing type.
The two choices are independent, so multiply. Precompute \cd{near[v][t]}, the number of neighbors of \cd{v} with
type \cd{t}, in one pass. All four types differ, so the four shops are different automatically.
Memory hook: \emph{fix the middle road, multiply the end choices, double for reverse.}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import permutations

def count_routes(shops, roads):
    near = [[0] * 4 for _ in shops]    # near[v][t]: neighbors of v with type t
    for a, b in roads:
        near[a][shops[b]] += 1
        near[b][shops[a]] += 1
    total = 0
    for a, b in roads:                 # each road as the middle p1 - p2
        if shops[a] == shops[b]:
            continue
        x, y = {0, 1, 2, 3} - {shops[a], shops[b]}   # types of the two ends
        total += near[a][x] * near[b][y] + near[a][y] * near[b][x]
    return 2 * total                   # every route also runs backwards

def brute(shops, roads):
    edge = {(a, b) for a, b in roads} | {(b, a) for a, b in roads}
    return sum(1 for p in permutations(range(len(shops)), 4)
               if {shops[v] for v in p} == {0, 1, 2, 3}
               and all((p[i], p[i + 1]) in edge for i in range(3)))

count_routes([0, 1, 2, 3], [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3]])            # -> 2
count_routes([0, 1, 2, 3], [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 0]])    # -> 8
shops = [0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0]
roads = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 0], [0, 4], [4, 5], [5, 3], [1, 5], [6, 4], [6, 2]]
count_routes(shops, roads) == brute(shops, roads)               # -> True
\end{pyex}
The general rule: pick the unique center of the pattern and multiply the counts on its sides.
A path with 2 edges has a middle node. A path with 3 edges has a middle edge. A triple $i < j < k$ in an array has
a middle index $j$. When labels can repeat, the side choices can overlap, and you must subtract the overlaps.
For example, count the unlabeled simple paths with 3 edges (a path and its reverse count once).
Start with $\sum (\deg(a) - 1)(\deg(b) - 1)$ over the edges $(a, b)$.
This sum also counts the case $p_0 = p_3$, which is a triangle and not a path.
Each triangle occurs 3 times, one time for each of its edges as the middle. So subtract 3 times the number of
triangles. For longer paths with distinct labels, use a bitmask DP over the set of used labels.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Name the nodes and the edges.} Is a fact ``before'' (directed), ``linked'' (undirected), or
        ``next'' (at most one outgoing edge)? Write the direction of one sample edge in a comment.
  \item \textbf{Find the edges.} Are they given, or must you derive them? Derived edges come from neighbors in a
        sorted list, from value neighbors such as $x + 1$, or from a shared key such as an email address.
  \item \textbf{Name the question.} An order or ``is it possible'' needs Template 1. Groups or a count of groups need
        Template 2. A first edge that breaks a property, or edges that arrive over time, need Template 3.
        A forced walk needs a successor map. A count of small patterns needs a fixed center.
  \item \textbf{Use the counting facts.} A tree has $n - 1$ edges. A connected graph with $n$ edges has exactly one
        cycle. Components equal $n$ minus the successful unions.
  \item \textbf{Cover every node.} Seed the queue or the outer loop with all $n$ nodes, not only the nodes in the
        edges.
  \item \textbf{Check the depth.} If a chain can be longer than about 1000 nodes, use a queue, an explicit stack
        or union-find with an iterative \cd{find}.
  \item \textbf{Check the extra rules.} A required order (smallest first) needs a heap. A number of rounds needs
        levels. A value for each node needs an update in topological order.
  \item \textbf{Test on small inputs.} Compare with a brute force: all permutations for an order, a fresh search
        for connectivity, or all tuples for a path count.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Edge direction.} The pair \cd{[a, b]} in ``take \cd{b} before \cd{a}'' is the edge \cd{b -> a}.
Reversed edges keep the yes/no answer of a cycle check, but they reverse the order.
Write the direction in a comment before you build the graph.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{One visited set in a directed DFS.} A single set cannot tell ``on the current path'' from ``finished''.
On a diamond, two paths reach the same finished node, and the DFS reports a false cycle. Use three colors.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def wrong_has_cycle(n, edges):         # one set for "on the path" and "finished"
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
    visited = set()
    def visit(u):
        if u in visited:
            return True                # wrong: u can be finished, not on the path
        visited.add(u)
        return any(visit(v) for v in graph[u])
    return any(visit(u) for u in range(n) if u not in visited)

diamond = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)]   # no cycle
wrong_has_cycle(4, diamond)            # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Union-find on a directed graph.} Union-find ignores direction. It reports a cycle for
\cd{0 -> 1 -> 2} plus \cd{0 -> 2}, which has none. Use it only for undirected connectivity.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Compare roots and link roots.} Two nodes of one group can have different parent entries.
Compare \cd{find(a)} with \cd{find(b)}, not \cd{parent[a]} with \cd{parent[b]}.
Link \cd{parent[ra] = rb}. The assignment \cd{parent[a] = b} moves only node \cd{a} and the nodes below it, and it
cuts them away from the rest of their old group.
Compare the roots before the union, not after it.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
parent = [1, 2, 2]                     # 0 -> 1 -> 2: one group with root 2
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x
parent[0] == parent[2]                 # -> False
find(0) == find(2)                     # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The final count check.} Nodes on a cycle never reach indegree 0. Kahn's algorithm then returns a short
order and raises no error. Compare \cd{len(order)} with $n$ and return the empty result.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Duplicate derived edges.} When you derive edges (for example from word pairs), the same edge can appear two
times. If the successors sit in a set, each copy still adds 1 to the indegree, but the set holds the node only one
time. The indegree then never reaches 0, and a valid input returns ``impossible''. Test \cd{b not in graph[a]}
before you add the edge and raise the indegree.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Isolated nodes.} A node that appears in no edge is still a node. It is a component, it is a free course, and
it must be in the order. Take the node count from $n$ (or from all letters), not from the edges.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion depth.} A recursive DFS or a recursive \cd{find} on a chain of 2000 nodes passes the CPython limit
of 1000 and raises \cd{RecursionError} (see the \cd{dfs_topo} example). Use Kahn's algorithm, an explicit stack,
or an iterative \cd{find}. \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit} helps only up to the size of the C stack
(Section~\ref{sec:recursion}).
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Undirected details.} Add each undirected edge in both directions. In a DFS cycle check, skip the edge back to
the parent, or every edge looks like a cycle. Build the adjacency list with \cd{[[] for _ in range(n)]}, never
with \cd{[[]] * n}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Group starts.} In the run-start pattern, loop over the set, not over the input list. Many copies of one run
start in the list repeat the full walk many times. Start \cd{longest} at 0 for an empty input.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Forced walks.} Put the start node in the visited set before the first step. Test the next node before you
move, or you return the repeated node instead of the node before it. A node that is never a source has no key in
the successor map; test with \cd{in} before you index.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Middle-edge counting.} Use both assignments of the two missing types. Multiply by 2 only if the loop visits
each undirected edge one time. Precompute the neighbor counts. A scan of the neighbor lists for each edge costs the
sum of the squared degrees, and that is too slow on a star.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Queues.} \cd{list.pop(0)} costs $O(n)$. Use \cd{collections.deque} and \cd{popleft()}.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Course Schedule & Only feasibility: Template 1 and the count \cd{taken == n}. &
  Take what is ready, free its dependents, check that you took everything. \\
Course Schedule II & Return the order; the pair \cd{[a, b]} is the edge \cd{b -> a}. &
  Count unmet prerequisites. Take any course at zero. A short order means a cycle. \\
Alien Dictionary & Derive the edges from the first difference of neighboring words; a longer word before its
  prefix fails. & Compare neighbors: a longer word before its prefix fails, else the first difference gives one
  edge. Kahn gives the order. A short order means a cycle. \\
Redundant Connection & Union-find in input order; return the first edge with the same root at both ends. &
  Same root already? That edge closes the cycle. \\
Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph & Count the flood starts (or $n$ minus the successful unions). &
  Count how many times you must start a new flood. \\
Graph Valid Tree & Check $n - 1$ edges, then one flood that reaches all nodes. &
  A tree has $n - 1$ edges and reaches everyone. \\
Longest Consecutive Sequence & Groups on values ($x$ and $x + 1$); walk only from the start of each run. &
  Only start counting where $x - 1$ is missing. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

% =====================================================================
\section{Weighted and advanced graphs}\label{tech:T14}

\subsection{The idea}
BFS finds the path with the fewest edges. When edges have different costs, this is not enough:
a path with more edges can cost less. Dijkstra fixes this with one change.
