The FIFO queue becomes a min-heap that orders the nodes by their distance so far.

Think of a wave that starts at the source and moves along all edges at the same time.
The wave reaches each node at its shortest distance, and it reaches the nodes in order of that distance.
The heap replays the wave. Each pop gives the next node that the wave reaches.

\textbf{Worked example.} The directed edges are A$\to$B (4), A$\to$C (1), C$\to$B (2) and B$\to$D (1).
Start at A with the heap \cd{[(0, A)]}.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Pop \cd{(0, A)}. A is final at 0. Push \cd{(4, B)} and \cd{(1, C)}.
  \item Pop \cd{(1, C)}. C is final at 1. Push \cd{(3, B)}, because $1 + 2 = 3$.
  \item Pop \cd{(3, B)}. B is final at 3. Push \cd{(4, D)}.
  \item Pop \cd{(4, B)}. B is already final, so skip this old copy.
  \item Pop \cd{(4, D)}. D is final at 4. The heap is empty, so stop.
\end{enumerate}
BFS puts B one edge from A, at cost 4. The cheaper route A$\to$C$\to$B has two edges.

Why is the first pop of a node final? Every entry that is still in the heap is at least as large.
An edge with a non-negative weight cannot make a longer path cheaper.
A brute force tries every path, and the number of paths can grow exponentially.
Dijkstra handles each edge one time, so it costs $O(E \log E)$.

The other problems of this family change one part of this picture.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{5.6cm}L{5.4cm}L{5.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & What changes & Tool \\
\midrule
Shortest time from one source; time until all nodes are reached & nothing & Dijkstra with \cd{d + w} \\
Lowest possible highest point on a route & combine with \cd{max} instead of \cd{+} & Dijkstra with \cd{max}, or binary search on the level \\
Cheapest set of edges that connects all nodes & the cost is the total of the chosen edges, not a path & minimum spanning tree: Prim or Kruskal \\
Cheapest path with at most $k$ edges & a second limit on the path & Bellman-Ford for $k$ rounds from a copy, or BFS by levels \\
Cheapest path under a limit on another resource & the state is (node, resource) & Dijkstra on states \\
Use every edge exactly one time & the answer is an order of edges, not a cost & Hierholzer (Euler path) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Edges carry a cost, time, price or distance, and the task asks for the minimum total from a source.
        Different weights rule out BFS. Non-negative weights allow Dijkstra.
  \item ``When do all nodes receive the signal'': each node gets it at its shortest distance.
        The answer is the maximum of these distances, not their sum.
  \item A route is usable only when every cell or edge on it is at or below some level.
        Phrases: ``earliest time that A and B connect'', ``minimum effort'', ``smallest limit so that a path exists''.
        This is a bottleneck (minimax) path.
        A higher level never removes a route, so binary search on the level also works.
  \item ``Connect all points at minimum total cost'', ``exactly one path between any two points'',
        ``no redundant link'': a minimum spanning tree (MST).
  \item A formula gives the cost of every pair, for example the distance between two points.
        The graph is complete and implicit. Compute each weight when you need it.
  \item ``At most $k$ stops, moves or edges'': the cheapest path overall can break the limit.
        Run one Bellman-Ford round, or one BFS level, for each edge that the path can use.
  \item A limit on another resource (fuel, time, coupons, obstacles to remove): put the resource in the state.
  \item ``Use every ticket, pair or domino exactly one time'', and the end of one item is the start of the next:
        an Euler path. Nodes can repeat; edges cannot.
  \item ``Visit every node exactly one time'' is a different problem (a Hamiltonian path).
        It needs backtracking or bitmask DP, and it is exponential.
  \item A negative weight rules out Dijkstra. Use Bellman-Ford.
  \item Sizes: a heap suits $E$ up to about $10^5$ to $10^6$. A complete graph with $V \approx 10^3$ has
        $5 \cdot 10^5$ edges. Do not store them; use an $O(V^2)$ scan.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
Dijkstra with lazy deletion. Do not decrease a key in the heap. Push a new entry instead,
and skip an entry at pop time when its node is already final.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

def dijkstra(graph, src):
    # graph[u] = list of (v, w), every w >= 0. Returns {node: shortest distance}.
    dist = {}                            # final distances; also the visited set
    heap = [(0, src)]                    # (distance so far, node): distance first
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if u in dist:                    # an old copy: u is already final
            continue
        dist[u] = d                      # the first pop gives the shortest distance
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if v not in dist:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, v))
    return dist

graph = defaultdict(list)
for u, v, w in [("A", "B", 4), ("A", "C", 1), ("C", "B", 2), ("B", "D", 1)]:
    graph[u].append((v, w))              # directed edge from u to v
dijkstra(graph, "A")                     # -> {'A': 0, 'C': 1, 'B': 3, 'D': 4}

def network_delay_time(times, n, k):     # Network Delay Time: nodes 1 .. n
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in times:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    dist = dijkstra(graph, k)
    return max(dist.values()) if len(dist) == n else -1

network_delay_time([[2, 1, 1], [2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1]], 4, 2)   # -> 2
network_delay_time([[1, 2, 1]], 2, 1)                         # -> 1
network_delay_time([[1, 2, 1]], 2, 2)                         # -> -1
network_delay_time([], 1, 1)                                  # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} \cd{dist} holds only final nodes, and each value is the true shortest distance.
The heap holds candidates, and some of them are old copies.
When a node pops for the first time, no other path can be shorter: every other entry is at least as large,
and no weight is negative.

Three small changes cover most uses.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{One target.} Return \cd{d} when the target pops. Do not return when it is pushed.
  \item \textbf{Several sources.} Start the heap with \cd{(0, s)} for each source.
  \item \textbf{Implicit graph.} Replace \cd{graph[u]} with code that makes the neighbors:
        the four cells around a grid cell, or the next states of a puzzle.
\end{itemize}
\begin{note}
The tuple puts the distance first, so the heap orders by distance. On a tie, Python compares the second item.
A one-item list \cd{[(0, src)]} is already a valid heap, so no \cd{heapify} call is necessary.
\end{note}

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Time until every node is reached}
Something spreads from one node along all edges at the same time. Each node gets it at its shortest distance.
So the answer is the largest final distance, or $-1$ when a node is not reached
(Network Delay Time). The core template already solves it.
Compare the number of final nodes with $n$. A node with no edges is not in the edge list, but it still counts.
Memory hook: \emph{the first pop of a node is its arrival time.}

\subsubsection{Bottleneck paths: the highest point on a route}
Here a route is usable at level $t$ only when every cell on it is at most $t$.
So the cost of a route is its highest cell, not a sum. The answer is the minimum over all routes of that maximum.
Dijkstra still works with \cd{max} in place of \cd{+}.
The reason: \cd{max} never makes a path cheaper when the path grows, so the first pop is still final
(Swim in Rising Water).
Memory hook: \emph{Dijkstra, but the path cost is the highest cell, so use max instead of plus.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq

def swim_in_water(grid):                 # Swim in Rising Water
    n = len(grid)
    heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]          # (highest cell on the path, row, col)
    visited = set()
    while heap:
        t, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if (r, c) in visited:
            continue                     # an old copy with a key that is not smaller
        visited.add((r, c))              # t is final for (r, c)
        if (r, c) == (n - 1, n - 1):
            return t
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and (nr, nc) not in visited:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (max(t, grid[nr][nc]), nr, nc))   # max, not +
    return -1

swim_in_water([[0, 2], [1, 3]])          # -> 3
swim_in_water([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [24, 23, 22, 21, 5], [12, 13, 14, 15, 16],
               [11, 17, 18, 19, 20], [10, 9, 8, 7, 6]])   # -> 16
swim_in_water([[0]])                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}
The heap key has a direct meaning: it is the earliest time at which you can reach that cell.
The start cell counts, so the heap starts with \cd{grid[0][0]}, not with 0.
For a cost on the edges, for example the height difference between two cells, change only the key formula.
A shorter form marks a cell when it is pushed. It has the same $O(n^2 \log n)$ cost, but it is correct only
because the cost to enter a cell depends on the cell alone. With a cost on the edges, it can give wrong answers.

\textbf{Other combine rules.} Dijkstra works when the combine step never makes a path better as it grows.
A sum of non-negative weights, a maximum, and a product of factors that are at least 1 all satisfy this.
To maximize a minimum, or a product of probabilities in $[0, 1]$, use a max-heap: push the negated key.

\textbf{Alternative: binary search on the level.} If the corners connect at level $t$, they connect at every
larger level. So binary search for the first level that connects them, with one BFS for each check.
This costs $O(n^2 \log n)$, the same as Dijkstra.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

def connected_at(grid, t):               # can you go corner to corner on cells <= t?
    n = len(grid)
    if grid[0][0] > t:
        return False
    seen = {(0, 0)}
    queue = deque([(0, 0)])
    while queue:
        r, c = queue.popleft()
        if (r, c) == (n - 1, n - 1):
            return True
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if (0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and (nr, nc) not in seen
                    and grid[nr][nc] <= t):
                seen.add((nr, nc))
                queue.append((nr, nc))
    return False

def swim_by_level(grid):
    lo, hi = grid[0][0], max(map(max, grid))   # the answer is in [lo, hi]
    while lo < hi:                       # find the first level that connects
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if connected_at(grid, mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

swim_by_level([[0, 2], [1, 3]])          # -> 3
grid = [[0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [24, 23, 22, 21, 5], [12, 13, 14, 15, 16],
        [11, 17, 18, 19, 20], [10, 9, 8, 7, 6]]
swim_by_level(grid)                      # -> 16
\end{pyex}
A third method adds the cells in increasing order of value and joins each new cell to its active neighbors
with union-find. The answer is the value at which the start and the end first share a root.
This is Kruskal's order (next subsection). The path between two nodes in an MST is always a minimax path.
\begin{note}
When the values are a permutation of $0$ to $N - 1$, store the position of each value in an array.
Then you can add the cells in value order without a sort.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Minimum spanning tree: connect everything at minimum total cost}
The goal is the total weight of the chosen edges, not the length of one path.
With non-negative weights, a cheapest connected set never needs a cycle:
remove the heaviest edge of a cycle, and all nodes stay connected.
So the answer is a minimum spanning tree (MST).
The \textbf{cut property} makes greedy growth safe: for any split of the nodes into two groups,
the cheapest edge across the split belongs to some MST.

\textbf{Prim} grows one tree from any node. Each round adds the outside node with the cheapest edge to the tree.
On a complete graph, keep one value for each outside node and scan the values.
This costs $O(V^2)$ time and $O(V)$ memory, and it stores no edges.
A dict that holds only the outside nodes is also the to-do list (Min Cost to Connect All Points).
Memory hook: \emph{keep a dict of outside points: pop the nearest, then let it lower the others.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_cost_connect_points(points):     # Min Cost to Connect All Points
    # cost[v] = cheapest edge from the outside point v to the tree
    cost = {v: float("inf") for v in range(len(points))}
    cost[0] = 0
    total = 0
    while cost:
        u = min(cost, key=cost.get)      # the nearest outside point joins the tree
        total += cost.pop(u)
        ux, uy = points[u]
        for v in cost:                   # the new tree point can lower the others
            d = abs(ux - points[v][0]) + abs(uy - points[v][1])
            if d < cost[v]:
                cost[v] = d
    return total

min_cost_connect_points([[0, 0], [2, 2], [3, 10], [5, 2], [7, 0]])   # -> 20
min_cost_connect_points([[3, 12], [-2, 5], [-4, 1]])                 # -> 18
min_cost_connect_points([[0, 0]])                                    # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Compare it with Dijkstra. Both grow a set from one node. Dijkstra keys a node by the whole path cost \cd{d + w}.
Prim keys a node by the single edge \cd{w}.

\textbf{Kruskal} suits an explicit, sparse edge list. Sort the edges by weight.
Keep an edge when its two ends are in different components of a union-find. Stop after $V - 1$ edges.
If fewer than $V - 1$ edges join components, the graph is not connected and no spanning tree exists.
Memory hook: \emph{cheapest edge first; keep it only when it joins two components.}
\begin{pyex}
def kruskal(n, edges):                   # edges = [(w, u, v)], nodes 0 .. n-1
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]   # path halving
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    total = used = 0
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):        # cheapest edge first
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru != rv:                     # the edge joins two components: keep it
            parent[ru] = rv
            total += w
            used += 1
            if used == n - 1:
                break
    return total if used == n - 1 else -1   # -1: the graph is not connected

kruskal(4, [(1, 0, 1), (4, 1, 2), (3, 0, 2), (2, 2, 3), (5, 1, 3)])   # -> 6
kruskal(3, [(1, 0, 1)])                  # -> -1
pts = [[0, 0], [2, 2], [3, 10], [5, 2], [7, 0]]
edges = [(abs(a[0] - b[0]) + abs(a[1] - b[1]), i, j)
         for i, a in enumerate(pts) for j, b in enumerate(pts) if i < j]
kruskal(len(pts), edges)                 # -> 20
\end{pyex}
Choose by density. A complete or formula-based graph: $O(V^2)$ Prim.
A sparse edge list: Kruskal in $O(E \log E)$, or Prim with a heap.
On the complete graph of Min Cost to Connect All Points ($n \le 1000$), heap Prim and Kruskal
cost $O(n^2 \log n)$ and are slower than the scan.
A list-based scan with an \cd{in_tree} flag array has the same $O(n^2)$ cost as the dict form.
\begin{note}
A node can sometimes connect to an outside source with its own cost (``build a well here'').
Add one virtual node, give it an edge to each such node, and run the MST on the larger graph.
For a maximum spanning tree, sort the edges in descending order.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Shortest path with at most k edges}
A limit on the number of edges breaks plain Dijkstra. Dijkstra keeps one best cost for each node,
but the cheapest arrival can use too many edges to continue.
\textbf{Bellman-Ford} relaxes every edge in rounds. If each round reads only the values of the previous round,
then after round $i$ each value is the cheapest cost with at most $i$ edges.
So run exactly $k + 1$ rounds for $k$ stops (Cheapest Flights Within K Stops).
Memory hook: \emph{$k + 1$ rounds: relax every flight from last round's copy.}
\begin{pyex}
def cheapest_price(n, flights, src, dst, k):   # Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
    INF = float("inf")
    prices = [INF] * n
    prices[src] = 0
    for _ in range(k + 1):               # k stops = k + 1 flights (edges)
        next_prices = prices.copy()      # read from prices, write to next_prices
        for u, v, cost in flights:
            if prices[u] == INF:
                continue
            if prices[u] + cost < next_prices[v]:
                next_prices[v] = prices[u] + cost
        prices = next_prices
    return -1 if prices[dst] == INF else prices[dst]

def cheapest_in_place(n, flights, src, dst, k):   # WRONG: no copy
    INF = float("inf")
    prices = [INF] * n
    prices[src] = 0
    for _ in range(k + 1):
        for u, v, cost in flights:
            if prices[u] + cost < prices[v]:
                prices[v] = prices[u] + cost       # a later edge reads this new value
    return -1 if prices[dst] == INF else prices[dst]

flights = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [2, 0, 100], [1, 3, 600], [2, 3, 200]]
cheapest_price(4, flights, 0, 3, 1)      # -> 700
short = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [0, 2, 500]]
cheapest_price(3, short, 0, 2, 1)        # -> 200
cheapest_price(3, short, 0, 2, 0)        # -> 500
cheapest_in_place(3, short, 0, 2, 0)     # -> 200
\end{pyex}
The last line is wrong. With $k = 0$, only the direct flight (500) is allowed.
The in-place round read the new price of city 1 and chained two flights in one round.
The cost is $O(k (V + E))$.
\begin{note}
The two-buffer rule applies to every layered computation in which layer $i$ must depend only on layer $i - 1$.
Two-row knapsack DP and synchronous grid updates use the same rule.
For ``exactly $k + 1$ edges'', start each new round at infinity instead of a copy of the old round.
\end{note}

\textbf{Alternative: BFS by stops.} A BFS level is the same as a round. Level $i$ holds the paths with
exactly $i$ edges, as (node, cost) pairs. Expand only the current level, and stop after $k + 1$ levels.
Push a neighbor only when its new cost is lower than the best cost so far.
A path that is cheaper and has fewer edges makes the other path useless.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def cheapest_bfs(n, flights, src, dst, k):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, p in flights:
        graph[u].append((v, p))
    best = [float("inf")] * n
    best[src] = 0
    level = [(src, 0)]                   # (node, cost) for paths with exactly i edges
    for _ in range(k + 1):               # one level for each flight
        next_level = []
        for u, cost in level:
            for v, p in graph[u]:
                if cost + p < best[v]:   # better than every path with fewer edges
                    best[v] = cost + p
                    next_level.append((v, cost + p))
        level = next_level
    return -1 if best[dst] == float("inf") else best[dst]

flights = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [2, 0, 100], [1, 3, 600], [2, 3, 200]]
cheapest_bfs(4, flights, 0, 3, 1)        # -> 700
short = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [0, 2, 500]]
cheapest_bfs(3, short, 0, 2, 0)          # -> 500
cheapest_bfs(3, short, 0, 2, 1)          # -> 200
\end{pyex}
Do not return when \cd{dst} first appears. A later level can reach it at a lower cost.

\subsubsection{Add a resource to the state}
The general tool for any limit is a larger state: (node, resource used).
Run Dijkstra on these states and order the heap by cost.
A state is useless when the same node already popped with a resource use that is not larger.
That earlier pop had a cost that is not larger, so it is at least as good in both ways.
This handles limits on fuel, total time, coupons or removed obstacles. The edge-count limit is one example.
Memory hook: \emph{put the limit in the state; pop by cost; skip a state that uses no less of the limit.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

def cheapest_by_state(n, flights, src, dst, k):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, p in flights:
        graph[u].append((v, p))
    fewest = {}                          # node -> fewest edges among its popped states
    heap = [(0, src, 0)]                 # (cost, node, edges used)
    while heap:
        cost, u, used = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if u == dst:
            return cost
        if u in fewest and fewest[u] <= used:
            continue                     # an earlier pop was cheaper and used fewer edges
        fewest[u] = used
        if used == k + 1:
            continue                     # no edges left in the budget
        for v, p in graph[u]:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (cost + p, v, used + 1))
    return -1

flights = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [2, 0, 100], [1, 3, 600], [2, 3, 200]]
cheapest_by_state(4, flights, 0, 3, 1)   # -> 700
cheapest_by_state(4, flights, 0, 3, 2)   # -> 400
short = [[0, 1, 100], [1, 2, 100], [0, 2, 500]]
cheapest_by_state(3, short, 0, 2, 0)     # -> 500
\end{pyex}
A node can pop more than one time here, each time with fewer edges used. A plain visited set is wrong.

\subsubsection{Use every edge exactly one time: Euler path}
Model the items as edges. An airport, a number or a letter is a node, and each ticket or pair is a directed edge.
``Use every ticket one time'' is then an Euler path. A greedy walk can get stuck too early.
The key fact: the first node where the walk gets stuck must be the last node of the path.
So write a node down when it has no unused edges (post-order), and reverse the list at the end.
After the reverse, a detour that the walk skipped comes before the dead end, so no choice needs an undo.
This is \textbf{Hierholzer's algorithm} (Reconstruct Itinerary).
Memory hook: \emph{take the smallest ticket, write the airport down when stuck, then reverse.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def find_itinerary(tickets):             # Reconstruct Itinerary
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for src, dst in sorted(tickets, reverse=True):
        graph[src].append(dst)           # each list ends with the smallest destination
    route = []
    def visit(airport):
        while graph[airport]:
            visit(graph[airport].pop())  # use the smallest unused ticket
        route.append(airport)            # stuck: write the airport down
    visit("JFK")
    return route[::-1]

find_itinerary([["MUC", "LHR"], ["JFK", "MUC"], ["SFO", "SJC"], ["LHR", "SFO"]])
# -> ['JFK', 'MUC', 'LHR', 'SFO', 'SJC']
find_itinerary([["JFK", "SFO"], ["JFK", "ATL"], ["SFO", "ATL"], ["ATL", "JFK"], ["ATL", "SFO"]])
# -> ['JFK', 'ATL', 'JFK', 'SFO', 'ATL', 'SFO']
find_itinerary([["JFK", "KUL"], ["JFK", "NRT"], ["NRT", "JFK"]])
# -> ['JFK', 'NRT', 'JFK', 'KUL']
\end{pyex}
In the last example, the greedy walk takes KUL first and gets stuck. KUL goes to the end of the route.
The walk then continues from JFK with the other tickets.
Sort each list in descending order and \cd{pop()} from the end: this removes the smallest destination in $O(1)$.
The total cost is $O(E \log E)$ for the sort and $O(E)$ for the walk.
Both tricks are reusable. A list sorted in descending order is a cheap static priority queue.
Use it when you take items only in ascending order and never add new items.
The post-order append and the final reverse also give a topological order by finish time
(DFS with three colors, Section~\ref{sec:graph-structure}).

\textbf{General form.} When the start is not given, start at the node with out-degree minus in-degree equal to 1.
If all nodes are balanced, the path is a circuit, so start at any node with an edge.
Use an explicit stack when $E$ is large, because the recursion depth is $E + 1$.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def euler_path(edges):                   # directed edges (u, v); a path is known to exist
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    balance = defaultdict(int)           # out-degree minus in-degree
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        balance[u] += 1
        balance[v] -= 1
    start = next((x for x in balance if balance[x] == 1), edges[0][0])
    stack, path = [start], []
    while stack:
        u = stack[-1]
        if graph[u]:
            stack.append(graph[u].pop())  # walk along an unused edge
        else:
            path.append(stack.pop())      # stuck: u takes the next place from the end
    return path[::-1]

euler_path([(3, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)])          # -> [3, 1, 2, 3, 4]
euler_path([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "a")])      # -> ['a', 'b', 'c', 'a']
euler_path([("a", "b"), ("a", "c")])                  # -> ['a', 'b', 'c']
\end{pyex}
In the first example, the walk goes $3 \to 4$ first and gets stuck. The cycle $3 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$ is put before it.

A directed Euler path exists when at most one node has out $-$ in $= 1$, at most one node has in $-$ out $= 1$,
all other nodes are balanced, and all edges are in one connected piece.
For an undirected graph, the number of odd-degree nodes must be 0 or 2. Start at an odd one,
and remove each edge from the lists of both ends.
When existence is not given, first check the degree conditions. Then check that the result has $E + 1$ nodes.
Fewer nodes mean that the edges are not in one connected piece.
The length check alone is not enough. The edges a$\to$b and a$\to$c have no Euler path,
but the last call above returns $E + 1 = 3$ nodes, and b$\to$c is not an edge.

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Name the nodes and the edges. Are the edges an explicit list, a grid, or a formula for every pair?
  \item Name the goal. A set of edges that connects all nodes: an MST, so go to step 7 to pick Prim or Kruskal.
        An order that uses every edge: an Euler path. Find the start from the degrees, then run Hierholzer.
        One path from a source: continue with step 3.
  \item For a path, find how the cost combines along the path: sum, max, min or product.
        Check that the combine never makes a path better as it grows. Then Dijkstra works.
        To maximize, use a max-heap. For max or min, binary search on the level also works.
  \item Check the weights. All equal: BFS. Only 0 and 1: 0-1 BFS with a deque. Non-negative: Dijkstra.
        Some negative: Bellman-Ford.
  \item Look for a second limit. A limit on the number of edges: Bellman-Ford rounds from a copy.
        A limit on another resource: Dijkstra on (node, resource) states.
  \item Decide when to stop. One target: return at its first pop. All nodes: take the maximum,
        and check that every node is reached.
  \item Check the density. A complete graph with $V \approx 10^3$: an $O(V^2)$ scan with no stored edges.
        A sparse graph: a heap, or Kruskal.
  \item Test the small and impossible cases: one node, an unreachable node, a disconnected graph, a limit of 0.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Final on pop, not on push.}
Wrong: mark a node as done when it is first pushed. A later push can carry a smaller distance.
Right: make a node final at its first pop, and skip its later copies.
Marking on push is correct only when the cost to enter a node does not depend on the edge.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

def build(edges):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    return graph

def dijkstra_mark_on_push(graph, src):   # WRONG
    dist = {src: 0}
    heap = [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if v not in dist:            # the first push fixes v too early
                dist[v] = d + w
                heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, v))
    return dist

def dijkstra(graph, src):                # right: final at the first pop
    dist = {}
    heap = [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if u in dist:
            continue
        dist[u] = d
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if v not in dist:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, v))
    return dist

g = build([("A", "B", 1), ("A", "C", 5), ("B", "C", 1)])
dijkstra_mark_on_push(g, "A")["C"]       # -> 5
dijkstra(g, "A")["C"]                    # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Heap entries that cannot be compared.}
Wrong: push \cd{(distance, obj)} where \cd{obj} is a dict, a node object or a list of mixed types.
On a tie in the distance, Python compares the second items and can raise \cd{TypeError}.
Right: put a counter between the key and the object, or push a node id instead of the object.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from itertools import count

heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, (3, {"name": "x"}))
heapq.heappush(heap, (3, {"name": "y"}))     # -> raises TypeError
tie = count()
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, (3, next(tie), {"name": "x"}))
heapq.heappush(heap, (3, next(tie), {"name": "y"}))
heapq.heappop(heap)[2]                       # -> {'name': 'x'}
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Read the graph correctly.}
Directed edges get one entry; undirected edges get two. Labels from 1 to $n$ need arrays of size $n + 1$.
Compare the number of reached nodes with $n$, not with the nodes that appear in the edge list.
Return $-1$ (or what the statement asks) when a node is not reached, not infinity.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative weights.} Dijkstra can give wrong answers with a negative edge, because a later path can be cheaper
than a node that is already final. Use Bellman-Ford. Zero weights are safe.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Bottleneck paths.} Do not sum the values; combine with \cd{max}.
Start the heap with the value of the start cell, not with 0. The value of the end cell also counts.
In a binary search, the lowest level is at least the start value.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Edge limits.} $k$ stops means $k + 1$ edges, so run $k + 1$ rounds.
Read from the old array and write to a copy. With a heap, do not keep one best cost for each node and
do not use a plain visited set: a node can need a second visit with fewer edges.
In a level BFS, do not return at the first arrival at the target: a later level can be cheaper.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{MST is not a shortest-path tree.}
Dijkstra minimizes the distance from one source. An MST minimizes the total of all chosen edges.
Example: edges A--B (2), B--C (2) and A--C (3). The MST costs 4 (A--B, B--C).
The shortest-path tree from A uses A--B and A--C, and costs 5.
On a graph that can be disconnected, Prim can pick a node with cost infinity. Then no spanning tree exists.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Euler paths.} Track used edges, not visited nodes: nodes repeat. Keep duplicate edges in a list, not a set.
Append a node after its loop, not before it, and reverse the list at the end.
\cd{list.pop(0)} costs $O(E)$; sort in descending order and pop from the end, or use a heap.
The recursion depth is $E + 1$. Above about 900 edges, use the explicit stack.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Network Delay Time (743) & Plain Dijkstra; the answer is the largest final distance, or $-1$ if a node is not reached. &
  The first pop of a node is its arrival time. \\
Swim in Rising Water (778) & The path cost is the highest cell, so combine with \cd{max}. Binary search on the level also works. &
  Dijkstra, but the path cost is the highest cell, so use max instead of plus. \\
Min Cost to Connect All Points (1584) & The goal is the total of the chosen edges: an MST on a complete graph, with an $O(n^2)$ Prim scan. &
  Keep a dict of outside points: pop the nearest, then let it lower the others. \\
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (787) & At most $k + 1$ edges: Bellman-Ford rounds that read from the previous round, or BFS by stops. &
  $k + 1$ rounds: relax every flight from last round's copy. \\
Reconstruct Itinerary (332) & Use every edge one time, smallest order first: Hierholzer with post-order and a reverse. &
  Take the smallest ticket, write the airport down when stuck, then reverse. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T14} (page~\pageref{drill:T14}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T14} (page~\pageref{ans:T14}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Dynamic programming: foundations and 1-D}\label{tech:T15}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
A brute force tries every sequence of choices. It explores a tree of calls, and many branches reach the same subproblem.
Dynamic programming (DP) gives each distinct subproblem a name, the \emph{state}.
DP solves each state one time and stores the answer.
The cost drops from the number of paths, which is often exponential, to the number of states times the work per state.

\textbf{Worked example.} Count the ways to climb 5 steps when each move climbs 1 step or 2 steps.
Look at the last move. It lands on step 5 from step 4 or from step 3.
These two groups of ways do not overlap, and together they contain every way.
So $\mathit{ways}(5) = \mathit{ways}(4) + \mathit{ways}(3)$, and the same rule holds for every step.
The plain recursion computes $\mathit{ways}(3)$ two times and $\mathit{ways}(2)$ three times. At $n = 45$ it makes about $3.7 \cdot 10^9$ calls.
A table that you fill from step 0 upward computes each value one time: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. The answer 8 costs 4 additions.

Every DP answers the five questions below. Write the answers in words before you write code.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.2cm}L{6.6cm}L{7.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Part & Question & Climbing Stairs \\
\midrule
State & What does one entry of the table mean, in words? & \cd{ways[i]} is the number of move sequences that end exactly on step \cd{i}. \\
Transition & What is the last decision? How do its cases combine? & The last move is 1 step or 2 steps: \cd{ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2]}. \\
Base case & What is the answer for the smallest input, often the empty prefix? & \cd{ways[0] = 1} (the empty climb is one way) and \cd{ways[1] = 1}. \\
Order & Which states must be ready before this state? & \cd{i} from 2 up to \cd{n}. \\
Answer & Which state, or which combination of states, is the answer? & \cd{ways[n]}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{note}
The question gives the combine operator. Use a sum for ``how many ways'', \cd{min} or \cd{max} for ``the best total'',
and \cd{any} (logical or) for ``is it possible''. The state and the order do not change.
Only the value of the base case changes with the operator: 1 way, cost 0, or true.
\end{note}

The transition must use only the state, not the path to it.
In Climbing Stairs, the ways to finish from step 3 do not depend on how you reached step 3.
When the future depends on more than the state, add that information to the state.
Examples are a flag ``the first house is robbed'' or a second value such as the minimum product.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The question asks ``how many ways'', ``the minimum or maximum total'', or ``is it possible''. It does not ask for the list of all solutions.
  \item Each step has a small set of choices: a move of 1 or 2, take or skip, a piece of length 1 or 2, extend or restart.
  \item A rule forbids two neighbors, such as ``no two adjacent items''. Decide take or skip for each item.
  \item The input must be cut into consecutive pieces (decode, segment, split), and each piece must pass a test.
        Use a state over the prefix length and list the cases of the last piece.
  \item A greedy choice fails on a small input. For example, the best houses in \cd{[2, 1, 1, 2]} are not every second house.
  \item The plain recursion calls the same arguments many times. Overlapping subproblems point to a cache or a table.
  \item The answer grows exponentially with $n$, and the statement promises that it fits in 32 bits or asks for it modulo $10^9 + 7$.
        You cannot list the solutions one by one, so you count them.
  \item The constraints allow $O(n)$ or $O(n^2)$, but not $O(2^n)$. A 1-D DP over $n \le 10^5$ needs $O(1)$ or $O(\log n)$ work per state.
        A limit of a few thousand allows $O(n)$ work per state, for example a look-back over all earlier indices.
  \item The answer is the best \emph{contiguous} segment (subarray, substring). Use a state that ends at index \cd{i}.
  \item A step can reverse the order of the candidates, for example a product with negative values.
        Then the best new result can come from the worst old result. Keep the minimum and the maximum that end at index \cd{i}.
  \item The answer is the longest \emph{subsequence} where each element relates to the previous chosen element. Use a chain that ends at index \cd{i}.
  \item The items form a circle, so the first item and the last item are neighbors. Cut the circle into lines by cases.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Write the same recurrence in one of two forms.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3cm}L{6.6cm}L{6.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
 & Memoized DFS (top-down) & Tabulation (bottom-up) \\
\midrule
How to write it & Write the brute-force recursion. Put \cd{@cache} on it. The arguments are the state. & Make a list for all states. Fill it in a loop from the base case upward. \\
Order of states & The recursion finds the order. & You choose the order. Each state must come after the states that it reads. \\
States computed & Only the states that the start state reaches. & All states. \\
Limits & CPython stops at about 1000 nested calls with \cd{RecursionError}. With \cd{@cache} on older versions, the limit is about 500. & No recursion limit. \\
Space compression & Not practical: the cache keeps every state that it computes. & Keep only the last few entries when the transition reads only them. \\
Best use & Many dimensions, an unclear order, or a sparse set of reachable states. & A clear order, such as prefix length, and large $n$. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{Tabulation over prefixes}
The state \cd{dp[i]} describes the prefix of length \cd{i}. Pad the table by one, so that \cd{dp[0]} is the empty prefix.
The template below counts the ways to reach step \cd{n} with moves from a set \cd{steps}.
Climbing Stairs is this template with \cd{steps = [1, 2]}.
\begin{pyex}
def count_ways(n, steps):
    ways = [0] * (n + 1)          # state: ways[i] = move sequences that end on step i
    ways[0] = 1                   # base case: the empty climb
    for i in range(1, n + 1):     # order: each state reads smaller states only
        for s in steps:           # transition: cases on the last move
            if i - s >= 0:
                ways[i] += ways[i - s]
    return ways[n]                # answer
count_ways(3, [1, 2])             # -> 3
count_ways(5, [1, 2])             # -> 8
count_ways(45, [1, 2])            # -> 1836311903
count_ways(4, [1, 3, 5])          # -> 3
\end{pyex}
Invariant: when the loop reaches \cd{i}, every entry \cd{ways[0..i-1]} is final.
The cases of the last move do not overlap, so each sequence is counted exactly one time.

\subsubsection{The same recurrence as a memoized DFS}
Start from the brute force: ``to finish at \cd{i}, try each last move''. Then cache by the arguments.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
def count_ways_memo(n, steps):
    @cache
    def ways(i):                  # the state is the argument list
        if i == 0:
            return 1              # base case
        return sum(ways(i - s) for s in steps if i - s >= 0)
    return ways(n)
count_ways_memo(5, [1, 2])        # -> 8
count_ways_memo(45, [1, 2])       # -> 1836311903
\end{pyex}
Define the cached function inside the solver. Then each call of the solver gets a new, empty cache.

\subsubsection{State that ends at index i}
Some problems do not fit ``the best over the prefix''. A contiguous segment, or a chain of chosen elements, must connect to its last element.
For these problems, let \cd{end[i]} be the best answer that \emph{ends exactly at} index \cd{i}.
The answer is then the best value over all \cd{i}, not the last entry.
The template below finds the longest chain where each element fits after the previous chosen element.
\begin{pyex}
def longest_chain(a, fits):
    end = [1] * len(a)            # end[i] = longest chain that ends at index i
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(i):        # a[j] is the element before a[i] in the chain
            if fits(a[j], a[i]):
                end[i] = max(end[i], end[j] + 1)
    return max(end)               # the chain can end at any index
nums = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]
longest_chain(nums, lambda x, y: x < y)                   # -> 4
longest_chain([1, 2, 4, 8, 3], lambda x, y: y % x == 0)   # -> 4
\end{pyex}
This is $O(n^2)$. For a contiguous segment, only index \cd{i - 1} can come before \cd{i}, so one pass of $O(n)$ is enough (Kadane, below).

\subsubsection{Compress the table to a few variables}
When \cd{dp[i]} reads only the last $k$ entries, keep $k$ variables instead of the table.
Update them in one tuple assignment, so that every new value uses the old values.
\begin{pyex}
def climb(n):
    prev, curr = 1, 1             # ways[0], ways[1]
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        prev, curr = curr, prev + curr    # both new values use the old ones
    return curr
[climb(n) for n in range(1, 7)]   # -> [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
def climb_bug(n):
    prev, curr = 1, 1
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        prev = curr               # overwrites prev too early
        curr = prev + curr
    return curr
[climb_bug(n) for n in range(1, 7)]   # -> [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
\end{pyex}
Write the full table first. Compress it only when the task asks for $O(1)$ extra space.
The table is easier to print, to check by hand, and to walk back for the chosen items.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Count the ways: sum over the last move}
The core template is the whole solution. Name the last move, add the counts of the states that it comes from, and set the empty prefix to 1.
Memory hook (Climbing Stairs): \emph{the last move is a 1-step or a 2-step, so add the ways for the two steps below.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Steps from a set $S$: sum \cd{ways[i - s]} over $s \in S$ with \cd{i - s >= 0}.
  \item A forbidden step: set its entry to 0 and keep the same transition.
  \item A large count: apply the modulo after each addition.
  \item Up to $k$ steps per move: keep a running sum of the last $k$ entries, so that each state costs $O(1)$.
  \item The positions are the outer loop, so the template counts ordered sequences (1+2 and 2+1 are two ways).
        For unordered combinations, put the move types in the outer loop. The knapsack section covers this case.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Best cost: min over the last move}
Replace the sum with \cd{min} and add the cost of the move.
Define exactly what the state includes. Below, \cd{dp[i]} is the cost to stand on step \cd{i} before you pay \cd{cost[i]}.
Both start steps are free, and the top is index \cd{n}, one past the last step.
Memory hook (Min Cost Climbing Stairs): \emph{to stand on step i, come from one back or two back, and pay the step you leave.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_cost_climb(cost):
    n = len(cost)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)            # dp[i] = cheapest cost to stand on step i; the top is i = n
    for i in range(2, n + 1):     # dp[0] = dp[1] = 0: both starts are free
        from_one_back = dp[i - 1] + cost[i - 1]
        from_two_back = dp[i - 2] + cost[i - 2]
        dp[i] = min(from_one_back, from_two_back)
    return dp[n]
min_cost_climb([10, 15, 20])                           # -> 15
min_cost_climb([1, 100, 1, 1, 1, 100, 1, 1, 100, 1])   # -> 6
min_cost_climb([1, 2, 3])                              # -> 2
\end{pyex}
The last case shows that greedy fails: the cheaper start step 0 costs at least 3, but the start step 1 costs 2.
For moves of size 1 to $k$, take the minimum of \cd{dp[j] + cost[j]} over the last $k$ indices \cd{j}.
For a large $k$, keep that minimum with a monotonic deque.

Some moves cover a span, not a fixed step. An example is a pass that covers 7 days.
The span can start before the first day. Then clamp the source index to the base state: \cd{dp[max(0, d - 7)] + cost}.
Do not skip the move with the guard \cd{if d - 7 >= 0}. That loses every plan where the first pass starts before day 1.
Memory hook (Minimum Cost For Tickets): \emph{the pass that covers today started up to 6 days ago; clamp at day 0.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_cost_tickets(days, costs):
    travel, last = set(days), days[-1]
    dp = [0] * (last + 1)         # dp[d] = cheapest cost to cover the travel days up to day d
    for d in range(1, last + 1):
        if d not in travel:
            dp[d] = dp[d - 1]     # no travel today: no new pass
            continue
        dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + costs[0],              # last move: a 1-day pass
                    dp[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1],      # clamp: the pass can start before day 1
                    dp[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2])
    return dp[last]
min_cost_tickets([1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 20], [2, 7, 15])   # -> 11
min_cost_tickets([1, 2, 3], [5, 6, 100])            # -> 6
\end{pyex}
With the guard instead of the clamp, the last case gives 15: three 1-day passes.

\subsubsection{Take or skip each item}
Each item is taken or skipped, and a rule forbids two neighbors.
Decide only about the last item. Skip it and keep the best of the shorter prefix.
Or take it and add it to the best of the prefix that ends before its forbidden neighbor.
Memory hook (House Robber): \emph{skip it and keep the last best, or rob it and add its money to the best two back.}
\begin{pyex}
def rob(nums):
    best = [0, 0]                 # two zeros for "no houses yet", so best[-2] exists
    for money in nums:
        skip = best[-1]           # leave this house: keep the best so far
        take = best[-2] + money   # rob it: the house before stays empty
        best.append(max(skip, take))
    return best[-1]
rob([1, 2, 3, 1])                 # -> 4
rob([2, 7, 9, 3, 1])              # -> 12
rob([2, 1, 1, 2])                 # -> 4
rob([5])                          # -> 5
\end{pyex}
The two leading zeros remove all base cases, so one house needs no special code.
When a take forbids the next $k$ items, the take reads \cd{best[-k-1]}. Start \cd{best} with $k + 1$ zeros, so that this entry exists.
When an item can be in one of several modes, keep one value per mode (a state machine).
The optimal form keeps \cd{best[-2]} and \cd{best[-1]} in two variables for $O(1)$ space.

\subsubsection{Recover the choices, not only the value}
Keep the full table. Then walk back from the answer and ask which case produced each entry.
Memory hook: \emph{walk back from the answer: which case made this entry?}
\begin{pyex}
def rob_plan(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)            # dp[i] = best total from the first i houses
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        take = (dp[i - 2] if i >= 2 else 0) + nums[i - 1]
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], take)
    plan, i = [], n
    while i > 0:                  # walk back: which case made dp[i]?
        if dp[i] == dp[i - 1]:
            i -= 1                # house i-1 was skipped
        else:
            plan.append(i - 1)    # house i-1 was robbed
            i -= 2
    return dp[n], plan[::-1]
rob_plan([2, 7, 9, 3, 1])         # -> (12, [0, 2, 4])
rob_plan([2, 1, 1, 2])            # -> (4, [0, 3])
\end{pyex}
For a state that ends at \cd{i}, store a parent index next to each entry. Then follow the parents from the best entry.

\subsubsection{Circular array: cut the circle by cases}
A circle is a line plus one extra link between the two ends.
Remove that link by cases on one end: one of the two end items is always unused.
Solve each case with the line solver and take the best result.
Memory hook (House Robber II): \emph{drop the first or drop the last, rob each row, take the max.}
\begin{pyex}
def rob_row(houses):
    two_back, one_back = 0, 0
    for money in houses:
        two_back, one_back = one_back, max(one_back, two_back + money)
    return one_back
def rob_circle(nums):
    if len(nums) == 1:
        return nums[0]            # one house has no neighbor
    return max(rob_row(nums[1:]), rob_row(nums[:-1]))   # drop the first, or drop the last
rob_circle([2, 3, 2])             # -> 3
rob_circle([1, 2, 3, 1])          # -> 4
rob_circle([5, 1, 1, 5])          # -> 6
rob_circle([7])                   # -> 7
rob_row([2, 3, 2])                # -> 4
\end{pyex}
The last line shows the bug of one run on the whole array: it robs both ends.
The general rule: fix the few possible states of one end item, solve each case as a line, and combine.
A best segment on a circle needs a different split: the segment wraps past the end, or it does not.
A wrapped segment is the whole array minus one segment that does not wrap.
The slices copy the list. Pass index bounds instead when the array is very large.

\subsubsection{Moves with validity guards}
The shape is Climbing Stairs, but each move is allowed only when a local test passes.
Put each test on its own transition. Do not handle the special values outside the DP.
Memory hook (Decode Ways): \emph{Climbing Stairs with guards: one step if the digit is not 0, two steps if the pair is 10 to 26.}
\begin{pyex}
def num_decodings(s):
    n = len(s)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)            # dp[i] = ways to decode s[:i]
    dp[0] = 1                     # the empty prefix has one way
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if s[i - 1] != "0":                          # last piece: one digit
            dp[i] += dp[i - 1]
        if i >= 2 and 10 <= int(s[i - 2:i]) <= 26:   # last piece: two digits
            dp[i] += dp[i - 2]
    return dp[n]
num_decodings("12")               # -> 2
num_decodings("226")              # -> 3
num_decodings("11106")            # -> 2
num_decodings("06")               # -> 0
num_decodings("30")               # -> 0
\end{pyex}
A \cd{"0"} cannot start a piece. It is valid only as the second digit of \cd{"10"} or \cd{"20"}.
The test \cd{10 <= value} rejects a two-digit piece with a leading zero, such as \cd{"05"}.
With \cd{dp} over prefix length, the last digit is \cd{s[i-1]}, and the last two digits are \cd{s[i-2:i]}.

\subsubsection{Split into pieces from a set}
The input must be cut into consecutive pieces, and each piece must come from an allowed set.
The rest of the string depends only on where it starts, not on the earlier cuts.
So cache the recursion by the start index.
Memory hook (Word Break): \emph{cut off a first word, ask if the rest can split, and cache by start index.}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
def word_break(s, word_dict):
    words = set(word_dict)
    @cache
    def can_split(start):         # True when s[start:] splits into words
        if start == len(s):
            return True           # nothing is left to split
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
            if s[start:end] in words and can_split(end):
                return True
        return False
    return can_split(0)
word_break("leetcode", ["leet", "code"])                         # -> True
word_break("applepenapple", ["apple", "pen"])                    # -> True
word_break("catsandog", ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"])   # -> False
word_break("cars", ["car", "ca", "rs"])                          # -> True
\end{pyex}
The optimal form is bottom-up over prefixes: \cd{dp[i]} is true when \cd{s[:i]} splits.
It looks back at most $L$ characters, where $L$ is the longest word length. So the slice work drops from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n L^2)$.
It also has no recursion limit, which matters for strings of thousands of characters.
The bottom-up form is the general partition template. Change only the combine operator.
\begin{pyex}
def split_count(s, word_dict):    # number of ways to split s into words
    words = set(word_dict)
    longest = max(map(len, words))
    n = len(s)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)            # dp[i] = ways to split the prefix s[:i]
    dp[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(max(0, i - longest), i):   # the last piece is s[j:i]
            if s[j:i] in words:
                dp[i] += dp[j]
    return dp[n]
split_count("catsanddog", ["cat", "cats", "and", "sand", "dog"])   # -> 2
split_count("aaaa", ["a", "aa"])                                   # -> 5
split_count("catsandog", ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"])    # -> 0
\end{pyex}
For a yes or no answer, use \cd{dp[i] = dp[i] or dp[j]}. For the fewest pieces, use \cd{dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)} with \cd{inf} as the start value.

\subsubsection{Best segment that ends here (Kadane)}
For the best contiguous segment, let \cd{cur} be the best sum of a segment that ends at the current index.
That segment is the current element alone, or the current element added to the best segment that ends one index earlier.
A negative earlier sum never helps, so clamp it at 0 before the addition.
Memory hook (Maximum Subarray): \emph{a negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_subarray(nums):
    best = nums[0]                # non-empty: do not start at 0
    cur = 0                       # best sum that ends at the previous index
    for x in nums:
        cur = max(cur, 0) + x     # extend a positive run, or restart at x
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])   # -> 6
max_subarray([5, 4, -1, 7, 8])                  # -> 23
max_subarray([-3, -1, -2])                      # -> -1
\end{pyex}
Restart when the running sum is negative, not when the current element is negative.
In \cd{[4, -1, 2, 1]} the \cd{-1} is part of the best segment.
When one state is not enough (a deletion is allowed, the sign flips), keep a small fixed set of states per index.

\subsubsection{Carry the max and the min}
A multiplication by a negative number reverses the order of the candidates. The smallest product becomes the largest.
So carry both the largest and the smallest product that end at the current index.
Memory hook (Maximum Product Subarray): \emph{Kadane, but carry the biggest and the smallest, because a negative swaps them.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_product(nums):
    best = nums[0]
    big = small = 1               # largest and smallest product that ends here
    for x in nums:
        candidates = (x, big * x, small * x)          # x alone, or an old run times x
        big, small = max(candidates), min(candidates)   # both from the OLD values
        best = max(best, big)
    return best
max_product([2, 3, -2, 4])        # -> 6
max_product([-2, 3, -4])          # -> 24
max_product([-2, 0, -1])          # -> 0
max_product([-2])                 # -> -2
\end{pyex}
The general rule applies to any step that is monotone but can reverse the order.
For such a step, the extremes of the new values come from the extremes of the old values.
So keep the range \cd{[min, max]} as the state. The candidate \cd{x} alone restarts the run after a zero.

\subsubsection{Longest chain: increasing subsequence}
The $O(n^2)$ form is the chain template above with \cd{fits = x < y}. It is enough for $n$ up to a few thousand.
The $O(n \log n)$ form keeps, for each chain length, only the smallest last value of any chain with that length.
A smaller last value is always at least as easy to extend. These best tails stay sorted, so a binary search finds the place of each new value.
Memory hook (Longest Increasing Subsequence): \emph{smallest tail per length: \cd{bisect_left}, then replace or append.}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
def lis_tails(nums, strict=True):
    find = bisect_left if strict else bisect_right
    tails = []                    # tails[k] = smallest last value of a chain of length k + 1
    for x in nums:
        pos = find(tails, x)      # first tail >= x (strict) or > x
        if pos == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)       # x extends the longest chain
        else:
            tails[pos] = x        # x is a smaller tail for length pos + 1
    return tails
len(lis_tails([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]))   # -> 4
len(lis_tails([0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3]))            # -> 4
len(lis_tails([7, 7, 7]))                     # -> 1
len(lis_tails([7, 7, 7], strict=False))       # -> 3
lis_tails([3, 4, 1])                          # -> [1, 4]
\end{pyex}
The last line shows that \cd{tails} is not a real subsequence: \cd{1} comes after \cd{4} in the input.
Only its length is correct. To rebuild a real chain, store a parent index for each element.
The general idea is dominance: of two partial solutions with the same score, keep the one that is easier to extend.
Many 2-D chain problems become this problem after a sort, when both keys must be strictly larger.
Sort by the first key going up. For equal first keys, sort the second key going down.
Then two items with the same first key cannot both be in a strictly increasing chain. Run the tails loop on the second key.
If equal first keys are sorted going up on the second key, items with the same first key chain, and the answer is too large.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Does the question ask for a count, a best value, or a yes or no answer? If it asks for all solutions, use backtracking instead.
  \item Write the brute force as a recursion over choices. Its arguments are a first try at the state.
  \item Does the rest of the problem depend only on these arguments? If it also depends on the path, add the missing fact to the state.
  \item Is the answer a contiguous segment or a chain? Then use a state that ends at index \cd{i}. Otherwise use the best over the prefix of length \cd{i}.
  \item What is the last decision: the last move, the last piece, take or skip the last item, extend or restart?
        List its cases. For a count, the cases must not overlap, and together they must cover every solution.
  \item Choose the combine operator: a sum, \cd{min} or \cd{max}, or \cd{any}.
  \item Set the base case. The empty prefix usually has 1 way, cost 0, or the value true. Pad the table by one to hold it.
  \item Choose the order, so that each state comes after the states that it reads.
  \item Find the answer: \cd{dp[n]} for a prefix state, or the best over all \cd{i} for an ``ends at i'' state.
  \item Multiply the number of states by the work per state. Compare the result with the constraints.
        If it is too slow, look for a dominance rule (keep only the best of equal candidates) or a bound on the look-back.
  \item Is there an extra link between the ends (a circle)? Fix the state of one end item, solve each case as a line, and combine.
  \item Check the code against a brute force on all small inputs. Then compress the table if the task asks for less space.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A wrong base case.} The empty prefix has 1 way to count, not 0. With 0, every count is 0.
Word Break needs \cd{dp[0] = True} for the same reason.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A non-empty answer that starts at 0.} When the segment must be non-empty and values can be negative, start the best at \cd{nums[0]}.
A start value of 0 returns 0 for \cd{[-3, -1, -2]}. For a product, starting both states at \cd{nums[0]} and then looping over all of \cd{nums}
counts \cd{nums[0]} two times: \cd{[2]} gives 4.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The last entry of an ``ends at i'' table.} The longest chain or the best segment can end anywhere.
Return the best over all \cd{i}, not \cd{end[n-1]}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Greedy instead of DP.} Every second item, the largest item first, or the longest word first can all fail.
Try a small counterexample before you trust a greedy rule.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def rob(nums):
    best = [0, 0]
    for money in nums:
        best.append(max(best[-1], best[-2] + money))
    return best[-1]
def rob_every_other(nums):        # greedy: the better of the even and the odd positions
    return max(sum(nums[0::2]), sum(nums[1::2]))
rob_every_other([2, 1, 1, 2]), rob([2, 1, 1, 2])   # -> (3, 4)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The recursion limit.} A memoized DFS goes as deep as the longest chain of states.
CPython raises \cd{RecursionError} at about 1000 nested calls.
On Python 3.11 and older, and on early 3.12 releases, the \cd{@cache} wrapper also counts. Then the limit is about 500 calls.
Use tabulation when the chain can be that long.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
@cache
def down(i):
    return 0 if i == 0 else down(i - 1)
down(400)                         # -> 0
down(5000)                        # -> raises RecursionError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A cache that outlives its input.} A module-level \cd{@cache} function that reads a global list keeps old answers for the next input.
The list is a hidden part of the state. Define the cached function inside the solver, so that each input gets a new cache.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache
nums = [1, 2, 3]
@cache
def best_from(i):                 # reads the global nums: a hidden part of the state
    if i >= len(nums):
        return 0
    return max(best_from(i + 1), nums[i] + best_from(i + 2))
best_from(0)                      # -> 4
nums = [10, 1, 10]
best_from(0)                      # -> 4
best_from.cache_clear()
best_from(0)                      # -> 20
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A negative slice start.} With \cd{dp} over prefix length, the two-digit piece \cd{s[i-2:i]} at \cd{i = 1} is \cd{s[-1:1]}.
It is an empty string, and \cd{int} of it raises \cd{ValueError}. Test \cd{i >= 2} first.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
s = "12"
i = 1
s[i - 2:i]                        # -> ''
int(s[i - 2:i])                   # -> raises ValueError
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Two separate updates of rolling variables.} \cd{prev = curr} followed by \cd{curr = prev + curr} reads the new \cd{prev}.
Use one tuple assignment, as in \cd{prev, curr = curr, prev + curr}. The same rule applies to the max and min of a product.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The circle edge cases.} With one item, both rows of the case split are empty, so return that item.
Do not exclude both ends in one run: that loses every plan that uses exactly one end, such as \cd{[5, 1, 1, 5]}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Strict or non-strict chains.} \cd{bisect_left} gives a strictly increasing chain. \cd{bisect_right} lets equal values chain.
In the $O(n^2)$ form, \cd{<} and \cd{<=} make the same difference.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Climbing Stairs & Count the ways: a sum over the last move (1 or 2 steps). The empty climb is 1 way. & The last move is a 1-step or a 2-step, so add the ways for the two steps below. \\
Min Cost Climbing Stairs & Best cost: a \cd{min} over the last move, plus the cost of the step you leave. The top is index \cd{n}. & To stand on step i, come from one back or two back, and pay the step you leave. \\
House Robber & Take or skip each item. A take reads the best two back. & Skip it and keep the last best, or rob it and add its money to the best two back. \\
House Robber II & A circle: run the line solver without the first item and without the last item. One item is a special case. & Drop the first or drop the last, rob each row, take the max. \\
Decode Ways & Count with guards: one digit if it is not \cd{"0"}, two digits if they are 10 to 26. & Climbing Stairs with guards: one step if the digit is not 0, two steps if the pair is 10 to 26. \\
Word Break & Yes or no over the last piece from a set. Memoized DFS on the start index, or bottom-up with a bounded look-back. & Cut off a first word, ask if the rest can split, and cache by start index. \\
Maximum Subarray & The best sum that ends at \cd{i}: extend or restart. The answer is the best over all \cd{i}. & A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart. \\
Maximum Product Subarray & Two states that end at \cd{i}: the max and the min product. & Kadane, but carry the biggest and the smallest, because a negative swaps them. \\
Longest Increasing Subsequence & A chain that ends at \cd{i} in $O(n^2)$, or the smallest tail per length with binary search in $O(n \log n)$. & Smallest tail per length: \cd{bisect_left}, then replace or append. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T15} (page~\pageref{drill:T15}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T15} (page~\pageref{ans:T15}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Dynamic programming: knapsack family}\label{tech:T16}

\subsection{The idea}
A knapsack problem picks items so that their sizes add up to a \emph{total}. The total can be an amount of
money, a capacity, a subset sum, or a position in a string. Brute force tries every subset or every sequence
of items. That is $2^n$ choices or more. But the future depends only on the total so far, not on the items
that made it. So merge all the choices with the same total into one cell. Keep one cell for each total
$0, 1, \dots, T$, and add the items one at a time. The work drops to $O(n \cdot T)$.

Each cell holds one answer for its total: the fewest items, the number of ways, the best value, or only
yes or no. Three questions fix the code:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.1cm}L{3.6cm}L{9.7cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Answer & Code \\
\midrule
Can an item repeat? & no: each item at most once (0/1) & Inner loop over the totals goes down: \cd{range(T, w - 1, -1)}. \\
 & yes: unlimited copies (unbounded) & Inner loop goes up: \cd{range(w, T + 1)}. \\
\midrule
What does the cell hold? & fewest items & \cd{dp[0] = 0}, other cells \cd{inf}; \cd{dp[t] = min(dp[t], dp[t - w] + 1)}. \\
 & number of ways & \cd{dp[0] = 1}, other cells \cd{0}; \cd{dp[t] += dp[t - w]}. \\
 & possible or not & \cd{dp[0] = True}, other cells \cd{False}; \cd{dp[t] = dp[t] or dp[t - w]}. \\
 & best value & \cd{dp[t] = max(dp[t], dp[t - w] + v)}. \\
\midrule
Does the order count? (counting only) & no: combinations & Items in the outer loop, totals inside. \\
 & yes: ordered sequences & Totals in the outer loop, items inside. Only with unlimited copies. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Worked example (fewest items).} Make the amount 6 from coins 1, 3 and 4, with unlimited copies.
Let \cd{dp[a]} be the fewest coins for the amount \cd{a}. Fix the last coin: \cd{dp[a]} is 1 plus the best
of \cd{dp[a - 1]}, \cd{dp[a - 3]} and \cd{dp[a - 4]}. Start with \cd{dp[0] = 0}. Then \cd{dp[1] = 1},
\cd{dp[2] = 2}, \cd{dp[3] = 1}, \cd{dp[4] = 1} and \cd{dp[5] = 2} (4 + 1). Last, \cd{dp[6]} is 1 plus the
best of \cd{dp[5]}, \cd{dp[3]} and \cd{dp[2]}, so it is 2 (3 + 3). A greedy choice takes the coin 4 first
and needs three coins (4 + 1 + 1).

\textbf{Worked example (loop direction).} One item of size 2, totals 0 to 4, yes or no. Loop up: \cd{t = 2}
reads \cd{dp[0]} and becomes \cd{True}. Then \cd{t = 4} reads \cd{dp[2]}, which is already \cd{True} in this
pass. So the one item counts two times. Loop down: \cd{t = 4} reads \cd{dp[2]} while it still holds the
old \cd{False}. Then \cd{t = 2} becomes \cd{True}. The item counts one time only.

A 1-D table is the 2-D table \cd{dp[i][t]} (``first \cd{i} items, total \cd{t}'') with only one row kept.
The downward loop reads cells that are still from the row before item \cd{i}. That is the 0/1 rule.
The upward loop reads cells that already include item \cd{i}. That is the ``take one more copy'' rule.

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Items must ``make an amount'', ``reach exactly a target sum'' or ``fit a capacity''.
  \item The question asks for the fewest items, the number of ways, the best value, or only yes or no.
  \item The target, or the sum of all values, is small (up to about $10^4$), and $n \cdot T$ is a few
        million at most. Index the table by the total, even when single values are huge.
  \item The total must be \emph{at least} a bound $P$, such as a profit of at least $P$. Cap the total at
        $P$. The table then has $P + 1$ cells, also when the sum of all values is large.
  \item The statement says that each item is used once, or it says ``unlimited supply'' or ``any number of
        times''.
  \item The statement says ``combinations'' (order does not matter), or ``different orders count as
        different'' (ordered sequences). Read the examples to be sure.
  \item Each item goes into one of two groups, or gets a plus or a minus sign. Rewrite it as a subset sum.
  \item A string must be cut into pieces from a set. The position in the string plays the total.
  \item A greedy choice fails on a small counterexample, such as coins 1, 3, 4 and the amount 6.
  \item $n \le 20$ and the items go into $k > 2$ groups. The total alone is not enough state. Use a
        bitmask of the used items.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
Remember this skeleton. Only the start values, the loop direction and the combine step change.
\begin{pyshow}
dp = [START] + [EMPTY] * T          # min: 0, inf   count: 1, 0   yes or no: True, False
for w in items:                     # items outside
    for t in range(T, w - 1, -1):   # each item once: down. Unlimited: range(w, T + 1)
        dp[t] = COMBINE(dp[t], dp[t - w])   # min(a, b + 1)   a + b   a or b
answer = dp[T]
\end{pyshow}
One tested function covers the three cell types and both loop directions. The items are in the outer loop.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import combinations, combinations_with_replacement

INF = float("inf")

def knapsack(items, T, reuse, kind):
    # dp[t] = answer for the total exactly t, with the items seen so far
    start = {"min": 0, "count": 1, "can": True}[kind]       # the empty choice
    empty = {"min": INF, "count": 0, "can": False}[kind]    # not reached yet
    dp = [start] + [empty] * T
    for w in items:                          # items outside: one build order
        if reuse:
            totals = range(w, T + 1)         # up: dp[t - w] may already use w
        else:
            totals = range(T, w - 1, -1)     # down: dp[t - w] is from before w
        for t in totals:
            if kind == "min":
                dp[t] = min(dp[t], dp[t - w] + 1)
            elif kind == "count":
                dp[t] += dp[t - w]
            else:
                dp[t] = dp[t] or dp[t - w]
    return dp[T]

knapsack([1, 3, 4], 6, True, "min")          # -> 2
knapsack([1, 3, 4], 6, False, "min")         # -> inf
knapsack([1, 3, 4], 7, False, "min")         # -> 2
knapsack([1, 2, 3], 3, True, "count")        # -> 3
knapsack([1, 2, 3], 3, False, "count")       # -> 2
knapsack([1, 5, 11, 5], 11, False, "can")    # -> True
knapsack([1, 3], 2, False, "can")            # -> False
knapsack([1, 3], 2, True, "can")             # -> True

def brute_subsets(items, T):                 # each item at most once
    return sum(sum(c) == T for r in range(len(items) + 1)
               for c in combinations(items, r))

def brute_multisets(items, T):               # unlimited copies
    return sum(sum(c) == T for r in range(T + 1)
               for c in combinations_with_replacement(items, r))

tests = [([1, 2, 3], 5), ([2, 3, 5, 7], 10), ([1, 4, 6], 8), ([3, 5], 7)]
all(knapsack(a, T, False, "count") == brute_subsets(a, T) and
    knapsack(a, T, True, "count") == brute_multisets(a, T) for a, T in tests)   # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: after the outer loop finishes item \cd{i}, \cd{dp[t]} is the answer for the total \cd{t} with only
the items \cd{0..i}. A total that no choice reaches keeps the ``empty'' value. Time $O(n \cdot T)$, space
$O(T)$.

\textbf{Best value with weights.} The classic knapsack gives each item a weight and a value. The cell holds
the best value. Start every cell at 0 for ``total weight at most \cd{c}''. Start only \cd{dp[0]} at 0 and the
other cells at minus infinity for ``total weight exactly \cd{c}''.
\begin{pyex}
def best_value(items, cap, reuse=False, exact=False):
    # items: (weight, value) pairs. dp[c] = best value for the weight c
    NEG = float("-inf")
    dp = [0] + [NEG if exact else 0] * cap
    for w, v in items:
        totals = range(w, cap + 1) if reuse else range(cap, w - 1, -1)
        for c in totals:
            dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v)
    return dp[cap]

items = [(2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)]
best_value(items, 7)                  # -> 9
best_value(items, 7, reuse=True)      # -> 10
best_value(items, 1)                  # -> 0
best_value(items, 1, exact=True)      # -> -inf
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
$O(n \cdot T)$ is \emph{pseudo-polynomial}. It grows with the value of $T$, not with its number of digits.
A table for $T = 10^9$ does not fit. Then look for a small $n$ (bitmask or meet in the middle) or for a
different state.
\end{note}

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Fewest items with unlimited copies}
Fix the last item. The rest is the same problem for a smaller total (Coin Change). The cell for \cd{a} is
1 plus the best cell for \cd{a - c} over every coin \cd{c <= a}. Fill the amounts upward. Memory hook:
\emph{pick the last coin: \cd{dp[a] = 1 + min of dp[a - coin]}, with \cd{dp[0] = 0}.}
\begin{pyex}
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount          # dp[a] = fewest coins for the amount a
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:                 # guard: a negative index reads the end of the list
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1

coin_change([1, 3, 4], 6)     # -> 2
coin_change([1, 2, 5], 11)    # -> 3
coin_change([2], 3)           # -> -1
coin_change([1], 0)           # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item For a min (or a max, or yes or no), the loop order does not change the result. The amounts can be
        outside, as here, or the coins can be outside, as in the core template.
  \item The items have a price: add the price instead of 1.
  \item The items are a fixed family, such as the squares $1, 4, 9, \dots$: generate them, then run the same
        loop.
  \item Each amount is a node and each coin is an edge of length 1. A BFS from 0 finds the same answer.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Count combinations or count ordered sequences}
When the cell counts ways, the loop order decides \emph{what} it counts. With the items outside, the items
join in one fixed order, so each multiset is built once: these are combinations (Coin Change II). With the
totals outside, each total tries every item as the last pick, so $1 + 2$ and $2 + 1$ are two different paths:
these are ordered sequences (Combination Sum IV). In both, \cd{dp[0] = 1} counts the empty choice.
Memory hooks: \emph{coins outside, amounts going up inside: \cd{ways[a] += ways[a - coin]}} (combinations);
\emph{ways to make a total: try every last number, add the ways for what is left} (ordered sequences).
\begin{pyex}
def change(amount, coins):              # combinations: coins outside
    ways = [1] + [0] * amount
    for coin in coins:
        for a in range(coin, amount + 1):     # up: the coin can repeat
            ways[a] += ways[a - coin]
    return ways[amount]

def combination_sum4(nums, target):     # ordered sequences: totals outside
    ways = [1] + [0] * target
    for total in range(1, target + 1):
        for last in nums:                     # every number can be the last pick
            if last <= total:
                ways[total] += ways[total - last]
    return ways[target]

change(4, [1, 2, 3])             # -> 4
combination_sum4([1, 2, 3], 4)   # -> 7
change(5, [1, 2, 5])             # -> 4
change(0, [7])                   # -> 1
combination_sum4([9], 3)         # -> 0
combination_sum4([1, 2], 5)      # -> 8
\end{pyex}
The last line is Climbing Stairs with 5 steps: ordered sequences of steps 1 and 2. General rule: the outer
loop of a counting DP fixes the order in which the choices are made. Choose it from the question: are two
orders of the same items one answer or two answers?
\begin{caution}
The title Combination Sum IV says ``combination'', but its examples count $(1, 1, 2)$, $(1, 2, 1)$ and
$(2, 1, 1)$ as three answers. Trust the examples, not the title.
\end{caution}

\subsubsection{Each item at most once: subset sum and equal split}
Two equal halves exist only if one subset reaches \cd{total / 2}. The other items form the second half
(Partition Equal Subset Sum). An odd total gives \cd{False} at once. The intuitive solution keeps the
\emph{set} of reachable sums. Memory hook: \emph{odd total means no; otherwise grow the set of reachable
sums and ask if half the total is in it.} The optimal solution keeps the same facts in a boolean list and
loops the totals down. It can stop early when the target cell becomes \cd{True}.
\begin{pyex}
def can_partition(nums):                # set of reachable sums
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % 2:
        return False
    sums = {0}                          # the empty subset
    for x in nums:
        sums |= {s + x for s in sums}   # skip x (old sums) or take x (s + x)
    return total // 2 in sums

def can_partition_table(nums):          # boolean list, totals go down
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % 2:
        return False
    target = total // 2
    dp = [True] + [False] * target
    for x in nums:
        for j in range(target, x - 1, -1):
            dp[j] = dp[j] or dp[j - x]
    return dp[target]

def wrong_upward(nums, target):         # BUG: one x is used many times
    dp = [True] + [False] * target
    for x in nums:
        for j in range(x, target + 1):
            dp[j] = dp[j] or dp[j - x]
    return dp[target]

can_partition([1, 5, 11, 5]), can_partition_table([1, 5, 11, 5])   # -> (True, True)
can_partition([1, 2, 3, 5]), can_partition_table([1, 2, 3, 5])     # -> (False, False)
wrong_upward([1, 3], 2)                 # -> True
\end{pyex}
The set comprehension reads only the old set, so each number is used once. The last line shows the bug:
the subsets of \cd{[1, 3]} cannot make 2, but the upward loop uses the 1 two times.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Two groups with the smallest difference: find the largest reachable sum \cd{s <= total // 2}.
        The difference is \cd{total - 2 * s}.
  \item Count the subsets with a given sum: same loop, with \cd{+=} and \cd{dp[0] = 1}.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Subset sums as a bitset}
For yes or no questions, store all the reachable sums as the bits of one Python integer. Bit \cd{s} is 1
when the sum \cd{s} is reachable. A shift by \cd{x} adds \cd{x} to every sum at the same time. CPython does
the shift and the OR in C, 30 bits per step. So this is much faster than a loop over a list. It works only
for yes or no. It cannot hold counts or minimums. Memory hook: \emph{one integer holds every sum; shift
by \cd{x} and OR to add \cd{x} to all of them.}
\begin{pyex}
def reachable_bits(nums):
