    bits = 1                         # bit 0: the empty subset has the sum 0
    for x in nums:
        bits |= bits << x            # each old sum s also gives s + x
    return bits

bits = reachable_bits([1, 5, 11, 5])
bits >> 11 & 1                       # -> 1
[s for s in range(bits.bit_length()) if bits >> s & 1]
# -> [0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12, 16, 17, 21, 22]
total = 22
max(s for s in range(total // 2 + 1) if bits >> s & 1)   # -> 11

def reachable_upto(nums, target):
    mask = (1 << (target + 1)) - 1   # keep the bits 0..target only
    bits = 1
    for x in nums:
        bits = (bits | bits << x) & mask
    return [s for s in range(target + 1) if bits >> s & 1]

reachable_upto([3, 4, 5], 7)         # -> [0, 3, 4, 5, 7]
\end{pyex}
The shift binds tighter than \cd{&}, so \cd{bits} \shr{} \cd{s & 1} reads bit \cd{s}. The mask keeps the
integer small when sums above the target can never help.

\subsubsection{Signs on every item: rewrite as a subset sum}
Each number gets a plus or a minus sign, and the question counts the sign choices that hit a target
(Target Sum). The intuitive solution is a memoized DFS on (index, running sum). The running sum stays in
$[-\mathit{total}, \mathit{total}]$, so there are at most $(n + 1) \cdot (2 \cdot \mathit{total} + 1)$ states.
Memory hook: \emph{plus or minus each number, cache on (index, running sum).}

The optimal solution removes the signs. Let $P$ be the sum of the plus group and $N$ the sum of the minus
group. Then $P - N = \mathit{target}$ and $P + N = \mathit{total}$, so $P = (\mathit{total} + \mathit{target}) / 2$.
Now count the subsets with the sum $P$: a 0/1 counting knapsack with the totals going down.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def target_sum_memo(nums, target):
    @cache
    def ways(i, running):              # sign choices for nums[i:] that end at target
        if i == len(nums):
            return 1 if running == target else 0
        return ways(i + 1, running + nums[i]) + ways(i + 1, running - nums[i])
    return ways(0, 0)

def target_sum_subset(nums, target):
    total = sum(nums)
    if abs(target) > total or (total + target) % 2:
        return 0
    goal = (total + target) // 2       # the sum of the plus group
    dp = [1] + [0] * goal
    for x in nums:
        for s in range(goal, x - 1, -1):    # down: each number once
            dp[s] += dp[s - x]
    return dp[goal]

target_sum_memo([1, 1, 1, 1, 1], 3), target_sum_subset([1, 1, 1, 1, 1], 3)   # -> (5, 5)
target_sum_memo([0, 0, 1], 1), target_sum_subset([0, 0, 1], 1)               # -> (4, 4)
target_sum_subset([1, 2], -4), target_sum_subset([1, 2], 2)                  # -> (0, 0)
\end{pyex}
The general trick: when a rule mixes a quantity with its complement, write the complement as the total minus
the quantity. This removes one unknown and turns a two-sided choice into a subset choice. The same move
turns ``two equal groups'' into ``one subset with half the total''.

\subsubsection{Segmentation: the total is a position}
Cut a string into dictionary words (Word Break). The position in the string plays the total. The words are
items with unlimited copies. The cell holds yes or no, so the combine step is \cd{or}. The intuitive solution
is a memoized DFS on the start index. Memory hook: \emph{cut off a first word, ask if the rest can split, and
cache by start index.} The optimal solution is the same idea bottom-up over prefixes: \cd{dp[i]} is
\cd{True} when \cd{s[:i]} splits. It looks back at most the longest word length and needs no recursion.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def word_break(s, word_dict):
    words = set(word_dict)
    @cache
    def can_split(start):              # True when s[start:] splits into words
        if start == len(s):
            return True
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
            if s[start:end] in words and can_split(end):
                return True
        return False
    return can_split(0)

def word_break_table(s, word_dict):    # dp[i]: the prefix s[:i] splits
    words = set(word_dict)
    longest = max(map(len, words))
    dp = [True] + [False] * len(s)
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        for j in range(max(0, i - longest), i):     # the last word is s[j:i]
            if dp[j] and s[j:i] in words:
                dp[i] = True
                break
    return dp[len(s)]

def count_splits(s, word_dict):        # the same table with a sum
    words = set(word_dict)
    dp = [1] + [0] * len(s)
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        dp[i] = sum(dp[j] for j in range(i) if s[j:i] in words)
    return dp[len(s)]

word_break("leetcode", ["leet", "code"])                          # -> True
word_break("catsandog", ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"])    # -> False
word_break("cars", ["car", "ca", "rs"]), word_break_table("cars", ["car", "ca", "rs"])   # -> (True, True)
count_splits("catsanddog", ["cat", "cats", "and", "sand", "dog"])   # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Change the combine step for related questions: a sum counts the splits, and \cd{min(dp[j] + 1)} finds the
fewest words. A greedy longest match fails: \cd{"cars"} needs \cd{"ca" + "rs"}, not \cd{"car"}.

\subsubsection{More than two groups: a bitmask of used items}
With two groups, one subset fixes the other, so a table over sums works. With $k > 2$ groups, one valid group
does not guarantee the rest (Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets). A greedy fails: for
\cd{[1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2]} and $k = 4$, the group $1 + 1 + 1$ leaves no valid split, but $1 + 2$ four
times works. So the state must be the \emph{set} of used items, as an $n$-bit mask. Fill one group at a time
to remove the symmetry between groups. The fill of the open group is the used sum modulo the group target,
so the mask alone fixes the state. Memory hook: \emph{mask of used numbers, fill is used sum mod target, try
every unused number that fits.}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def can_partition_k(nums, k):
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % k:
        return False
    target = total // k
    n = len(nums)
    all_used = (1 << n) - 1

    @cache
    def can_finish(used, fill):        # fill == (sum of the used numbers) % target
        if used == all_used:
            return True                # every group closed at exactly target
        for i in range(n):
            if used >> i & 1 or fill + nums[i] > target:
                continue               # already placed, or does not fit
            if can_finish(used | 1 << i, (fill + nums[i]) % target):
                return True
        return False

    return can_finish(0, 0)

can_partition_k([4, 3, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1], 4)       # -> True
can_partition_k([1, 2, 3, 4], 3)                # -> False
can_partition_k([1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2], 4)    # -> True
\end{pyex}
There are at most $2^n$ masks with $n$ steps each, so the cost is $O(n \cdot 2^n)$. In CPython that is
under half a second for $n \le 16$, but several seconds near $n = 20$. The optimal version adds pruning.
Sort the numbers, and return \cd{False} when the largest number exceeds the target. Stop the loop at the
first number that does not fit. Skip a value when an earlier equal copy is still unused. The pruning helps
most when values repeat. It does not change the bound.

The same state works for other ``assign $n \le 20$ items'' problems. Keep the used mask. Add only what the
future still needs: a fill, a count of closed groups, or the last item.

\subsubsection{Rebuild the chosen items}
The table gives a number. To list the items, store which item last improved each cell. Then walk back from
the target. Memory hook: \emph{a second list remembers the last item of each cell; follow it back to 0.}
\begin{pyex}
def fewest_coins_list(coins, amount):
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    last = [0] * (amount + 1)          # last[a] = the coin that set dp[a]
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:
                dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1
                last[a] = c
    if dp[amount] == INF:
        return None
    picked = []
    while amount:
        picked.append(last[amount])
        amount -= last[amount]
    return picked

fewest_coins_list([1, 3, 4], 6)    # -> [3, 3]
fewest_coins_list([2], 3)          # -> None
\end{pyex}
For a 0/1 problem, the 1-D table forgets which row a cell came from. Keep the full 2-D table
\cd{dp[i][t]} and walk back from \cd{i = n} to 1: if \cd{dp[i][t] != dp[i - 1][t]}, item \cd{i} is in the
answer, so subtract its size from \cd{t}. Otherwise skip item \cd{i}.

\subsubsection{More limits, groups and bounded copies}
Memory hook: \emph{one table dimension per limit; one new row per group.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Two capacities} (for example weight and volume): use one table dimension per capacity.
        For 0/1 items, loop every capacity down.
  \item \textbf{Exactly one item from each group}: build a new row for each group from the old row. Do not
        update in place. An in-place update lets two items of one group both count. It also keeps the old
        value, so a group can be skipped.
  \item \textbf{A fixed number of items}: add the count to the state, \cd{dp[count][t]}.
  \item \textbf{Item \cd{i} at most \cd{k} times}: for yes or no, min or max, split \cd{k} into the parts
        1, 2, 4, \dots{} and the rest, and run the 0/1 loop on the parts. A part of \cd{c} copies has the size
        \cd{c * w}, the value \cd{c * v}, and adds \cd{c} to an item count. For counts, do not split. The parts
        build some multisets in two ways. Use a sliding window sum over \cd{t - j * w} for \cd{j = 0..k}.
  \item \textbf{Huge values but $n \le 40$}: meet in the middle. List the sums of each half and match them
        with a hash map or with sorting.
  \item \textbf{A lower bound on one total} (a profit of at least $P$ with at most $G$ members): use one
        dimension per limit, and cap the lower-bounded total at $P$ (Profitable Schemes, LeetCode 879).
        The next variation shows the code.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{At least the total: cap the index}
Some questions ask for a total of \emph{at least} $P$, for example a profit of at least $P$. An exact table
needs one cell for each sum up to the sum of all values. In Profitable Schemes, that is $10^4$ profit cells
for each of 101 member counts and 100 items: about $10^8$ steps. But all totals of $P$ or more give the same
result: they pass. So merge them into one cell. Write to \cd{dp[min(P, t + w)]}, so the last cell means
``$P$ or more''. The table stays $P + 1$ cells wide. Memory hook: \emph{at least P: cap the index at P; the
last cell means P or more.}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import combinations

MOD = 10**9 + 7

def count_at_least(items, P):
    # dp[t] = subsets with the sum t; dp[P] = subsets with the sum P or more
    dp = [1] + [0] * P
    for w in items:
        for t in range(P, -1, -1):           # down, and every t is a source
            dp[min(P, t + w)] += dp[t]       # take w: the total t + w, capped at P
    return dp[P]

def brute(items, P):
    return sum(sum(c) >= P for r in range(len(items) + 1)
               for c in combinations(items, r))

count_at_least([2, 3, 5], 5)                 # -> 5
tests = [([2, 3, 5], 5), ([0, 1, 4], 3), ([6], 2), ([], 0), ([1, 1, 2, 7], 4)]
all(count_at_least(a, P) == brute(a, P) for a, P in tests)   # -> True

def profitable_schemes(n, min_profit, group, profit):
    P = min_profit
    # dp[m][p] = item sets with m members and the profit p (p == P means P or more)
    dp = [[0] * (P + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    dp[0][0] = 1
    for g, pr in zip(group, profit):
        for m in range(n - g, -1, -1):       # members: an upper limit, exact index
            for p in range(P, -1, -1):       # profit: a lower bound, capped index
                q = min(P, p + pr)
                dp[m + g][q] = (dp[m + g][q] + dp[m][p]) % MOD
    return sum(row[P] for row in dp) % MOD

profitable_schemes(5, 3, [2, 2], [2, 3])           # -> 2
profitable_schemes(10, 5, [2, 3, 5], [6, 7, 8])    # -> 7
\end{pyex}
The step pushes from the cell \cd{t} to a later cell. So the loop visits every \cd{t} from \cd{P} down to 0,
not only \cd{t >= w}. Each write goes to an index of \cd{t} or more. The loop goes down, so that cell is
already read in this pass, and each item counts one time only. At \cd{t = P} the step doubles \cd{dp[P]}:
with or without the item, the total stays $P$ or more. General rule: an upper limit drops the cells above
it, and a lower bound merges the cells above it into one.

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Do the items get signs, or go into two groups? Write the complement as the total minus the
        quantity. Then solve one subset sum, for example with the sum \cd{(total + target) // 2}.
  \item What is the total? A sum, a capacity, a length, a string position or a day. Is $n \cdot T$ at most
        a few million? If not, and $n \le 20$ (or $n \le 40$), use a mask (or meet in the middle).
  \item Is the total enough state? If $k > 2$ groups share the items, it is not. With $n \le 20$, use the
        mask of used items.
  \item Write the recurrence. Fix the last item (or the last piece of a string): \cd{dp[t]} comes from
        \cd{dp[t - w]}. Check the step on a tiny case by hand.
  \item Can one item repeat? No: loop the totals down. Yes: loop them up.
  \item What does the cell hold? Fewest items (min, start \cd{inf}), number of ways (sum, \cd{dp[0] = 1}),
        yes or no (or, \cd{dp[0] = True}), or best value (max).
  \item For counts: are two orders of the same items one answer or two? One answer: items outside.
        Two answers: totals outside (this needs unlimited copies).
  \item Exactly the total, at most the total, or at least the total? Exactly: only \cd{dp[0]} starts as
        reached. At most: solve for each exact total, then combine \cd{dp[0..T]} at the end (the best cell,
        or the sum for counts). For a best value, every cell can also start at 0. At least \cd{P}: cap the
        total at \cd{P} and write to \cd{dp[min(P, t + w)]}, so the last cell means ``\cd{P} or more''.
        Loop \cd{t} down from \cd{P} to 0. The table stays \cd{P + 1} cells wide, also when the sum of all
        values is large.
  \item Can an item be zero or negative? Zero items in a 0/1 count double the ways. Negative items in an
        unbounded count can give infinitely many sequences. Then add the length to the state.
  \item Are the items themselves part of the answer? Store the last item for each cell, or keep the 2-D table.
  \item Choose the form. A memoized DFS is fine when the depth stays below about 1000. Otherwise use
        the bottom-up loop. Test it against a brute force over subsets on small inputs.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Loop direction.} A 0/1 problem with the totals going up uses one item many times. An unbounded
problem with the totals going down uses each item only once. Both bugs give wrong answers and no error.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Loop order for counts.} Items outside counts combinations. Totals outside counts ordered sequences.
For \cd{[1, 2, 3]} and the target 4, the two orders give 4 and 7.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Base case.} A count needs \cd{dp[0] = 1}, a yes or no needs \cd{dp[0] = True}, and a min needs
\cd{dp[0] = 0}. With \cd{dp[0] = 0} in a count, every cell stays 0. The amount 0 has one way (the empty
choice) and needs zero coins.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative indexes.} Start the inner loop at \cd{w}, or test \cd{w <= t}, before you read
\cd{dp[t - w]}. A negative index reads from the end of the list and gives a silent wrong answer.
\end{caution}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The sentinel for ``not reachable'' must be larger than any real answer: \cd{inf} or
        \cd{amount + 1}, not \cd{amount}. Convert it to \cd{-1} (or what the statement asks) at the end.
  \item Greedy by the largest item fails on sets such as coins 1, 3, 4 and the amount 6. Test a small
        counterexample before you trust a greedy.
  \item Target Sum: test \cd{abs(target) > total} and the parity of \cd{total + target} before you size the
        table. A zero has two signs, so the inner loop must include \cd{s = x} (it then doubles \cd{dp[s]}).
  \item A memoized DFS over amounts up to $10^4$ goes deeper than the Python recursion limit of 1000. Use the
        bottom-up loop.
  \item Do not change a set while you iterate over it. Build the new sums in a comprehension first.
  \item A bitmask memo must have the mask in its key. A key of (index, fill) merges different used sets and
        gives wrong answers.
  \item Put the cached helper inside the function. A cache at module level keeps results from an earlier
        input.
  \item Turn the word list into a set before the DP. A list lookup scans every word.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Coin Change (322) & Unbounded, fewest items (min); sentinel for ``not reachable''. &
  Pick the last coin: dp[a] = 1 + min of dp[a - coin], with dp[0] = 0. \\
Coin Change II (518) & Unbounded count of combinations: coins outside, amounts up inside. &
  Coins outside, amounts going up inside: ways[a] += ways[a - coin]. \\
Combination Sum IV (377) & Unbounded count of ordered sequences: totals outside, items inside. &
  Ways to make a total: try every last number, add the ways for what is left. \\
Partition Equal Subset Sum (416) & 0/1 yes or no; equal halves become one subset with half the total. &
  Odd total means no. Otherwise grow the set of reachable sums and ask if half the total is in it. \\
Target Sum (494) & Signs become a subset with sum (total + target) / 2; 0/1 count. &
  Plus or minus each number, cache on (index, running sum). \\
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) & $k > 2$ groups: the state is the mask of used items, with fill = used sum mod target. &
  Mask of used numbers, fill is used sum mod target, try every unused number that fits. \\
Word Break (139) & The total is a string position; words are reusable items; combine with or. &
  Cut off a first word, ask if the rest can split, and cache by start index. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
