% =====================================================================
\section{Dynamic programming on strings and sequences}\label{tech:T17}

\subsection{The idea}
Many problems compare two sequences. They ask for the longest common part, the cheapest edit,
the number of ways that one sequence fits in the other, or a yes or no match.
A brute force tries every subsequence or every edit script. That work is exponential.

The work that remains after some choices depends only on how much of each sequence is used.
So a pair of positions $(i, j)$, one in each sequence, is a full state.
The brute force reaches the same pair by many different choice paths, and it solves that pair again each time.
There are only $(m + 1)(n + 1)$ pairs. Solve each pair one time and store the result in a table.
Cell \cd{dp[i][j]} holds the answer for the prefixes \cd{a[:i]} and \cd{b[:j]}.

To fill a cell, look only at the last element of each prefix: \cd{a[i - 1]} and \cd{b[j - 1]}.
Each move removes one or two of these elements and points to a smaller cell:
\begin{itemize}
\item Diagonal, cell $(i - 1, j - 1)$: use both last elements together (a match or a replace).
\item Up, cell $(i - 1, j)$: drop the last element of \cd{a}.
\item Left, cell $(i, j - 1)$: drop the last element of \cd{b}.
\end{itemize}
The problems in this family differ mainly in two things: which moves are legal, and how the moves combine.
Use \cd{max} for a longest value, \cd{min} for a cost, a sum for a number of ways, and \cd{or} for a yes or no answer.

\textbf{Worked example.} Find the length of the longest common subsequence (LCS) of \cd{"abcde"} and \cd{"ace"}.
Row 0 and column 0 stand for an empty prefix, so they hold 0.
Cell $(3, 2)$ compares \cd{c} with \cd{c}. They match, so the cell is the diagonal value plus 1, which is 2.
Cell $(4, 3)$ compares \cd{d} with \cd{e}. They do not match, so at least one of them is not in the answer.
Drop each one in turn: the cell is the larger of up (2) and left (2).
The bottom-right cell holds the answer: 3, for the subsequence \cd{"ace"}.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
 & \cd{""} & \cd{a} & \cd{c} & \cd{e} \\
\midrule
\cd{""} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\cd{a} & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
\cd{b} & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
\cd{c} & 0 & 1 & \textbf{2} & 2 \\
\cd{d} & 0 & 1 & 2 & \textbf{2} \\
\cd{e} & 0 & 1 & 2 & \textbf{3} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A second group of problems works on one string and asks about palindromes.
A window of a string is a palindrome when its two end characters are equal and the window just inside them is a palindrome.
So each window depends on one smaller window with the same center.
Start at a center and grow outward. Stop at the first mismatch, because no larger window on that center can be a palindrome.
A string of length $n$ has $2n - 1$ centers: $n$ characters for odd lengths and $n - 1$ gaps for even lengths.
This takes $O(n^2)$ time. The brute force checks each of the $O(n^2)$ windows from scratch and takes $O(n^3)$.

\textbf{Worked example.} Count the palindromic substrings of \cd{"aaa"}.
The center on index 1 grows to \cd{"a"} and then to \cd{"aaa"}, so it gives 2 palindromes.
Each of the two gaps gives \cd{"aa"} one time. Each end character gives \cd{"a"} one time.
The total is $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
\item Two strings or arrays, and the question is how well they match, align, merge or transform.
  Typical words: ``longest common'', ``minimum number of operations to convert'', ``number of ways to form'',
  ``can it be formed from'', ``does the pattern match the entire string''.
\item The word \emph{subsequence}: you can skip elements, but you must keep their order.
  A skip is one move and a match is another move.
\item Both lengths are up to about $10^3$. A table of about $10^6$ cells fits the budget.
\item Lengths of about 20 with wildcard or repeat symbols: a memoized search on $(i, j)$ is enough.
\item At some step two choices both look valid. For example, both sources match the next character,
  or a star can stop or continue. Greedy fails, so keep every reachable state.
  Counter-signal: when each step has only one legal choice (Is Subsequence), greedy two pointers are enough.
\item The answer type selects the combine step: longest or cheapest (\cd{max}, \cd{min}),
  how many (sum), is it possible (\cd{or}).
\item The output is one number, or true or false: you need only the value, so you can roll the rows.
  The output is the sequence itself (a common subsequence, an edit script): keep the full table and walk back.
\item One string, the words \emph{palindromic substring}, and $n$ up to a few thousand: expand around each center.
\item One string, and the words \emph{palindromic subsequence} or ``fewest inserts to make a palindrome'':
  use an interval table on \cd{s[i:j + 1]}.
\item Many questions of the form ``is this range a palindrome'', for example cuts into palindromes:
  build the palindrome table one time.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Decide five things before you write the code:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Meaning.} One sentence: \cd{dp[i][j]} is the answer for \cd{a[:i]} and \cd{b[:j]}.
\item \textbf{Border.} The values for an empty prefix: row 0 and column 0.
\item \textbf{Moves.} What can happen to \cd{a[i - 1]} and \cd{b[j - 1]}: diagonal, up or left.
\item \textbf{Combine.} \cd{max}, \cd{min}, a sum, or \cd{or}.
\item \textbf{Answer and order.} Usually \cd{dp[m][n]}. Fill the rows top to bottom and each row left to right.
\end{enumerate}
The template is the LCS. It returns the full table, so you can read the cells of the worked example.
\begin{pyex}
def lcs_table(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    # dp[i][j] = LCS length of the prefixes a[:i] and b[:j]
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]   # row 0 and column 0: empty prefix
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:             # cell (i, j) compares a[i-1] and b[j-1]
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1  # diagonal: pair the two last elements
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j],     # up: drop a[i-1]
                               dp[i][j - 1])     # left: drop b[j-1]
    return dp

dp = lcs_table("abcde", "ace")
dp[3]                                   # -> [0, 1, 2, 2]
dp[4]                                   # -> [0, 1, 2, 2]
dp[-1][-1]                              # -> 3
lcs_table("abc", "def")[-1][-1]         # -> 0
lcs_table([1, 4, 2], [1, 2, 4])[-1][-1] # -> 2
\end{pyex}
Invariant: when the loop reaches $(i, j)$, the cells up, left and diagonal are final.
They hold the answers for smaller prefix pairs. Time and space are $O(mn)$.
The table has $m + 1$ rows and $n + 1$ columns. The extra border row and column remove all index checks.

\textbf{Top-down form.} A memoized search fills the same states on demand.
Here \cd{dfs(i, j)} answers for the suffixes \cd{a[i:]} and \cd{b[j:]}, and the answer is \cd{dfs(0, 0)}.
This form is easier to write when the moves are irregular, for example with pattern symbols.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def lcs_memo(a, b):
    @cache
    def dfs(i, j):                      # LCS length of the suffixes a[i:] and b[j:]
        if i == len(a) or j == len(b):
            return 0
        if a[i] == b[j]:
            return 1 + dfs(i + 1, j + 1)
        return max(dfs(i + 1, j), dfs(i, j + 1))
    return dfs(0, 0)

lcs_memo("abcde", "ace")                # -> 3
lcs_memo("", "abc")                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
\cd{functools.cache} \since{3.9} is the short form of \cd{@lru_cache(maxsize=None)}. Use the long form on an older Python.
The recursion depth can reach $m + n$. The default limit is 1000, so two strings of length 500 already fail.
When $m + n$ can reach about 1000, use the table or call \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit}. In CPython, the memoized form is also often 2 to 3 times slower than the table.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Read the table}
Each problem in the family is one row of this table. Write the meaning of a cell first.
The border, the moves and the answer follow from that sentence.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.3cm}L{3.6cm}L{2.5cm}L{5.2cm}L{1.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & \cd{dp[i][j]} means & Border & Moves & Combine \\
\midrule
LCS & LCS length of \cd{a[:i]} and \cd{b[:j]} & all 0 & equal: diagonal + 1; else up, left & \cd{max} \\
Common substring & length of the longest common suffix of \cd{a[:i]} and \cd{b[:j]} & all 0 & equal: diagonal + 1; else 0. The answer is the max over all cells & \cd{max} \\
Edit distance & edits that turn \cd{a[:i]} into \cd{b[:j]} & \cd{dp[i][0] = i}, \cd{dp[0][j] = j} & equal: diagonal; else 1 + (up, left, diagonal) & \cd{min} \\
Distinct subsequences & ways to form \cd{t[:j]} from \cd{s[:i]} & \cd{dp[i][0] = 1} & up; equal: also diagonal & sum \\
Interleaving & \cd{s1[:i]} and \cd{s2[:j]} form \cd{s3[:i + j]} & \cd{dp[0][0]} is true & up if \cd{s1[i - 1]} equals \cd{s3[i + j - 1]}; left if \cd{s2[j - 1]} does & \cd{or} \\
Regular expression (suffix form) & \cd{s[i:]} matches \cd{p[j:]} & \cd{dp[m][n]} is true & token \cd{x*}: skip it, or eat one character and stay; else eat one character in each & \cd{or} \\
Palindromic subsequence (interval form) & longest palindromic subsequence of \cd{s[i:j + 1]} & \cd{dp[i][i] = 1} & equal ends: inside \cd{dp[i + 1][j - 1]} + 2; else drop the left end or the right end & \cd{max} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In the prefix form, the answer is \cd{dp[m][n]}. In the suffix form, the answer is \cd{dp[0][0]}.
In the interval form on one string, the answer is \cd{dp[0][n - 1]}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Maximize the matches: longest common subsequence}
Longest Common Subsequence is the core template.
Memory hook: \emph{last chars match: go diagonal plus one. Else take the best of up and left.}
On a match, take the diagonal, not up or left. Up plus 1 or left plus 1 uses one character two times.
The same table answers related questions. The minimum number of deletions that makes two strings equal is
$m + n - 2 \cdot \mathrm{LCS}$ (Delete Operation for Two Strings).
Non-crossing links between equal numbers of two arrays are an LCS on integers (Uncrossed Lines).

A \emph{substring} is contiguous. For the longest common substring, a cell holds the longest common
suffix of the two prefixes. A mismatch resets the cell to 0, and the answer is the largest cell anywhere.
Memory hook: \emph{substring breaks on a mismatch: reset to 0 and keep the best cell.}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_common_substring(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]   # longest common suffix of a[:i], b[:j]
    best = 0
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
                best = max(best, dp[i][j])
            # a mismatch leaves the cell at 0
    return best

longest_common_substring("abcde", "abfde")   # -> 2
longest_common_substring("abc", "xyz")       # -> 0
\end{pyex}
The LCS of \cd{"abcde"} and \cd{"abfde"} is 4 (\cd{"abde"}), but the longest common substring is only 2.

\subsubsection{Minimize a cost: edit distance}
Edit Distance asks for the minimum number of inserts, deletes and replaces that turn \cd{a} into \cd{b}.
Look at the last characters \cd{a[i - 1]} and \cd{b[j - 1]}. An optimal edit script pairs them (a free match or a replace),
deletes \cd{a[i - 1]}, or inserts \cd{b[j - 1]}. Each case leaves a smaller prefix pair.
Memory hook: \emph{look at the last chars: same is free diagonal, else 1 plus min of up, left, diagonal.}
Up deletes \cd{a[i - 1]}. Left inserts \cd{b[j - 1]}. Diagonal replaces \cd{a[i - 1]}.
The border is not 0: an empty \cd{a} needs \cd{j} inserts, and an empty \cd{b} needs \cd{i} deletes.
\begin{pyex}
def edit_distance(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]   # edits that turn a[:i] into b[:j]
    for i in range(m + 1):
        dp[i][0] = i                             # delete all i characters
    for j in range(n + 1):
        dp[0][j] = j                             # insert all j characters
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1]      # same last character: free
            else:
                dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i - 1][j],      # delete a[i-1]
                                   dp[i][j - 1],      # insert b[j-1]
                                   dp[i - 1][j - 1])  # replace a[i-1]
    return dp[m][n]

edit_distance("horse", "ros")           # -> 3
edit_distance("intention", "execution") # -> 5
edit_distance("", "abc")                # -> 3
edit_distance("abc", "abc")             # -> 0
\end{pyex}
With other costs per operation, the shape stays the same. Put each cost on its move, and use the costs in the border too.
The optimal solution keeps only two rows. See the rolling rows variation below.

\subsubsection{Count the ways: distinct subsequences}
Distinct Subsequences counts the index sets in \cd{s} that spell \cd{t}.
Split the ways to form \cd{t[:j]} from \cd{s[:i]} by the fate of the last character \cd{s[i - 1]}:
skip it, or use it as \cd{t[j - 1]}.
The two groups do not overlap, and together they cover every way. So add them.
Memory hook: \emph{ways equal skip plus use: \cd{dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]}, plus \cd{dp[i-1][j-1]} on a match.}
\begin{pyex}
def num_distinct(s, t):
    m, n = len(s), len(t)
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]   # ways to form t[:j] from s[:i]
    for i in range(m + 1):
        dp[i][0] = 1                             # empty t: choose nothing, one way
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j]              # skip s[i-1]
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] += dp[i - 1][j - 1]     # use s[i-1] as t[j-1]
    return dp[m][n]

num_distinct("rabbbit", "rabbit")       # -> 3
num_distinct("babgbag", "bag")          # -> 5
num_distinct("ba", "a")                 # -> 1
num_distinct("a", "aa")                 # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Set \cd{dp[i][0] = 1} for every \cd{i}, not only for \cd{i = 0}.
Without it, a character after index 0 cannot start a match: \cd{("ba", "a")} gives 0.
Python integers do not overflow. Counts for short prefixes of \cd{t} can be much larger than the final answer.
If a problem asks for a modulo, apply it at each addition.
The optimal solution keeps one row and updates \cd{j} from right to left (see rolling rows).

\subsubsection{Yes or no with a derived index: interleaving string}
Interleaving String asks if \cd{s3} uses each character of \cd{s1} and \cd{s2} one time
and keeps the order of each string.
Build \cd{s3} from left to right. The next position in \cd{s3} is \cd{k = i + j},
so \cd{k} adds nothing to the state. The state is only $(i, j)$.
When the next characters of \cd{s1} and \cd{s2} both match \cd{s3[k]}, either choice can be the right one.
So greedy fails, and the search must try both.
Memory hook: \emph{take from \cd{s1} or \cd{s2} if it matches \cd{s3[i + j]}; cache \cd{(i, j)}.}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def is_interleave(s1, s2, s3):
    if len(s1) + len(s2) != len(s3):
        return False

    @cache
    def can(i, j):                      # can s1[i:] and s2[j:] form s3[i + j:]?
        if i == len(s1) and j == len(s2):
            return True
        k = i + j                       # next character of s3 to match
        if i < len(s1) and s1[i] == s3[k] and can(i + 1, j):
            return True
        if j < len(s2) and s2[j] == s3[k] and can(i, j + 1):
            return True
        return False

    return can(0, 0)

def greedy(s1, s2, s3):                 # WRONG: prefers s1 when both match
    i = j = 0
    for ch in s3:
        if i < len(s1) and s1[i] == ch:
            i += 1
        elif j < len(s2) and s2[j] == ch:
            j += 1
        else:
            return False
    return i == len(s1) and j == len(s2)

is_interleave("aabcc", "dbbca", "aadbbcbcac")   # -> True
is_interleave("aabcc", "dbbca", "aadbbbaccc")   # -> False
is_interleave("ab", "ac", "acab")               # -> True
greedy("ab", "ac", "acab")                      # -> False
is_interleave("", "", "")                       # -> True
\end{pyex}
Check the lengths first. Without the check, a short \cd{s3} raises \cd{IndexError},
and a long \cd{s3} can return true with extra characters left over.
General rule: when one index follows from the others, drop it from the state.
For $k$ sources, the state is the $k$-tuple of prefix lengths.
The optimal solution is a rolling one-row table with $O(n)$ memory (see rolling rows).

\subsubsection{Pattern matching: regular expression}
Regular Expression Matching supports \cd{.} (any one character) and \cd{*} (zero or more of the element before it).
The pattern must match the entire string.
The trick: \cd{*} is a postfix modifier. Look at \cd{p[j + 1]} before you use \cd{p[j]},
and treat \cd{x*} as one token.
A token \cd{x*} has only two moves. Skip it (zero copies, \cd{j + 2}).
Or, if \cd{x} matches \cd{s[i]}, eat that character and stay on the same token (\cd{i + 1}, same \cd{j}).
Staying on the token covers every count of copies without a loop over counts.
Memory hook: \emph{peek for a star: skip it, or eat one and stay.}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def is_match(s, p):
    @cache
    def dfs(i, j):                      # does s[i:] match p[j:]?
        if j == len(p):
            return i == len(s)          # both must end together
        first = i < len(s) and p[j] in (s[i], ".")
        if j + 1 < len(p) and p[j + 1] == "*":
            # skip "x*", or eat one character and stay on "x*"
            return dfs(i, j + 2) or (first and dfs(i + 1, j))
        return first and dfs(i + 1, j + 1)
    return dfs(0, 0)

is_match("aa", "a")                     # -> False
is_match("aa", "a*")                    # -> True
is_match("ab", ".*")                    # -> True
is_match("aab", "c*a*b")                # -> True
is_match("aaa", "a*a")                  # -> True
is_match("mississippi", "mis*is*p*.")   # -> False
\end{pyex}
Each pattern token becomes a small set of moves on $(i, j)$.
Use this table to add a new symbol. Here ``eat'' means: \cd{x} matches \cd{s[i]}, and \cd{i} moves by 1.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3cm}L{12.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Token & Moves from $(i, j)$ \\
\midrule
\cd{x} or \cd{.} & eat, and move to the next token: $(i + 1, j + 1)$ \\
\cd{x*} (zero or more) & skip the token: $(i, j + 2)$; or eat and stay: $(i + 1, j)$ \\
\cd{x+} (one or more) & eat and stay: $(i + 1, j)$; or eat and leave: $(i + 1, j + 2)$. There is no skip move \\
\cd{x?} (zero or one) & skip the token: $(i, j + 2)$; or eat and leave: $(i + 1, j + 2)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The ``eat and stay'' move is the same idea as unlimited reuse of an item in the unbounded knapsack.
The optimal solution fills the same states bottom-up. Each state reads only cells with a larger \cd{i} or \cd{j},
so \cd{i} goes from \cd{m} down to 0 and \cd{j} goes from \cd{n - 1} down to 0.
Use it when the inputs are long enough to reach the recursion limit.
\begin{pyex}
def is_match_table(s, p):
    m, n = len(s), len(p)
    dp = [[False] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]   # s[i:] matches p[j:]
    dp[m][n] = True                                  # empty string, empty pattern
    for i in range(m, -1, -1):                       # i = m too: "a*b*" matches ""
        for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            first = i < m and p[j] in (s[i], ".")
            if j + 1 < n and p[j + 1] == "*":
                dp[i][j] = dp[i][j + 2] or (first and dp[i + 1][j])
            else:
                dp[i][j] = first and dp[i + 1][j + 1]
    return dp[0][0]

is_match_table("aab", "c*a*b")          # -> True
is_match_table("ab", ".*c")             # -> False
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Rolling rows: keep O(n) memory}
Row \cd{i} reads only row \cd{i - 1} and row \cd{i}. So keep two rows, or one row, instead of the full table.
The rule for the direction comes from the neighbors that a cell reads.
Memory hook: \emph{up and diagonal are old, left is new. Reads up and diagonal: scan right to left.
Reads up and left: scan left to right. Reads all three: keep two rows.}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.4cm}L{8.2cm}L{4cm}@{}}
\toprule
A cell reads & Keep & Examples \\
\midrule
up, left, diagonal & two rows \cd{prev} and \cd{cur}; or one row plus the old diagonal value in a variable & LCS, Edit Distance \\
up and diagonal & one row; \cd{j} from right to left, so \cd{dp[j - 1]} still holds the old row & Distinct Subsequences, 0/1 knapsack \\
up and left & one row; \cd{j} from left to right. Before the write, \cd{dp[j]} is up and \cd{dp[j - 1]} is left & Interleaving String \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
def edit_distance_2rows(a, b):
    n = len(b)
    prev = list(range(n + 1))           # row 0: j inserts
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        cur = [i] + [0] * n             # a NEW list for each row; cur[0] = i deletes
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                cur[j] = prev[j - 1]
            else:
                cur[j] = 1 + min(prev[j], cur[j - 1], prev[j - 1])
        prev = cur
    return prev[n]

def num_distinct_1row(s, t):
    n = len(t)
    dp = [1] + [0] * n                  # dp[j] = ways to form t[:j]
    for ch in s:
        for j in range(n, 0, -1):       # right to left: dp[j - 1] is still old
            if ch == t[j - 1]:
                dp[j] += dp[j - 1]
    return dp[n]

def num_distinct_wrong(s, t):           # WRONG: left to right
    n = len(t)
    dp = [1] + [0] * n
    for ch in s:
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if ch == t[j - 1]:
                dp[j] += dp[j - 1]      # reads a value of the NEW row
    return dp[n]

edit_distance_2rows("horse", "ros")     # -> 3
num_distinct_1row("babgbag", "bag")     # -> 5
num_distinct_1row("a", "aa")            # -> 0
num_distinct_wrong("a", "aa")           # -> 1
\end{pyex}
In the wrong version, one character of \cd{s} matches two characters of \cd{t}.
\begin{pyex}
def lcs_1row(a, b):
    dp = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    for x in a:
        diag = 0                        # old dp[j - 1]: the upper-left cell
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            up = dp[j]                  # save the old value before the write
            dp[j] = diag + 1 if x == b[j - 1] else max(up, dp[j - 1])
            diag = up
    return dp[-1]

def is_interleave_1row(s1, s2, s3):
    m, n = len(s1), len(s2)
    if m + n != len(s3):
        return False
    dp = [False] * (n + 1)              # dp[j]: s1[:i] and s2[:j] form s3[:i + j]
    for i in range(m + 1):
        for j in range(n + 1):
            if i == 0 and j == 0:
                dp[j] = True
                continue
            top = i > 0 and dp[j] and s1[i - 1] == s3[i + j - 1]
            left = j > 0 and dp[j - 1] and s2[j - 1] == s3[i + j - 1]
            dp[j] = top or left
    return dp[n]

lcs_1row("abcde", "ace")                            # -> 3
is_interleave_1row("aabcc", "dbbca", "aadbbcbcac")  # -> True
is_interleave_1row("ab", "ac", "acab")              # -> True
is_interleave_1row("a", "", "b")                    # -> False
\end{pyex}
When the two inputs can swap roles (LCS, Edit Distance, Interleaving String), make the shorter one the column sequence.
Then the memory is $O(\min(m, n))$.

\subsubsection{Rebuild the answer: walk back through the table}
A rolling table gives only the value. To get the sequence itself, keep the full table.
Start at $(m, n)$. At each cell, find the move that produced its value, and step to that neighbor.
Collect an element on each match move, and reverse the list at the end.
The same walk recovers an edit script or an alignment.
Memory hook: \emph{walk back from the corner along the move that made each value.}
\begin{pyex}
def lcs_string(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    out = []
    i, j = m, n
    while i > 0 and j > 0:
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:        # this cell came from the diagonal
            out.append(a[i - 1])
            i, j = i - 1, j - 1
        elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:
            i -= 1                      # the cell came from up
        else:
            j -= 1                      # the cell came from the left
    return "".join(reversed(out))

lcs_string("abcde", "ace")              # -> 'ace'
lcs_string("abcbdab", "bdcaba")         # -> 'bcba'
lcs_string("abc", "xyz")                # -> ''
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Palindromic substrings: expand around each center}
Longest Palindromic Substring returns the longest palindromic window.
Memory hook: \emph{every palindrome grows from a center: try each character and each gap,
expand while the ends match, keep the longest.}
Palindromic Substrings counts the palindromic windows by position, so \cd{"aaa"} gives 6, not 3.
Memory hook: \emph{every palindrome has a middle: expand from each middle, odd and even, and count each match.}

Both problems use one helper. It moves \cd{left} and \cd{right} outward while the two ends match.
The loop stops one step too far on each side. So the palindrome is \cd{s[left + 1:right]},
and its length is \cd{right - left - 1}.
Even-length palindromes have no middle character. Call the helper on the gap \cd{(c, c + 1)} too.
\begin{pyex}
def longest_palindrome(s):
    def expand(left, right):
        while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:
            left -= 1
            right += 1
        return s[left + 1:right]        # the loop stops one step too far
    best = ""
    for c in range(len(s)):
        best = max(best, expand(c, c), expand(c, c + 1), key=len)
    return best

def count_palindromes(s):
    n = len(s)
    def expand(left, right):
        count = 0
        while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right]:
            count += 1                  # s[left:right + 1] is one more palindrome
            left -= 1
            right += 1
        return count
    return sum(expand(i, i) + expand(i, i + 1) for i in range(n))

longest_palindrome("babad")             # -> 'bab'
longest_palindrome("cbbd")              # -> 'bb'
longest_palindrome("a")                 # -> 'a'
count_palindromes("abc")                # -> 3
count_palindromes("aaa")                # -> 6
\end{pyex}
The optimal versions use the same algorithm. For the longest window, store only the start and the length,
and slice one time at the end. For the count, one loop over the $2n - 1$ centers replaces the two calls.
Center \cd{c} gives \cd{left = c // 2} and \cd{right = left + c} \pct\ \cd{2}.
Even \cd{c} is a character and odd \cd{c} is a gap.
\begin{pyex}
def count_palindromes_one_loop(s):
    n = len(s)
    count = 0
    for c in range(2 * n - 1):
        left = c // 2
        right = left + c % 2            # even c: a character; odd c: a gap
        while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right]:
            count += 1
            left -= 1
            right += 1
    return count

count_palindromes_one_loop("aaa")       # -> 6
count_palindromes_one_loop("abba")      # -> 6
\end{pyex}
General rule: when a structure has two shapes (one middle item or two middle items), cover both shapes.
Seed each shape explicitly, as the two calls do.
Or encode both shapes in one index range, as the $2n - 1$ centers do. Then one loop body handles both cases.
Or transform the input so that only one shape remains.
For $n$ of $10^5$ or more, $O(n^2)$ is too slow. Then use Manacher's algorithm, which runs in $O(n)$.
It first puts a separator between all characters and at both ends, so every palindrome has a middle character.

\subsubsection{Palindromes by DP: the palindrome table}
The same recurrence fills a table. \cd{pal[i][j]} is true when \cd{s[i:j + 1]} is a palindrome:
the ends are equal, and the inside is a palindrome or has fewer than two characters.
A cell reads \cd{pal[i + 1][j - 1]}, so fill \cd{i} from right to left, or fill by increasing length.
The table costs $O(n^2)$ memory. Build it when many range questions follow,
for example Palindrome Partitioning, which tries each cut and needs each test in $O(1)$.
The number of true cells is the answer of Palindromic Substrings.
Memory hook: \emph{equal ends and a palindrome inside; fill \cd{i} from right to left.}
\begin{pyex}
def palindrome_table(s):
    n = len(s)
    pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):      # right to left: row i + 1 is ready
        for j in range(i, n):
            pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1])
    return pal

pal = palindrome_table("aab")
[(i, j) for i in range(3) for j in range(i, 3) if pal[i][j]]
# -> [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 2)]
sum(map(sum, palindrome_table("aaa")))  # -> 6
\end{pyex}
When a palindrome can skip characters (a palindromic \emph{subsequence}), a window has more than one move,
as in the LCS. Then the walk along one center does not work.
Use an interval table: \cd{dp[i][j]} is the answer for \cd{s[i:j + 1]}.
Equal ends go inside, to \cd{dp[i + 1][j - 1]}. Else drop the left end or the right end.
Fill \cd{i} from right to left, as in the palindrome table. The answer is \cd{dp[0][n - 1]}.
The fewest inserts (or deletes) that make \cd{s} a palindrome is \cd{n} minus the longest palindromic subsequence.
That length is also the LCS of \cd{s} and \cd{s[::-1]}, so the core template solves it too
(Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome, LeetCode 1312).
Memory hook: \emph{equal ends are free; else copy one end to the other side and pay 1.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_insertions(s):                  # fewest inserts that make s a palindrome
    n = len(s)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]    # dp[i][j] = inserts for s[i:j + 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):      # right to left: row i + 1 is ready
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if s[i] == s[j]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i + 1][j - 1]                     # equal ends: free
            else:
                dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])  # copy one end, pay 1
    return dp[0][n - 1] if n else 0

min_insertions("mbadm")                 # -> 2
min_insertions("leetcode")              # -> 5
min_insertions("zzazz")                 # -> 0
min_insertions("")                      # -> 0
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Which sequences does the process read in order? Give each one an index.
  If one index follows from the others (\cd{k = i + j}), drop it from the state.
\item Is the answer about a subsequence (skips allowed) or a substring (contiguous)?
  A substring of two sequences uses the ``common suffix'' cell. A palindromic substring uses centers.
  A palindromic subsequence uses an interval table.
\item Write the meaning of \cd{dp[i][j]} in one sentence. Choose prefixes (\cd{a[:i]}) for a table,
  or suffixes (\cd{a[i:]}) for a memoized search.
\item List what can happen to the last element of each prefix (the first element of each suffix):
  match both, skip one, skip the other, or a special move such as ``eat and stay''. Each move is one neighbor cell.
  For a pattern, turn each token into its moves with the token table.
\item Select the combine step from the question: \cd{max}, \cd{min}, sum, or \cd{or}.
  For a count, check that the cases do not overlap.
\item Fill the border. Ask: what is the answer for two empty prefixes, and for one empty prefix?
\item Select the order. Each cell must come after the cells that it reads.
  The prefix form goes up in \cd{i} and \cd{j}. The suffix form goes down.
\item Find the answer cell: \cd{dp[m][n]}, \cd{dp[0][0]}, or the best cell anywhere.
\item Check the size. In Python, about $10^6$ cells take about 0.3 s. If memory is tight, roll the rows.
  If the problem asks for the sequence itself, keep the full table and walk back.
\item Test on two empty inputs, on one empty input, on equal inputs, and on a case where greedy fails.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Off-by-one between the table and the strings.}
The table has size $(m + 1) \times (n + 1)$. Cell \cd{dp[i][j]} compares \cd{a[i - 1]} with \cd{b[j - 1]}, not
\cd{a[i]} with \cd{b[j]}. Build each row as a new list: \cd{[[0] * (n + 1)] * (m + 1)} repeats one row.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A wrong border.} Edit distance needs \cd{dp[i][0] = i} and \cd{dp[0][j] = j}, not 0.
Distinct subsequences needs \cd{dp[i][0] = 1} for every \cd{i}.
In interleaving, only \cd{dp[0][0]} is true without a character match.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A wrong match move.} LCS: diagonal plus 1, not up plus 1. Edit distance: a match is free, so do not add 1.
Distinct subsequences: on a match, add both cases (skip and use), not only the diagonal.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Greedy instead of a search.} When two choices both match the next character, a greedy choice can be wrong.
Interleaving \cd{("ab", "ac", "acab")} and the pattern \cd{"a*a"} on \cd{"aaa"} are small counterexamples.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Regular expression details.} Test for \cd{*} at \cd{p[j + 1]}, not at \cd{p[j]}.
Remember that \cd{x*} can match zero characters, so compute the row for an empty rest of the string.
A full match needs both indexes at the end together.
Each copy of \cd{.} in \cd{.*} matches any character, so \cd{.*} matches any string.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rolling rows.} A wrong direction reads a value of the new row.
\cd{prev = cur} with one shared list makes both names point to the same row, so build a new \cd{cur} for each row.
In edit distance, set \cd{cur[0] = i} at the start of each row.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Palindrome expansion.} Do not forget the even centers: \cd{"cbbd"} then gives \cd{"c"}, not \cd{"bb"}.
Test \cd{left >= 0} and \cd{right < n} before you compare characters.
Python accepts \cd{s[-1]}, so a missing left bound compares the wrong character and gives no error.
Count palindromes by position, not by distinct text.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion and speed.} A memoized search on two strings of length 1000 can go about 2000 levels deep.
Use the bottom-up table, or raise the recursion limit.
Keep the inner loop simple: no function calls and no slicing per cell.
A plain recursion without a cache is exponential. In the pattern case, a string of 18 \cd{a} with nine \cd{a*} tokens and a final \cd{b} makes about 11.6 million calls.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Longest Common Subsequence & The core table: match goes diagonal + 1, mismatch takes \cd{max} of up and left. & Last chars match: go diagonal plus one. Else take the best of up and left. \\
Edit Distance & Minimize a cost. The border is \cd{i} and \cd{j}. A mismatch costs 1 plus the \cd{min} of three moves. & Look at the last chars: same is free diagonal, else 1 plus min of up, left, diagonal. \\
Distinct Subsequences & Count the ways: always skip, and also use on a match. The border column is 1. & Ways equal skip plus use: \cd{dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]}, plus \cd{dp[i-1][j-1]} on a match. \\
Interleaving String & Yes or no. The third index is \cd{i + j}. Greedy fails, so search both sources. & Take from \cd{s1} or \cd{s2} if it matches \cd{s3[i + j]}; cache \cd{(i, j)}. \\
Regular Expression Matching & Pattern tokens become moves. \cd{x*} is skip or ``eat and stay''. Suffix form. & Peek for a star: skip it, or eat one and stay. \\
Longest Palindromic Substring & One string. Expand the $2n - 1$ centers and keep the longest window. & Every palindrome grows from a center: try each character and each gap, expand while the ends match, keep the longest. \\
Palindromic Substrings & Same centers. Add 1 for each matching pair instead of tracking the max. & Every palindrome has a middle: expand from each middle, odd and even, and count each match. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T17} (page~\pageref{drill:T17}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T17} (page~\pageref{ans:T17}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Dynamic programming on grids, intervals, games and states}\label{tech:T18}\label{sec:dp-shapes}

\subsection{The idea}
A brute force for these problems lists a set of histories that grows exponentially.
The histories are the paths through a grid, the orders of removal, the lines of play in a game,
or the sequences of buy and sell actions.
Many different histories reach the same situation, and the brute force solves the rest of the problem again each time.
Dynamic programming gives each situation a name, the \emph{state}. It solves each state one time and reuses the answer.
The work drops from the number of histories to the number of states times the number of choices per state.

In 1-D DP the state is a prefix index. In this section the state has other shapes.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.9cm}L{3.5cm}L{5.1cm}L{3.9cm}@{}}
\toprule
Shape & State & The choice that splits a state & Fill order \\
\midrule
Grid path & a cell $(r, c)$ & the last move into the cell & row by row \\
Path on an implicit DAG & a cell or a node & the first step out of the node & by a strict key, or a memoized DFS \\
Interval & an open range $(l, r)$ & the element that acts last (or the first cut) & by range length \\
Two-player game & the remaining range, seen by the player to move & the move of the player to move & by range length \\
State machine & (step, status) & the action at this step & step by step \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{A worked example.} Count the paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner of a $3 \times 3$ grid.
Each move goes one cell down or one cell right.
A brute force lists the paths one by one. The DP asks a smaller question for each cell: how many paths end here?
The last move into a cell comes from above or from the left. These two groups of paths do not overlap.
So the count of a cell is the count above plus the count to the left.
Each cell in row 0 and in column 0 has exactly one path, a straight line. Row 1 becomes $1, 2, 3$. Row 2 becomes $1, 3, 6$.
The answer is 6, and each cell costs one addition.
On a $100 \times 100$ grid the brute force lists about $2 \cdot 10^{58}$ paths. The DP does $10^4$ additions.

Every DP in this section comes from the same four decisions:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{State.} What is the minimum information about the past that the rest of the problem needs?
  \item \textbf{Split.} Which single choice breaks a state into smaller states that do not interact?
  \item \textbf{Base.} Which states are so small that their answer is known?
  \item \textbf{Order.} In which order is every smaller state ready before a larger state reads it?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The question asks for a count, a minimum, a maximum or a winner. It does not ask for the list of paths or orders.
        The output is one number or one boolean for the full input.
  \item Moves on a grid go only forward, for example down and right. Each cell depends only on cells before it.
  \item A rule must hold at every step of a path, for example a running total that stays above 0.
        The rule depends on the steps that come later, so fill the table backward from the target.
  \item Moves go in all directions, but each move strictly increases a key (a cell value, a length).
        The strict key removes all cycles, so the move graph is a DAG.
  \item Elements disappear or merge one at a time, and the score of a step depends on the neighbors at that moment.
        Or a cut splits a piece in two. The statement often says ``in any order'' or ``in an order that you choose''.
        Think of a DP over ranges with a split point.
  \item $n$ is a few hundred. Then $O(n^3)$ over all ranges with a split point fits.
  \item Two players alternate, both play optimally, and each move takes from an end of a row.
        The rest of the row is always one contiguous range $(i, j)$.
        $n \le 20$ allows a memoized recursion. $n \le 1000$ needs a bottom-up table of $O(n^2)$ ranges.
  \item Rules connect the actions over time: a cooldown, a fee per sale, at most one item held, at most $k$ uses.
        The past matters only through a small status.
  \item The recursion can go $n$ levels deep, and $n$ is 1000 or more. Plan a bottom-up loop from the start.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
Write the recurrence first. Then choose one of two forms.
The top-down form is a recursive function with \cd{@cache}. The cache finds a valid order by itself.
The bottom-up form fills a table in an order where every state that it reads is already final.
Both forms do the same work. The grid count is the smallest complete example.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def count_paths(m, n):                      # bottom-up table
    ways = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]      # row 0 and column 0: one straight path
    for r in range(1, m):                   # row by row: above and left are ready
        for c in range(1, n):
            ways[r][c] = ways[r - 1][c] + ways[r][c - 1]
    return ways[m - 1][n - 1]

def count_paths_memo(m, n):                 # top-down: the same recurrence
    @cache
    def ways(r, c):
        if r == 0 or c == 0:
            return 1
        return ways(r - 1, c) + ways(r, c - 1)
    return ways(m - 1, n - 1)

count_paths(3, 3), count_paths_memo(3, 3)   # -> (6, 6)
count_paths(3, 7), count_paths(3, 2)        # -> (28, 3)
count_paths(1, 1)                           # -> 1
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} When the loop reaches a state, every state that it reads holds its final value.
The fill order makes this true: row by row for a grid, decreasing key for a DAG,
increasing length for a range, and step by step for a state machine.

The same skeleton holds for every shape in this section:
\begin{pyshow}
dp = a table with one slot per state       # 1. state: dp[s] = answer for subproblem s
dp[smallest states] = known values         # 2. base (often sentinels)
for s in an order where the parts of s come first:          # 3. order
    dp[s] = combine(value of choice x for each choice x)   # 4. transition
answer = dp[full problem]
\end{pyshow}
The combine step depends on the question.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.6cm}L{11.2cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Combine \\
\midrule
number of ways & sum over the choices. The choices must split the paths into groups that do not overlap. \\
cheapest or best & min or max over the choices, plus the cost or score of the step \\
longest path & 1 plus the max over the next nodes \\
score in a two-player game & max over the moves of (gain now minus the value of the next state) \\
win or lose, no score & a state wins if some move reaches a state where the opponent loses \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{note}
Use the top-down form when the order is not clear, or when most states are never reached.
Use the bottom-up form when the recursion can go deeper than about 1000 calls (the default limit of CPython).
Also use it when speed matters: in CPython the top-down form of the same DP is often 2 to 3 times slower.
\end{note}

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Grid paths: count, cost and walls}
\textbf{Unique Paths} counts the paths of a robot that moves down or right on an $m \times n$ grid ($m, n \le 100$).
The core template is the intuitive solution.
Memory hook: \emph{fill the grid with ones, then each cell equals up plus left.}

Two changes give most other grid path problems.
A cost per cell changes the sum into a minimum plus the cell cost (Minimum Path Sum).
A wall gets the count 0. Then row 0 and column 0 are not all ones, so start with zeros,
seed only the start cell, and guard the indexes (Unique Paths II).
\begin{pyex}
def min_path_sum(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    INF = float("inf")
    best = [[INF] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if r == 0 and c == 0:
                best[r][c] = grid[0][0]
                continue
            up = best[r - 1][c] if r > 0 else INF
            left = best[r][c - 1] if c > 0 else INF
            best[r][c] = min(up, left) + grid[r][c]
    return best[rows - 1][cols - 1]

def paths_with_walls(grid):                 # 1 marks a wall
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    ways = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 1:
                continue                    # a wall keeps 0
            if r == 0 and c == 0:
                ways[r][c] = 1
                continue
            up = ways[r - 1][c] if r > 0 else 0
            left = ways[r][c - 1] if c > 0 else 0
            ways[r][c] = up + left
    return ways[rows - 1][cols - 1]

min_path_sum([[1, 3, 1], [1, 5, 1], [4, 2, 1]])        # -> 7
paths_with_walls([[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]])    # -> 2
paths_with_walls([[0, 1], [1, 0]])                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Each row reads only the row above, so one row is enough.
Update \cd{row[j] += row[j - 1]} from left to right. The old \cd{row[j]} is the cell above, and the new
\cd{row[j - 1]} is the cell to the left. This cuts the memory from $O(mn)$ to $O(n)$.
With no walls and no costs, the count also has a closed form. A path is a sequence of $m - 1$ downs and $n - 1$ rights,
so the answer is $\binom{m + n - 2}{m - 1}$.
\begin{pyex}
import math

def count_paths_row(m, n):
    row = [1] * n
    for _ in range(1, m):
        for j in range(1, n):
            row[j] += row[j - 1]            # old row[j] is above, new row[j - 1] is left
    return row[-1]

count_paths_row(3, 7), math.comb(3 + 7 - 2, 3 - 1)    # -> (28, 28)
count_paths_row(100, 100) == math.comb(198, 99)      # -> True
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Longest path on an implicit DAG: sorted order or memoized DFS}
\textbf{Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix}: from a cell, move up, down, left or right to a strictly larger value.
Return the number of cells on the longest such path ($m, n \le 200$).
In a general graph the longest simple path is NP-hard, and no fast algorithm for it is known.
The brute force tries every path from every cell, and the number of paths grows exponentially.
The strict increase removes the difficulty. A path can never come back to a cell, so the move graph is a DAG.
The best path from a cell then does not depend on how the path reached the cell.
So keep one number per cell, and use no visited set.

The intuitive solution visits the cells from the largest value to the smallest.
When it reaches a cell, every strictly larger neighbor already holds its final answer.
In \cd{[[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]]} the 9s get 1, the 6s get 2, the 2 gets 3,
and the 1 next to the 2 gets 4. That is the path 1, 2, 6, 9.
Memory hook: \emph{biggest first: each cell is 1 plus its best bigger neighbor.}
\begin{pyex}
def longest_increasing_path(matrix):
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    best = [[1] * cols for _ in range(rows)]    # one cell alone is a path of length 1
    cells = sorted(((matrix[r][c], r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols)),
                   reverse=True)                # largest value first
    for value, r, c in cells:
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and matrix[nr][nc] > value:
                best[r][c] = max(best[r][c], 1 + best[nr][nc])
    return max(max(row) for row in best)

longest_increasing_path([[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]])   # -> 4
longest_increasing_path([[3, 4, 5], [3, 2, 6], [2, 2, 1]])   # -> 4
longest_increasing_path([[1]])                               # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The sort costs $O(mn \log(mn))$ time. A memoized DFS takes $O(mn)$ time and needs no sort.
It is the general template for a DAG with no simple fill order: the recursion finds the order.
But a snake-shaped grid gives one path through all $mn$ cells, so the recursion can go 40000 calls deep.
Raise the recursion limit, or use the sorted order. Kahn's topological sort also gives an order with no recursion.
\begin{pyex}
import sys
from functools import cache

def longest_increasing_path_memo(matrix):
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    sys.setrecursionlimit(max(sys.getrecursionlimit(), rows * cols + 1000))
    @cache
    def longest_from(r, c):                 # longest path that starts at (r, c)
        best = 0
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and matrix[nr][nc] > matrix[r][c]:
                best = max(best, longest_from(nr, nc))
        return best + 1
    return max(longest_from(r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols))

longest_increasing_path_memo([[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]])   # -> 4
\end{pyex}
The same frame solves other DAGs with a strict key: longest increasing subsequence (an edge goes to a later,
larger element) and word chains (an edge goes to a longer word). To count paths instead, replace the max with a sum.

\subsubsection{Interval DP: choose the element that acts last}
\textbf{Burst Balloons}: burst all balloons in a row. Bursting balloon $i$ earns the product of its value and the values
of its two neighbors that are still present. A missing neighbor counts as 1. Maximize the total ($n \le 300$).

A split on the balloon that bursts \emph{first} does not work. Its two neighbors become adjacent, so the left part and
the right part still interact. Reverse the time. Choose the balloon $k$ that bursts \emph{last} in the open range $(l, r)$.
Until the end, $k$ stays alive and acts as a wall, so the balloons in $(l, k)$ and in $(k, r)$ never touch.
When $k$ bursts, its only neighbors are the walls $l$ and $r$, so it earns a known amount.
Pad the row with a 1 at each end, so that every range has two walls.
Memory hook: \emph{pick the balloon that pops last. It sees only the two walls.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_coins(nums):
    vals = [1] + nums + [1]                 # walls with the value 1 at both ends
    n = len(vals)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]        # dp[l][r]: best for balloons strictly between l and r
    for length in range(2, n):              # short ranges first
        for l in range(n - length):
            r = l + length
            best = 0
            for k in range(l + 1, r):       # k bursts LAST, so it sees only the walls
                coins = dp[l][k] + vals[l] * vals[k] * vals[r] + dp[k][r]
                if coins > best:
                    best = coins
            dp[l][r] = best
    return dp[0][n - 1]

max_coins([3, 1, 5, 8]), max_coins([1, 5])     # -> (167, 10)
max_coins([7])                                 # -> 7
\end{pyex}
In \cd{[3, 1, 5, 8]} one best plan bursts 8 last, between the walls 1 and 1, for $1 \cdot 8 \cdot 1 = 8$ coins.
The range $(3, 1, 5)$ to its left is then a smaller problem with the walls 1 and 8.
There are $O(n^2)$ ranges and $O(n)$ split points, so the time is $O(n^3)$.
At $n = 300$ this is about 4.5 million inner steps, about 1 second in CPython.
A top-down version with \cd{@cache} is 2 to 3 times slower in CPython and risks a timeout.
In the hot loop, a plain \cd{if} is faster than \cd{max()} over a generator.

The general rule: the split is the action that leaves two sides that cannot affect each other.
A removal or a merge joins two neighbors, so the \emph{last} action in a range is the clean split
(matrix chain multiplication, polygon triangulation). A cut separates two pieces, so the \emph{first} cut in a range is
the clean split. Add sentinels so that the ends of the row follow the same formula as the inside.
The reverse-time idea also works for deletions outside interval DP. Replay the deletions backward as insertions,
for example with union-find when the edges of a graph are removed one by one.

\subsubsection{Two-player games: store the score difference}
\textbf{Predict the Winner}: two players take turns. Each turn takes one number from either end of the array and adds it
to the score of the player. Both play optimally. Return true if player 1 wins or ties ($n \le 20$).

The brute force plays out every line of play, about $2^n$ of them. But after any sequence of moves,
the rest of the array is one range \cd{nums[i..j]} (both ends included). So only $O(n^2)$ different positions exist.
Do not store two scores and a turn flag. The scores so far make too many states, and the cache stops helping.
Store one number, the \emph{gap}: the best (mover minus opponent) score difference that the player to move
(the mover) can force on the range.
If the mover takes \cd{nums[i]}, the opponent becomes the mover on $(i + 1, j)$ and gets their own best gap.
So the mover gets \cd{nums[i] - gap(i + 1, j)}. One subtraction replaces a separate min layer for the opponent.
This form has the name negamax.
Memory hook: \emph{my pick minus your best gap, max of both ends. A tie wins.}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def predict_the_winner(nums):
    @cache
    def best_gap(i, j):                     # best (mover - opponent) on nums[i..j]
        if i > j:
            return 0
        take_left = nums[i] - best_gap(i + 1, j)
        take_right = nums[j] - best_gap(i, j - 1)
        return max(take_left, take_right)
    return best_gap(0, len(nums) - 1) >= 0  # a tie is a win for player 1

predict_the_winner([1, 5, 2])         # -> False
predict_the_winner([1, 5, 233, 7])    # -> True
predict_the_winner([0])               # -> True
\end{pyex}
In \cd{[1, 5, 233, 7]} the greedy pick 7 gives 233 to player 2. The DP takes 1 first and then gets 233.

\textbf{Score of the first player, not the winner}: the same game on cards with positive values and an even count
($n \le 1000$). Return the final score of player 1, not the winner.
The intuitive solution stores the actual score. The total of a range is fixed, so the mover gets the range total minus
what the opponent gets on the range that the mover leaves. The mover leaves the range where the opponent gets less.
The recursion would go $n$ levels deep, so fill a table by range length, with prefix sums for range totals.
Memory hook: \emph{my score is the range total minus the opponent's best on what I leave.}
\begin{pyex}
def first_player_score(cards):
    n = len(cards)
    prefix = [0]
    for card in cards:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + card)
    best = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]      # best[i][j]: most the mover collects from cards[i..j]
    for i in range(n):
        best[i][i] = cards[i]               # one card left: the mover takes it
    for length in range(2, n + 1):          # shorter ranges first
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            range_sum = prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]
            best[i][j] = range_sum - min(best[i + 1][j], best[i][j - 1])
    return best[0][n - 1]

first_player_score([2, 10, 3, 1])          # -> 11
first_player_score([5, 1, 7, 9, 2, 3])     # -> 15
\end{pyex}
In \cd{[2, 10, 3, 1]} the greedy pick 2 leaves 10 at the left end, and player 1 ends with 5.
The DP takes 1, then gets 10, for 11.

The optimal form keeps the gap in one array of length $n$ and needs no prefix sums.
For each right end $j$, it moves $i$ down from $j - 1$. Then \cd{gap[i + 1]} already holds the range that ends at $j$,
and \cd{gap[i]} still holds the range that ends at $j - 1$.
Convert the gap back to a score with $p_1 + p_2 = \text{total}$ and $p_1 - p_2 = \text{gap}$,
so $p_1 = (\text{total} + \text{gap}) / 2$. Use this identity whenever two values have a known sum and a known difference.
\begin{pyex}
def first_player_score_1d(cards):
    n = len(cards)
    gap = [0] * n                           # gap[i]: best gap on cards[i..j] for the current j
    for j in range(n):
        gap[j] = cards[j]
        for i in range(j - 1, -1, -1):      # i goes DOWN, so gap[i + 1] is already for this j
            gap[i] = max(cards[i] - gap[i + 1], cards[j] - gap[i])
    return (sum(cards) + gap[0]) // 2       # the sum is 2 * p1, so the division is exact

first_player_score_1d([2, 10, 3, 1]), first_player_score_1d([5, 1, 7, 9, 2, 3])   # -> (11, 15)
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
With an even number of items taken from the ends, player 1 can take all items at even indexes or all items at odd
indexes. So player 1 never loses (Stone Game). This argument gives only the winner, not the score.
For \cd{[5, 1, 7, 9, 2, 3]} the better parity sum is 14, but the optimal score is 15.
\end{note}
Other game shapes use the same negamax rule with a different state.
If each move takes a prefix, the state is one start index (plus any extra parameter of the rules).
If a move gives the same player another turn, add the next value instead of subtracting it.
The difference is enough when one player maximizes it and the other player minimizes it.
This is always true when the total of the two scores is fixed. It can also be true when the total changes with the order of the moves.
\textbf{Stone Game VII} (LeetCode 1690): a removal from either end scores the sum of the stones that remain.
Player 1 maximizes the difference and player 2 minimizes it. Only the gain of a move changes: it is the sum of the range that stays.
Memory hook: \emph{same gap rule; the gain is the sum of what stays.}
\begin{pyex}
def stone_game_vii(stones):
    n = len(stones)
    prefix = [0]
    for x in stones:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)
    gap = [0] * n                           # gap[i]: best gap on stones[i..j] for the current j
    for j in range(n):
        gap[j] = 0                          # one stone: its removal scores 0
        for i in range(j - 1, -1, -1):
            take_left = (prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i + 1]) - gap[i + 1]    # stones[i + 1..j] stay
            take_right = (prefix[j] - prefix[i]) - gap[i]               # stones[i..j - 1] stay
            gap[i] = max(take_left, take_right)
    return gap[0]

stone_game_vii([5, 3, 1, 4, 2]), stone_game_vii([7, 90, 5, 1, 100, 10, 10, 2])   # -> (6, 122)
\end{pyex}
Store a pair of scores only when each player maximizes their own score and the total is not fixed.

\subsubsection{State machines: a small status for each step}
\textbf{Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown}: buy and sell one share as often as you like, but hold at most one
share. After a sale you cannot buy on the next day. Maximize the profit ($n \le 5000$).

A brute force tries every sequence of buy, sell and wait actions, so the work grows exponentially with $n$.
But the future depends only on the day and on one status: you own a share, or you do not.
So two numbers per day are enough.
Walk the days backward and store the best profit from day $i$ to the end for each status.
In this backward table, the cooldown needs no third status: a sale on day $i$ jumps to day $i + 2$.
It only reads the answer that is already stored for day $i + 2$.
In \cd{[1, 2, 3, 0, 2]} the best plan is buy, sell, cooldown, buy, sell, for a profit of $1 + 2 = 3$.
Memory hook: \emph{walk the days backward. Free waits or buys, holding waits or sells, and a sale skips tomorrow.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_profit_cooldown(prices):
    n = len(prices)
    free = [0] * (n + 2)                    # best profit from day i on, with no share
    holding = [0] * (n + 2)                 # best profit from day i on, with one share
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        p = prices[i]
        free[i] = max(free[i + 1], holding[i + 1] - p)      # wait or buy
        holding[i] = max(holding[i + 1], free[i + 2] + p)   # wait or sell; a sale skips tomorrow
    return free[0]                          # day 0 starts with no share

max_profit_cooldown([1, 2, 3, 0, 2])   # -> 3
max_profit_cooldown([1])               # -> 0
max_profit_cooldown([5, 4, 3])         # -> 0
\end{pyex}
The optimal form runs forward with three variables and $O(1)$ memory.
In this forward form, the cooldown is a third status, \cd{sold}, that cannot go directly to \cd{hold}.
\cd{hold} owns a share, \cd{sold} sold today, and \cd{rest} owns nothing and did not sell today.
The legal arrows are: hold to hold (wait), rest to hold (buy), hold to sold (sell), sold to rest and rest to rest (wait).
A buy reads \cd{rest} and never \cd{sold}. That one arrow is the cooldown.
\begin{pyex}
def max_profit_states(prices):
    hold, sold, rest = float("-inf"), 0, 0  # holding before day 0 is impossible
    for p in prices:
        hold, sold, rest = max(hold, rest - p), hold + p, max(rest, sold)
    return max(sold, rest)                  # never end while holding

max_profit_states([1, 2, 3, 0, 2]), max_profit_states([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4])   # -> (3, 5)
\end{pyex}
The general method: list the statuses that the rules need, draw the legal arrows, and write one max per status per step.
\begin{itemize}
  \item A fee: subtract it on each sale. No new status.
  \item At most $k$ transactions: add the number of transactions to the state.
  \item A delay of $k$ steps after an event: add $k$ waiting statuses, or jump to step $i + k + 1$.
  \item A choice that blocks the next step (House Robber), or a color that the next house cannot repeat (Paint House):
        the status is the last choice.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Say the brute force in one sentence. Name what it lists: paths, orders, lines of play or action sequences.
  \item Ask what the rest of the problem needs to know about the past. That is the state.
        If the answer depends on the full path (a visited set), look for a strict key that removes the cycles.
  \item Find the split. Grid: the last move into the cell. DAG: the first step out of the node.
        Range: the action that leaves two independent sides (the last removal or merge, the first cut).
        Game: the move of the player to move. State machine: the action at this step.
  \item Choose the combine: sum, min, max, gain minus the next value, or ``some move reaches a losing state''.
  \item Find the order. Forward moves only: row by row. A strict key: sort by the key.
        A range: by length. Time: by step. If no order is clear, memoize.
  \item Fill from the end when the condition of a step depends on what comes after it.
        Then the value of a state means ``the best from here to the end''.
  \item Add sentinels so that the boundary states use the same formula:
        walls with value 1, extra zero cells after the last day, or the positions 0 and the full length.
  \item Check the size: states times choices. $n \le 20$: an exponential search can pass.
        $n$ up to a few hundred: $O(n^3)$. $n$ up to a few thousand: $O(n^2)$. $n$ up to $10^5$: $O(n)$ with a few statuses.
  \item Check the depth. If the recursion can go deeper than about 1000 calls, write the bottom-up form.
  \item Reduce memory last, and only if the limits need it (one row, three variables, one array).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Wrong fill order or wrong split in an interval DP.}
\cd{dp[l][r]} reads \cd{dp[k][r]} with $k > l$. If \cd{l} goes up, that value is not computed yet.
Fill by length, or move \cd{l} down and \cd{r} up. Also, a split on the element that acts first uses
neighbors that are not fixed, so the two sides interact.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def coins(nums, l_order):
    vals = [1] + nums + [1]
    n = len(vals)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for l in l_order(n):
        for r in range(l + 2, n):
            dp[l][r] = max(dp[l][k] + vals[l] * vals[k] * vals[r] + dp[k][r]
                           for k in range(l + 1, r))
    return dp[0][n - 1]

coins([3, 1, 5, 8], lambda n: range(n))                 # -> 63
coins([3, 1, 5, 8], lambda n: range(n - 1, -1, -1))     # -> 167
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Update all state variables at the same time.}
If \cd{hold}, \cd{sold} and \cd{rest} change one by one, later lines read new values of the same day.
In the example below, \cd{rest} then includes the sale of the same day. So the buy on the next day reads a sale
of the day before, and the cooldown disappears. The result is the profit with no cooldown.
Use one tuple assignment, or temporary variables.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def profit_one_by_one(prices):              # wrong
    hold, sold, rest = float("-inf"), 0, 0
    for p in prices:
        hold = max(hold, rest - p)
        sold = hold + p
        rest = max(rest, sold)
    return max(sold, rest)

def profit_together(prices):                # right
    hold, sold, rest = float("-inf"), 0, 0
    for p in prices:
        hold, sold, rest = max(hold, rest - p), hold + p, max(rest, sold)
    return max(sold, rest)

profit_one_by_one([1, 2, 3, 0, 2]), profit_together([1, 2, 3, 0, 2])   # -> (4, 3)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{A non-strict key makes cycles.}
With \cd{>=} instead of \cd{>}, two equal neighbors point to each other. A memoized DFS then calls itself
with no end, because the cache gets a value only after a call returns. Python stops it with a \cd{RecursionError}.
A strict comparison is the reason that the cache by cell is correct.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

def longest_non_strict(matrix):             # wrong: >= allows equal steps
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    @cache
    def f(r, c):
        best = 0
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and matrix[nr][nc] >= matrix[r][c]:
                best = max(best, f(nr, nc))
        return best + 1
    return f(0, 0)

longest_non_strict([[1, 1]])                # -> raises RecursionError
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Recursion depth.} A memoized DFS goes as deep as the longest chain of states.
A row of 5000 days, 1000 cards or a 40000-cell snake path is deeper than the default limit of 1000.
Write the bottom-up form, or raise the limit with \cd{sys.setrecursionlimit}.
A higher limit does not make the C stack larger, so very deep recursion can still crash the interpreter.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import cache

@cache
def suffix_best(i):                         # depth grows with i
    return 0 if i == 0 else 1 + suffix_best(i - 1)

suffix_best(5000)                           # -> raises RecursionError
suffix_best.cache_clear()
for i in range(0, 5001, 500):               # warm the cache in small steps
    suffix_best(i)
suffix_best(5000)                           # -> 5000
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Games: the tie rule and the memo marker.}
When a tie counts as a win, test \cd{gap >= 0}, not \cd{gap > 0}.
A difference of 0 or a negative difference is a valid result. Do not use 0 or $-1$ as the ``not computed'' mark
in a memo table. Use \cd{None} or \cd{@cache}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Base values and the final status.} In the forward stock form, \cd{hold} starts at minus infinity, not at 0.
A start at 0 pretends that you own a free share. The answer comes from a status with no share: \cd{max(sold, rest)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Shared rows.} \cd{[[0] * n] * n} repeats one inner list, so all rows change together.
Build each table with \cd{[[0] * n for _ in range(n)]}.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Greedy rules fail here.} Bursting the smallest balloon first gives 78 on \cd{[3, 1, 5, 8]}. The answer is 167.
Taking the larger end card gives player 1 a score of 5 on \cd{[2, 10, 3, 1]}. The answer is 11.
Test a greedy idea against the DP or a brute force on small inputs.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Unique Paths & Count paths with down and right moves. The base template: a sum of two predecessors, row by row. &
  Fill the grid with ones, then each cell equals up plus left. \\
Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix & Four directions. A strict increase makes a DAG. Order the cells by value; 1 plus a max. &
  Biggest first: each cell is 1 plus its best bigger neighbor. \\
Burst Balloons & State is an open range between two walls. The split is the balloon that bursts last. $O(n^3)$. &
  Pick the balloon that pops last. It sees only the two walls. \\
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown & State is (day, holding or not). Fill backward. A sale jumps to day $i + 2$. &
  Walk the days backward. Free waits or buys, holding waits or sells, and a sale skips tomorrow. \\
Predict the Winner & Two-player game on a range. Store the difference for the player to move. Answer: \cd{gap >= 0}. &
  My pick minus your best gap, max of both ends. A tie wins. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
