\section{Greedy}\label{tech:T19}

\subsection{The idea}
A greedy algorithm makes one local choice at each step and never undoes it.
Brute force tries every combination of choices, and that is exponential.
Dynamic programming keeps the best result for every state.
A greedy scan keeps one choice, or a small summary of all choices, and reads the input one time.
The scan costs $O(n)$. A sort before the scan adds $O(n \log n)$.

\begin{note}
A variant can take a choice back. It keeps its past choices in a heap.
When a budget breaks, it undoes the weakest choice and pays for that step in a different way.
Each choice goes into the heap and comes out at most one time, so the cost stays $O(n \log n)$
(Furthest Building You Can Reach). See the variation ``Take back the weakest choice'' below.
\end{note}

A small example shows how a set of choices collapses into one number.
In Jump Game, \cd{nums[i]} is the longest jump from index $i$, and every shorter jump is also allowed.
Take \cd{nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]}. From index 0, a search tries index 1 and index 2.
But a jump that can land on index 2 can also stop on index 1.
So the reachable indices always form a prefix \cd{0..farthest}, and one number describes them.
Index 0 sets \cd{farthest} to 2. Index 1 sets it to $1 + 3 = 4$, which is the last index. The answer is true.
For \cd{[3, 2, 1, 0, 4]}, \cd{farthest} stops at 3. Index 4 lies past it, so the answer is false.

A local choice can look good and still be wrong. So each greedy needs a reason.
The reason is usually one of the six in the table below.
The exchange argument is the most general reason. Take any optimal answer.
Change its choices into the greedy choices, one at a time, and show that the answer never becomes worse.
For example, to keep the most meetings that do not overlap, the greedy keeps the meeting that ends first.
An optimal answer starts with some meeting that ends at the same time or later.
Swap that meeting for the greedy one. The rest of the answer still fits, and the count does not change
(Non-overlapping Intervals). Task Scheduler and the wall-crossing walk below use the same argument.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.0cm}L{7.4cm}L{5.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Reason & Question to ask & Examples \\
\midrule
Forced choice & Does an extreme element (the smallest, the first) have only one possible role? & Hand of Straights \\
Exchange argument & Can you change an optimal answer into the greedy answer, one choice at a time, with no loss? & Task Scheduler, a walk that maximizes wall crossings, Furthest Building You Can Reach \\
Skip ahead & Does one failure rule out a whole range of candidates? & Gas Station, Maximum Subarray \\
Contiguous states & Is the set of reachable states always an interval? Then keep its ends. & Jump Game, Jump Game II, Partition Labels, Valid Parenthesis String \\
One-way operation & Can a value that passes the target ever come back? If not, drop that element. & Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet \\
Two lower bounds & Do the rules point to both neighbors? Meet each side in its own pass, then take the max per item. & Candy \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
If you cannot name the reason, test the greedy against a brute force on all small inputs.
The core template shows how.

\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The task asks for one number (a maximum, a minimum, a count) or for yes or no. It does not ask for all solutions.
  \item Typical phrases point to a variation below: ``can you reach'' (one frontier), ``the fewest jumps'' (BFS windows),
        ``the most parts'' (cut at the farthest end), ``at least $n$ slots apart'' (most frequent first),
        ``after any number of operations'' (filter, then combine),
        ``more than its neighbors'' (one pass per side).
  \item $n$ is $10^4$ to $10^5$ or more. A DP over pairs of indices, or over each possible move, is too slow.
  \item Each step has a choice that cannot hurt: extend or restart, the farthest reach, the smallest element, the most frequent item.
  \item A move allows any step up to a limit, or a wildcard changes a counter by $-1$, $0$ or $+1$.
        Then the reachable states have no gaps, and two numbers describe them.
  \item One failure at position $j$ rules out every candidate between the current start and $j$.
  \item An operation moves values in one direction only: max, min, bitwise OR, bitwise AND.
        An element that passes the target is useless.
  \item The input order does not matter. Sort it or count it, then start from an extreme element.
  \item Two kinds of budget pay for the costs, and the scarce kind must cover the largest costs.
        Give each cost the scarce kind first, then take back the smallest one from a heap.
  \item An action can repeat at a fixed cost, and the budget is huge.
        Pay a one-time cost to unlock the action, then repeat it with an integer division.
  \item Counter-signal: a small input where the local choice blocks a better choice later.
        The classic case is the largest coin first, which fails for coins $\{1, 3, 4\}$ and amount 6. Use DP there.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Core template}
Most greedy scans have the same shape. Keep a small state that summarizes all choices so far.
At each element, test for a failure first. Then apply the local choice. Then update the answer.
\begin{pyshow}
state = start_value               # a few numbers that summarize all choices so far
for x in items:                   # sorted or counted first when the order is free
    if failed(state, x):          # a gap, a negative balance, a missing card
        ...                       # return early, or reset the candidate
    state = choose(state, x)      # the local choice; it is never undone
    best = better(best, state)
\end{pyshow}
The frontier scan of Jump Game is the clearest example of this shape.
\begin{pyex}
def can_reach_end(nums):
    farthest = 0                         # right end of the reachable prefix
    for i, jump in enumerate(nums):
        if i > farthest:                 # gap: no reachable index jumps to i
            return False
        farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
    return True

can_reach_end([2, 3, 1, 1, 4])           # -> True
can_reach_end([3, 2, 1, 0, 4])           # -> False
can_reach_end([2, 0, 0])                 # -> True
can_reach_end([0])                       # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: before index $i$, every index in \cd{0..farthest} is reachable, and no jump from an index before $i$ goes past \cd{farthest}.
If $i$ is past \cd{farthest}, no reachable index jumps to $i$, so index $i$ and all later indices are cut off.

\subsubsection{Check a greedy against a brute force}
A greedy rule is easy to invent and easy to get wrong. Write the brute force that tries every choice.
Then compare the two solutions on every small input. Generate the inputs from the smallest size up.
The first difference is then the smallest counterexample, and you can trace it by hand.
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import product

def can_reach_end(nums):                 # the greedy under test
    farthest = 0
    for i, jump in enumerate(nums):
        if i > farthest:
            return False
        farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
    return True

def brute_reach(nums):                   # try every jump with a DFS
    seen, stack = {0}, [0]
    while stack:
        i = stack.pop()
        for j in range(i + 1, min(len(nums), i + nums[i] + 1)):
            if j not in seen:
                seen.add(j)
                stack.append(j)
    return len(nums) - 1 in seen

def first_counterexample(fast, slow, max_len=5, max_val=3):
    for n in range(1, max_len + 1):       # the smallest inputs first
        for t in product(range(max_val + 1), repeat=n):
            if fast(list(t)) != slow(list(t)):
                return list(t)
    return None

def zero_blocks(nums):                   # a plausible rule: "a zero blocks the path"
    return 0 not in nums[:-1]

first_counterexample(can_reach_end, brute_reach)     # -> None
first_counterexample(zero_blocks, brute_reach)       # -> [2, 0, 0]
\end{pyex}
Keep the value range small. Small ranges make zeros, ties and duplicates, and these break most wrong rules.
When the inputs are too many to list, use random small inputs from \cd{random.Random(seed)}.
A clean run on all small inputs is strong evidence for a greedy. It is not a proof, but it catches most wrong rules.

\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Extend or restart: drop a negative run}
The state is a running sum. The local choice is: extend the current run, or start a new run at this element.
The best subarray that ends at index $i$ either extends the best subarray that ends at $i - 1$, or it starts at $i$.
The extension helps only when the previous sum is positive.
So clamp the previous sum at 0, then add the current element (Maximum Subarray).
The reason is skip ahead: a run with a negative sum never helps a run that extends it to the right.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart.}
\begin{pyex}
def max_subarray(nums):
    best = nums[0]                 # the subarray is non-empty: never start at 0
    cur = 0                        # best sum of a subarray that ends at the previous index
    for x in nums:
        cur = max(cur, 0) + x      # extend a positive run, or restart at x
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])    # -> 6
max_subarray([-3, -1, -2])                       # -> -1
max_subarray([4, -1, 2, 1])                      # -> 6

def max_subarray_span(nums):       # also return (start, end) of one best subarray
    best, span = nums[0], (0, 0)
    cur = start = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if cur < 0:                # a negative run: restart here
            cur, start = 0, i
        cur += x
        if cur > best:
            best, span = cur, (start, i)
    return best, span

max_subarray_span([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])   # -> (6, (3, 6))
\end{pyex}
Restart when the running sum is negative, not when the current element is negative.
In \cd{[4, -1, 2, 1]} the $-1$ belongs to the best subarray.
When one state is not enough, keep a small fixed set of states for each index.
Examples are the largest and the smallest product (Maximum Product Subarray),
or ``no deletion used'' and ``one deletion used'' (Maximum Subarray Sum with One Deletion).

\subsubsection{Reachability: keep one frontier}
Each position allows any move up to a maximum, and the question is only yes or no (Jump Game).
The reachable positions are always a prefix, so keep its right end, \cd{farthest}.
The core template is the full solution. Test for a gap before you stretch \cd{farthest}.
A backward scan also works: move a \cd{goal} left to each index \cd{i} with \cd{i + nums[i] >= goal},
and test \cd{goal == 0} at the end.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Walk forward; if you pass farthest you are stuck, else stretch farthest.}

The same collapse works for other DPs. Suppose a cell is true when any cell in a window ahead of it is true.
Check whether only the nearest or the farthest true cell matters. If it does, the DP needs $O(1)$ state.

\subsubsection{BFS by levels on a line}
Now the question is the minimum number of moves (Jump Game II).
All moves cost the same, so this is a BFS. Each index reaches a contiguous range of next indices.
So each BFS layer is also a contiguous window \cd{[left, right]}, and two numbers replace the queue.
The next window starts at \cd{right + 1}. It ends at the farthest \cd{i + nums[i]} over the current window.
Each new window costs one more jump.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{BFS in windows: the next window runs from right + 1 to the farthest reach of this window.}
\begin{pyex}
from itertools import product

def min_jumps(nums):
    jumps = 0
    left = right = 0               # window: the indices whose fewest jumps is jumps
    while right < len(nums) - 1:
        farthest = max(i + nums[i] for i in range(left, right + 1))
        if farthest <= right:      # no progress: the last index is unreachable
            return -1
        left, right = right + 1, farthest
        jumps += 1
    return jumps

min_jumps([2, 3, 1, 1, 4])         # -> 2
min_jumps([2, 3, 0, 1, 4])         # -> 2
min_jumps([0])                     # -> 0
min_jumps([1, 0, 2])               # -> -1

def min_jumps_flat(nums):          # needs a reachable last index
    jumps = cur_end = farthest = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1): # stop before the last index
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
        if i == cur_end:           # the current layer ends here
            jumps += 1
            cur_end = farthest
    return jumps

small = [list(t) for n in range(1, 6) for t in product(range(4), repeat=n)]
all(min_jumps_flat(a) == min_jumps(a) for a in small if min_jumps(a) >= 0)   # -> True
\end{pyex}
The flat form is the usual optimal code. It has the same $O(n)$ time.
It closes a layer when \cd{i} equals \cd{cur_end}. Stop it at index $n - 2$.
If it also visits index $n - 1$, it counts one extra jump when \cd{cur_end} is exactly the last index.
Update \cd{farthest} before you test \cd{cur_end}.
To cover a line with the fewest intervals (Video Stitching), first store the farthest right end for each left end.
Then run the same window scan, and return $-1$ on a gap.

\subsubsection{Reset the start on failure}
A process must keep a balance at zero or more: fuel, money, energy, or stack depth.
Turn each step into one net change. On a circle, the question is which start works (Gas Station).
First check the total. If the total gas is less than the total cost, no start works.
Then drive one time from left to right. When the tank goes below zero at station $j$, the start moves to $j + 1$.
The reason is skip ahead. The car reached every station between the old start and $j$ with zero or more gas.
So a start at one of these stations drops a non-negative amount of gas, and it also fails at $j$.
The surviving start sits just after the lowest prefix sum, and the total check covers the wrap.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Not enough total gas means -1; out of gas means start after here.}
\begin{pyex}
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    if sum(gas) < sum(cost):       # not enough gas in total: no start works
        return -1
    start = tank = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:               # no start in start..i reaches i + 1
            start, tank = i + 1, 0
    return start

can_complete_circuit([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5, 1, 2])   # -> 3
can_complete_circuit([2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 3])               # -> -1
can_complete_circuit([2, 0], [0, 2])                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}
Maximum Subarray uses the same skip: a negative run is dropped, and the scan restarts after it.

\subsubsection{Forced choice at the smallest element}
All items must go into groups of a rigid shape, for example \cd{group_size} consecutive values (Hand of Straights).
Only the multiset matters, so count the values.
The smallest card that is left has no smaller neighbor. It cannot be the middle or the end of a straight.
So it must start a straight. The choice is forced, and a forced choice never needs backtracking.
Walk the sorted hand. Skip a card whose count is already 0, because an earlier straight used it.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Smallest card left starts a straight. Pull its next cards one by one.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def is_n_straight_hand(hand, group_size):
    if len(hand) % group_size:
        return False
    count = Counter(hand)
    for card in sorted(hand):
        if count[card] == 0:       # an earlier straight used this card
            continue
        for value in range(card, card + group_size):   # card starts a straight
            if count[value] == 0:
                return False
            count[value] -= 1
    return True

is_n_straight_hand([1, 2, 3, 6, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8], 3)   # -> True
is_n_straight_hand([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 4)               # -> False
is_n_straight_hand([3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1], 3)            # -> True
\end{pyex}
The optimal code walks only the distinct values and subtracts all copies at one time.
It tests \cd{count[v] < need}. The time is the same $O(n \log n)$, so use it only when the hand has many copies.
Values go up to $10^9$, so use a hash map and not an array indexed by value.
The same forced choice pairs \cd{x} with \cd{2 * x} when you process the values from the smallest
(Find Original Array From Doubled Array).

\subsubsection{Filter, then combine everything}
The operation combines elements with max, and you may apply it any number of times (Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet).
Max is associative, commutative and idempotent. So the order and the repeats do not matter.
Every reachable result is the coordinate-wise max of some subset.
Max never lowers a value. A triplet that passes the target in one coordinate can never be used, so drop it.
Every other triplet is harmless. Combine all of them, and compare the result with the target.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Drop any triplet that overshoots, max the rest, compare with target.}
\begin{pyex}
def merge_triplets(triplets, target):
    x, y, z = target
    best = [0, 0, 0]
    for a, b, c in triplets:
        if a <= x and b <= y and c <= z:     # an overshoot never comes back down
            best = [max(best[0], a), max(best[1], b), max(best[2], c)]
    return best == list(target)

merge_triplets([[2, 5, 3], [1, 8, 4], [1, 7, 5]], [2, 7, 5])   # -> True
merge_triplets([[3, 4, 5], [4, 5, 6]], [3, 2, 5])              # -> False
merge_triplets([[2, 2, 3], [1, 1, 2]], [2, 2, 2])              # -> False

def can_or_to(nums, target):       # the same idea for bitwise OR
    if target == 0:                # the empty selection does not count
        return 0 in nums
    acc = 0
    for v in nums:
        if v | target == target:   # v sets no bit outside target
            acc |= v
    return acc == target

can_or_to([1, 2, 8], 3)            # -> True
can_or_to([1, 6], 3)               # -> False
can_or_to([7, 1], 0)               # -> False
\end{pyex}
The accumulator starts at the identity value, so it equals the result of an empty selection.
If the target can be that value, test it by itself. In Merge Triplets every target value is at least 1.
Other one-way operations use the same filter. For AND, keep \cd{v} with \cd{v & target == target}.
For min, keep the elements that are at least the target in every coordinate. For gcd, keep the multiples of the target.

\subsubsection{Cut at the farthest required end}
Split a sequence into the most contiguous parts so that each value stays inside one part (Partition Labels).
Each letter forces a span from its first to its last occurrence.
Store the last index of each letter. Scan from the left, and push the end of the current part out to the
largest last index seen. When the scan index reaches that end, no letter on the left appears later. Cut there.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Each letter drags the cut to its last spot; cut when you catch up.}
\begin{pyex}
def partition_labels(s):
    last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}   # a later index overwrites: the last one wins
    sizes = []
    start = end = 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        end = max(end, last[c])    # this letter drags the end of the part
        if i == end:               # caught up: a legal cut
            sizes.append(end - start + 1)
            start = i + 1
    return sizes

partition_labels("ababcbacadefegdehijhklij")   # -> [9, 7, 8]
partition_labels("eccbbbbdec")                 # -> [10]
partition_labels("abc")                        # -> [1, 1, 1]
\end{pyex}
This is the running maximum of Jump Game again. The scan meets the start of each span in order, so the ends are enough.
A running maximum of the ends replaces a sort and a merge of intervals.
The same cut rule works whenever each element forces its part to reach some index, not only its last occurrence.

\subsubsection{Rules toward both neighbors: one pass per side}
Some rules compare an item with its left neighbor and with its right neighbor.
For example, each child gets at least one candy.
A child with a higher rating than a neighbor gets more candy than that neighbor (Candy).
One left-to-right pass sees only the left neighbor, so it breaks the rules toward the right.
One pass from the left meets every left rule with the smallest values. One pass from the right does the same for the right rules.
Each pass gives a lower bound that every valid answer must meet. So no valid answer is smaller than the max of the two bounds.
The max is also valid. When the rating goes up from $i - 1$ to $i$, the right pass gives $i - 1$ only 1.
So the max keeps the left rule. The right rules hold for the same reason.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Left pass for the left rules, right pass for the right rules, take the max per child.}
\begin{pyex}
def candy(ratings):
    n = len(ratings)
    left = [1] * n                 # meets every rule toward the left neighbor
    for i in range(1, n):
        if ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]:
            left[i] = left[i - 1] + 1
    right = [1] * n                # meets every rule toward the right neighbor
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        if ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]:
            right[i] = right[i + 1] + 1
    return sum(max(a, b) for a, b in zip(left, right))

def candy_left_only(ratings):      # wrong: it looks only at the left neighbor
    c = [1] * len(ratings)
    for i in range(1, len(ratings)):
        if ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]:
            c[i] = c[i - 1] + 1
    return sum(c)

candy([1, 0, 2])                   # -> 5
candy([1, 2, 2])                   # -> 4
candy([1, 3, 4, 5, 2])             # -> 11
candy_left_only([1, 0]), candy([1, 0])   # -> (2, 3)
\end{pyex}
Equal neighbors have no rule, so \cd{[1, 2, 2]} gives \cd{[1, 2, 1]}.
The same shape, a left pass, a right pass and a combine per item, also gives the product of all other elements
(Product of Array Except Self) and the water above each bar (Trapping Rain Water).

\subsubsection{Track a range of possible states}
A scan keeps a counter, and some steps are uncertain. In Valid Parenthesis String, each \cd{*} acts as
\cd{(}, as \cd{)}, or as nothing. Brute force tries $3^k$ assignments.
But the set of reachable open counts is always a contiguous range \cd{[lo, hi]}, because each step changes
the counter by a run of consecutive amounts. So keep only the two ends.
If \cd{hi} goes below zero, no assignment survives. If \cd{lo} goes below zero, clamp it to zero,
because a negative count is never legal. At the end, zero must be in the range, so test \cd{lo == 0}.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Range of open counts: fail if the most goes below zero, clamp the fewest at zero, and end with fewest == 0.}
\begin{pyex}
def check_valid_string(s):
    lo = hi = 0                    # fewest and most unmatched "(" after this prefix
    for c in s:
        if c == "(":
            lo, hi = lo + 1, hi + 1
        elif c == ")":
            lo, hi = lo - 1, hi - 1
        else:                      # "*" closes one, opens one, or does nothing
            lo, hi = lo - 1, hi + 1
        if hi < 0:                 # too many ")" even if every "*" opens
            return False
        lo = max(lo, 0)            # an open count is never negative
    return lo == 0                 # zero open is in the range

check_valid_string("(*))")         # -> True
check_valid_string("(*)(")         # -> False
check_valid_string(")*")           # -> False
check_valid_string("*(")           # -> False
\end{pyex}
The range works when each step maps an interval of states to an interval, and the legal states form an interval.
If a wildcard must be \cd{(} or \cd{)} and cannot be empty, all reachable counts have the same parity.
Then raise \cd{lo} by 2, not to 0, when it goes below zero.
To count the valid assignments, the range is not enough. Use a DP over (index, open count).

\subsubsection{Most frequent first, one window at a time}
Equal items need a gap of at least $n$ slots, and the question is the shortest schedule (Task Scheduler).
Only the counts matter. The most frequent task is the bottleneck: if you delay it, its copies pile up at the end
with idle slots between them. This is an exchange argument.
Fill each window of $n + 1$ slots with the most frequent different tasks, from a max-heap of counts.
A full window costs $n + 1$. The last window costs only the tasks that ran in it.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Fill each window of n + 1 with the most frequent different tasks. Only the last window has no idle tail.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def least_interval(tasks, n):
    heap = [-k for k in Counter(tasks).values()]   # max-heap of counts
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    time = 0
    while heap:
        ran = []                                   # one window of n + 1 slots
        while heap and len(ran) < n + 1:
            ran.append(heapq.heappop(heap) + 1)   # run one copy
        for k in ran:
            if k:                                  # copies remain
                heapq.heappush(heap, k)
        time += n + 1 if heap else len(ran)
    return time

def least_interval_formula(tasks, n):
    counts = list(Counter(tasks).values())
    m = max(counts)
    ties = counts.count(m)                         # kinds in the last window
    return max(len(tasks), (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties)

least_interval(list("AAABBB"), 2)                  # -> 8
least_interval(list("AAABBB"), 3)                  # -> 10
least_interval(list("ACABDB"), 1)                  # -> 6
least_interval(list("AAABBBCCCDDE"), 2)            # -> 12
least_interval_formula(list("AAABBBCCCDDE"), 2)    # -> 12
\end{pyex}
The closed form is the fastest to type: \cd{max(N, (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties)}.
Here \cd{N} is the number of tasks, \cd{m} is the top count, and \cd{ties} is the number of kinds with count \cd{m}.
Do not forget the \cd{max} with the task count: when many kinds fill every gap, there is no idle slot.
An event simulation with a FIFO queue of cooling tasks is the other optimal form.
For a different cooldown per task, the simulation code still runs: the queue becomes a min-heap keyed by the ready time.
But the most-frequent-first rule is then not always optimal, so check it against a brute force.
For example, take three B tasks with cooldown 0 and two A tasks with cooldown 5.
The greedy runs B first, so the second A cannot run before slot 8. A schedule that runs A first needs only 7 slots.

\subsubsection{Take back the weakest choice}
Two kinds of budget pay for a sequence of costs, and one kind is scarce.
For example, each climb to a taller building costs bricks equal to its height, or one ladder (Furthest Building You Can Reach).
A prefix of climbs is possible when the bricks pay for all climbs except the largest ones, one ladder for each.
But the scan does not know the later climbs. So give each climb a ladder first, and keep these climbs in a min-heap.
When the ladders run out, take back the smallest ladder climb and pay for it with bricks.
The heap then always holds the largest climbs so far. Each climb goes in and comes out at most one time.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Ladder first; when the ladders run out, the smallest ladder climb goes back to bricks.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq

def furthest_building(heights, bricks, ladders):
    climbs = []                          # min-heap: the climbs that use a ladder now
    for i in range(len(heights) - 1):
        d = heights[i + 1] - heights[i]
        if d <= 0:
            continue                     # a step down is free
        heapq.heappush(climbs, d)        # first give this climb a ladder
        if len(climbs) > ladders:        # one ladder too few: take one back
            bricks -= heapq.heappop(climbs)   # the smallest climb uses bricks
            if bricks < 0:
                return i
    return len(heights) - 1

furthest_building([4, 2, 7, 6, 9, 14, 12], 5, 1)          # -> 4
furthest_building([4, 12, 2, 7, 3, 18, 20, 3, 19], 10, 2) # -> 7
furthest_building([14, 3, 19, 3], 17, 0)                  # -> 3
\end{pyex}
The heap holds at most \cd{ladders + 1} climbs, so the time is $O(n \log k)$ for $k$ ladders.
The same take-back keeps a total under a limit. Take the courses in order of deadline.
When the time passes the deadline, drop the longest course taken so far (Course Schedule III).

\subsubsection{Unlock, then farm: case analysis with a brute-force check}
Some problems let you repeat one action at a fixed cost after a one-time cost to reach it.
For example, take a walk that starts at position 0 of a number line. Walls sit at half-integer positions.
A step costs 1, or the wall thickness \cd{t} when it crosses a wall, and each crossing is one hit.
Walls stay, so you can cross one wall again and again. Return the most hits with at most \cd{energy}.

Case analysis gives the plan. Take any walk, and let \cd{w} be the cheapest wall that it crosses.
Let $j$ be the number of walls between 0 and \cd{w}, and let \cd{base} be the cost to stand next to \cd{w}.
The inner walls give $j$ hits inside \cd{base}. Every other hit costs at least the thickness of \cd{w}.
This is an exchange argument: move every extra hit onto \cd{w}, and the cost does not grow.
So the walk has at most \cd{j + (energy - base) // t} hits, and the walk ``go straight to \cd{w}, then bounce'' reaches that bound.
Try each wall as the bounce wall. Sort each side by distance, keep a running cost, and score each wall in $O(1)$.

\textbf{Memory hook:} \emph{Walk out each side, and at every wall cash in all leftover energy as bounces.}
\begin{pyex}
import random
from functools import lru_cache

def max_wall_hits(walls, thickness, energy):
    # plain steps from 0 to the near side of each wall, one sorted list per side
    right = sorted((int(w - 0.5), t) for w, t in zip(walls, thickness) if w > 0)
    left = sorted((int(-w - 0.5), t) for w, t in zip(walls, thickness) if w < 0)
    best = 0
    for side in (right, left):
        spent = pos = 0                  # cost to stand here; distance walked
        for j, (dist, t) in enumerate(side):
            spent += dist - pos          # plain steps up to this wall
            if spent + t > energy:       # cannot cross it once; farther walls cost more
                break
            best = max(best, j + (energy - spent) // t)   # j inner hits, then bounce
            spent += t                   # cross once and go on
            pos = dist + 1
    return best

def brute_hits(walls, thickness, energy):   # try every walk; fine for a tiny energy
    cost = {int(w - 0.5): t for w, t in zip(walls, thickness)}   # key k: wall between k and k + 1
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def most(pos, left):
        best = 0
        for gap, nxt in ((pos, pos + 1), (pos - 1, pos - 1)):
            c = cost.get(gap, 1)
            if c <= left:
                best = max(best, (gap in cost) + most(nxt, left - c))
        return best
    return most(0, energy)

max_wall_hits([-1.5, 0.5, 1.5, 5.5], [2, 4, 8, 3], 3)   # -> 1
max_wall_hits([0.5], [2], 7)                             # -> 3
max_wall_hits([2.5], [1], 2)                             # -> 0
rng = random.Random(7)
ok = True
for _ in range(300):
    ks = rng.sample(range(-5, 5), rng.randint(0, 4))
    walls = [k + 0.5 for k in ks]
    thick = [rng.randint(1, 4) for _ in ks]
    e = rng.randint(0, 12)
    ok = ok and max_wall_hits(walls, thick, e) == brute_hits(walls, thick, e)
ok                                                       # -> True
\end{pyex}
Use this method for any greedy that comes from a case analysis.
State the canonical shape of an optimal answer, prove a bound, and confirm the code with a brute force on tiny inputs.
The energy can be $10^{12}$, so never simulate the bounces. Use an integer division, and keep all cost math in integers.
Convert the half-integer positions to integer step counts one time, before any cost math.

\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What is the output: one number, yes or no, or a construction? Does the input order matter?
        If it does not, sort the input or count it first.
  \item What does the brute force choose at each step, and what state does it carry?
  \item Can the state collapse into a summary? Look for a prefix (one frontier), an interval (two ends),
        a running sum that you can drop, or a frequency map.
  \item Which reason makes the local choice safe: forced choice, exchange argument, skip ahead,
        contiguous states, a one-way operation, or two lower bounds? If no reason fits, suspect DP.
        If a later item can show that an earlier choice was weak, keep the choices in a heap and take one back.
  \item In one step of the scan, what is the order? Usually: test for failure, apply the choice, update the answer.
        Write the invariant in one sentence.
  \item Which global checks come first? Examples are a total (Gas Station), a divisibility (Hand of Straights),
        and the impossible case ($-1$).
  \item Test the greedy against a brute force on all small inputs. Include zeros, ties, negative values and $n = 1$.
  \item If a counterexample appears, make the summary a DP state, and add the information that the greedy ignored.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong key for the local choice.}
Wrong: in Jump Game II, always jump as far as possible, or pick the next index with the largest \cd{nums[i]}.
Right: pick the next stop whose own reach \cd{i + nums[i]} is the farthest. The window scan does this for you.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def jump_longest_each_time(nums):        # wrong: always take the longest jump
    i = jumps = 0
    while i < len(nums) - 1:
        if nums[i] == 0:
            return -1                    # stuck
        i, jumps = min(len(nums) - 1, i + nums[i]), jumps + 1
    return jumps

def min_jumps(nums):                     # windows: compare reach positions
    jumps = left = right = 0
    while right < len(nums) - 1:
        farthest = max(i + nums[i] for i in range(left, right + 1))
        if farthest <= right:
            return -1
        left, right, jumps = right + 1, farthest, jumps + 1
    return jumps

jump_longest_each_time([2, 2, 0, 0]), min_jumps([2, 2, 0, 0])   # -> (-1, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Update and test in the wrong order.}
Wrong: in Jump Game, stretch \cd{farthest} before you test \cd{i > farthest}.
An unreachable index with a positive jump then extends the frontier.
Right: test for the gap first. In Partition Labels and Jump Game II the order is the other way.
Update the end with the current element first. Then test whether the scan reached it.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def can_reach_update_first(nums):        # wrong order
    farthest = 0
    for i, jump in enumerate(nums):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
        if i > farthest:
            return False
    return True

can_reach_update_first([0, 2, 0])        # -> True
\end{pyex}
The correct answer for \cd{[0, 2, 0]} is false: index 0 cannot move.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A strict test, and a missing global check.}
Wrong: in Gas Station, reset the start when the tank is 0, or skip the total check.
Right: reset only when the tank is below 0. Arriving with exactly zero gas is fine.
Check the total first, because the scan alone never returns $-1$.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def gas_start(gas, cost, reset_at_zero=False, check_total=True):
    if check_total and sum(gas) < sum(cost):
        return -1
    start = tank = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0 or (reset_at_zero and tank == 0):
            start, tank = i + 1, 0
    return start

gas_start([2, 0], [0, 2])                            # -> 0
gas_start([2, 0], [0, 2], reset_at_zero=True)        # -> 2
gas_start([2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 3])                      # -> -1
gas_start([2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 3], check_total=False)   # -> 2
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A range of states without the clamp or without the early failure.}
Wrong: in Valid Parenthesis String, let \cd{lo} go below zero, or test \cd{hi} only at the end.
Right: return false as soon as \cd{hi < 0}, then clamp \cd{lo} at zero after each character.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
STEP = {"(": (1, 1), ")": (-1, -1), "*": (-1, 1)}    # change of (lo, hi)

def valid_star(s, clamp=True, early_fail=True):
    lo = hi = 0
    for c in s:
        lo, hi = lo + STEP[c][0], hi + STEP[c][1]
        if early_fail and hi < 0:
            return False
        if clamp:
            lo = max(lo, 0)
    return lo == 0

valid_star("(*)("), valid_star("(*)(", clamp=False)          # -> (False, True)
valid_star(")*"), valid_star(")*", early_fail=False)         # -> (False, True)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong start value for the best answer.}
Wrong: start \cd{best = 0} in Maximum Subarray. An all-negative array then returns 0.
Right: the subarray is non-empty, so start \cd{best} at \cd{nums[0]} or at \cd{float("-inf")}.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A tuple compared with a list.}
Wrong: build the result as a tuple and compare it with the list \cd{target}. The result is always \cd{False}.
Right: compare two lists, or convert both sides to tuples.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
(2, 7, 5) == [2, 7, 5]                   # -> False
list((2, 7, 5)) == [2, 7, 5]             # -> True
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A simulation of a huge budget.}
Wrong: repeat one action at a time when the budget is $10^{12}$, or use \cd{/} on large integers.
Right: compute the repeat count with \cd{//}. A float loses precision above $2^{53}$.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
energy, t = 10**17 + 1, 3
energy // t                              # -> 33333333333333333
int(energy / t)                          # -> 33333333333333332
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A greedy rule with no reason.}
Wrong: trust a rule because it passes the given examples.
Right: name the reason from the table in the idea subsection. If you cannot, run the brute-force check.
A rule such as ``a zero blocks the path'' fails at \cd{[2, 0, 0]}.
\end{caution}

\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Maximum Subarray (53) & The state is a running sum. Clamp the previous sum at 0 before you add the element. & A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart. \\
Jump Game (55) & The reachable set is a prefix. Keep one frontier and fail on a gap. & Walk forward; if you pass farthest you are stuck, else stretch farthest. \\
Jump Game II (45) & The fewest moves. BFS layers are windows \cd{[left, right]}. & BFS in windows: the next window runs from right + 1 to the farthest reach of this window. \\
Gas Station (134) & A circle. Check the total, then move the start past each failure. & Not enough total gas means $-1$; out of gas means start after here. \\
Hand of Straights (846) & A partition of a multiset. The smallest card has a forced role. & Smallest card left starts a straight. Pull its next cards one by one. \\
Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet (1899) & A one-way operation (max). Drop the overshoots and combine the rest. & Drop any triplet that overshoots, max the rest, compare with target. \\
Partition Labels (763) & Each letter forces a span. Cut when the scan reaches the farthest required end. & Each letter drags the cut to its last spot; cut when you catch up. \\
Valid Parenthesis String (678) & Wildcards. Keep the range \cd{[lo, hi]} of open counts. & Range of open counts: fail if the most goes below zero, clamp the fewest at zero, and end with fewest == 0. \\
Task Scheduler (621) & A cooldown. Most frequent first, in windows of $n + 1$ slots. & Fill each window of n + 1 with the most frequent different tasks. Only the last window has no idle tail. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T19} (page~\pageref{drill:T19}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T19} (page~\pageref{ans:T19}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Intervals}\label{tech:T20}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
An interval is a piece of a line: a meeting, a booking, a range of values, a balloon.
Most interval questions are about pairs: do two intervals overlap, and which ones touch?
With $n$ intervals there are about $n^2 / 2$ pairs. At $n = 10^4$ that is $5 \cdot 10^7$ checks, which is too slow in Python.

Sort the intervals by one endpoint. Then each new interval can only touch a small state:
the last merged group, the last kept interval, or the set of intervals that are still open.
One pass over the sorted list then replaces all the pair checks. The total cost is $O(n \log n)$ for the sort.

A worked example: merge \cd{[[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6]]}.
Sort by start: \cd{[1, 3]}, \cd{[2, 6]}, \cd{[8, 10]}. Open a group with \cd{[1, 3]}.
The next interval starts at 2, and 2 is not after the group end 3. So extend the group to \cd{[1, 6]}.
The next interval starts at 8, after the group end 6. Every later interval starts at 8 or later,
so nothing can reach back to \cd{[1, 6]} any more. Close it and open \cd{[8, 10]}.
The result is \cd{[[1, 6], [8, 10]]}. The sweep compares each interval with one group only.

There are two main sort keys, and each one has a reason.
Sort by start when you must handle every interval in time order: merge, conflict check, room count.
Sort by end when you choose a subset: the interval that ends first leaves the most room for the rest.
The question decides the sort key and the state of the sweep:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.4cm}L{2.6cm}L{4.0cm}L{4.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Sort by & State during the sweep & Example \\
\midrule
Union, merge, covered length, free gaps & start & the last merged group & Merge Intervals \\
Does any pair conflict? & start & the previous end & Meeting Rooms \\
Keep the most, remove the fewest, stab with the fewest points & end & the end of the last kept interval & Non-overlapping Intervals \\
Peak number at one time, minimum resources & events \cd{(time, change)} & a running count & Meeting Rooms II \\
Best active interval for each query point & start, and the queries & a heap of active intervals & Minimum Interval to Include Each Query \\
Add one interval to a sorted, disjoint list & no sort & three buckets: left, middle, right & Insert Interval \\
Intersect two sorted, disjoint lists & no sort & two pointers & (Interval List Intersections) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Before any code, decide what happens at a shared endpoint.
For closed intervals \cd{[s, e]}, both ends belong to the interval, and two intervals that touch share a point.
For half-open intervals \cd{[s, e)}, the end does not belong, and touching intervals share no point.
Two closed intervals overlap when the larger start is at or before the smaller end.
Two half-open intervals overlap when the larger start is strictly before the smaller end.
\begin{pyex}
def overlap_closed(a, b):           # [s, e]: both ends belong to the interval
    return max(a[0], b[0]) <= min(a[1], b[1])
def overlap_half_open(a, b):        # [s, e): the end does not belong
    return max(a[0], b[0]) < min(a[1], b[1])
overlap_closed([1, 2], [2, 3]), overlap_half_open([1, 2], [2, 3])   # -> (True, False)
overlap_closed([1, 2], [3, 4]), overlap_closed([1, 9], [3, 4])      # -> (False, True)
max(1, 3), min(2, 4)                # the intersection [3, 2] is empty
# -> (3, 2)
\end{pyex}
The intersection of two intervals is \cd{[max of the starts, min of the ends]}. It is empty when that start is after that end.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The input is a list of \cd{[start, end]} pairs: meetings, bookings, trips, ranges, segments, time slots.
  \item The statement uses the words overlap, merge, conflict, attend all, rooms, cover, free time, or intersect.
  \item The answer does not depend on the input order. So you are free to sort.
  \item $n$ is $10^4$ to $10^5$. A check of all pairs is too slow, so the budget is one sort and one pass.
  \item The question asks for a minimum number of removals so that the rest do not conflict.
        Rewrite it as the maximum number that you can keep.
  \item The question asks how many things run at the same time, or for the minimum number of resources.
        The answer is the peak number of open intervals.
  \item Many point queries ask about one fixed set of intervals, and all queries are given at the start.
        Sort the queries too, and answer them in sorted order (offline).
  \item The statement defines what happens at a shared endpoint. This tells you to choose \cd{<} or \cd{<=} with care.
  \item The intervals are hidden. Each item spans from a first position to a last position:
        the first and last index of a character, a subarray, a trip from one stop to another.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Sort by start. Compare each interval with the last group of the output only.
Extend the group, or open a new group.
\begin{pyex}
def merge(intervals):                       # closed intervals: touching ones merge
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):          # sort by start; sorted() keeps the input
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:         # shares a point with the open group
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e) # max: a nested interval must not shrink it
        else:
            out.append([s, e])              # a new list, not the input row
    return out
merge([[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6]])            # -> [[1, 6], [8, 10]]
merge([[1, 4], [4, 5]])                     # -> [[1, 5]]
merge([[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]])            # -> [[1, 10]]
merge([[1, 2], [3, 4]])                     # -> [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
merge([[5, 5], [5, 5]]), merge([])          # -> ([[5, 5]], [])
\end{pyex}
Invariant: after $k$ intervals in sorted order, \cd{out} holds the union of these $k$ intervals as disjoint groups, sorted by start.
Every earlier group ends before \cd{out[-1]} starts. Every later interval starts at or after the start of \cd{out[-1]}.
So only \cd{out[-1]} can overlap a later interval.
For half-open intervals, where touching ones stay apart, change the test to \cd{s < out[-1][1]}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Merge, covered length and free gaps}
Merge Intervals is the core template.
Memory hook: \emph{Sort, then extend the last one or append a new one.}
The merged list answers more questions in one more step.
The total covered length is the sum of the group lengths.
The free gaps are the spaces between two neighbor groups (free time in a calendar, Employee Free Time).
\begin{pyex}
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out
def covered_length(intervals):              # length e - s (count integer points: e - s + 1)
    return sum(e - s for s, e in merge(intervals))
def free_gaps(intervals):                   # from the end of one group to the next start
    m = merge(intervals)
    return [[m[k][1], m[k + 1][0]] for k in range(len(m) - 1)]
covered_length([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10]])   # -> 7
free_gaps([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [12, 13]])   # -> [[6, 8], [10, 12]]
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Hidden intervals also merge. In Partition Labels, each character spans from its first to its last index.
The merged groups are the parts.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Insert into a sorted, disjoint list}
The list is already sorted and has no overlaps. One new interval arrives. Do not sort again.
Each old interval has exactly one relation to the new interval: it ends before the new start,
it starts after the new end, or it shares a point. Put each one in a bucket.
The overlapping ones melt into the new interval, which grows with \cd{min} and \cd{max}.
The buckets are already in order, so the answer is the left bucket, the merged interval, and the right bucket.
Memory hook (Insert Interval): \emph{Left stays left, right stays right, the middle melts into one.}
\begin{pyex}
def insert(intervals, new):     # intervals: sorted by start, disjoint, closed
    start, end = new
    left, right = [], []
    for s, e in intervals:
        if e < start:           # ends before the new interval starts
            left.append([s, e])
        elif s > end:           # starts after the new interval ends
            right.append([s, e])
        else:                   # shares a point: melt it into the new interval
            start, end = min(start, s), max(end, e)
    return left + [[start, end]] + right
insert([[1, 3], [6, 9]], [2, 5])                              # -> [[1, 5], [6, 9]]
insert([[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]], [4, 8])   # -> [[1, 2], [3, 10], [12, 16]]
insert([], [4, 8]), insert([[1, 2]], [2, 3])                  # -> ([[4, 8]], [[1, 3]])
insert([[1, 2], [5, 6]], [3, 4])                              # -> [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
\end{pyex}
This is $O(n)$. The common optimal form is the same idea with one index and two \cd{while} loops:
copy while \cd{e < start}, absorb while \cd{s <= end}, append the merged interval, then copy the rest with one slice.
The same classify-and-concatenate pattern removes a range from a set of disjoint intervals.
\begin{note}
For many inserts into a stored list (Range Module, My Calendar), find the middle block with binary search.
The intervals are disjoint, so the ends are sorted too.
\cd{bisect_left} on the ends gives the first interval with \cd{e >= start}.
\cd{bisect_right} on the starts gives the first interval with \cd{s > end}.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Conflict check: can one person attend all}
Sort by start. If any two intervals overlap, then some neighbor pair overlaps.
The reason: if each interval ends at or before the start of the next one, it also ends at or before every later start.
So compare each start with the previous end only.
Memory hook (Meeting Rooms): \emph{Sort by start. No meeting may start before the previous one ends.}
\begin{pyex}
def can_attend(intervals):              # a meeting that ends at t and one that starts at t do not conflict
    iv = sorted(intervals)
    for i in range(1, len(iv)):
        if iv[i][0] < iv[i - 1][1]:     # strict: touching meetings are fine
            return False
    return True
can_attend([[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]])   # -> False
can_attend([[7, 10], [2, 4]])              # -> True
can_attend([[1, 5], [5, 10]]), can_attend([])   # -> (True, True)
\end{pyex}
The comparison with the previous interval is enough here, because the first conflict returns at once.
In a merge, compare with the end of the open group instead. A long earlier interval can cover several later ones.

\subsubsection{Keep the most: sort by end}
The question ``remove the fewest so that the rest do not overlap'' is the same as ``keep the most''.
Keep the interval that ends first. It leaves the most room on the line for all later intervals.
An exchange argument proves it: any best selection can swap its first interval for the one that ends first, with no new conflict.
Then repeat on the intervals that start at or after that end.
Memory hook (Non-overlapping Intervals): \emph{Sort by end, keep what fits, remove the rest.}
\begin{pyex}
def min_removals(intervals):            # touching intervals do not overlap
    kept, prev_end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):   # earliest end first
        if s >= prev_end:               # it fits after the last kept interval
            kept += 1
            prev_end = e
    return len(intervals) - kept
min_removals([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 3]])     # -> 1
min_removals([[1, 2], [1, 2], [1, 2]])             # -> 2
min_removals([[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5], [6, 7]])   # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The same loop solves related questions with one changed test:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Return \cd{kept} itself for the longest chain of non-overlapping intervals.
        If the chain needs a strict order (\cd{b < c} for \cd{[a, b]} then \cd{[c, d]}), use \cd{s > prev_end}
        (Maximum Length of Pair Chain).
  \item Stab every interval with the fewest points: place a point at the end of each interval that the last point misses.
        For closed intervals, a point on a shared end hits both. So place a new point only when \cd{s > prev_end}
        (Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons).
  \item If the intervals have different values (profit, weight), the greedy fails.
        Use a DP over the intervals sorted by end, with \cd{bisect_right} on the ends to find the last compatible interval
        (Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Peak overlap: rooms and resources}
The minimum number of rooms equals the largest number of meetings in progress at one moment.
Fewer rooms fail at that moment. That many rooms are enough: give each meeting, in start order, any free room.
The count changes only at a start or an end. So turn each meeting into two events, sort them, and keep a running count.
Memory hook (Meeting Rooms II): \emph{Start is +1, end is -1, sort the events, and keep the peak.}
\begin{pyex}
def rooms(intervals):                   # half-open [s, e): an end at t frees a room for a start at t
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))           # a meeting starts: one more room busy
        events.append((e, -1))          # a meeting ends: one room frees
    events.sort()                       # at equal times, (t, -1) sorts before (t, 1)
    busy = most = 0
    for _, change in events:
        busy += change
        most = max(most, busy)
    return most
rooms([[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]])     # -> 2
rooms([[1, 5], [5, 10]])                # -> 1
rooms([[1, 10], [2, 3], [3, 4]])        # -> 2
\end{pyex}
The event sweep is the general tool: an event can also carry a weight, such as passengers or load.
When the coordinates are small, a difference array with a prefix sum replaces the sort (see the section on prefix sums).

Two other forms give the same count with the same $O(n \log n)$ cost. Treat them as asides.
The heap form sorts the meetings by start and keeps a min-heap with the end time of each room.
Each meeting takes the room that frees first if that room is free. Otherwise it opens a new room.
Use the heap when you must know which room frees first, for example to give out room numbers (Meeting Rooms III).
The two-list form sorts all starts and all ends in two separate lists, and walks them with two pointers.
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
def rooms_heap(intervals):
    ends = []                           # min-heap: the end time of the last meeting in each room
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if ends and ends[0] <= s:       # the room that frees first is free now: reuse it
            heapq.heappop(ends)
        heapq.heappush(ends, e)
    return len(ends)                    # one heap entry for each room
def rooms_two_lists(intervals):
    starts = sorted(s for s, _ in intervals)
    ends = sorted(e for _, e in intervals)
    count = j = 0
    for s in starts:
        if s >= ends[j]:                # some meeting ended: reuse its room
            j += 1
        else:
            count += 1                  # no room is free: open a new one
    return count
cases = [[[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]], [[7, 10], [2, 4]], [[1, 5], [5, 10]], [[1, 10], [2, 3], [3, 4]]]
[rooms_heap(c) for c in cases]          # -> [2, 1, 1, 2]
[rooms_two_lists(c) for c in cases]     # -> [2, 1, 1, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Best active interval for each query: offline sweep with a heap}
Many point queries ask about one fixed set of intervals. A scan of all intervals for each query costs $O(n m)$.
With $n = m = 10^5$, that is $10^{10}$ checks.
If all queries are known at the start, answer them in sorted order, and sweep a point from left to right.
An interval becomes active when the sweep passes its start. It is dead forever when the sweep passes its end.
Keep the active intervals in a min-heap, keyed by the value that you optimize.
Memory hook (Minimum Interval to Include Each Query): \emph{Sweep sorted queries, push started intervals by size, pop ended tops, read the top.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
def min_interval(intervals, queries):   # closed [l, r]; the size is r - l + 1
    intervals = sorted(intervals)
    order = sorted(range(len(queries)), key=lambda j: queries[j])   # indexes, not values
    ans = [-1] * len(queries)
    heap, i = [], 0                     # heap of (size, right); i is never reset
    for j in order:
        q = queries[j]
        while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][0] <= q:   # started: push it
            left, right = intervals[i]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (right - left + 1, right))
            i += 1
        while heap and heap[0][1] < q:  # the top ended before q: drop it for good
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        if heap:
            ans[j] = heap[0][0]         # write at the original index
    return ans
min_interval([[1, 4], [2, 4], [3, 6], [4, 4]], [2, 3, 4, 5])      # -> [3, 3, 1, 4]
min_interval([[2, 3], [2, 5], [1, 8], [20, 25]], [2, 19, 5, 22])  # -> [2, -1, 4, 6]
\end{pyex}
The trick is lazy deletion. An interval that ended stays in the heap until it reaches the top.
This is correct because the code reads only the top, and an ended interval never becomes valid again when the queries grow.
Use this rule for any heap whose items expire in the order of the sweep.
The same pointer-into-heap frame schedules work as time moves (Single-Threaded CPU, IPO).
\begin{note}
To count the intervals that contain each point, no heap is necessary.
The count is the number of starts at or before $q$ minus the number of ends before $q$. Two binary searches give both numbers.
\end{note}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
def count_containing(intervals, queries):   # closed intervals
    starts = sorted(s for s, _ in intervals)
    ends = sorted(e for _, e in intervals)
    return [bisect_right(starts, q) - bisect_left(ends, q) for q in queries]
count_containing([[1, 6], [3, 7], [9, 12], [4, 13]], [2, 3, 7, 11])   # -> [1, 2, 2, 2]
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Endpoint rules: closed and half-open}
Each problem fixes one rule for a shared endpoint. Read the rule from the statement or from an example.
Then let it decide every comparison in the code.
Memory hook: \emph{Closed ends touch, half-open ends do not. Decide once, then derive every \cd{<} or \cd{<=}.}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.2cm}L{4.6cm}L{6.8cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & Touching intervals & Test in the code \\
\midrule
Merge Intervals & share a point: they merge & extend when \cd{s <= out[-1][1]} \\
Insert Interval & share a point: they merge & left when \cd{e < start}, right when \cd{s > end} \\
Non-overlapping Intervals & do not overlap & keep when \cd{s >= prev_end} \\
Meeting Rooms & do not conflict & conflict when \cd{s < prev_end} \\
Meeting Rooms II & the room is free (half-open) & \cd{(t, -1)} sorts before \cd{(t, 1)}; reuse when \cd{ends[0] <= s} \\
Minimum Interval to Include Each Query & a query on an end is inside (closed) & drop the top when \cd{right < q} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
To switch a sweep from half-open to closed intervals, process starts before ends at equal times.
On integer coordinates, you can also keep ends first and free the room at \cd{e + 1}.
This works because \cd{[s, e]} holds the same integers as \cd{[s, e + 1)}.
\begin{pyex}
def peak(intervals, closed):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))
        events.append((e + 1 if closed else e, -1))   # closed: the end time is still busy
    events.sort()
    busy = most = 0
    for _, change in events:
        busy += change
        most = max(most, busy)
    return most
peak([[1, 5], [5, 10]], closed=False), peak([[1, 5], [5, 10]], closed=True)   # -> (1, 2)
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What is one interval? Some problems hide them: a trip from stop $a$ to stop $b$,
        the first and last index of a value, a subarray with a given sum.
  \item Do touching intervals overlap? Write the overlap test before the loop.
        Check it on the example that has a shared endpoint.
  \item Is the input already sorted and disjoint? Then do not sort again.
        For one new interval or one removed range, use three buckets. For two such lists, use two pointers.
  \item Must every interval be processed, or do you choose a subset?
        Process every interval (merge, conflicts, peak): sort by start, or sort events.
        Choose the most, or stab with the fewest points: sort by end.
  \item What is the smallest state that a later interval needs? The last group, the last kept end,
        a running count, or a heap of active intervals. Only this state may go into the loop.
  \item Are there ties in the sort order? Decide which one goes first: an end or a start at the same time,
        a longer or a shorter interval at the same start.
  \item Are there queries? If all of them are known at the start, sort their indexes and sweep once.
        If they arrive one at a time, keep a sorted list and use \cd{bisect}.
  \item Do the intervals carry different values? Then a greedy on the ends fails. Use a DP with binary search.
  \item Is the coordinate range small? A difference array or a marked line can replace the sort.
\end{enumerate}
Test with touching intervals, nested intervals, duplicates, point intervals \cd{[x, x]},
one interval, an empty list, and unsorted input.
For a merge, a slow oracle marks every covered point on a doubled line.
Doubling keeps a gap between \cd{[1, 2]} and \cd{[3, 4]}: the cells are 2 to 4 and 6 to 8, and cell 5 stays empty.
\begin{pyex}
import random
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out
def merge_brute(intervals):             # closed integer intervals; a test oracle only
    cells = sorted({x for s, e in intervals for x in range(2 * s, 2 * e + 1)})
    runs = []
    for x in cells:
        if runs and x == runs[-1][1] + 1:
            runs[-1][1] = x
        else:
            runs.append([x, x])
    return [[a // 2, b // 2] for a, b in runs]
merge_brute([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), merge_brute([[1, 2], [2, 4]])   # -> ([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[1, 4]])
random.seed(7)
def random_case():
    return [sorted([random.randint(0, 9), random.randint(0, 9)]) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 5))]
all(merge(c) == merge_brute(c) for c in (random_case() for _ in range(500)))   # -> True
\end{pyex}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The wrong strictness at a shared endpoint.}
Wrong: copy \cd{<} or \cd{<=} from another interval problem.
Right: read the rule for touching intervals in the statement, and use the table of endpoint rules.
Merge Intervals merges \cd{[1, 4]} and \cd{[4, 5]}. Meeting Rooms lets \cd{[1, 5]} and \cd{[5, 10]} both happen.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Compare with the open group, and take the max of the ends.}
Wrong: compare each interval with the previous input interval, or set the new end without \cd{max}.
A long interval can cover several later intervals, and a nested interval can shrink the group.
Right: compare with \cd{out[-1]}, and extend with \cd{max(out[-1][1], e)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def merge_wrong(intervals):
    iv = sorted(intervals)
    out = [list(iv[0])]
    for k in range(1, len(iv)):
        if iv[k][0] <= iv[k - 1][1]:        # the previous input interval, not the group
            out[-1][1] = iv[k][1]           # no max
        else:
            out.append(list(iv[k]))
    return out
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out
merge_wrong([[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]])      # -> [[1, 3], [4, 5]]
merge([[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]])            # -> [[1, 10]]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Rows of the input in the output.}
Wrong: append the input row itself to the output, and then change its end.
The caller's list changes too. Also, \cd{intervals.sort()} changes the order of the caller's list.
Right: append a new list \cd{[s, e]}. Use \cd{sorted(intervals)} when the caller needs the input unchanged.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def merge_alias(intervals):
    out = []
    for row in sorted(intervals):
        if out and row[0] <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], row[1])
        else:
            out.append(row)                 # the input row itself
    return out
data = [[1, 3], [2, 6]]
merge_alias(data)                           # -> [[1, 6]]
data                                        # -> [[1, 6], [2, 6]]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Sort by start for a selection problem.}
Wrong: sort by start and keep the current interval when the next one overlaps it.
A long early interval then blocks many short ones.
Right: sort by end and keep what fits. A sort by start works only if, on each overlap,
you keep the interval with the smaller end: \cd{prev_end = min(prev_end, e)}.
Also count removals, not overlapping pairs. One long interval can overlap many short ones, but it needs one removal.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
def min_removals_wrong(intervals):
    removed, prev_end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):          # by start
        if s < prev_end:
            removed += 1                    # always drops the new interval
        else:
            prev_end = e
    return removed
def min_removals(intervals):
    kept, prev_end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):
        if s >= prev_end:
            kept += 1
            prev_end = e
    return len(intervals) - kept
min_removals_wrong([[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]])   # -> 2
min_removals([[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]])         # -> 1
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{The tie order of events, and the size of the heap.}
Wrong: sort events so that a start comes before an end at the same time, for half-open meetings.
Wrong: pop every free room from the heap, and then return the final heap size.
Right: in Python, \cd{(t, -1)} sorts before \cd{(t, 1)}, so ends come first with no extra code.
Pop at most one room for each meeting. If you pop all free rooms, track the largest heap size.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
def rooms_starts_first(intervals):
    events = sorted([(s, 1) for s, e in intervals] + [(e, -1) for s, e in intervals],
                    key=lambda ev: (ev[0], -ev[1]))   # +1 before -1 at equal times
    busy = most = 0
    for _, change in events:
        busy += change
        most = max(most, busy)
    return most
def rooms_pop_all(intervals):
    ends = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        while ends and ends[0] <= s:        # frees every finished room
            heapq.heappop(ends)
        heapq.heappush(ends, e)
    return len(ends)                        # the size now can be below the peak
rooms_starts_first([[1, 5], [5, 10]])       # -> 2
rooms_pop_all([[1, 2], [1, 2], [5, 6]])     # -> 1
\end{pyex}
The correct answers are 1 and 2.
In the two-list form (all starts sorted, all ends sorted), do not pair \cd{starts[i]} with \cd{ends[i]}.
The sort breaks the pairs on purpose. Only the counts matter.

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Offline queries.}
Wrong: sort the query values and return the answers in sorted order, or reset the interval pointer for each query.
Right: sort a list of query indexes, write each answer at its original index, and keep one pointer for all queries.
A reset pointer makes the cost $O(n m)$. Also check the size formula \cd{r - l + 1} for closed integer intervals,
and the \cd{-1} for a query that no interval contains.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Work after the loop.}
Wrong: keep the open group in two variables and append it only when the next group starts.
The last group then never gets into the output.
Right: keep the open group as \cd{out[-1]}, as in the template. In Insert Interval, append the merged interval exactly once,
also when it goes at the very end.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Merge Intervals & Unsorted input; touching intervals merge. Sort by start and extend the open group. & Sort, then extend the last one or append a new one. \\
Insert Interval & The input is sorted and disjoint. No sort: three buckets in one $O(n)$ pass. & Left stays left, right stays right, the middle melts into one. \\
Non-overlapping Intervals & Choose a subset: minimum removals equals $n$ minus the most kept. Sort by end. & Sort by end, keep what fits, remove the rest. \\
Meeting Rooms & A yes or no conflict check. Sort by start and compare neighbors; touching is fine. & Sort by start. No meeting may start before the previous one ends. \\
Meeting Rooms II & The peak number of open intervals. Event sweep with ends before starts at a tie; or a heap of end times. & Start is +1, end is -1, sort the events, and keep the peak. \\
Minimum Interval to Include Each Query & Offline point queries. Sort the queries, push started intervals into a heap by size, drop ended tops lazily. & Sweep sorted queries, push started intervals by size, pop ended tops, read the top. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
