Many problems assume a 32-bit C \cd{int}. Emulate it with the mask \cd{0xFFFFFFFF}, and convert the sign
only at the end.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
\item The statement talks about bits: binary form, set bits, Hamming weight, XOR, powers of two.
\item Every value occurs an even number of times, except one or two values. The statement asks for
  $O(1)$ extra space, so a hash map is not allowed.
\item The input is a known range ($0..n$ or $1..n$) with one value missing or one value extra.
\item The output has one value for each integer $0..n$, and the value depends on the binary form of the integer.
\item The statement gives a fixed width, such as ``a 32-bit unsigned integer''. Leading zeros then count.
\item The output rearranges the bits or the digits of one number: reverse, rotate, complement, or a palindrome test.
\item The statement bans an operator (\cd{+}, \cd{-}, \cd{*}, \cd{/}). Build it from bit operations.
\item The statement says ``signed 32-bit'', ``overflow'' or ``return 0 if the result is out of range''.
\item The values are large (up to $10^9$), and the question is about pairs or about OR, AND, XOR.
  Count per bit position (30 or 32 columns), not per pair.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}

\subsubsection{The toolbox of identities}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4.6cm}L{11.6cm}@{}}
\toprule
Expression & Effect \\
\midrule
\cd{x & 1} & The last bit. It is 1 when \cd{x} is odd. \\
\cd{x} \shr\ \cd{1} & Remove the last bit. The same as \cd{x // 2}: in Python both round down, also for a negative \cd{x}. \\
\cd{(x} \shr\ \cd{k) & 1} & Read bit \cd{k}. \\
\cd{x | (1} \shl\ \cd{k)} & Set bit \cd{k}. \\
\cd{x & ~(1} \shl\ \cd{k)} & Clear bit \cd{k}. \\
\cd{x ^ (1} \shl\ \cd{k)} & Toggle bit \cd{k}. \\
\cd{x & (x - 1)} & Clear the lowest set bit. It is 0 only when \cd{x} is 0 or a power of two. \\
\cd{x & -x} & Keep only the lowest set bit. \\
\cd{(1} \shl\ \cd{k) - 1} & A mask of \cd{k} ones. \\
\cd{x ^ x}, \cd{x ^ 0} & 0 and \cd{x}: a value cancels itself, and 0 is the identity. \\
\cd{x.bit_length()} & The number of bits without leading zeros. \\
\cd{x.bit_count()} \since{3.10} & The number of set bits. Older versions: \cd{bin(x).count("1")}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{pyex}
x = 0b101100                 # 44
x & 1                        # -> 0
x >> 1                       # -> 0b10110
(x >> 2) & 1                 # -> 1
x | (1 << 0)                 # -> 0b101101
x & ~(1 << 2)                # -> 0b101000
x ^ (1 << 5)                 # -> 0b001100
x & (x - 1)                  # -> 0b101000
x & -x                       # -> 0b000100
(1 << 4) - 1                 # -> 0b1111
x ^ x, x ^ 0                 # -> (0, 44)
x.bit_length(), x.bit_count()   # -> (6, 3)
bin(x), format(x, "08b"), int("101100", 2)   # -> ('0b101100', '00101100', 44)
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Template 1: walk the bits}
Read the last bit, use it, then shift it away. Stop when the number is 0.
When the width is fixed, loop exactly \cd{width} times instead, because leading zeros count.
\begin{pyex}
def popcount(x):                     # x >= 0
    count = 0
    while x > 0:
        count += x & 1               # read the last bit
        x >>= 1                      # shift it away
    return count

def reverse_bits(x, width=32):       # fixed width: exactly width steps
    res = 0
    for _ in range(width):
        res = (res << 1) | (x & 1)   # push the last bit of x onto res
        x >>= 1                      # peel it off x
    return res

popcount(11)                         # -> 3
reverse_bits(0b0011, 4)              # -> 0b1100
reverse_bits(1) == 1 << 31           # -> True
\end{pyex}
Invariant: after $k$ steps, the work so far covers exactly the lowest $k$ bits of the input,
and \cd{x} holds the other bits, shifted down by $k$.

\subsubsection{Template 2: fold with XOR}
\begin{pyex}
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor

def odd_ones(values):
    acc = 0                          # 0 is the identity of XOR
    for v in values:
        acc ^= v                     # a value seen two times cancels
    return acc

odd_ones([4, 1, 2, 1, 2])            # -> 4
odd_ones([7, -3, 7])                 # -> -3
reduce(xor, [4, 1, 2, 1, 2], 0)      # -> 4
\end{pyex}
Invariant: \cd{acc} is the XOR of the values that occurred an odd number of times so far.
Negative values need no mask here. The XOR of two signed 32-bit values is again a signed 32-bit value.

\subsubsection{Template 3: emulate a 32-bit integer}
Use this template when the problem assumes a C \cd{int} and the values can be negative.
\begin{pyex}
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF                    # 32 ones
def to_u32(x):
    return x & MASK                  # the 32-bit pattern of x, as a value >= 0
def to_i32(u):
    return u if u <= 0x7FFFFFFF else u - (1 << 32)   # bit 31 set means negative

to_u32(-1) == MASK                   # -> True
to_u32(-5)                           # -> 0xFFFFFFFB
to_i32(0xFFFFFFFB)                   # -> -5
to_i32(to_u32(-2**31))               # -> -2147483648
to_i32((0x7FFFFFFF + 1) & MASK)      # -> -2147483648
\end{pyex}
Rule: mask after every step that can create bits above bit 31. Convert to a signed value only once, at the end.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Cancel pairs with XOR}
Every value occurs two times except one value. The space must be $O(1)$, so a hash map is not allowed.
Use Template 2 directly. Memory hook (Single Number): \emph{pairs cancel under XOR, so XOR everything.}
The same fold finds one extra item between two collections: fold both collections together.
\begin{pyex}
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor

def single_number(nums):
    result = 0
    for num in nums:
        result ^= num                # a pair cancels: x ^ x == 0, and x ^ 0 == x
    return result

single_number([2, 2, 1])             # -> 1
single_number([4, 1, 2, 1, 2])       # -> 4
single_number([-30000])              # -> -30000
s, t = "abcd", "dbcae"               # t is s, shuffled, with one extra letter
chr(reduce(xor, map(ord, s + t), 0)) # -> 'e'
\end{pyex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Two values without a pair: the fold gives \cd{a ^ b}. Any set bit of \cd{a ^ b} is a bit where \cd{a}
  and \cd{b} differ. Split all values into two groups by that bit, and fold each group.
\item Values that repeat three times: plain XOR fails. Use per-bit counts (see below) modulo 3.
\item One value repeated many times (Find the Duplicate Number): XOR fails. Use cycle detection.
\end{itemize}
(Single Number, Missing Number, Find the Difference.)

\subsubsection{Count the set bits of one number}
The question is about the bits of one number: how many are 1.
Use Template 1: add \cd{n & 1}, then shift. Memory hook (Number of 1 Bits): \emph{read the last bit, then shift it away.}
The optimal form uses \cd{n & (n - 1)}. Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 bit into 0 and every 0 below it into 1.
The AND then clears exactly the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit, not once per position.
The same fact gives a family of tools. For \cd{x > 0}, \cd{(x & (x - 1)) == 0} tests for a power of two.
\cd{x & -x} keeps only the lowest set bit, and a Fenwick tree uses it to move between nodes.
\cd{sub = (sub - 1) & mask} lists all submasks of \cd{mask} (Part I, ``Subsets as bitmasks'').
In each case, a subtraction of 1 changes only the lowest set bit and the zeros below it.
For 32-bit input both loops are fast. For many calls, use a 256-entry table of byte counts, or \cd{bit_count()}.
\begin{pyex}
def hamming_weight(n):               # intuitive: one step per bit position
    count = 0
    while n > 0:
        count += n & 1
        n >>= 1
    return count

def hamming_weight_fast(n):          # optimal: one step per set bit
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1                   # clear the lowest set bit
        count += 1
    return count

hamming_weight(11), hamming_weight_fast(11)       # -> (3, 3)
hamming_weight(2147483645)                        # -> 30
bin(0b101000 & (0b101000 - 1))                    # -> '0b100000'
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0
[k for k in range(1, 20) if is_power_of_two(k)]   # -> [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
hamming_weight_fast(-5 & 0xFFFFFFFF)              # -> 31
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
On a negative \cd{n}, both loops fail. The shift loop above tests \cd{n > 0}, so it stops at once and returns 0.
A loop that tests \cd{while n} never ends: \cd{n} \shr\ \cd{1} stops at \cd{-1}, and \cd{n & (n - 1)} never reaches 0.
If the input can be a signed 32-bit value, mask it first: \cd{n &= 0xFFFFFFFF}.
\end{caution}
(Number of 1 Bits, Hamming Distance as the count of \cd{x ^ y}, Power of Two.)

\subsubsection{Bit counts for every number: DP over bits}
The output has one answer for each \cd{i} in $0..n$. A separate loop for each number costs $O(n \log n)$.
Instead, reuse an answer that the table already holds.
\cd{i} \shr\ \cd{1} is \cd{i} without its last bit, so it is smaller than \cd{i}.
\cd{i & 1} is the bit that the shift removes.
So \cd{ans[i] = ans[i} \shr\ \cd{1] + (i & 1)}.
Memory hook (Counting Bits): \emph{drop the last bit, look it up, add the bit back.}
\begin{pyex}
def count_bits(n):
    ans = [0] * (n + 1)              # ans[0] = 0 is the base case
    for i in range(1, n + 1):        # increasing i: i >> 1 is already filled
        ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
    return ans

count_bits(5)                        # -> [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2]
count_bits(0)                        # -> [0]
n = 8
alt = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    alt[i] = alt[i & (i - 1)] + 1    # remove the lowest set bit: exactly one 1 fewer
alt == count_bits(8)                 # -> True
\end{pyex}
The general rule: when you need $f(i)$ for every $i$, find an $O(1)$ step that maps $i$ to a smaller $j$
with a known change in $f$. In base 2 the steps are \cd{i} \shr\ \cd{1}, \cd{i & (i - 1)}, and ``remove the top bit''.
In base 10 the steps are \cd{i // 10} and \cd{i} \pct\ \cd{10}.
Bitmask DP uses the same step: \cd{dp[mask]} comes from \cd{dp[mask & (mask - 1)]}.
(Counting Bits, Sort Integers by The Number of 1 Bits.)

\subsubsection{Fixed width: reverse the bits}
The statement fixes the width (32 bits), and the output moves bit \cd{i} to bit \cd{31 - i}.
Use Template 1 with exactly 32 steps: shift \cd{res} left, OR in the last bit of \cd{n}, then shift \cd{n} right.
The first bit that you read ends at the top.
Memory hook (Reverse Bits): \emph{peel the low bit off n, push it onto res, 32 times.}
\begin{pyex}
def reverse_bits(n):
    res = 0
    for _ in range(32):              # fixed width: exactly 32 steps
        res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)   # push the lowest bit of n onto res
        n >>= 1                      # peel that bit off n
    return res

def reverse_bits_wrong(n):           # stops when n is 0: the leading zeros are lost
    res = 0
    while n > 0:
        res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)
        n >>= 1
    return res

reverse_bits(43261596)               # -> 964176192
reverse_bits(2) == 1 << 30           # -> True
reverse_bits_wrong(2)                # -> 1
int(format(43261596, "032b")[::-1], 2)   # -> 964176192
\end{pyex}
For many calls on small fixed-width values, precompute the answer for every 8-bit chunk once.
Then each call combines four table entries. This idea answers most ``called many times'' follow-ups.
\begin{pyex}
REV8 = [int(format(b, "08b")[::-1], 2) for b in range(256)]
def reverse_bits_table(n):
    res = 0
    for _ in range(4):               # the bytes from low to high
        res = (res << 8) | REV8[n & 0xFF]
        n >>= 8
    return res
reverse_bits_table(43261596)         # -> 964176192
\end{pyex}
A second fast form swaps blocks: first the 16-bit halves, then the bytes, then the 4-bit, 2-bit and 1-bit blocks.
This is divide and conquer on bit blocks, with 5 steps for 32 bits.
The same masks count the set bits (SWAR popcount), with an addition of the two blocks in place of the swap.
\begin{pyex}
def reverse_bits_swap(n):
    n = ((n >> 16) | (n << 16)) & 0xFFFFFFFF                # swap the 16-bit halves
    n = ((n & 0xFF00FF00) >> 8) | ((n & 0x00FF00FF) << 8)   # swap the bytes
    n = ((n & 0xF0F0F0F0) >> 4) | ((n & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4)   # swap the 4-bit blocks
    n = ((n & 0xCCCCCCCC) >> 2) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)   # swap the 2-bit blocks
    n = ((n & 0xAAAAAAAA) >> 1) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)   # swap the single bits
    return n

reverse_bits_swap(43261596)          # -> 964176192
reverse_bits_swap(1) == 1 << 31      # -> True
\end{pyex}
(Reverse Bits, Number Complement, Binary Number with Alternating Bits.)

\subsubsection{Find the gap: expected minus actual}
You know the full collection before you read the input: all values $0..n$. One value is missing.
Compute an aggregate of the expected collection and subtract the aggregate of the actual one.
One unknown needs one equation. Memory hook (Missing Number): \emph{expected sum minus actual sum.}
The XOR form is the usual optimal answer, and it has the same cost. Seed the accumulator with \cd{n},
then XOR each index and each value. A present value meets its index and cancels.
XOR cannot overflow, so it is the safe choice in a fixed-width language.
\begin{pyex}
def missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    expected = n * (n + 1) // 2      # sum of 0, 1, ..., n
    return expected - sum(nums)

def missing_number_xor(nums):
    res = len(nums)                  # the indexes cover 0..n-1, so seed with n
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        res ^= i ^ x                 # a present value cancels its index
    return res

missing_number([3, 0, 1]), missing_number([0, 1]), missing_number([1])   # -> (2, 2, 0)
missing_number_xor([9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1])                          # -> 8
\end{pyex}
Two unknowns need two equations: the sum and the sum of squares,
or the XOR of the two values and then a split by one bit.
Many unknowns need index marking or a set.
(Missing Number, Find the Difference.)

\subsubsection{One column at a time: per-bit counts}
The answer depends on each bit position separately. Count the ones in each column over all numbers.
This takes $O(32 n)$ and needs no pairs. The XOR fold is a special case: bit \cd{k} of the single value is
the count of column \cd{k} modulo 2.
\begin{pyex}
def column_counts(nums, width=32):
    # counts[k] is how many numbers have bit k set
    return [sum((x >> k) & 1 for x in nums) for k in range(width)]

counts = column_counts([4, 1, 2, 1, 2], width=4)
counts                                             # -> [2, 2, 1, 0]
sum((c % 2) << k for k, c in enumerate(counts))    # -> 4
\end{pyex}
Change the rule per column to fit the problem: modulo $k$ when the other values repeat $k$ times,
or a count of pairs when the question is about pairs.
Memory hook (per-bit counting): \emph{count the ones in each column, then apply the rule to each column.}
For a negative value, \cd{(x} \shr\ \cd{k) & 1} still gives bit \cd{k} of the 32-bit pattern.
Rebuild the result as a 32-bit pattern, then convert it with \cd{to_i32}.
(Minimum Flips to Make a OR b Equal to c, Largest Combination With Bitwise AND Greater Than Zero.)

\subsubsection{Add without plus: XOR sum and AND carry}
The statement bans \cd{+} and \cd{-}. Add column by column, like a circuit.
The sum of two bits without the carry is their XOR. A carry appears only where both bits are 1, and it moves
one column left: \cd{(a & b)} \shl\ \cd{1}. So $a + b = (a \oplus b) + ((a \mathbin{\&} b) \ll 1)$.
Repeat this step until the carry is 0.

Worked example: $5 + 3$. In binary, \cd{101 ^ 011} is 110 (6), and the carry is \cd{001} shifted left, 010 (2).
Next, \cd{110 ^ 010} is 100 (4), and the carry is 100 (4). Next, \cd{100 ^ 100} is 0, and the carry is 1000 (8).
Next, the sum is 8, and the carry is 0. The result is 8.

In Python, the int has no top bit. When one operand is negative and the true sum is 0 or more,
the carry moves left forever. Some mixed-sign inputs still stop, such as $-3$ and $1$. So a few tests can hide this bug.
So mask both parts to 32 bits (Template 3). The carry then falls off bit 31, and the loop ends after at most 32 rounds.
Convert bit 31 to a sign at the end without a minus: \cd{~(a ^ MASK)}.
Memory hook (Sum of Two Integers): \emph{XOR is the sum, AND shifted left is the carry.
Repeat until no carry, mask to 32 bits, and fix the sign with} \cd{~(a ^ MASK)}.
\begin{pyex}
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF                    # keep 32 bits, like a C int
def get_sum(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        # sum without carry, and the carry moved one column left; both use the old a
        a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
    # bit 31 set means negative: flip the low 32 bits, then flip all bits
    return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ MASK)

get_sum(5, 3), get_sum(-1, 1), get_sum(-3, 5)     # -> (8, 0, 2)
get_sum(-1000, -1000)                             # -> -2000
all(get_sum(a, b) == a + b for a in range(-40, 41) for b in range(-40, 41))   # -> True

def unmasked_rounds(a, b, cap=200):  # the same loop without the mask, stopped at cap
    rounds = 0
    while b != 0 and rounds < cap:
        a, b = a ^ b, (a & b) << 1
        rounds += 1
    return rounds
unmasked_rounds(-3, 1), unmasked_rounds(-1, 1)    # -> (2, 200)
\end{pyex}
The same column-and-carry loop adds binary strings and digit lists.
Multiplication without \cd{*} is shift and add. Division without \cd{/} is shift and subtract.
(Sum of Two Integers, Add Binary.)

\subsubsection{Signs and 32-bit overflow}
The statement says that the result must fit a signed 32-bit int, and that no wider type exists.
Two rules handle most of these problems.
First, put the sign aside and work on the magnitude. Then Python rules for \cd{//} and \pct\ on negative values do not matter.
Second, test for overflow before the step that can overflow, not after it.
Solve the step for the old value: \cd{res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX} becomes \cd{res <= (INT_MAX - digit) // 10}.
The digit loop is the base-10 copy of Template 1: pop with \cd{divmod(x, 10)}, push with \cd{res * 10 + digit}.
Memory hook (Reverse Integer): \emph{put the sign aside. Pop a digit, solve} \cd{res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX}
\emph{for} \cd{res}\emph{, and push only if it holds.}
\begin{pyex}
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
def reverse_integer(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1        # put the sign aside
    x = abs(x)
    res = 0
    while x:
        x, digit = divmod(x, 10)     # pop the last digit
        if res > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10:   # res * 10 + digit would pass INT_MAX
            return 0
        res = res * 10 + digit       # push the digit
    return sign * res

reverse_integer(123), reverse_integer(-123), reverse_integer(120)   # -> (321, -321, 21)
reverse_integer(1534236469), reverse_integer(-2**31)               # -> (0, 0)
reverse_integer(-2147483412)                                        # -> -2143847412
-123 // 10, -123 % 10                # -> (-13, 7)
\end{pyex}
The usual optimal answer uses the classic two-part guard:
\cd{res > INT_MAX // 10}, or \cd{res == INT_MAX // 10} and \cd{digit > 7}.
It is equivalent for \cd{res >= 0} and digits 0 to 9. Most C and Java solutions use it.
One positive bound is enough for both signs here. No 32-bit input reverses to a magnitude of exactly $2^{31}$.
In a fixed-width language, keep \cd{x} signed, because \cd{abs(INT_MIN)} does not fit in 32 bits.
(Reverse Integer, Palindrome Number.)

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Write three or four small inputs in binary, one value in each row. Look down the columns, and look for a carry or a cancel.
\item Does each bit position behave on its own? Then solve one column and repeat for each of the 32 columns.
  Count the ones per column. Do not compare pairs.
\item Do equal items cancel? Pairs: fold with XOR. Groups of $k$: column counts modulo $k$.
  Two values without a pair: fold, then split by one set bit of the fold.
\item Do you know the full expected collection? Subtract the actual aggregate from the expected aggregate.
  One unknown needs one equation (sum or XOR). Two unknowns need two equations.
\item Do you need an answer for every number up to $n$? Fill a table from \cd{i} \shr\ \cd{1} or from \cd{i & (i - 1)}.
\item Is the width fixed? Loop exactly \cd{width} times. Build masks with \cd{(1} \shl\ \cd{w) - 1}.
  For many calls, use a table over 8-bit chunks.
\item Can a value be negative, or must the result fit in 32 bits? Mask every step with \cd{0xFFFFFFFF}
  and convert bit 31 at the end. Or put the sign aside and work on magnitudes.
  Guard each step that can overflow before you do it.
\item Is an operator banned? Copy the circuit or the long-hand method: XOR and AND for addition,
  shift and add for multiplication, shift and subtract for division.
\item Is the set of items small ($n \le 20$)? Store a subset as a mask: bit \cd{i} is item \cd{i}.
  \cd{range(1} \shl\ \cd{n)} then lists all subsets.
\item Check the bit solution against a brute force on all small values, negative values included.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Operator precedence.} In Python, \cd{+} and \cd{-} bind tighter than the shifts,
and the shifts bind tighter than \cd{&}, \cd{^} and \cd{|}. So \cd{ans[i} \shr\ \cd{1] + i & 1} means
\cd{(ans[i} \shr\ \cd{1] + i) & 1}, and \cd{1} \shl\ \cd{n - 1} means \cd{1} \shl\ \cd{(n - 1)}.
In Python, comparisons bind looser than all bit operators. In C and Java, \cd{==} binds tighter than \cd{&}, \cd{^} and \cd{|}.
Write the parentheses every time.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
ans, i = [0, 1, 1, 2], 3
ans[i >> 1] + i & 1, ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)        # -> (0, 2)
1 << 3 - 1                                        # -> 4
2 ^ 3, 2 ** 3                                     # -> (1, 8)
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{\cd{^} is XOR, not power.} Use \cd{**} for a power.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Negative values have infinite leading ones.} \cd{-1} \shr\ \cd{k} is always \cd{-1}, so a
``shift until 0'' loop never ends. \cd{~x} is \cd{-x - 1}, not a 32-bit flip: use \cd{x ^ 0xFFFFFFFF}.
\cd{bin(-5)} is \cd{'-0b101'}, not a two's complement pattern: use \cd{bin(x & 0xFFFFFFFF)}.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
-1 >> 10                             # -> -1
~5                                   # -> -6
5 ^ 0xFFFFFFFF                       # -> 4294967290
bin(-5), bin(-5 & 0xFF)              # -> ('-0b101', '0b11111011')
\end{pyex}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Mask both parts of the addition.} If only the carry has the mask, \cd{a} can stay a negative Python int,
and the final sign test is wrong. Do not use \cd{a - 2**32} to fix the sign when \cd{-} is banned.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Fixed width.} \cd{bin(x)} has a \cd{'0b'} prefix and no leading zeros. Use \cd{format(x, "032b")}.
A ``while x > 0'' loop also drops the leading zeros. Loop exactly 32 times.
Shift \cd{res} before the OR, not after it. Otherwise the result is two times too large.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Seeds and identities.} Start an XOR fold at 0. In the XOR form of the missing value, start at \cd{n}:
the indexes cover only $0..n-1$. Without the seed, \cd{[0, 1]} gives 0 instead of 2.
\end{caution}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{Floor division on negative values.} \cd{-123 // 10} is \cd{-13}, and \cd{-123} \pct\ \cd{10} is \cd{7}.
C and Java truncate toward zero. Put the sign aside, or use \cd{int(a / b)} and \cd{math.fmod} for small values.
\end{caution}
\begin{note}
\cd{int.bit_count()} needs Python 3.10 or later. Some judges run older versions, and some problems ban built-in bit counts.
Know the shift loop and the \cd{n & (n - 1)} loop.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
Single Number & All values occur two times except one; $O(1)$ space. XOR fold. & Pairs cancel under XOR, so XOR everything. \\
Number of 1 Bits & Count the set bits of one number. Shift loop; \cd{n & (n - 1)} is the optimal form. & Read the last bit, then shift it away. \\
Counting Bits & A count for every \cd{i} in $0..n$ in $O(n)$. DP from \cd{i} \shr\ \cd{1}. & Drop the last bit, look it up, add the bit back. \\
Reverse Bits & Fixed width of 32 bits; leading zeros count. Peel and push exactly 32 times. & Peel the low bit off n, push it onto res, 32 times. \\
Missing Number & The full range $0..n$ is known. Expected sum minus actual sum; XOR seeded with \cd{n} is the optimal form. & Expected sum minus actual sum. \\
Sum of Two Integers & \cd{+} and \cd{-} are banned; negative values. XOR sum, AND carry, 32-bit mask, sign fix. & XOR is the sum, AND shifted left is the carry. Repeat until no carry, mask to 32 bits, and fix the sign with \cd{~(a ^ MASK)}. \\
Reverse Integer & Base-10 digits, a sign, and no 64-bit values. Guard before each push. & Put the sign aside. Pop a digit, solve \cd{res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX} for \cd{res}, and push only if it holds. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent The transfer drills for this technique are in Section~\ref{drill:T23} (page~\pageref{drill:T23}). The answers are in Section~\ref{ans:T23} (page~\pageref{ans:T23}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Design problems: combining data structures}\label{tech:T24}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The idea}
A design problem asks for a class. The class has a constructor and a few methods.
The judge calls the methods many times, in any order, and checks each return value.
Each method has a cost target. The statement gives it (``$O(1)$ average''), or the call count implies it.
A brute-force design keeps one plain list and scans it on every call.
That design is correct, but each call costs $O(n)$, and $10^5$ calls cost $10^{10}$ steps.

Start from the operations, not from a structure.
Write each method and the access that it needs: by key, by order, by rank, by prefix, or the extreme value.
Then, for each access, pick the structure that makes it cheap.
When one structure cannot give every access, keep two structures that hold the same items.
The second structure removes the scan: it answers in one step the access that the first structure can only answer by a scan.
Each change then updates both structures, so they always agree.

\textbf{Worked example in words (LRU cache).}
The cache must find a value by key, mark a key as the newest on each use, and drop the oldest key when it is full.
A dict finds a key in $O(1)$, but it cannot tell which key is the oldest without a scan.
A list keeps an order, but it moves an item out of the middle in $O(n)$.
A doubly linked list moves any node in $O(1)$, but only when you already hold that node.
So keep a dict from key to node, and keep the nodes in a linked list in order of use.
The dict finds the node. The list moves the node to the newest end. Eviction removes the node at the oldest end.
For example, take capacity 2. Put key 1, then put key 2. The order is 1, 2.
A get of key 1 moves it to the newest end, so the order is 2, 1.
A put of key 3 makes the cache too full, so it evicts key 2 from the oldest end.
Each step is $O(1)$, and no step scans the keys.
The Python \cd{OrderedDict} is exactly this pair, written in C.

\subsubsection{Choose a structure from the access}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{5.6cm}L{7.4cm}L{3.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
Access that a method needs & Structure & Cost per call \\
\midrule
Find, add or delete by key; membership & \cd{dict}, \cd{set} & $O(1)$ average \\
Count equal items, duplicates allowed & \cd{Counter} (a dict of counts) & $O(1)$ \\
An aggregate (min, max, sum) of a stack; undo the last change & list of pairs (value, aggregate so far) & $O(1)$ \\
Order of use; move any key to one end; drop the other end & \cd{OrderedDict}, or dict + doubly linked list & $O(1)$ \\
Add and remove at both ends (FIFO, LIFO) & \cd{deque} & $O(1)$ \\
Smallest or largest item; removal only at the top & heap (\cd{heapq}) & $O(\log n)$ add, $O(1)$ peek \\
Smallest or largest item; items change or leave anywhere & a dict as the truth, plus a heap (or two) with lazy deletion: on a read, pop each top that disagrees with the dict & $O(\log n)$ amortized \\
Counts that change by $\pm 1$; a key with the smallest and with the largest count & doubly linked list of count buckets (sets of keys) in count order, plus a dict from key to bucket; a change moves the key to the next bucket or to the previous bucket & $O(1)$ \\
The $k$-th largest of all items so far & min-heap that keeps $k$ items & $O(\log k)$ \\
The median or another rank that moves with $n$ & two heaps: max-heap of the low half, min-heap of the high half & $O(\log n)$ \\
The first $k$ items of many sorted sources & heap with one cursor per source & $O(\log F)$ per item \\
Latest item at or before $x$; items arrive in sorted order & list per key + \cd{bisect} & $O(1)$ add, $O(\log n)$ query \\
Ordered queries; items arrive in any order & sorted list + \cd{insort}, or a balanced tree & $O(n)$ or $O(\log n)$ add \\
Prefix or wildcard queries on strings & trie (dict children + end flag) & $O(L)$ per insert or prefix walk \\
Shapes or tuples through a query point & \cd{Counter} of points; enumerate the free corner & $O(d)$ per query \\
Store or send a list or a tree as one string & length prefix, or tokens with a null marker & $O(n)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Here $F$ is the number of sources, $L$ is the word length, and $d$ is the number of distinct points.
\begin{note}
\textbf{Extremes over counts that change.} All O'one Data Structure (LeetCode 432) asks for \cd{inc}, \cd{dec},
a key with the largest count and a key with the smallest count, each in $O(1)$.
A heap version passes in practice: a dict from key to count, two heaps of (count, key), and lazy deletion
(see the section on heaps and priority queues).
The bucket list meets the $O(1)$ target. Each bucket holds the keys that have one count, and the list keeps only the buckets that are not empty.
A change of $\pm 1$ moves the key to the next bucket or to the previous bucket.
Create that bucket when it is missing, and unlink each bucket that becomes empty.
The first bucket then holds the smallest count, and the last bucket holds the largest count.
\end{note}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Recognize it}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The statement says ``Design'' or ``Implement the class'', and it lists a constructor and methods.
  \item The example input is two parallel lists: the method names and the argument lists.
  \item Each call has a cost target: $O(1)$, $O(1)$ average, or $O(\log n)$.
        Or the call count (for example $2 \cdot 10^5$) makes a scan per call too slow.
  \item Writes and reads interleave. The class must answer after each change, so one sort at the end does not work.
  \item The same items need two kinds of access, for example by key and by order.
        This points to two structures that index the same items.
  \item Typical words: cache, capacity, evict, recently used, stream, timestamp, ``as of time $t$'', feed,
        most recent, median, $k$-th largest, prefix, autocomplete, wildcard.
  \item Codec words: ``one string'', ``send over the network'', ``rebuild the original''.
        The decoder sees only the string, so the string must carry every boundary.
  \item Point words: ``add a point'', ``duplicate points count'', ``the number of ways to form'' a square or a rectangle
        with the query point. The answer is a count, not a list, so a \cd{Counter} of points is enough.
  \item A small bound in the statement: at most 2 wildcards, coordinates up to 1000, or a few thousand calls.
        A small bound allows a direct enumeration per query, so check it before you build a complex structure.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Core template}
Use the same five steps for every design problem.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Write a table of the operations: the method, what it reads, what it changes, and the target cost.
  \item For each access, pick a structure from the table above. Prefer the standard library:
        \cd{dict}, \cd{Counter}, \cd{defaultdict}, \cd{OrderedDict}, \cd{deque}, \cd{heapq}, \cd{bisect}.
  \item If two structures hold the same items, write the invariant that ties them.
        Decide what each item stores to find itself in the other structure: a key in a node, or an index in a map.
  \item Put each kind of change in one helper that updates every structure. The public methods call the helpers.
        Reads change nothing.
  \item Replay the example calls. Then compare the class with a slow, obviously correct model on many random calls.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{pyshow}
class Design:
    def __init__(self):
        self.by_key = {}          # access 1: find an item by key
        self.order = ...          # access 2: order, rank, prefix or extreme
        # invariant: by_key and order always hold the same items
    def _add(self, item): ...     # updates by_key AND order
    def _remove(self, item): ...  # updates by_key AND order
    def query(self, x): ...       # reads only; creates no entries
\end{pyshow}
The block below applies the steps to the LRU cache.
\cd{replay} runs an example that is given as two lists: the method names and the argument lists. \cd{agrees} runs random calls on the fast class and on a slow model.
The model check finds bugs that the example misses.
For example, a \cd{put} on an existing key must count as a use, but the example never puts an existing key.
\begin{pyex}
import random
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = OrderedDict()          # oldest key first, newest key last
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)         # a get is a use
        return self.cache[key]
    def put(self, key, value):
        self.cache[key] = value
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)         # a put is a use
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)  # evict the oldest key

def replay(cls, methods, args):
    obj = cls(*args[0])                     # methods[0] is the constructor
    return [None] + [getattr(obj, m)(*a) for m, a in zip(methods[1:], args[1:])]

methods = ["LRUCache", "put", "put", "get", "put", "get", "put", "get", "get", "get"]
args = [[2], [1, 1], [2, 2], [1], [3, 3], [2], [4, 4], [1], [3], [4]]
replay(LRUCache, methods, args)
# -> [None, None, None, 1, None, -1, None, -1, 3, 4]

class SlowLRU:                              # obviously correct, O(n) per call
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity, self.items = capacity, []     # (key, value), oldest first
    def get(self, key):
        for i, (k, v) in enumerate(self.items):
            if k == key:
                self.items.append(self.items.pop(i))
                return v
        return -1
    def put(self, key, value):
        self.items = [(k, v) for k, v in self.items if k != key] + [(key, value)]
        if len(self.items) > self.capacity:
            self.items.pop(0)

def agrees(fast_cls, slow_cls, init_args, make_call, rounds=300, calls=30, seed=1):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        fast, slow = fast_cls(*init_args), slow_cls(*init_args)
        for _ in range(calls):
            name, args = make_call(rng)
            if getattr(fast, name)(*args) != getattr(slow, name)(*args):
                return False
    return True

def lru_call(rng):
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        return "get", (rng.randint(0, 4),)
    return "put", (rng.randint(0, 4), rng.randint(0, 9))

all(agrees(LRUCache, SlowLRU, (cap,), lru_call) for cap in (1, 2, 3))   # -> True

class StalePutLRU(LRUCache):                # bug: a put on an existing key is not a use
    def put(self, key, value):
        self.cache[key] = value             # an existing key keeps its old place
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)

replay(StalePutLRU, methods, args) == replay(LRUCache, methods, args)   # -> True
agrees(StalePutLRU, SlowLRU, (2,), lru_call)   # -> False
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariant.} The \cd{OrderedDict} holds at most \cd{capacity} keys in order of last use.
The first key is the least recently used key, and the last key is the most recently used key.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Variations}

\subsubsection{Store the aggregate with each element}
\textbf{What changes.} A stack must also return its minimum (or maximum, or sum) in $O(1)$.
One variable for the minimum fails: when the minimum leaves, the variable cannot give the old minimum.
The minimum has no inverse, so arithmetic cannot undo it.
But a stack removes only the top, so each pop returns the stack to an earlier state exactly.
So store, with each element, the answer for the stack up to that element.
\textbf{Min Stack} uses one list of pairs (value, minimum so far).
Memory hook: \emph{Push the pair (value, min so far). Pop removes both.}
\begin{pyex}
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []                     # (value, min of this value and all below it)
    def push(self, val):
        low = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val
        self.stack.append((val, low))
    def pop(self):
        self.stack.pop()
    def top(self):
        return self.stack[-1][0]
    def getMin(self):
        return self.stack[-1][1]

s = MinStack()
for v in [5, 2, 7, 2]:
    s.push(v)
s.getMin()                                  # -> 2
s.pop(); s.pop(); s.top(), s.getMin()       # -> (2, 2)
s.pop(); s.top(), s.getMin()                # -> (5, 5)
\end{pyex}
The same idea works for any aggregate that grows by one element: max, sum, gcd, a count.
An undo operation is then a pop.
A queue with a minimum uses two such stacks: push to an in-stack, pop from an out-stack,
and move all items when the out-stack is empty.
For the maximum of a sliding window (FIFO), use a monotonic deque instead.
A common alternative keeps two parallel lists. It has the same cost, but each pop must remove from both lists.

\subsubsection{Find by key and keep an order of use}
\textbf{What changes.} Lookup by key, a move of any key to the newest end, and eviction at the oldest end, all in $O(1)$.
\textbf{LRU Cache} uses an \cd{OrderedDict} (see the core template).
Memory hook: \emph{Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow.}
Write the structure by hand when \cd{OrderedDict} is not allowed, or when the task asks for the linked list itself.
Keep a dict from key to node and a doubly linked list between two sentinel nodes.
The sentinels remove all checks for an empty list and for the ends.
Hook for this form: the map finds the node, the list keeps the order; remove, then insert at the right; evict \cd{left.next}.
\begin{pyex}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key, self.val = key, val       # the key lets eviction clean the map
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}   # map: key to node
        self.left, self.right = Node(), Node()      # sentinels: left.next is the LRU
        self.left.next, self.right.prev = self.right, self.left
    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev
    def _insert(self, node):                # insert just before the right sentinel
        prev = self.right.prev
        prev.next, node.prev, node.next, self.right.prev = node, prev, self.right, node
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._insert(node)
        return node.val
    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])     # unlink the old node: no ghost node stays
        node = self.map[key] = Node(key, value)
        self._insert(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            lru = self.left.next
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2); c.get(1)          # -> 1
c.put(3, 3); c.get(2)                       # -> -1
c.put(4, 4); c.get(1), c.get(3), c.get(4)   # -> (-1, 3, 4)
\end{pyex}
\begin{note}
Each node stores its key. Eviction holds only the node, so the key in the node is the only way to delete the map entry.
In general, when two structures index the same items, each item carries the data to find itself in the other structure.
Do not replace \cd{OrderedDict} with a plain dict and \cd{next(iter(d))}: in CPython that eviction is not $O(1)$.
\end{note}

\subsubsection{Find by key, then search an ordered timeline}
\textbf{What changes.} The query is ``the latest value at or before time $t$''.
Split it into two parts. The key is an exact match, so a hash map handles it.
The timestamp is a range match, so it needs a sorted list and binary search.
In \textbf{Time Based Key-Value Store}, the timestamps of \cd{set} strictly increase.
So an append keeps each list sorted for free, and \cd{set} is $O(1)$.
\cd{get} is a floor query: \cd{i = bisect_right(times, t)} is the count of timestamps $\le t$, so the answer is at index $i - 1$.
Memory hook: \emph{Two lists per key: times and values. \cd{bisect_right} counts times $\le t$, so take the value one left.}
\begin{pyex}
from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict

class TimeMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.times = defaultdict(list)      # key to timestamps, increasing
        self.values = defaultdict(list)     # key to values, same order as times
    def set(self, key, value, timestamp):
        self.times[key].append(timestamp)   # increasing timestamps: append keeps the order
        self.values[key].append(value)
    def get(self, key, timestamp):
        times = self.times.get(key, [])     # .get adds no entry for a missing key
        i = bisect_right(times, timestamp)  # i = count of times <= timestamp
        return self.values[key][i - 1] if i > 0 else ""

tm = TimeMap()
tm.set("foo", "bar", 1)
tm.get("foo", 1), tm.get("foo", 3)          # -> ('bar', 'bar')
tm.set("foo", "bar2", 4)
tm.get("foo", 4), tm.get("foo", 5), tm.get("foo", 0)   # -> ('bar2', 'bar2', '')
tm.get("nope", 9), "nope" in tm.times       # -> ('', False)
\end{pyex}
Always check whether the input order already sorts the data. If it does, a plain list replaces a balanced tree.
If the timestamps can arrive in any order, use \cd{bisect.insort} ($O(k)$ per insert) or a sorted container.
When the task asks for the search by hand, write it on (timestamp, value) pairs. The cost is the same.
Its loop is: while \cd{lo <= hi}, if the time at \cd{mid} is $\le t$, save the value and set \cd{lo = mid + 1}; else set \cd{hi = mid - 1}.

\subsubsection{Keep only the k best: one heap of size k}
\textbf{What changes.} Items only arrive, and each query asks for the $k$-th largest item so far.
The answer never decreases. So a value below the current answer can never be the answer again, and you can drop it.
\textbf{Kth Largest Element in a Stream} keeps a min-heap of the $k$ largest values.
The root is the weakest kept value, which is the $k$-th largest.
Memory hook: \emph{Keep the top $k$ in a min-heap. Every value goes through add: push, pop if over $k$, return the root.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq

class KthLargest:
    def __init__(self, k, nums):
        self.k, self.top_k = k, []          # min-heap of the k largest values so far
        for num in nums:
            self.add(num)                   # every value goes through the same gate
    def add(self, val):
        heapq.heappush(self.top_k, val)
        if len(self.top_k) > self.k:
            heapq.heappop(self.top_k)       # the weakest value can never be the answer again
        return self.top_k[0]

kl = KthLargest(3, [4, 5, 8, 2])
[kl.add(v) for v in [3, 5, 10, 9, 4]]       # -> [4, 5, 5, 8, 8]
KthLargest(1, []).add(-3)                   # -> -3
\end{pyex}
The heap has the opposite polarity of the request: a min-heap for ``largest'', a max-heap for ``smallest''.
The root is the threshold that a new value must beat.
An alternative constructor calls \cd{heapify} on a copy of the list and then pops down to $k$ values. The cost per \cd{add} is the same.
If items can also leave, a size-$k$ heap is not enough, because a dropped value can become the answer again.

\subsubsection{Two heaps that face each other at a moving rank}
\textbf{What changes.} The query asks for the median, a rank that moves as $n$ grows.
The median depends only on the boundary between the low half and the high half.
\textbf{Find Median from Data Stream} keeps the low half in a max-heap \cd{small} (negated values)
and the high half in a min-heap \cd{large}. The two tops face each other at the boundary.
Memory hook: \emph{Push into small, pass its top to large, give one back if large gets bigger.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq, random

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.small = []                     # max-heap of the low half (negated values)
        self.large = []                     # min-heap of the high half
    def addNum(self, num):
        heapq.heappush(self.small, -num)                         # enter through the low half
        heapq.heappush(self.large, -heapq.heappop(self.small))   # pass its top up
        if len(self.large) > len(self.small):
            heapq.heappush(self.small, -heapq.heappop(self.large))   # give one back
    def findMedian(self):
        if len(self.small) > len(self.large):
            return float(-self.small[0])
        return (-self.small[0] + self.large[0]) / 2

mf, out = MedianFinder(), []
for v in [5, 15, 1, 3]:
    mf.addNum(v)
    out.append(mf.findMedian())
out                                         # -> [5.0, 10.0, 5.0, 4.0]

rng, mf, seen, ok = random.Random(7), MedianFinder(), [], True
for _ in range(200):                        # compare with a sort after each insert
    v = rng.randint(-5, 5)
    mf.addNum(v)
    seen.append(v)
    s, n = sorted(seen), len(seen)
    ok = ok and mf.findMedian() == (s[n // 2] if n % 2 else (s[n // 2 - 1] + s[n // 2]) / 2)
ok                                          # -> True
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Invariants.} Every value in \cd{small} is $\le$ every value in \cd{large}.
\cd{len(small)} equals \cd{len(large)} or \cd{len(large) + 1}.
The route through \cd{small} needs no comparison with either top: the value that moves up is always the largest low value.
For a percentile $p$, keep \cd{small} at $\lceil p n \rceil$ values.
If values can also leave (a sliding window), add lazy deletion or use a sorted container.

\subsubsection{Merge many sorted sources with a heap of cursors}
\textbf{What changes.} The read combines many lists, and it needs only the first few items of the merge.
\textbf{Design Twitter} stamps each tweet with a global clock, because tweet IDs do not show the post order.
Each user has an append-only list of (time, tweetId), so each list is sorted for free.
Each user has a set of followees, so follow and unfollow are $O(1)$ and repeated calls are harmless.
The feed seeds a heap with the newest tweet of each relevant user.
It pops the newest tweet, then pushes the next older tweet of the same user, and stops at 10.
The heap holds at most one cursor per user, and the loop stops after 10 pops, so the old tweets are never read.
Memory hook: \emph{Stamp each tweet with a global clock. Merge the timelines with a heap: one cursor per user,
pop the newest, push that user's previous tweet, stop at ten.}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

class Twitter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.time = 0                       # global clock: one order across all users
        self.tweets = defaultdict(list)     # user to [(time, tweetId)], oldest first
        self.following = defaultdict(set)   # user to the set of followees
    def postTweet(self, userId, tweetId):
        self.tweets[userId].append((self.time, tweetId))
        self.time += 1
    def getNewsFeed(self, userId):
        heap = []
        for uid in self.following.get(userId, set()) | {userId}:   # temporary union: no side effect
            ts = self.tweets.get(uid)
            if ts:
                heap.append((-ts[-1][0], ts[-1][1], uid, len(ts) - 1))   # one cursor per user
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        feed = []
        while heap and len(feed) < 10:
            _, tid, uid, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
            feed.append(tid)
            if i > 0:                       # push the next older tweet of the same user
                t, prev_id = self.tweets[uid][i - 1]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-t, prev_id, uid, i - 1))
        return feed
    def follow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        if followerId != followeeId:
            self.following[followerId].add(followeeId)
    def unfollow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        self.following[followerId].discard(followeeId)     # no error if absent

tw = Twitter()
tw.postTweet(1, 5); tw.getNewsFeed(1)       # -> [5]
tw.follow(1, 2); tw.postTweet(2, 6); tw.getNewsFeed(1)  # -> [6, 5]
tw.unfollow(1, 2); tw.getNewsFeed(1)        # -> [5]
for tid in range(100, 112):
    tw.postTweet(3, tid)
tw.getNewsFeed(3) == list(range(111, 101, -1))         # -> True
\end{pyex}
A feed costs $O(F + 10 \log F)$ for $F$ sources. The cost depends on the sources and the output size, not on the total data.
The standard library has the same lazy merge: \cd{heapq.merge} with \cd{reverse=True} merges lists that are each sorted
from newest to oldest.
\begin{pyex}
from heapq import merge
from itertools import islice

def feed(tweets, users, k=10):              # tweets[u]: (time, id) pairs, oldest first
    newest_first = (reversed(tweets[u]) for u in users if u in tweets)
    return [tid for _, tid in islice(merge(*newest_first, reverse=True), k)]

tweets = {1: [(0, 5), (3, 8)], 2: [(1, 6), (2, 7)]}
feed(tweets, [1, 2])                        # -> [8, 7, 6, 5]
feed(tweets, [1, 2], k=3), feed(tweets, [9])   # -> ([8, 7, 6], [])
\end{pyex}

\subsubsection{Prefix tree classes}
\textbf{What changes.} Many stored strings, and queries about prefixes or about letters at fixed positions.
\textbf{Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)} stores each word as a path. Each node stands for one prefix.
A node has a dict of children and an end flag. One \cd{_walk} helper serves \cd{search} and \cd{startsWith};
only the final check differs.
Memory hook: \emph{One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end.}
A wildcard \cd{.} that matches one letter turns the walk into a DFS: a letter follows one edge, a dot follows every edge.
\begin{pyex}
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}                  # letter to child node
        self.is_end = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()
    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.is_end = True
    def _walk(self, s):                     # the node of prefix s, or None; creates nothing
        node = self.root
        for ch in s:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node
    def search(self, word):
        node = self._walk(word)
        return node is not None and node.is_end
    def startsWith(self, prefix):
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None
    def match(self, pattern):               # "." matches exactly one letter
        def dfs(i, node):
            if i == len(pattern):
                return node.is_end
            if pattern[i] == ".":
                return any(dfs(i + 1, child) for child in node.children.values())
            child = node.children.get(pattern[i])
            return child is not None and dfs(i + 1, child)
        return dfs(0, self.root)

t = Trie()
t.insert("apple")
t.search("apple"), t.search("app"), t.startsWith("app")   # -> (True, False, True)
t.insert("app")
t.search("app"), t.startsWith("apple")      # -> (True, True)
t.match("a.p"), t.match("..ple")           # -> (True, True)
t.match(".pl"), t.match("ap.")             # -> (False, True)
\end{pyex}
\textbf{Design Add and Search Words Data Structure} allows at most two dots per query and words of length at most 25.
The intuitive answer needs no trie. On add, store the word and each copy of it with one letter masked by a dot.
A query with at most one dot is then one set lookup.
A query with two dots fills its first dot with each letter and searches again.
Memory hook: \emph{Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search.}
\begin{pyex}
class WordDictionary:
    def __init__(self):
        self.patterns = set()               # each word, plus each copy with one letter masked
    def addWord(self, word):
        self.patterns.add(word)
        for i in range(len(word)):
            self.patterns.add(word[:i] + "." + word[i + 1:])
    def search(self, word):
        if word.count(".") <= 1:
            return word in self.patterns
        i = word.index(".")
        return any(self.search(word[:i] + c + word[i + 1:])
                   for c in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")

wd = WordDictionary()
for w in ["bad", "dad", "mad"]:
    wd.addWord(w)
wd.search("pad"), wd.search("bad")         # -> (False, True)
wd.search(".ad"), wd.search("b..")         # -> (True, True)
wd.search("..."), wd.search("b."), wd.search("..d.")   # -> (True, False, False)
\end{pyex}
An add costs $O(L^2)$. A search with $k \ge 1$ dots costs $26^{k-1}$ lookups, so the pattern set suits only a small dot limit.
The standard answer is the trie with the DFS (the \cd{match} method above).
Use it when the question asks for a trie, when you also need prefix queries, or when the dot limit is large.

\subsubsection{Count shapes with a point counter}
\textbf{What changes.} The class stores points, duplicates count, and a query counts the shapes that have the query point as a corner.
Fix the query corner, then enumerate the one free choice that fixes the whole shape.
In \textbf{Detect Squares}, the free choice is the diagonal corner $(x, y)$ with $x \ne q_x$ and $|x - q_x| = |y - q_y|$.
The other two corners are forced: $(x, q_y)$ and $(q_x, y)$. The number of ways is the product of the three counts.
Memory hook: \emph{Pick the diagonal, the other two corners are forced, multiply the counts.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

class DetectSquares:
    def __init__(self):
        self.points = Counter()             # (x, y) to the number of copies
    def add(self, point):
        self.points[tuple(point)] += 1      # a list is not hashable
    def count(self, point):
        qx, qy = point
        total = 0
        for (x, y), copies in self.points.items():
            if x == qx or abs(x - qx) != abs(y - qy):
                continue                    # not the diagonal corner of a square with area
            total += copies * self.points.get((x, qy), 0) * self.points.get((qx, y), 0)
        return total

ds = DetectSquares()
for p in [[3, 10], [11, 2], [3, 2]]:
    ds.add(p)
ds.count([11, 10]), ds.count([14, 8])       # -> (1, 0)
ds.add([11, 2])
ds.count([11, 10])                          # -> 2
\end{pyex}
\cd{add} is $O(1)$ and \cd{count} is $O(d)$ for $d$ distinct points.
The general move: find the fewest elements that fix the shape, enumerate them, and look up the rest in a hash map.
Two Sum is the one-dimensional case. Count rectangles by enumerating diagonal pairs.

\subsubsection{Codec classes: flatten and rebuild}
\textbf{What changes.} Two methods: one flattens a structure to a string, and the other rebuilds it from the string only.
The encoding must be self-delimiting: the decoder must know where each part ends.
\textbf{Encode and Decode Strings} allows any character in the data, so no delimiter is safe.
Write each string as its length, then \hsh, then the string.
The header holds only digits, so the first \hsh\ at or after the read position ends the header.
The payload is skipped by count, so it can contain \hsh.
Memory hook: \emph{Write length, hash, string; read length, then jump.}
\begin{pyex}
def encode(strs):
    return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)   # each item: length, "#", payload

def decode(s):
    res, i = [], 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = s.index("#", i)                 # the first "#" from i ends the header
        length = int(s[i:j])
        start = j + 1
        res.append(s[start:start + length])
        i = start + length                  # jump over the payload
    return res

encode(["a#b", ""])                         # -> '3#a#b0#'
cases = [["neet", "code"], [""], [], ["", ""], ["#", "12#", "a" * 12]]
all(decode(encode(c)) == c for c in cases)  # -> True
"#".join(["a#b"]) == "#".join(["a", "b"])   # -> True
\end{pyex}
The last line shows why a bare delimiter fails: two different lists give the same string.

\textbf{Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree} must keep the shape, not only the values.
Write a null marker \cd{N} for each empty child. The intuitive form follows the example list: level order with a queue.
The queue also holds the \cd{None} children. To decode, each real node in the queue takes the next two tokens as its children.
Memory hook: \emph{Write it level by level like the example list, with N for every null;
each real node in the queue takes the next two tokens as its kids.}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = x, None, None

class Codec:
    def serialize(self, root):
        out, queue = [], deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                out.append("N")             # the null marker keeps the shape
                continue
            out.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)         # the queue also holds None children
            queue.append(node.right)
        return ",".join(out)
    def deserialize(self, data):
        tokens = iter(data.split(","))
        def make(tok):
            return None if tok == "N" else TreeNode(int(tok))
        root = make(next(tokens))
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                continue                    # a null has no children to read
            node.left = make(next(tokens))  # the next two tokens are its children
            node.right = make(next(tokens))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
        return root

c = Codec()
s = "1,2,3,N,N,4,5,N,N,N,N"
c.serialize(c.deserialize(s)) == s          # -> True
c.serialize(None), c.deserialize("N") is None   # -> ('N', True)
root = TreeNode(1)
root.left = TreeNode(-20)
c.serialize(root)                           # -> '1,-20,N,N,N'
\end{pyex}
The standard optimal answer uses preorder DFS with the same null markers. It is shorter, and its grammar is
``tree = N, or a value, a tree and a tree''. The decoder is the same recursion as the encoder,
and it reads tokens in the same order.
A skewed tree of $10^4$ nodes goes past the default recursion limit of 1000, so raise the limit or use the level-order form.
\begin{pyex}
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = x, None, None

def serialize(root):
    out = []
    def dfs(node):
        if node is None:
            out.append("N")
            return
        out.append(str(node.val))
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)
    dfs(root)
    return ",".join(out)

def deserialize(data):
    tokens = iter(data.split(","))
    def build():                            # grammar: tree = N | value tree tree
        tok = next(tokens)
        if tok == "N":
            return None
        node = TreeNode(int(tok))
        node.left = build()                 # left first: the same order as the writer
        node.right = build()
        return node
    return build()

s = "1,2,N,N,3,4,N,N,5,N,N"
serialize(deserialize(s)) == s              # -> True
serialize(None)                             # -> 'N'
\end{pyex}
Test every codec with a round trip on hard inputs: an empty list, empty strings, the marker inside the data,
multi-digit lengths, negative values, and the empty tree.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Adapt it to a new problem}
Ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item What are the methods? For each one, what does it read, what does it change, and how often is it called?
  \item What is the cost target? Use the stated bound, or divide about $10^7$ simple steps by the number of calls.
  \item What access does each method need? By key, by order of arrival or use, by rank ($k$-th, median),
        by extreme (min, max), by prefix, or by a floor on time?
  \item Where do removals happen? Never, only at the top (stack), only at the front (queue),
        at the extreme (heap), or anywhere (dict + linked list, or lazy deletion)?
  \item Does the input order already sort the data? Increasing timestamps or a global counter make an append-only list sorted.
  \item Does a query need only a small part of the data, such as the top $k$, the boundary of two halves,
        or one cursor per source? Keep only that part.
  \item Does one structure give every access? If not, combine two. Write the invariant that ties them.
        Decide what each item stores to find itself in the other structure.
  \item Does the class flatten data to a string? Then ask what tells the decoder where each part ends:
        a length prefix, or a null marker for each empty slot.
  \item Route each change through one helper that updates every structure. Make each read free of side effects.
  \item Test the edge cases: an empty structure, a missing key, duplicates, capacity 1, ties, the value 0, the first call.
        Then compare with a slow model on random calls (see the core template).
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Pitfalls}
\begin{caution}
\textbf{The structures drift apart.} Wrong: remove a node from the list but leave its key in the map,
or create a new node for an existing key and leave the old node in the list.
The old node is a ghost: its later eviction deletes the map entry of the live node.
Right: put each change in one helper that updates every structure, and store in each item the key that finds it in the other structure.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A use that is not recorded.} In an LRU cache, a successful \cd{get} is a use, and a \cd{put} on an existing key is a use.
A \cd{put} on an existing key updates the value and does not evict. A \cd{get} on a missing key changes nothing.
Insert first, then evict only when the size is larger than the capacity.
This order is safe only because the new key is the newest key, so eviction never removes it.
If another rule picks the key to evict, check that the new key cannot be that key.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A read that writes.} Indexing a \cd{defaultdict} with a missing key creates an entry.
A later membership test then passes, the memory grows, and a loop over the same dict raises \cd{RuntimeError}.
Read with \cd{.get(key, default)}. A \cd{Counter} returns 0 for a missing key and does not insert it.
Also, 0 and the empty string are legal values: test membership with \cd{in}, not with truthiness.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
d = defaultdict(list)
len(d["missing"]), "missing" in d           # -> (0, True)
d.get("other", []), "other" in d            # -> ([], False)
c = Counter()
c["x"], "x" in c                            # -> (0, False)
pts = defaultdict(int, {(0, 0): 1})
for p in pts:
    pts[(p[0] + 1, p[1])]                   # -> raises RuntimeError
cache = {"k": 0}
bool(cache.get("k")), "k" in cache          # -> (False, True)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{State shared between objects.} A container in the class body, or a mutable default argument, is one object for every instance.
Create each container in \cd{__init__}. A codec must keep its state local to each call,
because the judge can use one object to encode and another object to decode.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
class Bad:
    items = []                              # one list for every instance
    def add(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)
a, b = Bad(), Bad()
a.add(1)
b.items                                     # -> [1]
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{A hidden $O(n)$ step.} \cd{min(self.stack)} inside \cd{getMin}, \cd{list.pop(0)}, a sort after each insert,
\cd{s = s[j:]} in a decode loop, and \cd{next(iter(d))} for eviction from a plain dict all look short.
Each one costs $O(n)$ or more per call. Move an index instead of a slice, and use \cd{deque} for a queue.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Heap details.} \cd{heapq} is a min-heap: negate the keys for a max-heap, on push and on pop.
Tuples compare field by field. If the first fields can tie, put a unique counter before any field that cannot compare, such as a node.
For the median of an even count, divide with \cd{/}, not \cd{//}: the median of 2 and 3 is 2.5.
\end{caution}
\begin{pyex}
import heapq
class Node:
    pass
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, Node()))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, Node()))              # -> raises TypeError
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, 0, Node()))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, 1, Node()))           # the counter breaks the tie
len(h), (2 + 3) / 2, (2 + 3) // 2           # -> (2, 2.5, 2)
\end{pyex}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Ambiguous encodings.} A bare delimiter fails when the data can contain it.
A separator between items cannot tell \cd{[]} from \cd{[""]}: give every item its own header.
A tree without null markers loses its shape: \cd{[1, 2]} and \cd{[1, null, 2]} give the same values.
Preorder plus inorder without markers fails when values repeat.
\end{caution}

\begin{caution}
\textbf{Names and signatures.} The judge calls the methods by the exact names of the statement, often in camelCase:
\cd{getMin}, \cd{startsWith}, \cd{addNum}, \cd{getNewsFeed}. A snake\_case name fails.
\end{caution}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Problems in this family}
\begin{longtable}{@{}L{4cm}L{6.2cm}L{6.3cm}@{}}
\toprule
Problem & What changes & Memory hook \\
\midrule
\endhead
Min Stack & Stack with an $O(1)$ minimum; store the minimum so far with each element. & Push the pair (value, min so far). Pop removes both. \\
LRU Cache & Lookup by key plus an order of use; evict the oldest key. \cd{OrderedDict}, or dict + doubly linked list. & Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow. \\
Time Based Key-Value Store & Lookup by key, then a floor search on timestamps that increase. & Two lists per key: times and values. \cd{bisect_right} counts times $\le t$, so take the value one left. \\
Design Twitter & Merge per-user timelines; the first 10 by a global clock; a heap of cursors. & Stamp each tweet with a global clock. Merge the timelines with a heap: one cursor per user, pop the newest, push that user's previous tweet, stop at ten. \\
Find Median from Data Stream & A rank that moves with $n$; two heaps meet at the boundary. & Push into small, pass its top to large, give one back if large gets bigger. \\
Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) & Prefix queries; one node per prefix with an end flag. & One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end. \\
Design Add and Search Words Data Structure & Wildcard letters; a set of masked patterns (or a trie DFS). & Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search. \\
Kth Largest Element in a Stream & A fixed rank $k$, inserts only; a min-heap of size $k$. & Keep the top $k$ in a min-heap. Every value goes through add: push, pop if over $k$, return the root. \\
Detect Squares & Count shapes through a query point; a \cd{Counter} of points. & Pick the diagonal, the other two corners are forced, multiply the counts. \\
Encode and Decode Strings & Flatten a list of any strings; a length prefix per item. & Write length, hash, string; read length, then jump. \\
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree & Flatten a tree; a null marker for each empty child. & Write it level by level like the example list, with N for every null; each real node in the queue takes the next two tokens as its kids. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

Hashing: counting, membership and canonical keys &
A pair with an exact sum, and the output is indexes.
Anagrams, or groups equal up to one detail. Consecutive runs in $O(n)$. &

The map holds only the items before $j$.

Prefix sums, running aggregates and offsets &
Count ranges with an exact sum and negative values.
``All except \cd{i}'' with no division. ``Buy before sell''. Many range updates, one read. &
Write a range as \cd{P[r + 1] - P[l]}.
Sweep: seed, extend, ask, add. Keep a count map or a running minimum of the past. &

Two pointers &
Sorted or sortable input, and a pair or a triple with a target sum.
A mirror check. A list cycle or middle. Remove in place. &

Fast and slow pointers on a list. Read and write pointers. &
Every answer pair stays inside \cd{[lo, hi]}.

Sliding window &
One contiguous segment: the longest, the shortest or the count.
A monotone rule: ``at most $k$'', ``contains all of''. A fixed length. &
Grow the right end. Longest: shrink the left while invalid. Shortest: shrink while valid.
Count when the rule survives shrinking: shrink while invalid, then add \cd{right - left + 1}.
Count with ``contains all of'' or ``at least'': shrink while valid, then add \cd{left}.
Exactly $k$: at most $k$ minus at most $k - 1$. &
The state updates in $O(1)$, and \cd{left} never moves back.
\emph{Window length minus top count must be at most k.} \\

Stacks and monotonic stacks &
Openers and closers that nest.
The nearest greater or smaller element. A minimum times a width. &
Push pending indexes. Pop each index that the new element beats: that is its \emph{next} answer.
The top is the \emph{previous} answer. &
Each index is pushed one time and popped at most one time: $O(n)$.
\emph{Pop what can never be an answer again.} \\
\midrule
Binary search &
Sorted or rotated data. ``The minimum $x$ such that it is possible'', with answers up to $10^9$.
The latest value at or before $t$. &
Write \cd{ok(x)}, and name why it flips one time.
Find the first true on a half-open range. \cd{bisect_left} gives the first \cd{a[i] >= x}. &
Below \cd{lo}, all fail. \cd{hi} passes or is the end.
\emph{If mid passes, keep it; if mid fails, skip it.} \\

Linked lists &
A chain of nodes, ``in place''. The head can change.
A position from the end, or the middle. &
Save the next node, then rewire. Build each output with a dummy and a tail.
Or copy the nodes into a list. &
\cd{prev} heads the reversed part, and \cd{curr} heads the rest.

Trees &
A node answer comes from its children or its ancestors.
``Level'', ``side view''. ``Path between any two nodes''. Order in a BST. &
Bottom-up DFS returns a summary. Top-down DFS passes the path state.
BFS goes by levels. A BST in-order walk is sorted. &
Height past 1000: use an explicit stack.

Many strings and prefix queries: ``starts with'', autocomplete.

A dot follows every edge. With 1 or 2 dots, a set of masked patterns is simpler:

The $k$th largest, the top $k$ or the $k$ closest, not the full order.
A running median. A $k$-way merge. &
Keep the $k$ best in a heap of the opposite polarity.
Or pop the best, push what follows. Two heaps for a median. Negate for a max-heap. &

``Return all'' or ``generate all''. Tiny bounds: $n \le 10$ to $20$.
A partial answer can break a rule. &
Choose, explore, un-choose. Pick a shape: take or skip, start index, pool, slots, grid path. Prune early.
Duplicates: sort, skip equal siblings. &
A call leaves the path as it found it.

Islands or regions in a grid. The fewest moves at equal cost.
A spread from many cells at once. A small move changes a state. &

Prerequisites: ``$b$ before $a$''. Return a valid order. Count the groups.

Union-find: a shared root means a cycle. &
A short order means a cycle.

Edge costs and a minimum total. The lowest level that allows a path.
Connect all points. At most $k$ stops. &

Minimax: max, not plus. $k$ stops: $k + 1$ Bellman-Ford rounds. &
\emph{The first pop of a node is its arrival time.}
MST on points (a complete graph): \emph{keep a dict of outside points: pop the nearest, then let it lower the others.}
Sparse edge list: \emph{cheapest edge first; keep it only when it joins two components.} \\

``How many ways'', a best total, or ``is it possible''.
A few choices at each step. Greedy fails. &
Recurse on the last move. The arguments are the state.
Cache it, or fill a table from the base case. Segments: a state that ends at \cd{i}. &
Combine with a sum, min, max or \cd{any}.

Items make an amount or fit a capacity.
``Each item once'' or ``unlimited''. Signs on items. &
Index a table by the total. Items outside: combinations. Totals outside: ordered sequences.
One copy: totals go down. Unlimited: totals go up. Signs: memo on (index, sum), or a subset sum. &
\emph{Coins outside, amounts going up inside: \cd{ways[a] += ways[a - coin]}.} \\

Two strings: longest common, fewest edits, ways to form, pattern match.
Lengths up to about $10^3$. &
\cd{dp[i][j]} answers \cd{a[:i]} and \cd{b[:j]}. Fill the border, then read up, left and diagonal.
Palindromes: expand from each center. &
\emph{Last chars match: go diagonal plus one. Else take the best of up and left.} \\

Forward-only grid moves. Removals ``in any order''.
Two players take from the ends. A cooldown. &
Split on the last move into a cell, the element that acts last, or the move of the player to move.
Fill by row, by length or by step. &

Greedy &
One number or yes or no, and $n$ up to $10^5$.
A choice that cannot hurt: the farthest reach. One failure rules out a range. &

Test it with a brute force. &
Before index $i$, every index in \cd{0..farthest} is reachable.
\emph{Walk forward; if you pass farthest you are stuck, else stretch farthest.} \\

With a copy, \cd{grid} never changes during a step. In place, one cell holds the old and the new state.

``Design'' or ``Implement the class'', with a cost target per call.

\emph{Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow.} \\

\subsection{Ten questions for any problem}
When no technique comes to mind, ask these questions in this order.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{What does the output ask for?} All solutions: backtracking. A count, a best value, yes or no: DP or greedy.
  \item \textbf{What do the bounds allow?} Plan for about $10^7$ Python steps. $n \le 20$: exponential search.
        $n \le 5000$: $O(n^2)$. $n \le 10^5$: $O(n \log n)$. An answer range up to $10^9$: binary search on it.
  \item \textbf{Which work does the brute force repeat?} Name its inner loop. The technique removes that work.
  \item \textbf{Does the input order matter?} If it does not, sort the input or count it first.
  \item \textbf{What is the shape of the answer?} A segment: a window or prefix sums. A pair: a hash map or two pointers.
        A subsequence: DP. The smallest subsequence after removals: a monotonic stack. A path: a graph.
  \item \textbf{Is the rule one expression?} Exact key: a lookup. Survives shrinking: a window.
        Survives growing: a shortest window, or a count that adds \cd{left}. Flips one time: binary search.
  \item \textbf{What must the rest know about the past?} That is the state. Keep it small: a frontier, a minimum, a count map.
  \item \textbf{What is a node, and what is an edge?} Equal costs: BFS. Costs 0 or 1: a 0-1 BFS.
        Non-negative weights: Dijkstra. Negative weights: Bellman-Ford. ``Before'': a topological order.
        ``Linked'': components. ``Two groups'' with no conflict inside a group: a two-coloring with BFS.
  \item \textbf{Which access does each step need?} By key, order, rank, extreme or prefix. Pick the structure for it.
  \item \textbf{Does it survive the edge cases?} Test empty, one element, ties, zeros and negatives. Past depth 1000, use a loop.
        Compare with a brute force.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Transfer drills}\label{sec:drills}
Each drill is a problem outside NeetCode 150 and Blind 75. Solve it with the method in Section~\ref{m1:method}. First name the signal, the technique and the key step. Then write the code. The answers are in Appendix~\ref{app:answers}. Start with the mixed drills in Section~\ref{drill:mixed}, because they test recognition. Each later set practices one technique. Its heading names the technique, and the line below the heading gives the sections of the technique and of its answers.

\subsection{Mixed drills}\label{drill:mixed}
These drills come from all techniques, in a random order. No heading names the technique. So for each drill, first name the signal and the technique. The answer key below the list gives the answer section and the item number.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Matrix Block Sum (LeetCode 1314).} You get an $m \times n$ matrix with $m, n \le 100$ and an integer \cd{k}.
        Return a matrix where \cd{answer[i][j]} is the sum of all \cd{mat[r][c]} with \cd{|r - i| <= k}, \cd{|c - j| <= k},
        and \cd{(r, c)} inside the matrix.
  \item \textbf{Find Peak Element (LeetCode 162).}
        An array of up to 1000 integers has no two equal neighbors. Treat the values outside the array as $-\infty$.
        A peak is a value greater than both of its neighbors.
        Return the index of any peak in $O(\log n)$ time. The array is not sorted.
  \item \textbf{Design Browser History (LeetCode 1472).}
        A browser starts on a home page. \cd{visit(url)} opens a new page after the current page and clears all forward history.
        \cd{back(steps)} and \cd{forward(steps)} move at most \cd{steps} pages and return the URL of the current page.
        When fewer pages are available, the move stops at the first page or at the last page.
        There are at most 5000 calls, and \cd{steps} is 1 to 100. Make each call $O(1)$ amortized, independent of \cd{steps}.
  \item \textbf{Divide Two Integers (LeetCode 29).} Divide two signed 32-bit integers without \cd{*},
  \cd{/} and \pct. Truncate the quotient toward zero, so $-7 / 2$ gives $-3$. The divisor is not 0.
  Clamp the quotient to $[-2^{31}, 2^{31} - 1]$: a quotient above $2^{31} - 1$ gives $2^{31} - 1$.
  \item \textbf{Shortest Bridge (LeetCode 934).} An $n \times n$ binary grid, $2 \le n \le 100$, has exactly two islands
  of 4-connected land. You can change water cells to land.
  Return the fewest changes that join the two islands into one island.
  \item \textbf{Prison Cells After N Days (LeetCode 957).} Eight cells in a row hold 0 or 1.
        Each day all cells change at the same time.
        An inner cell becomes 1 if its two neighbors are equal, else 0. The two end cells become 0.
