        Return the state after $n$ days, with $n$ up to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Array of Doubled Pairs (LeetCode 954).}
        You get an array of even length. It can hold negative values and zeros.
        Return true if you can reorder it so that \cd{arr[2 * i + 1] == 2 * arr[2 * i]} for every pair.
        $n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$ and $|a_i| \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Sudoku Solver (LeetCode 37).} You get a $9 \times 9$ board of characters. A digit cell holds \cd{"1"} to \cd{"9"},
        and \cd{"."} marks an empty cell. Fill every empty cell in place.
        Then each row, each column and each of the nine $3 \times 3$ boxes must hold each digit exactly one time.
        The input has exactly one solution.
  \item \textbf{Dungeon Game (LeetCode 174).} A knight starts in the top-left cell of an $m \times n$ grid and moves
        only right or down to the bottom-right cell. Each cell adds or removes health (values from $-1000$ to $1000$).
        The knight dies as soon as his health is 0 or less, also on the first and on the last cell.
        Return the minimum start health. $1 \le m, n \le 200$.
  \item \textbf{Single-Threaded CPU (LeetCode 1834).} Task $i$ is \cd{[enqueueTime, processingTime]}.
        When the CPU is idle, it starts the available task with the shortest processing time. A tie goes to the smallest index.
        A started task runs to the end. If no task is available, the CPU waits until the next task arrives.
        Return the order of the task indexes. There are up to $10^5$ tasks, and times go up to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (LeetCode 236).}
        A binary tree with 2 to $10^5$ nodes has unique values but no order rule.
        You get two different nodes $p$ and $q$ of the tree. Return their lowest common ancestor.
        A node is a descendant of itself.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses (LeetCode 1249).} A string has lowercase letters,
        \cd{(} and \cd{)}. Its length is up to $10^5$. Remove the minimum number of parentheses so that
        the result is a valid parentheses string, and return any such result. Letters stay in their order.
  \item \textbf{Shortest Common Supersequence (LeetCode 1092).}
  You get two strings \cd{str1} and \cd{str2} of lowercase letters. Each has length 1 to 1000.
  Return the shortest string that has both \cd{str1} and \cd{str2} as subsequences.
  If more than one answer exists, return any of them.
  \item \textbf{Count Number of Nice Subarrays (LeetCode 1248).}
        A contiguous subarray is nice when it contains exactly \cd{k} odd numbers.
        Return the number of nice subarrays of \cd{nums}.
        $1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^5$, $1 \le k \le n$.
  \item \textbf{Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II (LeetCode 80).}
  A sorted array has up to $3 \cdot 10^4$ elements.
  Change it in place so that each value appears at most two times, in the original order, and return the new length $k$.
  Use $O(1)$ extra memory. The judge reads only the first $k$ elements.
  \item \textbf{Sort List (LeetCode 148).} Sort a linked list in ascending order and return the head.
        The list has 0 to $5 \cdot 10^4$ nodes. The target is $O(n \log n)$ time. The follow-up asks for $O(1)$ extra memory.
  \item \textbf{Delete and Earn (LeetCode 740).} You get an integer array \cd{nums}.
        In one operation, pick an element \cd{x}, delete it, and earn \cd{x} points. Then delete every element equal to \cd{x - 1} or \cd{x + 1}.
        Return the maximum total of points. The limits are $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^4$ and $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^4$.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Score of a Node Sequence (LeetCode 2242).} An undirected graph has $n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$
        nodes with scores and up to $5 \cdot 10^4$ edges. A valid sequence has 4 different nodes, and each two
        consecutive nodes share an edge. Return the maximum sum of scores of a valid sequence, or $-1$ if none exists.
  \item \textbf{Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals (LeetCode 1481).} You get up to $10^5$ integers
        with values up to $10^9$, and an integer $k$. Remove exactly $k$ elements.
        Return the smallest possible number of distinct values that remain.
  \item \textbf{Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination (LeetCode 1976).}
        A connected undirected graph has up to 200 intersections. Each road takes a time from 1 to $10^9$.
        Count the routes from intersection 0 to intersection $n - 1$ that take the shortest possible time.
        Return the count modulo $10^9 + 7$.
  \item \textbf{Maximum XOR With an Element From Array (LeetCode 1707).} You get an array \cd{nums} and queries \cd{[x, m]}.
        For each query, return the largest \cd{x ^ v} over the values \cd{v} of \cd{nums} with \cd{v <= m},
        or \cd{-1} if no value qualifies. There are up to $10^5$ values and $10^5$ queries.
        All values, \cd{x} and \cd{m} are integers from 0 to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Number of Work Sessions to Finish the Tasks (LeetCode 1986).} You get $n \le 14$ tasks
        with durations from 1 to 10 hours, and a session length \cd{sessionTime} from the longest task up to
        15. A task must start and finish in the same session, and the tasks can go in any order. Return the
        fewest sessions that finish all the tasks.
  \item \textbf{Backward pass of max normalization.}
        Define $y = x / \max(x)$ for a vector $x$ of length up to $10^5$, with distinct values and a positive maximum.
        You get $x$ and the upstream gradient $v = \partial L / \partial y$.
        Return $\partial L / \partial x$ in the original order of $x$, in $O(n)$ time.
  \item \textbf{Car Pooling (LeetCode 1094).}
        A car drives east only and has \cd{capacity} empty seats.
        Each trip \cd{[p, start, end]} picks up \cd{p} passengers at kilometer \cd{start} and drops them at kilometer \cd{end}.
        At one kilometer, the passengers leave before new passengers get in.
        Up to 1000 trips, kilometers up to 1000. Return whether the car can do all trips.
\end{enumerate}
\noindent\textbf{Answer key.} 1: \ref{ans:T02} item 5; 2: \ref{ans:T06} item 6; 3: \ref{ans:T24} item 3; 4: \ref{ans:T23} item 6; 5: \ref{ans:T12} item 6; 6: \ref{ans:T21} item 4; 7: \ref{ans:T19} item 3; 8: \ref{ans:T11} item 6; 9: \ref{ans:T18} item 1; 10: \ref{ans:T10} item 4; 11: \ref{ans:T08} item 6; 12: \ref{ans:T05} item 1; 13: \ref{ans:T17} item 3; 14: \ref{ans:T04} item 4; 15: \ref{ans:T03} item 4; 16: \ref{ans:T07} item 5; 17: \ref{ans:T15} item 1; 18: \ref{ans:T13} item 6; 19: \ref{ans:T01} item 4; 20: \ref{ans:T14} item 3; 21: \ref{ans:T09} item 6; 22: \ref{ans:T16} item 6; 23: \ref{ans:T22} item 6; 24: \ref{ans:T20} item 3.

\subsection{Hashing: counting, membership and canonical keys}\label{drill:T01}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T01} (page~\pageref{tech:T01}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T01} (page~\pageref{ans:T01}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{4Sum II (LeetCode 454).} You get four integer arrays $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, each of length $n \le 200$.
        Count the tuples $(i, j, k, l)$ with $a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] = 0$.
        The values go up to $2^{28}$ in absolute value. A check of all $n^4 \approx 1.6 \cdot 10^9$ tuples is too slow.
  \item \textbf{Count Nice Pairs in an Array (LeetCode 1814).} You get an array \cd{nums} of up to $10^5$ integers,
        each from 0 to $10^9$. The function \cd{rev(x)} writes the digits of $x$ in reverse order, so \cd{rev(120) == 21}.
        A pair of indexes $i < j$ is nice when \cd{nums[i] + rev(nums[j]) == nums[j] + rev(nums[i])}.
        Return the number of nice pairs modulo $10^9 + 7$.
  \item \textbf{Group Shifted Strings (LeetCode 249).} A shift moves every letter of a word one step forward
        in the alphabet, and \cd{z} becomes \cd{a}. So \cd{abc}, \cd{bcd} and \cd{xyz} belong to one shifting sequence.
        Group up to 200 lowercase words (each up to 50 letters) by shifting sequence. The order of the groups does not matter.
  \item \textbf{Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals (LeetCode 1481).} You get up to $10^5$ integers
        with values up to $10^9$, and an integer $k$. Remove exactly $k$ elements.
        Return the smallest possible number of distinct values that remain.
  \item \textbf{Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference (LeetCode 1218).} You get an array \cd{arr} of up to $10^5$
        integers and an integer \cd{difference}. All values are from $-10^4$ to $10^4$.
        Return the length of the longest subsequence in which each element minus the element before it equals \cd{difference}.
        A subsequence keeps the order of the array. An $O(n^2)$ check of all pairs is too slow.
  \item \textbf{Number of Boomerangs (LeetCode 447).} You get $n \le 500$ distinct points with integer coordinates.
        A boomerang is an ordered tuple of points $(i, j, k)$ in which the distance from $i$ to $j$
        equals the distance from $i$ to $k$. Count the boomerangs. An $O(n^3)$ check of all tuples is too slow.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Prefix sums, running aggregates and offsets}\label{drill:T02}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T02} (page~\pageref{tech:T02}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T02} (page~\pageref{ans:T02}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Contiguous Array (LeetCode 525).} You get a binary array \cd{nums} with up to $10^5$ elements.
        Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that has the same number of 0s and 1s.
        Return 0 if no such subarray exists.
  \item \textbf{Shifting Letters II (LeetCode 2381).} You get a string \cd{s} of lowercase letters and a list \cd{shifts}.
        Each shift \cd{[start, end, direction]} moves every letter in \cd{s[start..end]} one step forward if \cd{direction} is 1,
        or one step backward if it is 0. The alphabet wraps: \cd{z} goes to \cd{a}, and \cd{a} goes back to \cd{z}.
        Both lengths are up to $5 \cdot 10^4$. Return the final string.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Value of an Ordered Triplet II (LeetCode 2874).} You get an array \cd{nums} with $3 \le n \le 10^5$.
        Each value is an integer from 1 to $10^6$.
        A triplet of indexes \cd{i < j < k} has the value \cd{(nums[i] - nums[j]) * nums[k]}.
        Return the largest value of a triplet, or 0 if all triplets have a negative value.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray (LeetCode 1749).} You get an array \cd{nums} of up to $10^5$ integers.
        Each value is from $-10^4$ to $10^4$.
        The absolute sum of a contiguous subarray is the absolute value of its sum. An empty subarray has the absolute sum 0.
        Return the largest absolute sum of a contiguous subarray.
  \item \textbf{Matrix Block Sum (LeetCode 1314).} You get an $m \times n$ matrix with $m, n \le 100$ and an integer \cd{k}.
        Return a matrix where \cd{answer[i][j]} is the sum of all \cd{mat[r][c]} with \cd{|r - i| <= k}, \cd{|c - j| <= k},
        and \cd{(r, c)} inside the matrix.
  \item \textbf{Find All Good Indices (LeetCode 2420).} You get an array of up to $10^5$ integers and \cd{k} with $1 \le k \le n / 2$.
        Only an index \cd{i} with \cd{k <= i < n - k} can be good.
        It is good when the \cd{k} elements just before \cd{i} are non-increasing and the \cd{k} elements just after \cd{i} are non-decreasing.
        Return all good indices in increasing order.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Two pointers}\label{drill:T03}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T03} (page~\pageref{tech:T03}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T03} (page~\pageref{ans:T03}).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Valid Palindrome II (LeetCode 680).}
  A string \cd{s} of lowercase letters has a length of up to $10^5$.
  Return \cd{True} if \cd{s} can become a palindrome after you delete at most one character.
  A test of every possible deletion costs $O(n^2)$ and is too slow.
\item \textbf{Boats to Save People (LeetCode 881).}
  \cd{people[i]} is the weight of person $i$, and no weight is more than \cd{limit}.
  A boat carries at most two people, and their total weight is at most \cd{limit}.
  Return the minimum number of boats that carry all $n \leq 5 \cdot 10^4$ people.
\item \textbf{Valid Triangle Number (LeetCode 611).}
  Count the index triples $i < j < k$ whose three values can be the sides of a triangle:
  the sum of any two sides is larger than the third side.
  $n \leq 1000$ and $0 \leq$ \cd{nums[i]} $\leq 1000$. Equal values at different indexes give different triples.
\item \textbf{Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II (LeetCode 80).}
  A sorted array has up to $3 \cdot 10^4$ elements.
  Change it in place so that each value appears at most two times, in the original order, and return the new length $k$.
  Use $O(1)$ extra memory. The judge reads only the first $k$ elements.
\item \textbf{Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List (LeetCode 2095).}
  A singly linked list has $n$ nodes, with $1 \leq n \leq 10^5$.
  Delete the node at the 0-based index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and return the head.
  A list of one node becomes empty.
\item \textbf{Merge Sorted Array (LeetCode 88).}
  \cd{nums1} has the length $m + n$. Its first $m$ values are sorted, and its last $n$ slots hold placeholder zeros.
  \cd{nums2} holds $n$ sorted values.
  Merge \cd{nums2} into \cd{nums1} in place, so that \cd{nums1} is sorted. Use $O(m + n)$ time and no second array.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Sliding window}\label{drill:T04}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T04} (page~\pageref{tech:T04}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T04} (page~\pageref{ans:T04}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Frequency of the Most Frequent Element (LeetCode 1838).}
        You get an integer array \cd{nums} and an integer \cd{k}. In one operation, you add 1 to one element.
        Return the largest possible count of one value after at most \cd{k} operations.
        $1 \le n \le 10^5$, $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^5$, $1 \le k \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Replace the Substring for Balanced String (LeetCode 1234).}
        A string \cd{s} has only the letters \cd{Q}, \cd{W}, \cd{E} and \cd{R}. Its length $n$ is a multiple of 4.
        The string is balanced when each letter appears exactly $n/4$ times.
        You may replace one substring with any string of the same length. Return the minimum length of that
        substring, or 0 if \cd{s} is already balanced. $4 \le n \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Subarray Product Less Than K (LeetCode 713).}
        You get an array \cd{nums} of positive integers and an integer \cd{k}.
        Return the number of contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than \cd{k}.
        $1 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$, $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 1000$, $0 \le k \le 10^6$.
  \item \textbf{Count Number of Nice Subarrays (LeetCode 1248).}
        A contiguous subarray is nice when it contains exactly \cd{k} odd numbers.
        Return the number of nice subarrays of \cd{nums}.
        $1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^5$, $1 \le k \le n$.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards (LeetCode 1423).}
        Cards lie in a row, and each card has a number of points. In each step, you take the card at the left
        end or the card at the right end of the row. You take exactly \cd{k} cards.
        Return the largest possible total of points. $1 \le k \le n \le 10^5$, $1 \le$ points $\le 10^4$.
  \item \textbf{Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit (LeetCode 1438).}
        Return the length of the longest non-empty contiguous subarray in which the absolute difference of
        any two elements is at most \cd{limit}.
        $1 \le n \le 10^5$, $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^9$, $0 \le$ \cd{limit} $\le 10^9$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Stacks and monotonic stacks}\label{drill:T05}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T05} (page~\pageref{tech:T05}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T05} (page~\pageref{ans:T05}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses (LeetCode 1249).} A string has lowercase letters,
        \cd{(} and \cd{)}. Its length is up to $10^5$. Remove the minimum number of parentheses so that
        the result is a valid parentheses string, and return any such result. Letters stay in their order.
  \item \textbf{Decode String (LeetCode 394).} An encoded string uses the rule \cd{k[text]}: repeat
        \cd{text} exactly \cd{k} times. Brackets can nest, as in \cd{3[a2[c]]}, and \cd{k} can have
        several digits (up to 300). The input is always valid, and the decoded length is at most $10^5$.
        Return the decoded string.
  \item \textbf{Basic Calculator II (LeetCode 227).} A string holds non-negative integers, the operators
        \cd{+ - * /} and spaces, but no parentheses. Its length is up to $3 \cdot 10^5$. Evaluate it with
        the usual precedence, and truncate each division toward zero. Do not use \cd{eval}.
  \item \textbf{Asteroid Collision (LeetCode 735).} A row of up to $10^4$ asteroids is given as non-zero
        integers. The absolute value is the size, and the sign is the direction (positive moves right,
        negative moves left). All asteroids move at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one
        explodes, and equal sizes both explode. Return the asteroids that remain.
  \item \textbf{Online Stock Span (LeetCode 901).} Design a class with \cd{next(price)}. It returns the
        span of today's price. The span is the number of consecutive days that end today (today included)
        with a price less than or equal to today's price. There are up to $10^4$ calls, and each call must
        be amortized $O(1)$.
  \item \textbf{Sum of Subarray Minimums (LeetCode 907).} An array has up to $3 \cdot 10^4$ integers from 1
        to $3 \cdot 10^4$, and values can repeat. Return the sum of \cd{min(sub)} over every contiguous
        subarray \cd{sub}, modulo $10^9 + 7$. An $O(n^2)$ scan is too slow.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Binary search}\label{drill:T06}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T06} (page~\pageref{tech:T06}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T06} (page~\pageref{ans:T06}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (LeetCode 1011).}
        Up to $5 \cdot 10^4$ packages, each with a weight from 1 to 500, must ship in the given order.
        Each day, the ship loads the next packages in order, and the total load must not exceed its capacity.
        Return the smallest capacity that ships all packages within \cd{days} days.
  \item \textbf{Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (LeetCode 1552).}
        You get up to $10^5$ distinct basket positions, each up to $10^9$, and $m \ge 2$ balls.
        Put each ball in a different basket.
        Make the smallest distance between two balls as large as possible, and return that distance.
  \item \textbf{Snapshot Array (LeetCode 1146).}
        Design an array of length up to $5 \cdot 10^4$. All values are 0 at the start.
        \cd{set(index, val)} changes one value. \cd{snap()} takes a snapshot and returns its id: 0, then 1, then 2.
        \cd{get(index, snap_id)} returns the value at that index when that snapshot was taken.
        Up to $5 \cdot 10^4$ calls occur, so a full copy of the array at each snapshot is too slow.
  \item \textbf{Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (LeetCode 378).}
        Each row and each column of an $n \times n$ matrix ($n \le 300$) is sorted in ascending order.
        The values are in $[-10^9, 10^9]$.
        Return the $k$-th smallest of all $n^2$ values, with duplicates counted.
        Use less than $O(n^2)$ extra memory.
  \item \textbf{Russian Doll Envelopes (LeetCode 354).}
        You get up to $10^5$ envelopes as pairs \cd{[w, h]}, and each side is from 1 to $10^5$.
        One envelope fits in another only when its width and its height are both strictly smaller.
        Return the largest number of envelopes that you can put one inside the other. You cannot rotate an envelope.
  \item \textbf{Find Peak Element (LeetCode 162).}
        An array of up to 1000 integers has no two equal neighbors. Treat the values outside the array as $-\infty$.
        A peak is a value greater than both of its neighbors.
        Return the index of any peak in $O(\log n)$ time. The array is not sorted.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Linked lists}\label{drill:T07}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T07} (page~\pageref{tech:T07}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T07} (page~\pageref{ans:T07}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Palindrome Linked List (LeetCode 234).} Return \cd{True} if the values of a singly linked list read the
        same forward and backward. The list has 1 to $10^5$ nodes. The follow-up asks for $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory.
  \item \textbf{Reverse Linked List II (LeetCode 92).} Reverse only the nodes from position \cd{left} to position \cd{right}
        (1-indexed, $1 \le left \le right \le n$), and return the head. The list has 1 to 500 nodes.
        Change the links, not the values. The follow-up asks for one pass.
  \item \textbf{Rotate List (LeetCode 61).} Rotate a list to the right by $k$ places: the last $k$ nodes move to the front
        in the same order. The list has 0 to 500 nodes, and $k$ can be as large as $2 \cdot 10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Partition List (LeetCode 86).} Given a list and a value $x$, put all nodes with a value less than $x$ before
        all nodes with a value of $x$ or more. Keep the original relative order inside each part.
        The list has 0 to 200 nodes. Rewire the given nodes.
  \item \textbf{Sort List (LeetCode 148).} Sort a linked list in ascending order and return the head.
        The list has 0 to $5 \cdot 10^4$ nodes. The target is $O(n \log n)$ time. The follow-up asks for $O(1)$ extra memory.
  \item \textbf{Linked List Cycle II (LeetCode 142).} Return the node where the cycle of a list begins, or \cd{None} if there is
        no cycle. The list has 0 to $10^4$ nodes. Do not change the list. The follow-up asks for $O(1)$ extra memory.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Trees}\label{drill:T08}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T08} (page~\pageref{tech:T08}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T08} (page~\pageref{ans:T08}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Maximum Difference Between Node and Ancestor (LeetCode 1026).}
        A binary tree has 2 to 5000 nodes, with values from 0 to $10^5$.
        Find the largest value of $|a.val - b.val|$, where node $a$ is an ancestor of node $b$.
        The tree can be skewed (one child at each node), so a check of every ancestor-descendant pair is $O(n^2)$.
  \item \textbf{Longest Univalue Path (LeetCode 687).}
        Return the number of edges on the longest path in a binary tree where all nodes have the same value.
        The path can start and end at any node. It does not need to pass through the root.
        The tree has up to $10^4$ nodes and a depth of at most 1000.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Width of Binary Tree (LeetCode 662).}
        The width of a level is the number of positions from its leftmost to its rightmost non-null node.
        The null positions between them count, as if the level were full. Return the largest width of all levels.
        The tree has up to 3000 nodes, and it can be skewed, 3000 levels deep.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Absolute Difference in BST (LeetCode 530).}
        A binary search tree has 2 to $10^4$ nodes, with values from 0 to $10^5$.
        Return the smallest difference between the values of two different nodes.
        A check of all pairs is $O(n^2)$.
  \item \textbf{Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal (LeetCode 106).}
        You get the in-order list and the postorder list of a binary tree with up to 3000 nodes.
        All values are unique. Rebuild the tree and return its root.
  \item \textbf{Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (LeetCode 236).}
        A binary tree with 2 to $10^5$ nodes has unique values but no order rule.
        You get two different nodes $p$ and $q$ of the tree. Return their lowest common ancestor.
        A node is a descendant of itself.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Tries}\label{drill:T09}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T09} (page~\pageref{tech:T09}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T09} (page~\pageref{ans:T09}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Map Sum Pairs (LeetCode 677).} Design a class with \cd{insert(key, val)} and \cd{sum(prefix)}.
        An insert of a key that exists replaces its old value.
        \cd{sum(prefix)} returns the sum of the values of all keys that start with \cd{prefix}.
        Design each call to cost $O(\text{length of its string argument})$, not $O(\text{number of keys})$.
  \item \textbf{Implement Magic Dictionary (LeetCode 676).} \cd{buildDict(words)} stores distinct lowercase words.
        The method \cd{search(w)} returns \cd{True} if a change of exactly one letter of \cd{w} gives a stored word.
        A stored word equal to \cd{w} does not count. There are up to 100 words of length up to 100, and up to 100 searches.
  \item \textbf{Search Suggestions System (LeetCode 1268).} You get distinct product names and a search word.
        After each typed letter of the search word, return up to three products that start with the typed prefix,
        in lexicographic order. There are up to 1000 products with a total length up to $2 \cdot 10^4$,
        and the search word has up to 1000 letters.
  \item \textbf{Concatenated Words (LeetCode 472).} You get up to $10^4$ distinct lowercase words.
        Each word has up to 30 letters, and the total length is up to $10^5$.
        Return every word that is a concatenation of at least two shorter words of the same list.
        A shorter word can appear more than one time in a concatenation, for example \cd{catcat}.
  \item \textbf{Stream of Characters (LeetCode 1032).} You get up to 2000 words of length up to 200.
        Then letters arrive one at a time, in up to $4 \cdot 10^4$ calls.
        After each letter, return \cd{True} if some suffix of the stream so far is one of the words.
  \item \textbf{Maximum XOR With an Element From Array (LeetCode 1707).} You get an array \cd{nums} and queries \cd{[x, m]}.
        For each query, return the largest \cd{x ^ v} over the values \cd{v} of \cd{nums} with \cd{v <= m},
        or \cd{-1} if no value qualifies. There are up to $10^5$ values and $10^5$ queries.
        All values, \cd{x} and \cd{m} are integers from 0 to $10^9$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Heaps and priority queues}\label{drill:T10}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T10} (page~\pageref{tech:T10}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T10} (page~\pageref{ans:T10}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Top K Frequent Words (LeetCode 692).} You get a list of words and an integer $k$.
        Return the $k$ most frequent words, sorted by frequency from high to low.
        Words with the same frequency come in lexicographic order.
        There are at most 500 words of at most 10 lowercase letters. The follow-up asks for $O(n \log k)$ time.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Operations to Halve Array Sum (LeetCode 2208).} You get an array of positive integers.
        One operation picks any number and replaces it with exactly half of it. A later operation can pick the same number again.
        Return the minimum number of operations that reduce the sum of the array by at least half.
        There are up to $10^5$ numbers, and each number is at most $10^7$.
  \item \textbf{Reorganize String (LeetCode 767).} Rearrange the characters of a string \cd{s} so that no two adjacent characters are equal.
        Return any valid arrangement, or an empty string if no arrangement exists.
        \cd{s} has up to 500 lowercase letters.
  \item \textbf{Single-Threaded CPU (LeetCode 1834).} Task $i$ is \cd{[enqueueTime, processingTime]}.
        When the CPU is idle, it starts the available task with the shortest processing time. A tie goes to the smallest index.
        A started task runs to the end. If no task is available, the CPU waits until the next task arrives.
        Return the order of the task indexes. There are up to $10^5$ tasks, and times go up to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums (LeetCode 373).} Two arrays \cd{nums1} and \cd{nums2} are sorted in non-decreasing order.
        Each has up to $10^5$ items, and $k$ is at most $10^4$.
        Return the $k$ pairs \cd{(u, v)}, with \cd{u} from \cd{nums1} and \cd{v} from \cd{nums2}, that have the smallest sums.
        A list of all $n_1 \cdot n_2$ pairs is too large.
  \item \textbf{Sliding Window Median (LeetCode 480).} You get an array \cd{nums} and a window size $k$.
        Return the median of each window of size $k$ as the window moves right by one position.
        For an even $k$, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
        $n$ is up to $10^5$, the values are 32-bit integers, and answers within $10^{-5}$ are accepted.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Backtracking}\label{drill:T11}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T11} (page~\pageref{tech:T11}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T11} (page~\pageref{ans:T11}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Permutations II (LeetCode 47).} You get a list of 1 to 8 integers from $-10$ to $10$, and values can repeat.
        Return all distinct orderings of the list.
        Two orderings are the same when they have the same value at each position.
  \item \textbf{Combination Sum III (LeetCode 216).} Find all sets of exactly $k$ distinct numbers from 1 to 9 with the sum $n$.
        Each number is used at most one time, and the order inside a set does not matter.
        The bounds are $2 \le k \le 9$ and $1 \le n \le 60$.
  \item \textbf{Restore IP Addresses (LeetCode 93).} You get a string of 1 to 20 digits.
        Insert three dots to make a valid IPv4 address, and return all such addresses.
        Each of the four parts is a number from 0 to 255 without a leading zero: \cd{"0"} is valid, \cd{"01"} is not.
  \item \textbf{Path with Maximum Gold (LeetCode 1219).} A grid of at most $15 \times 15$ cells holds gold amounts from 0 to 100,
        and at most 25 cells hold gold. Start at any gold cell and move up, down, left or right.
        Never enter a cell with 0 gold, and never visit a cell two times. Return the largest total gold of one walk.
  \item \textbf{Find Minimum Time to Finish All Jobs (LeetCode 1723).} You get $n$ job durations of up to $10^7$ each and $k$ workers,
        with $1 \le k \le n \le 12$. Each job goes to exactly one worker, and the time of a worker is the sum of its jobs.
        Return the smallest possible value of the largest worker time.
  \item \textbf{Sudoku Solver (LeetCode 37).} You get a $9 \times 9$ board of characters. A digit cell holds \cd{"1"} to \cd{"9"},
        and \cd{"."} marks an empty cell. Fill every empty cell in place.
        Then each row, each column and each of the nine $3 \times 3$ boxes must hold each digit exactly one time.
        The input has exactly one solution.
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================
\subsection{Graph traversal: grids and implicit graphs}\label{drill:T12}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T12} (page~\pageref{tech:T12}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T12} (page~\pageref{ans:T12}).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Count Sub Islands (LeetCode 1905).} Two binary grids \cd{grid1} and \cd{grid2} have the same shape,
  up to $500 \times 500$. Islands connect 4-directionally. An island of \cd{grid2} is a sub-island if each of its
  cells is land in \cd{grid1}. Return the number of sub-islands in \cd{grid2}.
\item \textbf{Number of Enclaves (LeetCode 1020).} A binary grid, up to $500 \times 500$, holds land (1) and sea (0).
  One move goes from a land cell to a 4-directionally adjacent land cell, or off the edge of the grid.
  Return the number of land cells from which no sequence of moves leaves the grid.
\item \textbf{As Far from Land as Possible (LeetCode 1162).} An $n \times n$ grid, $n \le 100$, holds water (0) and
  land (1). Find the water cell with the largest Manhattan distance to its nearest land cell, and return that
  distance. Return $-1$ if the grid has no land or no water.
\item \textbf{Detonate the Maximum Bombs (LeetCode 2101).} There are up to 100 bombs.
  Bomb $i$ is a list $[x_i, y_i, r_i]$: a center and a blast radius, with values up to $10^5$.
  A bomb that explodes detonates every bomb whose center is at a distance of $r_i$ or less, and the chain continues.
  You detonate exactly one bomb. Return the largest number of bombs that can explode.
\item \textbf{Sliding Puzzle (LeetCode 773).} A $2 \times 3$ board holds the tiles 1 to 5 and one empty square 0.
  One move swaps the 0 with a tile that shares an edge with it.
  Return the fewest moves to reach \cd{[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 0]]}, or $-1$ if the board cannot reach it.
\item \textbf{Shortest Bridge (LeetCode 934).} An $n \times n$ binary grid, $2 \le n \le 100$, has exactly two islands
  of 4-connected land. You can change water cells to land.
  Return the fewest changes that join the two islands into one island.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Graph structure: ordering, cycles and connectivity}\label{drill:T13}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T13} (page~\pageref{tech:T13}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T13} (page~\pageref{ans:T13}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Parallel Courses III (LeetCode 2050).} There are $n$ courses and pairs \cd{[prev, next]}:
        course \cd{prev} must finish before course \cd{next} starts. Course $i$ takes \cd{time[i]} months, and any
        number of courses can run at the same time. Return the minimum number of months to finish all courses.
        $n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, at most $5 \cdot 10^4$ pairs, and the pairs form no cycle.
  \item \textbf{Find Eventual Safe States (LeetCode 802).} A directed graph with $n \le 10^4$ nodes comes as
        adjacency lists with up to $4 \cdot 10^4$ edges. Self-loops are possible. A node is safe if every path from it
        ends at a node with no outgoing edge. Return all safe nodes in increasing order.
  \item \textbf{Satisfiability of Equality Equations (LeetCode 990).} You get up to 500 strings of the form
        \cd{"a==b"} or \cd{"a!=b"}. Each lowercase letter is a variable. Return \cd{True} if you can give each
        variable an integer so that every equation holds.
  \item \textbf{Number of Operations to Make Network Connected (LeetCode 1319).} There are $n \le 10^5$ computers
        and up to $10^5$ cables, each between two computers. One operation removes a cable and uses it to join any
        two computers. Return the minimum number of operations to connect all computers, or $-1$ if it is impossible.
  \item \textbf{Longest Cycle in a Graph (LeetCode 2360).} A directed graph has $n \le 10^5$ nodes. Each node has
        at most one outgoing edge: \cd{edges[i]} is its target, or $-1$. Return the length of the longest cycle,
        or $-1$ if there is no cycle.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Score of a Node Sequence (LeetCode 2242).} An undirected graph has $n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$
        nodes with scores and up to $5 \cdot 10^4$ edges. A valid sequence has 4 different nodes, and each two
        consecutive nodes share an edge. Return the maximum sum of scores of a valid sequence, or $-1$ if none exists.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Weighted and advanced graphs}\label{drill:T14}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T14} (page~\pageref{tech:T14}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T14} (page~\pageref{ans:T14}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Path With Minimum Effort (LeetCode 1631).}
        A grid of heights has up to $100 \times 100$ cells, and each height is from 1 to $10^6$.
        You walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell in 4 directions.
        The effort of a route is the largest absolute height difference between two consecutive cells on it.
        Return the minimum effort.
  \item \textbf{Path with Maximum Probability (LeetCode 1514).}
        An undirected graph has up to $10^4$ nodes and $2 \cdot 10^4$ edges.
        Each edge has a success probability in $[0, 1]$, and the probability of a path is the product
        of its edge probabilities. Return the maximum probability of a path from \cd{start} to \cd{end},
        or 0 when no path exists.
  \item \textbf{Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination (LeetCode 1976).}
        A connected undirected graph has up to 200 intersections. Each road takes a time from 1 to $10^9$.
        Count the routes from intersection 0 to intersection $n - 1$ that take the shortest possible time.
        Return the count modulo $10^9 + 7$.
  \item \textbf{Optimize Water Distribution in a Village (LeetCode 1168).}
        A village has up to $10^4$ houses, labeled 1 to $n$. A well in house $i$ costs \cd{wells[i - 1]}.
        A pipe \cd{[a, b, c]} joins houses $a$ and $b$ in both directions at cost $c$, and there are up to $10^4$ pipes.
        A house has water when it has a well, or when pipes connect it to a house with a well.
        Return the minimum total cost to give water to every house.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time (LeetCode 1928).}
        An undirected graph has up to 1000 cities and 1000 roads, and two cities can have more than one road.
        Each road takes 1 to 1000 minutes. Each city has a fee from 1 to 1000, which you pay for every city
        on the route, the first and the last included.
        Return the minimum total fee from city 0 to city $n - 1$ in at most \cd{maxTime} minutes ($\le 1000$),
        or $-1$.
  \item \textbf{Valid Arrangement of Pairs (LeetCode 2097).}
        You get up to $10^5$ distinct pairs \cd{[start, end]} of integers up to $10^9$, with \cd{start != end}.
        Put all the pairs in a list so that the end of each pair equals the start of the next pair.
        A valid arrangement is known to exist. Return any one.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Dynamic programming: foundations and 1-D}\label{drill:T15}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T15} (page~\pageref{tech:T15}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T15} (page~\pageref{ans:T15}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Delete and Earn (LeetCode 740).} You get an integer array \cd{nums}.
        In one operation, pick an element \cd{x}, delete it, and earn \cd{x} points. Then delete every element equal to \cd{x - 1} or \cd{x + 1}.
        Return the maximum total of points. The limits are $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^4$ and $1 \le$ \cd{nums[i]} $\le 10^4$.
  \item \textbf{Count Number of Texts (LeetCode 2266).} A phone keypad maps the digits 2 to 9 to letters.
        The keys 7 and 9 have four letters, and the other keys have three letters. To type the $k$-th letter of a key, press that key $k$ times.
        You get the string \cd{pressedKeys} of the pressed digits, with a length up to $10^5$.
        Return the number of text messages that produce it, modulo $10^9 + 7$.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Cost For Tickets (LeetCode 983).} You get the travel days of one year in increasing order, each from 1 to 365.
        A pass costs \cd{costs[0]} for 1 day, \cd{costs[1]} for 7 days, and \cd{costs[2]} for 30 days.
        A pass covers that number of consecutive days from the day of purchase. Each cost is at most 1000.
        Return the minimum total cost that covers every travel day.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Sum Circular Subarray (LeetCode 918).} You get a circular integer array \cd{nums}, so the last element is next to the first element.
        Return the maximum sum of a non-empty subarray. A subarray can wrap past the end, but it uses each element at most one time.
        The limits are $n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$ and values from $-3 \cdot 10^4$ to $3 \cdot 10^4$.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Length of Subarray With Positive Product (LeetCode 1567).} You get an integer array \cd{nums} with $n \le 10^5$
        and values from $-10^9$ to $10^9$, zeros included.
        Return the maximum length of a contiguous subarray whose product is positive.
  \item \textbf{Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence (LeetCode 673).} You get an integer array \cd{nums} with $n \le 2000$
        and values from $-10^6$ to $10^6$.
        Return the number of strictly increasing subsequences that have the maximum length.
        Two subsequences are different when they use different indices.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Dynamic programming: knapsack family}\label{drill:T16}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T16} (page~\pageref{tech:T16}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T16} (page~\pageref{ans:T16}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Last Stone Weight II (LeetCode 1049).} You get the weights of up to 30 stones, each from 1 to
        100. In each turn, smash any two stones with weights $x \le y$. Equal stones both disappear; otherwise
        only one stone of weight $y - x$ stays. Return the smallest possible weight of the last stone, or 0
        if no stone stays.
  \item \textbf{Ones and Zeroes (LeetCode 474).} You get up to 600 binary strings (each of length at most
        100) and two limits $m$ and $n$ (each at most 100). Return the size of the largest subset of the
        strings that contains at most $m$ zeros and at most $n$ ones in total.
  \item \textbf{Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum (LeetCode 1155).} You roll $n$ dice, and each die has the
        faces $1$ to $k$. Count the roll results (out of $k^n$, so the order of the dice matters) whose sum is
        exactly \cd{target}. Return the count modulo $10^9 + 7$. Limits: $1 \le n, k \le 30$ and
        $1 \le \mathit{target} \le 1000$.
  \item \textbf{Count Ways To Build Good Strings (LeetCode 2466).} Start with an empty string. In each step,
        append the character \cd{0} exactly \cd{zero} times, or the character \cd{1} exactly \cd{one} times.
        Count the different strings that you can build with a length from \cd{low} to \cd{high}, modulo
        $10^9 + 7$. Limits: $1 \le \mathit{zero}, \mathit{one} \le \mathit{low} \le \mathit{high} \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Extra Characters in a String (LeetCode 2707).} Break a string \cd{s} into non-overlapping
        substrings that are dictionary words. Characters that are in no chosen word are extra. Return the
        fewest extra characters. The string and each word have at most 50 characters, and there are at most
        50 distinct words.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Number of Work Sessions to Finish the Tasks (LeetCode 1986).} You get $n \le 14$ tasks
        with durations from 1 to 10 hours, and a session length \cd{sessionTime} from the longest task up to
        15. A task must start and finish in the same session, and the tasks can go in any order. Return the
        fewest sessions that finish all the tasks.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Dynamic programming on strings and sequences}\label{drill:T17}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T17} (page~\pageref{tech:T17}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T17} (page~\pageref{ans:T17}).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Minimum ASCII Delete Sum for Two Strings (LeetCode 712).}
  You get two strings \cd{s1} and \cd{s2} of lowercase letters. Each has length 1 to 1000.
  Delete characters from either string until the two strings are equal.
  Return the lowest possible sum of the ASCII codes of the deleted characters.
\item \textbf{Number of Ways to Form a Target String Given a Dictionary (LeetCode 1639).}
  You get up to 1000 words, all of the same length $L \le 1000$, and a string \cd{target} of length up to 1000.
  Build \cd{target} from left to right. Each character comes from column $k$ of any word,
  and the columns that you use must strictly increase.
  Return the number of ways modulo $10^9 + 7$. A different word or a different column gives a different way.
\item \textbf{Shortest Common Supersequence (LeetCode 1092).}
  You get two strings \cd{str1} and \cd{str2} of lowercase letters. Each has length 1 to 1000.
  Return the shortest string that has both \cd{str1} and \cd{str2} as subsequences.
  If more than one answer exists, return any of them.
\item \textbf{Wildcard Matching (LeetCode 44).}
  You get a string \cd{s} of lowercase letters and a pattern \cd{p} of letters, \cd{?} and \cd{*}.
  Each has length 0 to 2000. The symbol \cd{?} matches any one character.
  The symbol \cd{*} matches any sequence of characters, also the empty sequence.
  Return true if \cd{p} matches all of \cd{s}.
\item \textbf{Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LeetCode 516).}
  You get a string \cd{s} of lowercase letters with length 1 to 1000.
  Return the length of the longest subsequence of \cd{s} that is a palindrome.
  The characters of the subsequence do not need to be contiguous.
\item \textbf{Max Dot Product of Two Subsequences (LeetCode 1458).}
  You get two integer arrays \cd{nums1} and \cd{nums2}. Each has length 1 to 500, with values from $-1000$ to $1000$.
  Pick a non-empty subsequence from each array. The two subsequences must have the same length.
  Their dot product is the sum of the products of the values at the same position.
  Return the largest possible dot product.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Dynamic programming on grids, intervals, games and states}\label{drill:T18}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T18} (page~\pageref{tech:T18}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T18} (page~\pageref{ans:T18}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Dungeon Game (LeetCode 174).} A knight starts in the top-left cell of an $m \times n$ grid and moves
        only right or down to the bottom-right cell. Each cell adds or removes health (values from $-1000$ to $1000$).
        The knight dies as soon as his health is 0 or less, also on the first and on the last cell.
        Return the minimum start health. $1 \le m, n \le 200$.
  \item \textbf{Number of Increasing Paths in a Grid (LeetCode 2328).} Count all strictly increasing paths in an
        $m \times n$ grid. A path moves up, down, left or right. It can start and end at any cell, and one cell alone is a path.
        Return the count modulo $10^9 + 7$. $m \cdot n \le 10^5$, and the values are from 1 to $10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick (LeetCode 1547).} A stick has the length $n \le 10^6$.
        You must cut it at each of the given positions (at most 100 distinct positions), in an order that you choose.
        A cut costs the length of the piece that it cuts. Return the minimum total cost.
  \item \textbf{Stone Game III (LeetCode 1406).} Stones in a row have values from $-1000$ to $1000$ ($n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$).
        Alice and Bob alternate, and Alice starts. Each turn takes the first 1, 2 or 3 remaining stones and adds their
        values to the score of the player. Both play optimally. Return \cd{"Alice"}, \cd{"Bob"} or \cd{"Tie"}.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Swaps To Make Sequences Increasing (LeetCode 801).} Two arrays have the same length $n$
        ($2 \le n \le 10^5$). One operation swaps \cd{nums1[i]} and \cd{nums2[i]} at the same index $i$.
        Return the minimum number of operations that makes both arrays strictly increasing.
        The input guarantees that this is possible.
  \item \textbf{Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV (LeetCode 188).} You get daily prices ($n \le 1000$, prices from 0 to 1000)
        and an integer $k \le 100$. You may complete at most $k$ transactions, and you hold at most one share at a time.
        Return the maximum profit.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Greedy}\label{drill:T19}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T19} (page~\pageref{tech:T19}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T19} (page~\pageref{ans:T19}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Two City Scheduling (LeetCode 1029).}
        You get $2n$ people. Person $i$ costs \cd{costs[i][0]} to fly to city A and \cd{costs[i][1]} to fly to city B.
        Send exactly $n$ people to each city. Return the smallest total cost.
        $2n \le 100$, and each cost is from 1 to 1000.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden (LeetCode 1326).}
        A garden covers the interval $[0, n]$ of a line. The tap at each integer point $i$ waters $[i - r_i, i + r_i]$.
        Return the fewest taps that water the whole garden, or $-1$ if no set of taps does.
        $n \le 10^4$ and $0 \le r_i \le 100$.
  \item \textbf{Array of Doubled Pairs (LeetCode 954).}
        You get an array of even length. It can hold negative values and zeros.
        Return true if you can reorder it so that \cd{arr[2 * i + 1] == 2 * arr[2 * i]} for every pair.
        $n \le 3 \cdot 10^4$ and $|a_i| \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Max Chunks To Make Sorted (LeetCode 769).}
        The array is a permutation of $0, 1, \ldots, n - 1$. Split it into contiguous chunks, sort each chunk, and join the chunks.
        The result must be the sorted array. Return the largest possible number of chunks.
        Find an $O(n)$ method.
  \item \textbf{Check if a Parentheses String Can Be Valid (LeetCode 2116).}
        You get a string of \cd{(} and \cd{)}, and a binary string \cd{locked} of the same length.
        You can change each character whose \cd{locked} value is \cd{0} into \cd{(} or \cd{)}. You cannot delete a character.
        Return true if some set of changes makes a valid bracket sequence. $n \le 10^5$.
  \item \textbf{Candy (LeetCode 135).}
        Children stand in a line, and each child has a rating.
        Give each child at least one candy. A child with a higher rating than a neighbor must get more candies than that neighbor.
        Return the smallest total number of candies. $n \le 2 \cdot 10^4$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Intervals}\label{drill:T20}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T20} (page~\pageref{tech:T20}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T20} (page~\pageref{ans:T20}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Remove Covered Intervals (LeetCode 1288).}
        You get up to 1000 distinct half-open intervals \cd{[a, b)}.
        An interval \cd{[a, b)} is covered by \cd{[c, d)} when \cd{c <= a} and \cd{b <= d}.
        Remove every covered interval and return the number of intervals that remain. Aim for $O(n \log n)$.
  \item \textbf{Interval List Intersections (LeetCode 986).}
        You get two lists of closed intervals. Each list is sorted by start, and its intervals are pairwise disjoint.
        Each list has up to 1000 intervals. Return the intersection of the two sets as a sorted list of closed intervals.
        A shared single point, such as \cd{[5, 5]}, is a valid interval of the answer.
  \item \textbf{Car Pooling (LeetCode 1094).}
        A car drives east only and has \cd{capacity} empty seats.
        Each trip \cd{[p, start, end]} picks up \cd{p} passengers at kilometer \cd{start} and drops them at kilometer \cd{end}.
        At one kilometer, the passengers leave before new passengers get in.
        Up to 1000 trips, kilometers up to 1000. Return whether the car can do all trips.
  \item \textbf{Remove Interval (LeetCode 1272).}
        A set of numbers is a sorted list of disjoint half-open intervals \cd{[a, b)}.
        Remove every number in the half-open range \cd{[lo, hi)}. Return the rest as a sorted list of disjoint intervals.
        Up to $10^4$ intervals; the values can be negative. Aim for one $O(n)$ pass.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended (LeetCode 1353).}
        Each event \cd{[s, e]} can be attended on any one day \cd{d} with \cd{s <= d <= e}.
        You can attend at most one event per day. Return the largest number of events that you can attend.
        Up to $10^5$ events, days up to $10^5$, so $O(n \log n)$ is the target.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Subarrays With Sum Equals Target (LeetCode 1546).}
        You get an array \cd{nums} of up to $10^5$ integers, with negative values allowed, and an integer \cd{target}.
        Return the largest number of non-empty subarrays that have the sum \cd{target} and share no index.
        Aim for $O(n)$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Matrices and simulation}\label{drill:T21}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T21} (page~\pageref{tech:T21}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T21} (page~\pageref{ans:T21}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Walking Robot Simulation (LeetCode 874).} A robot starts at $(0, 0)$ on an infinite plane and faces north.
        Command $-2$ turns it left, $-1$ turns it right, and $k$ in $1..9$ moves it $k$ unit steps forward.
        If the next unit cell is an obstacle, the robot stays on its current cell and goes to the next command.
        Return the largest squared distance from the origin at any time. There are up to $10^4$ commands
        and $10^4$ obstacles.
  \item \textbf{Cyclically Rotating a Grid (LeetCode 1914).} An $m \times n$ grid has even $m$ and $n$ ($2..50$).
        It is a set of nested rings (layers).
        One rotation moves every element of every ring one place counterclockwise.
        Return the grid after $k$ rotations, with $k$ up to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Rotating the Box (LeetCode 1861).} An $m \times n$ box holds stones (\hsh), fixed obstacles
        (\cd{*}) and empty cells (\cd{.}).
        Rotate the box 90 degrees clockwise. Then each stone falls down until it lands on an obstacle,
        another stone or the floor. Obstacles do not move.
        Return the $n \times m$ result. $m$ and $n$ are up to 500.
  \item \textbf{Prison Cells After N Days (LeetCode 957).} Eight cells in a row hold 0 or 1.
        Each day all cells change at the same time.
        An inner cell becomes 1 if its two neighbors are equal, else 0. The two end cells become 0.
        Return the state after $n$ days, with $n$ up to $10^9$.
  \item \textbf{Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array (LeetCode 448).} An array of $n$ integers holds values
        in $1..n$. Some values repeat and some values are missing.
        Return all missing values in $O(n)$ time with no extra space except the output list.
  \item \textbf{Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing (LeetCode 1909).}
        Remove exactly one element of \cd{nums} ($2 \le n \le 1000$).
        Return \cd{True} if the rest is strictly increasing.
        An array that is already strictly increasing also gives \cd{True}.
        The $O(n^2)$ replay fits, but find the $O(n)$ answer.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Math and number manipulation}\label{drill:T22}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T22} (page~\pageref{tech:T22}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T22} (page~\pageref{ans:T22}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Add to Array-Form of Integer (LeetCode 989).}
        You get a digit array \cd{num}, most significant digit first, with up to $10^4$ digits,
        and an integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le 10^4$.
        Return the digit array of $\text{num} + k$. Do not convert the whole array to an integer.
  \item \textbf{String to Integer (atoi) (LeetCode 8).}
        Parse a string of up to 200 characters. Skip the leading spaces, read an optional sign,
        and then read digits until the first character that is not a digit.
        Clamp the result to $[-2^{31}, 2^{31} - 1]$, and return 0 if there are no digits.
        Assume that no 64-bit type exists, so the value must never leave the range while you build it.
  \item \textbf{Smallest Integer Divisible by K (LeetCode 1015).}
        For $1 \le k \le 10^5$, find the length of the smallest positive integer that is divisible by $k$
        and has only the digit 1 (1, 11, 111, \dots). Return $-1$ if no such integer exists.
        The integer itself can have up to $10^5$ digits.
  \item \textbf{Count Good Numbers (LeetCode 1922).}
        A digit string of length $n$ is good when each digit at an even index is even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8)
        and each digit at an odd index is a prime (2, 3, 5, 7). Leading zeros are allowed.
        Return the number of good strings of length $n$ modulo $10^9 + 7$, for $1 \le n \le 10^{15}$.
  \item \textbf{Minimum Area Rectangle (LeetCode 939).}
        You get up to 500 distinct points with coordinates from 0 to $4 \cdot 10^4$.
        Return the minimum area of a rectangle with sides parallel to the axes and all four corners in the set.
        Return 0 if no such rectangle exists.
  \item \textbf{Backward pass of max normalization.}
        Define $y = x / \max(x)$ for a vector $x$ of length up to $10^5$, with distinct values and a positive maximum.
        You get $x$ and the upstream gradient $v = \partial L / \partial y$.
        Return $\partial L / \partial x$ in the original order of $x$, in $O(n)$ time.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Bit manipulation}\label{drill:T23}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T23} (page~\pageref{tech:T23}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T23} (page~\pageref{ans:T23}).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Single Number II (LeetCode 137).} In an array of 32-bit signed integers, every value occurs
  three times, except one value that occurs once. Return that value.
  The array has up to $3 \cdot 10^4$ values, and the values can be negative.
  Use $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.
\item \textbf{Single Number III (LeetCode 260).} In an array of 32-bit signed integers, exactly two values
  occur once, and every other value occurs exactly two times. Return the two values in any order.
  Use $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.
\item \textbf{Set Mismatch (LeetCode 645).} An array of length $n$ must hold each value $1..n$ one time.
  One value was overwritten with a copy of another value. So one value occurs two times, and one value is missing.
  Return \cd{[duplicate, missing]}. The length is $2 \le n \le 10^4$, and the values can be in any order.
\item \textbf{Total Hamming Distance (LeetCode 477).} The Hamming distance of two integers is the number
  of bit positions where they differ. Return the sum of the Hamming distances over all pairs in an array.
  The array has up to $10^4$ values, each in $[0, 10^9]$. A loop over all pairs is too slow in Python.
\item \textbf{Concatenation of Consecutive Binary Numbers (LeetCode 1680).} Write each integer from 1 to $n$
  in binary, without leading zeros, and join the strings in order. Return the value of the joined binary string
  modulo $10^9 + 7$. The bound is $1 \le n \le 10^5$, so the joined string has about $1.6 \cdot 10^6$ bits.
  For $n = 3$, the string is 11011, and the answer is 27.
\item \textbf{Divide Two Integers (LeetCode 29).} Divide two signed 32-bit integers without \cd{*},
  \cd{/} and \pct. Truncate the quotient toward zero, so $-7 / 2$ gives $-3$. The divisor is not 0.
  Clamp the quotient to $[-2^{31}, 2^{31} - 1]$: a quotient above $2^{31} - 1$ gives $2^{31} - 1$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Design problems: combining data structures}\label{drill:T24}
\noindent Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T24} (page~\pageref{tech:T24}). Answers: Section~\ref{ans:T24} (page~\pageref{ans:T24}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) (LeetCode 380).}
        Design a set of integers. \cd{insert(val)} and \cd{remove(val)} return \cd{True} only when they change the set.
        \cd{getRandom()} returns a stored value, and each stored value must have the same probability.
        Each method must run in $O(1)$ average time. There are at most $2 \cdot 10^5$ calls,
        and \cd{getRandom} is called only on a non-empty set.
  \item \textbf{Maximum Frequency Stack (LeetCode 895).}
        Design a stack with \cd{push(val)} and \cd{pop()}. \cd{pop} removes and returns the most frequent value in the stack.
        On a tie, it removes the tied value that is closest to the top.
        Values are up to $10^9$, there are at most $2 \cdot 10^4$ calls, and \cd{pop} is called only on a non-empty stack.
  \item \textbf{Design Browser History (LeetCode 1472).}
        A browser starts on a home page. \cd{visit(url)} opens a new page after the current page and clears all forward history.
        \cd{back(steps)} and \cd{forward(steps)} move at most \cd{steps} pages and return the URL of the current page.
        When fewer pages are available, the move stops at the first page or at the last page.
        There are at most 5000 calls, and \cd{steps} is 1 to 100. Make each call $O(1)$ amortized, independent of \cd{steps}.
  \item \textbf{LFU Cache (LeetCode 460).}
        Design a cache with \cd{get(key)} and \cd{put(key, value)}, each in $O(1)$ average time.
        When the cache is full, \cd{put} of a new key evicts the key with the smallest use count.
        On a tie, it evicts the least recently used of those keys. A \cd{get} of a stored key and every \cd{put} count as a use.
        The capacity is 1 to $10^4$, and there are at most $2 \cdot 10^5$ calls.
  \item \textbf{Stock Price Fluctuation (LeetCode 2034).}
        Records \cd{update(timestamp, price)} arrive out of order. A later record for the same timestamp corrects the earlier price.
        \cd{current()} returns the price at the latest timestamp. \cd{maximum()} and \cd{minimum()} return the largest and
        the smallest current price over all timestamps. There are at most $10^5$ calls,
        and the queries come only after at least one update.
  \item \textbf{Serialize and Deserialize BST (LeetCode 449).}
        Encode a binary search tree to a string and decode the string back to the same tree.
        The string must be as compact as possible, and the decoder sees only the string.
        The tree has 0 to $10^4$ nodes, with values from 0 to $10^4$.
\end{enumerate}

\appendix

\section{Answers to the transfer drills}\label{app:answers}

\subsection{Hashing: counting, membership and canonical keys}\label{ans:T01}
\noindent Drills: Section~\ref{drill:T01} (page~\pageref{drill:T01}). Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T01} (page~\pageref{tech:T01}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{4Sum II.} \textbf{Signal:} an exact sum over four independent choices, and $n^2 = 40{,}000$ is cheap.
        \textbf{Technique:} complement lookup on pair sums (meet in the middle).
        \textbf{Key step:} count every sum $a[i] + b[j]$ in a \cd{Counter}. Then, for every sum $c[k] + d[l]$,
        add the count of its negation. Time and space are $O(n^2)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} Two Sum on pair sums.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def four_sum_count(a, b, c, d):
    pair = Counter(x + y for x in a for y in b)
    return sum(pair[-(x + y)] for x in c for y in d)

four_sum_count([1, 2], [-2, -1], [-1, 2], [0, 2])   # -> 2
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Count Nice Pairs in an Array.} \textbf{Signal:} pairs $i < j$ with $n = 10^5$, and a relation in which each side mixes both indexes.
        \textbf{Technique:} rewrite the relation so that each side depends on one index only.
        Move the terms: a pair is nice when \cd{nums[i] - rev(nums[i]) == nums[j] - rev(nums[j])}.
        An equality of two keys is a hash lookup.
        \textbf{Key step:} count the pairs with the ask-then-record scan on the key \cd{x - rev(x)}.
        A value has at most 10 digits, so the time is $O(n)$.
        If the relation is an inequality, count the equal keys and subtract them from $n(n-1)/2$.
        \textbf{Hook:} put all terms of $i$ on one side; equal keys make the pairs.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def nice_pairs(nums):
    seen = Counter()
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        key = x - int(str(x)[::-1])      # x - rev(x)
        total += seen[key]               # ask
        seen[key] += 1                   # record
    return total % (10**9 + 7)

nice_pairs([42, 11, 1, 97])              # -> 2
nice_pairs([13, 10, 35, 24, 76])         # -> 4
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Group Shifted Strings.} \textbf{Signal:} group items that are equal up to one detail, here the same shift of every letter.
        \textbf{Technique:} canonical key and a dict of lists.
        \textbf{Key step:} the key is the tuple of differences of neighbor letters, modulo 26.
        It also fixes the length. All one-letter words get the empty key, so they form one group.
        \textbf{Hook:} the gaps between neighbor letters, modulo 26, are the key.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import defaultdict

def group_shifted(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        key = tuple((ord(b) - ord(a)) % 26 for a, b in zip(w, w[1:]))
        groups[key].append(w)
    return list(groups.values())

group_shifted(["abc", "bcd", "acef", "xyz", "az", "ba", "a", "z"])
# -> [['abc', 'bcd', 'xyz'], ['acef'], ['az', 'ba'], ['a', 'z']]
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals.} \textbf{Signal:} the answer depends on how often each value occurs, not on the values.
        \textbf{Technique:} count, then select by count. A greedy choice removes the rarest values first,
        because a value leaves the array only when all its copies go.
        \textbf{Key step:} walk the counts from small to large and remove whole values while $k$ covers the count.
        A count is at most $n$, so buckets indexed by count give $O(n)$. A sort of the counts gives $O(n \log n)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} count, then delete the rarest values first.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def least_unique(arr, k):
    left = len(set(arr))
    for f in sorted(Counter(arr).values()):   # rarest values first
        if k < f:
            break
        k -= f
        left -= 1
    return left

least_unique([5, 5, 4], 1)               # -> 1
least_unique([4, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2], 3)   # -> 2
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference.} \textbf{Signal:} a chain of neighbors in value space,
        where the neighbor of $x$ is $x + d$. But the chain is a subsequence, so the order in the array matters.
        A set and a walk from each run start, as in Longest Consecutive Sequence, ignore the order.
        For \cd{[3, 1, 2]} and $d = 1$, the walk finds 3 values, but the answer is 2.
        \textbf{Technique:} a dict from a value to the length of the longest chain that ends at that value.
        This is a 1-D DP with a hash map as the table.
        \textbf{Key step:} scan from left to right and set \cd{best[x] = best.get(x - d, 0) + 1}.
        The dict holds only earlier elements, so each chain keeps the array order. The time is $O(n)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} each value extends the best chain that ends at $x - d$.
\begin{pyex}
def longest_subseq(arr, d):
    best = {}                            # longest chain that ends at each value
    for x in arr:
        best[x] = best.get(x - d, 0) + 1
    return max(best.values())

longest_subseq([1, 5, 7, 8, 5, 3, 4, 2, 1], -2)   # -> 4
longest_subseq([3, 1, 2], 1)             # -> 2
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Number of Boomerangs.} \textbf{Signal:} count shapes through a fixed point. The vertex $i$ anchors the shape, as the query corner does in Detect Squares.
        \textbf{Technique:} fix the anchor, then group the other points by a key in a \cd{Counter}.
        \textbf{Key step:} for each anchor, count the other points by squared distance. The squared distance is an exact integer key.
        A distance shared by $c$ points gives $c(c - 1)$ ordered pairs $(j, k)$. Time is $O(n^2)$.
        The code also counts the anchor itself at distance 0. The points are distinct, so that count is 1 and adds 0.
        \textbf{Hook:} fix the vertex, count by distance, add $c(c - 1)$.
\begin{pyex}
from collections import Counter

def boomerangs(points):
    total = 0
    for ax, ay in points:
        dist = Counter((x - ax) ** 2 + (y - ay) ** 2 for x, y in points)
        total += sum(c * (c - 1) for c in dist.values())
    return total

boomerangs([(0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0)])     # -> 2
boomerangs([(1, 1)])                     # -> 0
\end{pyex}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Prefix sums, running aggregates and offsets}\label{ans:T02}
\noindent Drills: Section~\ref{drill:T02} (page~\pageref{drill:T02}). Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T02} (page~\pageref{tech:T02}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} the longest range with a balance of two kinds of items.
        \textbf{Technique:} prefix sums and a hash map of first indexes.
        \textbf{Key step:} map 0 to $-1$ and 1 to $+1$. A balanced range starts and ends at equal prefix values.
        Seed \cd{first = {0: -1}}, keep only the first index of each value, and maximize \cd{j - first[balance]}.
        $O(n)$. \textbf{Hook:} equal prefixes, first index wins.
\begin{pyex}
def find_max_length(nums):
    first = {0: -1}
    balance = best = 0
    for j, x in enumerate(nums):
        balance += 1 if x == 1 else -1
        if balance in first:
            best = max(best, j - first[balance])
        else:
            first[balance] = j
    return best

find_max_length([0, 1]), find_max_length([0, 1, 0])   # -> (2, 2)
find_max_length([0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1])             # -> 6
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} many updates that each add to a whole range, then one read of the final values.
        \textbf{Technique:} a difference array over the indexes.
        \textbf{Key step:} map the direction to $+1$ or $-1$. Do \cd{diff[start] += v} and \cd{diff[end + 1] -= v}.
        Run the prefix sum to get the net shift at each index. Apply it with \cd{(ord(c) - 97 + shift)} \pct{} \cd{26}.
        Python gives a non-negative remainder, so backward shifts wrap correctly. $O(n + q)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} plus at the start, minus just past the end, then run the sum.
\begin{pyex}
def shifting_letters(s, shifts):
    diff = [0] * (len(s) + 1)
    for start, end, direction in shifts:
        v = 1 if direction == 1 else -1
        diff[start] += v
        diff[end + 1] -= v
    out, shift = [], 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        shift += diff[i]
        out.append(chr((ord(c) - 97 + shift) % 26 + 97))
    return "".join(out)

shifting_letters("abc", [[0, 1, 0], [1, 2, 1], [0, 2, 1]])   # -> 'ace'
shifting_letters("dztz", [[0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]])             # -> 'catz'
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} the best triplet with \cd{i < j < k}. Each index adds one part of the score.
        \textbf{Technique:} a chain of running maximums.
        \textbf{Key step:} keep \cd{best_left}, the largest \cd{nums[i]}, and \cd{best_diff}, the largest \cd{nums[i] - nums[j]}.
        At each value \cd{x}, first update the answer with \cd{best_diff * x}, then \cd{best_diff} with \cd{best_left - x}, then \cd{best_left} with \cd{x}.
        This update order makes sure that \cd{i < j < k}. All values are positive, so the largest difference gives the largest product.
        Seed all three with 0. A seed never gives a product above 0, and 0 is the lowest answer. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space.
        A prefix maximum before \cd{j} and a suffix maximum after \cd{j} also work: fix the middle.
        \textbf{Hook:} best left, then best left minus middle, then times right.
\begin{pyex}
def max_triplet_value(nums):
    best_left = best_diff = answer = 0
    for x in nums:
        answer = max(answer, best_diff * x)        # x is nums[k]
        best_diff = max(best_diff, best_left - x)  # x is nums[j]
        best_left = max(best_left, x)              # x is nums[i]
    return answer

max_triplet_value([12, 6, 1, 2, 7])    # -> 77
max_triplet_value([1, 10, 3, 4, 19])   # -> 133
max_triplet_value([1, 2, 3])           # -> 0
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} the best range sum, but the absolute value removes the order of the two prefixes.
        \textbf{Technique:} the extremes of the prefix sum.
        \textbf{Key step:} a range sum is \cd{P[j] - P[i]}, so its absolute value is the distance between two prefix values.
        The order of \cd{i} and \cd{j} does not matter, so the global maximum and the global minimum of the prefixes give the answer.
        Include the empty prefix 0. The answer is \cd{max(P) - min(P)}. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space.
        Two Kadane scans, one for the largest sum and one for the smallest sum, also work.
        \textbf{Hook:} the absolute sum is the spread of the prefixes: highest minus lowest.
\begin{pyex}
def max_absolute_sum(nums):
    prefix = high = low = 0              # the empty prefix counts
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        high, low = max(high, prefix), min(low, prefix)
    return high - low

max_absolute_sum([1, -3, 2, 3, -4])       # -> 5
max_absolute_sum([2, -5, 1, -4, 3, -2])   # -> 8
\end{pyex}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} one rectangle sum for each cell of a static grid.
        \textbf{Technique:} a padded 2D prefix table.
        \textbf{Key step:} clamp the box: \cd{r1 = max(0, i - k)}, \cd{r2 = min(m - 1, i + k)}, and the same for the columns.
        Then use four lookups: the whole block, minus the top strip, minus the left strip, plus the corner. $O(mn)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} clamp the box, then whole minus strips plus corner.
  \item \textbf{Signal:} a condition on the left side of \cd{i} and a separate condition on the right side of \cd{i}.
        The aggregate is a run length, so it has no inverse.
        \textbf{Technique:} a prefix pass and a suffix pass.
        \textbf{Key step:} \cd{dec[i]} is the length of the non-increasing run that ends at \cd{i} (left to right).
        \cd{inc[i]} is the length of the non-decreasing run that starts at \cd{i} (right to left).
        Index \cd{i} is good when \cd{dec[i - 1] >= k} and \cd{inc[i + 1] >= k}. $O(n)$.
        \textbf{Hook:} left run before \cd{i}, right run after \cd{i}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Two pointers}\label{ans:T03}
\noindent Drills: Section~\ref{drill:T03} (page~\pageref{drill:T03}). Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T03} (page~\pageref{tech:T03}).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Signal:} a symmetry check from both ends, with one allowed fix.
  \textbf{Technique:} converging pointers.
  \textbf{Key step:} move inward while the two ends match.
  At the first mismatch $(i, j)$, all outer pairs already match, so the deleted character is \cd{s[i]} or \cd{s[j]}.
  Test \cd{s[i+1..j]} and \cd{s[i..j-1]} with one more converging scan each. The total is $O(n)$.
  \textbf{Hook:} first mismatch: skip the left or the right, one time.
\begin{pyex}
def is_pal_range(s, i, j):
    while i < j:
        if s[i] != s[j]:
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True

def valid_palindrome_ii(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        if s[i] != s[j]:
            return is_pal_range(s, i + 1, j) or is_pal_range(s, i, j - 1)
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True

valid_palindrome_ii("aba"), valid_palindrome_ii("abca"), valid_palindrome_ii("abc")
# -> (True, True, False)
\end{pyex}

\item \textbf{Signal:} pairs under a sum limit and a minimum count. The order of the people does not matter, so sort.
  \textbf{Technique:} converging pointers with a greedy discard.
  \textbf{Key step:} the heaviest person who is left always needs a boat, so every step moves \cd{hi}.
  The lightest person is the best partner for that person. If the lightest does not fit, nobody fits, and the heaviest rides alone.
  Move \cd{lo} only when the pair fits. Loop while \cd{lo <= hi}, because one person can be left in the middle.
  \textbf{Hook:} each boat takes the heaviest who is left; the lightest joins if it fits.
\begin{pyex}
def num_boats(people, limit):
    a = sorted(people)
    lo, hi, boats = 0, len(a) - 1, 0
    while lo <= hi:
        if a[lo] + a[hi] <= limit:
            lo += 1                  # the lightest rides with the heaviest
        hi -= 1                      # the heaviest always takes this boat
        boats += 1
    return boats

num_boats([1, 2], 3), num_boats([3, 2, 2, 1], 3), num_boats([3, 5, 3, 4], 5)
# -> (1, 3, 4)
\end{pyex}

\item \textbf{Signal:} count triples with a sum condition; $n \leq 1000$ allows $O(n^2)$.
  \textbf{Technique:} sort, fix one element, and count pairs with converging pointers.
  \textbf{Key step:} fix the longest side \cd{a[k]}. Then one test is enough:
  \cd{a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]} implies the two other triangle rules, because \cd{a[k]} is the largest side.
  For \cd{lo < hi < k}: if \cd{a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]}, every index from \cd{lo} to \cd{hi - 1} also works with \cd{hi}.
  Add \cd{hi - lo} and move \cd{hi} down. Otherwise move \cd{lo} up. A side of length 0 never counts.
  \textbf{Hook:} fix the longest side, count the pairs that beat it.
\begin{pyex}
def triangle_number(nums):
    a = sorted(nums)
    count = 0
    for k in range(len(a) - 1, 1, -1):      # a[k] is the longest side
        lo, hi = 0, k - 1
        while lo < hi:
            if a[lo] + a[hi] > a[k]:
                count += hi - lo            # lo..hi-1 all work with hi
                hi -= 1
            else:
                lo += 1
    return count

triangle_number([2, 2, 3, 4]), triangle_number([4, 2, 3, 4]), triangle_number([0, 0, 1])
# -> (3, 4, 0)
\end{pyex}

\item \textbf{Signal:} an in-place filter of a sorted array with $O(1)$ extra memory.
  \textbf{Technique:} read and write pointers.
  \textbf{Invariant:} \cd{a[:w]} is the answer so far, and it is sorted.
  So a value \cd{x} already has two copies in the output exactly when \cd{a[w - 2] == x}.
  Keep \cd{x} when \cd{w < 2} or \cd{a[w - 2] != x}. Compare with the written part, not with the read part.
  The same rule with \cd{w - m} keeps at most $m$ copies.
  \textbf{Hook:} look two slots back in the written part.
\begin{pyex}
def remove_duplicates_ii(a):
    w = 0
    for x in a:
        if w < 2 or a[w - 2] != x:
            a[w] = x
            w += 1
    return w

b = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3]
k = remove_duplicates_ii(b)
k, b[:k]                     # -> (7, [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3])
\end{pyex}

\item \textbf{Signal:} the middle of a forward-only list, in one pass.
  \textbf{Technique:} fast and slow pointers, plus a dummy node.
  \textbf{Key step:} a deletion needs the node before the middle. Put \cd{slow} on a dummy node in front of the head and \cd{fast} on the head.
  While \cd{fast and fast.next} exist, move \cd{slow} one node and \cd{fast} two nodes.
  Then \cd{slow} is at index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1$, or on the dummy when $n = 1$.
  Set \cd{slow.next = slow.next.next} and return \cd{dummy.next}.
  \textbf{Hook:} slow starts one node behind, on a dummy.

\item \textbf{Signal:} two sorted inputs, one sorted output, in place, with the free space at the end of the first array.
  \textbf{Technique:} merge with one pointer per input, from the back.
  \textbf{Key step:} compare the largest values that are not placed yet, \cd{nums1[i]} and \cd{nums2[j]}.
  Write the larger value at \cd{w}, and move that pointer and \cd{w}.
  \textbf{Invariant:} \cd{w == i + j + 1}, so \cd{w > i} while \cd{nums2} has values left.
  A write never destroys an unread value of \cd{nums1}. Stop when \cd{nums2} is empty: the rest of \cd{nums1} is already in place.
  \textbf{Hook:} fill from the back; the larger of the two last values takes the last free slot.
\begin{pyex}
def merge_in_place(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    i, j, w = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1
    while j >= 0:
        if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]:
            nums1[w] = nums1[i]
            i -= 1
        else:
            nums1[w] = nums2[j]
            j -= 1
        w -= 1

x = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]
merge_in_place(x, 3, [2, 5, 6], 3)
x                            # -> [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]
y = [0]
merge_in_place(y, 0, [1], 1)
y                            # -> [1]
\end{pyex}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Sliding window}\label{ans:T04}
\noindent Drills: Section~\ref{drill:T04} (page~\pageref{drill:T04}). Technique: Section~\ref{tech:T04} (page~\pageref{tech:T04}).

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Signal:} ``at most $k$ operations'' is a budget. After a sort, the best group is a contiguous
        block that you raise to its largest value.
        \textbf{Technique:} longest window under a budget, on the sorted array.
        \textbf{Key step:} the cost of the window is \cd{nums[right] * length - window_sum}. The cost never drops when
